# I. Introduction

*[…] man is among the most wondrous things in nature, by virtue of which he exists. We say, then, that there are many things in man, but that he is man only through the sum of them all. Indeed, the nutritive faculty exists in him, but it does not receive the form [proper to man]. He also possesses the sensitive, imaginative and memorative faculties, but neither do these receive his essence nor necessarily accompany it. [Finally] he has the rational faculty, and by this he is characterized [as man].*[^p8-1]

[^p8-1]: Excerpt from *The Regimen of the Solitary* by Avempace (Spanish translation by Joaquín Lomba).

Welcome. The Iberian Tribunal is the gateway to the refined culture of the East, through which the rest of Mythic Europe receives the influences of Persia, Damascus, Baghdad, Syria and Egypt. The magi of Iberia have been both witnesses to and actors in a first medieval renaissance of arts and letters, pioneers in reading the classical treatises (translated into Arabic in the East and brought to al-Andalus by the Umayyads) and in incorporating Aristotelian and Platonic theses into religion, science, philosophy and magic theory. They have been the foremost disseminators of these teachings among their peers, in an Iberia that has become the cradle of Western culture, thanks to poets of the stature of Abū ʿAmir ibn Šuhayd, Abū Muḥammad ʿAlī ibn Ḥazm, Wallāda ḅint Al-Mustakfī and Al-Fatḥ ibn Jāqān, to mystics such as Ibn Masarra and Muḥammad ibn al-ʿArabī, and to polymaths such as ʿAbbās ibn Firnās, Abraham ben Meʾir ibn Ezrá, Abū Bakr ibn Ṭufayl, Abū Marwān ibn Zuhr, Abū Bakr ibn Bāŷŷa, Rabbi Mosé ben Maimón and Ibn Rušd.

The influence of the old Umayyad dynasty has left an echo that can still be felt in the covenants and society of Iberia. The eldest magi remember the old ways and miss the legacy of the taifa kingdoms, cursing in their prayers the moment when the reactionary Almohad doctrines of Ibn Tūrmat, with which they must contend in 1220, arrived in Iberia.

## Some Preliminary Considerations

The Iberian Tribunal has been written from numerous sources, which you will find in the bibliography appendix. All the historical and philosophical material in this book has been built from them, so we hope it serves you as a starting point for further research into this magnificent and sometimes little-known period of the Iberian Peninsula. Remember that the Iberian Tribunal is not a history book; to better recreate the atmosphere of Mythic Europe we have taken a few minimal liberties, always avoiding anachronisms and within the bounds of historical rigor. Of course, any historical error that may remain is our own oversight and not that of the authors we have cited.

### On the Organization of the Book

The book opens with this introduction and devotes the following chapter to mundane and mythic history. Chapter three describes the covenants of the Tribunal, organized according to the kingdoms of the Peninsula as they stood in 1220. Each kingdom is in turn subdivided into regional units (counties or *kuwar*) where, after a brief introduction to the historical present, first the inhabited covenants are presented and then those lying in ruins, always ordered chronologically by the year their charter was ratified (which coincides with the years in which the ordinary Tribunals were held). Chapter four of the book covers the various magical traditions native to the Peninsula, a section devoted to characters, which presents new Abilities, Virtues and Flaws specific to Iberia, and a short section describing two mythic places of the Peninsula. Finally, six appendices are provided: an impressive, historical mundane library to give color to your saga, an index of names in which to consult the list of the many names that appear in the book, the compilation of the Peripheral Code of the Iberia of 1220, a compendium of the covenants and their magae, an index of the book's illustrations and, lastly, a bibliography.

#### On the Story Seeds

Numerous story seeds are presented throughout the book. Although they can be used with the game's canonical starting date in mind (that is, 1220), unless a different date is indicated, they are also designed to be used from the time periods in which they are set. For example, if you wanted to set the start of your saga at the beginning of the Umayyad Caliphate, you could use all the seeds presented up to that date (clearly defined in the second section, or what would be up to the subsection on the Arabization of the Iberian Tribunal in the third section, page 74); what's more, some of the seeds fit better in the era with which they are contemporary, such as those concerning the *mayús* (see page 286).

<!-- p. 9 -->

#### On Canonical Mythic Europe

This book has been written with the utmost respect for the canon of Mythic Europe in the fifth edition of Ars Magica, which means it can be used in play alongside the other books without any kind of adaptation. However, owing to the historical reality of the Peninsula, we have had to update references to certain Iberia-related content that appeared in other books in order to fit it properly within our historical and social framework.

#### On Aspects of Society

Although we have tried to maintain historical rigor and the religious and social reality of the Middle Ages in the Peninsula, we wish to remind you that roleplaying games are inclusive by definition: there must be no room for any kind of discrimination, whether of gender, religion or ethnicity. However the historical, religious and social reality may have been, never allow anyone to feel offended in your games.

#### On the Book's Quotations

This introduction opens with a quotation, and you will find many more throughout the book. All of them (except those from the *Codex Calixtinus*, which was presumably written by a Frank) are by authors who lived in the Peninsula between the ninth and thirteenth centuries. To make them easier to identify, we have added a footnote indicating the work (whose full reference you will find in the bibliography appendix), its author and its translator.

#### On Dates and Time

In almost all the Christian kingdoms of the Peninsula (with the exception of the Crown of Aragon, which since Alfonso II has used the date of the birth of Christ to date the Crown's documents) the "Hispanic era" is used, which begins with the conquest of Iberia by the Roman emperor Augustus, that is, 38 years before the birth of Christ (which is the reference used in the rest of Mythic Europe). However, for the sake of clarity, the dates in this book are given according to the present-day calendar, disregarding the Muslims' Hiŷra (when Muḥammad fled from Mecca to Medina, in the year 622), the calendar of the Jews (who count the years from the creation of the world), and the Christians' Hispanic era. Furthermore, we have tried to leave out as many dates as possible to make the book lighter reading, offering instead as a reference for the period the emir or king who ruled at the time, and, where dates have been kept, we would point out that the sources sometimes disagree about them, so wherever we could we have opted for those which, in our view, were best documented.

#### On the Transcription System

We have respected the transcription of the Arabic alphabet into Castilian in order to preserve the sound of Arabic names in the Peninsula. To that end, we have used the transliteration system found in the sources, which is usually the one used by the school of Spanish Arabists, established in its day by the journal *al-Andalus*. As this lies beyond the aims of this book, we have omitted the table of equivalences for this system, although you will find it in many of the books in the bibliography.

As for Hebrew names, we have respected the spelling that appears in the translations and studies we used for our research, all of them listed in the bibliography appendix.

#### On Arabic Names

The Arabic naming system is somewhat complex, so a brief guide follows. The personal name is known as the *ism*, and it usually contains religious references. Thus we have, for example, the name ʿAbd Allāh, which means "slave of God," or ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, which means "slave of the Merciful," or, outside the theological sphere, Ŷaʿfar, which means "stream." Next comes the *nasab*, which sets out the individual's male ancestry, that is, the name of the father, grandfather and so on, joined by the word *ibn* (or *ḅint* for women), meaning "son/daughter of," or in the case of magi, the name of the *parens* and those before them (the Order does not restrict the *nasab* to male Hermetic ancestry). Naturally, those magi of Iberia who belong to the True Lineages of Hermes can trace their lineage back to the Founders, and bear truly long names. The third part of the name is the *nisba*, which indicates the individual's tribal, family or professional affiliation, as for example al-Umawī (meaning "the Umayyad") or al-Qurṭubī (which refers to the city where one lives or from which one comes, in this case "the Cordoban"). A name may bear several *nisbas*, and more can be added over time. Thus, for example, we might have ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ŷaʿfar al-Qurṭubī. Names may also bear another element called the *kunya*, in which the word *abū*, meaning "father," appears linked to the name of a son, to a family tradition, or to a particular virtue or quality. Thus, for example, Abū Ŷaʿfar would be "father of Ŷaʿfar." Some magi of the Peninsula have even come to be known by the apprentices they had, so that history has remembered them this way and their names reflect it, as might be the case with Abū Ǧamīla, for example. Finally, the name may contain a nickname or *laqab*, which may refer to a physical trait (such as al-Ṣagīr, meaning "the small") or to an honorific title, such as those borne by the caliphs. For example, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān bore the epithet al-Nāṣir, meaning "the conqueror."

With the cultural revolution of Ǧamīla (see page 75), the magi of the Peninsula began to adopt Arabic names. Many of these names appear in the book, sometimes as *laqab*, *ism* or *nisba* (or a combination of all of them), depending on how their bearers came to be known. Below is a table of the *nisbas* (in their feminine and masculine forms) of the Hermetic Houses, a nomenclature most magi of the Tribunal tend to prefer over the one used in the rest of the Order beyond the borders of Iberia.

| House | Feminine Nisba | Masculine Nisba |

| Bjornaer | al-Biŷorniyya | al-Biŷornī |
| Bonisagus | al-Bonisagiyya | al-Bonisagī |
| Bonisagus (Trianomae) | al-Trianomiyya | al-Trianomī |

#### On the Mythic Dīnār

*[…] as to the amount that must be paid [of the parias], opinions differ, for Malik holds that the amount owed […] is that prescribed by Umar, consisting of four dīnārs [or doblas] for peoples on the gold standard, and forty drachmas for peoples who use silver, besides provisions for the Muslims and a right to three days' lodging […].*[^p10-2]

[^p10-2]: Excerpt from *The Book of the Ŷihād* by Averroes (Spanish translation by Carlos Quirós).

To adapt the existing nomenclature for money in Ars Magica, and without going into considerations of relative value, exact weight or the great diversity of coins in circulation, we can speak of two basic coins in the Iberia of 1220: the gold dīnār muminī, or mithqal, issued by the Almohads (a square coin over 90% pure and weighing about 4.5 grams), and the silver dirham (about 2.75 grams), at a ratio of 1 to 8 with the mithqal. Given that a pound of silver weighs 460 grams, it would be worth about 150 dirhams (rounding down to the nearest whole number), and if 8 dirhams are worth one dīnār (according to some sources), we could draw up a first table of equivalences (which you can of course adapt according to other sources).

|  | Gold Dīnārs | Silver Dirhams |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Mythic Pound | 20 | 150 |

To give a few examples from the bibliography: in the tenth century, a merchant earned about 5.5 dīnārs a year, and a house might cost around 10 dīnārs; in the eleventh century, during the taifa kingdoms, the last Zirid king of Granada, ʿAbd Allāh (see page 36), paid an initial sum of 30,000 mithqals to Alfonso VI of Leon to avoid being attacked by the Christian armies, and undertook to pay 10,000 mithqals a year to maintain the agreement. On that basis, the figure in Mythic Pounds would be an initial 1,500 pounds (the value of a castle and a half!) and some 500 pounds a year.

#### On the Climate of Iberia

*Our country, which is al-Andalus, lies at the beginning of the fifth clime, and autumn there lasts approximately two months.*[^p10-3]

[^p10-3]: Excerpt from *The Book of the Generalities of Medicine* by Averroes (Spanish translation by Vázquez de Benito and Álvarez Morales).

Until the first half of the ninth century, the climate in the Peninsula was colder and drier. From the second half of the ninth century up to 1220, Iberia experienced the so-called "medieval climate anomaly," which brought marked changes in temperature and rainfall across the whole western hemisphere: temperatures rose (which led to the thawing of the North Atlantic and allowed the Norsemen to reach Greenland and America) and winters were warmer and drier than in previous centuries, especially on the central plateau of the Peninsula, since in the north the climate was more like that of central Europe, with mild temperatures, though with less rainfall.

These times saw numerous extreme events. In 974 and 1010 the Guadalquivir flooded, causing (in the latter case) the deaths of as many as 5,000 people in Cordoba and bringing on a terrible plague. Droughts were frequent (we have records of them in 867, 887, 915, 926, 941, 946, between 960 and 980, and so on) and caused many deaths, and in some extreme cases the Guadalquivir reached Cordoba dry (to give two examples, in the drought of 964 Al-Ḥakam II distributed tons of food among the people of the suburbs, and in 968 he handed out 12,000 loaves a day among the Cordobans). Droughts raised prices, halted military campaigns and increased crime. Moreover, they were divine signs denouncing the Andalusi governors for ruling badly, and so popular revolts broke out.

The chroniclers also recorded several earthquakes, such as that of the summer of 944, which struck in the small hours between Sunday and Monday, after the last prayer, whose aftershocks were felt throughout the night and drove the people of Cordoba to take refuge in the mosques; and that of the summer of 955, which had aftershocks over the following days and was accompanied by strong winds and rain.

#### On Place Names

Throughout the book, place names are given in the form most commonly rendered in the language in which the book was written, Castilian, which does not always match the term used by their inhabitants. Thus, although transcriptions of the corresponding place names in Arabic or Hebrew are sometimes included, as a rule the name of a place always appears in Castilian: Córdoba and not Qurtuba, Gerona and not Girona, and so on.

#### On the Hermetic Population

To build the Tribunal we have used a variation of the study by *Shirley* (2014): we assume a mundane population of 6.9 million inhabitants, to which we have applied the birth rate of children with the Gift. However, we have departed from the average population, set at about 100 magi per Tribunal, since Iberia is large enough to hold a greater number, and certain peculiarities of its history could justify this. Thus, in these pages you will find descriptions of thirty-one inhabited covenants and twenty-seven in ruins, with a total of 155 magi (among them twenty-four Redcaps), which makes it the most populous Tribunal in the Order (ahead of the Rhine, which has some 130 magi).

### How to Use This Book

The Iberian Tribunal is designed for gaming groups who want to run their sagas in the Iberian Peninsula, although its ideas can also be put to use in other Tribunals, since many of them can be transferred or adapted to other lands. In principle, all of the book's content could become known to the players, so the storyguide should seek the best way to introduce it into the game.

This book offers abundant information and ideas for you to fit into your saga. This means there is not a single Iberian Tribunal, but one for each gaming group. Do not feel obliged to use the many covenants and magi described here, and adapt any content to the standards of your own saga. In any case, we have chosen to offer as complete a picture of the Tribunal as possible, so that it can be fully developed without your needing to add anything more.

We hope you enjoy reading it and the cultural richness of Iberia.

# II. Mythic History

*Since man is nothing more than the story he leaves behind him, be thou a fair story for the one who must gather them.*[^p12-1]

[^p12-1]: Lines from *In Praise of Spanish Islam* by Al-Šaqundī (Spanish translation by Emilio García Gómez).

This section covers the mythic history of the Peninsula from the arrival of the Umayyad ʿAbd al-Raḥmān to the canonical starting year of the game (that is, 1220), when the Almohads ruled al-Andalus. The events of this section begin more than fifty years before the founding of the Order of Hermes, so they are presented as background to the Order's own mythic history. By way of preamble, it offers a short introduction to the three religions that coexist in the Iberian Tribunal; the section is then organized according to the mundane rulers of al-Andalus, namely:

- the Umayyad emirate (from 756 to 912);
- the Umayyad Caliphate (from 913 to 1013);
- the *fitna*, or civil war (from 1013 to 1031);
- the taifa kingdoms (from 1031 to 1086);
- the Almoravid Empire (from 1086 to 1145) and the second taifas (from 1145 to 1160);
- the Almohad Empire (from 1160 to 1220).

These periods form the backbone of Iberian history, in the magical landscape as well as the mundane. Each opens with a schematic map of the Peninsula's geopolitical borders and goes on to describe the most notable events in Muslim, Jewish and Christian Iberia during the existence of the Order of Hermes.

## The Three Religions

Although three religions (Muslim, Jewish and Christian) coexist in the Mythic Iberia of 1220, the two majority faiths are Islam and Christianity; the Jews live alongside both. Lacking a language of their own (Hebrew is used only by the rabbis), they are tolerated because the dominant religions are unable to wipe them out. As will be seen below, this does not mean that the Jews live under oppression, at least not until the Almohads arrive in the Peninsula.

### The Muslims

*[…] the Law makes the study of the books of the ancient sages obligatory, if their aim and intention are the same as those the Law preaches. And so, if someone forbids the study of such books to another who is fit to read them, […] then he is closing to people the door which, according to the Law, is the entrance to knowledge of God; that is, the reflection that leads to true knowledge of God. This is extreme ignorance […].*[^p12-2]

[^p12-2]: Excerpt from *The Decisive Treatise* by Averroes (Spanish translation by A. Yacine and P. Chabrera Calpe).

Islam is the restoration of the original religion of Abraham, founder of all the monotheistic religions. Muslims live according to Islamic law (or *šarīʿa*), which draws on four sources: the Qurʾan (the holy book that gathers the revelations Allāh made to Muḥammad); the sunna, or tradition (a compendium of sayings and deeds handed down orally in the form of *ḥadīṯ*, or narrations, by the followers who accompanied Muḥammad, and set down in writing in the ninth century); the *iŷmāʿ* (the consensus of the community or of the fuqahāʾ, the scholars of the law), used to resolve problems that neither the Qurʾan nor the sunna addresses; and the *qiyās*, the interpretation made by the ulama, or doctors of the law, to fill the legal gaps left by the three previous sources (by analogy or *qiyās*, by deduction or *iŷtihād*, or by reasoning or *raʾy*).

In Iberia, all the Muslim rulers (Umayyads, taifa petty kings, Almoravids and Almohads) have been Sunni. Sunnis believe that the Prophet named no successor and that the first caliph, Abū Bakr (Muḥammad's father-in-law), was chosen by the Muslim community in accordance with the dictates of the sunna. The Shiʿa (from the Arabic for the followers, or *šīʿat*, of ʿAlī), on the other hand, claim that Muḥammad chose his son-in-law and cousin ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib as his successor, and so only the blood heirs of his marriage to Fāṭīma (one of the Prophet's daughters) may serve as guides of the Muslim community. The Kharijites, for their part, maintain that the only requirement for being caliph is to be the best among Muslims.

To Islam, Christians and Jews are the People of the Book (*ahl al-Kitāb*), that is, readers of the revealed book. As descendants of Abraham, Christians and Jews must be respected, as dictated by the word *ḏimma*, which means both "protection" and "contract." The protected, that is, the dhimmis, may not be converted by force; they may live among Muslims and are allowed to practice their religion as long as they do not insult Islam, which is punishable by death. Dhimmis are subject to far heavier taxes than Muslims, and must pay the *ǧizya* (a head tax, or capitation) and the *jarāŷ* (on the lands they hold). Muslims, in contrast, must fund the holy war through an annual tax, must pay for their lands (if they have any) and must pay the tithe (*ʿušr*), ranging from 5% to 10% of the produce of their earnings in general (however, the obligation to pay lapses after a year, and minors, slaves, the insane and those unable to fend for themselves are exempt).

<!-- p. 13 -->

The contract of the *ḏimma* restricts the participation of non-Muslims in the social and economic life of the city. In general, the status of dhimmis is inferior: their testimony against Muslims is not valid, they may not hold processions or public demonstrations, they may not ring church bells, and they may not practice certain trades or professions or, barring exceptions, hold administrative, political or military office. Furthermore, they may not dress like Muslims, ride noble mounts (such as horses) or carry weapons. Nonetheless, they are guaranteed their lives, freedom of religion and possession of their property, and under Islamic law they may have their own leaders and courts so that they can be judged by their own laws and customs.

For all their respect toward the People of the Book, Muslims do not forget that the dhimmis have distorted God's message: the Jews reviled the Virgin and Christ, and the Christians committed the sin of making Christ into a god. For these reasons Muslims may take up arms against them and wage holy war (the *ŷihād*), for anyone who does not live within the abode of Islam (*dār al-islām*), which comprises the lands ruled by Islam, dwells in the abode of war (*dār al-ḥarb*) and must therefore be fought. It should be borne in mind, however, that for Muslims there are two holy wars: the greater *ŷihād*, waged within every man to master his passions and temptations, and the lesser *ŷihād*, which fights the unbelievers.

The *ŷihād* is a religious instrument and, in part, a political one as well, for it has allowed the Muslim peoples to expand since the eighth century without fighting among themselves. In holy war, the Muslim who dies fighting wins paradise, and enemies who surrender must be pardoned (they must be granted the *amān*): pagans are forced to embrace Islam, while the People of the Book are allowed to keep their beliefs as long as they accept the protection of Islam. Indeed, it is preferable that they keep their faith, go on working their lands and retain their possessions, since in this way they can go on paying tribute so that the Muslims can go on waging holy war. No Muslim, however, may force anyone to convert, since the Qurʾan dictates that there is no compulsion in faith; instead, the aim is to place the dhimmis under Islamic law so that the faith grows of its own accord.

*[…] it would never be lawful to put the prisoner to death after the amān has been granted; on this particular point there is no disagreement whatsoever among the Muslims. The differences begin when it comes to knowing who may lawfully grant the amān and who may not. All agree that it may be granted by the* imam*, but the majority of the doctors decide for the lawfulness of an amān granted by a Muslim who is male and of free condition […].*[^p13-3]

[^p13-3]: Excerpt from *The Book of the Ŷihād* by Averroes (Spanish translation by Carlos Quirós).

In Islam there is no separation between the powers of Church and State; the caliph holds all power, and he delegates judicial power to the qadi (*qādī*) and legislative power to the fuqahāʾ. The qadi is the axis on which the whole legal structure rests, and his final decision cannot be appealed, though he may take counsel from the fuqahāʾ. The qadi serves as mediator between the people and the caliph, so he must always remain impartial; therefore, in his private life he must not associate with officials or fuqahāʾ, may not accept gifts, should not receive many visitors, may not attend any celebration (except weddings), must not administer justice on rainy days and may not be seen riding with the same people on different occasions. Furthermore, the qadi must lead a humble life, dress fittingly, know the Qurʾan and the sunna, and be rich, so that he never needs to accept money. He may also appoint a secondary judge, called a *hākim* (a learned and wealthy man), to try lesser matters, and he has the authority to appoint the qadis of each community (in cities or farming villages). Finally, the *qādī* is responsible for education in the realm and for the administration of justice throughout its territory, and he has access to the treasury of the pious foundations (*bayt māl al-muslimīn*) to sow fields or repair buildings, pay salaries, organize campaigns, strengthen the frontiers or prepare the defense of the Muslims against Christian raids. To carry out their duties, the *qādī* and the *hākim* have a body of attendants (*ʿawān*) at their service.

> #### Prayers
>
> *The imam is responsible before the umma (the Muslim community) for every decision that must be taken regarding the ŷihād.*[^p13-I]
>
> Prayer is one of the five pillars of Islam (the others being the profession of faith, almsgiving, fasting and the pilgrimage to Mecca), and in the mosques it is led by the *imām*. The prayers divide time for Muslims (for example, they determine when water may or may not be drawn from the irrigation channel and provide the temporal frame of daily life), and they are announced by the muezzins from the minarets of the mosques. At their call, Muslims find the direction of Mecca and set aside whatever they are doing to prostrate themselves before Allah.
>
> The day is divided by five prayers:
>
> - *salāh al-faǧr*, before dawn;
>
> - *salāh aẓ-ẓuhr*, at midday;
>
> - *salāh al-ʿaṣr*, in mid-afternoon, before the sun turns orange;
>
> - *salāh al-maghrib*, after sunset;
>
> - *salāh al-ʿishaaʾ*, when night has fully fallen, roughly an hour and a half after sunset.
>
> [^p13-I]: Excerpt from *The Book of the Ŷihād* by Averroes (Spanish translation by Carlos Quirós).

<!-- p. 14 -->

Each day, on a rotating basis, the *qādī* must gather the fuqahāʾ in his court (where the *hākim* must be present so that the qadi can consult him on the day's cases) to take their counsel and make his rulings more just. There must be no more than four of these advisors: two from the *qādī*'s court and two from the Great Mosque.

The remaining posts of public responsibility are held by the officers of the State described below.

- The *ḥāŷib* is in charge of the administration, the land army and the fleet. He presides over the council of ministers (the viziers, or *wuzarāʾ*, singular *wazīr*) and is assisted by a secretary of State, or *kātib*.
- The *wālī* (walis) govern the provinces, or *kuwar* (singular *kūra*), into which al-Andalus is divided, and owe obedience to the central power (during the emirate and Caliphate of Cordoba, the *kuwar* that served as frontiers between the central power and the Christian kingdoms were grouped into Marches: the Lower March with its capital at Badajoz, the Middle March with its capital at Toledo and the Upper March with its capital at Saragossa).
- The muhtasib is charged with enforcing Islamic law and is appointed by the *qādī* (who must first consult the *ḥāŷib*).
- The market-tax collector's task is to levy the market taxes, though always under the strict supervision of the *qādī*, since it is a post that tends toward corruption for illicit gain.
- The *ṣāḥib al-madīna*, or city prefect, is in charge of public order and taxes (which makes him a much-hated figure), though he must first consult the qadi before taking important decisions. Under his command are the officers (responsible for investigating crimes, taking statements and administering floggings), the patrols (which watch over the cities by night and arrest possible suspects) and the constables; together they form a police force that keeps public order. The prison (which he must visit two or three times a month) and the jailers answer to the *ṣāḥib al-madīna*. If the prison holds many prisoners, he must release those who have already been punished and are serving the lightest sentences. He must also grant all prisoners an amnesty every year at the end of *ramadān*. Naturally, women may not share cells with men.
- Jailers must be older men, married and of good reputation. They may not mistreat the prisoners, and must allow them to receive visits and alms (on which they live). The prisoners must also have an *imām*, assigned by the qadi, to lead them in prayer at the times of prayer. The jailer is also in charge of the stocks, which are reserved for the most dangerous criminals. Even so, he is obliged to release them during the hours of prayer and when they need to relieve themselves.

> #### Punishments
>
> *If an evildoer or incorrigible criminal is caught, the amputation of his hand or crucifixion in his own town must be imposed on him, which will be the swiftest way to put an end to his wickedness, better than applying a mere corporal punishment, and no plea in his favor shall be heeded.*[^p14-II]
>
> The most common punishments are described below.
>
> - **Flogging:** for any minor offense (never theft or murder) detected by the *ṣāḥib al-madīna* or one of his agents, the caliph, the *ḥāŷib*, the *ṣāḥib al-madīna*, the qadis, the muhtasib or the *hākim* (and no one else) may have the culprit flogged. Floggings must be measured, and no one who has made the pilgrimage to Mecca may ever be flogged. Furthermore, floggings may not be pardoned unless they are meant for a member of the nobility, in which case the noble is publicly reprimanded to shame him.
> - **Amputation of the hand:** this punishment is meant for thieves. Afterward the thief is expelled from the city and must live on charity until he heals or perishes.
> - **Prison (and the stocks):** prison may only be imposed by the caliph or the *qādī*.
> - **Crucifixion:** this is the harshest punishment that can be imposed; the criminal may only be crucified after his sentence has been confirmed three times.
>
> [^p14-II]: Excerpt from *The Treatise of Ibn ʿAbdūn* (Spanish translation by Emilio García Gómez and E. Levi-Provençal).

### The Jews

*[…] there are […] matters of equal concern to […] Jews, Christians and Muslims;* e.g.*, the doctrine of the "temporal creation of the world," on whose truth that of miracles depends, and others. But in the remaining questions, […] such as the question of the Trinity and, among some sects, the "prophetic word," they had to resort to certain hypotheses of their own devising in defense of the principles in which they were involved […]. Of all this we have no need whatsoever.*[^p14-4]

[^p14-4]: Excerpt from *The Guide for the Perplexed* by Maimonides (Spanish translation by David Gonzalo Maeso).

The Jews share many similarities with the Muslims: both have temples without images, practice circumcision, do not eat pork and, by the precepts of their religion, are extremely scrupulous about personal hygiene. Yet what brings them together is also what sets them apart from the uncircumcised.

The Jews lived under oppression once the Visigothic king Reccared adopted Christianity in the sixth century. Later, the decisions of King Sisebut in the eighth century (who decreed that they must convert to Christianity and receive baptism if they did not wish to live as slaves) drove them to help the Muslims in the conquest of Iberia, which allowed them to live in a favorable and tolerant climate after the arrival of the Umayyads. After long centuries of sorrow and persecution, they were at last able to flourish under the pact of the *ḏimma* in cities such as Granada, Saragossa, Tarragona, Jaén, Seville, Almería, Barcelona and Lucena. Indeed, Lucena was inhabited exclusively by Jews until 1148, and it had an important rabbinical school and a house of *fatà* (eunuchs, on whom the Jews operated with great care) destined for the harems of al-Andalus, where they served as spies, guards and go-betweens in harem politics.

<!-- p. 15 -->

> #### Oremos pro perfidis iuadeis
>
> *Cedant gentilium herrorum perfida secta, Cedat homnigena monstrorum perfida secta: Ecce Xρi signo centri conuexa refulgent.*[^p15-III]
>
> The statesman Ḥasdāy ibn Šaprūṭ, founder of Talmudic study in Cordoba and physician and counselor to the caliph ʿAbd al-Raḥmān III, was at the center of a movement through which the Jews of Iberia sought to clear themselves of the death of Jesus. According to its tenets, the diaspora had brought the Sephardic Jews to Iberia long before the crucifixion of Jesus, and so they had had nothing to do with his trial or death. Ḥasdāy ibn Šaprūṭ even argued that some Jews of Toledo had written to Pontius Pilate asking him not to crucify him. Though it may have been obvious that the Jews of Iberia had no connection with the deicide, they could not keep the Church in Iberia from repeating the prayer *oremos pro perfidis iuadeis* every Good Friday for many centuries.
>
> #### The Law of the Jewish People
>
> Judaism is based on the Hebrew Bible, a collection of twenty-four sacred books divided into the Torah (also called the Pentateuch, as it corresponds to the first five books), the Prophets (*Nebiím*) and the Writings (*Quetubim*).
>
> The Torah is the Law par excellence, and it was given to Moses by God on Mount Sinai. The Torah is complemented and interpreted through a body of legal traditions called the Mishnah, while the Talmud is the compendium of the traditional doctrines of Judaism, which arose from the decisions and debates of the rabbis who taught in the academies of Palestine and Babylon. The body of legislative material of Hebrew law found in both the Bible and the Talmud is thus called the Halakhah.
>
> [^p15-III]: Excerpt from a poem by Álbaro of Cordoba in which he attacks the unbelief of the Jews, urging them to acknowledge that Christ is the Messiah. Spanish translation by Miguel Rodríguez-Pantoja, which reads: *Away with the perfidious sect of pagan errors, / away with the perfidious sect that engenders monsters: / behold, the heights shine with the sign of Christ*; taken from "Los mozárabes y sus poemas en el siglo ix" (in *Los mozárabes. Historia cultura y religión de los cristianos de al Ándalus*).

<!-- p. 16 -->

With the fall of Toledo and the invasion of the Almoravids, the Jews lost their status. The Almoravids considered the sultans of the taifa kingdoms corrupt and impious, and imposed Islamic orthodoxy and purity of custom. They barred Jews from positions of responsibility in public bodies and expelled those who held positions of power. For this reason, the Jews emigrated en masse to the Christian kingdoms, where the monarchs welcomed them warmly. One example is the *Carta inter Christianos et Iudaeos*, promulgated by Alfonso VI, king of Castile and Leon, which laid down that Jews were to be treated much like Christians. Not for nothing did this king have as his physician Yūsuf ben Ferruziel, called Cidiello by the Christians, who was the monarch's favorite at the court of Toledo.

With the coming of the Almohads, nearly all the Jews who remained emigrated from al-Andalus; this time they left by the thousands. Some went to Provence (the Jewish physicians took refuge in Montpellier, founding an important school that eventually became a faculty in 1220), others to the Christian kingdoms of Castile and Aragon, and the great majority to the Islamic lands of the East or North Africa. Even the Jews of Lucena, who had escaped the Almoravid danger by paying them great sums of money, were forced to abandon the city. The persecution they suffered then was a cultural and economic step backward for Andalusi society (the philosopher Maimonides was one of the many Jews who had to live in exile). Those who could not leave were forced to embrace Islam, and the caliph Abū Yūsuf Yaʿqūb al-Manṣūr forced the few who kept their religion to dress in blue so that they could be told apart from Muslims.

> #### The Court of Justice
>
> Jews who do not follow the law of the Torah (for instance, by failing to keep the Sabbath) can be brought before the court of justice to be tried. There, sentences are carried out by the officers of the Christian monarch of the kingdom.
>
> Although the Law can be broken in many ways, an especially grave crime is that by which a Jew endangers the very existence of the aljama, such as spreading lies about the Jewish religion among the Christians and stirring up fear, envy or wrath. Such criminals are called *malsines* (informers), and for them the *herem* is reserved: an excommunication that carries the harshest punishments, from amputation to death (there are records of the punishments imposed on Jewish women for lying with Christians, whose noses were cut off, and of informers being hanged or bled to death).
>
> In addition, the following crimes are punished by death in the Jewish courts of justice: idolatry (worshipping idols, prophesying in the name of idols, passing newborns through fire to grant them the idols' protection, and practicing evocation, magic or sorcery), adultery, incest (but only the most shameful kinds), murder, profaning the Sabbath, false prophecy, striking or cursing one's parents, abduction and robbery with violence.
>
> #### The Aljamas
>
> In both Muslim and Christian cities, the Jews live in aljamas, or *kahal* (quarters), as they call them. The aljamas are not territorial groupings, nor are they regarded as Jewish quarters, but rather communities with enough authority to govern themselves by their own laws. Bear in mind that Jews are not forced to live together; if they do, it is to be near the synagogue and the butchers' shops (where they can buy food prepared according to the Torah), as well as the Jewish baths, hospitals and libraries.
>
> Every aljama has the following bodies and facilities: the civil authority, the court of justice, the synagogue and the cemetery.
>
> The civil authority, which includes judges, treasurers, officers and so on, is represented by a council of elders or *mucaddemim* that handles the internal affairs of the aljama (such as the collection and apportionment of taxes) and serves as the body that represents the royal authority. Traditionally, the *mucaddemim* are elected annually from among the inhabitants of the aljama and, when there is no consensus, they are chosen by the rabbi. In the thirteenth century, however, these posts have become hereditary, so that control of the aljama falls to a few families who hoard all the power. As a result, this body is a source of social inequality.
>
> The court of justice is established according to Talmudic law and is made up of the judges, or *dayaním* (the equivalent of the Christian alcalde). In Iberia, unlike the rest of Mythic Europe, Jewish justice has authority over both criminal and civil matters. When a case involves more than one religion, the court requires the presence of a Christian or Muslim representative and a Jewish one so that it can proceed according to their laws; cases between Jews follow Jewish law alone, that is, the Torah.
>
> The synagogue houses the Talmudic school, where the rabbis interpret the law and teach it to the children. In the school, all children, whatever their social status, learn to read and write until the age of ten so that they can interpret the Torah. They then go on to study the Talmud. One or more rabbis and priests may be in charge of the synagogue.
>
> Lastly, the Jews have their own cemetery and are buried with the head toward the west and the feet toward the east, so that at the moment of the resurrection their faces will be turned toward Jerusalem. If the aljama is small and has no cemetery, the Jews must bury their dead in another town that has one (bear in mind that moving corpses can be difficult on the roads of thirteenth-century Iberia).

<!-- p. 17 -->

The Christian monarchs benefited greatly from this, for a cultural elite was arriving in their kingdoms that could help them organize the vast resettled lands they had on their hands. Among them were also great merchants and craftsmen, some so rich that they could advance money to the monarchs in times of severe financial crisis (so that they could keep fighting the Muslims). Moreover, the Jews also spoke and wrote Arabic (as well as Aramaic, Latin and the Romance languages), which made them perfect intermediaries in dealings with the Muslim kings. In Aragon, Jewish money financed the campaigns to conquer Valencia, and Alfonso VIII of Castile took out a loan from the Jew Joseph ben Salomón ben Shoshan to fund the military campaign that ended in the great victory of Las Navas de Tolosa.

Although under civil law Jews may not hold positions of authority over Christians, they have wielded great power among the monarchs, in Castile as well as in Leon and Aragon.

In 1220, in the kingdom of Castile (for in Aragon and Navarre the aljamas are autonomous), the king appoints a rabbi or chief judge who has authority over all the Jews of his kingdom and serves as intermediary between them and the Crown, since all Jews are the king's property (and the aljamas ultimately depend on the monarch); the Crown therefore protects them. In the tenth century, the fuero of Castrojeriz (see page 32) states: "whoever kills a Jew shall pay the same fine as whoever kills a Christian."

> #### The Jews in Iberia
>
> *[…] he who aspires to be truly a man, and not a beast with human shape and features, must strive to curb all the appetites of matter with respect to food, drink, sex, anger and all the other vices that derive from the concupiscible and irascible appetites, to be ashamed of them, and to set limits on them in his soul.*[^p17-IV]
>
> In Christian Iberia there were few Jewish communities before the fall of the Caliphate of Cordoba: Sahagún, Leon, Astorga, Aguilar de Campoo, Burgos, Nájera, Haro, Palencia, Ávila and Sepúlveda. Later, with the coming of the Almoravids and the Almohads, the Christian kingdoms of the thirteenth century came to have some 20,000 Jews, mainly distributed among the cities listed below.
>
> - **Castile:** Burgos, Segovia (5 synagogues), Toledo (10 synagogues), Hervás.
> - **Navarre:** Tudela, Pamplona.
> - **Aragon:** Saragossa, Huesca and Calatayud.
> - **The County of Barcelona:** Barcelona, Villafranca del Panadés, Tarragona, Montblanch, Lérida, Balaguer, Tárrega, Gerona and Besalú.
> - **Valencia:** Valencia, Játiva, Castellón, Denia and Murviedro.
> - **Majorca:** there is a community of Jewish merchants, renowned as great navigators and explorers. The Jews of Majorca trade across the Mediterranean, and above all with North Africa.
>
> [^p17-IV]: Excerpt from *The Guide for the Perplexed* by Maimonides (Spanish translation by David Gonzalo Maeso).

### The Christians

*Per diem salbasti nos, Domine, in nocte custodi nos, Ihesu Xȓe. Deo gratias semper. Benedictus Dominus Amen. Deo gratjas semper.*[^p17-5]

[^p17-5]: Excerpt from an anonymous exorcism, translated into Spanish by Miguel Rodríguez-Pantoja as: *By day you have saved us, Lord; guard us in the night, Jesus Christ. Thanks be to God always. Blessed be the Lord. Amen. Thanks be to God always*; taken from "Los mozárabes y sus poemas en el siglo ix" (in *Los mozárabes. Historia cultura y religión de los cristianos de al Ándalus*).

Christians are scattered throughout Iberia, both in the Christian kingdoms of the north and in al-Andalus. Those of Hispano-Visigothic origin who live in al-Andalus are called Mozarabs, and the children of Mozarabs who have embraced Islam are called muwalladūn. The influence of Islam has managed to convert more than half of the Hispano-Visigothic population of al-Andalus. This conversion is due to three factors. First, self-interest: in al-Andalus, Christians who convert to Islam do not pay the *ǧizya* tax (see above). Second, faith: many Christians have come to love the laws of Islam and to find in its principles the spiritual guidance they needed. And last, law: once a man has converted to Islam, his children are considered Muslims in turn and so cannot choose their religion, for although conversion to Islam is voluntary, apostasy is punishable by death.

The Mozarabs have three civil authorities: a *comes*, who exercises the authority of civil government; a *judex* (or *qādī*), who acts as lawgiver; and an *exceptor*, who is in charge of collecting taxes. All three are elected by the Mozarabs, although as a rule they must be approved by the city's Muslim governor. The Mozarabs have freedom of worship and may gather in their churches to celebrate their offices according to the Mozarabic rite, whose liturgy is in Latin even though they themselves speak Arabic (see the sidebar on the next page).

The Christians who do not live under the influence of Islam, north of the Central System, are organized around a court or *palatium* that does not reside permanently in any one place. It is an itinerant court, usually made up of high-ranking personages such as clerics, Jews, magnates and knights (nobles), in which the king holds absolute power. In his absence, the *alférez* (the royal standard-bearer, at the head of the royal guard) leads the army. At court, the scribes draft the royal ordinances, which are reviewed by a notary; the alcalde performs his duties as the court's judge; and the majordomo (a post held by members of powerful lineages) directs a number of household officers, such as the treasurers, the huntsmen and the chaplains.

<!-- p. 18 -->

For all his omnipotence, the king is advised in his government by a council or curia (called the *Curia Regis* in Leon and Castile) made up of powerful and prominent figures. Its members advise the king and can authorize (by a signature with power of attorney) royal documents that have been reviewed by the court's notaries. There is thus an ordinary curia, made up of the royal family, the court officers, the magnates and the clergy (the king summons this curia to decide on the affairs of the Crown and to hear appeals brought by lesser powers), and an extraordinary curia which, besides the members of the ordinary curia, includes the aristocracy, the bishops, the abbots and the masters of the military orders, as well as the representatives of the cities (the extraordinary curia deals with the oaths of the heirs to the throne, the marriages of monarchs and declarations of war, and serves as a court of justice).

The presence of the cities' representatives in the extraordinary curia gave rise to another assembly: the Cortes. The Cortes are summoned by the monarch at irregular intervals and, besides serving as a council chamber, they legislate on justice, peace and compensation for damages. As the cities have grown, some merchants have grown so rich that the monarchs have turned to them to cover the financial troubles of their kingdoms (as Alfonso VIII of Castile and Pedro II of Aragon did). Thanks to the merchants' money, the cities have won a voice in the Crown's decisions and are now represented in the Cortes by an elected procurator who acts as spokesman for their interests and casts a single vote.

For their part, the cities and towns are governed by the *concilium*, or town council, which rules over its whole district (*alfoz*)[^p18-6]. The councils meet on Sundays after Mass and are presided over by a representative of the king called the *senior* or *dominus villae*; also present is the governor of the fortress (in charge of military command), called the castellan (*alcaide*), *tenente* or *princeps militae*.

[^p18-6]: A group of villages that share the same legal ordinances and form a geographical district.

The council elects its officers and representatives each year from among the wealthiest families. Furthermore, since the Cortes delegate royal justice to that of the councils, the alcaldes lay down the law in cities as well as in towns and villages; they also collect the *caloñas* (fines), set and collect the *portazgos* (tolls), and profit from other royal levies such as the *pontazgo* (for crossing a bridge), the *montazgo* (for driving livestock across hill land), the *colodrazgo* (for selling wine), the *barcaje* (for using a boat to cross a river) or the *castillería* (for passing through a castle's lands).

The *concilium* also decides on the exploitation of common resources, such as woods, meadows and mills, and may sell or grant lands to nobles and monasteries.

> #### The Mozarabic Rite
>
> The apostles brought to Iberia the rites of the Christian offices they had earlier formalized in Rome. Once in Iberia, however, the divine rite was enriched by the contributions of various prelates and scholars, such as Saint Isidore and Saint Leander during the Visigothic occupation of the Peninsula. These changes, together with those that had taken place in the Roman rite outside Iberia, eventually set the offices of the two Churches apart and drove them further from each other.
>
> The Mozarabs of the Peninsula inherited the Visigothic office and, owing to its influence, called their breviary the *Officium Isidori et Leandri*. In 924, amid suspicions that it diverged from the Roman rite, Pope John X sent a legate to Iberia to confirm the conformity of the Mozarabic rite. Although the legate found no significant differences, the Holy See tried without success to introduce the Roman rite, and tried again in the mid-eleventh century with the same result (although it did succeed in introducing it in Aragon in 1071, as King Sancho I Ramírez had to make his fledgling kingdom a fief of the Holy See to secure his control over it).
>
> When the reform promoted by Pope Gregory VII began (see page 39), the Gothic-Mozarabic rite and office were censured. In 1088, Urban II confirmed in the bull *Cunctis Sanctorum* the primacy of the archbishopric of Toledo (of the Roman office) over the other churches of Iberia. The pope, however, failed to establish the Roman rite throughout the Peninsula because of opposition from the prelates and the Christian people of some cities. Although the Mozarabs of Aragon accepted the rite unanimously, the same did not happen in other kingdoms. When the bishop of Coimbra (in the kingdom of Portugal), Gonçalo Pais, tried to impose the Roman rite on the Mozarabs, they rebelled, and the pope had to intervene with a bull urging the citizens to obey him. Tension between the two Churches increased after the murder of the Mozarabic bishop during the conquest of Lisbon and after the arrival of the relics of Saint Vincent in the city in 1173.
>
> The Mozarabic liturgy has remained in use in Toledo and Lisbon up to 1220, as well as in some monasteries outside the ordinary jurisdiction and in Mozarabic churches under Muslim rule, for example in Valencia (where the liturgy is still celebrated in the church of the Holy Sepulcher) and Majorca (in the church of Santa Eulalia in Palma and the underground sanctuary of San Martín in La Alcudia), where the Christian monarchs have been unable to suppress it. The Mozarabs, however, have been dwindling over the years, and by 1220 few remain, for nearly all have ended up accepting either the Latin Roman rite or Islam.
>
> In game terms, the Mozarabic rite is considered a specialty of the Academic Ability Theology.

<!-- p. 19 -->

In the mid-twelfth century, the councils began to be divided into administrative districts (*sexmos*, *cuartos*, *ochavos*) to make them easier to run. As a result, villages throughout the kingdom have been grouped into territorial units.

> #### On Time
>
> *[…] time itself also belongs to created things, since it accompanies motion, which is an accident of the thing moved, which likewise was created and brought into being after its nonexistence.* [^p19-V]
>
> Muslims and Jews follow a lunar calendar. The former divide the year into twelve months of 29 or 30 days, called *muḥarram* (which marks the beginning of the year), *ṣafar*, *rabīʿ I*, *rabīʿ II*, *ŷumāda I*, *ŷumāda II*, *raŷab*, *šaʿbān*, *ramadān* (the month of fasting), *šawwāl*, *ḏū l-qaʿda* and *ḏū l-ḥiŷŷa* (which marks the end of the year and is when the pilgrimages to Mecca begin). Ramadan is the month in which the first revelation of the Qurʾan to the Prophet took place, and during it every healthy adult Muslim must abstain from eating, drinking and sexual relations during the hours of daylight. Ramadan ends with the "Festival of Breaking the Fast," or *ʿĪd al-Fiṭr*, celebrated on the 1st of *šawwāl*. The other great date is the "Festival of the Sacrifice," or *ʿĪd al-aḍḥà*, on the 10th of *ḏū l-ḥiŷŷa*, which recalls Abraham's (unconsummated) sacrifice of Isaac.
>
> For the Jews, one of the most important celebrations is *Yom-Kippur*, the day of atonement for sins, which brings with it a strict fast and a complete cessation of all work and activity. It is celebrated on the tenth day of the month of *Tishrí*, nine days after the Hebrew new year, or *Rosh ha-shaná*. The intervening days between the two dates are known as the *yamim noraím*, or days of repentance.
>
> For the Christians, winter begins with Advent, which precedes Christmas, a feast that lasts until the first Sunday after the 6th of January, which they call the Appearance of the Lord. Weeks later, the villages celebrate a day of games, masks and madness: Carnival. After this feast, still in winter, Christians begin the period of Lent, in which they prepare for Easter by purifying body and soul through fasting. Lent always begins on a Sunday, which they call *In Carnes Tollendas*, and it has a festive character. In spring come Easter (which commemorates the resurrection of Christ), the Ascension and Pentecost. Summer begins with the fire rite of Saint John, and the fertility of the harvests is celebrated with the Assumption. Finally, in September the rents are collected under the auspices of Saints Matthew and Michael. All the Sundays from the beginning of Christmas to Lent, and from Pentecost to Advent, are called *De Cotidiano*.
>
> [^p19-V]: Excerpt from *The Guide for the Perplexed* by Maimonides (Spanish translation by David Gonzalo Maeso).
>
> #### Adoptionism
>
> The arrival of Islam in Iberia and the coexistence of the two religions shook the foundations of the Church, where, thanks to the backing of figures of the stature of Elipandus, bishop of Toledo, the Adoptionist heresy resurfaced: an anti-Trinitarian theological doctrine holding that Jesus had been adopted by God at his baptism and had risen again thanks to his immaculate devotion. Its theses were declared heretical at the end of the second century, at the First Council of Nicaea.
>
> The doctrine resurfaced in Iberia in the eighth century, however, when Elipandus, the highest authority of the Visigothic church of Toledo, together with Felix, bishop of Urgell, maintained that Jesus's human nature was adoptive of God, while his divine nature was part of the Father. Their thesis held that his human nature was independent of his divine being. This error, which fell into the Adoptionist heresy of the second century, was immediately condemned by Pope Adrian I, who called on the bishop to recant. Elipandus nevertheless defended his position even when his teachings were condemned as heretical at the Second Ecumenical Council of Nicaea, at the synod of Regensburg (where Felix of Urgell was forced to abjure his beliefs) and at that of Frankfurt.
>
> Elipandus's doctrines spread throughout Iberia, though they never passed beyond the bounds of the Peninsula. He was refuted by great scholars of the age, such as Beatus of Liébana (who wrote an anti-Adoptionist treatise for the purpose, the *Apologeticus*, in which one could read: "Elipandus is a heretic and a testicle of the Antichrist") and his disciple Eterius, bishop of Osma. Later, Pope Leo III again condemned Elipandus's teachings at the synod of Rome and, a year later, none other than Alcuin of York (the *Alcuinus Flaccus Albinus* of Charlemagne's court) engaged in a theological debate against Elipandus's teachings at the Council of Aachen.
>
> Elipandus always upheld a stance of collaboration with the Muslims and showed his wish to remain connected with the culture of the East. His Church was the Mozarabic Church, the same one that was opposed and finally eliminated by the Church of Rome. After his death, at the beginning of the ninth century, the Adoptionist doctrine began to lose strength until it disappeared completely from Iberia.

<!-- p. 20 -->

## The Umayyad Emirate

The Umayyads ruled al-Andalus as emirs independent of Baghdad from 756 to 912, maintaining throughout the territory under their control[^p20-7] the system of government that had existed since the Muslims arrived in the Peninsula in 711.

### The Kingdom of al-Andalus

The following Umayyad emirs succeeded one another in this period:[^p20-8]

| Emirs | Years |
| --- | --- |
| ʿAbd al-Raḥmān I | 756–788 |
| Hišām I | 788–796 |
| Al-Ḥakam I | 796–822 |
| ʿAbd al-Raḥmān II | 822–852 |
| Muḥammad I | 852–886 |
| Al-Munḍir | 886–888 |
| ʿAbd Allāh | 888–912 |

The Umayyad prince ʿAbd al-Raḥmān I (fair-haired,[^p20-9] and called the Falcon of Qurayš by the chroniclers)[^p20-10] fled Baghdad after the Abbasid clan's coup and took refuge in North Africa among his mother's kin. From there he sought allies in the Peninsula to seize power in Cordoba (then a province dependent on Baghdad), which at the time was governed by the Abbasid emir Yūsuf al-Fihrī. ʿAbd al-Raḥmān won the support he needed from the commanders of the Syrian armies (*aŷnād*)[^p20-11] who held regions such as Jaén, Seville, Algeciras and Elvira, and who had once served the Umayyads. With their help, the Falcon of Qurayš defeated the Abbasid emir of Cordoba and laid the foundations of Umayyad rule in Iberia.

[^p20-7]: The Muslims never settled north of the Sistema Central; the Christians controlled all the territory from there to the Cantabrian Sea, and from the edges of the northern Meseta to the Atlantic Ocean.

[^p20-8]: The numbering of the emirs and caliphs (see below) is no more than a convention. In their own time they were known by their *laqab*, such as ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Nāṣir (the conqueror) or Al-Ḥakam al-Rabḍī (he of the suburb).

[^p20-9]: Fair hair was a distinctive trait of the Umayyads, who, according to the chronicles, always preferred women of their own hair color, especially those from the Basque lands and the north of Iberia. Their taste spread through society, and the preference took hold among the members of the court.

[^p20-10]: The saker is a type of falcon, and *qurayš* was the family of the Prophet that eventually founded the Umayyad dynasty of Damascus.

[^p20-11]: The *aŷnād* (singular *ŷund*), created for the Arab conquest of Syria, controlled the territory and the army settled in it; they ended up in Iberia after putting down the Berber revolt in the Peninsula in 741.

ʿAbd al-Raḥmān I refused to recognize the caliphal authority of the Abbasids, but neither did he wish to claim the caliphate, so as not to defy the caliph of Baghdad. He therefore proclaimed himself an independent prince and, once established in power, had to confront great cultural diversity—Arabs, Berbers, muwalladūn, Mozarabs and Jews—all of whom he had to manage so that they would respect his authority.

> #### The Banū Qasī
>
> The Qasī clan descended from an old Visigothic count of the middle Ebro basin who traveled to Damascus to swear obedience to the Umayyad caliph and embrace Islam before the arrival of ʿAbd al-Raḥmān I.
>
> The Qasī reached their zenith under Musā ibn Musā during the reigns of ʿAbd al-Raḥmān II and Muḥammad I. Musā transformed the *muwalladūn* clan of the Qasī from a local family into a power to be reckoned with by Christian kings and emirs of Cordoba alike. Among his many feats were the rescue of ʿAbd al-Raḥmān II from the Vikings who sacked Seville, the union of his house with the royalty of Pamplona, the expulsion of the Franks from Pamplona (halting the Carolingian advance into the Peninsula with the help of the Christian Arista family), and winning the title of *wālī* of the Upper March at the battle of Albelda (Huesca), where he defeated the Christians despite taking 35 lance thrusts. So great were his military achievements that he became known as the third king of Iberia (alongside the kings of Asturias and al-Andalus).
>
> On his death, however, his realm crumbled: one of his sons swore obedience to the king of Asturias and the other to the emir of Cordoba, tearing apart the lands and authority that the great Musā had won. Before the clan's end, one of the third king of Iberia's descendants sold Saragossa to the emir of Cordoba, Muḥammad I.

Although the Arabs were a minority, they held the most important posts in government and ruled the frontier regions of al-Andalus. The Berbers formed the largest group (they had made up the bulk of the armies during the invasion of Iberia in 711) and worked the land. The Arabs, who considered themselves superior, also treated them with contempt. The native inhabitants who had converted to Islam were called *musālim*. Like the Berbers, they were scorned by the Arabs. In time the *musālim* came to outnumber the Berbers, since their children, the *muwalladūn* (muwallads), were born Muslim. Another group ʿAbd al-Raḥmān had to deal with were the Christians living in al-Andalus, whom the Muslims called *mustaʿribūn* (Mozarabs); they still practiced their religion and were not hostile to the Muslims. Over time they came to use Arabic as their mother tongue and adopted many Arab customs. Finally, the smallest group were the Jews.

<!-- p. 21 -->

> #### The Great Mosque of Cordoba
>
> *As for the Great Mosque, you will have heard that its lamps were cast from the bells of the Christians, and that the enlargement Ibn Abī ʿĀmir made to its fabric was built with earth the Christians carried on their shoulders from the churches he destroyed in their lands.*[^p21-VI]
>
> Of the more than one hundred mosques in Cordoba, the greatest is the Great Mosque, built by order of ʿAbd al-Raḥmān I. It was raised on the foundations of the church of San Vicente, bought from the Christians for 100,000 dīnāres, who were then forbidden to build new churches. It was later enlarged by the emirs ʿAbd al-Raḥmān II and Al-Ḥakam II (raising its capacity to 7,000 people) and by the *ḥāŷib* Almanzor, during the last years of the Caliphate of Cordoba.
>
> The mosques of Cordoba were each the center of an urban parish (*ḥawma*), whose residents and workers were obliged to come and pray at least five times a day. Although one could pray at home, the religious authorities censured those who did not attend the mosque for the Friday afternoon prayer. Indeed, it was precisely at that hour that the caliph and the chief members of his court usually attended the Great Mosque, so the crowds were larger. When that prayer ended it was not unusual to find the town crier making announcements and proclaiming state ordinances on the west side of the Great Mosque, at the so-called House of Alms (*Dār al-Ṣadaqa*).
>
> The interior of the Great Mosque is a single hall filled with columns that open toward the ceiling, as if forming an immense palm grove. For the Umayyads, palms are more than trees: they are a memory of their homeland. ʿAbd al-Raḥmān I himself planted vines, pomegranates, palms and other fruit trees brought from Syria on his country estate (*almunia*) of al-Ruṣāfa, to remind him of his childhood. Hence the great importance the Arabs give to the hall of palms in the great mosque. Yet it is not only a memory but also a symbol of the absence of an ecclesiastical hierarchy in Islam: it is infinity, broken only by the niche of lights (the *miḥrāb*), whose sole purpose is to point toward Mecca.
>
> The *miḥrāb* is entered through an arch leading to a small heptagonal chamber with a domed, fluted ceiling like a seashell. Here the word of God revealed in the Qurʾan is recited: the word, deposited in and transmitted from within the *miḥrāb*, is transmuted as it reaches the listeners, crystallizing within them as though it were a pearl. Facing the *miḥrāb* is the *maqsura*, the space reserved for the caliph.
>
> The great mosque is a space open to all. There teachers give lessons explaining the faith, always standing, always beside the same column, and always from memory. Around them lie many mats where their students, or anyone who wishes to listen, may sit. It is also where the qadi dispenses justice and where citizens' petitions and complaints are heard. All activity, however, stops at the call to prayer from the minaret (see the sidebar on page 12).
>
> [^p21-VI]: Fragment of *In Praise of Spanish Islam* by Al-Šaqundī (Ibn Abī ʿĀmir is Almanzor; Spanish translation by E. García Gómez).

ʿAbd al-Raḥmān I also had to show his strength by crushing the many threats that arose throughout his reign, always relying on the troops of the Syrian *aŷnād*. His armies fought the Christians of the kingdom of Asturias, clashed with the Franks, had to subdue the powerful muwallad families of the Ebro basin, crushed the supporters of the Abbasids and the Arab chieftains of the frontier regions, and fought and triumphed over the Berbers (who rose up repeatedly in Toledo and Mérida).

The first Umayyad emir of al-Andalus was not only a great statesman but also a cultivated man of letters. During his reign he used poetry as a means to instruct while delighting in the values and ideals of his rule; panegyrics were the most important form of political propaganda (his panegyrist was the first Andalusi poet, Abū-l-Majšī). Thus, from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān I onward, the Andalusi Umayyad family promoted not only the import, copying and making of books (always in contact with the Arab East) but also the founding of libraries.

ʿAbd al-Raḥmān I was succeeded by his son, Hišām I. Hišām went down in history as a holy man who always dressed humbly in simple clothes. During his reign he spent much time among the sick in the suburbs of Cordoba, beyond the city walls, tending to them at the expense of the state treasury. Apart from the revolts he faced on taking the throne, his short reign was prosperous and peaceful, just as the court magus, Al-Ḍabbī (see page 74), had foretold. During his rule he clothed Cordoba in culture, ordered the city's Roman bridge rebuilt, and waged *ŷihād* against the Christian kingdoms.

Hišām I's son, Al-Ḥakam I, would be remembered as the most bloodthirsty and despotic of the Umayyads. He is said to have had a great passion for drink, even though the Qurʾan forbids it (the abundance of vineyards in al-Andalus was always a great temptation for the country's entire ruling class), and for this he was nicknamed "the Drunkard."

Al-Ḥakam I made his protégé, the Christian Goth Rabí ben Teodoulfo, commander of Cordoba's armies, and greatly enlarged the mercenary forces created by ʿAbd al-Raḥmān I. For his personal protection he surrounded himself with a powerful Slavic guard known as "the mutes," since they could not speak Arabic. During his reign he raised taxes and harshly repressed every popular rebellion, among which the following stand out:

<!-- p. 22 -->

- the Revolt of the Suburb of Cordoba, in which Berbers and muwalladūn demanded equality with the Arabs, who considered themselves superior and entitled to more rights. It was put down on the emir's orders and carried out by Rabí ben Teodoulfo. The suburb was razed, more than 3,000 Cordobans were executed, and hundreds of families (the chronicles speak of a quarter of Cordoba's population) were deported to Fez, Alexandria and the island of Crete;

- an attempted coup. The attack was thwarted and punished with more than 70 crucifixions (Islamic law inherited this capital punishment from Roman law);

- the rebellion of Toledo, capital of the Middle March. Toledo's continual insurrections in its struggle against the central power of Cordoba ended with the ill-fated Day of the Ditch.

> #### Islamic Law: The Mālikī School
>
> In the ninth century, the main ways of interpreting legal questions crystallized into four schools among the Sunnis: Ḥanafī, Mālikī, Šāfiʿī and Ḥanbalī. When one of the two books containing the codification of Mālikī principles on the *šarīʿa* reached Iberia, the emir Al-Ḥakam I had to give the Mālikī rite a degree of official recognition, since it had taken firm root among the townsfolk thanks to the ulama (the citizens preferred a strict Islamic law that would curb the tyrannical capacity of the central power in Cordoba). Even so, it was not recognized as the official rite until the reign of his son, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān II.
>
> The Mālikī school takes the Qurʾan and the sunna as its primary sources, accepts the use of *iŷmāʿ* and *qiyās* (though without innovation), forbids the qadi from adopting solutions from other schools, and holds the faqih to be infallible and his authority unquestionable.
>
> The Umayyad state tolerated the other Sunni schools that coexisted in al-Andalus, at least until the coming of Almanzor, as shown by the fact that during three centuries of Umayyad rule there were only six accusations of heresy (*zandaqa*), and of these only two ended in the death penalty. The legal system applied in the Umayyad period endured without much change in later centuries under the taifas, the Almoravids and the Almohads.

> #### The Day of the Ditch of Toledo
>
> At the end of the eighth century, the poet Girbib ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jamir raised the city of Toledo in revolt. The city, home to Visigoths, Hispano-Romans, Jews and Berbers, managed to free itself from the grip of the despot Al-Ḥakam I.
>
> To put down the rebellion the emir used the forces of Talavera and, to prevent further uprisings, placed Toledo under the command of ʿAmrus ibn Yūsuf al-Muwalad, governor of Talavera and a muwallad trusted by the emir. To that end, the new governor resolved to do away with everyone who had ever quarreled with the Umayyad regime of Cordoba. Taking advantage of his investiture in his new post, he held a "feast" in his palace to which he invited more than 400 people (mostly muwalladūn) deemed subversive. Once they were gathered there, he shut the doors and had them all put to the sword. They were beheaded one by one and their heads thrown into a ditch dug for the occasion.

When Al-Ḥakam I named his son ʿAbd al-Raḥmān as his successor, he resolved to wipe out what remained of Visigothic power in al-Andalus to guarantee the Umayyad succession. He therefore presented his son with the head of his former protégé and army commander, the Goth Rabí ben Teodoulfo. Al-Ḥakam I also invited the poet Ziryāb to the court of Cordoba (see the sidebar on the next page), which brought Persian poetic influences, chess and the game of polo into al-Andalus.

With the accession of ʿAbd al-Raḥmān II (one of Al-Ḥakam I's nineteen sons), and with his father having crushed all the insurrections that had challenged the central power of Cordoba, the course of al-Andalus's government changed and ceased to be expansionist. His reign enjoyed a measure of stability and fostered the rooting of the Eastern customs Ziryāb had brought, as well as the research of the brilliant ʿAbbās ibn Firnās (see Appendix I).

Among the courtiers who served him, two stood out: the influential muwallad and chief of the eunuchs, Abū-l-Fath Nasr, who died when the emir ordered him to drink the poison he himself had had prepared for his master (the muwallad was involved in a conspiracy over the succession to the throne); and the singing slave girl, woman of letters and scribe Qalam (from the Arabic for "reed pen"), of Basque origin and educated in the school of Medina.

Despite the stability of his government, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān II had to face the movement of the voluntary martyrs (see the sidebar on page 24) and, abroad, the attacks of the Scandinavian Vikings, against whom he had a network of watchtowers built along the entire Andalusi coast (see page 286).

Of his more than 100 children, his daughter Bahaʾ (from the Arabic for "splendor") led an ascetic life devoted to copying Qurʾans, which became pious endowments (*habices*). ʿAbd al-Raḥmān II also had the mosque of Seville built and approved the construction and restoration of Cordoba's old Roman aqueducts to supply the capital with water.

<!-- p. 23 -->

> #### Ziryāb
>
> Abū l-Hasan ʿAlī ibn Nāfiʿ, nicknamed Ziryāb (from the Arabic for "blackbird," for his dark complexion), was a singer, poet, composer, teacher and lute player with great knowledge of astronomy, chemistry, geography, meteorology and botany. He spent his early years in Baghdad, at the court of the Abbasid caliph. However, because of his talent as a musician, his own master had him banished, fearing the caliph would prefer his pupil to him.
>
> In exile, Ziryāb received an invitation from the emir Al-Ḥakam I to come to the court of al-Andalus. He had heard that Cordoba could be compared only to fabulous Constantinople, so he crossed the Strait of Gibraltar and traveled to the Umayyad capital of Iberia. When he reached the city the emir had died, and it was his son, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān II, who renewed the invitation. Without even hearing him play, the emir gave him a palace and granted him a handsome income—such was his fame! Under ʿAbd al-Raḥmān's protection Ziryāb could express himself freely, changing forever the social and cultural standards of Iberia and of Europe (which the Muslim chroniclers called the Great Land).
>
> Ziryāb spread the ideal of the perfect man, according to which every Muslim must show himself to be in love, must write love poetry, must exchange letters in verse (or rhymed prose) with other men of letters, accompany his writings with gifts, and adorn his garments with embroidered verses. According to the Eastern ideal, men should be elegant and decorate their rooms with verses alluding to each room's purpose.
>
> The singer from Baghdad also revolutionized the world of music. Each string of his lute was dyed a different color, in sympathy with the four bodily humors (see *Ars Magica Fifth Edition*, page 265), and depending on which he played he could influence the mood and health of his listeners. However, to fully encompass the nature of man, he added a fifth string (between the second and third) which he called "breath." This string represented the vital spirit and served as a bridge between the body (the other four strings) and the soul. With his lute he brought the Eastern sounds of Persia and Greece and created a unique style of performance that spread throughout al-Andalus. His songs were handed down for generations and gave rise to Andalusi music. Ziryāb founded Cordoba's first school of music, which admitted both men and women, and where Basque women (highly prized by the caliphs of his day) learned all manner of vocal techniques and dances. His school outlived him, and its fame as a center of cultural reference spread throughout the Muslim world.
>
> Ziryāb introduced the custom of dressing according to the seasons of the year (linking them to different colors and garments), and even got people to dress differently in the morning, afternoon and evening. This aesthetic concern extended to hairstyles: he popularized the fringe and cuts that left the ears and nape bare; under his influence men began to shave, and smooth faces came to be thought handsome.
>
> Among his virtues was also a deep respect for personal hygiene, in which he set the example: he bathed every morning and every evening. Ziryāb invented a deodorant made with litharge to eliminate body odor and prevent sweating, and a perfumed toothpaste that became popular throughout al-Andalus. Moreover, when he discovered that the emir washed his hair with rosewater, the poet taught him the use of salts and essences to improve its shine and cleanliness.
>
> Ziryāb imported new fruits and vegetables, such as asparagus, and introduced new rules that spread to every table in al-Andalus: "every meal must be served in three successive courses: first, a soup; a main course of meat or fish; and a dessert"; always served, of course, on tablecloths of fine leather, where until then tables had been bare. Among his many other contributions, Ziryāb also introduced glass for wine, for the sight of it fired men's imaginations. Thus, from his arrival onward, gold and silver cups were no longer used on the tables of al-Andalus.

Muḥammad I, son of ʿAbd al-Raḥmān II, had to face constant revolts and rebellions by muwalladūn and Mozarabs: his reign marked the beginning of the crisis of the independent emirate of Cordoba. Although he subdued the Banū Qasī of the Upper March and the rebels of Toledo in the Middle March, he could not overcome the muwalladūn of the Lower March nor the semi-independent government of Seville. To make matters worse, the revolts that broke out in the mountains of Malaga, led by the muwallad ʿUmar ibn Ḥafṣūn (see the sidebar on the next page), finished destabilizing the Umayyad emirate.

Muḥammad I founded the *ribāṭ* of Majrīṭ, Talamanca and Peñafora (buildings, at once military and religious, built at strategic points to defend the frontiers, housing a garrison and a number of devotees who freely submitted to military service to earn the merits that go hand in hand with *ŷihād*), and imported Persian and Byzantine technology to build siege engines with which to fight the Christian kingdoms of the north. In addition, according to the chronicles, during his reign he assembled the largest library in all Cordoba.

The brief reign of Al-Munḍir, in a Cordoba stifled by the growth of local powers, was marked by internal strife and the war against the rebel Ibn Ḥafṣūn, whom, like his father, he could not defeat. Al-Munḍir was poisoned by his physician during the siege of Bobastro—at the behest, they say, of his brother (and the next emir) ʿAbd Allāh. His death hastened the disintegration of the Umayyad state.

During his reign, ʿAbd Allāh faced widespread rebellions that cost him control of all the Muslim territories (Cordoba was the only *kūra* under Umayyad rule), which Alfonso III of Asturias exploited to consolidate his rule in Asturias. To forge alliances with the Christian kingdoms, ʿAbd Allāh married Onneca Fortúnez, daughter of the king of Pamplona, Fortún Garcés.

In his old age ʿAbd Allāh lived in fear of assassination, and so imprisoned and condemned many of his relatives.
