By his death most of al-Andalus had slipped from Umayyad control, and the Fatimid Caliphate had established itself in the Maghreb, making matters even harder for the dynasty that had been settled in Iberia for more than 150 years.

<!-- p. 24 -->

> #### ʿUmar ibn Ḥafṣūn
>
> This muwallad fought alongside other Mozarab and Berber rebels against the humiliating treatment and heavy taxes that the emirs of Cordoba imposed on non-Arabs.
>
> Ibn Ḥafṣūn proved a great strategist and exploited the instability of the emirate to seize numerous fortresses between Jaén and Seville. As his base of operations he chose the old Roman settlement of *Municipium Singiliense Bobastrense* (Bobastro) in the mountains of Malaga. Once fortified, the stronghold withstood Cordoba's sieges for more than fifty years. Other men-at-arms fought at his side, such as the powerful Ibn Mastana, lord of Priego and Luque.
>
> Ibn Ḥafṣūn was baptized to win supporters among the Christians and secure an alliance with the king of Asturias. However, the promised support never came, and in converting he lost many muwallad allies. Defeated by the emir ʿAbd Allāh, he returned to Islam and sought support in North Africa. After he swore obedience to the Fatimid caliph, the latter showered him with gifts and sent him two preachers so that he might fight the Umayyads and defeat them. Even so, he never regained his power and, after many defeats at the hands of ʿAbd al-Raḥmān III, he died in 918, still independent of Cordoba.
>
> Although his sons continued the rebellion, the Ḥafṣūnids were finally wiped out and Bobastro was taken by Cordoba in 928. According to the chronicles, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān III went to Bobastro the following year and, after praying in the mosque, ordered all the churches destroyed and Ibn Ḥafṣūn's body exhumed; the rebel's remains were taken to Cordoba and hung atop a pole between the crucified bodies of his two sons. Ibn Ḥafṣūn's body remained there until 942, when a flood of the Guadalquivir carried it away.

### The Christian Kingdoms during the Emirate

During the emirate of al-Andalus (756–912), the following Christian kingdoms existed in the north of the Peninsula (see below). They were forced to pay tribute to Cordoba and lived harassed by its summer raids, which Alfonso II of Asturias managed to curb. Later, with the crisis of the emirate, the Christian monarchs pushed their borders south, eroding the power of the Marches and limiting that of Cordoba itself.

<!-- p. 25 -->

| Kingdoms | Years |
| --- | --- |
| The kingdom of Asturias | 756–912 |
| The kingdom of Pamplona | 824–912 |
| The kingdom of Leon | 910–912 |
| The kingdom of Galicia | 910–912 |

The emirate of al-Andalus witnessed the waning power of the kingdom of Asturias, whose gradual disintegration led to the rise of the kingdom of Pamplona under the rule of the Íñigo and Jimeno families (Cordoba made and broke alliances with this kingdom many times during the Umayyad domination of al-Andalus), and of the counties of Aragon, Castile, Leon, Portucale and Álava, which came under the command of powerful noble families with more influence than the monarch himself and with authority over the succession to the Asturian crown (under Gothic law).

> #### The Voluntary Martyrs
>
> *Heu pro dolor, legem suam nesciunt Xpīani et linguam propriam non aduertunt Latini, ita ut omini Xp¯i collegio uix inueniatur unus in milleno hominum numero qui salutatorias fratri possit ratjonauiliter dirigere litteras [...].*[^p25-VII]
>
> During the reign of ʿAbd al-Raḥmān II, the abbot of the monastery of Santa Clara, Esperaindeo, violently criticized the laxity of the Christians of Cordoba at the council of 839, for conversions to Islam were increasing year after year. In his address he exalted Christian sentiment and urged rebellion against Islam and preaching against Christian converts, at a time when no one knew for certain who Muḥammad was and Islam was fought as though it were just another anti-Trinitarian doctrine. This council was the prelude to what would become the era of the martyrs of Cordoba.
>
> Esperaindeo's work was carried on by the clerics Eulogius and Samsón (his disciples) and the laymen Pablo, Cipriano, Vicente and Álbaro (also his disciple, and Eulogius's friend and biographer). Eleven years after that council, Perfecto, a monk of the Tabanense monastery (apparently goaded by a group of Muslims), defamed Muḥammad (a crime punishable by death under Islamic law), which led to his imprisonment and execution. The following year, other Christians began insulting the Prophet in public or renouncing Islam, and were likewise executed. When Saint Eulogius,[^p25-VIII] now bishop of Toledo, publicly supported the first acts of martyrdom, the bishop of Seville, Recafredo, had him imprisoned, and there Eulogius wrote the *Memoriale Sanctorum* and the *Documentum Martyriale* (a work exhorting to martyrdom the young women Flora—daughter of a Muslim father and therefore an apostate—and María).
>
> Faced with the city's bloody wave of martyrs, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān II, now in the last years of his reign, tried to put an end to the matter, since tension in the capital was mounting. He asked Recafredo to convene the Third Christian Council of Cordoba, which forbade Christians to insult Islam so as to prevent their martyrdom and, although it sanctified those who had already died, condemned any future martyrdom. But the council failed in its purpose: the martyrdoms continued to be encouraged by the doctors of the church of Cordoba. Álbaro wrote the *Indiculus Luminosus* (which urged Christians to suffer martyrdom) and, after his journey to Pamplona, his *Apologetic against Muhammad* (in which he counted Islam among the currents Christian orthodoxy must combat).
>
> On the death of ʿAbd al-Raḥmān II, the matter of the martyrs passed to his son, Muḥammad I, and ended in 859, when Saint Eulogius was caught instructing Leocricia (a young woman of Muslim parents) in the Christian faith. Eulogius was imprisoned and, when the qadi asked him to recant, he refused. Eulogius was therefore beheaded, and his death ended the nearly fifty executions that had taken place in Cordoba between 850 and 859. The martyrs included not only Andalusis but also Franks, Arabs, Syrians, Greeks and Berbers.
>
> In 883, the king of Asturias, Alfonso III, sent an embassy to the emir Muḥammad I to request the remains of Saint Eulogius, and a year later they were handed over together with several codices that passed into the royal library (among them the so-called *Codex Ovetensis*, containing the only four surviving works of Eulogius).
>
> In 1220, Christians prize having martyrs among their ancestors.
>
> [^p25-VII]: Fragment of the *Indiculus Luminosus* of Álbaro of Cordoba, translated into Spanish by Feliciano Delgado León as: "Alas, the pain! The Christians do not know their own law and the Latins do not understand their own tongue, so that in the whole Christian community scarcely one man in a thousand can be found who can write a letter to a brother in correct Latin [...]."
>
> [^p25-VIII]: On his journey to Pamplona, Saint Eulogius discovered in the monastery of Leire (Aragon) works that had reached its library thanks to Carolingian influence, such as the *City of God* (Saint Augustine), the *Aeneid* (Virgil), the poems of Juvenal and Horace, the treatises of Porphyry, the fables of Avianus and a disparaging biography of the prophet Muḥammad, which offered a glimpse of the extent of Islam in Iberia.

Meanwhile, the influence of the Franks (of the Carolingian Empire) of Provence eventually vanished from the Aragonese Pyrenees, and the Catalan counties won independence from them by making their titles hereditary (the last count of Barcelona to pay homage to the Frankish kings was Wifredo II Borrell).

The end of this period coincided with the reign of Alfonso III of Asturias (called *Hispaniae rex*). Alfonso freed dozens of strongholds from Muslim rule and pushed the Christian frontier south, fixing it on the line of the Duero and securing the settlements in the conquered lands. He also strengthened the crown's power over the nobility by binding the landowners to the monarchy. Alfonso also achieved a major milestone by defeating the rebel armies of the Umayyad prince Ibn al-Qitt at the so-called Day of Zamora (see the sidebar on the next page) during the crisis of the emirate.

<!-- p. 26 -->

> #### The Day of Zamora
>
> With the coming of the tenth century, in the twilight of the emirate of Cordoba, the prophet and Umayyad prince Ibn al-Qitt had a vision revealing to him the coming of the end of days. Determined to play the role of redeemer, he rebelled against his kinsman, the emir ʿAbd Allāh, and proclaimed himself Al-Mahdī, the figure who for the Shiʿa appears shortly before the end of time to rid the world of evil. Through magic, and with the help of the mystic Abū ʿAlī al-Sarray, he won the support of the Berber chieftains who held the Middle and Lower Marches, proclaiming *ŷihād* against the Christian kingdoms. His first target was Zamora, an important stronghold taken by Alfonso III of Asturias.
>
> On his march north he led the largest army ever sent against the kingdom of Asturias, more than 40,000 men. So vast was it that his whole host took a full day to pass a single point. At the vanguard, Al-Mahdī declared that with a single word the walls of Zamora would fall like wheat before the scythe.
>
> Alfonso III, warned of this army, deployed his forces around the city. When the monarch saw the army he faced, he commended himself to God and fought bravely beside the Duero. But Ibn al-Qitt's hosts defeated the Christians, who had to fall back inside the city. Al-Mahdī announced that unless they all converted to Islam they would be put to death in the name of God. Alfonso III made no reply to the threat, and when all seemed lost the Berber armies miraculously collapsed, the phalanxes broke apart, and Ibn al-Qitt was left abandoned by his armies. The Christian forces sallied from the city and for three days pursued and slaughtered the fleeing Muslims. Thus Ibn al-Qitt was killed, and his head, together with those of his men, adorned the gates of Zamora.

On the death of Alfonso III of Asturias, shortly before the first caliph came to power in Cordoba, his sons broke up the unity of the kingdom, creating the kingdom of Leon (ruled by García I) and the kingdom of Galicia (governed by Ordoño II), leaving the old kingdom of Asturias (under his third son, Fruela II the Leper) diminished in both extent and power. Leon stood at the head of these three kingdoms, known together as the Astur-Leonese kingdom.

## The Umayyad Caliphate

The word caliph (Arabic *jalīfa*) means "lieutenant" and is applied to the successor of the Prophet in his temporal (but not spiritual) powers: the caliph is the leader of the Muslims (*imām*), the one charged with transmitting the Law, and the supreme commander of the army.

The rule of the Umayyad caliphs brought great economic and social stability to al-Andalus. Indeed, the reigns of ʿAbd al-Raḥmān III and Al-Ḥakam II saw the greatest number of Christian conversions to Islam in Iberia.

### The Kingdom of al-Andalus

During this period there were three Umayyad caliphs before the civil war of al-Andalus, or *fitna*:

| Caliphs | Years |
| --- | --- |
| ʿAbd al-Raḥmān III | 912–961 |
| Al-Ḥakam II | 961–976 |
| Hišām II | 976–1013 |

<!-- p. 27 -->

> #### The Gold of *bilad al-Sūdān*
>
> The path to pacifying al-Andalus also depended on its economic stability, so the caliph turned to the gold of the Sudan, in the lands of *bilad al-Sūdān* (as the Arabs called the lands south of the Sahara; literally "the land of the blacks"), thanks to the protectorate he had established over the western and central Maghreb.
>
> To bring the metal to al-Andalus, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān III used caravans of more than 1,000 camels that traveled the gold routes across the Sahara. The convoys set out in autumn from the territories controlled by the Maghrebi clans (on good terms with the Umayyads) and had to make their way past the Fatimid forces and cross the desert to winter in *bilad al-Sūdān*. There they stocked up on gold, rock salt, spices, ivory, copper, mercury, hides and, above all, slaves captured in Senegal and Gāna. The caravans returned in spring, traveling in the afternoon and at night and camping in the mornings.
>
> With all that gold, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān III opened the mints (*dār al-sikka*) of Cordoba, Madīnat al-Zahrāʾ, Seville and Fez (Madīnat Fās), with which he put his kingdom's finances in order and brought al-Andalus out of crisis (the chronicles say that Al-Ḥakam II's caliphal treasury held more than forty million dīnāres).
>
> With the fall of the Umayyad Caliphate, the Sudanese gold routes passed under the control of the Almoravids and later of the Almohads. The high quality of Sudanese gold allowed them to issue coins of great purity that rivaled the ever-powerful Byzantine gold coinage.

> #### Madīnat al-Zahrāʾ
>
> In an overcrowded Cordoba (its population at this time is estimated at 100,000) and wishing to establish a separate capital as a political and social alternative to aged Cordoba, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān III had the court city of Madīnat al-Zahrāʾ built on the lower slopes of the last foothills of *Ŷabal al-ʿArus* (Arabic for "the mountain of the bride," that is, Sierra Morena), as the seat of the spiritual and governmental power of the new caliphate; its area exceeded that of the medina of Cordoba itself. Raised in honor of his beloved, Al-Zahrāʾ, the caliph had the mountainsides replanted with almond and fig trees to create an idyllic landscape.
>
> The palace city was built on three terraces on the mountainside. On the upper level were the caliphal quarters, whose bureaucracy was served by some 3,500 slaves. There the streets were paved with black marble and green jade laid out like a chessboard, and the lush gardens held cages for wild beasts and aviaries with thousands of birds. On the middle terrace stood the buildings of the administration and the court, the palaces of the viziers and the residences of high state officials; finally, on the lowest level were the baths, the schools, the homes of craftsmen and merchants and those of the common people; from here one entered the city and reached the souk.
>
> The interior of the city's Umayyad palace was supported by more than 4,000 marble columns (brought from Constantinople, Rome, Carthage, Tunis and the finest quarries of al-Andalus), and its walls were adorned with hundreds of precious stones; the ceilings were covered in gold, and of gold were the statues of the fountains. The palace also held a basin filled with mercury: the pool was flanked by eight arches of ivory and ebony, with marble arabesques inlaid with gold and seed pearls, and the arches rested on colored columns. To impress his visitors, the caliph would have a slave stir the mercury, which gave off lovely flashes and produced astonishing plays of light. Thus the caliphal palace was opulent, like those built by the Abbasids,[^p27-IX] while the caliph himself was humble, wearing simple, unadorned clothes. ʿAbd al-Raḥmān III used to say: "All are small before me, but before God I am nothing."
>
> [^p27-IX]: After the fall of the Abbasid Caliphate in Baghdad, al-Andalus sought to imitate its opulence.

ʿAbd al-Raḥmān III was the eighth and last emir and also the first caliph of al-Andalus. He was the grandson of the emir ʿAbd Allāh and the son of a Christian concubine of Frankish origin. He had deep blue eyes and red hair, though he always wore it dyed black. When he came to the throne at twenty-one, al-Andalus was mired in civil war: the Arab nobility was plotting against the central power, the lords of the Marches had risen up, numerous hotbeds of discord had sprung up, fanned by false prophets, the realm was going through a terrible financial crisis (see the sidebar "The Gold of *bilad al-Sūdān*"), and the Fatimid Caliphate had established itself in Ifrīqiya[^p27-12] and threatened from the coasts of Tunis to expand its territories into the Peninsula.

[^p27-12]: This roughly corresponds to North Africa, in what would be Tunisia, eastern Algeria and western Libya.

Of all the dangers he faced, the Fatimids were the worst, and to keep their armies from crossing the strait he had the coastal cities of al-Andalus and the naval base of Algeciras fortified. Moreover, to halt the spread in Iberia of heterodoxy akin to Fatimid ideology, he had the Masarrīs (see page 79) persecuted, along with anyone who might pose a political threat to his rule; in this he had the crucial support of the ulama, without whom he might well never have secured the throne.

ʿAbd al-Raḥmān III enlarged the mercenary army created by the first emir of Iberia, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān I, to serve the Umayyads. To fill its ranks and staff the palace services, he imported Slavic, Frankish and northern slaves (*ṣaqāliba*)[^p28-13] en masse, and with them he subjugated the Berber lords of the Middle, Lower and Upper Marches: Saragossa capitulated after being besieged by ʿAbd al-Raḥmān III; Toledo withstood a two-year siege before paying homage to the emir; and Mérida, having remained independent since the reign of the emir Muḥammad I, was forced to recognize the sovereignty of the central power once more. ʿAbd al-Raḥmān III was also the one who finally ended the rebellion of the Ḥafṣūnids.

[^p28-13]: The *ṣaqāliba* were bought in the markets as children, so that they grew up according to Muslim customs. It was not unusual for them to earn their freedom on coming of age, thanks to their services.

<!-- p. 28 -->

In 929, to make himself wholly independent of Baghdad and partly quell the political threat of the Fatimids, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān proclaimed himself *jalīfa rasul-Allah* ("caliph") and *amīr al-mu´minīn* ("prince of the believers"), and took the epithet "defender of the religion of God" (*al-Nāṣir li-dīn Allāh*). After nineteen years as emir, he claimed his right of blood as a descendant of the Umayyad caliphs of Damascus to confirm his independence from any higher Muslim authority. From then on, the public Friday prayer no longer asked blessings for the Abbasid caliph of Baghdad but for ʿAbd al-Raḥmān III.

After pacifying his realm, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān III took Melilla and Ceuta. With them he could dominate the strait and exercise indirect control over much of the Maghreb. After all the measures ʿAbd al-Raḥmān III had taken to secure his power, al-Andalus knew the greatest unity in its entire history.

The foreign policy of the Umayyads and of ʿAbd al-Raḥmān III changed after the terrible defeat suffered at the battle of Alhándega (see the sidebar on page 32). The Umayyad military machine proved neither functional nor flexible, so the caliphate abandoned the summer raids in which the emirs had always led their armies in person: although victory could add to their prestige, defeat carried greater physical and political danger.

In his last years ʿAbd al-Raḥmān III did not exert himself as a warrior (nor would his son, Al-Ḥakam II), and he built his policy on three main pillars. First, he strengthened the Andalusi frontiers by fortifying and repairing strategic sites. Lacking garrisons for all the frontier fortresses, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān granted the frontier lineages control over the lands they held, making it hereditary (the heads of these families became kings in the taifa period). With this second pillar, al-Andalus could launch numerous localized attacks along the frontier. Finally, the third pillar consisted of putting truce before conflict, encouraging trade with distant cities (Franks, Catalans, Byzantines, etc.), and exerting influence over the Christian kingdoms, whose political and economic power was far inferior to the caliphate's. For example, after the death of Ramiro II of Leon, the internal disputes that followed weakened the Astur-Leonese kingdom, so ʿAbd al-Raḥmān III got the king of Leon, the queen of Navarre and the counts of Castile and Barcelona to recognize his hegemony and pay him annual tribute on pain of raids into their lands. Thus, during those years, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān came to act as mediator and arbiter in the investiture of some Christian monarchs.

<!-- p. 29 -->

<!-- p. 30 -->

This diplomacy, unprecedented in al-Andalus (it would reach its height under Al-Ḥakam II), allowed the Franks to trade in Andalusi ports without fear of attack by Mediterranean pirates, the Christian counts and kings to visit Madīnat al-Zahrāʾ regularly, and economic and cultural exchanges with the city of Constantinople: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān III exchanged many embassies with the Byzantine emperor, and in one of them he received a Greek copy, written in gold and silver letters, of Dioscorides' medical work *De Materia Medica*, wonderfully bound and illustrated with drawings of medicinal plants. The emperor sent a monk named Nicholas to the court of Cordoba so that he and the caliph's counselor and physician, the Jew Ḥasdāy ibn Šaprūṭ, could translate it into Arabic. Such a book was of incalculable value, for like any other man the caliph suffered all manner of illnesses.

When ʿAbd al-Raḥmān III's firstborn died, Al-Ḥakam II, next in the line of succession, was named heir. The son of a Christian slave, he inherited a pacified empire with a strong diplomatic component, which allowed him to devote himself to the arts and letters. Al-Ḥakam was a man of great learning who followed his father's policy and took Umayyad splendor a step further. His impressive library of knowledge (*jizanatu-hu l-ʿilmiya*) held more than 400,000 volumes (many annotated by his own hand), recorded in a catalogue of forty-four volumes of more than twenty folios each. The caliph's magnificent library held the medical treatises of Hippocrates and Galen and the mathematical works of Ptolemy and Euclid, nor did it lack the authorities on philosophy: Aristotle, Plato, Plotinus and Empedocles. To assemble such a library, Al-Ḥakam II relied on a network of merchants spread throughout the known world to seek out and buy every kind of learned work.

At a time when Arabic, not Latin, was the language of progress, Cordoba, the cultural capital of Mythic Europe, had dozens of workshops copying and translating documents from the Arab world (Persia, Syria and Egypt) and the Byzantine Empire. Indeed, during the reign of Al-Ḥakam II there was a quarter of Cordoba called *al-raqqaqīn* ("the parchment makers") for leatherworkers and bookmakers. The city produced several thousand books a year, and the alcázares of the Cordoban Umayyads employed the finest binders, illuminators, decorators and copyists in al-Andalus, supervised by grammarians and scholars from Sicily and Baghdad. Among the scribes and calligraphers who worked for Al-Ḥakam were the Cordoban man of letters and lexicographer Muḥammad ibn al-Husayn al-Fihri and the copyist from Jaén Muḥammad ibn Muʿammar; both copied and corrected the first Arabic dictionary, the *Kitab al-ʿayn*. Women also worked in Al-Ḥakam's scriptoria (such as Lubnà al-Katiba and Fāṭīma bint al-Sabullari), since copying Qurʾans and books was considered a pious trade well suited to them. And if the emir's library was of such dimensions, no minister could afford to own fewer than a hundred volumes.

Hermetic covenants could use their copyists or craftsmen to copy or make the materials needed for this great book trade. To do so, consider the sources of income described in *Covenants* under "Manufacturing" and "Service" (pages 84 and 86, respectively); in this case, controlling the copying work of Cordoba could count as a legendary source of income.

Al-Ḥakam II had the Great Mosque of Cordoba enlarged and its walls faced with carved marble and with mosaics sent from Constantinople by the emperor Nikephoros II Phokas. He expanded free medical care for the poor and the care of lepers in the suburbs, and the confinement and protection of the insane, and he sought to make education universal, founding numerous public schools and acting as protector and patron of the intellectuals of his time.

Al-Ḥakam II's rule was not free of struggle and conflict, however. In 966 the Norsemen attacked the Andalusi coasts, and Al-Ḥakam II had to send his fleet to defeat them. In 972, to check the threat of the Fatimid Caliphate[^p30-14] of North Africa and the Idrisid uprising led by the chieftain Ḥasan ibn Qannūn, Al-Ḥakam mobilized between 5,000 and 10,000 troops to subdue the Berber chieftains who rejected his authority and bowed to the Fatimid caliphs of northwest Africa. This campaign had grave consequences that would ultimately lead to the *fitna*.[^p30-15] First, the war dragged on until 974 and carried great costs, both material and human. In the course of the war the caliphal workshops produced eight thousand swords and spears, ten thousand round shields (*turs*), and a similar quantity of leather adargas, mail hauberks and bows (made from deer antler); all this, together with the troops' pay, drained great reserves from the public treasury. Added to this was the cost of Al-Ḥakam's diplomacy, which induced many of these chieftains to come to Cordoba, laden with goods and life pensions, to reside in the city indefinitely and so keep them from leading any further rebellion against the Umayyads. Second, when the general of Marrākeš, Gālib, managed to defeat the Idrisid chieftain Ḥasan ibn Qannūn, the war came to an end and the defeated chieftains were moved and housed in Cordoba. With them came their retinues, which were incorporated into the Umayyad army and were deeply unpopular with the populace. The Berbers became indispensable to the Umayyad administration and, after Al-Ḥakam's death, Al-Manṣūr made them his main military instrument, getting rid of the Syrian *aŷnād* who had served in the army since the days of ʿAbd al-Raḥmān I.

[^p30-14]: The Umayyads used their court poets to spread propaganda for their rule and to vilify the Fatimids.

[^p30-15]: On the other hand, by recovering a significant part of North Africa from the Fatimids, the Umayyads gained control of the cities that opened the way for the caravans of *bilad al-Sūdān*, so Cordoba received a great quantity of gold (see the sidebar on page 26).

<!-- p. 31 -->

In 975, a year after the war in North Africa ended, Al-Ḥakam II had to face a rebellion by Leon, Castile and Navarre, which had besieged the castle of Gormaz on the upper Duero: the siege was broken in the summer of that same year and the Christian forces were scattered.

Al-Ḥakam II did not have his first son until after the age of forty-five, by the Basque slave Ṣubḥ. The baby, named ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, died young, however. In 965 Ṣubḥ bore him another male heir, whom they named Hišām.

In the last years of his life, Al-Ḥakam II sought to have Hišām accepted as heir, though at his tender age he had no right to inherit under Islamic law. So before he died he carried out various maneuvers to smooth the way for the community to accept the boy as his successor. On his death, however, all those who thought it madness to be ruled by an eleven-year-old turned their eyes to Al-Mugīra, one of Al-Ḥakam's brothers. Although Al-Mugīra had never tried to seize power, Hišām's supporters saw him as a threat to be eliminated, since the opposition could use him as a candidate against their interests. So one of the late Al-Ḥakam's favorites, a vizier of the court, sent a squad of soldiers to Al-Mugīra's house with orders to kill him. At its head was Muḥammad ibn Abī ʿAmir (better known as Al-Manṣūr), steward of the properties of Ṣubḥ, the late caliph's wife, with whom, according to wagging tongues, he was having a love affair. Despite Al-Mugīra's promises to support Hišām, the soldiers strangled him, and his death (which marked the beginning of the end of the caliphate) was presented at court as a suicide.

Then the court's *ḥaŷib*, Al-Muṣḥafī, with the support of Al-Manṣūr, had Hišām II proclaimed caliph at just eleven years old. After this maneuver Al-Manṣūr, who had been gaining more and more power during the years of Al-Ḥakam II's rule, managed to oust Al-Muṣḥafī with the support of the general Galīb (not for nothing had he married the general's daughter) and won the title of *ḥaŷib* for himself. To entrench himself in office, Al-Manṣūr sought the support of the fuqahāʾ: to that end he copied the Qurʾan with his own hands, persecuted the philosophers of al-Andalus, and burned the works in Al-Ḥakam II's library that the fuqahāʾ considered "heretical."

Once established in power, Al-Manṣūr let the young caliph Hišām II have every kind of sensual pleasure at hand and nullified him completely, without his mother, Ṣubḥ, being able to do anything to prevent it.

Al-Manṣūr had the Great Mosque enlarged and a new city built east of Cordoba to serve as the seat of government and office of administration and finance. The new palace city, Madīnat al-Zaḥirāʾ, was raised in only two years; new markets were established there and state receptions held. Surrounded by walls, it saw the court's secretaries and ministers vie for the *ḥaŷib*'s favor to obtain land and plots within its precincts. The old city of Madīnat al-Zahrāʾ, the caliph's residence, ceased to be the destination of ambassadors from other realms, which contributed to Hišām's isolation. To justify his complete absence from affairs of state, the ministers announced that the caliph had devoted himself to piety and had handed full power over the realm to the *ḥaŷib* Al-Manṣūr.

<!-- p. 32 -->

In 980, Al-Manṣūr ordered Hišām's palace precinct closed to all visitors, and its gates and passageways were sealed. Hišām thus never came to rule, living as a captive in his dazzling prison while Al-Manṣūr governed the realm in his name. To show his influence, Al-Manṣūr had his own name pronounced after Hišām's in the Friday midday prayer.

Al-Manṣūr became the absolute dictator of the empire. He disbanded the Syrian *aŷnād* and made the Berbers his personal troops, hiring them in vast numbers. He broke with the diplomatic policy of ʿAbd al-Raḥmān III and Al-Ḥakam II and once again took command of the summer campaigns against the Christian kingdoms, relying on his Berber armies.

### The Fitna

*The "fitna" came dressed in darkness like the night, which favors crimes, and our dreams drifted away to turn into hallucinations... The one who was the tail put himself at the head, and the most exalted became a servant...*

*as if we were led blind by other blind men in the darkness.*[^p32-16]

[^p32-16]: Poem by Ibn Shuhayd taken from *The Treatise of Familiar Spirits and Demons* (Spanish translation by Salvador Barberá).

In the first years of the *fitna*, numerous caliphs were proclaimed in various corners of the territory of al-Andalus:

| Caliphs | Years |
| --- | --- |
| Proclamation of six Umayyads | 1009–1031 |
| Proclamation of three Hammudids | 1016–1027 |

On Al-Manṣūr's death, his powers passed to his firstborn son and, when he died after a brief rule of seven years, they fell on the shoulders of his second-eldest son, whom the people called Sanŷul (a diminutive of the name of his maternal grandfather, Sancho Garcés II Abarca, king of Navarre).

Sanŷul drank wine in public and lived a life given over to sin. His folly led him to disregard his father's counsel and, with the leave of Hišām II (who had no offspring), he had himself publicly proclaimed as the caliph's heir. The Banū Omeya would not tolerate this. Muḥammad al-Mahdī rose up with his army and, followed by the people, hid Hišām away, then killed and crucified Sanŷul. In his victory he proclaimed himself caliph for a short time. When the provincial governors learned of this, each rebelled against the central power, bringing about the end of the caliphate and a long period of civil war known as the *fitna*. The huge Berber mercenary armies recruited by Al-Manṣūr, left without pay and never integrated into a society that loathed them, became a force that laid waste to al-Andalus and plunged the empire into utter chaos. In 1013 the Berbers, who had once attacked the Christian kingdoms, besieged and sacked the city of Cordoba. Before long, the palace and administrative cities of Madīnat al-Zahrāʾ and Madīnat al-Zaḥirāʾ were repeatedly burned and looted by the mob, and were finally stripped bare and abandoned. During the revolts, almost all the Umayyads departed for the east of al-Andalus.

> #### The Summer Campaigns of Al-Manṣūr
>
> *One day I dined with Almanzor […] at al-Zaḥirā, a place of blossoming beauty, for it holds flowerbeds and pools. And when the day anointed itself with the saffron of evening and the black raven of darkness spread its wings, the night let fall its shadows, Arcturus brandished his lance, the Vulture made ready to fly and the boat of the moon sailed across the sky, we lit the lamps of wine, wrapped ourselves in the cloaks of contentment, and the clouds spread over us a canopy covered with dew.*[^p32-X]
>
> The former ulema and now *ḥaŷib*, Muḥammad ibn Abī ʿAmir, bore the byname Al-Manṣūr (Arabic for "the victorious"), and was known to the Christians as Almanzor. Al-Manṣūr unleashed his fury on the northern kingdoms with yearly summer campaigns that ended in the destruction and plunder of important Christian cities, such as Leon (of which he left only a single tower standing as the sole witness of its former glory), Santiago (where he razed everything in his path except the apostle's tomb, forcing Christian captives to carry the cathedral's heavy bells on their shoulders so they could be used as lamps in the Great Mosque of Cordoba) and, in 985, Barcelona, with which Al-Ḥakam II had always enjoyed good relations: Al-Manṣūr launched a brutal attack to ruin the port city's economy, and in the sack he burned documents and attacked the Jewish community.
>
> Al-Manṣūr also enlarged the already disproportionate mercenary army created by ʿAbd al-Raḥmān I on his arrival in the Peninsula. Made up of African Berbers, Catalan Christians and Slavs, the army grew very large in many cities. With it he was victorious in almost every campaign he launched against the Christian kingdoms; in fact, he was defeated only on his last incursion (these campaigns were sung by his court poet, the Berber from al-Gharb Ibn Darraŷ al-Qasṭallī). He also used it to fight off attempts to restore the caliph Hišām II and to put an end to the general Galīb, who had allied with the Christian kings and plotted against his rule.
>
> The *ḥaŷib* died on the Night of Destiny (*laylat al-qadr*)[^p32-XI] and was buried in the alcázar of Medinaceli together with the dust that had gathered on his cloak during the campaigns he had led against the Christian kingdoms.
>
> [^p32-X]: Poem by Abū l-Mugīra ibn Ḥazm (Spanish translation by Teresa Garulo).
>
> [^p32-XI]: The Night of Destiny is the 27th night of the month of Ramadan, the same night on which the revelation of the Qurʾan began (that is, when the Qurʾan came down to earth). It is a notable night of great celebration.

<!-- p. 33 -->

The caliph Hišām II was freed by the great-grandson of ʿAbd al-Raḥmān III, the Hammudid Sulaymān al-Mustaʿīn, after the latter fought the armies of Al-Mahdī. However, instead of returning him to the throne, Sulaymān proclaimed himself caliph. Amid the chaos two opposing parties arose: the Hammudids of Malaga and Algeciras, and the supporters of Hišām, led by the ʿAbbādids of Seville. By then Hišām had been murdered, so to keep their hold on power the Sevillians used a double, a deception the poet Ibn Hazm criticized in his writings.

> #### The Battle of Alhándega
>
> Following his forebears' custom of the usual summer campaigns, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān III called for *ŷihād* against the northern kingdoms. He set out from Cordoba for Toledo at the head of his army, and there nearly 100,000 men-at-arms gathered once the armies of the lords of the Upper March joined him. On hearing of such a host, the king of Leon, Ramiro II, summoned the armies of the counts of Castile and of the king of Pamplona, along with the Galician and Asturian troops, to march out and meet it.
>
> Two days before the battle, when both armies stood face to face, there was a total eclipse of the sun; so deep was the darkness that the caliph, on the last day of Ramadan, broke his fast at the wrong moment, an event the sorcerers of his court judged an evil omen.
>
> The two armies met on the plain of the Pisuerga, northeast of Simancas. For several days the outnumbered Christians fought the Muslims until, unable to hold them back, they had to fall back toward the fortress that gave the battle its name. Then a warrior appeared, dressed in a black tunic and clad in shining armor, dealing death as he passed through the Muslim ranks. With a sword in his right hand and a banner in his left, he broke the siege of the fortress and scattered the forces of ʿAbd al-Raḥmān III across the bloodied battlefield. The warrior was none other than Saint Millán, sent to grant victory to the armies of Ramiro II (from that day on, Saint Millán was named patron saint of Castile).
>
> In their flight the Muslims were defeated, and the caliph himself was wounded. Among the treasures the Christians captured were the caliph's favorite coat of golden mail and a valuable Qurʾan. As punishment, when ʿAbd al-Raḥmān III returned to Cordoba, he had 300 officers of his army crucified.

<!-- p. 34 -->

During the *fitna* more than ten men proclaimed themselves caliph, the city of Cordoba was besieged and sacked many times (to cope with the famine, what remained of Al-Ḥakam II's library was publicly auctioned off) and, finally, it became the capital of a taifa kingdom, witness to the last breath of the dynasty founded almost 300 years earlier by the Falcon of Qurayš, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān I.

### The Christian Kingdoms during the Caliphate

During the caliphate of al-Andalus and the *fitna* (912–1031), the following Christian kingdoms existed:

| Kingdoms | Years |
| --- | --- |
| The kingdom of Asturias | 912–924 |
| The kingdom of Pamplona | 912–1031 |
| The kingdom of Leon | 912–1031 |
| The kingdom of Galicia | 912–1031 |
| The kingdom of Viguera | 970–1005 |

The kingdoms of Leon and Asturias ended up governed by a single sovereign, Ramiro II of Leon (who managed to make his monarchy hereditary), who also ruled the kingdom of Galicia intermittently, always keeping his capital at Leon. In this period the short-lived county of Monzón appeared (created by Ramiro II) to limit the power of the counties of Saldaña and Castile (the latter eventually absorbed it), and the county of Aragon passed into the hands of the kingdom of Pamplona, its title being handed down to the monarch's sons. The small kingdom of Viguera (La Rioja) was also created; after being ruled by three monarchs, it was annexed back into the crown of Pamplona. For its part, the House of Barcelona managed, for the first time in its history, to have a count free of ties to the Carolingian and Capetian dynasties of France, to whom it had always paid homage.

> #### The Fuero of Castrojeriz
>
> Faced with the Muslim threat on his borders, the count of Castile, García Fernández, granted rights, privileges and obligations (set down in a fuero)[^p33-XII] to the town of Castrojeriz, near Burgos, expressed in the following terms:
>
> - Every peasant who owns a horse (and has the money to keep it) is to be held in the same regard as an *infanzón*[^p33-XIII] (though without a noble title) and is therefore exempt from paying council and royal taxes.
> - Peasants with these privileges may exercise their authority over any frontier land they are the first to break with the plow.
> - In return for this dispensation, the members of the town council are obliged to give military support to the count of Castile whenever he requires it.
>
> The granting of these fueros in all the count's towns created an armed force of considerable strategic value. These so-called commoner knights (known as "pardos" in some places) were decisive in many battles fought against the Muslims (such as Las Navas de Tolosa).
>
> The proliferation of commoner knights in the mid-twelfth century broke the neighborly "equality" of the fueros, as they came to control the town councils in the Castilian-Leonese Extremadura. Moreover, at the end of the twelfth century this social status became harder to attain (a minimum income was required, among other things), closing the group to potential new knights.
>
> In the Iberia of 1220, the *pardo* knights dominate the town councils, where they hold reserved seats. In payment for their rights they must take part in the war against the Muslims (the so-called *fonsado*) once a year and permanently defend the city they live in, which they may leave only between October and May (a season of almost obligatory truce), and only if they leave a substitute. Furthermore, the knights' sons inherit their fathers' status and privileges and, once they come of age, must take part in the war.
>
> [^p33-XII]: Fueros set down the laws of coexistence of the town councils (see "The Christians," page 16).
>
> [^p33-XIII]: *Infanzones* are knights of the lesser nobility.

Nobles and kings expanded their domains by taking advantage of the weakness or absence of neighboring lords. To do so, they forged alliances not only with Christians but also with the Muslims of al-Andalus. Power struggles set members of noble families against one another, and murders, mutilations and preventive imprisonments were common (it is said that Ramiro II ordered the eyes of his predecessor, Alfonso IV the Monk, who had abdicated, to be put out).

The Christian monarchs also fought the Muslim armies: they pushed the frontier south from the county of Portugal, gained ground in Navarre and Saragossa, and forced the Berber governors of the *kuwar* of Badajoz and Mérida to pay them tribute.

Alliances among the Christian monarchs helped win the Battle of Alhándega (see the sidebar on the previous page) and, although they went so far as to form a coalition against Al-Manṣūr, the kingdoms did not offer unified resistance to the Muslim attacks until the arrival, in 1004, of Sancho III the Great, king of Pamplona, count of Aragon and a renowned warrior. Sancho created a league of Christian princes joined by the king of Leon, the count of Castile and the Cluniac order (charged with protecting pilgrims on the Way of Saint James). At the end of the caliphate, after the murder of the count of Castile, the Castilian nobles handed the county over to Sancho III, who ended his reign ruling the counties of Aragon, Castile, Álava, Sobrarbe and Ribagorza.

The Christian monarchs also had to face the "Northmen" once again; Viking attacks on the Cantabrian coasts continued, sometimes with terrible battles inland which, as in the case of Portugal, cost the lives of two of its counts, Menendo Gonçalves and Alvito Nunes (see page 286).

The Christian kingdoms began to develop their legal systems during the period of the Umayyad Caliphate. The *presura* (the old practice of peasants occupying frontier lands, whose owners had to defend themselves against Muslim attacks) gave way to settlement charters (*cartas pueblas*) or fueros that shaped the new Hispano-Christian society, based on grouping the territory into geographical districts. In addition, at the beginning of the eleventh century, the royal court of Alfonso V of Leon for the first time approved a set of laws to be obeyed both in the city of Leon and throughout the kingdom. In the Catalan counties, Abbot Oliba proclaimed the *Pau i Treva de Déu* at the synod of Toluges in response to the abuses committed by feudal nobles against the Church and the peasantry.

> #### Pau i Treva de Déu
>
> In the eleventh century, in the Catalan counties, the nobles rebelled against the counts in order to rule the land of the free farmers and bring them into vassalage. Under their dominion, the villeins lived exposed to the violence of their lords, who extorted, punished and threatened them. Although they had the right of *sagrera* (a consecrated area with a radius of 30 meters around churches, where no act of violence could be committed on pain of excommunication), the farmers needed an authority able to forbid the violence and mistreatment they suffered anywhere in the territory.
>
> In answer to this need, Abbot Oliba, acting on behalf of the bishop and under the protection of the *sagrera,* proclaimed the *Pau i Treva de Déu* (Catalan for "Peace and Truce of God"), obliging the inhabitants of the county of Roussillon and the diocese of Elna not to engage in fights or brawls between Saturday and Monday (for churchmen the protection extended to every day of the week), on pain of excommunication.
>
> In 1030, Abbot Oliba managed to extend the period of peace from Thursday to Monday (and to extend the penalty of excommunication to counterfeiters and to those who assaulted merchants) and, although not all the Catalan counties embraced it at first, it reached the lands of Provence and won over the counts there. The count of Barcelona himself convened peace councils in his domains and eventually incorporated them into the *Usatges* of Barcelona (the civil law of the county of Barcelona). Thus the counts of Catalonia will use the *Pau i Treva de Déu* to keep their domains at peace until the end of the thirteenth century.

<!-- p. 35 -->

## The Taifa Kingdoms

*When the ʿāmirí dynasty came to an end and the people were left without an imām, every qaid rose up with his city or entrenched himself in his castle, after weighing his chances, raising an army and laying in stores of provisions. These qaids soon began to vie with one another for riches, and each began to covet the other's goods.*[^p35-17]

[^p35-17]: Excerpt from *The Eleventh Century in the First Person* by ʿAbd Allāh (Spanish translation by E. García Gómez). The qaids are the generals.

The factions or *ṭawāʿif* (singular *tāʿifa*) referred to the three ethnic groups present in al-Andalus after the fall of the Caliphate of Cordoba: Berbers, Slavs and Andalusis.

- **Berbers**: such as the Hammudid dynasties of Cordoba, Malaga and Algeciras, the Afṭasids of Badajoz and the Zirids of Granada.
- **Slavs**: such as the governors of Almería, Denia and the Balearic Islands (none of them founded dynasties).
- **Andalusis**: such as the ʿAbbādids of Seville, the Banū ḏī-l-Nūn of Toledo or the Hūdids of Saragossa.

The former governors of the *kuwar* proclaimed themselves emirs, and as a result dozens of independent kingdoms sprang up throughout the caliphate. The taifa kings set up their own administrative and political structures, which replicated the Umayyad state on a smaller scale and were forced to pay *parias* to the Christian kingdoms to preserve their independence.

This was a period of great cultural splendor. The courts of al-Andalus competed in the arts and sciences and acted as patrons of learning. Almost all the sovereigns were poets or notable men of letters: the sultans[^p35-18] of the taifas no longer wished to imitate the East, but rather to establish an ideal society inspired by the ʿAbbāsid Baghdad of the ninth century.

[^p35-18]: Until the eleventh century, *sulṭān* was used as a symbol of the central power embodied in the caliph. From the eleventh century onward, it was used as a title to distinguish the ruler's temporal power from the purely religious authority that the caliphs, ever more nominally, still held in the Near East.

### Al-Andalus after the Fitna

*Qurtuba the beautiful, is there hope of having you?*

*A heart athirst from separation,*

*can it ever be soothed? Will your famous nights return, when beauty showed itself in you*

*and your delights reached our ears?*[^p35-19]

[^p35-19]: Eleventh-century poem by Ibn Zaydūn (Spanish translation by José Miguel Puerta Vilches).

Of the more than twenty taifas that arose after the breakup of the caliphate, the most powerful were those of Seville, Saragossa, Granada, Badajoz, Toledo and Denia (which was eventually absorbed by Saragossa in 1076).

| Taifas | Years |
| --- | --- |
| The taifa of Seville | 1023–1091 |
| The taifa of Saragossa | 1018–1110 |
| The taifa of Granada | 1013–1090 |
| The taifa of Badajoz | 1013–1093 |
| The taifa of Toledo | 1023–1085 |
| The taifa of Denia | 1010–1076 |

#### The Taifa of Seville

The qadi of Seville, Abū al-Qasim Muḥammad ibn ʿAbbād, broke away from Cordoba during the *fitna* and founded the dynasty of the Banū ʿAbbād, which ruled the taifa of Seville until the Almoravids arrived in the Peninsula. Seville claimed to be the heir of the Umayyads: the ʿAbbādids kept up the relations the Umayyads had had with the Maghreb and, with them, access to the gold of *bilad al-Sūdān*.

After the death of the dynasty's founder, the throne passed to his son, Al-Muʿtaḍid, who conquered and annexed the small taifas of Ronda, Jerez and Arcos, and promoted an anti-Berber movement in al-Andalus with the aim of conquering the taifas of Badajoz and Granada (to prevent this, those taifas joined with Almería and Malaga in a Berber coalition). In the end, Seville conquered all the land south of Badajoz, the taifa of Cordoba, Murcia, Cartagena and Lorca.

At his court, Al-Muʿtaḍid appointed the famous poet Ibn Zaydūn as vizier and encouraged the arrival of great poets and panegyrists who extolled his rule and improved the image his own people and the other taifa kingdoms had of him. So it was that the poet and adventurer Ibn ʿAmmār came to Seville, and he soon struck up a friendship with the sultan's son and heir to the throne, Al-Muʿtamid.

The poet king Al-Muʿtamid made Seville a true magnet for the poets of the Islamic West, the cradle of countless men of letters who carried poetry to its peak. It is said of him that, after the conquest of Cordoba, he went to wander the ruins of the palace city of Madīnat al-Zahrāʾ to admire its ancient, decaying splendor, an early instance of romantic evocation that also inspired many verses from the poets of his time.

<!-- p. 36 -->

Seville always had a tense relationship with Alfonso VI of Leon, to whom it paid tribute intermittently throughout his reign. Under the fiscal and military pressure exerted by the Christian emperor, Al-Muʿtamid was the first of the taifa kings to write to the Almoravids asking for help. Although he knew that once in Iberia they might take his kingdom from him, he always preferred that possibility to the growing certainty that the Christian monarch would conquer his lands. Unfortunately, just as he had feared, the third time the Almoravids entered Iberia they resolved to conquer the taifa kingdoms and their riches.

Before conquering Seville, the Almoravids decided to take Cordoba, governed by Al-Muʿtamid's son, Al-Maʿmūn. Faced with Almoravid military superiority, Al-Maʿmūn chose to bring his wife, Zaida, to safety, sending her outside the walls with an escort. When the Almoravids entered the city's alcazaba they arrested Al-Maʿmūn and executed him; once he was dead, the soldiers paraded his head on a pike through the streets of Cordoba. In her flight, Zaida took refuge at the court of Alfonso VI, where she converted to Christianity and was baptized with the name Isabel. There Alfonso made her his concubine and fathered on her the *infante* Sancho Alfónsez.

After the fall of Cordoba, Seville endured a long siege and was conquered in 1091, having been defended by both its militias and its inhabitants (it was the only taifa to stand up to the Almoravid invaders). Al-Muʿtamid was exiled to Agmāt, in North Africa, where he lived on for four more years as a captive and where he wrote many poems.

*I was the ally of the dew, lord of tolerance, beloved of souls. My right hand was generous in giving*

*and bloody in combat. My left hand held the reins*

*that guided men into battle.*

*Today I am hostage to these chains; to poverty, to dishonor. A bird with broken wings.*[^p36-20]

[^p36-20]: Verses by Al-Muʿtamid (Spanish translation by Emilio González Ferrín, 2016).

> #### Ibn ʿAmmār
>
> *[…] With gold embroidery I stitched my qasida with your name, and in your praise I crumble it like balls of musk. None could compete with me, for your fame is sandalwood, and my thought serves it as a burning brazier […]*[^p36-XIV]
>
> The adventurer and poet Ibn ʿAmmār quickly hit it off with Al-Muʿtamid, for both were lovers of pleasure and poetry. However, the sultan of Seville never considered him a good influence on his son and, to keep them apart, sent him to Silves. Even so, distance could not erase their affection: when Al-Muʿtamid ascended the throne of Seville he made his friend governor of Silves and, after the death of the sage Ibn Zaydūn, vizier.
>
> The story goes that, after an incident with the Christian emperor's envoy at the court of Seville, Al-Muʿtamid refused to pay the agreed *parias*, so Alfonso VI of Leon[^p36-XV] led his army toward the city. When the Christians were at the gates and the inhabitants had given up all hope, the vizier Ibn ʿAmmār rode out to meet the emperor and negotiate with him, equipped only with his proverbial chess set (made with pieces of sandalwood, ebony and aloe wood inlaid with gold). When he reached the camp, Alfonso VI received him with honors and invited him into his tent. Seeing the set he carried, the emperor asked him to show it, for he was a great player and truly coveted it. Ibn ʿAmmār then proposed a game on the following condition: "If you win, the set shall be yours; but if you lose, you must hear a single request." Though he knew it was unwise, the emperor accepted... and lost. As a result, he had to withdraw his armies from the borders of the kingdom of Seville.
>
> For all his brilliance, Ibn ʿAmmār was a greedy man, a flaw that worsened with time. To gain more influence and wealth he urged the sultan to make war on Granada with the help of Alfonso VI, with whom he had secretly agreed to betray his friend Al-Muʿtamid. When that plan failed he seized the government of Murcia, wresting it from Seville, but he was eventually deposed and exiled from there. With nowhere to go, he sought the protection of other Muslim princes and of Alfonso, who refused his services. His intrigues were so many that his old friend Al-Muʿtamid ended up executing him with his own hands.
>
> [^p36-XIV]: Poem by Ibn ʿAmmār dedicated to Al-Muʿtaḍid; Spanish translation by E. García Gómez (1976), taken from *Arabic Literature of al-Andalus in the Eleventh Century*.
>
> [^p36-XV]: Alfonso VI's adviser on Muslim affairs was Sisnando Davídiz.

#### The Taifa of Saragossa

When the *fitna* broke out in Cordoba, the taifa of Saragossa was ruled by the Hispano-Arab dynasty of the Tujibids, who had come to Iberia in the eighth century. Like the other governors of the *kuwar* of al-Andalus, the governor Al-Munḍir ibn Yahya al-Tuŷībī proclaimed himself *ḥaŷib* of Saragossa and declared his independence from the other powers of al-Andalus.

Saragossa was ruled by the Tujibids until the corruption of their line led to the death of their last monarch at the hands of one of his cousins. The then sultan of the taifa of Lérida, Sulaymān ibn Hūd al-Mustaʿīn, won the affection of the people of Saragossa and seized the opportunity to conquer the city and proclaim himself sultan, placing his sons at the head of the territories of Huesca, Tudela and Lérida.

On the death of Al-Mustaʿīn, Saragossa was inherited by his son, Al-Muqtadir, who took the chance to seize control of the kingdom's other districts, governed by his four brothers.

<!-- p. 37 -->

Al-Muqtadir brought the taifa of Saragossa to its greatest splendor. He had the beautiful *Qasr al-Jaʿfariya* (Arabic for "Palace of the Aljafería") built and used it as the seat of his court and a meeting place for an intellectual elite of al-Andalus in search of an atmosphere of tolerance and patronage. Poets, musicians, philosophers and mystics came together in Saragossa; *al-Jaʿfariya* saw the birth of the Islamic school of philosophy that embraced the rational thought of Aristotle, a cultural movement in which great scholars such as Avicenna, Avempace and Averroes took part.

During Al-Muqtadir's rule, Saragossa extended its borders by conquering the taifa of Tortosa, through which it reached the sea and thus the commercial gateways of the Mediterranean. He also made the sultan of Valencia his vassal and, without even fighting, forced the surrender of the splendid taifa of Denia and annexed it to his kingdom. However, the long northern frontier of the kingdom left it vulnerable to constant attacks from the county of Barcelona, the kingdom of Aragon and the kingdom of Castile.

As his father had done, Al-Muqtadir divided his kingdom between his two sons at his death. He left Saragossa and its districts to Al-Muʾtamin, and Lérida, Tortosa and Denia to Al-Munḍir, which sparked a civil war between them. To pursue their interests, both made use of Christian troops: Al-Muʾtamin allied himself with the Cid and Al-Munḍir with the king of Aragon, Sancho Ramírez.

Al-Muʾtamin was a wise king, a protector of the arts and sciences rather than of poetry (see Appendix I). His rule lasted only three years, for he died in 1085, the year Toledo was conquered. He was succeeded by his son, Al-Mustaʿīn II, called "the Lesser" to distinguish him from his great-grandfather, the first Hūdid of Saragossa.

Al-Mustaʿīn II continued the policy of his father, a champion of culture and art in Iberia, and when the Almoravids arrived he managed to stay on good terms with them, becoming the only taifa sultan to keep his independence. As a result, he had to do without the services of the Cid, who returned to serving Alfonso VI. The sultan lived to see the end of the cultural splendor of the white city and, shortly after his death, the city was absorbed by the Almoravids and conquered by the crusaders.

#### The Taifa of Granada

*[…] they beheld a lovely plain, full of streams and groves, which, like all the surrounding land, is watered by the river Genil* [Wādī Šanīlī]*, which comes down from the Sierra Nevada* [Ŷabal Šulair]*. They likewise beheld the hill on which the city of Granada now stands, and understood that it was the center of the whole region […]. The place delighted them, for they saw that it combined every advantage and realized that [...], if an enemy came to attack it, he would be unable to lay siege to it […].*[^p37-21]

[^p37-21]: Excerpt from *The Eleventh Century in the First Person* by ʿAbd Allāh (Spanish translation by Emilio García Gómez).

The Berber clan of the Zirids came to al-Andalus to serve in Al-Manṣūr's mercenary army. During the *fitna*, the clan's founder, Zāwī ben Zīrī, supported the Hammudid Sulaymān al-Mustaʿīn in his rise to the throne, and in return received the region of Elvira as a fief. As Elvira was hard to defend, they moved to a more suitable site, and so the city of Granada was born. When the armies of the taifas learned that the Zirids were fortifying the old Umayyad castle they marched to its borders, but they were defeated. After the victory, Ben Zīrī returned to North Africa, where he died of poison, and the young principality passed to his nephew, Ḥabūs ibn Māksan. Ḥabūs took the title of *ḥaŷib* and, to win the favor of Granada's large Jewish community, appointed the sage Ismāʿīl ibn al-Nagrela as vizier.

After the death of Ḥabūs ibn Māksan, his son Bādīs ibn Ḥabūs came to the throne. His first great victory was over the eunuch prince of the taifa of Almería, Zuhayr, who had decided to invade Granada on learning of Ibn Māksan's death. But the Zirids marched out to meet him, defeated his army and conquered Almería, whose court had gathered all the eunuchs of al-Andalus during the *fitna*.

Bādīs cast off the vassalage he owed to the Hammudid prince of Malaga and in 1057 conquered that taifa and annexed it to his kingdom, banishing all the Hammudid princes to Africa. He also had to face the anti-Berber movement of the prince of Seville, to which he tried to respond by exterminating the Arabs who lived in his kingdom (something the Jewish vizier Ismāʿīl ibn al-Nagrela prevented) and by invading the taifa of Seville. However, his armies were defeated and, taking advantage of his failure, the Arabs of Malaga rebelled and asked the prince of Seville for help. Although the Sevillian armies made their way to Malaga without difficulty, Bādīs managed to drive them out and recover the city, punishing the rebels bloodily. With the help of the taifa of Toledo, the prince made the sultan of Valencia his vassal.

On Bādīs's death the last Zirid prince of Granada, his grandson ʿAbd Allāh, came to the throne. He signed a peace treaty with Seville after the death of the vizier Ibn ʿAmmār (see the sidebar on the previous page). His reign witnessed the arrival of the Almoravids in the Peninsula. Alongside them he fought the forces of Alfonso VI of Leon at the battles of Sagrajas and Aledo, and when the Almoravids came to conquer al-Andalus, Granada was taken without resistance, ʿAbd Allāh was exiled to North Africa (where he spent his last years in comfort) and his treasures were seized: the chronicles speak of chambers full of gold, silver, jewelry, gems, precious fabrics and glass vessels. To keep the Almoravids from accusing him of treason, ʿAbd Allāh expelled all the Jews from the city before their arrival.

The Berber sovereigns of Granada were always scorned by the poets of al-Andalus, who held that they did not know how to value poetry as the other taifa courts did.

#### The Taifa of Badajoz

The vast kingdom of Badajoz (seat of the Berber Afṭasids) was devastated as a result of its sultan's refusal to pay *parias* to the kingdom of Leon. To fight this taifa, the Christian king sought the help of the sultan of Toledo, who in turn called on the sultan of Seville. The wars that followed from this decision plunged the kingdom of Badajoz and its inhabitants into poverty. Badajoz lost many of its southern territories to the ʿAbbādids of Seville and, at the height of Seville's anti-Berber movement, it bore the brunt. To its misfortune, the struggles with Seville and Toledo weakened it still further.

<!-- p. 38 -->

The princes of Badajoz were cultured men and lovers of poetry. As would happen with other taifa princes, Al-Muẓaffar ibn al-Afṭas took great interest in the image of his kingdom, and so he used poetry and panegyrist poets to publicize his rule favorably.

The last Afṭasid king, Al-Mutawakkil, briefly ruled the taifa of Toledo (which he abandoned, leaving it ripe for surrender) and, when the Almoravids reached the borders of his kingdom, he would not abandon the city or his subjects. With the first Almoravid conquests in Iberia, Al-Mutawakkil sought to keep his throne by siding both with the Muslim forces (against Alfonso VI of Leon) and with the Christian ones (against the Almoravids), so when the Almoravid emir intercepted one of the letters in which he professed loyalty to Alfonso, he stormed Badajoz. The Almoravids took the alcazaba in a surprise night attack and, once the stronghold was taken, Al-Mutawakkil was executed together with two of his sons (his wives and daughters were treated as spoils by the Almoravids).

When Al-Mutawakkil's third son, Al-Manṣūr (who was away from the city), learned what had happened, he joined the Christian armies to fight the Almoravids and avenge his father's death.

#### The Taifa of Toledo

The taifa of Toledo was the largest in al-Andalus and was ruled by the Berber Banū Ḏū-l-Nūn, who had come to the Peninsula with the arrival of Islam in the eighth century. Its most flourishing period was fostered by the taifa's second sultan, Al-Maʿmūn, who appointed as qadi the historian and scientist Ṣāʿid al-Andalusī. Acting as the court's patron, Ṣāʿid gathered under his protection a group of scholars that included the botanist Ibn Baṣṣāl, the scholar Ibn Wāfid (a Toledan physician and botanist and apprentice of Abulcasis) and the great astronomer Al-Zarqālī. Thanks to Ṣāʿid, Toledo could rival the scientific splendor of the Saragossa of the Banū Hūd.

As a tributary of Leon, Al-Maʿmūn sheltered Alfonso VI when the latter lost his throne to his brother Sancho II the Strong. However, after Sancho was murdered at the siege of Zamora, Alfonso was able to ascend the throne, and from then on he kept up his close friendship with Al-Maʿmūn, respecting the borders of the taifa of Toledo all his life. Thanks to this, Toledo was able to expand by conquering the taifas of Valencia and Cordoba. However, just as his court astrologers had foretold, Al-Maʿmūn died of poison after conquering Cordoba, for "all that reaches its apogee must begin its decline."

On Al-Maʿmūn's death, the throne passed to Ibn Ḏū-l-Nūn's grandson, whom Alfonso VI forced to pay *parias*, to buy a fortress near Toledo for 150,000 mithqals, and to hand over 500 almudes of grain for every night Alfonso spent in Toledo. Under such fiscal pressure the taifa fell into poverty and lost its hold over Valencia and Cordoba. As a result, the sultan was forced to tax his subjects excessively, and in such dire straits they split into two factions: those who favored remaining under the protection of Alfonso VI (including Ibn Ḏū-l-Nūn's grandson) and those who favored seeking help from other Muslims. Since many held the Christian monarch to blame, the second faction prevailed, and Toledo asked for help from the taifa of Badajoz, which ended up annexing Toledo and exiling Ibn Ḏū-l-Nūn's grandson. However, once in power, the sultan of Badajoz, Al-Mutawakkil, merely occupied the capital to enrich himself and then fled. When Ibn Ḏū-l-Nūn's grandson returned to rule the city, Toledo was ripe for surrender. Alfonso VI conquered it peacefully in 1085: his entry into the city marked the beginning of the end of the taifa kingdoms.

<!-- p. 39 -->

### The Almoravids and the Taifa Kingdoms

While al-Andalus was living through a time of great political instability during the *fitna*, the seed of a powerful empire was beginning to sprout in the Senegal basin. Made up of Berber warrior monks, the fundamentalist sect of the Almoravids conquered the desert until it reached Marrākeš, where it established its capital, and from there it heeded the pleas of the taifa kings of al-Andalus to free them from the growing pressure of the Christian kingdoms.

In 1078 Al-Muʿtamid, the poet king of the taifa of Seville, wrote to the Almoravid emir Yūsuf ibn Tāšufīn asking him to come to his aid and cross the strait, but the Almoravid showed no interest and turned down his request. In 1081 Al-Mutawakkil of Badajoz also wrote to him, with the same result. The same answer was given to Tamīn ibn Būluggīn of Malaga when, a year later, he asked for help against his brother, the last Zirid king of Granada, ʿAbd Allāh. But when Toledo too asked Yūsuf for help, the Almoravids began to weigh the situation in al-Andalus.

Given the need for unity in the face of the fragmentation of the taifas, and as the only effective way of resisting the expansionism of the Christian kingdoms, a sentiment favorable to the Almoravids began to grow in al-Andalus. Finally, after Alfonso VI of Leon conquered Toledo in 1085, the taifa kings of Seville, Badajoz and Granada sent their ambassadors to the Almoravid court at Marrākeš to request their help on the following terms:

- the Almoravid army could cross the strait to fight alongside the Andalusis against the Christian forces;
- during their stay in al-Andalus, the Almoravids undertook to respect the taifa kings and their kingdoms;
- the king of Seville placed the city of Algeciras at the Almoravids' disposal for the landing and quartering of their troops.

So, in 1086, the Almoravids crossed the strait and, after fortifying Algeciras, went on to the kingdom of Seville, where the Almoravid emir called for *ŷihād*. With the troops of Seville, Badajoz, Malaga, Granada and Almería, the Muslim army crushed the Christian troops of Alfonso VI at Sagrajas (Zallāqa to the Muslims), pacifying the west of al-Andalus. But instead of pressing on with the campaign, the Almoravid emir had to return to Marrākeš with his armies because of the sudden death of his son.

In 1088 the kings of Valencia, Murcia, Baeza and Lorca again asked the Almoravid emir for help, and he returned that same year to conquer Aledo. But the campaign failed and they soon went back to Marrākeš. After their departure, the taifa kings came to terms with Alfonso VI once more, as they were still at a disadvantage against him. So when Yūsuf heard of these events, given the lack of morale and disunity among the monarchs of al-Andalus (and as a pretext for seizing the great riches they possessed), he decided to take control of the taifa kingdoms and their possessions.

In 1090 Yūsuf entered Iberia for the third time and won over the resentful militias of the taifa kingdoms; one by one, the garrisons of the fortresses defending the lands of al-Andalus swore loyalty to him, leaving the capitals of the kingdoms unprotected. The Almoravids conquered Granada and Malaga effortlessly and banished their kings to North Africa. The Almoravid emir then left for Marrākeš, entrusting his cousin Sīr ibn Abī Bakr with the task of subduing the remaining taifas. The following year the city of Cordoba fell, and with it the splendid taifa of Seville. Faced with the unstoppable advance of the Almoravids, the king of Badajoz, Al-Mutawakkil, wrote to Alfonso VI asking for help. In response, Sīr ibn Abī Bakr invaded his kingdom, killed the sultan and took power in the capital.

The Almoravids were unable to take the taifas of the Levant because of the Cid's blockade at Valencia. Although they tried to take the city on several occasions, their armies were always defeated by the forces of the Campeador. Together with Saragossa, with which the Almoravids reached an agreement, these were the only cities that did not fall during the Almoravids' third visit to the Peninsula.

The banishment of the princes of the taifa kingdoms was a hard blow for the poets of al-Andalus. With their departure they lost the protection and patronage of cultured lords and the chance of joining the state administration. They were thus forced to live precariously, combining their poetic calling with a trade such as copyist, smith or even butcher, or to wander in search of a patron, which was not always possible.

### The Christian Kingdoms during the Taifas

*If they snatch the outlying regions from us, it is not impossible that the same will happen to the center… The time has come for the blind to look, the idle to act, the sleepers to awaken and the cowards to be brave.*[^p39-22]

[^p39-22]: Excerpt from a letter by Abū Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Barr after the conquest of Barbastro by the Christians in 1064 (Spanish translation by Teresa Garulo, taken from *Arabic Literature of al-Andalus in the Eleventh Century*).

During this period the first crusades against the Muslim kingdoms were proclaimed, the first military order in Europe was founded (see page 56), and the last Viking attack on Galicia took place, repelled thanks to the restoration of seven defensive towers known as *Castellum Honesti* or the Torres del Oeste. The taifa kingdoms also witnessed the birth of Rodrigo Díaz (the Cid; see the sidebar on page 40) and the growing popularity of pilgrimages by nobles to the Holy Land.

As for the Church, at this time the Gregorian reform was introduced (giving rise to the concept of the Reconquest), and in Castile the Mozarabic rite was replaced by the Roman one, which bound Hispania to the Holy See. The inhabitants of Iberia saw bigamy and marriage to a brother's wife forbidden, and clerics were required to give up bearing arms and to leave their wives. In this period work began on the cathedral of Compostela, and the pope excommunicated the bishop of Iria Flavia for proclaiming his diocese an apostolic see without his permission.

<!-- p. 40 -->

> #### The Gregorian Reform
>
> Promoted by Pope Gregory VII (1073–1085), the reform sought to carry out an ideological reinforcement to restore the rights of the Western Church and achieve peace among Christians through a universal Truce of God. To maintain unity, the reform created a new enemy, Islam, which led to the promotion of crusades in Iberia (see page 41).
>
> The Gregorian reform put an end to the Mozarabic Hispanic liturgy and allowed the pope to act as the organizing authority in Iberia, which the king of Castile and Leon, Alfonso VI, opposed. The reform also brought Frankish (Cluniac) clergy into Iberia and papal legates into Hispania; monasteries ceased to depend on the feudal lords of Hispania and came to depend on Rome.
>
> In the four centuries that the Order of Hermes has existed in Iberia, wars between kingdoms (the division between Muslims and Christians would make little sense here) have been constant. However, they have not always had a religious character. Before the Gregorian reform, wars were territorial, fought for booty and land; there was no talk of reconquest, for the movements of the Christian armies did not answer to such aspirations. However, once the reform took shape with the call to the First Crusade, war became sacred. Even so, it will not be until the thirteenth century, after 1220, that authors such as Ramón Martí, Ramón Llull and Pedro Pascual mark out the definitive religious distance between the two worlds and manipulate the imagination of Christians, creating terrible images of the Muslims.

During the taifa period in al-Andalus (1031–1086), the following Christian kingdoms existed:

| Kingdoms | Years |
| --- | --- |
| The kingdom of Pamplona | 1031–1086 |
| The kingdom of Leon | 1031–1086 |
| The kingdom of Galicia | 1031–1071[^p40-23] |
| The kingdom of Aragon | 1035–1086 |
| The kingdom of Castile | 1065–1086 |

[^p40-23]: The kingdom of Galicia could be considered to have disappeared in 1090, after the death of García II, rather than after its absorption by Alfonso VI in 1071.

#### The Offspring of Sancho III of Pamplona

On the death of the king of Pamplona, Sancho III the Great, who also ruled the counties of Aragon, Castile, Álava, and Sobrarbe and Ribagorza, the empire broke apart and, in accordance with his will, was divided among his four sons:

- The firstborn, García Sánchez III, received the kingdom of Pamplona, the county of Álava and part of the county of Castile.
- Fernando I inherited a diminished county of Castile.
- Ramiro I inherited the lands of Navarre and the new kingdom of Aragon (dependent on the kingdom of Pamplona). After his death the throne passed to his son, Sancho I Ramírez.
- Gonzalo I inherited the lands of Sobrarbe and Ribagorza (dependent on Pamplona).

García and Fernando joined forces to defend themselves against the invasion of the king of Leon, Bermudo III, whom they defeated and killed at the Battle of Tamarón (Burgos). As a result, the throne passed to his sister Sancha, who delegated the crown to her husband, the count of Castile, Fernando I. However, the alliance of blood did not last long. Fernando invaded the kingdom of Pamplona and, backed by a powerful army, defeated and killed his own brother, García. With the kingdom decimated, the dead king's son ascended the throne and was forced to pay homage to his uncle Fernando, who thus amassed great power and influence over the Christian lands. Fernando was also the first to demand payment from the taifa kingdoms, in 1055.

#### The Offspring of Fernando I of Leon

When Fernando I died, he did as his father had done and divided his lands among his sons and daughters, separating the crowns once again:

- The firstborn, Sancho II, inherited what was now the kingdom of Castile (and the tribute of Saragossa).
- Alfonso VI inherited the kingdom of Leon (and the tribute of Toledo).
- García II inherited Galicia and the lands of Portugal as far as Coimbra (and the tribute of Seville and Badajoz).
- Elvira received the lordship of Toro.
- Urraca inherited the lordship of Zamora.

However, Sancho II always considered himself the sole legitimate heir to his father's kingdoms and, after forging an alliance with his brother Alfonso VI, the two decided to share out the lands García II had inherited. García, for his part, had annexed the county of Portugal after doing away with Count Nuño Méndez, but he could not stop his brothers from conquering his kingdom: Sancho II took the lands of Galicia and Alfonso VI those of Portugal. To keep him from reclaiming what he had lost, García II was imprisoned for almost twenty years and then exiled to the vassal court of the taifa of Seville, where the poet king Al-Muʿtamid gave him shelter and protection.

Pursuing his hegemonic policy, Sancho II invaded Leon. His armies, led by his champion Rodrigo Díaz, defeated the Leonese forces, and Alfonso VI was imprisoned. However, thanks to the mediation of his sister Urraca, Alfonso was moved to the monastery of Sahagún, from which he escaped to take refuge at the vassal court of Toledo, under the protection of the sultan Al-Maʿmūn.

<!-- p. 41 -->

Sancho II's coronation in Leon was not well received by the Leonese nobility. Many remained loyal to Alfonso VI and, to escape Sancho's wrath, took refuge in Zamora, the fief of Doña Urraca. When Sancho came to Zamora to subdue the city, he was killed by the thrust of a lance.

On Sancho's death, Alfonso VI was able to claim his brother's kingdoms for himself, uniting the crowns of Leon, Castile and Galicia. García II was not so lucky. On hearing the news of Sancho's death, he sought to reclaim his former kingdom, and was summoned by Alfonso. However, on his arrival he was taken prisoner (on the advice of his sister Urraca) and locked away in the mighty castle of Luna, where he lived in confinement for seventeen years until his death.

According to the chronicles, Alfonso VI took part in the conspiracy that ended in the murder of his cousin, Sancho Garcés IV of Pamplona, which led to the annexation of the kingdom of Pamplona to the crown of Aragon. Pamplona came under the control of the king of Aragon, Alfonso VI's cousin Sancho I Ramírez, who styled himself "king of the Aragonese and the Pamplonese." A large part of the territory (Álava, La Rioja, and parts of Biscay, Guipúzcoa and Navarre) was also joined to the crowns of Castile and Leon. Furthermore, since Sancho Garcés had died without heirs, the French houses of Poitiers, Armagnac and Aquitaine took the duchy of Gascony.

With control of almost all of northern Iberia, Alfonso VI adopted the title *Imperator totius Hispaniae* and attacked the taifa of Seville, penetrating its domains and punishing the sultan Al-Muʿtamid for having refused to pay him. It is said that he rode his horse all the way to the sea, and that his punishment was so excessive that the sultan threatened to turn to the Almoravids, to which Alfonso replied: "The religious fanaticism of the Almoravids would sit ill on your court in Seville."

> #### The Cid
>
> *And from then on Moors and Christians called this Ruy Díaz de Bivar the Cid Campeador, which is to say battler.*[^p41-XVI]
>
> Rodrigo Díaz was knighted by his companion and friend, the *infante* Sancho (firstborn son of Fernando I of Leon), the future Sancho II of Castile. Together they fought the armies of the king of Aragon at the siege of Graus (Huesca) to aid the emir of Saragossa, and there Rodrigo showed his great gifts as a warrior.
>
> Once crowned, Sancho named him *armiger regis,* making him the keeper of the king's arms.
>
