> In his youth the Cid served as royal champion and fought alongside his friend for supremacy over the kingdoms of the empire that Sancho's father, Fernando I, had broken apart; his feats of arms earned him the byname of Campeador (from *campi ductor*, meaning "leader on the battlefield").
>
> When Alfonso VI returned from his exile in Toledo after the death of his brother Sancho, the Cid demanded, in the name of all the Castilian knights, that he swear he had had nothing to do with his brother's death. Alfonso did so, but he never forgave the Cid for it. Even so, in his first years of service to Alfonso, the Cid was on good terms with the monarch. But after the Campeador's raid on the eastern part of the taifa of Toledo (which was under Alfonso's protection), and on the advice of the powerful count of Castile and enemy of the Cid, García Ordóñez, the monarch banished him.
>
> In his exile, accompanied by his son Diego, the Cid offered his services to the count of Barcelona and, after being turned away, entered the service of the sultan of Saragossa, Al-Muʾtamin. Under his protection he defeated the armies of the count of Barcelona and those of the king of Aragon and Pamplona, taking many prisoners, whom he freed after collecting hefty ransoms. On his return to Saragossa, the crowds greeted him with the cry of *sīdi,* Andalusi Arabic for "lord."
>
> With the arrival of the Almoravids, the sultan of Saragossa, Al-Mustaʿīn II, had to do without the Campeador's services. The presence of a Christian military leader at the sultan's court was hard to justify before the Almoravids. Consequently, after the defeat suffered against the Almoravids at Sagrajas, Alfonso VI pardoned the Campeador, granting him many domains and the promise of governing the strongholds they might conquer in the Levant. But the Cid was banished again for failing to join the royal troops to help lift the Almoravid siege of Aledo: he was accused of treason, and the king confiscated all his property and exiled him a second time. From then on Rodrigo acted as an independent lord and made the Muslim governor of Valencia, Al-Qādir, pay him tribute.
>
> After Al-Qādir's death the Cid lost a considerable source of income and decided to besiege the city. After a siege of more than a year, the Cid took the city and, wresting it from the Almoravids, proclaimed himself independent lord of the kingdom of Valencia. Once inside, he condemned the city's former qadi to be burned alive for the murder of Al-Qādir. During this period many Muslims joined the Cid; their countrymen considered them vile, perverse and corrupt (they were called *dawāʾir*, "marauders"), for they renounced their faith and launched raids against Muslim cities.
>
> Rodrigo fought alongside the king of Aragon and the count of Barcelona to halt the Almoravid advance and, as a token of friendship, sent his only son, Diego, at the head of a powerful army to help Alfonso VI against the Muslims; however, Diego died at the Battle of Consuegra (Toledo), where the Christians suffered a severe defeat.
>
> The Cid then humbled the Almoravid emir, Yūsuf ibn Tāšufīn, by driving back his armies at Valencia. However, Rodrigo was struck and killed by an arrow. His widow, Jimena, took up the defense of Valencia against the Almoravids and held it until the beginning of the twelfth century. Then, with the help of her uncle Alfonso VI, she had to abandon the principality under the overwhelming pressure of the Almoravid forces, who went on to conquer the city. Before abandoning Valencia, Alfonso ordered it burned to the ground: the Almoravids gained nothing but its ashes.
>
> [^p41-XVI]: Excerpt from the *Cantar de mio Cid*, anonymous (Old Spanish text edited by Ramón Menéndez Pidal).

<!-- p. 42 -->

## The Crusades of Iberia

*[…] Had you seen, O Muslims, your brothers in faith, stripped of their riches and their families; power was given to the swords, and death was sovereign over them; wounds covered them, for the points of the lances made sport of them; the clamor, the moans and the laments swelled, blood ran down their legs as rain runs down the roads, they lost their reason […] And the voices rose, evil deeds spread, the wicked rebelled, tyranny prevailed, the crosses appeared, the bells spoke, the demons fell upon their prey, the chiefs of the swine set fire to everything, and the houses became ovens.*[^p42-XVII]

[^p42-XVII]: Fragment of an epistle by Abū Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Barr after the Christian conquest of Barbastro in 1064 (Spanish translation by Teresa Garulo, taken from *La literatura árabe de al-Andalus durante el siglo XI*).

To understand the meaning of the Christian struggles against the Muslims in Iberia, the terms "crusade" and "reconquest" must be defined. A crusade is any military action whose aim is the defense of the Church and its interests, regardless of the place or the identity of the enemy; it therefore does not imply the liberation of the holy places, as the crusades overseas do. Crusades are directed by the popes, seek the spiritual salvation of the individual, and have a universal scope that affects all of Christendom. The reconquest, by contrast, is led by the Hispanic monarchs, aims to recover the lands and the Church their forebears lost, and is therefore a phenomenon that operates on a local scale.

The crusades in Iberia were a consequence of Almoravid rigorism and the Gregorian reform of the eleventh century. From the time of Pope Alexander II (1061–1073), the Holy See's interest in Iberia took shape through the crusades. This pope already spoke of the *regnum Hispaniae* as the property of Saint Peter, which was a threat to the kings of the Peninsula, who saw their power endangered. Those monarchs were therefore quick to make holy war a Hispanic affair and to assert the power of the monarchy against pontifical power. Alfonso VI, for example, never submitted to the pope's authority and sought an alliance with the Cluniacs in Castile to prevent the Holy Father from intervening in his kingdom. To escape excommunication, the Castilian monarch declared himself a soldier of Christ, but not of Rome. Likewise, the creation of the military orders in Iberia (see page 56) and the nationalization of the local church were moves designed to keep Rome from meddling.

The crusades are holy wars, so whoever takes part in one receives the pope's indulgence. Indulgences are not a sacrament (see *Ars Magica Fifth Edition*, page 301) and do not forgive sins; rather, they remit before God the temporal punishment that souls must expiate, whether on earth or in purgatory.

The first crusade was a consequence of the death of the king of Aragon, Ramiro I, in 1063. The monarch died at the hands of a Saracen who, disguised as a Christian soldier, ran him through with a lance during the siege of Graus. In the wake of this event, Pope Alexander II sent letters to the bishops of Hispania reminding them that the shedding of blood was condemned except to punish the Saracens, and granted plenary indulgences to the warriors who joined the taking of Barbastro (held by the sultan of Saragossa). The pope's call echoed across Europe: nobles came from Aquitaine, Burgundy, Poitou, Vermandois, Champagne and southern Italy, under the command of the Norman William of Montreuil, the pope's standard-bearer.

After the conquest, the crusaders massacred the population of Barbastro and seized a vast booty that included hundreds of Muslim maidens. In response, the Muslim population of the nearby cities murdered many Mozarabs.

When news of the massacre reached Europe, the Benedictine monk Amatus of Montecassino condemned the crusaders' deeds and warned them of God's judgment. And although Barbastro returned to Muslim hands nine months later, the memory of the massacre endured. It was from this moment that the Christians first set out to reconquer the land and spread "the faith in Christ": before, they had always fought for booty or territorial conquest, and the struggle against the Muslims had never been sacralized (see "The Gregorian Reform," page 39).

The second crusade of Iberia took shape in 1068. At the time, the king of Aragon, Sancho I Ramírez, was politically isolated by the monarchs of Pamplona and Castile and by the Catalan nobility. Sancho sought help from Rome to break the blockade. Alexander II heeded his petition and reached an agreement with him: in exchange for becoming a vassal of the Holy See, recognizing Rome's direct superiority over the Aragonese bishoprics and admitting the Roman rite in the kingdom's monasteries, he was named *miles Sancti Petri*, which allowed Rome's armies to intervene in the kingdom. As a result, in 1073 Pope Gregory VII summoned all the *milites* of the Holy See to fight the Muslims and annex their lands to the kingdom of Aragon. Count Ebles II of Roucy (the king of Aragon's brother-in-law) came from Champagne to govern the conquered land and make it a fief of Rome. The crusade, however, was a failure, and almost all the Normans who had come to fight ended up settling in Aragon.

After the defeat suffered against the Almoravids at Sagrajas in 1086, Pope Victor III called the third crusade in Iberia. To conquer Tudela, the armies of Burgundy, Languedoc, Provence and Normandy gathered in Iberia, led by Duke Odo I of Burgundy (nephew of Alfonso VI's wife). The Christians, however, failed to take the city.

At the beginning of the twelfth century the Catalans tried to conquer the Mediterranean cities with the pope's support, but both they and the Pisans (the foremost maritime power in Christendom) clashed with the Muslim pirates who plagued the western Mediterranean. In 1113, the Pisans persuaded Paschal II to call a crusade to conquer Majorca and free the Christian prisoners on the island. In 1114 the Pisans reached an agreement with Ramón Berenguer III, count of Barcelona, for his participation in what would be the fourth Hispanic crusade (though under Pisan right). The Pisan and Catalan armies and the soldiers of Rome, Lucca and southern France embarked in 100 ships and conquered Majorca in 1115, thus destroying an important nest of Muslim piracy. The crusaders freed the Christian captives and put every Muslim male living there to the sword. A year later, the Catalans learned that the Almoravids planned to assault the islands, so they abandoned their houses, burned them and departed. When the Almoravids arrived, they found the islands deserted.

<!-- p. 43 -->

Two years later, in 1118, Alfonso I of Aragon and his friend, the veteran Gaston IV of Béarn, planned the conquest of Saragossa, and Alfonso I issued a call to all the kings of Christendom. When the news reached Rome, Pope Gelasius II granted a crusade bull to those who took part in the siege of the White City. The fifth crusade drew many Frankish, Gascon, Occitan, Catalan and Béarnais lords, who under the orders of Alfonso I (at the head of his own army of Aragonese, Riojans and Navarrese) besieged the city of Saragossa for more than six months. Because of the long siege, the bishop of Huesca had to pay out a large sum of money so that the crusaders would not abandon the enterprise, and Gelasius II promised them eternal life and absolution of all their sins. Saragossa fell in 1118, and Alfonso I agreed a surrender with the Banū Hūd that allowed the roughly 20,000 Muslims of the city to go on living there: the Muslims could leave for Islamic lands with their movable goods, or spend a year in the city and then reside in the suburbs, keeping their freedom and their trades as long as they paid the king a tithe of their income. Moreover, they could not be made slaves of the Jews nor be called up for forced labor (azofras). Many Muslims left, and since they carried their riches and goods with them, the Aragonese monarch granted them an escort so that no one could rob them.

In the middle of the twelfth century, Alfonso VII of Leon (in the first crusading intervention by Castile since the death of Alfonso VI) agreed on the assault of Almería, base of the Almohad fleet and a nest of Muslim piracy, with Ramón Berenguer IV, count of Barcelona, and with the Pisan and Genoese forces, who provided naval support in exchange for money and other commercial advantages in the conquered ports. The attack was blessed as a crusade by Eugene III in the bull issued in 1148, which required the participants to fight until conquest or death. The bishops of Leon and Toledo urged the Christians to take part in this sixth crusade, and the troubadour Marcabru composed a song to draw the knights of Provence. Alfonso VII led an army made up of troops from Castile, Leon and Navarre (with its king García V at their head), from the counties of Barcelona and Urgell, from the republics of Genoa and Pisa and from the lordship of Montpellier. Templars, Hospitallers and a great number of Anglo-Normans from England, whose original destination was Damascus, also took part. Almería fell in less than a week: the crusading forces razed it and murdered more than 28,000 inhabitants. After the conquest, the city was left in the hands of the Genoese Ottone di Bonvillano, and the pope honored Alfonso VII with the Golden Rose.

A year after the conquest of Almería, Ramón Berenguer IV, count of Barcelona, organized the seventh crusade (with papal leave) to conquer the city of Tortosa. Catalan and Provençal nobles, Templar and Hospitaller knights, Flemish and Norman crusaders, the Genoese fleet, the bishop of Barcelona and the Englishman Nicholas Breakspear (the future Pope Adrian IV) all took part. The city, and the whole region of the lower Ebro, fell to the Christian forces and was made a marquisate.

In 1172, Cardinal Hyacinth (the future Celestine III), acting as papal legate, granted the benefits of crusade to those who defended Huete from the Almoravids. Five years later, the same cardinal issued the same bull for the conquest of Cuenca. During these two actions, however, no forces from beyond the Pyrenees were present (the bulk of the Christian armies was made up of Aragonese warriors).

The benefits of crusade were not issued only against the Muslims. In 1191, Alfonso IX of Leon signed a five-year truce with the Almohads. As a consequence, Pope Celestine III (1191–1198) released the Leonese from their fealty to the monarch and proclaimed that those who fought him would enjoy a plenary indulgence. However, when the battle of Alarcos was lost in 1195, Pope Celestine III issued a general call to crusade against the Almohads; the aim was no longer the conquest of cities, but dominion over the whole Peninsula.

In 1211 all of Castile was forging weapons and minting coin to pay for the campaign of Las Navas de Tolosa. All of Hispania mobilized to gain the widest possible support: the bishop of Segovia, Gerardo, went to Rome to obtain from Innocent III a crusade bull and an exhortation to the French and Provençal bishops to spread the call to crusade or contribute money; the archbishop of Toledo, Rodrigo Jiménez de Rada, traveled to France to ask the king for help against the Almohads, and, as an inducement, Alfonso VIII of Castile undertook to pay for the transport of his armies and promised him rich booty; Master Arnaldo, Alfonso VIII's physician, traveled to Poitou, Anjou and Gascony for the same purpose; and, lastly, the troubadour Gavaudan the Elder composed a song according to which salvation could be won through the service of God. All this propaganda bore fruit. In 1212 the armies of Poitou, Anjou, Brittany, Limoges, Périgord, Gascony, Guyenne, Provence, Lyon, Vienne and Valentinois gathered in Toledo. Before setting out, the European crusaders attacked and killed the Jews and Mudéjars of Toledo, and to avoid further trouble the king had to remove them from the city. On the way, the crusaders took the fortress of Malagón (Ciudad Real) and killed all its occupants. On reaching Calatrava they conquered it, and then almost all the European crusaders abandoned the campaign. Jiménez de Rada explained their departure by claiming that the Muslims had bewitched them. The eighth crusade culminated in the victory of Las Navas de Tolosa.

The year 1212 marked the papacy's final estrangement from the Hispanic crusade, which had drifted away from the centralizing project of Gregorian reformism: when the pope proclaimed a crusade he aspired to control the conquered territory, which clashed with Hispanic interests. In 1213, Innocent III issued a bull (*Quia Maior*) revoking the crusading privileges of those who had come to the Peninsula to fight the Muslims. In 1218, Honorius III issued a bull forbidding German and Dutch crusaders to fight the Muslims of the Peninsula as crusaders. In this context, Honorius preached a new crusade against the Muslims of the Peninsula in 1219, in order to spur the king of Castile to follow the combative example of the king of Aragon. But the call was addressed to the Hispanics alone; European crusaders no longer took part. The campaign, led by Jiménez de Rada, took the fortresses of Sierra, Mira and Utiel (between Cuenca and Valencia), and in trying to conquer Requena (Valencia) the army lost more than two thousand Christians in a failed siege that lasted more than three months. This ninth crusade extended the borders of Castile as far as the fortress of Utiel.

Bear in mind that in 1220 the Hispanics consider crusaders depraved, cruel and cowardly folk, for whenever crusading armies gather, looting and rape always follow.

<!-- p. 44 -->

Alfonso did not use his armies to seize Muslim cities or besiege castles, undertakings in which he would have had to spend great sums of money and would have lost many men; instead, he applied heavy fiscal pressure to strangle the taifa kings and so prepare their kingdoms for capitulation. As a demonstration of this policy, Toledo surrendered peacefully to the Castilian monarch. Alfonso entered the city through the Old Bisagra Gate and in 1085 returned the capital of the ancient Visigoths to the crown of Castile.

After the conquest of Toledo, Alfonso VI conquered Albarracín, and its governor, Ḥusām al-Sawla ibn Razīn, king of the Banū Razīn, asked him to confirm him in his rule. Alfonso accepted him as a vassal, and in gratitude Ibn Razīn gave him a monkey. But Alfonso did not stop there: when the sultan of Seville again refused to pay him the *parias*, war between the two monarchs broke out anew. Under the Castilian's pressure, the emir of Seville, representing the taifas of Seville, Badajoz, Granada and Almería, desperately summoned Yūsuf ibn Tāšufīn, Almoravid emir and lord of all the Maghreb (see "The Almoravids and the Taifa Kingdoms," above).

#### The Offspring of Ramón Berenguer I, Count of Barcelona

The county of Barcelona was torn by disputes over the succession, which led to the excommunication of Count Ramón Berenguer I by Pope Victor II. This count published the *Usatges* and bought the Frankish counties of Carcassonne, Razès and Narbonne, gaining power over an extensive territory. On his death he left his lands to his twin sons: Ramón Berenguer II, called *Cap d'estopes* (for his straw-blond hair), and Berenguer Ramón II. Disobeying their father's last wishes, however, the twins quarreled over the inheritance and ended up dividing the lands they had been left.

Ramón Berenguer II could not exercise his rule, for he was murdered in 1082 at the pool in the forest of the Perxa de l'Astor by unknown assailants. The chief suspect in the crime was his brother, who was therefore nicknamed "the Fratricide." Indeed, Berenguer Ramón II was found guilty of the crime when he lost a judicial combat convened by Alfonso VI and, according to the chronicles, set out for the Holy Land when the First Crusade was called, where he lost his life in the taking of Jerusalem. On his death, the county of Barcelona lost possession of the county of Carcassonne, which was occupied by the viscount of Albi and Nîmes.

## The Almoravid Dynasty

The Almoravids, or "the veiled ones,"[^p44-24] rigorously observed the Mālikī doctrine, which led them to combat every heresy of the western Maghreb. During their rule, the Almoravids favored the *fuqahāʾ*, who were enemies of philosophy and mysticism, and encouraged the censorship and exile of philosophers and scientists who put forward treatises deemed heretical. The Almoravid dynasty made Granada the capital of its dominions in al-Andalus, though the capital of its empire was established in Marrākeš, from where the following caliphs ruled:

[^p44-24]: The Almoravid ruling class (though not only they, but also the Berbers who had come from North Africa to fight the Christians) wore a kind of veil that covered the face (called the *liṯām*), and so they were known as "the veiled ones."

<!-- p. 45 -->

| Caliphs | Years |
| --- | --- |
| Yūsuf ibn Tāšufīn | 1086–1106 |
| ʿAlī ibn Yūsuf | 1106–1143 |
| Tāšufīn ibn ʿAlī | 1143–1145 |

### Al-Andalus under Almoravid Rule

Yūsuf ibn Tāšufīn came to the Peninsula four times. During his third incursion he managed to conquer and annex to his empire almost all the taifas of Iberia, and the few that remained were absorbed a few years later.

In 1097, Yūsuf crossed the strait a fourth and final time to see to the *ŷihād* in person. He won a great victory against Alfonso VI of Leon at Consuegra and suffered a heavy defeat against the forces of the Cid when he tried to conquer Valencia (indeed, the Cid's Valencia held out until 1102). Afterward, the taifa of Albarracín was conquered in 1104 and, after the death of the last sultan of Saragossa, the city fell into Almoravid hands in 1110; the last taifa kingdom of Iberia, Majorca, surrendered in 1116. Once their supremacy in the Peninsula was secured, the Almoravids were able to launch a general offensive against the Christian kingdoms: they attacked and besieged Toledo on several occasions, launched a failed attack on Barcelona that had grievous consequences for the Christians (the count of Barcelona could not go to the aid of Carcassonne because he was defending his own city, and lost the Provençal city to the count of Toulouse), and crushed the armies of Alfonso VI at Sagrajas (1086), Consuegra (1097) and Uclés (1108).

After Yūsuf's death his son, ʿAlī ibn Yūsuf, was named caliph. To maintain his defensive bulwarks, he launched systematic attacks on strategic points along the borders of the Christian kingdoms, which did not prevent Alfonso I the Battler, king of Aragon and Pamplona, from penetrating into the heart of Granada and freeing thousands of Mozarabs, nor Alfonso VII of Leon from cutting the empire in two and ruining the Almoravids' reputation among the Andalusis.

### The Almoravids and the Almohads: The Second Taifas

While the Almoravids fought the taifa kings and the Christian monarchs, the scholar Ibn Tūrmat preached in Marrākeš the orthodoxy that was the seed of the Almohad reform movement. Rather than imprison or execute him for the unrest he was causing, the Almoravids exiled him to the mountains, where he went on preaching and swelling the ranks of his followers with the clans of the region. Ibn Tūrmat proclaimed himself al-Mahdī and launched a reformist movement that called for the purification of customs, holy war, and the return of the degenerate Almoravids to the Qurʾan. Aware of the threat, the Almoravids attacked the rebels in the mountains and, although they inflicted great defeats on them, could not wipe them out. The withdrawal of Almoravid troops from Iberia to fight the Almohads in the Maghreb was exploited by the inhabitants of Cordoba to begin a rebellion in 1121, which was provoked by the loss of the entire Ebro valley to the great Christian warrior Alfonso I of Aragon.

The death of the caliph ʿAlī ibn Yūsuf in 1143 provoked a succession crisis fought out between two factions. The losers joined the Almohads, who were advancing relentlessly over Almoravid territory. In Iberia, the discontent of the people of al-Andalus grew until, in 1144, a general revolt broke out that gave rise to the second taifas: Santarém, Jerez, Cadiz, Badajoz, Cordoba, Malaga, Valencia, Lérida and Tortosa, among others, proclaimed their independence.

In Marrākeš, the rule of Tāšufīn ibn ʿAlī (son of ʿAlī ibn Yūsuf) was brief. In 1145 his armies were overwhelmed by the Almohads, and he died falling from a cliff as he fled from them. As a result, his ten-year-old son was named caliph, and ruled for two months before his uncle seized power from him. Meanwhile, the Almohads went on conquering Almoravid cities.

In 1146, the commander of the Almoravid fleet, Abū-l-Ḥasan ʿAlī ibn Maymūn, who was in Cadiz, went over to the Almohads. That same year they laid siege to Marrākeš, and they took it in 1147. Soon after, the last Almoravid emir was beheaded. In this situation, many exiled Mozarabs who had served alongside the Almoravid troops left North Africa and returned to Iberia to settle in the city of Toledo.

The second taifas remained independent until the Almohads were firmly established in the Peninsula, around 1160. During this period the figure of Ibn Mardanīš, "the Wolf King," stood out; he kept control over the whole of eastern Iberia until 1172.

### The Christian Kingdoms during the Almoravid Dynasty

During this period, the Christians faced the Almoravid troops arriving from Marrākeš. Although they lost important strongholds and suffered serious defeats, they shattered the reputation of the Muslim generals, encouraged their subjects to rebel and fragmented their fragile unity, already damaged by the Almohad movement.

<!-- p. 46 -->

> #### The Pilgrims' Hospitals of Iberia
>
> *The clothes of a leper, a Jew, a Christian, or a libertine must not be sold unless the buyer is made aware of their origin […]. Nor shall eggs, chickens, milk or any other product be bought from lepers; rather, they must trade among themselves.*[^p46-XVIII]
>
> Along the Way of Saint James there are many buildings that can lodge pilgrims. So that they can be recognized, they mark their doors or façades with crosses or scallop shells, and in remote hermitages they even ring a small bell after nightfall to guide pilgrims to the safety of the hospice.
>
> In the hospitals, pilgrims receive shelter, are given a fire to warm themselves, water and some food, and are cared for if they are sick. They admit Christians, Jews and Muslims alike, and are tended by honest women.
>
> In the larger hospices, pilgrims may stay for up to three days, and men and women must rest in separate quarters. In these places pilgrims are given dinner and supper, have baths and interpreters at their disposal, can count on cobblers to mend their footwear, and can even find scribes to take down their last will should they be gravely ill; if a pilgrim dies in a hospital, the clerics in charge are bound to bury him in a church or a Christian cemetery, sometimes created solely for that purpose. Hospitals may be maintained and staffed by monastic or military orders, by officials of the crown, or even by covenants (such as Duresca).
>
> In Iberia, the most important hospital is that of Santa Cristina, at the Somport (Huesca, although from the Hermetic point of view it belongs to the Provençal Tribunal), considered one of the three most important in all Christendom, together with those of Jerusalem and Montjoux (which serves the pilgrims bound for Rome). Santa Cristina has always occupied a strategic position and was granted privileges by the kings of Aragon Pedro I and Alfonso I, and by Popes Paschal II and Eugene III. It reached its height in the middle of the twelfth century.
>
> Despite being hospitals, these buildings do not treat lepers (in Arabic, *mardà*, singular *marīd*), for leprosy is considered not a disease but a punishment for sins committed: the flesh rots while it still houses a soul! When a case is detected, the leper is expelled from the city or town with the following implements: a gray hood, a pair of leather shoes, a walking staff, a set of sheets so that his skin touches nothing while he sleeps, a pair of clappers to announce his presence, and a cup, a knife and a plate for eating and drinking. Moreover, to prevent contagion, the leper may not approach churches, markets, mills or taverns, may not lean on the posts of bridges, touch the water of streams, or walk downwind.
>
> [^p46-XVIII]: Fragment of *The Treatise of Ibn ʿAbdūn* (Spanish translation by Emilio García Gómez and E. Levi-Provençal).

<!-- p. 47 -->

During the Almoravid domination of al-Andalus, Compostela received the blessing of the pontiffs of Rome: Paschal II encouraged pilgrimage to the city, and the hospital of Santa Cristina at the Somport became one of the most important in Christendom, after the pilgrims' hospital of Jerusalem; furthermore, Calixtus II, by the bull *Omnipotentis dispositione*, made the city an archbishopric and instituted the Jacobean Holy Year (granting an indulgence[^p47-25] to pilgrims who reached Santiago in a year when the feast of Saint James, July 25, fell on a Sunday), so that the kingdom of Castile grew rich from the flow of pilgrims.

The Christian kingdoms of Iberia also saw their first tournament, already a popular pastime in northern Europe, witnessed the birth of the school of translators of Toledo, and had to face a great famine that struck all the powers of the Tribunal and decimated the population throughout their territories.

The Almoravids of al-Andalus (1086–1145) coexisted with the following Christian kingdoms:

| Kingdoms | Years |
| --- | --- |
| The kingdom of Aragon | 1086–1137 |
| The kingdom of Leon | 1086–1145 |
| The kingdom of Castile | 1086–1145 |
| The kingdom of Monzón | 1089–1143 |
| The kingdom of Pamplona | 1134–1145 |
| The Crown of Aragon | 1137–1145 |
| The kingdom of Portugal | 1143–1145 |

#### The Kingdom of Aragon and the Kingdom of Monzón

On the borders of the kingdom of Aragon arose the small kingdom of Monzón, a fief of Aragon, which, after being held by the Muslims for four years, ended up in the hands of the Order of the Temple.

The son of Sancho I Ramírez, Pedro I of Aragon, king of Pamplona, Sobrarbe, Ribagorza, Culla, Oropesa and Castellón, extended the borders of his kingdom at the expense of the taifa kingdom of Saragossa. Thanks to Almoravid pressure on the borders of Castile, Pedro was able to force his way into the Ebro valley, conquering more than 30,000 square kilometers between 1080 and 1120.

- In 1096 he took Huesca at the battle of Alcoraz thanks to the intervention of Saint George, his patron saint, making it his capital and moving the kingdom's diocese there from Jaca.
- In 1101 he conquered Barbastro and attacked Saragossa, although he failed to take it. His armies bore the *vexillum Christi* and besieged the city with the crusaders' cry of "God wills it!"

Pedro I took the crusader's vow, and although he wished to go to the Holy Land, he could never fulfill it because Pope Urban II forbade it (see "The Crusades Overseas," page 48). He obeyed this command because he needed the papacy to consolidate his crown against the imperialist advance of Alfonso VI.

> #### The Crusades Overseas
>
> *Whoever dies here fighting face to the foe, I take his sins upon me, and God shall have his soul.*[^p49-XIX]
>
> In 1095, while the Christians were fighting the Almoravids in the Peninsula, the emperor of Constantinople, Alexios I Komnenos, appealed to Rome for help against the Seljuk Turks. In response, Urban II summoned the Christian kingdoms of the West to the First Crusade. With this call, Urban gave definitive shape to Gregorian reformism, for he created a political doctrine with a theological foundation aimed at the triumph of Christianity and the Church of Rome. The Christian kingdoms of the Peninsula sent more than seven thousand men (most of them Catalans) to the Holy Land; veteran soldiers who fought alongside Gaston of Béarn and the count of Toulouse. The First Crusade culminated in the conquest of Jerusalem in 1099, an event that shook Europe and inspired many nobles to follow in the wake of the valiant crusaders. However, to keep the warriors of Iberia from going to fight in the Holy Land, Pope Paschal II issued repeated bulls forbidding them to abandon their struggle against the Almoravids.
>
> In 1145, in response to the fall of the county of Edessa (Turkey), Eugene III called the Second Crusade. To answer his call, more than a hundred ships set out from England carrying English, Scots, Flemings, Normans and Germans. As was customary, the crusaders from overseas stopped at Santiago to venerate the saint (with the consequent sack of the city) and then put in at Porto, where many took part in the taking of Lisbon and stayed on in Portuguese lands. Those who continued on their way to the Holy Land joined the Hispanic crusade to conquer Almería, and those who did not stay to conquer Tarragona (and keep winning booty) carried on across the Mediterranean and fought in the failed siege of Damascus.
>
> The Third Crusade was called by Gregory VIII in 1187 to conquer Jerusalem, which had been taken by the sultan of Egypt, Saladin, after his crushing victory over the Christian armies at the battle of the Horns of Hattin (Israel). As in the Second Crusade, the armies from overseas (3,500 Germans, Danes, Flemings and Englishmen) stopped at Santiago and then in Portugal, where they took part in the (temporary) conquest of Alcácer do Sal and Silves.
>
> Despite their efforts, the crusaders failed to "liberate" the Holy City, and although in 1192 Saladin allowed Christians to enter Jerusalem on pilgrimage, in 1202 a military expedition was called to conquer it. The so-called Fourth Crusade, however, ended up sacking Constantinople (to the great sorrow of House Jerbiton) without even reaching Palestine. As in the two previous crusades, the northerners passed through Lisbon, made a pact with the king of Portugal, razed the city of Silves and handed it over to the monarch.
>
> In 1217, Pope Honorius III called on Christians to recover Jerusalem in the Fifth Crusade. The crusaders again passed through Santiago and Lisbon, where a good number of them took part in the conquest of Alcácer do Sal, although on this occasion the pope did not let them stay in Portugal and urged them on to the Holy Land. The crusaders, however, failed to take Jerusalem at the first assault, so in 1218 they chose to attack Damietta in order to conquer Egypt and take the Holy City from there. For the assault, the pope named the Leonese cardinal Pelagio Galván as legate. While the crusaders were besieging Damietta, the sultan of Egypt, al-Kāmil, offered Pelagio the kingdom of Jerusalem if the crusaders lifted the siege. Pelagio flatly refused, and after eighteen months of siege, in November 1219, the city finally fell. The valiant Aragonese warrior Pere de Montagut and fifty knights from the Peninsula armed by the bishop of Barcelona took part in the battle.
>
> [^p49-XIX]: Fragment of the *Cantar de mio Cid*, anonymous (Old Spanish text edited by Ramón Menéndez Pidal).

Pedro I's only heir died the same year as he did, so he was succeeded by his half-brother Alfonso I, nicknamed the Battler. At thirty-six Alfonso married his second cousin, Urraca, daughter and heiress of the emperor Alfonso VI, so that when the latter died, Alfonso I became ruler of Castile and Leon and proclaimed himself "emperor of all the Spains." However, the interests of his wife and of the Castilian, Leonese and Galician nobility caused a civil war that scourged the kingdom with great misfortunes for five years. In that war the nobility and the clergy rallied around Urraca, while the peasants and the burghers supported Alfonso. The nobles' party won the war, and afterward several papal bulls ordered the burghers to return all the lands confiscated from the monasteries at the start of the revolt. The fighting did not end until the pope declared the marriage of Alfonso and Urraca null and the two separated; Alfonso kept his original kingdoms: Aragon and Pamplona.

After the civil war, Alfonso concentrated on conquering the Ebro valley. He took the city of Saragossa and then Soria and Calatayud. He secured the passage of his armies into the heart of the Muslim empire in the Peninsula and, together with his friend Gaston IV, set out to free the Christians from Almoravid fanaticism, intending to establish a Christian principality in Granada with the help of the Mozarabs. He did not manage to take Granada, though he attacked and took many Muslim strongholds and carried his campaign of liberation through the plain of Granada, the south of Cordoba and the coast of Malaga, defeating the Almoravids who faced his army. In this way he freed 10,000 Mozarabs, with whom he resettled the Ebro valley, and broke Almoravid unity. Pope Urban II compared the conquests of Alfonso I to the victories of the crusaders in the East.

Alfonso I tried without success to conquer Valencia and dreamed of organizing a crusade to the Holy Land. In the end he died (with no legitimate or illegitimate offspring) trying to take Fraga, which was held by one of the best Almoravid generals of Cordoba, and in that battle he lost a fragment of the True Cross that he had brought to the camp. In his strange will he left his kingdoms to the military orders of the East: the Knights Templar, the Hospitallers of Saint John, and the Order of the Holy Sepulchre (probably inspired by his friend Gaston, who did the same). His death left the crown in a serious economic crisis and set the Navarrese and Aragonese nobility against each other; they ignored his will and each proclaimed their own king, splitting the crown into two kingdoms: Aragon and Pamplona. The kingdom of Aragon passed to Ramiro II (a bishop before his coronation, and Alfonso I's brother), who had to face the monarch of Leon and the internal noble revolts that gave rise to the events of the bell of Huesca.

> #### The Bell of Huesca
>
> When King Alfonso I died without issue, the kingdom passed to his brother, the bishop Ramiro II of Aragon. Faced with the instability created by the kingdom's financial and political crisis, Ramiro ordered a great bell to be cast, to serve as a pretext for summoning all the great lords of his realm. Rumor had it that it was so large that its peal would be heard from every corner of the kingdom.
>
> At such news, all the great lords answered the king's call. Allies and rebels alike came to his palace to behold the immense bell. Ramiro picked out those who were causing the greatest trouble in the kingdom and had them enter, one by one, the hall where it was kept. As they entered, the king beheaded them and arranged their heads in a great circle. When he had punished his greatest enemy (the bishop of Huesca), he hung his head as the clapper and invited the rest of the nobles to contemplate the punishment that awaited them if they rose against the royal power.

When Ramiro had his only daughter, Petronila, the monarch of Leon proposed a marriage with his firstborn son. The Aragonese king, however, returned to his monastery and gave the throne and his daughter's hand to the count of Barcelona, Ramón Berenguer IV; thus was born the Crown of Aragon. As Berenguer IV was a Templar, the Holy See accepted the decision, for it saw in it the fulfillment of the will of the late Alfonso I of Aragon.

[^p47-25]: To gain the indulgence one must make the pilgrimage to Santiago, and confess and take communion in the days immediately following.

<!-- p. 48 -->

#### The County of Barcelona

The county of Barcelona absorbed the Frankish and Catalan counties of Cerdanya, Conflent, Besalú and Osona when their holders died without issue. On his death, the count of Barcelona, Ramón Berenguer III, divided his counties between his twin sons: Ramón Berenguer IV kept the Catalan counties and Berenguer Ramón I inherited the Occitan counties, although the Provençals resisted Catalan domination.

The expansion of the county of Barcelona culminated at the end of this period with the county's union with the kingdom of Aragon and the birth of the Crown of Aragon (1137) under the rule of Ramón Berenguer IV. He could not, however, recover Carcassonne, harried as he was by the Almoravid troops, whom he fought fiercely.

During this period, and thanks to Pope Gelasius II, the county ended more than three centuries of obedience to the archbishopric of Narbonne and put into practice the *remença* (a payment the peasant had to make to his lord on leaving the land he worked; see the "*Ius Maletractandi*" sidebar, page 52) to stem the exodus of peasants to the newly conquered lands.

#### The Kingdoms of Leon and Castile

The powerful monarch of the kingdom of Leon, Alfonso VI, fought the Almoravids fiercely. His only legitimate son, Sancho Alfónsez, died in 1108 fighting the Almoravids at the battle of Uclés, so Alfonso assembled the royal *curia* in Toledo and decided to marry his heiress, Urraca, to Alfonso of Aragon, in order to give the crown of the kingdom to the son of that marriage.

On the death of Alfonso VI (1109), the kingdom was plunged into a bloody civil war (see "The Kingdom of Aragon and the Kingdom of Monzón," above), in which his daughter Urraca could not defend her rights in Castile, where Alfonso I, her husband, was considered the sole monarch. When Urraca died, her son, Alfonso VII, recovered the power lost through his mother's disastrous rule, proclaiming himself sovereign of Leon, Castile, Galicia and Toledo and prevailing over the power of his stepfather, the king of Aragon, who renounced the imperial title in his favor.

Alfonso VII obtained the vassalage of the king of Aragon, the counts of Barcelona, King Zafadola and the Almoravid governor of Cordoba. He also proclaimed himself emperor of Hispania and drew up general laws for the whole empire, declaring, for the first time in his kingdom, the Peace and Truce of God. In his struggles against the Almoravids he reached the heart of al-Andalus, sacking Cordoba, Seville, Granada and Carmona and destroying Almoravid unity in the Peninsula.

> #### Zafadola
>
> Aḥmad ibn Hūd (known to the Christians as Zafadola, from his honorific title *Sayf al-Dawla*) was the last king of the Hūdid dynasty and grandson of al-Mustaʿīn II. When Alfonso I conquered Saragossa, he left the city and remained in his fortress of Rueda de Jalón until 1130.
>
> Alfonso VII, in his obsession with becoming emperor of Hispania, beguiled Zafadola in order to make al-Andalus a vassal province of Castile. In his letters he asked him to proclaim himself king of the Muslims and pay him homage: "The Almoravids are laying waste to the kingdom and the Andalusis loathe them; your blood makes you the only legitimate heir of al-Andalus; they have no other king but Zafadola!" Spellbound, Zafadola paid homage to Alfonso VII and handed over the fortress of Rueda de Jalón in exchange for fiefs in Castile. The last Hūdid king rode out with his armies and took part in the conquest of Saragossa and in the raids (*algaras*) Alfonso sent against the regions of Cordoba, Seville and Granada, thereby coming to rule a good part of the southeast of the Peninsula. The Muslims, however, never saw him as an ally nor supported his actions, for they considered him an uprooted man.
>
> As a vassal of Alfonso VII, he asked him for help to subdue the lords of Baeza, Jaén and Úbeda, who refused to pay him tribute. The emperor sent a group of Christian counts to his aid, and they laid waste to the rebel strongholds. In desperation, the insurgents surrendered to Zafadola in exchange for his protection against the counts' troops, who, despite the Hūdid's requests, did not stop their attacks and plundering. In an attempt to stop them, Zafadola gave them battle on the fields of al-Luŷŷ (near Albacete), where he was defeated and taken prisoner. Despite his title, Zafadola was murdered by the counts' soldiers in the camp where he was being held. With his death the line of the Banū Hūd came to an end, and with it Alfonso VII's aspirations of crowning his loyal ally as vassal king of all al-Andalus.

<!-- p. 49 -->

#### The Kingdom of Pamplona

The kingdom of Pamplona was bound to that of Aragon until the death of Alfonso I, when the Navarrese proclaimed García Ramírez, grandson of the Cid, monarch of Pamplona and Monzón. On his death, his son, Sancho VI of Navarre, was the first to adopt the title of king of Navarre rather than of Pamplona.

#### The Kingdom of Portugal

The county of Portugal, having abandoned its ambitions to expand northward at the expense of Galicia, turned its gaze south to fight the Almoravids. To this end, Count Afonso Henriques built the fortress of Leiria, with which he tried to stabilize the region south of Coimbra, so often attacked by the Muslim hosts, and which he used to launch attacks against Santarém, which served as the rearguard for the Almoravid incursions. Although the fortress was soon taken and burned by the Muslims, the count set his sights beyond Coimbra and began to make war on the Muslims, which would eventually bring him victory at the decisive battle of Ourique in 1139, the moment from which the count began to appear in documents with the royal title (*Rex Portugallensis*).

After Ourique, Guimarães ceased to be the nerve center of the county and Coimbra began to emerge, which increased the importance of the frontier knights and allowed a lesser nobility to gather in the area to increase its fortunes. Thanks to the victory of Ourique, the emperor Alfonso VII recognized the kingdom's independence and its king in 1143: thus was born the kingdom of Portugal. That same year, Afonso I Henriques sent the pope a letter of vassalage (known as *Claves regnum ceelorum*) in which he declared himself *miles Sancti Petri* (knight of Saint Peter) and placed himself in the pope's service, paying him an annual census in exchange for the protection of the kingdom (papal recognition, however, would not come until 1179, with the bull *Manifestis probatum est*; see page 53).

<!-- p. 50 -->

## The Almohad Dynasty

*The fuqahāʾ whom I revile are only those who seek to make their fortune through their learning; who study the Law to win fame and renown […] and so that people speak of them; who devote themselves constantly to disputes and controversies; and who, moreover, dare to contradict the religious men who love only the life to come and who fear God […].*[^p50-26]

[^p50-26]: Excerpt from *The Epistle of Holiness* by Ibn ʿArabī (Spanish translation by Miguel Asín Palacios).

The founder of the Almohad movement (from the Arabic *al-muwaḥḥidūn*, "those who profess the unity of God"), the Berber Abū ʿAbd Allāh Muḥammad ibn Tūrmat, was born in 1078 and studied in Cordoba and the East, where he learned philosophy, astrology and theology. Averroes himself bore witness to his wisdom in his commentaries on Aristotle.

The Almohads laid down powerful ideological foundations and, after being driven out by the Almoravids, took refuge in the mountains of the High Atlas. From there they set out to put an end to the depraved and impious Almoravids, their religious corruption and their unlawful taxes, and to establish justice in the world, seizing the Almoravids' riches as plunder by the right their revolution claimed for itself.

Almohad doctrine rests on the abstract unity of the divine essence, called *tawḥīd*, which is the fundamental dogma of Islam: this unity denies any likeness between God and the creatures He has made. Indeed, since the Almoravids had come to attribute human form to the divinity, the Almohads accused them of anthropomorphism; their moral and religious decadence ended with the arrival of the Almohads.

By 1220, the Almohads have had five caliphs since they conquered al-Andalus. The first of them, ʿAbd al-Muʾmin, succeeded in establishing a dynastic principle by naming his son as his successor and heir:

| Caliphs | Years |
| --- | --- |
| ʿAbd al-Muʾmin | 1160–1163 |
| Abū Yaʿqūb Yūsuf | 1163–1184 |
| Abū Yūsuf Yaʿqūb al-Manṣūr | 1184–1199 |
| Abū ʿAbd Allāh Muḥammad al-Nāṣir | 1199–1213 |
| Abū Yaʿqūb Yūsuf II al-Muntanṣir | 1213–1224 |

When the founder of the Almohad movement, Ibn Tūrmat, died, he was succeeded by ʿAbd al-Muʾmin, who kept up heavy military and propaganda pressure on the Almoravids; combined with the actions of the Christian kingdoms, this brought about their collapse. The wars against the Almohads forced the Almoravids to tax their subjects even more heavily, which led to growing discontent among the inhabitants of North Africa and al-Andalus.

After gaining control of North Africa and the Maghreb, the Almohads seized the Almoravid capital, Marrākeš, but it was not until 1160 that ʿAbd al-Muʾmin planned the final subjugation of al-Andalus, setting up his base of operations for the conquest at Gibraltar.

When the Almohads took control of Muslim Iberia, ʿAbd al-Muʾmin decreed the forced conversion of all non-Muslims on pain of death (though in practice this was not always enforced) and confiscation of their property, for the Almohads did not recognize the protection of the dhimmis (see page 12). Consequently, Christians and Jews with the necessary means emigrated north; those who could not leave and embraced Islam went on living in their communities; those who refused were expelled or executed; and the rest lived under the strict observance of the Unitarians. Andalusi opposition to the Almohad regime then became clear and open.

Broadly speaking, the Almohads preserved the administrative divisions of the Almoravids. However, when they made the caliphate hereditary, they introduced some changes: to reward the local support they had received against the Almoravids, they maintained the independence of the governors of al-Gharb, although they eventually annexed it to Seville in 1157–58. During the caliphate of Abū Yaʿqūb Yūsuf, they split it into two provinces again, though at times a single governor ruled both regions. The region of Malaga was initially joined to the province of Granada (which also governed Ceuta), but became independent during the caliphate of Abū Yaʿqūb Yūsuf II.

### The Almohads in al-Andalus

After subduing the kingdoms of the second taifas, the first Almohad caliph, ʿAbd al-Muʾmin, established his Iberian capital at Cordoba and appointed his two sons, Abū Yaʿqūb Yūsuf and Abū Saʿīd ʿUṯmān, governors of Seville and Granada, to rule the province of al-Andalus in his name. Although he left for Marrākeš to consolidate his rule in North Africa, he continued to send troops to Iberia to put an end to the Wolf King.

<!-- p. 51 -->

> #### The Wolf King
>
> At the end of the Almoravid Empire, Ibn Mardanīš, a muwallad born in Peñíscola, proclaimed himself emir of Murcia, Valencia and Almería, controlling the whole eastern seaboard of al-Andalus during the second taifas. The Wolf King, as the Christians called him, paid *parias* to the count of Barcelona to avoid attack from the north and so be free to expand into Muslim lands. To this end he recruited an army of mercenaries in Castile and Aragon, with which he conquered Jaén, Baeza, Granada and Carmona, and laid siege to the cities of Seville and Cordoba.
>
> Ibn Mardanīš twice rejected the Almohad caliph's invitations to join his reformist movement. The Wolf King fought the Almohad Empire and defied its authority until his death. During his reign, Murcia grew rich on agriculture, boosted by the hydraulic works (waterwheels, irrigation channels and weirs) that for centuries had harnessed the waters of the Segura. Ibn Mardanīš introduced vermicelli, silkworm breeding and the cultivation of the white mulberry to his kingdom, and saw Murcian pottery exported to Genoa and Pisa. Harnessing the power of its mills, his kingdom was the first in Mythic Europe to make paper from rice straw (an industry that would keep growing over the years in Iberia).
>
> Nevertheless, the economic splendor of his reign began to decline when his father-in-law, Ibn Hamušk, lord of Jaén, went over to the Almohads. With the Almohad raids on the fertile plains and rich market gardens of Murcia, his rule began to languish, and although the capital withstood every attempt to take it, Ibn Mardanīš subjected its people to heavy fiscal and social pressure that ended up turning them in favor of the Almohads. One by one, the Almohads recovered the cities the Wolf King had conquered.
>
> With hardly any allies left, Ibn Mardanīš died in Murcia in 1172, while the city was under siege by the Almohad armies of Seville. His son, following his father's advice, submitted to them and let them into the city in exchange for being named governor of Murcia. With its conquest, the Almohads managed to unite all of al-Andalus under their banner (except the Balearic Islands, the last Almoravid stronghold, which would also eventually fall).

<!-- p. 52 -->

ʿAbd al-Muʾmin died unexpectedly, so the throne passed to his son, the governor of Seville, Abū Yaʿqūb Yūsuf. After his father's sudden death, the newly named caliph had to leave for the Maghreb to consolidate his power, and in his absence the Wolf King ravaged al-Andalus. The raids of the man from Peñíscola threatened the survival of the Almohad province of Iberia, so Abū Yaʿqūb Yūsuf put down the succession crisis in the Maghreb and returned to Seville to lead a military expedition and finish off the Wolf King for good.

During his reign, Yūsuf moved the capital to Seville, and the city he had governed since the age of sixteen underwent a true urban revolution. He had a pontoon bridge built across the Guadalquivir, planned the construction of the Great Mosque (with room for 16,000 people), rebuilt the Roman aqueduct (seventeen kilometers long) to supply the city with drinking water, organized the province's farmland and ordered the building of the minaret for the Great Mosque (known as the Giralda), completed in 1184. Atop it was set a spectacular *yâmûr*: an architectural finial made of four spheres of pure gold, of decreasing size, threaded on a spire (the largest sphere was so enormous that part of one of the city gates had to be demolished to bring it in). In 1220, the gleam of the spheres can be seen from a day's journey away.

Yūsuf lavished particular attention on Muslim philosophers and scientists, whom he always treated with great deference. Indeed, he was one of the foremost champions of the spread of Aristotelian thought in al-Andalus (and therefore in Mythic Europe), a factor that helped Averroes write his famous and excellent commentaries (see page 322).

Yūsuf had to return to the Maghreb to set his domains in order, and the Christian monarchs took advantage of this to raid deep into the heart of al-Andalus. In the face of such incursions, the caliph returned to Iberia in 1184, chiefly to halt the Portuguese. However, he lost his life in the campaign of Santarém (Portugal), while withdrawing toward Seville.

Yūsuf was no great soldier, but he stood out for his culture, asceticism, piety and sense of justice. On his death, his son Abū Yūsuf Yaʿqūb al-Manṣūr was proclaimed caliph. Unlike his father, he was a great strategist and also a great censor, possibly under the influence of the fuqahāʾ, who were truly responsible for the intellectual repression of his time. Proof of this was his legislation against alcohol, his ban on musicians and on excess in dress, his requirement that the Jews of al-Andalus dress in blue, the order of exile he issued against the great philosopher Averroes and his edict for the destruction of books that did not deal with the religious sciences. Curiously, the caliph entrusted this task to the physician Avenzoar, whom he allowed to keep as many forbidden books as he wished on condition that no one find out.

After his appointment, al-Manṣūr had to go to the Maghreb to put down the revolts that followed his father's death, taking with him a good number of the Mozarabs remaining in al-Andalus as his personal guard. Seizing the opportunity, the Banū Gāniya, the last Almoravids holding power in Iberia, attacked several African ports from their stronghold in the Balearic Islands, wresting them from the Almohads for a short time.

After stabilizing the situation in the Maghreb in 1188, the caliph returned to Iberia and took the fight to the Christian kingdoms, with whom he signed a five-year peace treaty in 1190. When it expired, the caliph returned to the Peninsula to defend himself against the attacks of the armies of Alfonso VIII of Castile, on whom he inflicted a terrible defeat at the battle of Alarcos.

> #### The Battle of Las Navas de Tolosa
>
> After the battle of Alarcos, Alfonso VIII of Castile signed numerous truces with the Almohads until, in 1210, he resumed the war against them together with the kingdom of Aragon. In response, in 1211, the caliph Abū ʿAbd Allāh Muḥammad al-Nāṣir stormed the fortress of Salvatierra (Ciudad Real), seat of the Order of Calatrava; its loss shook all of Christendom in the Peninsula. Faced with this situation, Alfonso VIII began preparing a great campaign with the support of Pope Innocent III, who preached a crusade to see it through. The monarchs Pedro II of Aragon and Sancho VII of Navarre joined it, and although Alfonso IX of Leon and Afonso II of Portugal did not appear in person, they sent part of their armies.
>
> Alfonso VIII gathered in Toledo an army such as had never been seen before. His men were joined by the forces of the military orders of Castile, the Templars, the Hospitallers and the armies of Aragon and Navarre, each led by its king. The crusader army took the fortresses it found in its path until it reached Sierra Morena, where, thanks to a shepherd, it found a safe pass through which to meet the Almohad army waiting for it at Las Navas de Tolosa (Jaén). The Christians, 12,000 strong, divided their forces into three bodies commanded by Alfonso VIII (with the archbishop of Toledo, Jiménez de Rada), Pedro II and Sancho VII, and arranged each of these in turn into three units: vanguard, center and rearguard. The Almohad army, 20,000 strong, was divided into five bodies — Arabs, Berbers, volunteers, Andalusis and Almohads — and strengthened its defenses with a palisade where the caliph took shelter.
>
> The two armies clashed in a bloody struggle in which Sancho broke through the palisade and, swollen with rage, smashed the Muslim lines and cut through with his sword the chains protecting the caliph's camp, putting him to flight and routing his army. Alfonso VIII captured the caliph's tent and standard, which he sent as gifts to Innocent III. In their rich plunder, the Christians found an enormous emerald.
>
> With this victory, the Christian kingdoms paved the way for the conquest and surrender of the Guadalquivir valley.

<!-- p. 53 -->

Afterward, al-Manṣūr ordered the establishment of a defensive system for the entire frontier march of present-day Extremadura, since it was essential to the protection of Seville; he set its defensive center at Badajoz and restored the walls of Cáceres and Trujillo after conquering them in 1196. Two years later he fell ill and returned to Marrākeš, where he died in 1199.

After al-Manṣūr's death, his seventeen-year-old son Abū ʿAbd Allāh Muḥammad al-Nāṣir was proclaimed caliph. He took advantage of the empire's stability to defeat the Banū Gāniya, the last Almoravid enclave in the Balearic Islands and North Africa. However, al-Nāṣir could not defeat the crusader armies at Las Navas de Tolosa (al-ʿUqāb in Arabic) and was murdered a year later. The next caliph in the line of succession was Abū Yaʿqūb Yūsuf II al-Muntanṣir, son of the Christian slave Qamar, who was named caliph at the age of sixteen.

### The Christian Kingdoms under the Almohad Dynasty

The Holy See wielded powerful influence over Mythic Iberia during the Almohad dominion of al-Andalus. Thanks to indulgences, many men-at-arms fought in God's name against the Muslims; united under a single banner, they won important battles and conquered strategic strongholds. During this time, as a sign of favor toward the Christian lords of Iberia, Pope Alexander III issued the bull *Regis aeterni*, which made perpetual the bull *Omnipotentis dispositione* granted by Callixtus II (see page 46). Also in this period, Saint Dominic de Guzmán of Burgos began to combat the Cathar heresy in the Languedoc (in southern France), and Saint Francis of Assisi (the Italian monk who founded the Franciscan Order) traveled to the Peninsula to walk the Way of Saint James, working many miracles on his wanderings through Iberia.

During the Almohad dominion of al-Andalus (1145–1224), the following Christian kingdoms existed:

| Kingdoms | Years |
| --- | --- |
| The Crown of Aragon | 1145–Present |
| The kingdom of Portugal | 1145–Present |
| The kingdom of Leon | 1145–Present |
| The kingdom of Pamplona | 1145–Present |
| The kingdom of Navarre | 1150–Present |
| The kingdom of Castile | 1157–Present |
| The lordship of Albarracín | 1168–Present |

#### The Crown of Aragon

After the death of Ramon Berenguer IV, his son Alfonso II ascended the throne of Aragon. Alfonso adopted the date of Christ's birth for dating the Crown's documents and summoned the first Cortes of Aragon, where he proclaimed the Peace and Truce of God (see page 33) throughout his territory. In this way he placed public order in the hands of the Crown and reduced the power of the nobility. To strengthen the monarchy still further, he decreed the royal peace, by which he protected holy places and roads and forbade waging war without a prior public challenge; in this edict he also limited reprisals between merchants of different cities and towns, preventing conflicts among his vassals.

In 1179 the Third Lateran Council was held in Rome, where the Cathar heresy that had spread through Provence was condemned. As a result, the powerful Occitan lords Roger II Trencavel, viscount of Carcassonne and Béziers, and Bernat Ató III, viscount of Nîmes and Agde, turned to Alfonso II to try to protect themselves from the threat of excommunication. With their vassalage, Alfonso II's authority was recognized throughout southern France, from Béarn to the Alps. On his death, his titles were divided between his two sons: Pedro II inherited the kingdom of Aragon and the counties of Barcelona, Gerona, Osona, Besalú, Cerdanya, Conflent, Roussillon, Pallars Jussà and Ribagorza, while Alfonso II of Provence inherited the Occitan lands that lay apart from Catalonia.

> #### Ius Maletractandi
>
> During the reign of Pedro II of Aragon, the assembly of Cervera (Lérida) was held. There, serfs were bound to pay their lords a feudal rent in the form of dues. Thus the feudal lords won the right to mistreat their peasants with numerous obligations (which lay beyond the king's power to intervene).
>
> - ***Arçia***: if the peasant's land suffered damage (such as a fire), he was obliged to pay his lord for the losses caused by the disaster.
>
> - ***Cugucia***: if the peasant induced his wife to commit adultery, the lord could keep the wife's dowry.
>
> - ***Eixorchia (or mañería)***: if the peasant died without issue, his feudal lord could keep most of his estate.
>
> - ***Firma d'espoli***: the peasant could only mortgage the land if his lord allowed it and after paying him his due.
>
> - ***Intestia***: if the peasant died without making a will, his lord could keep part of his estate.
>
> - **Farmyard privilege**: the lord could take hens, pigs and rams without paying for them.
>
> - ***Remença***: if the peasant wished to leave the land he worked and so win his freedom, he had to pay his lord to be allowed to go.
>
> - **Saca**: the peasant was obliged to pay to take grain beyond the bounds of the lordship.
>
> - **Tercería**: if the lord so wished, he could hand the management of his property to a peasant, who had to answer for any losses.

<!-- p. 54 -->

The monarch of Aragon, Pedro II, was crowned in Rome by Pope Innocent III, becoming his vassal and enfeoffing the kingdom to the Holy See; the monarch therefore undertook to pay Rome an annual census. However, his relations with the pope broke down when Innocent III declared a crusade against the Cathars of Provence, all of them vassals of Pedro II; Pedro refused to carry out the crusade and was excommunicated. Despite his journeys to Rome and his constant pleas for clemency, Pedro could not change the dire fate of his domains in Occitania. The king of Aragon died defending Toulouse from the crusaders at the tragic battle of Muret. His body was taken to the monastery of Sigena (Huesca), but, being excommunicate, he was buried outside the consecrated ground. After his death, Aragon was plunged into a serious financial crisis and passed into the hands of Jaume I, a five-year-old boy who had lost both his parents. With the defeat at Muret, the Crown lost forever the Occitan lands that had been its fiefs, fixing its border at the Pyrenees.

Jaume I's minority caused disputes over the regency of the kingdom. He was confined and kept away from power until finally, at the request of Innocent III, he was released and granted his birthright. During his minority, Aragon signed a three-year truce with the Almohads.

#### The Kingdom of Portugal

In 1147, the Anglo-Norman crusaders on their way to fight at Damascus set out from the English city of Devon and stopped over in the Portuguese city of Porto. With no king to lead the crusaders, Bishop Pedro Pitões persuaded them to help Afonso I Henriques conquer Lisbon. To win them over, the king of Portugal swapped the pope's spiritual message for a more material one: "If you help me conquer the city, I will give you everything taken as plunder." Afonso I also promised tax exemptions and land to any crusaders who wished to stay in Portugal. Lisbon was thus sacked by the crusaders and handed over to Afonso I after its conquest. That same year, the city of Santarém also fell to the Portuguese armies.

After the Portuguese attempt to conquer Badajoz, the king of Leon allied with the Almohads to halt the advance of the Portuguese monarch, Afonso I Henriques, who had also planned the conquest of important strongholds in the territories of Galicia and Salamanca. To end hostilities between the two kingdoms, a marriage was arranged between the descendants of the monarchs of Leon and Portugal. But this alliance of blood did not stop the hostilities, and the kingdoms kept fighting over the border territories during the early years of this period.

In 1179, the Holy See recognized the independence of the kingdom of Portugal with the bull *Manifestis probatum est*, issued by Pope Alexander III. The kingdom became a vassal of the Holy See and, as a result, Fernando II of Leon was forced to recognize the sovereignty of the kingdom of Portugal.

After the death of Afonso I, his son Sancho I of Portugal ascended the throne, though his accession did not come under the best of circumstances. On the one hand, the unification of al-Andalus under the Almohads endangered the kingdom's conquests (Almohad pressure forced the monarch to cede frontier strongholds to the military orders and to grant fueros and privileges to strengthen settlement in the center of the territory and the Tagus area); on the other, the Christian monarchs would have to face bad harvests and outbreaks of plague (such as the one that took the life of Dulce of Aragon, Sancho's consort).

During Sancho's reign, the conflicts with Leon flared up again after the separation of Teresa and Alfonso IX (see the "Interdicts" sidebar on the next page), and dragged on until 1200 with wars on both sides of the border. At the end of his reign, disputes began with the bishops of Porto and Coimbra, which would set off the monarchy's clashes with the Portuguese prelates.

The next Portuguese monarch in the line of succession, after the death of Sancho I, was Afonso II of Portugal, who from the outset set about strengthening royal power with a series of innovative, centralizing measures (such as the *inquirições gerais* approved in 1220, which aimed to identify which properties in northern Portugal belonged to the Crown). However, his short reign was beset from the beginning by disputes over the lordships Sancho I had left to his daughters, the *infantas*, which set him at odds with the military orders and even with Alfonso IX of Leon, in a conflict that outlived him. He also inherited from his father the disputes with the Portuguese prelates, especially after the bishop of Coimbra went to the Fourth Lateran Council (see page 305) to denounce before the Holy See the old affronts he had suffered at the hands of the Crown. On his return, the king received him with violence, and his relationship with the Church soured to such a degree that Pope Honorius III ruled that the king's decisions to demand undue tribute from ecclesiastical institutions amounted to the enslavement of the Church. On the other hand, as his grandfather had done, Afonso made use of crusaders bound for the Holy Land to conquer the stronghold of Alcácer do Sal once and for all, in a crucial victory for Portugal.

#### The Kingdom of Leon

On the death of the emperor Alfonso VII, the kingdom of Leon passed to his son, Fernando II. Taking advantage of the untimely death of his brother, Sancho III of Castile, and the civil war that had broken out over the regency, Fernando entered Castile and proclaimed himself guardian of his nephew, the child Alfonso VIII, whom he held prisoner until those loyal to Castile managed to free him.

To halt the Portuguese advance, Fernando II forged an alliance with the Almohad caliph, Abū Yaʿqūb Yūsuf, which provoked the wrath of the pope in Rome. Moreover, through his poor management he bankrupted the kingdom, and on his death his firstborn, Alfonso IX, proclaimed himself king of Leon against the opposition of his stepmother, Urraca López de Haro, who sought to crown her own son, the *infante* Sancho Fernández. To prevent this, Alfonso IX turned to his cousin, King Alfonso VIII of Castile, and, at the cost of subjugating his kingdom, paid him homage in order to secure the crown of Leon. To resolve the bankruptcy inherited from his father, Alfonso IX held a *Curia Regis* in which, for the first time, burghers and representatives of the cities took part with voice and vote, giving rise to the Cortes of the kingdom of Leon.

Taking advantage of Castile's weakness after the defeat at Alarcos, Alfonso IX signed a truce with the Almohads to obtain money and troops with which to invade the neighboring kingdom. However, he failed to defeat his cousin, Alfonso VIII of Castile, and, as a result of his pact, Pope Celestine III excommunicated him.

<!-- p. 55 -->

When the child heir to the kingdom of Castile, Enrique I, died (see below), the crown fell to Berenguela, wife of Alfonso IX of Leon and daughter of Alfonso VIII of Castile. However, Alfonso IX ended up renouncing the Castilian crown and allowed his firstborn son, Fernando III, to take the title of king of Castile.

> #### The Interdicts
>
> At the end of the twelfth century, the kingdom of Leon was placed under interdict at the behest of Celestine III, who thus punished the marriage contracted in 1191 by Alfonso IX of Leon and Teresa, daughter of Sancho I of Portugal, on the grounds of consanguinity. Despite the pope's prohibition, the couple refused to dissolve the union until, in 1196, Alfonso VIII of Castile, at the papacy's urging, forced Alfonso to separate from Teresa. Thus the kingdom lay under interdict for five years, during which the auras of the Dominion weakened.
>
> Shortly afterward, in 1197, Alfonso IX married Berenguela (daughter of Alfonso VIII of Castile and Eleanor Plantagenet), who was also related to him in the fourth degree. However, Celestine III did not declare the marriage null (perhaps because the union was so necessary to end the war between the kingdoms and so fight Islam), and it fell to Innocent III to send a papal legate to put an end to such monstrous incest. But Alfonso IX ignored the papal warnings, and Innocent excommunicated the couple and placed the kingdom under interdict. Of all the bishops, only the bishop of Oviedo sided with the pope, so Alfonso confiscated his lands, deposed him and banished him.
>
> This interdict was a serious problem for Alfonso IX, since it allowed heretics to spread through his lands (at a moment of great Almohad strength) and, moreover, ruined the priests: unable to administer the sacraments or ask for offerings, they had to take to begging or enter the service of Jewish families. Faced with this situation, the archbishop of Toledo wrote to the pope in 1199 asking him to issue a papal bull that would legalize the marriage and so end the interdict; although Innocent refused, he did lessen its severity. Nevertheless, the anathema was not lifted until 1204, when Berenguela wrote to Rome asking that her excommunication be removed, under promise of separating from her husband. In June of that same year, Alfonso renounced his wife and the pope granted him absolution.
>
> #### Story Seeds: Interdicts
>
> While a kingdom is under interdict, the level of the Dominion aura drops by one each year; the aura around towns and villages wanes when the bells stop ringing, and that of churches may dwindle almost to nothing if they stand empty.
>
> The storyguide can use these facts to let other powers thrive in the absence of the Dominion. This would be a fine opportunity for infernal (or faerie) hotspots to appear that might affect the covenants of the kingdom of Leon in the late twelfth and early thirteenth centuries. In any case, these anathemas could fuel major story arcs in your sagas.

#### The Kingdom of Pamplona and Navarre

The monarch of Navarre, Sancho VI, took advantage of the Castilian civil war to make peace with Aragon and set out to recover Logroño, Álava, Guipúzcoa and La Rioja from the king of Castile. His attacks were answered by Castile, which counterattacked by conquering several Navarrese strongholds. After years of war, they decided to end the conflict by submitting to the arbitration of the Castilian monarch's father-in-law, Henry II of England. Henry ruled that both kings must return the strongholds they had taken and restore their borders, and that the king of Castile must pay Sancho VI compensation for ten years for the damage caused.

Hemmed in between two kingdoms more powerful than his own, and with no chance of expanding at the Almohads' expense, Sancho VI strengthened his rule within the kingdom and expanded north of the Pyrenees. To this end he married his daughter to the king of England, Richard the Lionheart, who was the nominal lord of the lands north of Navarre.

On the death of Sancho VI, his son Sancho VII the Strong ascended the throne; he was said to stand more than two meters tall. His feats of arms in Gascony, alongside his friend King Richard of England, reached the ears of every monarch in Iberia. Sancho was recognized by the pope as *rex Navarrae*, which did not stop the monarch from ignoring the pope's requests that he give up the *parias* from the Almohads and begin waging war on them. Instead, he signed a perpetual peace with the Almohad caliph under which, in exchange for Sancho's help in Africa, the caliph undertook to hand over numerous domains in the Peninsula to him. Sancho VII fought for years in Africa in the service of the Almohads and, in his absence, the kings of Aragon and Castile signed an agreement to divide Navarre between them and attack his kingdom. Despite the help he had given the caliph, the Castilians conquered Vitoria and all of Álava, cutting Navarre off from the sea forever. Enraged, Sancho VII claimed the caliph's lands in Iberia, but the Almohad went back on his word, breaking the oath he had sworn. To try to mitigate this loss, Sancho signed a treaty of friendship with the king of England, John Lackland, which allowed Bayonne (France) to be used as a port of the kingdom of Navarre.

<!-- p. 56 -->

Sancho VII received the homage of the lords beyond the Pyrenees at Agramont (in Gascony) and of twenty-seven other nobles of the land of Mixe and the viscounty of Soule, extending his borders northward. At home he followed his father's policy: by unifying taxes and pursuing a sound policy of collecting border dues and urban censuses (as well as his many raids against the Muslims, from which he took great plunder), he enriched the kingdom's coffers, which allowed him to invest in infrastructure and act as a moneylender. Indeed, he was able to lend large sums of money to the monarch of Aragon, Pedro II, who in exchange handed over to him the strongholds of Peña, Escó, Petilla de Aragón, Gallur and Trasmoz (of the Aragonese kingdom).

Sancho went to the battle of Las Navas de Tolosa at the head of his own army. Determined to make the Almohad caliph pay for the loss of the Basque provinces, he fought his way to the caliph's tent, killing many Muslims. His exploits at Las Navas de Tolosa were spread throughout Iberia and beyond the Pyrenees. In 1217 he took part in the Fifth Crusade, which led to the conquest of Alcácer do Sal, and in 1219 his army took part in the ninth Iberian crusade. The pope entrusted the care of the Navarrese lands to the papal legate, Jiménez de Rada, on condition that Sancho cross the kingdom of Aragon without causing damage (which he certainly did). However, while the Navarrese monarch was fighting in the east, the knights of the dioceses of Saragossa, Tarazona and Calahorra burst into Navarre and plundered it.

#### The Kingdom of Castile

The kingdom of Castile was united with the kingdom of Leon under the crown of the emperor Alfonso VII. On his death, he divided the realm between his two sons: Sancho III inherited Castile and Fernando II inherited Leon. However, a year after his coronation, Sancho III died, leaving as heir his three-year-old son, Alfonso VIII. The struggle for control and the power of the regency plunged the kingdom into a civil war that pitted the powerful houses of Lara and Castro against each other and drew in the king of Leon, Fernando II, who was Alfonso VIII's uncle.

On turning fourteen, Alfonso was declared of age and began his reign. He married Eleanor Plantagenet of England (aged seven), daughter of King Henry II of England. The girl brought as her dowry the duchy of Gascony, which the Crown ultimately could not annex for want of the necessary vassalages, but which served to strengthen the kingdom with the arrival of many Gascon knights. Alfonso began to mint gold coins and conquered the important Almohad economic center of Mandrona la Grande (Cuenca), where saffron was grown and there was extensive stockbreeding for the sale of wool and the making of carpets.

Alfonso VIII fixed the borders between Castile and Leon in the treaty of Fresno-Lavandera, in which his uncle Fernando II and the magnates and bishops of both kingdoms took part. The peace this treaty brought allowed them to raid the Almohad territories of al-Andalus. But with the death of his uncle and the coronation of his cousin, Alfonso IX, in Leon, Alfonso VIII achieved for the first time in history that Leon paid homage to Castile, reversing the balance of power between the two kingdoms. Castile then began an aggressive policy against its neighbors. In response, the monarchs under attack signed the Treaty of Huesca, attacked Castile and began a series of battles that ended with the mediation of Pope Celestine III (see the sidebar on the previous page).

<!-- p. 57 -->

> #### The Treaty of Huesca
>
