> By this treaty, signed in the city of Huesca in 1191, the monarchs of Aragon, Leon, Portugal and Navarre agreed to make war on the kingdom of Castile to curb the growing power of Alfonso VIII, provided that none of them went to war without the approval of the others.
>
> This treaty clashed with Celestine III's wish that the Christian kingdoms fight Islam, so in 1192 he sent a papal legate: the cardinal of Sant'Angelo. The pope's aim soon bore fruit. In a short time the legate brought about peace between Castile and Aragon, and in 1194 he got Leon and Castile to sign a treaty at Tordehumos ending the war. As for Navarre, the death of Sancho VI ended that kingdom's membership in the league.
>
> However, the pope's hopes came to nothing after the defeat at Alarcos, since the Leonese monarch took advantage of Castile's weakness to start the war again.
>
> #### Studia generalia
>
> The *studia generalia* (*studium generale* in the singular) were the institutions from which the first universities of Christian Mythic Europe sprang. For a cathedral or episcopal school to merit the title of *studium generale* (granted by a monarch or the pope), it had to stand out notably in its teaching. This title came with substantial annual revenues and the following obligations:
>
> - they had to admit students from anywhere in Mythic Europe (both secular and regular);
>
> - they had to provide higher teaching in some of the established fields of knowledge (liberal arts, civil and canon law, or theology);
>
> - they had to have several masters for each of the branches of knowledge taught (the masters of the *studia* often moved from one to another to broaden their knowledge and share it with their colleagues).
>
> Shortly after the battle of Las Navas de Tolosa, Bishop Tello Téllez de Meneses urged Alfonso VIII of Castile to found the first *studium generale* in Iberia from the episcopal school of Palencia, where Saints Dominic de Guzmán and Julian (bishop of Cuenca) had studied. Its founding encouraged other *studia generalia* to arise in Mythic Europe (such as Bologna, Cambridge, Oxford or Paris). With the death of Alfonso VIII, the *studium generale* of Palencia lost royal favor and sank into a serious financial crisis.
>
> In 1218, Alfonso IX of Leon granted the title of *studium generale* to the cathedral school of Salamanca, creating the *Studii Salmantini*. This *studium* follows the model of Bologna (focused on civil law rather than on the liberal arts and theology, like Oxford and Paris), and in 1220 it is drawing many of the masters from the Palencia school.

Pursuing his expansionist policy, Alfonso VIII took advantage of the king of Navarre's absence in Africa, fighting alongside the Almohads, to seize from him the Basque provinces bordering the sea, giving Castile a northern border with Gascony. Finally, and despite his belligerent past, Alfonso signed a fifty-year peace with the monarchs of Leon, Navarre and Aragon.

> #### The Military Orders of Iberia
>
> Born to enjoy the benefits of crusade on a permanent basis, the military orders of Iberia fought the Muslims and acquired great power, both political and economic. Although this section presents them alongside the confraternities of the Peninsula (Belchite, Monreal, Barbastro and the Militia of Toledo), bear in mind that the latter take no monastic vows and so cannot be considered military orders.
>
> The lands of the military orders are organized into commanderies, the smallest administrative unit within the order. Each commandery is ruled by a commander, who is overseen by a grand commander, who in turn is overseen by a master, the highest-ranking office within the order.
>
> The first confraternity in the Peninsula was the *Militia Christi* of Belchite, founded by Alfonso I of Aragon. Its aims were to defend the southern frontier against the Muslims (especially Saragossa), to fortify and resettle the lands conquered from the infidels and to liberate the holy places, including distant Jerusalem. Four years later, Alfonso I founded the Confraternity of Monreal (Teruel), which would absorb that of Belchite in the mid-twelfth century and would in turn be absorbed by the Temple a few years later. In those years two more confraternities appeared in the Peninsula: the Confraternity of Barbastro (founded by Bishop Gaufredo) and the Militia of Toledo (founded by the emperor Alfonso VII of Leon to fight the Muslims).
>
> After the disappearance of the Confraternity of Monreal, a group of knights from Salamanca founded the Order of Knighthood of San Julián del Pereiro beside the river Coa. When, in 1218, Alfonso IX of Leon entrusted them with the defense of the city of Alcántara, the order adopted the town as its seat. By 1220 it is starting to be known as the Order of Alcántara.
>
> In 1158, under pressure from the Almohad armies, the Templars abandoned the city of Calatrava, and Sancho III of Castile summoned the Cortes to offer the strategic city to whoever could defend it. Amid the silence of all the nobles, the Cistercian abbot Raimundo Serra of Fitero, encouraged by one of his monks, the former warrior Diego de Velázquez, volunteered. The king, resigned, entrusted the city and its defense to the monastery of Fitero: thus was born the mighty Order of Calatrava, initially charged with defending the crossings of the Tagus.
>
> After Fernando II of Leon conquered Cáceres, he entrusted the defense of the city to thirteen knights. At the head of the defenders was Pedro Fernández de Castro, who, having witnessed the power of the Templars in the Holy Land, founded with his companions the *Congregatio* of Cáceres. Despite their courage, they could not defend the city against the Almohads and had to flee. The knights of Cáceres devoted their lives to protecting the pilgrims on the Way of Saint James and watching over the borders of the Leonese Extremadura and the Tagus (together with the knights of Calatrava). In the last quarter of the twelfth century, the knights joined the canons regular of Saint Augustine to form the Order of Santiago.
>
> The Order of Saint Mary of Mountjoy of Jerusalem was created in Aragon by one of the counts who founded the Order of Santiago. A detachment of these knights fought and died at the battle of the Horns of Hattin against the armies of the sultan of Egypt, Saladin. At the end of the twelfth century the order was absorbed by the Temple, and the knights who rejected the union founded the Order of Monfragüe in the castle of Cáceres. In 1220 they are on the point of merging with the Order of Calatrava by order of Fernando III of Castile.
>
> After the conquest of Lisbon, a group of Portuguese knights banded together to fight the Muslims wherever they found them. Afonso I Henriques of Portugal entrusted the defense of the city of Évora to these knights, who went on to form the Order of Évora. The Portuguese order (always supported by the Order of Calatrava) conquered the town of Avis in 1211 and moved its seat there, after which it became known as the Order of Avis.
>
> With the coming of the thirteenth century, Pedro II of Aragon founded the Order of Saint George of Alfama in honor of his patron saint. The knights of Saint George fought at the battle of Las Navas de Tolosa and accompanied their king when he fought on the side of the Cathars against the crusader armies sent by the pope. The knights faced the dilemma of having to fight on behalf of heretics and, when Pedro II fell at the battle of Muret in 1213, the order was dissolved.
>
> In 1203, a Barcelona cloth merchant named Pedro Nolasco began to organize expeditions, at his own expense, to free Christian captives from Muslim hands. In 1218 the Virgin Mary appeared to him and commanded him to found a religious order to carry on his work. Jaume I of Aragon thus authorized the founding of the Order of Mercy, whose knights are ready to give their lives in exchange for the freedom of Christian captives and slaves.

<!-- p. 58 -->

On the death of Alfonso VIII, his ten-year-old son Enrique I was crowned, becoming king of Castile and lord of Guipúzcoa. The young monarch never came to govern, for three years later he died when a roof tile fell on his head while he was playing. The crown passed to the boy's elder sister, Berenguela, who was the queen consort of the king of Leon (Alfonso IX). However, the monarchs of Leon ended up renouncing the crown in favor of their son Fernando. As a result, Fernando III took the title of king of Castile and ratified the peace that Alfonso VIII had signed with Leon, Navarre and Aragon. In 1219, Fernando III was knighted and married Beatrice of Swabia (of the Holy Roman Empire).

#### The Lordship of Albarracín

In 1168, the Wolf King gave this taifa to Pedro Ruiz de Azagra, lord of Estella and vassal of the king of Navarre, in gratitude for the help the Navarrese monarch had given him against the Almohads. The king of Navarre legitimized his possession of the lordship two years later and, after the Wolf King's death in 1172, Ruiz de Azagra relied on the archbishop of Toledo to consecrate Martín of Toledo as bishop of Arcábica, thereby making the episcopal see of his lordship independent of Aragon.

## Iberia in 1220

In 1220, barely eight years after the battle of Las Navas de Tolosa and three since the battle of Alcácer do Sal, the Christian crowns have signed lasting peace agreements, creating a climate of harmony and unity in which to fight the waning Almohad dynasty.

### The Almohad Empire

The Almohad caliph al-Muntanṣir has neglected the government of his realm and delegated all his power to an oligarchy made up of members of his family: his uncles rule in Iberia, and his second cousin in Tunis. While in North Africa the Almohads have put down the threat of the Banū Marin (who did in fact manage to conquer Melilla), in Iberia, lacking a figure to centralize power and after the army's defeat in the decisive battles of Las Navas de Tolosa and Alcácer do Sal, they face numerous revolts that help destabilize a government already battered by the relentless advance of the Christian monarchs.

In 1220, the governor and prince of Seville has ordered the construction of *Borg-al-Azajal* (the Torre del Oro, or Tower of Gold), to complete the defenses of the empire's splendid capital in the Peninsula.

<!-- p. 59 -->

> #### Markets, Fairs and Souks
>
> ##### Christian Markets and Fairs
>
> The first network of fairs in Christian Iberia appeared in the mid-twelfth century in cities such as Palencia, Carrión, Valladolid, Sahagún and Castrogonzalo, whose main activity takes place during the summer months. At the fairs, magi or their servants can find a great many products that would be hard to obtain otherwise, such as manufactured goods (cloth, timber, iron), livestock (from Asturias, Cantabria and the kingdom of Leon), fish (conger eels, dried and salted fish, mainly from Galicia) and grain (rye, wheat and barley).
>
> In 1220, the main fairs of Iberia are spread across the whole of the Christian peninsula.
>
> - **Valladolid:** possibly the most important fair in Christian Iberia (established in 1155).
>
> - **Sahagún:** under the control of the monastery of Sahagún (in Leon, established in 1155).
>
> - **Carrión:** under the control of the monastery of Carrión (in Palencia, established in 1169).
>
> - **Santa Marina de Castrogonzalo:** will move to the city of Benavente in 1220.
>
> - **Mondoñedo:** the town holds an annual fair in August (in Lugo, since the twelfth century).
>
> - **Alcalá:** in Madrid (since 1184).
>
> - **Brihuega:** in Guadalajara (since 1215).
>
> ##### Muslim Souks
>
> The most prominent place in the souks of the main cities of al-Andalus (such as Seville, Granada and Jaén) is the bakery, where every family goes to knead the bread it eats. To do so they must buy the wheat they need in the souk and then take it to the mill, which belongs to the State (but is leased to an official), to grind it into flour. The bakery houses the communal ovens, tended by a baker who is paid in kind: each family gives him a piece of its dough, which he takes as his wage, to bake and sell in the market along with all kinds of sweets. Among these are Persian *falúdh* (made with wheat seeds and bees' honey), *jabis* (fried wheat cakes, crushed and mixed with plenty of honey, made with lard, egg white and spices such as saffron, cinnamon or pepper), *al-qubaitá* (sesame paste cooked with honey), dates stuffed with starch and *al-muŷabbana* (a sort of fritter made with flour, sugar and cheese and filled with honey).
>
> The next most important establishment in the souks is the butcher's, which sells fried fish, *harīsa* (boiled wheat toasted with chicken), sausages, skewers of meatballs of minced lamb, beef or goat, cured meat and rabbit (*qunilya*, which makes up a good part of the diet in the Muslim cities of Spain). Bear in mind that livestock is never slaughtered in the souk, but outside the city.
>
> In the souks one can also buy fats (such as oils and lard, the latter considered a luxury item), pulses, fruits and nuts (figs and melons being especially prized), spices (indeed, the spice-sellers' guild is grouped in one area of the souk named after them: *al-ʿat-tārīn*) and fruit and vegetables sold by the *muʿālich*. One can also find building tradesmen, such as masons, carpenters and makers of tiles and bricks; hire the services of craftsmen (cabinetmakers, potters, glassmakers and ivory workers); or buy lime from the lads who prepare it. Nor is there any lack of blacksmiths, nail makers, farriers, brass workers, basket makers and esparto weavers and, of course, makers of parchment and paper (indeed, many magi travel to the city of Játiva to obtain the best paper in Mythic Europe).
>
> The souk is also the place to buy slaves (mostly from Gāna and northern Europe) and animals such as donkeys, mules, magnificent chargers and mares (such as those of Seville).
>
> Those who wish to buy clothing or garments (such as the costly tunics of cloth of gold bought by the richest magi of Iberia) must go to a special market called the *marqatān*, home to weavers, dyers, tailors (*jayyāt*), embroiderers, furriers, tanners and shoemakers (*jarrāz*), where all kinds of materials, such as linen and silk, are worked.
>
> Besides the souks and markets, the streets of the great cities are full of storytellers (*quṣṣāṣ*), fortune-tellers (*jussāb*), bathhouse owners (with masseurs, barbers and hairdressers, or *al-maššāṭīn*), physicians, apothecaries, musicians, dancers and prostitutes.

### The Christian Kingdoms

The lordship of Albarracín keeps its independence after numerous attempts at conquest by Castile and Aragon. In 1220, the lord of Albarracín, Pedro Fernández de Azagra, will start the first noble revolt against Jaume I of Aragon. The young monarch will respond by besieging the city, which will put down the revolt, but he will fail to annex the lordship.

Aragon is ruled by Jaume I, who at only twelve years old has signed an alliance with the king of Navarre, Sancho VII the Strong. Thanks to it, in the coming years he will be able to expand his kingdom southward at the Almohads' expense.

The young monarch Fernando III of Castile has not yet begun to fight the Almohads (he will sign a truce with their caliph in 1221), although in 1224 he will take up the terms of the crusade preached by the pope and set out to conquer new lands to the south of his kingdom.

The monarch of Leon, Alfonso IX, has made peace with his neighboring kingdoms: Castile (ruled by his son) and Portugal. Alfonso is keen to strengthen his kingdom, stop his subjects from emigrating to other lands and curb the growing power of the bishops and nobles. In 1220 he will lead a raid against Seville that will bring him rich plunder.

Sancho VII the Strong, monarch of Navarre, continues his policy of expansion beyond the Pyrenees, adding to his holdings of strategic strongholds beyond Navarre's borders.

In Portugal, Afonso II the Fat has managed to stabilize his kingdom, which is free to fight the Muslims since it enjoys a peace treaty with the monarchs of Castile and Leon. However, he must contend with the Portuguese prelates, in a conflict that will end with his excommunication in mid-1220.

<!-- p. 60 -->

## Iberia beyond 1220

What follows is a very brief chronology of the most notable mundane events after the canonical start of the game.

- 1225. Jaume I, aged sixteen, launches the conquest of the eastern Peninsula, beginning with Peñíscola so as to reach Valencia.
- 1230. Concord of Benavente: union of the crowns of Castile and Leon.
- 1229. Jaume I the Conqueror begins his campaigns to conquer Valencia (the whole territory taken by 1245) and Majorca (until 1231).
- 1236. Conquest of Cordoba by Fernando III of Castile, known as "the Saint."
- 1238. The Nasrid kingdom of Granada is created.
- 1246. Conquest and Pact of Jaén: the Nasrid king of Granada declares himself a vassal of Fernando III and must pay him *parias* to keep his independence.
- 1248. Conquest of Seville by Fernando III of Castile.
- 1269. Fall of the capital and last stronghold of the Almohads, and therefore of their empire: Marrākeš surrenders to the Marinid Berbers.
- 1284. Pedro III of Aragon conquers the independent lordship of Albarracín, which until then had been held by the Azagra family.

> #### Story Seeds: The Thieving Pigeons
>
> When one of the covenant's magi is interrupted by a pigeon bursting into his study, he discovers that it is no ordinary bird, but a beast of virtue (see *Realms of Power: Magic*, page 69). After capturing it and looking into where it came from, he learns that one of the covenant's grogs bought it in the souk of the nearest city. Questioning the grog, he finds out that he bought it to steal a brooch from one of the local nobles and give it to a lady of the covenant with whom he is in love. Luckily for the magus, the grog didn't buy just one pigeon but half a dozen — all of them beasts of virtue!
>
> When he goes with the grog to the souk stall where he bought them, he finds that it has been replaced by another selling donkeys. Where is the strange merchant who sold pigeons? Unfortunately, the sale of thieving pigeons is banned in the cities, and he has most likely been arrested by the ṣāḥib al-madīna. Will the characters arrive in time, before the merchant is executed? If so, where did he get the beasts of virtue? And, more importantly, has he managed to breed a magical lineage of pigeons? On the other hand, what if the grog had succeeded in stealing the coveted brooch? What if the lady had walked through the city wearing it? Could the magi be linked to the theft?

> #### Some Historical Notes
>
> To add more color to your saga, here are three curiosities to bear in mind.
>
> - In Iberia the heater shield is not used (as it is in the rest of Europe); instead, the adarga is used (though it uses the heater shield's statistics). This shield of Islamic origin consists of one or two overlapping oval pieces and is made by joining several layers of leather hardened with vinegar.
>
> - Although there were foot soldiers who used swords (*suyūf*), they were normally equipped with spears, shields, maces (*dammāgāt*) or a kind of axe known as *ṭabarzināt* (a word of Persian origin). For all weapons, see the statistics on page 260 of *Ars Magica Fifth Edition*.
>
> - As a general rule (and again unlike the rest of Europe), the moats of Iberian fortresses are dry: no fortress beyond the Pyrenees fills them with water.

# III. Hermetic History and Culture

*[…] true human perfection […] consists in the acquisition of the intellectual virtues, that is, in conceiving intelligible forms that can give us sound ideas on metaphysical matters. Herein lies the ultimate end of man, which confers on the human being a true perfection; it belongs to him alone, through it he attains immortality, and through it man is truly man.*[^p63-27]

[^p63-27]: Excerpt from Maimonides' *The Guide for the Perplexed* (Spanish translation by David Gonzalo Maeso).

The Hermetic history and culture of Iberia is deeply intertwined with its mythic history and society; mundane politics has left its mark on the attitudes of the Tribunal ever since the Order first occupied it, following the second meeting of the First Tribunal, and since its official constitution at the seventh Grand Tribunal (898).

This section briefly recounts the most important events in the Iberian Tribunal in chronological order. Throughout it you will find numerous entries of the Peripheral Code, marked with the year of their approval according to the official Iberian chronology (established by the covenant of Duresca) and with the presiding Quaesitor in parentheses. Since the Tribunal was officially founded in 898, the earlier entries were assimilated into the Peripheral Code after the fact, although for the sake of simplicity they are recorded in the same way. Unless otherwise stated, all the entries were approved at the subsequent Grand Tribunals.

Any character who succeeds in an Intelligence + Iberian Tribunal Lore roll against an Ease Factor of 6 knows the broad outline of the events detailed in this section. Likewise, anyone who succeeds in an Intelligence + Code of Hermes roll of 6+ can draw upon the entries of the Iberian Peripheral Code described here. Bear in mind that there are several exceptions to this rule: first, the meetings held at Lucis up to 799 were recorded at that covenant, which vanished a year later. Furthermore, any minutes predating the Duresca manuscripts may have been lost or destroyed. Finally, the clause approved at the Tribunal of 1025 (see the Peripheral Code entry "On the Diedne Legacy") means that the records relating to House Diedne may have been altered or deleted. Such knowledge is therefore left in the storyguide's hands, to be used as she sees fit.

## The First Settlers

The Order of Hermes was founded at Durenmar (domus magna of House Bonisagus) in the year 767; Bonisagus and the rest of the Founders swore the Hermetic Oath at what became known as the first meeting of the Order's First Tribunal. That same year, Flambeau departed with several of his followers for the Pyrenees, where between 767 and 773 he founded the powerful and legendary covenant of Val-Negra (the former domus magna of House Flambeau, officially constituted in 774), around which a regional Tribunal would eventually form. Many other magi set out after the Founders at that time and settled in other parts of Mythic Europe, following the model of the covenant of Durenmar.

In those days the regional Tribunals had not yet been created. Indeed, it was not until 773, at the second meeting of the First Tribunal of the Rhine (also held at Durenmar), that they were officially constituted. However, this meeting did not define their borders, nor all of the present-day boundaries; the Tribunals were no more than groupings of like-minded covenants, and to be constituted they had to comprise at least four covenants and twelve magi.

Scattered though they were, there were few members of the Order in Europe, and magi still had to travel to Durenmar to stay in touch with the central authority and to settle any disputes that arose among them. In those times trust among the magi of the Order was not especially firm, so the region that would become the future Iberian Tribunal saw a modest flowering of small covenants inhabited by one or two Hermetic magi. The first four Hermetic settlements on the Peninsula avoided the pull of mighty Val-Negra in the Pyrenees; they were founded after the second meeting of the First Tribunal and constituted during the first Rhine Tribunal, in the year 780. Thus were born Salionca, Brigantia, Duresca and Lucis, all of them in the north of the Peninsula and therefore far from the dreaded *saḥirs* (non-Hermetic sorcerers who had killed Flambeau's master and who lived in al-Andalus).

Of these four covenants, Salionca and Brigantia (both still inhabited today) were conceived by Flambeau as strongholds from which to coordinate the Order's expansion through the magical conquest of the broad lands of Iberia. For that reason, when the future founders of Salionca and Brigantia crossed the Pyrenees, they settled near the Ebro, not far from Val-Negra but at a sufficient distance to rule a vast region independent of the Founder's covenant. There they held a meeting of which no written record survives, since it was nothing more than a council of war to debate the best strategies for attacking the non-Hermetic enclaves known to the magi of that time; the site of Brigantia may also have been chosen at that point.

<!-- p. 64 -->

> #### The Campaigns of Grimoald Niger
>
> Some followers of House Flambeau in the Tribunal consider the Basque Grimoald Niger *filius* Flambeau (one of the founders of Salionca) to have been a key figure in the creation of the Iberian Tribunal. This powerful magus took part in the first campaigns waged to subdue the Peninsula, and a chronicle of his deeds survives, probably written by one of his followers or perhaps one of his apprentices (no one agrees on this point), which proved an important source of knowledge for the mapping work the Mercere later undertook to locate the Peninsula's magical resources. Furthermore, it is customary among the Flambeau to follow the route described in this chronicle to commemorate Grimoald's exploits.
>
> Although the original manuscript was lost, the magi of Salionca keep a transcription from the early ninth century, from which numerous copies were made. As a result, anyone interested in these chronicles can find them in Salionca's library, where for one pawn of vis they may copy or study them as they wish.
>
> ##### Comentarii de Bello Iberico
>
> *Tractatus* on Iberian Tribunal Lore<br>
> Quality 6
>
> Narrated in the third person and written in verse, the book is divided into three parts of unequal size (the length shrinks and the detail fades as the text goes on, so that the third part is substantially shorter than the first).
>
> In the first part of the tale, which covers his journeys through northern Iberia, the chronicler sets the beginning of the action on Mount *Orçiren çorita*, which he says was their first stop after leaving Val-Negra in the Pyrenees. Some have turned to this text in the hope of finding some evidence of the whereabouts of the old Flambeau domus magna; however, as with many parts of this tale, the text is convoluted and obscure, and offers nothing but misleading clues from which no one has been able to make anything clear, although that does not stop someone in every generation from wanting to try again.
>
> In the text, after coming down from the mountain, Grimoald and his band cross Roncesvalles and follow the old Roman road of the Ebro until they reach a cliff beside a river, where a white stone the size of a small table is described. Today it is fully accepted that this must have been the place Grimoald and his people chose to establish the stronghold of Salionca. From here the text describes how the company follows the Roman road across the land of the Vascones until it reaches Abelania, where the chronicler relates with hardly any embellishment how Grimoald stops to pray at the foot of the tomb of King Pelagius and his queen Gaudiosa. From this point on, various encounters with non-Hermetic sorcerers are described, possibly former members of the cult of Mercury or of the Roman cult of Mithras. The end of this part describes Grimoald's battle with the sorcerer Leuvigild, whom he managed to defeat after nine months of fighting. According to the chronicler, this victory was a great step forward for the Order in Iberia: "besides pacifying the lands nearest to Val-Negra, with the surrender of Leuvigild the rest of the sorcerers belonging to the old Roman cults throughout Iberia joined." Scholars of the treatise consider this assessment an exaggeration, although it is true that the old followers of Mercury on the Peninsula emigrated to Provence (their cult was revitalized at Val-Negra under the guidance of Priamitus of Mercere with the help of Apromor of Flambeau), where their legacy can still be found in 1220.
>
> After his struggle with Leuvigild, Grimoald and his band continue their journey until they reach the lands of the Pataric giants (see page 146), where, after a violent battle described in more than a hundred verses, the chronicler abruptly concludes with the triumph of the Flambeau over Equión, king of the giants. Without further ado, the narrative continues, amid geographical references now lost (although they are believed to have been in the old kingdom of Asturias), with the magical assault that Grimoald's Flambeau launched against the Astur vates, or augurs. In the narrative, the leader of the Astur hosts, a *hieroskópo* priest,[^p64-XX] is named Balaudos Petrocirios. Despite the importance of this encounter, the chronicler dispatches it in barely fifty verses; in his account, the confrontation ends at the beginning of the second year, when, at the summer solstice of 778, Grimoald slays Balaudos and leaves the fighting in the hands of one of his apprentices, whom he does not name, in order to press on westward.
>
> The tale continues into the Galician lands, where, at the end of the world, Grimoald confronts what by all appearances are tempestarii (see page 299). This encounter is even briefer than the last. According to the chronicler, Grimoald destroys the leader of the tempestarii and annihilates all his followers, making possible the founding of the covenant of Brigantia, which he calls Geriona. Of course, the historical value of this encounter is slight, since the conflicts with the tempestarii dragged on until the end of the eighth century. With this encounter over, the copyist gives thanks to God and brings the first part of the chronicles of Grimoald Niger to a close.
>
> In the second part of the book, the chronicler relates the journey of Grimoald and his companions-in-arms toward the south of Iberia. It mentions their passage through the city of Velegia and the region of the Bardulias, and their arrival on the banks of the river Durius. After they cross it, the tale focuses on describing several places of power and touches briefly on some encounters with non-Hermetic sorcerers whom Grimoald subdues without difficulty. This part concludes with the conquest of Augusta Emerita, where Grimoald defeats the worshippers of the daimons (see *Realms of Power: Magic*, page 106) of the second sphere in twenty-one days. The copyist adds the date on which he finished copying this part and appends an epilogue extolling the valor of the Flambeau over the rest of the Founders.
>
> The third part of the book is the shortest and recounts Grimoald's battles against the *saḥirs*. The style changes in these last pages, shifting from verse to rhymed prose (perhaps because of the death of the previous chronicler, or because it is an apocryphal text added later). The epic culminates with Grimoald's battle and victory against a dozen *jinn* at the Pillars of Hercules, described cursorily in fewer than a hundred lines. Its ending is ambiguous, for it hints that after his victory Grimoald fell into a Twilight from which he has yet to return: "he pursued the demons in their flight and vanished from the world." The book ends with a copyist's epilogue that Salionca never discloses with the copies it provides to visitors. The reason? They have never been willing to explain it.
>
> [^p64-XX]: Described by the Greek geographer Strabo (first century BC), they were a priestly caste of Asturias (augurs) charged with sacrificing prisoners of war and making predictions by studying their entrails, with powers of divination based on observing the flight of birds and lightning.

<!-- p. 65 -->

### De belli flambonis

*[…] if the warrior perceives the fire that announces war […], he readies himself for battle and prepares* *for it as if he had seen the battle itself with his senses. […] His judgment of future things proceeds from his judgment of present things.*[^p65-28]

[^p65-28]: Excerpt from Averroes' *Middle Commentary on Aristotle's "On the Soul"* (Spanish translation by Abdelali Elamrani-Yamȃl, taken from the treatise *On the Intellect*).

Described in great detail in the book of the campaigns of Grimoald Niger, the wars waged by the Flambeau pacified the regions bordering the Pyrenees, the northwestern quarter of the Peninsula (except the domains of the Galician sorcerers, both tempestarii and vates) and the central plateau as far as the Sierra Morena, where the domain of the *saḥirs* began. Naturally, both Salionca and Brigantia played a leading role during this first period.

During the battles to conquer the Peninsula, the non-Hermetic groups that could not hold back the onslaughts of the Flambeau ended up joining the Order. Yet despite the Flambeau's efforts, not all of Iberia was conquered during this first period. Indeed, the magi who abhor those years of barbarity point out that only a small part of the territory of the present Tribunal was conquered; for all the blood that was shed, not even northern Iberia came over to the Order's side, for the vates and the tempestarii mounted a formidable resistance to the Hermetic occupation.

The dismal results of these campaigns have often been held up by the Criamon of the Peninsula in contrast to the successes achieved through diplomacy in the following years. According to them, that was when the identity of the future Iberian Tribunal took shape. To add insult to injury, some stress that this eighth-century treatise describes a great many non-Hermetic traditions of which nothing remains today, some of them truly wondrous, to judge by its account of them. The Flambeau scorn such ideas, and on more than one occasion disputes of this kind have been taken to the Tribunals or settled through *certamina* or Wizard's Wars.

## The Preaching

Hermetic scholars mark the year 782 as the start of a period they call "the Preaching," and agree that it ended in the year 800, a year after the third Grand Tribunal was held.

This period marked the beginning of a change in the policy of the region's magi, for the first truces were made and negotiations began with the non-Hermetic traditions of the Peninsula, setting aside the armed conflicts that had prevailed until then. The most important figures were Ranemiro of Sahagún (see the insert on the next page) and Tancoystl of Diedne, foundress of Duresca.

In the year 780, shortly after the disappearance of Grimoald Niger, the magi of the Peninsula traveled to the Rhine to hold their first Tribunal. During the meeting, Ranemiro of Guernicus set out the difficulties being encountered on the Peninsula: vates, tempestarii and *saḥirs* were fiercely resisting the Order's advances and, after seven years of fighting, the conflict had intensified. Ranemiro and Tancoystl then called for a vote to have the Flambeau fighting on the Peninsula grant them a truce, which the Flambeau accepted only after the *saḥirs* were excluded from any kind of negotiation. The Rhine Tribunal endorsed the agreement among the magi of the Peninsula, and Ranemiro summoned his *sodales* to Lucis to settle the details of the truce.

### Lucis, the First Peninsular Meeting

In 782 Ranemiro hosted the meeting at Lucis to define the terms of the truce between the Order and the Galician tempestarii and Astur vates, opening what would be the first regional minutes of the Peninsula, attended by the region's only four covenants: Lucis, Salionca, Duresca and Brigantia.

The meeting framed the terms of the truce in light of the harm the war was causing them, and set a deadline of no more than ten years (until 792) to bring the lineages of the north of the Peninsula into the Order. If no agreement had been reached after that time, negotiations would be deemed over and the lineages would be subdued by force.

### Negotiations with the Vates and the Tempestarii

Tancoystl of Diedne was charged with conveying the decision to the spiritual leader of the vates, Clutoso, and to his *hieroskópo* priest, Ágila (son of Balaudos Petrocirios), since she was on good terms with them. Both agreed to meet Ranemiro at Lucis, where he recorded their interviews in meticulous detail, and where, two years later, the vates agreed to join the Order on condition that their mysteries remain within House Diedne and that their places of worship be respected.

> #### The Sorginas
>
> The history of the Basque and Navarrese witches is told in the sourcebook for the Provençal Tribunal (see the bibliography), since its borders encompass most of their lands. This witch tradition remained outside the Order when other minor traditions joined House Ex Miscellanea. Attempts to annex it failed, and in 1220 they are still not part of the Order of Hermes.

<!-- p. 66 -->

> #### Ranemiro of Sahagún
>
> Ranemiro was born in Sahagún, near the shrine of *Domnos Sanctos*, which held the relics of Saints Facundus and Primitivus. While he was still a child, his uncle Alfonso, a Mozarab of the Toledan nobility, decided to send him to study at the abbey of Monte Cassino, in the *Terra Sancti Benedicti*.
>
> Ranemiro took the vows of the Benedictine order and studied the 73 chapters of the *Regula Sancti Benedicti*. Although he could have stayed at Monte Cassino, he decided to return to Iberia to join a small group of religious led by Máximo and Fromestano who, with the leave of the king of Asturias, Fruela I, were building a monastery at Oueto (not far from the Roman ruins of Lucus Asturum) dedicated to the Valencian martyr Saint Vincent.
>
> Ranemiro first heard of the Order of Hermes during his second winter in the now completed monastery of San Vicente, from the lips of an Italian nobleman named Oderisio. The knight, who had sought shelter from the storm, told them of this new Order: "made up of women and men, and inspired by the writings of the holy Bonisagus." When he left, everyone took him for a madman… However, a week after his departure, Ranemiro had a revelation as he slept: Saint Benedict spoke into his right ear and charged him with watching over the new Order, so that it would not fall into sin and would thus remain in the service of God.
>
> Although at first Ranemiro paid no heed to that "dream," within a week his ears began to bleed and his eyes to weep, signs he interpreted as punishment for his disobedience. To set matters right, Ranemiro asked Abbot Fromestano for permission to leave the monastery and carry out his holy mission. He knew at once that he had done the right thing, for the very next day his ears stopped bleeding and his sight was no longer clouded by tears. Before leaving the Peninsula, he visited his uncle Alfonso in Toledo and made his confession before none other than Elipandus, archbishop of the city, who confirmed him in his task. And so, at Santa María de Alfizén, Ranemiro swore to carry out what Saint Benedict had asked of him.
>
> With little to go on, Ranemiro followed the few leads Oderisio had left, and his inquiries took him to Piedmont, from where he reached Harco, domus magna of House Mercere (not far away, Flambeau was fighting the sorcerer Varstus in the Alps, and in Iberia, Grimoald and his band were blazing a path southward through the Peninsula). At Harco, Ranemiro was received by one of Mercere's sons, Priamitus, who, after conversing with him for a few days, granted him passage to Durenmar, where he was trained in the Arts and in Hermetic theory by the Founder Guernicus. When his apprenticeship was over, Ranemiro returned to Oviedo, where he began to devise a way to carry out his holy task.

<!-- p. 67 -->

Their capitulation was a turning point for many other sorcerers of smaller traditions, for whom the peace with the vates served as an incentive to come to Duresca or Lucis to learn about the Order without running any risk. But it was not so with the tempestarii. In 785 Ranemiro was gravely wounded when he violated one of their sanctuaries, and Tancoystl had to take charge of the negotiations. Despite the warnings of Ágila (his prophecies foretold nothing but war), the Diedne maga kept drawing closer to them until she was accepted among the priests of the storms, at which point she managed to seat one of their elders across from Ranemiro, in 787, after he swore an oath to keep the cult's secrets. Four years later, the Peninsula's magi went to the Rhine Tribunal to announce the success of their negotiations. To the Flambeau's displeasure, the Tribunal was so pleased that the negotiations were extended by another ten years.

That same year, Ranemiro again summoned the Peninsula's magi to renew the terms of the truce the Flambeau had signed in 782 and to address certain matters of concern to the magi of the Peninsula, so that these could be presented at the next Rhine Tribunal. However, a season after that meeting, Tancoystl discovered that the situation had changed radically. The tempestarii seemed to have lost what little interest they had in belonging to the Order and barred her from their sanctuaries. The Diedne heard nothing more until the summer of 792, when one of the elders appeared at Duresca to tell her that they were willing to reach an agreement on certain conditions: the tempestarii were to form a new House to keep their mysteries safe, and Ranemiro had to expel the Christian priests who lived near their sanctuaries. Tancoystl knew then that no negotiation was possible, and when she passed this on to Ranemiro, he refused to go any further. That same year, Tancoystl again summoned all the magi to Duresca and announced that the negotiations had failed.

### The Fall of the Tempestarii

Ranemiro stepped aside to make way for the Flambeau and the Tremere of the Peninsula, now led by the leader of Brigantia, Dehewint of Flambeau. To Tancoystl's dismay, Ranemiro broke his word and gave them all the information he had obtained in the negotiations with the tempestarii: identities, known powers, settlements and sanctuaries, although he could not hand over the secrets that only she knew and kept to herself.

The magi attacked the northern settlements where they knew the sorcerers lived, but without bringing down a single tempestarius: it was as if they could foresee their movements. However, many innocent lives were taken, and when the tempestarii struck back, their response was terrible: storms ravaged the north of the Peninsula for months; lands were flooded, the sea grew so wild that it could not be sailed, Brigantia was destroyed, and Dehewint and two Tremere who had left the short-lived covenant of Prima died. The scale of the conflict drew the attention of the mundanes of the kingdom of Asturias, and Tancoystl again summoned the Peninsula's magi to her covenant of Duresca in the year 794.

<!-- p. 68 -->

During the meeting Tancoystl and the former vates were accused of having collaborated with the tempestarii, and Ranemiro forced them to share the secrets of the storm sorcerers and to remain at Duresca. Using unorthodox methods, Ranemiro obtained from his old friend the information the magi of the Order craved: the location of the tempestarii's most important sanctuary and focus of power, on the western coast of Asturias. At the spring equinox of 794 the Peninsula's magi performed a ritual to devastate the beach where the tempestarii worshipped their gods, destroying the focus of their power and, possibly, the richest vis source in Iberia. The blow was decisive. After the battle, most of the tempestarii chose death over joining the Order; those who did join (mostly the young) entered House Diedne, so the inner mysteries of the tempestarii were lost, and the descendants of the survivors possess no more than a small fraction of their power (see page 299).

### The Expulsion of Ranemiro and the Disappearance of Lucis

The consequences of the battle against the tempestarii reached the Rhine Tribunal, and Ranemiro, as the Quaesitor in charge of the negotiations, had to appear before the Grand Tribunal of 799. Guernicus ruled that the battle against the tempestarii had violated the Code, so Ranemiro lost his quaesitorial authority and was expelled from the Order. The rest of the Peninsula's magi were admonished and fined, the fine to be paid over seven years.

After his expulsion, the aged Ranemiro, who had never performed his Longevity Ritual because he believed it contrary to God's will, returned to his covenant, shut himself in his chapel and began to pray. That is how Grimoald's former apprentice, Égica of Flambeau, should have found him when he came to carry out the Grand Tribunal's sentence in the spring of the year 800; however, on reaching Lucis he found nothing but ruins, inexplicably ancient in appearance. According to the covenant's sole survivor, Tello of Guernicus *filius* Ranemiro, his *parens* and Lucis had ascended to the Divine realm. Strange as the statement was, Égica confirmed the presence of a powerful Divine aura at the site.

## The Transition

The disappearance of Lucis marks the end of the second period of Iberia's history and the start of what scholars call "the Transition." In this period the Carolingian Empire began to break apart, the regional Tribunals became distinct from one another, and the Order suffered its first crisis. The most prominent figure of this time is Somnus of Tremere, an aged magus who arrived from Lycaneon in 801, whose end coincides with the close of this period and the Sundering.

After the disappearance of Lucis, Salionca called a meeting in 801 to settle how to pay the fine the Grand Tribunal had imposed on them. To cover the fine and the losses they had suffered in the wars, the magi drafted the first clause of what would become the future Peripheral Code of Iberia, which in the end would serve to finance the wars against the *saḥirs* until the year 864 (see below). However, when they brought their proposal before the Grand Tribunal of 817, the gathering did not approve it, and the Peninsula's magi decided to apply it in their territory even though they had not been constituted as a regional Tribunal for lack of a *quorum*.

***801 AD, On the Iberian Tax*** *(Quinto of Guernicus)* Any covenant on the Peninsula that can demonstrate its work on behalf of the Order may request a payment to defray the costs of its labors. To meet such demands, every covenant on the Peninsula must deliver three pawns of vis of any Art to the treasury of Salionca every five years. The same covenant may not request this service twice within a period of less than ten years. Requests will be assessed by the judges of the Peninsula, and the vis will be kept at Salionca.

The meeting also decided to gather the existing minutes of the Peninsula and keep them at the covenant of Salionca. In compliance with this rule, Duresca handed over the minutes of the meeting it had held in 794, at which the attack on the tempestarii's focus of power had been agreed.

***801 AD, On the Peninsular Minutes*** *(Quinto of Guernicus)* The minutes of the Peninsula shall be kept at the covenant of Salionca.

### The Struggle against Damhan-Allaidh

The Order suffered its first Order-wide crisis during this second period of the future Iberian Tribunal. While the Peninsula's magi were still fighting the *saḥirs* in al-Andalus, the sorcerer Damhan-Allaidh appeared in the British Isles and brought the Order's advances in those lands to a dead halt (see *Ars Magica Fifth Edition*, page 12). Among the magae who had gone to fight Damhan-Allaidh was Tancoystl, for she knew well the terrain over which the guerrilla war was being fought. However, when the conflict ended and Pralix surprised the Order by creating the Ordo Miscellanea, Tancoystl joined it.

When the news reached Duresca, the former tempestarii and vates of House Diedne joined it as well, and those who did not left the covenant and founded the Diedne covenant of Mons Vindius. Duresca was therefore inhabited by renegades, although it was not outlawed for even two years. At the fourth Grand Tribunal of 817 House Ex Miscellanea was created, and the Order pardoned its members' offenses. Despite the demands of the Flambeau of the Peninsula, Duresca escaped punishment, and its crimes in connection with the Ordo Miscellanea were annulled. As a result, Duresca once more came under the protection of the Code of Hermes and was thereafter inhabited entirely by magi of House Ex Miscellanea.

### The Arrival of Priamitus of Mercere

Four years after the death of the Founder Mercere, his son Priamitus (founder of the Hermetic cult of Mercury) and Priamitus's own son (a Mozarab Redcap named Don Šaybān) came to the Peninsula to embark on an ambitious plan: the construction of the first Mercer House on the Peninsula and of the Mercere portals. To that end they contacted Somnus of Tremere, of the covenant of Secunda, and the aged magus summoned all the Peninsula's magi in the year 822, this time fully emulating the meetings of the Rhine, in the hope of founding a regional Tribunal at the next Grand Tribunal (which would be the fifth, in 832).

<!-- p. 69 -->

> #### The Portals of Iberia
>
> Priamitus of Mercere agreed with Somnus of Tremere, the Quaesitores and the leaders of all the Peninsula's covenants present at the meeting of 822 on the creation of five Mercere portals in Iberia. Priamitus made it a condition that all of them must connect to the Mercer House of Aedes Saturni, from which it would be possible to travel to Harco, the domus magna of his House, by means of a portal built for that purpose.
>
> Of the five portals, two were shut down during the Schism War, since they were not housed inside any covenant, and the Mercere disabled them after the events at the domus magna of House Bonisagus (see *Houses of Hermes: True Lineages*, page 87). The other three, located at the covenants of Duresca and Salionca (connected to the portal hall of Aedes Saturni) and at Aedes Saturni itself (connected to Harco), are still in operation today.
>
> All the pairs of portals in Iberia were numbered in the order of their creation, so the magi of the Tribunal know them by their ordinal names.
>
> - ***Primus:*** the first pair of portals in Iberia. It joins Aedes Saturni with Harco.
> - ***Secundus:*** this pair links Duresca with Aedes Saturni.
> - ***Tertius* and *Quartus:*** where the blind arches of Aedes Saturni lead is unknown.
> - ***Quintus:*** links Salionca with Aedes Saturni.
>
> Later, with the creation of the Portuguese Mercer House of Porta Pandere (see below), the construction of four more pairs of portals was approved, numbered from ten onward.
>
> - ***Decimus:*** links Porta Pandere with Aedes Saturni.
> - ***Undecimus:*** links Porta Pandere with the covenant of Harra.
> - ***Duodecimus:*** links Porta Pandere with the covenant of Duresca.
> - ***Tertius Decimus:*** linked Porta Pandere with the Mercer House of Tāfīlālt, Aedes Iris (this portal was shut down with the destruction of Aedes Iris).
>
> Finally, during the breakup of the Tribunal, Porta Pandere approved the creation of a new pair of portals to communicate with the covenant of Dār Malīḥaʾ.
>
> - ***Vicesimus:*** links Porta Pandere with Dār Malīḥaʾ.

> #### Story Seeds: The *Sextus* Portal
>
> When one of the players' magi finds a blind arch in the cellars of some building in the Tribunal (such as an abbey, an old Mercer House or the ruins of some covenant), he notices that the alfiz framing it clearly bears a carving of the Roman numeral six set within the emblem of House Mercere. With an Intelligence + Iberian Tribunal Lore roll of 6+, the magus knows that this same notation is the one the Mercere have traditionally used when creating the Tribunal's portals. Of course, in the portal hall of Aedes Saturni there is no arch numbered VI. Has the magus found the *Sextus* portal? Where will it lead if he unblocks it?

The meeting held at Secunda focused on Priamitus's request for the founding of the first Mercer House on the Peninsula and the construction of the Mercere portals. The Peninsula's magi welcomed them, and it was agreed to purchase (in equal shares between the covenants of the Peninsula and the covenant of Harco) a magnificent building within the Roman walls of the city of Barcelona, which Priamitus named Aedes Saturni. In addition, the Peninsula's magi approved the amendment and creation of the following entries in their unofficial minutes.

***822 AD, On the Iberian Tax II*** *(Tello of Guernicus)* As "On the Iberian Tax" (801), but without the reference to the Peninsula's treasury.

***822 AD, On the Iberian Treasury*** *(Tello of Guernicus)* The treasury of the Peninsula shall be kept at Aedes Saturni.

***822 AD, On the Privileges of the Mercere*** *(Tello of Guernicus)* The treasury shall set aside 5% of the Iberian tax for the use of the Mercere, with which to create and maintain the network of portals of Iberia.

During this historic meeting, the Peninsula's magi wrote once again in their own minutes, adding to the complexity of the seed of their Peripheral Code, which only strengthened the identity of the region's magi. But what was happening in Iberia was no isolated case: throughout Mythic Europe the other regions were also beginning to take shape. To regulate this new situation, the fifth Grand Tribunal of 832 set the intervals between Tribunal meetings from 836 onward: Grand Tribunals would meet every thirty-three years and regional Tribunals every seven. However, to the sorrow of the Peninsula's magi, the Grand Tribunal refused to create a regional Tribunal in Iberia, since they could not count on the members of Brigantia, whose covenant had recently been destroyed by the Vikings. Nevertheless, the Grand Tribunal ratified the creation of the Mercere portals and the founding of Aedes Saturni.

<!-- p. 70 -->

With Don Šaybān established in Iberia, the Redcaps carried out the first census of the vis sources of the north of the Peninsula, with the help of the Diedne and the Guernicus of Iberia. Later, in 836, the Peninsula's magi met at Secunda to amend, yet again, the entry on the Iberian tax and to create a new ruling on vis sources:

***836 AD, On the Iberian Tax III*** *(Tello of Guernicus)* As "On the Iberian Tax II" (822), except that payment is standardized at every seven years, coinciding with the summer meetings of the ordinary Rhine Tribunals.

***836 AD, On Vis Sources*** *(Tello of Guernicus)* Every declared vis source shall be reviewed, assessed and registered by a Quaesitor and a Mercere, to avoid conflict with other covenants.

### Magicis per ignem finem imposuit

In the year 845, the most powerful political figures on the Peninsula were Tremere or under their influence (among them Somnus of Tremere; Teodoric of Guernicus, also a member of Secunda; and Átropo of Tremere, of the covenant of Tertia), and they counted the covenant of Duresca as their bitter enemy. For the Transylvanian Founder's plan, its opposition posed a real obstacle to the rise of House Tremere's power.

In those years the king of Asturias, Ramiro I, was consolidating his hold on the throne, and Átropo of Tremere used his influence among the Asturian nobility to bring about the decree *Magicis per ignem finem imposuit*, by which Ramiro I ordered that all the sorcerers of the kingdom be burned for opposing the Christians who supported his coronation.

When this news reached the ears of Tancoystl Ex Miscellanea, she summoned the Peninsula's magi to her covenant to deal with the matter, since the next Rhine Tribunal was still far off. At the meeting, Tancoystl set out the problem and framed it within the wider advance of the mundane world: the discovery of the tomb of the apostle Saint James had considerably diminished many of Duresca's vis sources, and the Astur king's decree was a threat to all the magi of the kingdom. To keep the situation from worsening, and to prevent Duresca and other covenants from being harmed or destroyed, Tancoystl asked the assembly for help in halting the advance of the Dominion and abolishing Ramiro I's decree. However, after she had spoken, the Quaesitor Teodoric called those present to order and dissolved the meeting, deeming it "an incitement to violence against mundanes and, therefore, a high crime under the Code of Hermes."

When, months later, a *filia* of Tancoystl died at the king's stake, the old Ex Miscellanea and other magae of Duresca (former tempestarii and vates) resolved to assassinate King Ramiro to put an end to his edict and so avenge the maga's death. However, the regicide was never carried out: seven days after the summer solstice of 845, the magae involved were ambushed and handed over to the king in Oviedo, who ordered an immense pyre built on the slopes of Mount Naranco, facing the Aula Regia of the Asturian court. Thus Tancoystl Ex Miscellanea, one of the first Hermetic inhabitants of Iberia and a former member of the Ordo Miscellanea, died at the stake together with her companions, and the Tremere cleared the ground still further for their bid for supremacy in the Order.

<!-- p. 71 -->

The Asturian king's decree prompted some Asturian magi to leave for the south of the Peninsula, where they decided to try their luck in the lands of al-Andalus despite the danger of the *saḥirs*. This, together with the discord caused by Baldiccione's decisions (see below), contributed to the lack of a *quorum* at the Grand Tribunal of 865 for the official constitution of the Iberian Tribunal, since a good number of them took several lustra to settle down.

### The Sundering

*There is no doubt that you are the most guileless man in the world,* *and the one with the best faith, intentions and conscience. But wake up, for one of those who were here yesterday* *keeping us company was hatching ugly schemes. Mark that not every prostration is a prayer, and that not everyone with eyes in his face can see.*[^p71-29]

[^p71-29]: Excerpt from Ibn Ḥazm's *The Ring of the Dove* (Spanish translation by Emilio García Gómez).

The Sundering of 848 (see *Houses of Hermes: True Lineages*, "The Last Founder," page 120) brought about the destruction of the minds of Somnus and Átropo, Tremere's lieutenants, when the plot of the Transylvanian magi was foiled. When the Quaesitor Qatr al-Nadà, who was in charge of the investigations carried out on the Peninsula, publicly announced the Tremere's treachery, she summoned the Peninsula's magi to the covenant of Dār Malīḥaʾ, which no Tremere attended. This meeting was the prelude to the Rhine meeting of 850, where Qatr al-Nadà raised the inclusion of a new ruling in the Code, called "On the Praeco" (see the next page), to prevent a repetition of what the Order had just been through. However, the Tribunal did not support the motion, which would finally be rejected outright at the Grand Tribunal of 865. Even so, this ruling would later be included after the official constitution of the Tribunal (see below).

## The Days of Nuʿmān

*Do not trust the darkness, for the dawn comes after it, nor be deceived by the light, for the sun also sets.*[^p71-30]

[^p71-30]: *Ibidem.*

The scholars of Iberia regard this period as fundamental in the history of the Tribunal, for it laid the foundations for the long-desired peace with the *saḥirs*, and the official constitution of the Iberian Tribunal was at last achieved at the seventh Grand Tribunal of 898. Many refer to this period as the days of Nuʿmān, in allusion to the well-known legend of the king of Hira, of whom it was said that he had two days, on which he might either punish the innocent or shower them with gifts; such was the instability of this time.

The most important figure of this period was Baldiccione of Guernicus, one of the Founder's apprentices, who came to the north of the Peninsula to found the covenant of Campus Stellae.

Baldiccione was welcomed with great hope by the Peninsula's magi, who saw embodied in him their longing for a stability that never quite seemed to arrive. Indeed, after the Tribunal was constituted in 898, Baldiccione was named the first Praeco at the first Iberian Tribunal.

| Praeco | Years |
| --- | --- |
| Baldiccione of Guernicus | 899–906 |

### Baldiccione of Guernicus and the Peace with the Saḥirs

Before officially establishing his covenant, Baldiccione took the opportunity to travel the Tribunal and learn about its inhabitants and customs. In this he had the invaluable help of Àlvar, a Redcap of Aedes Saturni, whose diligence in his work was such that it proved crucial in improving the image the Peninsula's magi had of the Redcaps, whom they considered lesser members of the Order for lacking the Gift.

On his travels Baldiccione visited many covenants and concluded that the greatest problem facing the covenants of the Peninsula was the war that for almost a century had been wearing away their identity and their wealth, as well as the trust of their members and between covenants. The region's constant conflicts had prevented a *quorum* at the Grand Tribunals of 817 and 832, so he resolved to make ending the wars and intrigues of the Peninsula his priority.

It took Baldiccione some years to grasp the idiosyncrasies of the Peninsula's magi, for there were great differences between those who lived in the Christian kingdoms and those who dwelt in the domains of the Umayyad emirate. What surprised him most on his travels was that many of the northern magi used their own laws outside the Order's legal framework, which were kept at the covenant of Salionca. However, hardly any Andalusi magus abided by them, and the eminent judge Qatr al-Nadà had denounced their existence on several occasions at the Rhine Tribunals.

Baldiccione resolved to seek Qatr al-Nadà's help in abolishing these laws on the Peninsula and, since the maga had been in contact with the *saḥirs* in her youth, he also enlisted her to open peace negotiations with the Muslim sorcerers. For this second undertaking, the judge contacted Tareyja of Apromor, a maga of Brigantia blessed with the Gentle Gift, believing that her involvement might calm the tempers of the Flambeau of Salionca when it was announced that peace with the *saḥirs* was being sought, though unfortunately it did not.

The two judges brought the abolition of the Iberian Peripheral Code, and an end to hostilities with the *saḥirs* so as to achieve peace, before the Rhine Tribunal of 864. At the meeting, the assembly ruled in favor of both measures and resolved to seize the Iberian treasury at Aedes Saturni, which was stripped of the wealth it had accumulated over more than fifty years. Many of the northern magi of the Peninsula lodged complaints, led by the then *dictator* of Salionca, Ruiz Sánchez de Esco. The meeting was a disaster from the political standpoint Baldiccione sought, for not only did he earn the enmity of numerous covenants in Iberia for having stripped them of their identity at that Tribunal, but it ended up defining two factions on the Peninsula: those who favored war and those who did not.

<!-- p. 72 -->

The Tribunal of 864 had its echo a year later, at the sixth Grand Tribunal. At that meeting the regional Tribunals of the Rhine, the West Franks, Lotharingia, Britain, Rome, Thebes, the Levant and the Greater Alps were constituted, but not that of Iberia. Many of the Peninsula's magi did not attend the assembly because of the schism caused by the decisions of Baldiccione and Qatr al-Nadà, so the *quorum* needed to constitute the Tribunal could not be established. On the other hand, and making up for the Hermetic diplomatic failure, the ceasefire with the *saḥirs* allowed negotiations to progress until, in 870, the Order signed its first truce with them, which was ratified by the Rhine Tribunal in 871. This was a time of peace and prosperity that culminated in the creation of the Isidorian Circle (see page 103).

### The Grand Tribunal of 898

The peace of 871 allowed the Peninsula's magi to live free of the threat of the *saḥirs* for the first time, and Hermetic society on the Peninsula grew stable. Thanks to this, the Andalusi magi agreed to attend the Grand Tribunal of 898 with the intention of forming the regional Tribunal of Iberia, and the Iberian covenants agreed to add to the *quorum* if the Peripheral Code abolished in 864 were restored and the treasures Durenmar had seized were returned. The Rhine ruled in favor of the proposal, and the Iberian Tribunal was created and registered with sixteen covenants (Salionca, Brigantia, Duresca, Aedes Saturni, Mons Vindius, Barzaj, Tertia, Campus Stellae, Fafḥṣ al-Luŷŷ, Dār Malīḥaʾ, Ipagrum, Nebula, Ajabeba, Inverneira, Tremébriga and Qasr Dār al-Muchaddad) and thirty magi.

### The First Iberian Tribunal

In 899 the first Iberian Tribunal was held at Campus Stellae, with Baldiccione as Praeco and his *filius* Ṭāmis al-Išbīlī al-Gernikī as presiding Quaesitor. During the meeting the earlier minutes of the Peninsula were recovered and amended, the clause proposed by Qatr al-Nadà in 850 ("On the Praeco") was included, and new rules were approved. In addition, Durenmar handed over the treasury seized in 864, which was returned to the coffers of Aedes Saturni.

***899 AD, On the Iberian Treasury*** *(Ṭāmis al-Išbīlī al-Gernikī)* The treasury of the Tribunal shall be kept at Aedes Saturni and shall be regulated and protected by a Flambeau and a Guernicus, who shall hold the titles of *praefectus praetorio* and *quaestor aerarii*, respectively (see "New Virtues and Flaws," page 305).

***899 AD, On the Iberian Tax*** *(Ṭāmis al-Išbīlī al-Gernikī)* Any covenant of the Iberian Tribunal that can demonstrate its work on behalf of the Order may request a payment to defray the costs of its labors. To meet such demands, every covenant of the Tribunal must deliver to the Iberian treasury an amount of vis determined by the wealth of its declared sources[^p72-31].

The vis may be of any Art and must be delivered every seven years, coinciding with the ordinary meetings of the Iberian Tribunal.

The same covenant may not request this service twice within a period of less than ten years. Requests will be assessed by the Quaesitores of the Iberian Tribunal, and the vis will be kept in the Tribunal's treasury. No war, whatever its nature, may be financed with the treasury's funds.

[^p72-31]: In game terms, Spring covenants pay one pawn of vis, Summer covenants five, Autumn covenants seven and Winter covenants two.

***899 AD, On the Privileges of the Mercere*** *(Ṭāmis al-Išbīlī al-Gernikī)* The treasury shall set aside 5% of the Iberian tax for the use of the Mercere, to be used to create and maintain the network of portals of Iberia.

***899 AD, On Vis Sources*** *(Ṭāmis al-Išbīlī al-Gernikī)* Every declared vis source shall be reviewed, assessed and registered by a Quaesitor and a Mercere, so that its possession does not come into conflict with other covenants.

The following clause was not only amended but also renamed to suit the new reality of the Iberian Tribunal.

***899 AD, On the Minutes of Iberia*** *(Ṭāmis al-Išbīlī al-Gernikī)* The minutes of the Tribunal shall be kept at the covenant of Salionca.

***899 AD, On the Praeco*** *(Ṭāmis al-Išbīlī al-Gernikī)* The Praeco shall be chosen at the close of each Tribunal from among the five eldest magi (unless there is no Praeco at the start of the Tribunal). Furthermore, the candidates must be members of a covenant of Iberia, and must therefore belong to the Tribunal and be registered in it.

Once the business of the Tribunal has been concluded, the presiding Quaesitor must ask the assembly whether it wishes to choose a new Praeco. In the vote, each member of the Tribunal has a single vote (Tremere without their voting sigils may vote, and those who hold their *filii*'s sigils may cast only their own),[^p72-32] and neither the Quaesitores, the Redcaps nor the Praeco may vote. The five candidates must be in full possession of their mental faculties, and may not come from the same covenant or belong to the same House. Should that be the case, the youngest of them must be replaced by the next-eldest magus of the Tribunal. Furthermore, the five candidates may not excuse themselves from their obligations, and therefore may not decline the office; to do so is classed as a high crime and may therefore lead to the magus's expulsion.

Finally, a Quaesitor may never be Praeco.

As a result of this last clause, Baldiccione agreed to renounce his title of Quaesitor so as to continue serving as Praeco and be able to bring the peace with the *saḥirs* to fruition.

[^p72-32]: Note that this invalidates voting by proxy; see *Houses of Hermes: True Lineages*, page 55.

<!-- p. 73 -->

### The End of the Truce with the Saḥirs and the Fall of Baldiccione

Although the recovery of the Iberian treasury had given the northern covenants a certain preeminence, the Flambeau did not forget what Baldiccione, Qatr al-Nadà and Tareyja had done. Ruiz Sánchez de Esco led a campaign to discredit the Tribunal's "peacemakers," for not only had they defied the judgment the Rhine handed down in 780, which barred the *saḥirs* from any diplomatic approach toward peace, but they had also insulted the memory of the Founder.

Baldiccione, Qatr al-Nadà and Tareyja received numerous declarations of Wizard's War during this period, which finally ended in the deaths of the two magae in 907, at the very moment they were meeting a group of *saḥirs* in a *ribāṭ* north of Jaén. The Flambeau killed them all and discovered that the magae were carrying a substantial cargo of mundane riches and vis, plainly intended for the Andalusi sorcerers. Ruiz Sánchez de Esco knew then that Baldiccione's end was near.

A few months later, after more than forty years of truce, the *saḥirs* launched an attack on the northwest of the Peninsula that destroyed the covenants of Inverneira and Ipagrum and inflicted heavy damage, and more than one Hermetic casualty, on Occelum Durii, Fafḥṣ al-Luŷŷ and Duresca (from which they stole a great quantity of vis, murdering all its apprentices).

To deal with the crisis and repair the havoc wrought by the *saḥir* raid, the dean of Duresca, Briatiz de Moncharro of Diedne (who was deeply shaken by the loss of her apprentice in the attack), summoned an extraordinary Tribunal at her covenant. The meeting, however, took an unexpected turn when the *quaestor aerarii* announced that the coffers held neither the vis nor the money needed to repair the damage, even though the Rhine Tribunal had returned the entire treasury. Briatiz de Moncharro then demanded that he share all the account books with the assembly, and the Quaesitores agreed.

After long and tedious hours, the judges denounced a considerable embezzlement from the coffers and prepared to question the *quaestor aerarii*. They never got the chance: Baldiccione took the floor and, to everyone's astonishment, took the blame upon himself. The Praeco confessed to having taken the Tribunal's goods to negotiate peace with the *saḥirs* and to having paid a certain Al-Muzaffar to prevent war and bring the conflict to an end, though he stressed that he had only drawn on the treasury during the last eight years. In his speech he also accused Ruiz Sánchez de Esco of having broken the truce, holding him responsible for everything that had happened; but his rejoinder sounded desperate, and the Flambeau of Salionca took shelter behind the Wizard's War he had declared, then went on to speculate that the *saḥirs* might have attacked not because the truce had been broken, but because they had never received the *parias* of vis the magae were going to pay them. And so, although Baldiccione denied it, by then he had earned the enmity of the whole assembly: it was obvious that the peace had been bought, and that Baldiccione, in the name of the Order of Hermes, had been paying *parias* to keep it.

After the statements and the quaesitorial interrogations, the assembly began debating whether or not to exile Baldiccione when Briatiz de Moncharro rose, bathed in tears, and blamed him for the death of her apprentice. Although the aged magus tried to reason with her and did everything he could to ease the Diedne's grief, the maga declared Wizard's War on him for the following full moon and killed Baldiccione at the end of that same year. His death also brought to a close what would come to be known as the days of Nuʿmān.

<!-- p. 74 -->

> #### Baldiccione's Contribution to the Code
>
> Many magi of the Tribunal today (no Flambeau among them) consider Baldiccione a model of Hermetic social work. Part of his policy took shape in amendments to the rulings of the Peninsula's old Peripheral Code (such as scaling vis payments according to the age of each covenant, or the appointment of the *praefectus praetorio* and the *quaestor aerarii*) and in limiting the power of the Praecones in the Tribunal through the following entry:
>
> ***906 AD, On the Praeco II*** *(Ṭāmis al-Išbīlī al-Gernikī)* As "On the Praeco" (899), with the addition: under no circumstances may the Praeco of the Tribunal be an archimagus or a Primus.
>
> He was, however, also responsible for the curious inclusion of this singular entry:
>
> ***906 AD, On the Gentle Gift*** *(Ṭāmis al-Išbīlī al-Gernikī)* A magus's first apprentice with the Gentle Gift may be claimed from his masters by the Quaesitores of Iberia. This claim does not outrank that of the Bonisagus; that is, if a Bonisagus wants the same apprentice as a Guernicus, the Bonisagus's preference shall always prevail.
>
> Scholars of the Tribunal today believe this ruling may have been connected in some way with the Duresca manuscripts, but no one has ever been able to prove it conclusively. Unusual as it is, the entry has never been revoked, and the Quaesitores of the Tribunal can still make use of it.

> #### The Perfumers
>
> *[…] the soul expands at good odors, feeling itself drawn to them; but it shrinks back from bad odors and shuns them.*[^p74-XXI]
>
> In the tenth century the perfumer's trade began to flourish in al-Andalus, and many magi of the Peninsula turned to this mundane source of income. Perfumers did not merely make essences: their customers also called on them to cast out or ward off the evil eye, to prepare love philters, or to buy a spell that would put an end to their lovesickness. In tenth-century Cordoba, anyone could find a magic shop of this sort.
>
> Even before Ǧamīla was elected Praeco, Eastern-style perfumes (that is, sweet and heavy ones) had begun to spread among the magi, who burned them to scent their covenants or wore them beneath their clothes to perfume themselves: they used ambergris, civet, musk and scented oils, perfumes that only the highest classes of society could obtain because of their great cost. However, as Ǧamīla rightly pointed out, to use them properly one had to take into account the season in which they were to be worn (by passing a stress roll of Intelligence + Etiquette against an Ease Factor of 6+), unless one wished to look like a moneyed boor.
>
> - **Winter:** the time for musk, civet and jasmine oil.
> - **Spring:** gives way to gentler perfumes, such as orange-blossom water, narcissus, jasmine, marshmallow and basil.
> - **Summer:** fresh fragrances are advisable, such as moss and sandalwood powder, and apple water.
> - **Autumn:** the season for rosewater.
>

Indeed, every magus of the Tribunal knows the story of a magus of that era named Abū-l-Walīd Muḥammad al-Ŷerbitonī, whom masters often use as a cautionary tale for their apprentices. According to the story, Abū-l-Walīd Muḥammad lacked the means to buy expensive perfumes, so he overused this spell throughout his life and brought on his Final Twilight at an early age (for another perfume-related spell, see page 3 of the *Códice Hermético*, the spell booklet included with Holocubierta's Spanish-edition Storyguide screen).

## The Arabization of the Tribunal

Hermetic scholars place the beginning of Muslim influence on the Iberian Tribunal at this point. After almost two centuries of learning from Eastern culture through the many journeys Hispanians made to the East, al-Andalus became a wellspring of knowledge in its own right. With Umayyad rule at its zenith, the magi of the Tribunal fell under the spell of al-Andalus's cultural sophistication; all the works and learning of the classical thinkers were gathered in Cordoba and, like a lodestone, drew magi from the Peninsula and from every corner of the Order.

The person most responsible for spreading this culture among the members of the Order was the venerable Ǧamīla al-Qurṭubiyya al-Ŷerbitoniyya, of the covenant of Qasr Dār al-Muchaddad, also known as the Hermetic Ziryāb. Such was her reputation that she was elected Praeco at the Tribunal of 913.

| Praecones | Years |
| --- | --- |
| Ǧamīla al-Qurṭubiyya al-Ŷerbitoniyya | 913–941 |
| ʿAbbās ibn Munḏīr al-Bonisagī | 948–990 |
| Ibn Sahl al-Tremerī | 996 |

During this period the magi of Iberia lived through a social revolution (which culminated in the building of the covenant of al-Zahrāʾ), and witnessed the peace with the *saḥirs*, the revolt of the Kharijites, the scandal of the Duresca manuscripts, and the expansion beyond the Pillars of Hercules.

> #### The Astronomers
>
> *[…] the distance between the center of the earth and the summit of the sphere of Saturn is a journey of some eight thousand seven hundred years […]. Consider so enormous and terrifying a distance.*[^p75-XXII]
>
> Astronomy reached al-Andalus from Baghdad, which had received it from India. ʿAbd al-Raḥmān II sent ʿAbbās ibn Firnās (see Appendix I) to Iraq on a scientific mission together with a group of scholars. When they returned they brought with them, among many other things, an Indian astronomy book called the *Sind-hind* (*Siddhānta* in Sanskrit), which was studied by the emir's court astronomer, ʿAbd Allāh ibn Assimir (a contemporary of Ziryāb).
>
> Many scholars regard astronomy as a way of worshipping God, and their studies cover not only horoscopes but also the weather, for on it rests the economic foundation of empires and kingdoms; in an agricultural world, predicting a drought is vital. The astronomers claimed they could do so by studying the position of the planets: for instance, the presence of Saturn and Jupiter in the fire signs of the zodiac (Aries, Leo and Sagittarius) foretold drought.
>
> Horoscopes, for their part, are of great importance in Mythic Europe, for they mark the destiny of men. The heirs of the astrological traditions of India believe that the messages conveyed by the heavenly bodies (which lie beyond the lunar sphere and therefore cannot be touched by magic) contain absolute truth, and they choose their rulers by horoscope rather than by ability, for what can the will of man do against destiny? Indeed, some magi cast their vote for Praeco guided by their horoscope. Even so, a small number of Andalusi astronomers hold this belief to be utterly false, and some argue that astronomy can only obtain indications of what is right or wrong, since the absolute terms of these concepts lie in God's hands alone (in the tenth section you will find two non-Hermetic traditions with powerful astronomical foundations, the riadiins and the astral sorcerers).
>
> ##### The Code of Hermes and the Court Astronomers
>
> At the beginning of the tenth century, Abū Šakir ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Ŷerbitonī, of the Granadan covenant of Qasr Dār al-Muchaddad, laid before the Tribunal the grievous consequences of the magi's constant presence at royal courts.
