For almost two centuries the magi had influenced royal decisions to a greater or lesser degree, and the results had almost always been disastrous. Abū Šakir gave two examples. The first concerned King Ramiro I and his decree against the sorcerers of Asturias, issued under the influence of Átropo of Tremere. The second, narrower in scope but no less serious, concerned the emir Hišām I, who summoned the wandering magus of the city of al-Ŷazīra al-Jaḍrāʾ, ʿAbd al-Wāḥid ibn Isāḥq al-Ḍabbī al-Ŷerbitonī, to read the stars and foretell the length of his reign. Although Al-Ḍabbī refused to answer, the emir begged him until he had no choice but to give his verdict. "Six to seven," was all he said. After this accurate prediction, the following emirs called him to the palace, where he was obliged to reside and where he lived in great luxury until, almost a century later, Hišām I's grandson, the emir Muḥammad I, tired of Al-Ḍabbī airing his secrets at court, exiled him to Tortosa and condemned him to death. Al-Ḍabbī used magic to defend himself and, although he managed to hold out for a time, he was finally overpowered and executed, endangering the rest of Iberia's covenants. Following Abū Šakir's presentation, the Tribunal approved the following entry in the Peripheral Code:
>
> ***920 AD, On Court Astronomers*** *(Ṭāmis al-Išbīlī al-Gernikī)* No Hermetic magus may serve as a court astronomer. When this judgment was passed, the magi of Salionca had already spent some time at the court of Leon, where Alfonso Álvarez of Flambeau served as counselor to Ordoño II, a post he had to give up for good when the Grand Tribunal of 931 broadened the entry of the Code of Hermes on dealings with mundanes (see "Interfering with Mundanes," *Ars Magica Fifth Edition*, page 18), definitively condemning the participation of members of the Order as court wizards.
>
> [^p75-XXII]: From Maimonides' *The Guide for the Perplexed* (Spanish translation by David Gonzalo Maeso).

<!-- p. 76 -->

### Ǧamīla's Cultural Revolution

*Had the Persians seen the fire of your cheeks, they would have done without emperors and magi.*[^p76-33]

[^p76-33]: From Ibn Ḥazm's *The Ring of the Dove* (Spanish translation by Emilio García Gómez).

With the proclamation of ʿAbd al-Raḥmān III as caliph of al-Andalus, the first school of medicine in Mythic Europe was founded in Cordoba. Social and medical advances were such that the average age of Cordoba's citizens reached seventy. The city began to attract every scholar of the Islamic world, including the Praeco of the Tribunal, Ǧamīla al-Qurṭubiyya al-Ŷerbitoniyya, who began to draw closer to the Umayyad court (a rapprochement later seized upon and exploited to the full by her successor, the Trianomae ʿAbbās ibn Munḏīr al-Bonisagī).

> #### Story Seeds: The Perfumers
>
> ##### The Magical Perfume
>
> One of the covenant's magi has persuaded the most renowned perfumer of an important city of al-Andalus (someone who might well work for an emir or a caliph) to distill his perfumes for him. By chance he detects traces of magic in one of them, and decides to look into the matter, discovering that it is distilled from one of the following ingredients: ambergris, musk or civet. But where do they come from, and how are they obtained? The player characters will have to investigate the origin of the perfumes and which animals produce them: if it is ambergris, they will have to put to sea and hunt for the sperm whale that produced it; in the case of musk or civet, the animal is probably already dead, but what if there were some magical lineage among musk deer or civets? Perhaps the magi will have to travel to Africa and cross the Sahara in search of magical civets, or visit the far East or frozen Siberia in pursuit of musk deer. Either way, the mundane price of these ingredients (if they could be obtained in bulk) would make for a legendary source of income (see *Covenants*, page 79).
>
> ##### The Censer-Bearer
>
> The ṣāḥib al-madīna of a powerful Muslim city near the characters' covenant comes to the magi to ask for their help. According to his account, all the inhabitants of the city's suburb have risen against their prince. The riots are constant, and the rioters seem blinded by hatred. Despite the crucifixions that have been carried out, the insurgents attack the prince's soldiers and, deaf to all reason, throw themselves into martyrdom. The prince and his family are terrified!
>
> If the magi go to investigate, they will find that the suburbs are not safe for them either; their inhabitants will attack them in a frenzy, possessed by a blind rage. If they spend a full day investigating, their grogs (unless they have Magic Resistance) will end up infected by the madness around them and will start attacking their masters. The culprit behind all this is nothing more than a censer-bearer (*bajjār*), a street vendor who, for a tip, perfumes his customers with sprinklings of scented water, fumigations of incense or fragrant wood. Who is this man, what kind of magic is he using, and why does he want to overthrow the established order? If the magi set things right the prince will surely reward them, but what if the censer-bearer offered them something better? Or worse still, what if he were another Hermetic magus?

> #### Story Seeds: The Astronomers
>
> ##### A Delicate Commission
>
> A companion of the covenant works as a perfumer in a large city and is commissioned by a servant of a powerful and regular customer to prepare a love philter. After talking with the servant, the companion discovers that his lord wishes to lie with a humble girl from the suburbs.
>
> Making the elixir could mean the girl's death, for the difference in their social standing would end up condemning her once the powerful lord's carnal desires were satisfied. He himself, in turn, could fall into disgrace with his family, which would cost him his standing and sink the reputation of the magi's perfumery. Yet refusing could also lose them the client, who would end up going to another perfumer. And then again, is the lord truly in love?
>
> ##### The Court Astronomer
>
> One fine day a mundane messenger arrives at the characters' covenant. He says he has been sent by his lord (an emir, a caliph or perhaps a king) to claim the services of one of the magi. To the characters' astonishment, the envoy knows the Hermetic name of the magus in question, and asks him to present himself at court within no more than twenty-eight days.
>
> Serving in such a capacity would be a violation of the Code of Hermes, but ignoring the summons of a powerful lord could cause him trouble (in Castile, royal wrath meant banishment from the kingdom). How did the mundane lord come to hear the magus's name and the location of the covenant? Could it be a ruse by one of his enemies?

<!-- p. 77 -->

Ǧamīla brought the Eastern customs of al-Andalus to the Order. Magi began to adopt the Muslim ideal of the perfect man (see the "Ziryāb" sidebar, page 22), took to embroidering verses or spell formulas on their clothes, and to wearing perfumes as a symbol of power and influence. Thanks to her, covenants began to be built around gardens, as a representation of paradise, and the walls of *sancta* filled with verses alluding to the magical affinities of their owners. Under Ǧamīla the aesthetic aspects of magic were developed to the full, not merely its practical ones.

Of course, these changes did not permeate the Iberian Tribunal evenly: the north of the Peninsula was much less receptive, although their influence was felt there too to a greater or lesser degree (with the possible exception of Salionca).

### The Peace with the Saḥirs

The Tribunal resumed peace negotiations with the *saḥirs* in the year 920, once again with one of Apromor's followers, a magus of Brigantia, as ambassador. To spare him the fate of young Tareyja, the negotiator's identity was kept secret (and remains so to this day, though some students of the Tribunal's history claim to have inferred it from certain evidence; see "Harra," page 173), as were the meeting places of both parties.

Thanks to the Tribunal's efforts, the negotiations proceeded almost without incident and, in less than five years, the judge Ṭāmis ibn Baldiccione al-Išbīlī al-Gernikī (founder of the covenant of Pico Sacro) and the judge Zaynab ḅint Qatr al-Nadà al-Gernikiyya (Quaesitor of the covenant of Dār Malīḥaʾ) summoned Ǧamīla to inform her that the *saḥirs* were prepared to make peace with the Order and become part of it. To formalize the agreement, Ǧamīla convened an extraordinary Tribunal at her covenant in the year 925. All the magi of the Tribunal attended the meeting, along with almost two dozen *saḥirs*, represented by the non-Hermetic sorcerer Al-Muzaffar. Before them all, Al-Muzaffar signed a peace agreement whose sole condition was that the Order should found no covenant in Africa for a period of 300 years (see the sidebar on the next page). When the Praeco and the Quaesitor signed on behalf of the Order, the *saḥirs* swore the Hermetic Oath and joined House Ex Miscellanea, adopting the *nisba* al-Praliḥī and al-Praliḥiyya (in honor of Pralix). The Tribunal, however, created no ruling of the Peripheral Code to reflect the *saḥirs*' request, which in time proved to be a mistake (see "*Non plus ultra*").

After the reading of the oath, Ruiz Sánchez of Flambeau asked for the floor and urged everyone present to rise up against those who wished to desecrate the memory of the magi who had lost their lives fighting the *saḥir* threat. His speech, however, did not meet with the reception he had hoped for: nobody wanted to go on fighting that war. And so, before the Tribunal was brought to a close, Ruiz Sánchez left the hall together with some of his followers. The Flambeau magus never forgave the Order for extending its hand to those who had murdered so many valiant Hermetic magi.

Despite their oath, the *saḥirs* did not fully integrate into the Order until five years later (after the destruction of the *ribāṭ* of al-ʿAbraj in the year 930), when the Andalusi covenants of Bayt al-Ḥikma, Dār Malīḥaʾ and Qasr Dār al-Muchaddad opened their doors to teach them Hermetic theory and the Parma Magica, of which they had known nothing until then.

### The Duresca Manuscripts

To understand these events we must go back a few years. After Briatiz de Moncharro of Diedne had killed Baldiccione of Guernicus in the year 907, she plundered his *sanctum* (as Hermetic law entitled her to) and carried all his belongings off to Duresca. Among the magus's possessions were hundreds of writings that the maga left in a corner, since they had no immediate Hermetic value. Consequently, it was not until 920 that she finally began cataloguing the manuscripts from the Guernicus's *sanctum*, embarking on a task that would take years. Thus, in 937 she found some parchments containing the correspondence Baldiccione had kept up with the Founder Guernicus and other Quaesitores, notably Ranemiro and Fenicil. Although all the letters contained important information, Briatiz was surprised to discover that a series of them spoke, in confidential terms, of the course of action the House was to follow: first to dominate the Order and then the world.

> #### Story Seeds: Non nobis, Flambo, non nobis sed nomini tuo da gloriam
>
> One spring day a badly wounded grog arrives at the players' covenant begging for help. The characters take him in and ask him what has happened. According to his account, his lord was attacked nearby while traveling north: his whole retinue was wiped out by fire. The grog, whose name is Yazīz, also says he heard the following litany during the attack: *Non nobis, Flambo, non nobis sed nomini tuo da gloriam*. An Intelligence + Theology roll against an Ease Factor of 9 tells the characters that it is an alteration of a psalm of the Bible spoken by David, king of Israel and father of Solomon (the same one the Knights Templar, also present in the Peninsula, use after a victory).[^p77-XXIII]
>
> The characters must investigate the murder (perhaps one of them is a Quaesitor and can lead the investigation), discovering that it is no isolated attack: assaults on the *saḥirs* of the Peninsula have been recurring for almost two centuries. Could the heirs of Clara of Apromor be responsible? But why has the Tribunal done nothing? And what if Duresca itself were aware of the attacks and looking the other way?
>
> [^p77-XXIII]: For sagas set before the game's canonical starting date, bear in mind that the Templars were founded in Jerusalem in the year 1119, and the first donations to the order in the Peninsula do not appear until 1132 (or 1127–1129 according to other sources).

<!-- p. 78 -->

Briatiz did not know quite what to do with the documents, so she called a council with the presiding Quaesitor Ṭāmis al-Išbīlī al-Gernikī, the judge Zaynab ḅint Qatr al-Nadà al-Gernikiyya, the *ductor* of the covenant of Brigantia, Al-Harqal al-Apromorī al-Flambī, and Arnau al-Merkerī, a member of the Mercer House of Aedes Saturni. At the meeting, Ṭāmis was able to confirm that the letters were in his master's hand; their contents, however, were too disconcerting to assume they were authentic, so they made copies of the documents and Ṭāmis requested an urgent hearing before the lower chamber of Magvillus.

The events that followed, known today to every magus of the Tribunal, were these:
- Arnau al-Merkerī spread news of the manuscripts both in Iberia (through his network of Redcaps) and in Europe (through Harco's communication networks).
- Ṭāmis went to Magvillus, where he was stripped of the title of Quaesitor.
- The upper chamber sent five Guernicus, led by Alvarra of Guernicus, to investigate the Duresca manuscripts.
- Three years later, in the winter of 940, the two foremost defenders of the authenticity of the Duresca manuscripts, Briatiz of Diedne and Ṭāmis, lost their lives at the battle of Frías.
- At the Tribunal of 941, the new presiding Quaesitor, Maryam ḅint Tello al-Gernikiyya, presented the evidence needed to declare the manuscripts fraudulent and have them destroyed.

The Tribunal of 941 cost the Praeco her reelection. To keep control of the Tribunal, Ǧamīla had to silence several magi after Quaesitor Maryam's statements. Her conduct was considered despotic and roused the distrust of many magi, especially after the Guernicus of Dār Malīḥaʾ accused Maryam of having let herself be bought by Magvillus's envoys (not without reason, for Maryam had accepted a position of responsibility in her new covenant, Duresca). As a result, at the conclusion of the Tribunal, the assembly elected the Andalusi Trianomae ʿAbbās ibn Munḏīr al-Bonisagī.

In the years that followed, numerous copies of the Duresca manuscripts came to light, so many that at the next Tribunal the judges of Duresca classed their dissemination as a low crime (which did nothing to cool the opinion Iberia's inhabitants held of the judges), and centralized at Duresca the records that until then had been kept at Salionca.

> #### The Conditions of Al-Muzaffar
>
> The *saḥirs* might have imposed other conditions for joining the Order of Hermes. This point can be left open so that each gaming group may freely add whatever clauses it sees fit to flavor its saga.

<!-- p. 79 -->

***941 AD, On the Records of Iberia II*** *(Maryam al-Gernikiyya)* Amendment to "On the Records of Iberia" (899). The records of Iberia shall be kept at the covenant of Duresca.

***948 AD, On the Duresca Manuscripts*** *(Alvarra of Guernicus)* Any reference to or dissemination of the proven-fraudulent "Duresca manuscripts" contributes to undermining the integrity of the Order and shall therefore be considered a low crime. Repeated offenses may come to be considered a high crime.

In those years the discredit of the Guernicus of Magvillus was keenly felt among the inhabitants of Iberia, and it was not until the purge of House Tytalus at the end of the tenth century that the magi of the Tribunal began to see them in a different light.

> #### The Fall of Ruiz Sánchez de Esco
>
> When Ruiz Sánchez of Flambeau walked out of the extraordinary Tribunal of 925, no one suspected that he was in fact walking out of the Order. Five years later, he led the attack on the covenant of al-ʿAbraj, inhabited solely by Ex Miscellanea *saḥirs*, without any declaration of Wizard's War. These deeds earned him expulsion at the Tribunal of 934, where Ṭāmis al-Išbīlī al-Gernikī served as presiding Quaesitor. Other Hermetic magi left the Order along with him, nearly all of them members of Salionca, among them Diego of Flambeau, Clara follower of Apromor, and Klynoites of Tytalus.
>
> Despite their expulsion, Ruiz Sánchez and his followers went on living at Salionca and attacking the Order's *saḥirs* with total impunity; although some magi tried to stop them, they were no match for the renegade Flambeau. Shortly after the scandal of the Duresca manuscripts, Ṭāmis obtained an Arcane Connection to Ruiz Sánchez (by unorthodox methods, it is said) and, together with Briatiz of Diedne, planned the attack, in which the magi of Duresca, Ṭāmis, the *saḥir* Al-Muzaffar al-Praliḥī, and Alvarra of Guernicus, newly arrived from Magvillus, all took part.
>
> The renegades were intercepted crossing the Ebro and defeated near Frías in the winter of 940. The battle cost the lives of Briatiz de Moncharro and Ṭāmis al-Išbīlī (curiously, the foremost defenders of the truth of the Duresca manuscripts) on one side, and those of Ruiz Sánchez de Esco and his followers on the other (although no one ever found the body of Clara of Apromor).

### The Kharijites

*In this state in which you see me, if you consider it carefully, I am the happiest of men. My dwelling is whatever spot I choose on the whole face of the earth. [...] I own no garments that I fear may arouse envy, nor will you see any money on me. For a pillow I use my right arm and, when I turn over, my left. I have neither father nor son and, since I reached the age of reason, I have founded no family. Some things once gave me pleasure; but I reflected upon them and saw that they were phantoms.*[^p79-34]

[^p79-34]: Verses by Abū Wahb al-ʿAbbāsī al-Qurṭubī (ninth century), taken from *In Praise of Spanish Islam* (Spanish translation by E. García Gómez).

After the scandal of the Duresca manuscripts, the Criamon of the covenant of Bayt al-Ḥikma, in the mountains of Almería, began preaching their ideas at the ordinary Tribunals. They claimed to be disciples of Aḥmed and Omar al-Harranī (those who had come to the Peninsula from distant Harran, the city of magic and wisdom), of Ibn Masarra of Cordoba (see the sidebar on the next page), and of the epistles of the Brethren of Purity.

They soon became known as the Kharijites (from the Arabic for "dissenters"), for their resemblance to the Islamic branch of the same name. This group advocated detachment from worldly things and the abolition of private property. To show the Order that things could be done differently, they opened the doors of Bayt al-Ḥikma to every magus who wished to benefit from their knowledge. Leaving aside the inherent obscurity of their mystery (which, as is customary in the House, they also offered to share), the rest of their knowledge was of general use, and so word began to spread among the magi of the Tribunal. Thus, at a time when justice had been corrupted by power, the Criamon shared their material and spiritual riches with the rest of the Order as a protest.

Bayt al-Ḥikma became a center of learning of the first rank for all the magi of the Peninsula and for those who came from abroad. The Criamon always devoted their time to teaching those who knocked at their door, never putting their own interests before those of others. They wove their doctrines into their teachings, for in doing so they claimed to be walking the path: "the intellect is a divine Gift, bestowed by the one God, which man has received so that he may rise above revealed knowledge and attain to, and become part of, the absolute one (or *tawhīd*)."

The Criamon of Bayt al-Ḥikma began to use their magical knowledge and riches to give shelter not only to members of the Order but also to mundanes, for according to their ideas the Founder's salvation was within reach of all mortals.

When this news reached the court of Madīnat al-Zahrāʾ, where the Masarrī doctrines had been condemned less than twenty years before, an order was issued for the arrest of the Criamon of Bayt al-Ḥikma. And so the Kharijites were condemned by the Mālikī fuqahāʾ in the spring of 963, and seized by the caliph's authorities that same summer.

<!-- p. 80 -->

When the magi of al-Andalus raised their voices to halt the execution, the Guernicus of Duresca reminded them that any action they took would be a violation of the Code and would put all the magi of Iberia in great danger. Reluctantly, the Praeco, ʿAbbās ibn Munḏīr al-Bonisagī, backed the Quaesitores of Duresca, for he did not wish to wreck the negotiations he was conducting with Al-Ḥakam II.

In so hostile a climate, civil war was averted only by the intervention of the Criamon of Barzaj, who spoke out in defense of the Order and of the inaction of the Tribunal's magi. "It is their decision," they said and, although many found it hard to accept Duresca's victory, they let the matter rest.

The Kharijites were crucified at the end of the summer of 963 on the roof terrace (*saṭḥ*) of the Azuda Gate, or *bāb al-Sudda*, and their covenant was plundered by the Order and, a month later, by the mundane forces of Cordoba. Since then the term "Kharijite" has been used to describe those who oppose the Order's policies.

> #### Ibn Masarra
>
> Abū ʿAbd Allāh Muḥammad ibn Masarra al-Ŷabalī (see page 316) is considered the first Andalusi mystic (twice anathematized and persecuted by the Mālikī fuqahāʾ of Cordoba) and the instigator of a class revolution during the tenth century. His doctrines and thought were deeply influenced by the Greek philosophy of Plato, Plotinus and Empedocles, as well as by Sufism, a branch of Muslim mysticism. Although profoundly Gnostic, he believed that the theses of Plotinus concealed the keys to deciphering certain esoteric meanings of the Qurʾan. For Ibn Masarra, however, rational knowledge (*falsafa*, or human intellect) could not be considered superior to the knowledge revealed by God, for inner knowledge could only be attained through intuition and never through rational or philosophical discourse (and he therefore criticized the philosophers, for they followed the wrong path, that of rationality).
>
> According to his doctrine, to become one with the *Spharios* (or to attain recognition of the divine unity, which is the one and final truth), one had to read the book of the universe (which confirms everything set forth in the Revealed Book) with the eyes of thought.
>
> After Ibn Masarra fled to Africa with two of his apprentices, Ibn Abdullah al-Roʿayni founded a Masarrī school in Almería, whose members came to be known as "the madmen of Pechina." One of his apprentices, Ibn al-ʿArif, gathered all the followers of this school in the mountains of Almería and drew up rules for the spiritual life, which he entrusted to three of his disciples to spread: Abū Bakū al-Mallorquī took charge of preaching them in the *kūra* of Granada; Ibn Qasī spread them in the *kūra* of al-Gharb, where he created a kind of religious militia (see "Chazāʾir," page 230); and Ibn Barraŷán went off to the remote *kūra* of Seville to preach them.
>
> The school of Masarra's followers was condemned in Madīnat al-Zahrāʾ and its members were persecuted until it was finally dissolved.

### The Tribunal and the Umayyads

The Praeco and Trianomae ʿAbbās ibn Munḏīr completed the cultural revolution begun by his lover, Ǧamīla. He made the Tribunal prosper through his relationship with the Umayyads and achieved an unprecedented milestone when, in 969, the Tribunal approved the use of the Great Mosque as a place of teaching for Hermetic magi with the Gentle Gift or their agents. Ibn Munḏīr drew on the Kharijites' good reputation to achieve this, with a speech that has often been studied by scholars of Hermetic law and was wielded as a thesis by the followers of Simprim in the twelfth century (see *Houses of Hermes: True Lineages*, page 46). An excerpt follows:

<!-- p. 81 -->

*[…] The Kharijites have not abandoned us, not while their teachings live on, not while we keep their memory alive. We must continue their work, but clearing the heresy from their doctrines, lest we provoke the wrath of mundanes and fall into violation of the Code of Hermes […].*

*[…] On the second anniversary of the death of the great lexicographer Abū ʿAli al-Qalī al-Bagdadī, from whom I had the good fortune to receive many lessons in the Great Mosque of Cordoba, I summon you, brothers. You who have traveled to Qayrawān, Alexandria, Fusṭāṭ, Damascus, Constantinople and Baghdad to learn from the masters of the East. […] All of you, sisters, for you have changed the course of the history of al-Andalus. Let us give back what we have learned, so that we may go on growing! […]*

***969 AD, On the Great Mosque of Cordoba*** *(Qāsim ibn Muṭarrif al-Gernikī)* Any magus with the Gentle Gift, or any of his agents, may claim a free column of the Great Mosque of Cordoba in order to teach classes in Hermetic or mundane knowledge. The classes must remain within the bounds of the Mālikī school so as not to violate the Code of Hermes. In any case, responsibility rests with the teacher, who must on no account make known his connection with the Order of Hermes, on pain of expulsion. Naturally, classes must be suspended for the daily prayers, and the teacher must always first attend the hall of ablutions, in accordance with the precepts of Islamic law. Where there are children, the teacher shall be responsible for their care and for ensuring that they do not soil the mats on which the faithful must prostrate themselves. Under no circumstances shall teachers be entitled to receive any payment for their classes.

### Al-ʿIdwa:[^p81-35] Beyond the Pillars of Hercules

The Tribunal's relations with the caliphate allowed the Order to spread into the protectorates al-Andalus had established in Africa and, although in 925 the Order had agreed not to occupy Africa for a period of 300 years, the magi of Iberia set out to explore the African continent all the same; their justification was that they did not wish to found a covenant *per se*, but a Mercer House, and the judges agreed that this did not constitute a violation of the treaty. And so, after the Tribunal of 976, a group of Redcaps led by the maga Umm al-Kirām al-Merkeriyya was sent to Africa. Their travels lasted five years and were recorded by a Redcap of Porta Pandere in a long *risāla* of epic character, which the Merinitae have more than once used as inspiration for organizing what they call the Great Game (see *Houses of Hermes: Mystery Cults*, page 146).

[^p81-35]: From the Arabic, "the other shore of the strait."

<!-- p. 82 -->

> #### Bilad al-Sūdān
>
> When the Arabs crossed the great Sahara Desert in the mid-eighth century, they discovered the riches of the ancient kingdom of Awkār, which they called the land of gold. According to the writings of Abū Ishāq Ibrāhīm ibn al-Ḥabīb al-Fazārī, the kingdom was created by the *soninké* clan, descendants of the mythical *sissé* clan, which had made a pact with a huge and terrible black serpent they called Bida: in exchange for the yearly sacrifice of one of the virgins of the city of Wagadu (Gāna, as the Berbers called it), the serpent made gold fall with the rain.
>
> The kingdom grew rich thanks to this pact until the coming of the young warrior Mamadi who, driven by the imminent sacrifice of his beloved, went to the place where Bida made its lair. There, after a hard fight, Mamadi managed to defeat the serpent and cut off its head. Then a curse fell upon Wagadu: a terrible drought. With the rains gone, gold ceased to fall from the sky, and the kingdom sank into a deep crisis that brought about its disappearance.
>
> Although the Arabs and Berbers settled in *bilad al-Sūdān*, fighting the tribes of the western Sudan, they did not succeed in imposing their religion until the coming of the Almoravids; until then Islam coexisted openly with the native pagan cults of the ancient kingdom of Awkār.

> #### Story Seeds: The Curse of the Kingdom of Awkār
>
> One of the magi of the characters' covenant gets hold of the *risāla* of Umm al-Kirām al-Merkeriyya and is struck by the legend of the serpent Bida. After some thought, he believes it would be possible to travel to the ancient ruins of the Mercer House of Tāfīlālt and try to undo the curse that brought drought to the kingdom of Awkār and, with it, the scarcity of gold. A stress roll of Intelligence + Iberian Tribunal Lore of 6+ reveals that the Mercer House of Tāfīlālt was destroyed in mysterious circumstances, and a stress roll of Intelligence + Code of Hermes of 6+ reveals that the Tribunal agreed not to settle on the African continent until 1225. Perhaps the characters can turn to the only surviving African covenant (al-Minẓār) for more information, or venture into the African continent on their own.

> #### Story Seeds: The Magical Gold Coins
>
> From 1160 onward the Christian presence in the Maghreb increased, as the Almohad caliphs signed trade treaties with the republics of Genoa and Pisa. As a result, by the end of the twelfth century, Ceuta had become an important base of operations for the Genoese.
>
> While one of the magi of the characters' covenant is reviewing his autocrat's accounts of the income from their businesses in Ceuta, he discovers by chance that one of the gold coins holds vis, and not just any vis, but extraordinary vis (see *Realms of Power: Magic*, page 147). Puzzled, the magus examines the coin, on which the following can be read in Arabic:
>
> **Obverse** *There is no god but the One God; none may be associated with Him.*[^p82-XXIV]
>
> **Reverse** *In the name of God this dinar was struck in the dār al-sikka of Madīnat al-Zahrāʾ.*
>
> Vis cannot be preserved in any manufactured object, yet this dinar belies it. Moreover, what path has the dinar, minted during the caliphate of al-Andalus, followed? Could more be obtained by following that trail? The characters will have to investigate the dinar and, with it, its history. Perhaps they will have to travel to their trading posts in Ceuta and track down the Genoese merchant who gave them the coin in order to find its twins. In the course of the story they will discover that all the caliphs' gold came from *bilad al-Sūdān*, where the destroyed Mercer House of Aedes Iris once stood. Their inquiries will lead them to the Mercer Houses of the Tribunal to investigate the transport of the gold (see the sidebar on page 26) and, finally, to the vis sources of the old covenant of Aedes Iris, where they may delve into, and even uncover, the secret that claimed the few Hermetic magi who reached those lands.
>
> [^p82-XXIV]: Spanish translation by José Luis de Villar.

When Umm al-Kirām returned, the Tribunal approved the creation of the Mercer House of Aedes Iris (for more on the possible truthfulness of this *risāla*, take a look at the sidebar "The Mystery of *bilad al-Sūdān*" on page 272).

Once fully established in Africa, the Tribunal approved the creation of a second Mercer House in the Peninsula, which the Mercere named Porta Pandere (subsidiary to Aedes Saturni). For communication between them, new Mercere portals were agreed upon and, to distinguish them from the first ones, they began numbering them from ten. Thus four new portals were built: *Decimus*, *Undecimus*, *Duodecimus* and *Tertius Decimus*. Nevertheless, until Porta Pandere was created, the Peninsula had no direct communication with Africa, for the Redcaps of Aedes Saturni did not wish to risk exposure to the possible repercussions of the Hermetic settlement in Africa.

Aedes Iris opened the gold of *bilad al-Sūdān* to the coffers of the Tribunal, which began exporting great riches to Harco. This contributed to the economic rise of House Mercere in particular and of the Order in general. The magical horizon opened up by the first Hermetic expeditions to Africa helped the Tribunal's magical expansion and the mapping of numerous African vis sources by the Mercere of Aedes Iris… whose secrets died with them.

<!-- p. 83 -->

### The Corruption of House Tytalus

When the corruption of House Tytalus was revealed, the Guernicus seized the opportunity to divert attention from the scandal of the Duresca manuscripts, since they had been unable to restore their House's image. Although no Tytalus in Iberia was implicated, the events further undermined what little confidence the magi of al-Andalus had in the Order.

The corruption of the Tytalus coincided with the publication of the meetings held in 962 between ʿAbbās and the caliph Al-Ḥakam II. According to the minutes revealed by the Redcaps, the Praeco had denounced the Kharijites to advance himself at the Umayyad court. At such news, the discontent of Iberia's inhabitants, with the Schism War already brewing, turned to fury: the covenant of al-Zahrāʾ was denounced to the fuqahāʾ of Cordoba, the magi who lived there scattered across the Peninsula, and the Praeco fled the Tribunal. The ordinary Tribunal of 996[^p83-36] was therefore held at Duresca and, to make up for the Praeco's absence, the magi of northern Iberia (no Andalusi magus answered the summons) voted at its opening to elect the "ephemeral" and aged *ductor* of the covenant of Tremébriga, Ibn Sahl al-Tremerī, whose reputation as a hoplite preceded him. Duresca, for its part, supported his term of office, having taken an active part alongside the Guernicus of Magvillus in the purge of House Tytalus.

[^p83-36]: The Tribunal should have been held in 997, but since that coincided with the Grand Tribunal it was held a year early.

The Tribunal of 996 was a prelude to what was to come. Ibn Sahl al-Tremerī lashed out at the Tribunal's Diedne, silencing them and expelling them from Duresca one after another, until the *ductor* of the Autumn covenant of Mons Vindius, Tridio of Diedne, refused to leave the hall. The Tribunal then came to an abrupt end when Tremébriga declared Wizard's War on Mons Vindius, marking the end of the period of the Arabization of the Iberian Tribunal.

> #### The Repression of the Philosophers (I): Almanzor
>
> When Almanzor seized temporal power in al-Andalus, the *ductor* of the covenant of al-Zahrāʾ managed to stay on good terms with him by presenting him with sumptuous gifts, among them precious codices on Mālikī legal doctrine, robes of Almerían cloth-of-gold, and a mechanical ostrich built by the Verditius of the Majorcan covenant of Ajabeba. In this way ʿAbbās was able to save many works from the royal library of Al-Ḥakam II, which Almanzor himself had ordered burned. The Praeco also took advantage of the droughts of 989 and 992 to improve his reputation, donating 22,000 loaves a day to be distributed among the populace.
>
> The fortunes of the wealthy Cordoban covenant changed radically, however, with the publication of the negotiations the Praeco had held with the caliph Al-Ḥakam II in 962: an anonymous member of the Order informed a powerful faqih that the covenant of al-Zahrāʾ held forbidden writings, and Almanzor found himself obliged to order the covenant searched. When the fuqahāʾ found countless books of philosophy, Hermetic knowledge and natural history in its immense library, the former Praeco was found guilty of heresy and condemned in the Great Mosque of Cordoba. To avoid capture, ʿAbbās ibn Munḏīr abandoned the covenant of al-Zahrāʾ and escaped both mundane justice and Hermetic disgrace. No one ever saw him again.

> #### Story Seeds: The Ruins of al-Zahrāʾ
>
> The magi of the player characters' covenant use a grog to harvest the vis from the source on the slopes of *Ŷabal al-ʿArus*, but the grog has not come back. After waiting a reasonable time, they send one of the covenant's young magi to find out what has happened to him. Although they will probably suspect another covenant, the trail of the missing grog leads them to an old silo among the rubble of the ancient city of Madīnat al-Zahrāʾ. The grog's body lies lifeless before an ancient portico carved in green marble. The grog does not appear to have died a violent death, and he still carries all the vis he harvested. What if he had discovered an entrance to the cellars of the sumptuous covenant of al-Zahrāʾ?

## The Fate of ʿĀd and Tamūd:[^p83-37] The Schism War

*Their traces have been erased, their vestiges have vanished [...]. Ruin has overturned everything. Prosperity has turned into barren desert; society, into dreadful solitude; beauty, into scattered rubble; tranquility, into terrifying crossroads. Now the places where they dwelt are a refuge for wolves, a plaything for ogres, a pastime for jinn and a lair for wild beasts […]. Their company has been broken up […]. Those halls full of inscriptions, those adorned chambers […], now […] are like the gaping jaws of ferocious beasts that proclaim how transient this world is; they make you see the end that awaits its dwellers; they make you know where everything you see in it will come to rest, and they make you give up desiring it, after having long made you unable to give it up.*[^p83-38]

[^p83-37]: The legendary and mighty peoples of ʿĀd and Tamūd in Arabia were destroyed by God for their impiety. For the Arabs they exemplify the instability of all that men build.

[^p83-38]: From Ibn Ḥazm's *The Ring of the Dove* (Spanish translation by Emilio García Gómez).

<!-- p. 84 -->

Almost all the Hermetic scholars of Iberia consider that the events of the Schism War deserve a chapter of their own. During those years no ordinary Tribunal was held in the Peninsula; the consequences in Iberia were the tearing apart of the social fabric and the disintegration of the Tribunal.

Violence between House Diedne and House Tremere grew *in crescendo* in Iberia until the rule of law disappeared, so that in 1004 the Tribunal could not be held, and when the year 1010 arrived House Tremere declared war on the Diedne. The Tremere of the Peninsula were joined by the Flambeau of Salionca and by the Jerbiton, a representative sample of what was happening throughout the Order.

The Guernicus then decided to put an end to the conflicts, and the Primus of the House convened an extraordinary Grand Tribunal in 1011 (in place of the ordinary regional Tribunals) to resolve a problem that had by now become universal.

Thanks to the Tribunal's Redcaps, the most important bodies of Iberia were able to go to Magvillus to decide the fate of the two warring Houses. The Grand Tribunal decreed the expulsion of House Diedne and all its members and, when the news reached Iberia, the *ductor* of Mons Vindius, Tridio of Diedne, summoned the Diedne of the Tribunal to take refuge in his covenant. They did not fight alone in the Peninsula, however: the Flambeau of Brigantia stood at their side and joined them in the subsequent failed assaults on the covenants of Tertia, Duresca and Salionca, and in the war that ended with the destruction of Tremébriga, where the Praeco of the Tribunal, Ibn Sahl al-Tremerī, met his death.

For her part, when the Trianomae Ḥafṣa ibn ʿAbbās al-Bonisagiyya of the Andalusi covenant of Dār Malīḥaʾ returned from the extraordinary Grand Tribunal of 1011, she issued a communiqué inviting all the covenants of Iberia to disregard the resolution passed there. To the surprise of the northern magi of the Peninsula, almost every covenant of al-Andalus endorsed this manifesto, and most of the *saḥirs*, fearing they would share the fate of House Diedne, stayed out of the conflict. And so, in the winter of 1012, virtually all the Andalusi covenants voted at an extraordinary tribunal to split from the Iberian Tribunal and form the Tribunal of al-Andalus, a decision many took following the prophecy made by Maslama, the head of the school of mathematics of Majrīṭ (see page 287). This meeting thus became the first Tribunal of al-Andalus (see below).

While the magi of the south of the Peninsula kept out of the war, in the north the magi toiled in their struggle against the Diedne. After the ritual of the Curse of Thoth (see *Houses of Hermes: True Lineages*, page 82), however, the renegades began to lose a battle they had seemed certain to win, and their allies began to fall back with them. Thus the Flambeau of Salionca at last managed to subdue those of Brigantia, who were tried at Salionca in 1016, in a proceeding that came to be known as the Concord of Fire. At its conclusion the *ductor* of Brigantia was executed, and the rest of the covenant's magi were punished, placed under surveillance and pardoned in exchange for taking part in the next assault on Mons Vindius. Thanks to the Concord of Fire, the Order obtained all the information it needed to raze the last Diedne stronghold in the Peninsula in the autumn of 1016. Before he died, Tridio was able to witness two of his *filii* escaping to Nebula, from where they presumably fled to the covenant of the Diedne Primus, in Wales.

A year later, the Order saw the end of the war with the destruction of the last Diedne stronghold in all of Mythic Europe. The Order nonetheless went on hunting down the remaining renegades for several more years, which prolonged the conflict, albeit on a local scale.

The Schism War also led the covenants that survived the fighting in the region north of the Pyrenees to decide to pay tribute to the Provençal Tribunal and become part of it. The decision was taken partly in order to resist the southward advance of the Tytalus, who intended to claim the treasure of the fallen Diedne covenants. In any case, the Tribunal hardly felt the loss, for Aedes Saturni had always organized Iberia's communications and had a powerful base in the Peninsula. It is worth noting that the covenant of Val-Negra, once the *domus magna* of the Flambeau and now vanished, also fell during the Schism War; many of its surviving members withdrew to the temple of Mercury founded by Priamitus, to create Aedes Mercurii.

## The Disintegration of the Iberian Tribunal

Hermetic scholars decided to group the events of the Iberian Tribunal and of al-Andalus under a single period, which they chose to call "the disintegration of the Iberian Tribunal," since the Tribunal of al-Andalus was never recognized de facto by the powers of the Order. Each region, however, acted independently of the other, and while the north recovered from the ravages of the Schism War, in the south currents of thought began to germinate that would have a profound impact on what was to come. What follows recounts the most significant events in each of the regions after the Schism War.

During this period the following Praecones held office in Iberia and, although never officially recognized, in al-Andalus:

| Praecones of al-Andalus | Years |
| --- | --- |
| Ḥafṣa ibn ʿAbbās al-Bonisagiyya | 1012–1068 |
| Al-ʿĀsmarun al-Ŷerbitonī | 1075–1103 |

| Praecones of Iberia | Years |
| --- | --- |
| Bruto of Flambeau | 1018–1074 |
| Yulyān ibn Muhŷa al-Bonisagī | 1081–1109 |

<!-- p. 85 -->

### The Tribunal of al-Andalus: Between Scylla and Charybdis[^p85-39]

*If our world is of noble origin, how then does it serve as food for dogs, stinking carrion to which flies swarm?*[^p85-40]

The Tribunal of al-Andalus was born as a regional Tribunal by popular vote and without the approval of the Order's powers: its founders were starting a revolution. The one who began the movement, the elderly Ḥafṣa ibn ʿAbbās al-Bonisagiyya, was elected Praeco before the Schism War ended. While the magi of the rest of Mythic Europe fought a war on a global scale, virtually all the magi of al-Andalus refused to take part in it, thereby showing their discontent with the Order's policies. Moreover, by then there was no living Diedne covenant in al-Andalus, for, apart from Ipagrum, destroyed during the *saḥir* attack of 907, the members of that House had always shown a preference for the domains of the ancient druids, located in northern Iberia.

Not without some controversy, Porta Pandere and Aedes Iris joined the Andalusi movement, withdrawing the support the northern magi needed in their struggle against the Diedne. The loss of the Iberian tax revenues from the covenants of al-Andalus, and the departure of the magical and mundane treasure that reached the Portuguese Mercer House from Aedes Iris, left the Order's combatants in difficulty, and many blamed the Andalusis for depriving the rest of the Peninsula's magi of the resources they needed. Indeed, the Tremere still remember that if Porta Pandere, Aedes Iris and the covenants of al-Andalus had remained at their side, the powerful covenant of Tremébriga would not have been lost. However, House Mercere had its own internal conflicts in the Tribunal, which Porta Pandere and Aedes Iris exploited to make themselves independent of Aedes Saturni.

Broadly speaking, the Tribunal of al-Andalus enjoyed a long period of well-being and harmony while the rest of Europe recovered from a long war. Keeping out of events contributed to the prosperity the Tribunal would enjoy in the years after the Schism War, in the so-called Tribunals of Joy. But that long idyll, which all knew could not last, also had its dark moments: while in Europe the Order was granting almost absolute powers to House Guernicus to prevent any repetition of a new Schism, al-Andalus lived through the fall of the caliphate, the destruction of the palatine cities of Madīnat al-Zahrāʾ and Madīnat al-Zaḥirāʾ, the rise of the taifa kingdoms and the beginning of the Gregorian Reform.

[^p85-39]: The nymph Scylla was turned into a monster by Circe the sorceress, for she was loved by the sea god Glaucus, whom Circe desired. Charybdis, daughter of Poseidon, was turned into a monster by Zeus as punishment for helping her father flood the land. According to Homer, the two monsters dwell on opposite shores of a strait, so that avoiding one means falling into the clutches of the other. This is how the magi of al-Andalus felt when they had to choose between independence and annexation to the Iberian Tribunal.

[^p85-40]: Poem from *The Treatise of Familiar Spirits and Demons* by Ibn Shuhayd (Spanish translation by Salvador Barberá).

<!-- p. 86 -->

#### The First Tribunal of al-Andalus

Al-Andalus held its first Tribunal in the winter of 1012, at Dār Malīḥaʾ, where the magi voted for independence following Maslama's prophecies and where the first two rulings of its Peripheral Code were approved, building on the legislative foundation of the Iberian Tribunal. Especially noteworthy was the decision to abolish the Iberian tax after approving the construction of a mint at Porta Pandere, using the metal that came from *bilad al-Sūdān* via Aedes Iris. As for magical resources, Aedes Iris undertook to donate to the Tribunal's treasury as much vis as was needed to meet any needs that might arise among the members of al-Andalus, provided that the presiding judge and the Praeco agreed and that there was at least a Tribunal vote passing by half plus one.

***1012 AD, On the Andalusi Treasury*** *(ʿAdlun al-Gernikī)* As "On the Iberian Treasury" (822), with the following amendment: the Tribunal's treasury shall be kept at the covenant of Porta Pandere and guarded by two magi bearing the titles of *ḥárisun* and *jāzin*, who need not reside at that covenant.

***1012 AD, Abolition of the Iberian Tax*** *(ʿAdlun al-Gernikī)* The Iberian tax is revoked for all the covenants of the Tribunal of al-Andalus.

#### The Collapse of the Cities of Madīnat al-Zahrāʾ and Madīnat al-Zaḥirāʾ

Maslama's predictions came true, and many Andalusis saw the end of an era with the fall of the palatine cities of Madīnat al-Zahrāʾ and Madīnat al-Zaḥirāʾ. When the governor of Cordoba, Abu-l-Walid al-Rasid, decided to sell what remained of the cities and allowed them to be plundered, the Praeco and Trianomae Ḥafṣa ibn ʿAbbās al-Bonisagiyya sent word to the Redcaps of Porta Pandere and Aedes Iris to gather all the money at their disposal and go to Cordoba to buy what was being auctioned there. The Redcaps were able to buy marble, beautiful columns, fine woods, worked copper and a great many books that had been seized from the royal library of Al-Ḥakam II and from the covenant of al-Zahrāʾ, and that had been saved from Almanzor's burning. The bidding was fierce, however, for despite the gold the Redcaps had brought, the Verditius of the covenant of Ajabeba turned up with countless riches to recover, in their words, the works their House brothers had left there, since along with the rest of the materials for sale, Cordoba was auctioning the marvelous devices that the Verditius of al-Zahrāʾ and Ajabeba had created (see the insert on the previous page).

> #### The Verditius Devices of Cordoba
>
> Among the goods auctioned by the governor of Cordoba were the marvels that the covenant of al-Zahrāʾ had crafted in its workshops or had bought from the Verditius of Ajabeba, many of them given as gifts to the caliphs of Cordoba to win their favor and used to dazzle the ambassadors of other kingdoms.
>
> This is not a complete list of all the devices that existed in Madīnat al-Zahrāʾ; feel free to create new contrivances with your troupe. Bear in mind that in many cases what is prized is not the Hermetic power of the object but the uniqueness of its craftsmanship. These pieces are one-of-a-kind works, and although their invested effects may be simple, their value is incalculable.
>
> - The mechanical ostrich. When the ostrich of the *ḥāŷib* Almanzor died, shortly before the negotiations of ʿAbbās ibn Munḏīr came to light, the latter gave him a beautiful automaton that imitated the bird's movements. Its mechanical workings allowed it to run at great speed, and every lunar month it laid a delicious egg that the court cooks fried for the enjoyment of the courtiers.
>
> - The swimmer of the Sudan. When the ambassador of Constantinople presented the caliph ʿAbd al-Raḥmān III with the copy of Dioscorides' book, the caliph was able to marvel at a black automaton swimming in one of the palace pools. Besides imitating the movements of a swimmer (without the water damaging its gears), the automaton had the power to plunge whoever watched it into a placid hypnotic calm, delightful for anyone wishing to think clearly about grave matters. This automaton is believed to have been commissioned from the Verditius of Ajabeba by the workshops of Madīnat al-Zahrāʾ.
>
> - The golden nightingale. Among the thousand-colored birds caged in the palace of Madīnat al-Zahrāʾ hid a precious mechanical device given by ʿAbbās ibn Munḏīr to the caliph Al-Ḥakam II. The courtiers played at finding it with their eyes closed among the other birds of the palace's great aviaries. Its song is said to have been so beautiful that it inspired memorable verses.
>
> - The great bronze griffin. More than a meter tall, the griffin, which the Arabs considered a protective and beneficent creature, had Kufic bands carved on its belly bearing the following message: "blessing, profit, joy, health and complete and lasting happiness be upon its owner." On the upper part of the forelegs the craftsmen engraved the figure of a lion, and on the hind legs that of an eagle. The wings and head were decorated with stylized feathers, and the body with incised circles. This true masterpiece formed part of the riches of the covenant of al-Zahrāʾ until it was bought by the Verditius of Ajabeba (see *Houses of Hermes: Mystery Cults*, page 233).
>
> - The peacock-shaped ewer was one of the many gifts the Praeco made to the caliph. This cast and chased bronze ewer, thirty-two centimeters tall, was decorated with plant motifs and had delicate plumage carved along its whole body. When tipped as if to pour, pure, crystal-clear water flowed from its beak; however, if the word *jamrun* was spoken first, a delicious white wine poured from the beak. If instead one said *nabīḏun ʾaḥmarun*, a spiced red wine flowed. Those who tasted it said it was even better than the wines of Malaga. This object is especially useful when its owner is in places where Qurʾanic law is strictly enforced, since that law forbids the drinking of wine.
>
> - The bronze tripod brazier. This large circular brazier stands on three legs. Its body is decorated with carvings of numerous animals, and its chain-shaped handles are joined to the body by small horse figures. Without any other fire, the brazier warms and softly lights the room it stands in. The atmosphere it creates is so welcoming that any mundane becomes inclined to listen to, or even close, any deal that is handsomely presented to him.
>
> - The mercury of the Hall of Kings. Unfortunately, the basin of mercury was lost at some point during the burning of the palatine city in the Cordoban civil war. The Verditius say that the mercury was enchanted with powerful Imaginem spells, which could create marvelous lights and atmospheres capable of swaying the most important decisions toward the caliph's interests. Its Penetration is said to have been so great that not even magi were safe from its influence.

<!-- p. 87 -->

Ajabeba bought numerous Hermetic and mundane works, and the Praeco summoned its magi to Dār Malīḥaʾ to reach an agreement with them, for she planned that much of the Cordoban riches would go to a Great Hall that was to serve as a common space for all the magi of the new Tribunal of al-Andalus. However, the Verditius of Ajabeba did not appear. This only increased the tension between the Tribunal's magi and Ajabeba; it began to be said that the latter had sold magic items to the Diedne and Flambeau of Brigantia during the Schism War, something that, however, has never been proven.

#### The Tribunals of Joy

During the second ordinary Tribunal of al-Andalus, the magi present agreed to create a common space to house their meetings and to serve as neutral ground for sharing knowledge. Although at first they considered the city of Cordoba, its instability due to the civil war (and the great plague that had ravaged it in 1011) forced the magi to look for a better site. The Praeco again turned to the mathematicians of Madrid and, thanks to their predictions, they decided to build the Great Hall in a powerful *lacuna*[^p87-41] in the city of Saragossa, which at that time was ruled by the Tujibid petty king Al-Munḍir ibn Yahya al-Tuŷībī.

[^p87-41]: *Lacunae* (singular *lacuna*) are spaces in the urban fabric that are not affected by the Dominion and may have, as in this case, a Magic aura.

Throughout the life of the Tribunal of al-Andalus, the Great Hall housed the best books (mundane and Hermetic) and laboratory texts of all the Tribunal's magi. In fact, the Andalusi Bonisagi copied their research for the Great Hall before sending it to Durenmar. In time it became the residence of a cultural elite of the Order, endowed with great facilities thanks to the immeasurable riches that arrived from the lands of *bilad al-Sūdān* through the Mercer House of Aedes Iris.

The most significant aspects of the Hermetic law of al-Andalus were recorded in two entries of the Peripheral Code.

***1019 AD, The Tribunals of Joy*** *(ʿAdlun al-Gernikī)* For the sharing of knowledge among all the magi of the Tribunal of al-Andalus, and for the growth of the Order, all magi of al-Andalus shall have the right to use the common spaces, library and laboratories of the Great Hall, and shall be guaranteed a seat in the forum of Ḥafṣa[^p87-42]. Ordinary Tribunals shall begin one day before the winter solstice and, before it begins, all those present shall have the duty to take part in casting the *Aegis of the Hearth*. The Praeco shall be responsible for performing the ritual (as well as for keeping the tokens generated by the casting), and the necessary vis shall come from the treasury kept at Porta Pandere. The Great Hall shall house all the records of the Tribunals and the copies of the Andalusi Bonisagi's research, as well as any research carried out by any member of the Order in the facilities of the Great Hall.

To protect the Great Hall, a magus from among the Tribunal's covenants shall be required, who must volunteer to hold the office of *al-gay’yūrun*. This magus shall live in the Great Hall in the period between Tribunals. The office shall be filled anew at each Tribunal, and no member shall in any case be compelled to hold it. Should the office be left vacant, it shall be filled by popular vote.

Finally, to reinforce security and avoid attracting the attention of mundane powers, all members of the Tribunal must hold an Arcane Connection to the Great Hall, and access to it by any means other than magic shall be forbidden save with the express permission of the Praeco and the Quaesitores.

[^p87-42]: This was the name given to the meeting hall of the ordinary Tribunals.

***1026 AD, On the Official Language of the Tribunal*** *(ʿAdlun al-Gernikī)* The official language of the Tribunal of al-Andalus shall be Arabic. (See insert.)

> #### Arabic as a Language of Iberia
>
> At the Tribunal of 1026, Classical Arabic was chosen as the official language; from it derived Andalusi Arabic (a dialect quite distant from Classical Arabic) and Mozarabic (in this case a Romance dialect). Next, since Arabic has two main scripts (Kufic, used chiefly for ornament, and Naskh, a cursive script that is easier to read), the Tribunal voted on which one to use. The fact that Naskh was the script mainly used by the copyists of that time led to its choice as the official script of the Tribunal of al-Andalus (later, the Almoravids would choose Kufic as their official script).
>
> During the Tribunals of Joy, all texts were written in Arabic.

In 1061, the Order forbade Hermetic magi to sell their magic items to mundane society without intermediaries. Moreover, one of House Verditius's edicts limited such sales to one magic item per year at most. For this reason the Verditius negotiated with the magi of al-Andalus an entry in the Peripheral Code that would improve their selling conditions under the protection of the law, and as a gesture of goodwill they gave them seven bronze and silver automata to guard the Tribunal of al-Andalus's flagship building. This also helped ease the tensions with the Verditius of Ajabeba that had lingered since the incident at the auctions of the riches of the Cordoban palatine cities. Thus the following entry of the Peripheral Code was approved:

<!-- p. 88 -->

***1068 AD, On the Exchange of Enchantments with Mundanes*** *(Danāʾ al-Gernikiyya)* A single magus may sell as many magical enchantments per year as he has clients under the rule of different mundane princes, and always through mundane intermediaries. That is, in a single year (as of the date this entry was approved), a magus may sell, for example, one item to a man of Granada, one to a man of Cordoba and one to a man of Valencia, since all three are subject to different mundane powers.

This entry remained unamended, so with the end of the taifas the Verditius lost much of the diversity of their sales when all the kingdoms were gathered under the banner of the Almoravids.

With the arrival of the Banū Hūd in Saragossa, the beautiful *Qasr al-Jaʿfariya* was built, and the magi of al-Andalus took part in the cultural revolution the dynasty brought with it. In this climate a charismatic magus was elected Praeco: the poet Al-ʿĀsmarun al-Ŷerbitonī of Dār Malīḥaʾ, a native of Baghdad. Al-ʿĀsmarun was an extremely intelligent man with great social gifts; the magi of al-Andalus had chosen him in part to keep the newly begun Gregorian Reform from harming them and to return to the bosom of the Order. Al-ʿĀsmarun therefore put an end to the revolution Ḥafṣa had begun and started the legal process to establish the Tribunal of al-Andalus officially. Like the other Andalusi magi, Al-ʿĀsmarun knew that the magi of Iberia had not brought the Andalusi case before the Grand Tribunals of 1030 and 1063, so the Tribunal of al-Andalus sent a letter to the Iberian Tribunal asking that its Praeco be granted an audience at the next ordinary meeting. His wish was to settle that hidden debt and lay the foundations needed for al-Andalus to establish itself at last as an independent regional Tribunal recognized by the Order. Thus, at the Iberian Tribunal of 1081, the Praeco attended as ambassador of the Tribunal of al-Andalus to negotiate its independence. However, the northern covenants, especially Duresca and Aedes Saturni, had been waiting for that meeting, and they would on no account accept the departure of more than half of the Peninsula's covenants.

> #### The Court Poets
>
> During the period of the taifa kingdoms, their petty kings and magnates acted as protectors and patrons of the arts and sciences and held poets and poetry in the highest esteem. To take advantage of this cultural boom, some magi became protégés of the sultans, from whom they obtained favors, riches or lands on which to build their covenants or exploit their vis sources.

> #### Story Seeds: The Poetry Contest
>
> The characters have just passed their Gauntlet in Iberia and are eager to found a covenant. After seeking the advice of their *parentes*, they settle on a wonderful site whose nearest vis source has not yet been claimed. However, after they have been settled there for a season, they receive a visit from an emissary of the sultan. Escorted by a dozen armed men, he urges them to accompany him to the palace, where they will be judged for occupying his lord's land without permission. The player characters may want to win the sultan's favor, and what better way than through a poetry contest?
>
> In these contests the challengers must pass a test of improvisation: the poet and protégé of the court speaks the opening of the poem, and the challenger must continue it in the same meter and rhyme. Challenger and protégé make opposed Communication + Arabic (poetic improvisation specialty) rolls over five rounds. The contest is won by whoever doubles the opponent's result in a single roll, or by whoever wins more rounds than the rival (in case of a tie, the one with the higher Presence wins). But what if the protégé were a faerie?
>
> The character's poetic skills will be put to the test, and the future of their lives and their Spring covenant will depend on their ability. On the other hand, if the character wins the contest, he will no doubt make an enemy of the former protégé, now displaced by the player character. In any case, if he dazzles the sultan, the sultan will gladly lift his punishment, and the covenant's lands will be the first of his many gifts.
>
> Bear in mind that Arab folklore attributes the ability to write poetry, or to improvise it before an audience, to the *jinn*. Other possible poetry-related specialties of Arabic include poetic improvisation, the muwashshah, the kharja, the zajal and panegyric poetry.

The meeting was tense on both sides and ended with an ultimatum from the Iberian Tribunal: al-Andalus had the span of one full Tribunal (that is, seven years) to dissolve its separate meetings and hand over its administration and riches to the powers of Iberia. Otherwise, Iberia would denounce its situation to the Grand Tribunal, and all the Andalusi magi would be condemned and possibly cast out.

The following year, the members of al-Andalus met in Saragossa for the next ordinary Tribunal. The Guernicus of al-Andalus advised the gathering to vote for the dissolution of the Tribunal, for a confrontation with the Order had to be avoided at all costs (the Schism War had ended barely fifty years before and was still very present in the magi's minds). Then, to everyone's surprise, Porta Pandere announced that if the Tribunal ruled for independence, the Mercere would stop providing their services, a stance which, however, Aedes Iris did not support. At the close of the meeting, the Praeco Al-ʿĀsmarun asked all those present to reflect on the matter until the next Tribunal.

<!-- p. 89 -->

#### The Gregorian Reform

The reform promoted by Pope Gregory VII (see page 39) brought about a change of mentality for the magi of the Tribunal. Rome had made a new enemy of the men and women alongside whom the magi had lived for years.

The Tribunal's *sodales* received this news with sorrow, and many began to foresee an unpromising future; after all, all the cultural enrichment they had experienced was owed almost entirely to the people on whom Rome had declared war. The Reform ominously foreshadowed the fate that seemed to await the Tribunal of al-Andalus.

> #### Story Seeds: The Gregorian Reform
>
> When the player characters' magi, in a covenant in northern Iberia, learn of Gregory VII's pronouncements, they applaud his decisions and look to the future with optimism. A year later, however, they receive a letter from the bishop: the church that stands on the covenant's lands, which brings them considerable income from the tithe and the donations of local nobles, will from next year become part of the parish dependent on the bishopric in question. Before the Reform, churches could be under the control of monasteries or laymen, but the centralizing reform movement forbade this.
>
> The magi are about to lose their greatest source of income, without which they will be unable to support all the covenant's inhabitants. The looming crisis has no easy solution, for how could they get the bishopric to let them keep the benefits of the Church's tithe? Will they face poverty (with all that it entails), or will they defy the Church, and therefore Rome, even at the risk of the Quaesitores opening a case against them?

#### The Tribunal of al-Andalus of 1089

During the seven years of reflection, on their visits to the Tribunal's covenants, the Redcaps of Porta Pandere waged a propaganda campaign urging the magi of al-Andalus, male and female, to vote in favor of union with the Iberian Tribunal.

The ordinary Tribunal of 1089 was attended by the Trianomae of Durato, Domingo Garcés, as guest and mediator for Iberia, and by the Quaesitor of Duresca, Iustum of Guernicus. During the proceedings, Porta Pandere reaffirmed its decision to support the Andalusis no longer, and Aedes Iris ended up being dragged along by the Portuguese Mercer House and by the threats of the powerful Aedes Saturni. For their part, the Quaesitores supported the dissolution of the illegitimate Tribunal, and the Trianomae Domingo Garcés spoke shrewdly to all present to avert a confrontation that he described as inevitable if they did not return to Iberia. To the dismay of the Praeco of al-Andalus, the Tribunal decided by a narrow majority to join the Iberian Tribunal. Al-Andalus was thus granted fourteen years to hand over its records to Duresca, return its treasury to the coffers of Iberia, and dissolve itself.

The Tribunals of Joy were held until 1103, when the Tribunal of al-Andalus was peacefully absorbed by the Iberian Tribunal, barely seven years before Saragossa was handed over to the Almoravids.

> #### The Repression of the Philosophers (II): Yūsuf ibn Tāšufīn
>
> When the caliph Yūsuf ibn Tāšufīn seized power in the Peninsula, the Almoravids granted the Mālikī *fuqahāʾ* great privileges and great power; it was in this period that they enjoyed their greatest influence.
>
> Opposed to Aristotelian thought and intolerant of all knowledge outside the juridical sciences, they hunted down philosophical writings (Hermetic codices included) in the libraries of al-Andalus to destroy or censor them.
>
> This was a time of darkness; the magi had to redouble their efforts not to be seen casting magic in the great cities of the south. Indeed, Porta Pandere and Aedes Saturni issued warnings to all the covenants of the Tribunal to avoid any behavior that could be denounced to the Mālikī *fuqahāʾ* in the cities of al-Andalus.

### The Iberian Tribunal: The Search for Unity

Unlike al-Andalus, which had remained neutral during the Schism War, the magi of northern Iberia suffered the loss of almost all the Tremere, more than half the Flambeau and a third of the Jerbiton and Ex Miscellanea; casualties among the other Houses were scarcely significant. In addition, the covenants of Tremébriga, Mons Vindius, Nebula and Pico Sacro were destroyed during the conflict.

#### Iberian Legislation after the Schism

The Tribunal of 1018 was a meeting without a *quorum* held at Duresca, where those present decided to elect as the new Praeco (since Ibn Sahl al-Tremerī had died in the battle in which Tremébriga fell) the Peninsula's hero and survivor of the Schism War, Brutus of Flambeau. Brutus had destroyed the covenant of Mons Vindius and traveled to Stonehenge after taking part in the destruction of the Diedne covenant of Nebula, which was said to serve as a communication hub between the rebel covenants. When the Redcaps asked him to come back to attend the Tribunal of 1018, he did so with abundant spoils, which he stored in his covenant of Salionca, and on condition that he return to fight the renegades still hiding at Stonehenge once the Tribunal meeting was over.

<!-- p. 90 -->

A descendant of Grimoald Niger, Brutus has had his deeds told to Flambeau apprentices for generations, and will for generations more. There is no Flambeau who does not know that name, and many apprentices end up taking it as their own in homage and out of respect for the hero of the Schism.

As happened in the rest of Mythic Europe, the Iberian Tribunal granted greater freedoms to House Guernicus, which the Grand Tribunal would later ratify with the powers of cooperation and inquisitorial freedom (see *Houses of Hermes: True Lineages*, page 68).

For their part, Duresca, Durato and Aedes Saturni took advantage of the absence of the Andalusi magi to lay the legislative foundations of the Tribunal, creating the Iberian Chamber and erasing historical memory: the Diedne records were removed from the minutes, and their symbols, history and legacy were destroyed; the locations of Mons Vindius and Nebula were deleted from the records kept by Aedes Saturni, and deliberately searching for them was made a low crime; their vis sources were distributed among those who had taken part in the Schism War.

***1018 AD, On the Iberian Chamber*** *(Iustum of Guernicus)* Duresca shall host every decade (from 1020 onward, at the autumn equinox) a meeting of the Tribunal's magi in what is called the Iberian Chamber, which may be attended by the members of Duresca, the Trianomae, the heads of the Tribunal's Mercer Houses, the Praeco, the Quaesitores, and the *praefectus praetorio* and *quaestor aerarii*. In addition, the chamber shall have three further seats that may be used by any other member invited by the *disceptator* of Duresca, the Praeco or the Trianomae (one seat for each of these powers).

The purpose of the chamber shall be to discuss the state of the Tribunal for its overall analysis: it shall in no case serve as a legislative instrument, so the Iberian Chamber shall have no power over the meetings of the Tribunals and shall for all purposes be considered of lower rank. However, the Iberian Chamber shall have the authority to audit the accounts of the Tribunal's treasury and may take control of them if the ordinary Tribunal approves.

***1025 AD, On the Diedne Legacy*** *(Iustum of Guernicus)* House Diedne shall be erased from the records of Iberian history. All knowledge of or reference to it shall be purged, and its possession shall be grounds for punishment (deemed a high crime) by the forces of the Tribunal.

Deliberately seeking any knowledge related to this House shall be deemed a low crime, for which the one responsible shall answer before the Tribunal. Likewise, protecting or sheltering a magus of this House shall be grounds for expulsion.

#### The Conflict with the Tribunal of al-Andalus

When news of the independence of al-Andalus reached the ears of the magi who were giving their lives in the Schism War, dismay spread among the warriors, for they feared the Diedne might end up taking refuge in those lands. Their dejection turned to hatred, however, when Aedes Saturni announced that Porta Pandere and Aedes Iris had declared their independence along with the other Andalusi covenants.

Iberia could do nothing about it until the end of the Schism War, when they discovered that their Andalusi *sodales* were enjoying great prosperity at the expense of the crisis suffered by the rest of the Order.

The conflict between north and south was managed and postponed by the Praeco, Brutus of Flambeau, the Quaesitor Iustum of Duresca and the Tenens of Autumn, Domingo Garcés al-Trianomī, who in the first half of the eleventh century pledged to bring the magi of al-Andalus back to Iberia peacefully. His first success came in 1067, when he persuaded the Andalusi covenant of Fafḥṣ al-Luŷŷ to join the Iberian Tribunal.

At the Tribunal of 1074, Brutus announced his retirement from Hermetic life after contracting a strange illness, so at the end of the meeting the rector of the covenant of Fafḥṣ al-Luŷŷ, Yulyān ibn Muhŷa al-Bonisagī, who knew the inner workings of the self-proclaimed neighboring Tribunal perfectly, was elected Praeco.

After Brutus's departure, the negotiations for Iberian unity were taken over entirely by Domingo Garcés, who two years later received a request from the Praeco of al-Andalus to negotiate independence at the next ordinary meeting. Those five years were a time of frantic activity for the Trianomae.

> #### The Grand Tribunals of 1030 and 1063
>
> Brutus of Flambeau, Iustum of Guernicus and Domingo Garcés al-Trianomī did not bring the situation of the Tribunal of al-Andalus before the Grand Tribunals of 1030 and 1063, for they knew the Andalusis would not turn to the Order's powers to define the boundaries of their illegitimate Tribunal. Instead, they chose to follow a strategy that would yield better returns in the long run. They thus took advantage of the absence of the Andalusi magi to create a governing body from which to control the most important aspects of the Tribunal.
>
> Their intention was always to prevent al-Andalus from officially constituting itself as an independent Tribunal, to which end Domingo Garcés used all his influence and resources. In this way, when al-Andalus returned to Iberia, it handed over part of its riches and, most importantly, had to abide by a law that none of its magi had approved.

<!-- p. 91 -->

The Tribunal of 1081 was attended by the Praeco of al-Andalus, Al-ʿĀsmarun al-Ŷerbitonī, and was the longest meeting recorded in the entire history of Iberia; all those attending lost their season of study. It was a difficult meeting which Yulyān nevertheless conducted masterfully, managing to bring the Tribunal to a close without any altercation. At its conclusion, Iberia was able to issue its verdict and deliver the aforementioned ultimatum to the Tribunal of al-Andalus.

With the union of the Tribunal of al-Andalus with Iberia in 1103, scholars of Hermetic history consider the period known as "the Disintegration" to have come to an end.

## The Time of the fiʿāl

After a century of convulsive change, the magi of Iberia, male and female, experienced a withdrawal from Hermetic political life: after the Schism War and the attempted independence of the Tribunal of al-Andalus, many grew used to living with uncertainty, wondering when and where the next conflict would arise.

By analogy, scholars name this period after the children's game that Hermetic apprentices still enjoy. To play *fiʿāl*, one hides something under a heap of sand and then makes other similar heaps to disguise the first; whoever guesses where the object is wins.

During this era the Almoravids (or "veiled ones") had taken control of almost all of al-Andalus, although their presence in the Peninsula was never looked upon kindly by the Andalusis; their strict observance burst violently into their lives, and many magi mourned all they had lost with the fall of the taifa kingdoms.

The Tribunal of 1109, the first after the annexation of al-Andalus, was a slow, complicated and at times tedious process, in which it had to be decided what to do with each of the entries of the Peripheral Code of Andalusi law. Although Yulyān ibn Muhŷa al-Bonisagī again proved to be an exceptional Praeco, his lack of popularity among the southern magi cost him his post. At the close of the assembly, the Andalusis came out en bloc for the elderly Criamon of Barzaj, Fawd ḅint Abī Yaʿqūb.

The maga, who had attended hardly any Tribunals in her life, performed her role diligently, but without the authority the Tribunal's magi were used to. Her neutrality was applauded and criticized in equal measure: her supporters found in her conduct the calm the Tribunal needed, while her detractors saw nothing but weakness and laxity.

| Praeco | Years |
| --- | --- |
| Fawd ḅint Abī Yaʿqūb al-Criamoniyya | 1116-1144 |

In this period, the Tribunal lost its dominion over Africa with the destruction of the Mercer House of Aedes Iris, and lived through the intellectual revolution of the perfect ones, which threatened the established order.

### The Peripheral Code after the Merger

The Tribunal invalidated the entries "Abolition of the Iberian Tax" (1012) and, for obvious reasons, the ruling "The Tribunals of Joy" (1019). However, it agreed to keep Arabic as an official language, which is why many magi still speak Arabic in the Tribunal and it is a tradition for Andalusi covenants to teach it to their apprentices.

***1116 AD, On the Iberian Treasury II*** *(Danāʾ al-Gernikiyya)* As "On the Iberian Treasury" (899), but amended by adapting the Andalusi ruling "On the Andalusi Treasury" (1012): the Tribunal's treasury shall be divided between the Mercer Houses of Porta Pandere and Aedes Saturni. The former shall keep the Tribunal treasury of the covenants in the territory of al-Andalus and the kingdom of Portugal, and the latter that of the territories of the kingdoms of Leon, Castile and Navarre, the Crown of Aragon and the Catalan counties. To this end, they shall have the oversight and protection of two magi (traditionally a Flambeau and a Guernicus), who shall bear the titles of *praefectus praetorio* (*ḥárisun*) and *quaestor aerarii* (*jāzin*), respectively.

***1116 AD, On Arabic*** *(Danāʾ al-Gernikiyya)* Adaptation of the Andalusi ruling "On the Official Language of the Tribunal" (1026): the Iberian Tribunal recognizes Arabic as a second language. Under these terms, the magi of the Iberian Tribunal may address their *sodales* in Arabic, both orally and in writing.

***1116 AD, On the Exchange of Enchantments with Mundanes*** *(Danāʾ al-Gernikiyya)* As the Andalusi ruling of the same name: "On the Exchange of Enchantments with Mundanes" (1068).

### Non Plus Ultra[^p91-43]

The Tribunal of 1123 received the news of the destruction of Aedes Iris from the lips of Pasífae al-Merkeriyya. The covenant was razed by night in an attack that began at astronomical dusk. According to her account, Porta Pandere had no time to react; the *quaestor aerarii* only saw the members of Aedes Iris seal the portal of *Tertius Decimus*.

When the magi tried to reach the covenant by magic, they discovered that none of the Arcane Connections to Aedes Iris worked any longer. Whatever it was that destroyed the covenant razed the building and, it seems, took the lives of all its inhabitants.
