[^p91-43]: According to legend, Hercules carved this phrase at the Strait of Gibraltar to let all travelers know that there was no land beyond that point; it was the end of the known world.

<!-- p. 92 -->

When the Redcaps of Porta Pandere reached the site more than a month later, they found no sign that anyone had survived, although they did discover that much farther north the African covenant of al-Minẓār had been raised without the Tribunal's permission, and had suffered no attack in its more than one hundred years of existence.

The Tribunal speculated about the possible attack. The Merinitae, Tremere, Jerbiton and Mercere who had traveled to Africa said that the region was suffering a civil war that had devastated the city of Siŷilmāsa and that, being so close, might have reached the nearby oasis of Tāfīlālt, where Aedes Iris stood. For their part, the judges brought up the old clause of the agreement signed with the *saḥirs* in 925, which forbade the Order to settle in Africa until 1225, though this did not explain why the newly discovered covenant of al-Minẓār was still alive.

In the end, the Tribunal forbade the settlement of new covenants in Africa, and the members of al-Minẓār managed to keep their covenant from being closed down on condition that they include a Guernicus among their ranks.

***1123 AD, On al-ʿIdwa*** *(Danāʾ al-Gernikiyya)* The founding of any covenant beyond the Pillars of Hercules shall be deemed a high crime. This prohibition shall remain in force until the year 1225.

### The Perfect Order

*[...] the perfect society is the only thing that is natural to the soul. [...] the solitary, given his nature, must not keep company with material men, nor with those whose spiritual end is mixed with materiality [...].*[^p92-44]

In the shadow of the cryptic Praeco a new current of thought sprouted, whose seed was planted in the halls of the *Qasr al-Jaʿfariya* in Saragossa and whose philosophy was influenced by Avempace, Ibn Ṭufayl and Al-Fārābī (see Appendix I). The revolution of the Perfect Order emerged during the time of the fiʿāl and was stamped out during the exodus.

Born of the discontent of a generation that came after the Schism War, the perfect magi (as they became known in the Tribunal) criticized the denial of individual freedom imposed by the Order of Hermes, and its implicit imperfection. To them, the Order was sunk in vice and error; it was an organization governed by speculation about the truth and by a material life divorced from the Arts. The perfect ones showed that the Order was riddled with unjust acts and false judgments, and that virtues and vices were so intermingled that its members had grown accustomed to it and were unable to escape that reality, so that they had become slaves of the Order.

To avoid this alienation and loss of freedom, the perfect ones preached the figure of the solitary (in the plural, *mutawaḥḥid*), who, in the absence of perfection, must isolate himself spiritually from the community so as not to be contaminated by it, and seek perfection in solitude through reason, which is ultimately the supreme end of every man and a personal and inalienable right and duty. This did not, however, imply that the perfect ones segregated themselves from the community, for they could go on living within it without taking part in it, following the doctrine of the solitude of the superior man.

In their quest, the *mutawaḥḥid* must take on all the political and governing powers proper to the leaders of the Order in order to govern themselves and lead themselves to the ultimate end of intellectual union, given the incapacity the Primi, Trianomae and Quaesitores have shown in accomplishing this task for the whole community. This is the only path by which magi can attain the fullness of their selves and complete mastery of themselves and of others.

The perfect ones preached at the Tribunals of the Praeco Fawd that their *sodales* should not stop after leaving Plato's cave; they should not content themselves with the light of the sun, for it was not the ultimate reality; they must transform themselves into the light itself and attain perfection through spiritual solitude.

When their foremost representative, Ḥayy ibn Yaqẓān al-Bonisagī (of the covenant of Qasr Dār al-Muchaddad), emerged victorious from a dialectical duel with the Praeco, the magi of Barzaj came to her defense, for, as mystics, they did not believe salvation could be reached through the pure intellectual act. Ḥayy ibn Yaqẓān then lashed out at the Ṣūfīs of Barzaj with the following speech:

*For you, the ultimate end of man lies not in reflection or knowledge, but in the pleasurable union of the sensible faculties, which, as you well know, give man images, feelings and pleasures that, once unified, make you believe they are complete happiness and perfection. Which is an error.*

*Furthermore, you content yourselves with individual spiritual forms, you have misunderstood the* Spharios *and you are incapable of reaching the contemplation and knowledge of the pure and universal spiritual forms… You show nothing but a false asceticism, and you allow others to go astray so that you may go on living without stain. That, without doubt, is your worst sin!*

The Criamon burst into sobs, and Fawd punished them by silencing them during the Tribunals, which in the end led to her removal from the office of Praeco, once her inability to control the conflict became plain. As a result, the doctrines of the perfect ones spread among the magi until they were numerous enough to create the covenant of ʾAlif.

Seeking to achieve the perfect society (which they called *al-madīna al-fāḍila*), the perfect ones of ʾAlif drafted a new Hermetic Code in which only just actions would have a place and opinions would always be true through the use of right reason, so that vice could be separated from virtue. Its first and most controversial ruling was based on the non-existence of Quaesitores, Primi and Praecones, for in a flawless Order made up of perfect individuals there would be no laws to break and no assemblies to regulate. *Al-madīna al-fāḍila* entailed renouncing the material world and unifying thought and opinion in what was called the "agent intellect": a community of brotherly love among its members and of everlasting contemplation.

[^p92-44]: Fragment from *The Self-Taught Philosopher* by Ibn Ṭufayl (Spanish translation by Ángel González Palencia).

<!-- p. 93 -->

When the number of perfect ones at ʾAlif reached twenty or so, the Iberian Chamber of 1150 (by which time Fawd was no longer Praeco) resolved to study the possible consequences for the Tribunal and the Order. At that meeting, those present came to a terrible conclusion: if the doctrines of the perfect ones kept attracting new followers, the Order could face a new schism. However, the meeting was attended by one of the founders of ʾAlif, Salāmān al-Gernikī, who helped them dismantle the philosophy the perfect ones had created and draft the following three points, derived from the doctrines of *al-madīna al-fāḍila*, to put an end to it:

- Ultimate union with the agent intellect entails the destruction of identity and the denial of the personal immortality of the human soul, from which, moreover, it may be inferred that it denies life after death.
- The doctrines of the perfect ones condone suicide (as a last resort, admittedly) by endorsing detachment from matter as one of the means of attaining perfection.
- They claim that only the Perfect Order can heal the corruption that has been festering in the Order of Hermes for more than three centuries. But their social revolution does not use the tools of the Order of Hermes; instead it rests on contemplation, and therefore on inaction. That is, the perfect one does not seek to change or improve the Order, but to create a new one out of the *mutawaḥḥid*.

When the minutes were closed, it was agreed to take the resolution to the Grand Tribunal of 1162, where the magi spoke out against the slogans of the *mutawaḥḥid* and ʾAlif was accused of undermining the Order's power through its prerogatives. ʾAlif then faced a charge of high crime, from which it was saved when Ḥayy ibn Yaqẓān al-Bonisagī gave his word to destroy the code he was drafting and to give up his preaching.

The Order's threats had their effect. In the following years ʾAlif lost half its members and, with the arrival of the Almohads, many left for the East in the hope of continuing to develop the Perfect Order there. Since then, the Tribunal has not regarded them as a threat.

The meeting of the Iberian Chamber in 1150 and the arrival of the Almohads mark the end of the fiʿāl.

## The Exodus

The Peninsula's Hermetic scholars speak of an exodus beginning with the arrival of the Almohads in Iberia. Over the more than half a century they have ruled in the Peninsula, the Almohads have driven this migration of the magi of al-Andalus toward the East and northern Iberia.

During the exodus, two Praecones of very different attitudes were elected.

| Praecones | Years |
| --- | --- |
| Munio Alfonso Garcés al-Flambī | 1151-1193 |
| ʿEzraʾ ben Šēlomoh al-Bonisagī | 1200-Present |

> #### The Repression of the Philosophers (III): Abū Yūsuf Yaʿqūb al-Manṣūr
>
> *Whoever forbids the study of the books of wisdom to one who is fit to read them, because base and suspect people have gone astray in interpreting them, is like one who forbids cool, delicious water to the thirsty until they die of thirst, and only because there are people who have choked on it and died. For death by choking is accidental, whereas thirst is essential and necessary.*[^p93-XXV]
>
> In 1190, the illustrious Avenzoar, in the name of the Almohad caliph Abū Yūsuf Yaʿqūb al-Manṣūr, published an edict in the principal cities of al-Andalus (Seville, Granada, Jaén, Malaga, Almería, Alcácer do Sal, and so on) that not only ordered all books of the ancient sciences (above all of logic and philosophy) to be handed over to the local *ṣāḥib al-madīna*, but also condemned the use of magic and called on the citizenry to take part in denouncing any sorcerer to the officials or the *fuqahāʾ*.
>
> Four years later, the caliph's censorship claimed its first victim: the Redcap Muhŷa was interrogated, tortured and stoned in the outskirts of Seville; her lifeless body was thrown into the Guadalquivir. She had not even used magic, only a magic item to change her appearance. The last time a member of the Order saw her alive was in the Mozarabic quarter of Triana.
>
> A week after her execution, a group of officials and soldiers left Seville under the command of the elderly faqih Al-Aʿmaš al-Išbīlī, bound for the covenants that had been assigned to the Redcap. Fearful of breaking the 1193 ruling of the Peripheral Code, the covenants submitted to searches, and the libraries that their covenants could not hide were seized and, in some cases, burned. Especially harrowing was the destruction of the covenant of ʾAlif: the civil authorities ordered its inhabitants arrested and its buildings demolished.
>
> [^p93-XXV]: Fragment from *The Decisive Treatise* by Averroes (Spanish translation by A. Yacine and P. Chabrera Calpe).

<!-- p. 94 -->

### The Tribunal and the Almohads

The first Tribunal at which Munio Alfonso Garcés served as Praeco was the same one at which the *rosh yeshiva* of ʿÔlām wā-ʿed, Meʾir ibn Yosef al-Ŷerbitonī, reported the irretrievable loss of the covenant of Lucena. His account was the most notorious of the many that followed the arrival of the Almohads, and the one that would mark the beginning of the period of the exodus from al-Andalus.

Munio was known in the Tribunal for the relations his covenant had with the Wolf King of the lands of *Xarq al-Andalus* (see page 50). His gifts as a leader and his analytical ability had earned him the title of Praeco and, after Meʾir ibn Yosef's account, he agreed that the Almohads could become a threat to the Tribunal in al-Andalus, since they did not recognize the protection of the dhimmis. To assess the situation, the Tribunal approved the creation of an embassy to approach the Almohads in the Peninsula, led by the Jew ʿEzraʾ ben Šēlomoh al-Bonisagī. Moreover, so that it might succeed, Munio Alfonso undertook not to meddle in the mundane conflicts between his protégé, the Wolf King, and the caliph Abū Yaʿqūb Yūsuf. As a consequence, the Wolf King fell and the Almohads took all of al-Andalus except the Balearic Islands.

The Tribunal lived in peace until Abū Yaʿqūb Yūsuf died a violent death and his son, Abū Yūsuf Yaʿqūb al-Manṣūr, was crowned. During his rule, all the progress made by the Hermetic ambassadors dissolved under pressure from the *fuqahāʾ*: in 1190, the qadi of Seville condemned practitioners of magic in the Great Mosque of al-ʿUdays. As a result, the covenants near the great population centers of al-Andalus were subjected to searches, and the Hermetic books and books of the ancient sciences that had not been hidden were burned. To resolve the crisis, the Tribunal of 1193 was attended by the Order's Tenens of Winter, who guided the meeting throughout and secured the approval of the Peripheral Code entry concerning mundane relations in al-Andalus, even though it might worsen the migration of the Andalusi magi. The Tribunal's resolution did not please Munio Alfonso Garcés, however, so he resigned his duties and another Praeco was elected at the close of the meeting.

<!-- p. 95 -->

***1193 AD, On Mundane Relations in al-Andalus*** *(Jayrān al-Gernikī)* No covenant or magus may enter into an agreement with a mundane party, whatever its terms. In addition, any agreement in progress must be handled by a Quaesitor, so that he may take the appropriate actions and recommend the course of action to follow at every step.

Finally, no magus may use magic or any magic item in a population center of al-Andalus or its surroundings, or in any other place where his life would be endangered by a possible denunciation to the authorities.

> #### Story Seeds: The Arrival of the Faqih
>
> The autocrat of the player characters' covenant (which must be located in al-Andalus) calls an urgent council and summons all the covenant's members. As he explains, not without some apprehension, that very morning an official visited the covenant and said that in a week a faqih will come to search the building for heretical works. What will the characters do? Will they call on a Quaesitor for advice? Will they leave for the north of the Peninsula? Will they hide their library? Will they oppose the mundane authorities, with all the consequences that may follow? Will they seek out Avenzoar to try to save the situation?
>
> When the faqih arrives (if the characters are still at the covenant and try to affect him with a spell), they will discover that he has True Faith, so it will not be so easy to get rid of him.

#### The Other Tribunal of Harra

In 1193, at the conclusion of the ordinary Tribunal, a small number of magi stayed at Harra to debate how to stop the Almohads. At "the Other Tribunal of Harra," as this meeting came to be known, the following magi were present: Munio Alfonso Garcés al-Flambī, Abū-l-Āfiya al-Flambī, Šuʿlatun al-Ŷerbitoniyya, Nāārun al-Flambī, Focus of Apromor, and Birbón and Remond of Flambeau (these two former triumvirs of Salionca), of the covenant of Harra; ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUbayd Allāh al-Praliḥī, of the covenant of Chazāʾir; Guzmán Garcés of Flambeau, of the covenant of Praesidium Abditus; and, lastly, Prosérpina of Tremere, of the covenant of Victrix.

During the meeting, the magi agreed that they would go to fight the Almohad armies in the next war, of which they would be forewarned by Munio's many contacts at the Castilian court. But when in 1195 the armies of Alfonso VIII of Castile went out to face the Almohad troops at Alarcos, Abū-l-Āfiya, Nāārun and Focus refused, and the rest went off to meet their deaths on the fields of Calatrava; shortly afterward, Harra was destroyed.

### The Iberian Tribunal Today

The Tribunal of 1200 was held at the covenant of ʿĂrābôt, in Gerona, with the Rationalist ʿEzraʾ ben Šēlomoh al-Bonisagī as Praeco; there the Hermetic magi learned of the mysterious events surrounding the deaths of the magi of the Other Tribunal of Harra and the destruction of the Flambeau covenant.

Since his election, ʿEzraʾ has fought the exodus in many ways together with the covenant of Durato, and although in 1220 the Almohads appear to be in decline, he is not optimistic. Meanwhile, the approaching expiry of the clause imposed by the *saḥirs* in the year 925 has led many magi to set their sights on the African continent, especially since the Mozarabs who fought in the Maghreb alongside the caliph Al-Manṣūr testified that those lands enjoyed greater freedoms than the Almohad province of al-Andalus. Preparing for what he foresees will be a race to obtain those riches, ʿEzraʾ has secured the approval of a clause by which Iberia comes to encompass the lands of North Africa as far as the Atlas Mountains, which will give Iberian magi an advantage when the time comes. The measure exploits a legal loophole in the agreement with the *saḥirs*, since it establishes no real Hermetic presence in those lands.

These are the entries approved during ʿEzraʾ's tenure, to be submitted for review at the next Grand Tribunal (to be held in 1228) so that they may be included in the Peripheral Code. For his part, ʿEzraʾ fears that the clause of 1214 will be challenged and even discarded at the Grand Tribunal, since many interests will clash once the restriction imposed by the *saḥirs* expires.

***1207 AD, On Tenure in the Tribunal*** *(Lía al-Gernikiyya)* Every magus who passes the Gauntlet in Iberia must remain in the Tribunal for at least seven years. If after this period he finds no covenant in which to lodge, his *parens* shall be obliged to give him shelter.

***1214 AD, On the Southern Border*** *(Lía al-Gernikiyya)* The southern limit of Iberia shall extend south as far as the bounds set by the Atlas Mountains, namely the Anti-Atlas, High Atlas, Middle Atlas and Saharan Atlas. All covenants in these new territories shall fall under the jurisdiction of the Iberian Tribunal.[^p95-45]

[^p95-45]: Note that this conflicts with the Tytalus cabal of the Shining Eye, which aims to have the Rhine Tribunal colonize North Africa.

# IV. The Kingdom of Portugal

The nearly eighty years that have passed since the creation of Portugal in 1143 have been rather turbulent for the kingdom, which in 1220 stretches from south of the Miño river to the region of the Alto Alentejo, Évora being one of its southernmost towns. To the west it is bounded by the Atlantic, while to the east it borders the kingdom of Leon and the Almohad Empire. Its capital and most important city is Coimbra, although Lisbon has grown enormously in recent times and is destined to become the kingdom's new capital before the end of the thirteenth century. Porto and Braga are also important towns.

In 1220 the monarch of Portugal, Alfonso II the Fat, is thirty-five years old and enjoys complete freedom to expand his kingdom at the expense of the Muslims, thanks to the peace treaty he has signed with the monarchs of Castile and Leon. At present he is in conflict with the head of the Church in Portugal, the archbishop of Braga, Estévão Soares, who is fighting on behalf of Pope Honorius III after the Portuguese monarch was accused of demanding improper tribute from ecclesiastical institutions, thereby violating the immunities of the clergy, which in the pontiff's eyes amounted to the enslavement of the Church.

As a result of this conflict, the monarch will be excommunicated in mid-1220; he will respond by issuing an order for the occupation and destruction of the archbishop's properties and by occupying and requisitioning the goods of the archiepiscopal church of Braga. Seeing his properties laid waste, Estévão will set out for Rome that same year, where, together with the pope, he will keep up the pressure on the Portuguese monarch, to the point of threatening to place the kingdom under interdict (see page 53). In the end, Alfonso II will yield to the pressure (above all because of his poor health) and Estévão will return to Braga in 1222. However, the monarch's death in 1223 will leave the damage done to the Church unresolved, and it will fall to his successor on the throne, Sancho II of Portugal, to answer for it.

## The Covenants of the Kingdom of Portugal

All the covenants of Portugal belong to the Iberian Tribunal, although the kingdom has never had much of a Hermetic presence throughout its history. The magi of the Peninsula have traditionally divided the region along the natural barrier formed by the mountain system that begins at *serra Montejunto* (where Porta Pandere stands, the second most important Mercer House in the Tribunal after Aedes Saturni in Barcelona) and ends at *serra da Estrela*, which holds the highest point in the kingdom, at almost 2,000 meters, and where the Mondego river rises; several megalithic monuments can be found along its course.

## The Northern Region

This regional unit is furrowed by rivers such as the Duero, the Mondego, the Limia and the Ave; it borders the kingdom of Leon to the north and east and is washed by the Atlantic Ocean to the west. Unlike the south, it is a much more rugged and colder region, where there are still tracts of forest to be felled and pasture to be brought under cultivation. Deciduous woods and scrub predominate here. On the highest points of the ranges, where temperatures are lower and the snow lasts all winter, heather and juniper prevail, and as the land descends there appear oak woods, yews and some pines, together with smaller hollies and laurels. In the Duero valley oaks, chestnuts and holm oaks abound, giving way to cork oaks and olive trees as the river nears its mouth, until they disappear in wetter areas, where poplars, willows, ashes and elders are plentiful. Rushes grow in great numbers along the riverbanks and the brackish estuaries, and undergrowth is abundant in the dune lands of the coast.

> #### Galician-Portuguese
>
> This is the everyday language of the inhabitants of the northwest of Iberia, and the language sung in the noble courts of the north and northwest of the Peninsula (it will come to replace Latin as the political and administrative language of the territory in the last quarter of the thirteenth century). In 1220 it has the status of a literary language, a standing it has held since at least 1196, when João Soares de Paiva composed the oldest known troubadour song in this tongue. This troubadour of noble family, author of satirical poems and of *cantares de amigo*, was a contemporary of Alfonso I Henriques and frequented the court of Sancho I and Alfonso II (the present king of Portugal), as well as that of the king of Aragon, whose vassal he was. Indeed, many troubadours and minstrels frequented the courts of the first three kings of Portugal, among whom also deserves mention the troubadour of the house of Sousa, Garcia Mendes de Eixo, who served at the court of Sancho I.

<!-- p. 99 -->

In this region lie the forests of Talhada, Mesão Frio and Uja (between the Duero and the mouth of the Vouga), where thieves and murderers take refuge and wild beasts abound (unfortunately for the region's Bjornaer, the forest of Alcobaça, in the Portuguese Extremadura, has been felled to make way for farming). These are not the only dangers the region's inhabitants face, however: in his will, Sancho I recorded how dangerous the moorlands with stagnant water were because of the swarms of mosquitoes.

The northern region has important urban centers, such as Guimarães, Braga, Porto, Lamego and the capital of the Portucalense county, Coimbra. Although a great many bridges have been built to improve the roads (which are always dangerous) thanks to the numerous pious bequests of the *ricos hombres*, much of this infrastructure has yet to be built.

In 1220 the northern region of Portugal has only one living covenant, the modest Serra da Lousã, although the ruins of two more can be found in the territory.

### Serra da Lousã

>**Lifespan:** 934–Present<br>
>**Founder:** Fadrique de Lousã Ex Miscellanea<br>
>**Season:** Spring<br>
>**Aura (type and strength):** Magic, strength 3<br>
>**Reputations:** Lesser Magi (Iberian Tribunal) 3<br>
>**Votes:** 2

Serra da Lousã is a wholly atypical covenant for Iberia. It is made up entirely of *rusticani* magi, members of a minor tradition of House Ex Miscellanea that has practically no presence in the rest of Europe and is characterized by the magical skill with which its members can work various mundane materials. Settled in a small hamlet near the Alto de Trevim, the highest point in the range, the covenant's magi have been fully accepted by the nearby mundane population, with whom they actively cooperate, together forming a community of most unusual character.

<!-- p. 100 -->

#### History

The Serra da Lousã has never been densely populated. Towns such as Lousã, Cerdeira and Miranda do Corvo have always been self-sufficient, and so have had no need to trade with larger towns outside the range. The impressive natural landscapes of the area have also fostered the presence of natural magic auras, which in turn have affected some of the region's natives. Since time immemorial, in fact, there have been inhabitants of the range who developed a special talent for craftsmanship that can only be described as magical. The first of them known to the Order was Fadrique de Lousã, a local man whose evident magical abilities caught the attention of a Bjornaer magus on his way to Mare Iacum. After the magus convinced him that the Order of Hermes could offer him special protection and took him to his covenant, Fadrique learned the rudiments of magic theory and the Parma Magica, but shortly afterward, overwhelmed by the complexity of Hermetic life, he decided to return home and carry on with the life he had led before. Although he was a nominal member of the Order, he never took an active part in its politics, but he did establish a covenant on the Alto de Trevim, a hamlet where he began taking as apprentices other local youths in whom he detected the same magical abilities as his own. Soon a line of *rusticani* magi arose, specializing in the creation of lesser magic items that they used to help with their daily tasks. The covenant was always on good terms with the nearby towns and recruited potential apprentices who, in many cases, ended up returning to their homes. At the same time, it has always kept a very low profile, so much so that even matters as momentous as the Schism War or the secession of al-Andalus passed almost unnoticed by its magi, who very rarely attend Tribunals.

Fadrique's line continued more or less unbroken until the middle of the eleventh century, when, at the height of the mundane struggle for territory, one of the covenant's apprentices, Hernando de Miranda, decided to offer his magical abilities in the service of the Christian lords who were fighting to expand southward. The magi of Serra da Lousã took an active part in the wars of the Coimbra region, but their ignorance of the most basic Hermetic laws earned them heavy fines when the magi of Duresca discovered their involvement. This, combined with the deaths of two of the magi in the fighting (Hernando himself among them), led the inhabitants of Serra da Lousã to abandon that course of action and withdraw once more into the mountains that were their home. Many local families then helped them to go unnoticed whenever some suspicious-looking visitor asked about the presence of witches or sorcerers in the range. The *rusticani* had decided to live with their backs to the world, and they were not going to change their minds.

After that period, the only thing that drew them out of their isolation again was the intrusion of the mundane powers into the region when, after the final reconquest of Coimbra, the nearby castle of Lousã became the administrative center of the area. The castle, around which many legends had grown (see insert on page 102, "Story Seeds: Princess Peralta"), sought to take control of the surrounding lands, and joint action by the town council and the *rusticani* themselves was needed to reach an agreement with the castellan and so keep him from overly disrupting local traditions and customs.

Today Serra da Lousã remains the same quiet, remote place it has been since its foundation. Not even the Redcaps visit it often, and many of them would have trouble even finding it. And that is just how its magi want it.

#### Setting and Physical Description

Serra da Lousã lies on the Alto de Trevim, the highest point in the range, at an altitude of 1,200 meters. It is an imposing spot, constantly buffeted by the winds, from which there is a commanding view over the whole range. The covenant consists of half a dozen small stone houses with thatched roofs, surrounded by a stone wall a little under a meter high, which became necessary in order to cast the *Aegis of the Hearth* each year. Many of these houses might be considered the magi's *sancta*, were it not that each is rather a combination of workshop and dwelling for its *rusticanus*. They are spacious places and, despite their evidently rustic appearance, are well equipped for the magi to create their items and tools.

A somewhat larger, elongated building serves as a barracks for the covenant's turb, which consists essentially of half a dozen young men from the region who have received special combat training so that they can carry out their duties as guards, although they are far from being a well-trained, disciplined unit. They are, however, fiercely loyal to the *rusticani*, and they also have less obvious but equally useful skills for the covenant, such as a perfect knowledge of the range that surrounds their home.

One last structure stands out on the Alto de Trevim, outside the main enclosure, near the steepest edge overlooking the western slope. It is a small wooden watchtower that has stood there for centuries; its existence is already recorded in the covenant's own founding records. On clear days the whole region surrounding the range can be seen from the watchtower for several dozen kilometers around, and some even claim that Porto can be seen from it, though the city is more than 150 kilometers away. That would be impossible under normal circumstances, but there are rumors that the watchtower has magical properties and that the covenant's *rusticani* have enchanted it with some Hermetic effect…

#### Society and Customs

Serra da Lousã is a very small covenant, and at any given time it has no more than three magi, all of them *rusticani*, representing three different generations, each of whom usually acts as master to the next youngest generation. The *rusticani* have hardly any hierarchy, as they are a scattered and very loosely organized tradition. In fact, calling Serra da Lousã a covenant is almost an exaggeration, as it can scarcely be described as one. The hamlet on the Alto de Trevim has hardly any fortifications or defenses, nor a library or treasury worthy of the name. The magi do, however, meet the minimum requirements to remain members of the Order, and indeed the covenant has an *Aegis of the Hearth*, cast each year by a Quaesitor who is paid in vis for doing so.

<!-- p. 101 -->

The covenant's three magi hold three positions: the *mestre* acts as teacher, training a pupil known as the *jovem*. When his training ends, the *jovem* becomes the new *mestre*, and if his master remains at the covenant, the latter becomes known as the *velho*, and holds the greatest moral (though not actual) authority in the covenant. Serra da Lousã is not used to Hermetic guests, although its doors are not closed to them either. When such visits occur, the magi offer the hospitality expected of any Hermetic host, suited to the resources they have, no more and no less. Should those guests prove aggressive or hostile, the magi know they can count on all the inhabitants of the range to come to their aid if need be.

#### The Magi of Serra da Lousã

##### Sesnando Ex Miscellanea, *mestre*

The covenant's current *mestre* is Sesnando, a magus of a little over fifty, a native of the nearby village of Cerdeira. Trained as a carpenter in his youth, he soon discovered that he had certain special abilities and, as the people of the area have done since time immemorial, his family sent him to the hamlet atop the hill of Trevim so that the *rusticani* could teach him to control those gifts. Throughout his apprenticeship under Facundo, Sesnando divided his time between the hamlet and his own home in Cerdeira, until, once he had passed his Gauntlet, he settled permanently on the Alto. Although the covenant lacks any structure or government, Sesnando is the nearest thing it has to a leader, and he is also the only visible, known face of Serra da Lousã in the Hermetic world, for he has even traveled to a couple of Tribunals.

Sesnando's skill at carpentry, combined with his magical arts, has filled his house with small marvels: superbly crafted wooden objects which at the same time produce minor magical effects, making life much easier for the covenant's other inhabitants in this remote area.

##### Facundo Ex Miscellanea, *velho*

Facundo is the oldest inhabitant of Serra da Lousã. Although he is nearly eighty, he bears his years with great dignity thanks to a good longevity ritual he obtained from a magus, whom he paid with several lesser magic items. Facundo was a blacksmith, and his magical gifts were discovered by the then *mestre* of Serra da Lousã on a business visit to his village, Miranda do Corvo. Facundo has never fully come to terms with his capacity to work what he calls "miracles," and he struggles to reconcile his strong religious convictions with those abilities. His apprenticeship was arduous and full of incidents, and although he passed his Gauntlet, he never took the covenant very seriously and flatly refused to travel to distant places to attend "blasphemous gatherings," as he calls Tribunals. Despite all this, he accepted Sesnando as his apprentice.

Sesnando has trouble handling Facundo. On the one hand, the old man's age and experience make him a recognized and respected figure not only in the covenant but throughout the range. On the other hand, his ideas and reactions are often controversial, and Sesnando sometimes fears they may lead the covenant, and even the nearby villages, to make decisions they might come to regret. Sesnando dreams of the day when Facundo will keep his eternal promise to leave Serra da Lousã, return to his native village and spend the rest of his life there…

<!-- p. 102 -->

##### Ágata, *jovem*

Ágata is the latest apprentice to arrive at Serra da Lousã, a girl of barely seventeen born in the nearby town of Penela who, shortly before reaching adolescence, began to develop an inexplicable ability to shape and work stone with prodigious precision. Her parents, a family of herders, thought they could turn their daughter's talent to their own advantage and tried to have a local stonemason take her on as an apprentice, but a series of inexplicable incidents soon occurred in his workshop, and the girl was promptly sent back to her parents. Resigned to continuing their humble life, and somewhat intimidated by the strange phenomena that surrounded Ágata ever more often, they decided to climb up to visit the eccentric Sesnando at the top of the range. If anyone could train her, it was he.

>**Appearance:** Ágata is a girl of barely seventeen springs whose innate beauty can be seen even through the grime that usually covers her face and the humble garments she wears.
