## Galicia

*Next comes the land of the Galicians, once past the borders of Leon and the passes of Mounts Irago and Cebrero. It is a leafy land, with rivers, meadows, extraordinary orchards, good fruits and the clearest springs, but poor in cities, towns and arable land. It is scant in bread, wheat and wine, but plentiful in rye bread and cider, well stocked with cattle and horses, with milk and honey, and with sea fish […]; rich in gold, silver, cloth, wild furs and other riches, and even most abundant in precious Saracen wares. Of all the other uncultured peoples of Spain, the Galicians are the ones who most resemble our Gallic nation, were it not that they are very wrathful and litigious.*[^p115-1]

[^p115-1]: Excerpt from the *Codex Calixtinus*, anonymous (Spanish translation by Millán Bravo Lozano).

The regional unit of Galicia lies in the westernmost part of the kingdom. Its terrain is gentle, although many of its rivers have deep valleys, and a great number of rias (drowned estuaries) give the landscape a very distinctive character. Its coasts are washed by the Atlantic Ocean to the west and by the Cantabrian Sea to the north, which throughout its history has exposed it to attacks by the *al-Mayús* (see page 286) and Muslim pirates; indeed, at the beginning of the twelfth century the archbishop of Santiago, Gelmírez, brought engineers from Genoa and Pisa to build ships with which to fight piracy. It is said that from them the Galicians learned the art of seamanship.

Galicia is home to important town councils such as those of Compostela, Noya, Pontevedra and Ribadavia, among others, and to the south it borders the kingdom of Portugal.

In Hermetic terms, Galicia has traditionally been densely populated, and in 1220 it is home to the covenants of Brigantia and Beit Midrash.

<!-- p. 116 -->

### Brigantia

*If you can overcome him, kill him, but do not burn him with fire, for only the Lord of fire may burn with Fire.*[^p116-2]

[^p116-2]: Saying of the Prophet concerning a certain individual, from *The Book of the Ŷihād* by Averroes (Spanish translation by C. Quirós).

>**Lifespan:** 780–Present<br>
>**Founder:** Dehewint of Flambeau<br>
>**Season:** Spring<br>
>**Aura (type and strength):** Magic, strength 7<br>
>**Reputations:** Controversial (Iberian Tribunal) 3, Honorable (Iberian Tribunal) 2<br>
>**Votes:** 6

Brigantia is the second-oldest living covenant in the Tribunal after Salionca (not counting Barzaj), and it has a long tradition of followers of Apromor. Its name stirs mixed feelings among the magi of the Peninsula; those who do not despise it for its subversive past revere it for the high moral values it has shown throughout its history.

#### History

Dehewint, a pagan magus from the kingdom of Gwynedd (Wales), crossed the Pyrenees under Flambeau's orders and, like his *sodales* of Salionca, sought a place to settle from which to fight the non-Hermetic wizards. The covenant was established in Galicia for three reasons: Dehewint had found a powerful magic aura, from that spot he controlled the northwestern edge of the Peninsula, and it was one of the places farthest from the border with al-Andalus and, therefore, from the *saḥirs*.

In 792, after Ranemiro's failed negotiations with the tempestarii, Dehewint took command in order to crush the Galician wizards. The Welshman led the Flambeau and Tremere of the abandoned covenant of Prima, and together they laid waste to the places Ranemiro had marked as targets. However, only the wizards' families were there, and these they massacred. The tempestarii's response was terrible: Brigantia was swallowed by storms that lashed the coast for months, two of its Tremere lost their lives, and Dehewint died disemboweled when one of the ñuberus' lightning bolts pierced his body; nothing was left of the covenant but its foundations. It took years for Brigantia to be rebuilt by Dehewint's *filius*, the Zoroastrian Petrus of Flambeau, who together with the rest of the warriors of Iberia took part in the ritual that destroyed the tempestarii's center of power and ended with their surrender.

<!-- p. 117 -->

To raise Brigantia once more, Petrus had to fight in several mundane wars, taking part in the Galician battles that pitted the armies of the emir of Cordoba, Hišām I, against the *mesnadas* of Alfonso II of Asturias. In this way Petrus won plentiful plunder with which to rebuild Brigantia, and many slaves to raise it. However, when the *mayús* attacked the coasts of Galicia at the beginning of the ninth century, Brigantia was assaulted and devastated a second time, which prevented its members from attending the fifth Grand Tribunal. Fortunately, the constant Viking attacks on the coast also had their bright side: mundanes moved away from the peninsula of Faro, so when Brigantia was rebuilt years later it was able to live entirely apart from society throughout the ninth and tenth centuries, and in relative seclusion until the beginning of the thirteenth, when the area began to be resettled.

During the ninth century, Brigantia took part in the war against Damhan-Allaidh; when in 845 Ramiro I of Asturias ordered all the wizards of his kingdom burned, Petrus declared Wizard's War on Átropo of Tremere, who was responsible for it, and the magus died in that war. The leadership of Brigantia then passed to Eio, and the covenant's policy began to center on diplomacy.

Thanks to the magae of Brigantia, the Order managed to make peace with the *saḥirs* in 925 (see page 76), after which Eio left the covenant in the hands of the Andalusi Al-Harqal al-Apromorī, who a few years later would be involved in the affair of the Duresca manuscripts and would be one of those chiefly responsible for spreading them after they were declared fraudulent.

The name of Brigantia appeared for the last time in the pages of the Tribunal's history during the Schism War. The covenant sided with the Diedne of Mons Vindius and Nebula, and took part in the attacks on Tertia, Duresca, Salionca and Tremébriga. For years the war went in the Diedne's favor until, for some reason, the druids began to falter (see page 83). The Flambeau of Brigantia were then subdued in 1016 and tried at Salionca, in a proceeding that became known as the Concord of Fire. After the trial, the *ductor* of Brigantia was executed and the rest of its magi punished. The covenant was placed under strict watch and the Tribunal seized its vis sources and stores, which plunged it into a deep Winter from which it emerged only with the arrival of three magi expelled from the covenant of Harra at the end of the twelfth century.

Brigantia has drawn on the vigor and power of the Andalusi magi to rise again, and it is now struggling to recover the vis sources taken from it in 1016. Meanwhile, it must deal with the considerable mundane growth taking place in the area since 1208, when Alfonso IX of Leon decided to refound the city of Corunna with inhabitants of O Burgo and Betanzos under the privileges of the fuero of Benavente (under which the city is free of vassalage to the Church and the nobles and answers only to the crown).

#### Setting and Physical Description

Brigantia stands on the cliffs of the peninsula of Faro, beside the ancient Roman ruins of Brigantium. The influx of mundanes into the nearby city of Corunna has caused the Divine auras of its two Romanesque churches to begin spreading, and the building of the friary of San Francisco in 1214 has only made matters worse.

The oldest buildings of Brigantia, despite having been rebuilt several times, still bear the names Dehewint gave them when he raised them: *tŷ*, *ystafell* and *du*,[^p117-3] from old Cymraeg, while the newest (barely ten years old) was named *novo*, after the local tongue.

[^p117-3]: Although in 1220 no one at the covenant knows this language, the words mean "house," "bedchamber" and "black," respectively.

*Tŷ* is the largest building. It houses the magi's *sancta* (up to ten), the library, a small council chamber, the treasure rooms and the kitchens. It is of magical make and is the building nearest the water. After the Concord of Fire, its owners were required to pierce windows in its walls and pull down its defensive towers, for *tŷ* had been designed as a compact fortress, impregnable in time of war.

*Ystafell* is the building that houses the common rooms: the council hall, the guest chambers, the kitchens, the old lighthouse (which the inhabitants of Brigantia keep lit to prevent ships from running aground on their coast), and the quarters needed to lodge all the magi of the Tribunal and allow them to meet should Brigantia host a Tribunal. In the cellars of *Ystafell* lies the burial chamber of the giant Geryon.

*Du* is the only building that survives from its creation in 776. Built by mundane means by Brigantia's first settlers, this small tower of black stone has been rebuilt several times over its history and, in 1220, lies in ruins and abandoned. *Du* is a tower some seven meters high with a "D"-shaped plan, standing on a small rocky island to the north of Brigantia. It was abandoned after the Concord of Fire and no one now remembers its purpose. When the Andalusi magi arrived they looked into the matter, but found nothing but inscriptions on its walls, made illegible by the passage of time. For want of any other explanation, they ascribed a religious meaning to it. In 1207 the tower partly collapsed and fell into the sea, and although the magi keep an Arcane Connection to it, they never use it, for neither the building nor the island holds anything of interest.

Finally, the newest building of Brigantia is *novo*, raised barely ten years ago in the heart of the newly founded city of Corunna to keep a close eye on the spread of the Dominion and on the activities of the mundanes. Thanks to it, they have learned that Corunna promises to become an important center of maritime trade, and so they intend to gain a place on its town council to prevent its decisions from harming the covenant.

#### Society and Customs

Brigantia is a young democracy that has been transformed (both aesthetically and politically) by its new inhabitants. The Andalusis have filled it with wall hangings and carpets, and have perfumed it with sandalwood to recall their old home of Harra. Since their arrival, Brigantia has met every lunar year at night in the council chamber of *tŷ* to debate the covenant's affairs, dealing first with finances (when the annual budgets are approved), then with magical resources (when the vis is shared out), then with the plan of action toward the mundanes of Corunna and, lastly, with Hermetic matters (all of it in Arabic). Following tradition, every council is recorded in the so-called *Chronicle of Brigantia*, in which reliable information can be found from at least 1016 onward, for everything before the Concord of Fire was audited and altered by the magi of Salionca.

<!-- p. 118 -->

Brigantia has a nominal leader who bears the title of *ductor*. This title is all the magi have kept of Brigantia's old political organization (albeit with restricted powers), and they did so in honor of the aged Ouro. The *ductor* is responsible for moderating the annual meetings and holds a casting vote that he cannot delegate. He also acts as spokesman at ordinary Tribunals. Otherwise, he has no additional privilege or responsibility.

The covenant has kept two mundane customs since the days of Dehewint: the lighthouse and the watching of the tides. The lighthouse of Brigantia is never allowed to go out. The family of grogs that tends it holds a special status within the covenant and, in fact, the autocrats are normally chosen from among them. The other family that enjoys similar status is the one charged with recording the hours of low and high tide and ringing Dehewint's ancient enchanted bronze bell when they occur. The bell hangs on the flat roof of *tŷ* and can be heard clearly in all the covenant's *sancta* and, curiously, in the abandoned tower of *du* as well. Beyond that, it does not seem to possess any other powers.

#### The Magi of Brigantia

##### Ductor, Ouro of Flambeau, Follower of Apromor

Ouro is the oldest magus in Brigantia and one of the most ancient in Iberia. At the close of the Tribunal of 1214 he fell a couple of votes short of being elected Praeco, and in 1221 his covenant-mates hope the vote will go his way. Ouro has lived through two turns of the century and in all his life has never seen Brigantia as he sees it now. This aged follower of Apromor grew up in Brigantia, passed his Gauntlet with honors and stayed on in the ruinous covenant, where he ended up infected by the apathy within its walls and for years suffered the ill-treatment of the then *ductrix*, Judit of Flambeau. As he often says, his life was in ruins until he met Abū-l-Āfiya al-Apromorī, whose intelligence won his heart. Since then Ouro has enjoyed a second youth and has taken a renewed interest in Hermetic life and in his own covenant. He is thrilled at the prospect of becoming Praeco and has many plans for the Tribunal. Furthermore, although his *sodales* have tried to dissuade him, he has begun looking for someone to challenge in order to win the title of archmage; Ouro feels his time is near and, in some way, he wants to leave his mark on a world through which he has passed on tiptoe.

Ouro is always accompanied by his familiar, an aged black dog who has gone blind and devotedly serves the members of the covenant. Old Barzelay likes to walk along the edge of the nearby cliffs, and often spends days away from the covenant sleeping in the open, for, as he says, he loves to rest lulled by the sea.

##### Judit of Flambeau

The aged Judit is utterly consumed by Twilight. She barely eats, barely speaks; dark embers glow in her eyes that will not let her sleep. Judit has lost almost all her Hermetic knowledge; her Arts are comparable to those of a fifteen-year-old apprentice; her life is no more than a shadow. She was once the *ductrix* of Brigantia and used her position to enrich herself and prosper at the covenant's expense. She was a despotic, wretched woman who projected her fears and complexes onto others. If someone asked her for vis, she threw it into the sea; when someone wanted a book, she burned it; she spoiled her companions' food merely because she had had a bad night. She turned the lives of Brigantia's members into a hell, and her *sodales* abandoned the covenant one by one… all except Ouro. The magus had to endure Judit's abuse for years, until one winter night the deranged Judit suffered a Twilight she could not control and that left her with terrible aftereffects. Inexplicably, Judit went on suffering ever longer Twilights, until in 1185 magic finally destroyed her mind. Abū-l-Āfiya suspects that Ouro may have been responsible for those Twilights, although, knowing what he suffered, he would never dare to blame him.

##### Abū-l-Āfiya al-Fassād al-Apromorī al-Flambī

Abū-l-Āfiya is a mature magus, a native of the Sudan. During his apprenticeship he received the *laqab* al-Fassād ("the Bleeder" or "the Phlebotomist") for using one of his Perdo Corpus spells to cure his master's shield grog. Abū-l-Āfiya lived at Harra until 1195, when he was expelled from the covenant for refusing to go to Alarcos.

Although he has been in Galicia for more than twenty years, he has still not grown used to it: the color of his skin, his language, his religion and his Gift keep him shut away in Brigantia and cut off from the world, which is slowly embittering him. Moreover, he cannot abide the falseness and selfishness of the northern magi and, above all, he hates their megalomania.

Abū-l-Āfiya al-Apromorī is chiefly responsible for the rebirth of Brigantia. It was he who persuaded Ouro to take them in, and he has brought prosperity to the covenant, which now has a sizeable fishing fleet and a few merchant ships that ply the coasts of the kingdom of Portugal to keep it supplied (thanks to which they are on good terms with the Portuguese covenant of Resurgens). Thanks to his deep knowledge of Hermetic law, Abū-l-Āfiya is fighting for Brigantia to win back the old vis sources the Tribunal took from it in 1016 and, in truth, he is very close to succeeding, which could bring about the coming of Summer, and perhaps the backing Ouro needs to be elected Praeco.

##### Nāārun al-Apromorī al-Flambī

*He was, however, a witty man and a joker, though when he jested he never said what was not true; thus he liked to make jokes with the truth, and he so abhorred lies and liars that he could not bear them.*[^p118-4]

[^p118-4]: Excerpt from *The Epistle of Holiness* by Ibn ʿArabī (Spanish translation by Miguel Asín Palacios).

Nāārun is Abū-l-Āfiya's *filius* and, like him, a lover of poetry and the sciences, although, unlike his master, he has a great sense of humor. Like Abū-l-Āfiya, he was expelled from Harra, which ended up saving his life. At present the young follower of Apromor is charged, together with Xana al-Merinitiyya, with overseeing the mundane growth of the new city of Corunna. Although the fieldwork is done mainly by his *sodalis* and their covenant companions, it is Nāārun who has to make the decisions so that the efforts of the Merinita and the rest are not in vain.

<!-- p. 119 -->

##### Xana al-Merinitiyya

The young Xana is the covenant's newest member. A native of Asturias recruited by Abū-l-Āfiya, the Merinita was first brought in to negotiate for an important vis source with a powerful sea faerie who lives some ten kilometers out to sea from Brigantia. Xana managed to win an invitation to the faerie's court, but had to leave it when, because of her Gentle Gift, Abū-l-Āfiya asked her to help Nāārun with his duties. Since then she has not been able to shake off the idea that the tower of *du* has something to do with the faeries, although she does not yet know what.

> #### Story Seeds: The Head of Geryon
>
> It is said that Brigantia's center of power emanates from one of the heads of the giant Geryon, son of Chrysaor and Callirrhoe (daughter of Oceanus), who lived on the island of Erytheia.[^p119-I] According to Apollodorus, Geryon was a giant with the bodies of three men, joined into one at the waist but split into three from the flanks and thighs. On Erytheia the giant kept a herd of red cattle, tended by the herdsman Eurytion and guarded by Orthrus, the two-headed dog born of Typhon and Echidna. In his tenth labor, Hercules stole Geryon's cattle (with the help of the cup of Helios) and sailed back toward Tartessos. In other sources, Geryon is the son of Erebus and Night, ruler of Erytheia and king of the giants, who was slain by Hercules and buried on the peninsula of Faro. These mythographers say that he used his face to work his deceits, for it was that of a kindly man, while his body was that of a serpent, mottled in many colors, with a tail ending in a scorpion's sting that oozed a deadly venom.
>
> Whatever its origin, the head lay for centuries in its burial chamber until, a little under two years ago, Abū-l-Āfiya opened it to study it. Unbeknownst to him, the smell released when he broke the seal was carried along the north coast and then inland, as far as the source of the Naverón river, in Asturias. There a middle-aged cuélebre, thirsting for magic, came out of the mar Cuayada in pursuit of the intoxicating scent. On reaching the covenant, she found that the *Aegis* barred her way. Since then she has not stopped seeking a way to breach it, and she has taken refuge on the coast, sheltered by Brigantia's magic aura. Naturally, her presence has not gone unnoticed. The shepherds have reported the disappearance of many goats, and one of the families of Corunna has lost one of its children, so the matter has reached the town council.
>
> Xana has already told Nāārun, and he has told Abū-l-Āfiya, who has asked Šuʿlatun to pass word to the Redcaps so that some covenant will come to help them. Will the player characters get involved in Brigantia's affair? What will they ask in return for their services?
>
> [^p119-I]: This was the name of one of the islands of the Gadeira archipelago, in what is now the Bay of Cadiz.

>
> Cuélebres delight in the fear of men, so they begin by hunting cattle to terrify them and then children to get their attention. Once panic has spread among the populace, the cuélebre picks some shepherd with whom to negotiate the delivery of animal or human sacrifices, under threat of destroying the church and the village where he lives. The cuélebre loathes speaking, for it knows only a few words and, although it is hard to understand (its hissing hampers its diction), it generally manages to convey a simple message about what it wants. Usually the terrified shepherd goes to the village with its message, and the villagers agree to leave the agreed head of cattle at a certain spot. The interval between sacrifices is purely a matter of trial and error: if it is too long, the cuélebre starts killing on its own account, and if it is too short, the offerings are usually not claimed until a day or two later.
>
> The fangs of cuélebres can be enriched (see *Realms of Power: Magic*, page 153) if they are left steeping in the creature's own blood and venom for a season. After that time the fangs will have partly dissolved, so the largest piece must be taken and wrapped in the hair of a pregnant woman until it forms a ball, which must then be bathed in water and left to dry. If this is done, anyone who carries these fangs gains the Virtue Lesser Immunity to the venom of cuélebres, serpents and basilisks.

##### Šuʿlatun al-Ŷerbitoniyya

Šuʿlatun is a mature maga who was expelled from Harra for refusing to abandon her husband, Abū-l-Āfiya. Since her former covenant-mates perished at Alarcos, her relationship with her husband has been cold and distant; she no longer loves him. She believes that had they all gone to war, they would have won the battle and Harra would still be standing. Šuʿlatun hates the north of Iberia, so she uses her work for the covenant as an intermediary to keep abreast of the Almohad situation in al-Andalus, in the hope of returning to the *kūra* of Jaén, where she grew up.

<!-- p. 121 -->

### Beit Midrash

>**Lifespan:** 1151–Present<br>
>**Founders:** Šôfēṭ al-Gernikī, Raḥûm al-Tŷtalī<br>
>**Season:** Spring<br>
>**Aura (type and strength):** Magic, strength 2<br>
>**Reputations:** Troublemakers (Iberian Tribunal) 4, Defiant (Iberian Tribunal) 2<br>
>**Votes:** 4

*Beit midrash* (plural *batei midrash*) is the Hebrew for "house of learning," and it was the name its two founders chose in order to carry on the legacy of the fallen covenant of ʿÔlām wā-ʿed, in Lucena. Although they thought they could rebuild their home, the lands of northern Iberia have proved surly and unfriendly, and their people dirty, illiterate and stammering. And so the grief of its founders ended up stamped on the high white walls of the ever-melancholy Jewish covenant of Beit Midrash.

#### History

When the *rosh yeshiva* of the Lucena covenant, Meʾir ibn Yosef, announced the destruction of ʿÔlām wā-ʿed in 1151, his Hermetic brothers Šôfēṭ al-Gernikī and Raḥûm al-Tŷtalī had already resolved to found a covenant of their own; at that same Tribunal they had their charter approved and set off westward, where, after a few months, they found a powerful magic aura in which to settle, in the deep canyons of the Sil. But when they attended the Tribunal of 1158 to report their location and register their vis sources, the Quaesitores informed them that they were too close to Duresca and asked them to move at least ten days' journey away. As a gesture of goodwill, Duresca gave them books, vis and gold to start again, and Šôfēṭ and Raḥûm left the Sil in 1173. After two years they decided to settle in Monforte, where there was a thriving Jewish community… and where they were even closer to Duresca.

The Tribunal of 1179 was marked by the dispute between the two covenants. Although Duresca tried to have them exiled, Šôfēṭ argued that there was no precedent in the Peripheral Code to justify its wish, and the Quaesitores of Duresca had to validate Beit Midrash's new location. Since then the Jewish covenant has been the target of constant attacks by Duresca: its resources have been expropriated, Duresca has meddled in the mundane politics of Monforte to try to ruin it, and it has incited others to challenge its members to Wizard's War. Beit Midrash, however, has held out stoically, and although it seems frozen in its Spring, it continues to advance little by little. What is more, to Duresca's exasperation, it has not yet lodged a single complaint.

<!-- p. 122 -->

#### Setting and Physical Description

Beit Midrash lies in a deep grove protected by one of the meanders of the Chalibe river, some six kilometers northwest of Monforte. This town has a thriving Jewish community, where the Sephardim do not live in an aljama but share the streets and squares with the Christians (although they do have a cluster of buildings around the rúa Vella where they keep their synagogue, *micvé*[^p122-5] and butcher's shop, very near the hill on which the fortress of the town's lord stands). Monforte holds licenses to hold fairs and markets (see page 58), so the magi of Beit Midrash generally need not travel to other towns to obtain their laboratory materials, which is especially advantageous.

[^p122-5]: The Jewish ritual bath.

Beit Midrash is a building of clearly magical make, squat and compact, with an octagonal plan. Its walls of polished alabaster, almost always wrapped in the mists of the river, have neither windows nor doors, and are covered in Hebrew inscriptions bearing phrases from the Pentateuch. Although the covenant has no more than two floors and a cellar (so that it does not rise above the woodland), it is large enough to house up to four *sancta* of standard size. Inside, despite the lack of windows, light enters through certain points in the walls and ceilings, enchanted so that one can see through them. The building has only one entrance, guarded from within by an automaton dog and facing Jerusalem. The entrance becomes visible only if one of the members of Beit Midrash speaks the word *menorá*. At the center of the covenant is a courtyard giving access to the cellars, where the forge and laboratory of the artisan Ferraria al-Verditiyya are located, from which a pleasant scent of wormwood always drifts.

The grove of Beit Midrash is protected by the spell *The Shrouded Glen* (ReMe 40), which, together with the *Aegis of the Hearth*, the members of the covenant take great care to renew every year. This has led the people of Lucena to set candles and crosses on the paths that cross the grove, and many carry wolf's claws in the folds of their clothes to ward off the *mal güeyu*.

#### Society and Customs

The government of Beit Midrash is pure anarchy: each of its members does whatever lies in his power to protect and improve the covenant, and none (regardless of experience, title or age) has to account for his activities to the rest in council. In Beit Midrash there is no infighting; resources are used with restraint and always for the good of the covenant; matters are approached according to the abilities of its members, so it is rare for any of its undertakings to fail. Indeed, they have proved so competent that Duresca considers them a threat, and so the judges' covenant began, years ago, a campaign of disparagement that by 1220 is firmly entrenched. As a result, in the eyes of the Tribunal Beit Midrash is a harmful covenant with which almost no one wants dealings. Despite all this, the members of Beit Midrash seem not to care, though only outwardly. Neither Šôfēṭ al-Gernikī nor Raḥûm al-Tŷtalī has forgotten Duresca's offenses, and they have gathered to their side others who, like them, repudiate Hermetic society.

All the magi of Beit Midrash are Jews, so they speak Hebrew as their first language and Arabic as their second, and they share (except, at times, the young Orraca) the rites of their religion in the small synagogue inside the covenant, where, unlike among mundanes, men and women may remain in the same chamber. Nevertheless, the members of Beit Midrash usually attend the synagogue of Monforte once a year; there, despite the discomfort their Gift causes, they share the space for a few hours with their Sephardic brethren.

On the magical side, the covenant is sustained by a powerful vis source that welled up in the river when Beit Midrash settled near the Chalibe. These waters, traditionally rich in iron (the Celtiberian warriors came to them to temper their swords), began to produce Corpus, Terram and Vim vis in such quantities that the covenant was able to begin raising a powerful *Aegis* each year to protect itself, above all from the snares of the hated Duresca. As for its mundane needs, Beit Midrash earns its wealth by selling its silverwork at the town's fairs and markets, for which it relies on Ferraria's contacts, the ever-willing companions Samuel Lemos, Salomón Ferraz and Moisés Gaibor.

#### The Magi of Beit Midrash

##### Archmage Raḥûm al-Tŷtalī

Raḥûm (Hebrew for "merciful") is a warrior magus, the former defender of the Lucena covenant of ʿÔlām wā-ʿed and, as such, the one chiefly responsible for having failed to prevent its fall. Raḥûm is a Rationalist philosopher who did not end up at Iššáh because of the philosophical differences that separated him from his former *sodalis*, Abraham ben David. But their differences did not keep him from going to his aid in 1212, when news came of the terrible pogrom taking place in Toledo.

The archmage Raḥûm seeks to discredit Duresca through his own suffering. Although he has managed to expose the great Iberian covenant on more than one occasion, it is as if his *sodales* had no memory: by dint of repeating its lies, Duresca always prevails. For Raḥûm it is a matter of time; the Tribunal will come to see the truth for itself, without his having to use the same methods as the Order.

##### Šôfēṭ al-Gernikī

Like his *amicus* Raḥûm, Šôfēṭ declined the invitation extended to him at Iššáh and chose not to follow the path of ʿEzraʾ ben Šēlomoh. Šôfēṭ seeks the same thing as Raḥûm: to establish a new order that will put an end to the corruption of a system that, after more than four centuries without change, has become obsolete. He also believes that the Order cannot be changed from within, which is why he gave up his title of Quaesitor at the beginning of the twelfth century. After meeting and learning from Maimonides, he began to write the foundations of a Hermetic law whose formal structure of legal reasoning rested on the operations (such as analogy and syllogism) that make up the core of Aristotelian metaphysics. However, after the doctrines of the *mutawaḥḥid*, or Perfects, were condemned at the Grand Tribunal of 1162, Šôfēṭ lost heart and chose not to publish his studies, which Raḥûm has still not forgiven him.

<!-- p. 123 -->

##### Ferraria al-Verditiyya

Trained at Ajabeba, Ferraria was still an apprentice when she heard the details of the destruction of ʿÔlām wā-ʿed recounted. The tale affected her so deeply that, after passing her Gauntlet, she set out in the footsteps of the Lucena covenant. She knew its members had gone their separate ways, so she went first to Iššáh, where she was not admitted, and then had to wait until the Tribunal of 1179 (when Duresca cruelly attacked the two magi of Beit Midrash) to meet the rest of the magi of ʿÔlām wā-ʿed. She then asked to join them and was accepted as a full member. Since then she has never stopped improving the covenant, whose impressive appearance and main sources of mundane income are due above all to her overflowing talent. Over the years, Ferraria converted to Judaism and abandoned her Muslim faith.

##### ʿOg al-Praliḥī

ʿOg Ex Miscellanea is a tempestarius (see page 299). His height of over two meters betrays his giant blood, inherited from the ancient pataricos of northern Iberia (see page 147). ʿOg came to the covenant after being manipulated into challenging Šôfēṭ to Wizard's War. It was not until he faced Raḥûm that he realized it: without words or magic, the archmage showed him the mistake he had made. To make amends, and as a token of honor, ʿOg asked to join the covenant, and Beit Midrash welcomed him as an equal.

ʿOg converted to Judaism in 1212, after the pogrom in Toledo. Since then he has become what the Asturians call a *vedorio*, someone with the gift of the Calderín (see insert), able to see the spirits of the dead. No one in the covenant knows the cause of his new power, but Raḥûm considers it a sign from God for having embraced the true faith.

> #### Story Seeds: The Güestia
>
> The so-called *vedorios* are those who possess the gift of the Calderín: the ability to see and speak with the spirits of the dead and to foretell when a person is going to die. The local people say this gift is acquired only by those who were baptized with the oils used to anoint the dead (usually walnut oil), although the magi believe it is due to some kind of supernatural ability gained through contact with some magical agent (in game terms, it would be an application of the Virtues Second Sight and Premonitions).
>
> According to the magi who have studied the affairs of the soul, after death or burial the separation from the body and the release of the soul take place a year later, which is the time the soul needs to sever its ties, although it usually stays near the body after the process. In February the freed souls are purified, and it is customary for the living to take food to the cemeteries to celebrate the feast of Saint Peter in their memory. After Easter, in spring, the freed souls that have been purified can leave their bodies behind and set out on the road to the next world in a procession that the local people call the "güestia."
>
> The *vedorios* who have seen it say that the spirits that form it go wrapped in shrouds and carry burning bones in their hands, like candles. On April 25 (Saint Mark's Day) the people of northern Iberia commonly do not leave their homes at night for fear of meeting the güestia, for they say it is the only day on which men can see it, and that all who see it die soon after.
>
> The souls leave the world on All Souls' Day, during the ancient Celtic celebration of Samain. On that day fishermen leave off their labors, for their nets tend to come out of the water laden with bones, and the local people do not sleep in their beds and leave cauldrons of water and food on their doorsteps; all of them practices the Church considers pagan.
>
> One day in late autumn, the player characters (preferably from a covenant located in northern Iberia) are asked by their autocrat to hold a council. At it, the mysterious death of several head of the covenant's cattle is set out. The animals have been found dead, with no sign of violence. A magical investigation will confirm this, but will shed no further light on the matter. The following week, one of the covenant's workers is found dead outside its walls, again without any mark of violence, although questioning him with the spell *Whispers through the Black Gate* (InCo[Me] 15) will reveal a frightened soul who describes, as his last memory, a shadow woven in the wind.
>
> The magi face a spirit that has been unable to leave the world, a soul that lost the trail of the güestia on its journey to the hereafter because of its unresolved deeds on earth. Once they deduce that it is a spirit, if they lack the abilities needed to locate it, perhaps they can seek out the *vedorio* of Beit Midrash (ʿOg) to help them. The magi will first have to locate the spirit in order to negotiate with it (which will mean helping it resolve whatever binds it to the earth) or destroy it so that it stops killing their people.

##### Orraca al-Merkeriyya (Redcap)

Orraca is the youngest member of Beit Midrash. Although she was raised and educated at Porta Pandere, the Redcap is not very comfortable following rules. Her lack of discipline led to her expulsion from the Portuguese covenant. Although the Mercere gave her the chance to find another covenant where she could practice her profession with more freedom, Orraca did not take it well. Fond of wine, poetry and chess, she wandered across Iberia until she fell, quite literally, into Beit Midrash. ʿOg found her collapsed in the covenant's magical grove, utterly drunk. When she awoke, Orraca discovered that she could stay at the covenant, and she was admitted as a member of Beit Midrash in the autumn of 1216.

In her four years she has managed to buy a stone house on the rúa Vella in Monforte, where she spends the night during her rare visits to Beit Midrash. Although her mother was Jewish, Orraca is not very devout, and at times she wonders why the magi of the covenant have not yet thrown her out; she herself feels that she does nothing for the covenant and, by all appearances, anyone would think the same. Yet everyone in Beit Midrash is fond of her and treats her as one of their own during her short stays.

Orraca was denounced by Duresca a couple of seasons ago; she was carrying an important message and lost it while playing chess at a hospice on the Way of Saint James. Although she fears being expelled from House Mercere at the ordinary Tribunal of 1221, she seldom stays sober long enough to worry about it.

### Lucis

*Hinc fons prespicuis paradisi surgit a limphis,*<br>
*Hic dulcis austus effluit in pectoris antro,*<br>
*Hic largos latices per mundi compita mittit,*<br>
*Hęc forisque renidet argenti claro metallo*<br>
*Et intus cluit spiritalis gratję dono.*[^p124-6]

[^p124-6]: Excerpt from the poem by Cyprian, archpriest of Cordoba, which Miguel Rodríguez-Pantoja translates as: *Here from the clean stream of paradise a spring wells up; / it pours its sweet draughts into the depths of the breast, / these abundant jets it sprinkles over all the world; / with the bright metal of silver it gleams without / and the grace of the spirit shines within;* (*Los mozárabes. Historia cultura y religión de los cristianos de al Ándalus*).

>**Lifespan:** 780–799<br>
>**Founder:** Ranemiro of Guernicus<br>
>**Aura (type and strength):** Divine, strength 6<br>
>**Reputations:** Saintly (Iberian Tribunal) 3

The ancient covenant of Lucis still arouses curiosity and reverence among the magi of Iberia in 1220. Built at the dawn of the Order's arrival in Iberia, Lucis took an active part in Hermetic politics and, despite its short life, laid the first stone in defining the identity of the Tribunal; its light went on casting inspiration over the generations to come and, because of the events surrounding its disappearance, many are beginning to regard its founder, Ranemiro, as a saint.

#### History

When the Galician kingdom rose against the kingdom of Asturias, King Silo marched with his army to put down the revolt. The two kingdoms clashed and fought in the shadow of Mount Cupeiro, where the Asturians defeated the Galicians. After the victory, Silo granted the conquered lands to Abbot Esperautano so that he might build on them a monastery from which to restore the Christian religion in the region.

At that time the Benedictine Ranemiro had returned from Durenmar and settled in the monastery of Oviedo. His friendship with Esperautano allowed him to build a hermitage in the abbot's monastery, from which he could carry out his sacred task. In exchange, Ranemiro pledged to the abbot to evangelize as many pagan Galicians as he could. Thanks to this agreement, Ranemiro's hermitage became part of the religious and ecclesiastical restoration of the Galician district at the end of the eighth century. His influence thus spread through the north, and he succeeded in bringing the vates and some lesser wizards of the region into the fold, so that he had to enlarge the covenant, which came to reach the size of a small monastery. He failed, however, with the tempestarii in the year 792.

When Ranemiro was expelled from the Order at the Grand Tribunal of 799, the aged magus returned to his covenant and, without saying a word, shut himself away in the private chapel of his *sanctum*. When his *filius*, Tello, returned from Cordoba a year later, he found nothing but ruins where Lucis should have stood: all its inhabitants, magi and mundanes alike, had vanished with it. When Égica of Flambeau arrived in the spring of 800 intent on finishing off the expelled Ranemiro, Tello received him and confessed that his master and Lucis had ascended to the Divine Realm.

After the disappearance of Lucis, Tello encouraged pilgrimage to the ruins of the covenant, a movement that became popular during the tenth century and has lost momentum by 1220. Nevertheless, there are still Christian magi who make the pilgrimage to Lucis from many parts of Mythic Europe, considering the place a point of singularity between the Divine and Magic Realms (see insert).

> #### Story Seeds: The White Blackbird
>
> For more than a hundred years, the notebooks of the Hermetic pilgrims to Lucis have mentioned a white bird resembling a blackbird among the ruins. Many of these accounts agree on the beauty of its song during spring and summer, while those who have seen it in autumn and winter describe it as a silent and elusive bird.
>
> At the Tribunal of 1207, a Redcap from Porta Pandere spoke of this. Accustomed to listening to travelers, she was struck by the fact that the accounts, sometimes far apart in time, always agreed about this white bird. Since then she has devoted herself to tracking down the notes of the magi who had made the pilgrimage to Lucis, asking permission for this from the covenants that kept them. According to her, the oldest record was made by a magus of the covenant of Durato in 1106.
>
> The chances of these being different birds are remote; white blackbirds are far too rare for several of the same kind to have been in the same place over the course of a century. According to the Redcap, it must be a divine bird that, for some reason, chose to nest in the ruins of Lucis. However, although she has been back to Lucis several times since then, the bird avoids her and will not let her approach. What kind of creature is it, and what are its aims? Perhaps the player characters have to face some infernal being and want to go to Lucis in search of help; or perhaps they have to wash away their sins and their only remaining hope is that the supposed divine animal can ease their burden. As always, the storyguide has the final word on the motives of this century-old bird.

#### Setting and Physical Description

The ruins of Lucis lie lost somewhere between the Eo, Masma, Alesancia and Mera rivers, surrounded by a not very dense forest of beech, chestnut, oak, yew and cork oak. Near the old walls is a small artificial lake that Ranemiro's people once used as a fishpond. The pool, fed by a natural stream, has stayed crystal clear over the centuries, and some trout and, at times, eels can be found in its waters.

<!-- p. 125 -->

It is customary for pilgrims to spend seven nights among the ruins of Lucis to pray and meditate. At some point in the tenth century, a magus left his voting *sigil* as an offering on the spot where Ranemiro's private chapel had stood. Since then some have followed his example, although in the twelfth century they began to leave a symbolic object in its place.

### Campus Stellae

>**Lifespan:** 836–913<br>
>**Founder:** Baldiccione of Guernicus<br>
>**Aura (type and strength):** Divine, strength 2<br>
>**Reputations:** Monastery (local) 6

The covenant of Campus Stellae is, above all, the covenant of Baldiccione of Guernicus: it was born with him and, when he was gone, it ceased to exist. Founded by one of Guernicus's *filii*, it played an outstanding legislative role in bringing about the formation of the regional Iberian Tribunal in 898, and a fundamental one in achieving peace with the *saḥirs*.

#### History

When the second Grand Tribunal, in 817, granted *certamen* the power to settle any dispute, Guernicus's *filius* Baldiccione left the forum of Hermes together with his *parens* to return to Rome, where a few years later news reached them of the discovery of the tomb of the apostle Saint James the Greater in Iberia. Baldiccione then took leave of his *parens* and set out for the Galician lands. On arriving, he met the Benedictines of Antealtares, who were charged with caring for the apostle's remains, and the magi of Alma Mater on their annual pilgrimages. Baldiccione spent some time at Antealtares and, after making the pilgrimage to Lucis, decided to found his own covenant near the apostle's tomb, two years before Fenicil was named Primus of House Guernicus.

In his early years, Baldiccione built bridges with the diocese of Iria Flavia, and the relationship grew stronger from the second half of the ninth century, when Campus began to take in pilgrims bound for the apostle's tomb. The fact that it was always home to few magi, and that all of them had the Gentle Gift, favored its integration into the social fabric of Iria Flavia, to the point that by the end of the ninth century part of the covenant was already serving as a convent for some Benedictine monks.

When in 907 the *saḥirs* killed the apprentice of Briatiz de Moncharro of Diedne (the dean of Duresca), Briatiz declared Wizard's War on Baldiccione, holding him responsible for the death of her *filius*. Baldiccione died in that conflict and the covenant became a monastery. All its members (except Ṭāmis *filius* Baldiccione) left the Order behind to pursue their monastic life. In this way the covenant was absorbed by the diocese of Iria Flavia, which at that time was governed by Abbot Teodomiro.

Years later, Baldiccione was linked to the supposedly fraudulent Duresca manuscripts, when Briatiz de Moncharro brought them to light in 937 (see page 76).

#### Setting and Physical Description

What was once Campus Stellae is now a peaceful monastery inhabited by Benedictine monks near Iria Flavia. The weak magic aura of the place eventually disappeared in favor of a faint Divine aura. The sharp-eyed observer may still discover Hermetic motifs in the carvings of the cloister and in the old chapel of Campus Stellae.

> #### Story Seeds: The Last Days of Flambeau
>
> Some believe that Flambeau spent his last days at the covenant of Campus Stellae. This idea, which many find preposterous, is supported by those who claim to have copies of letters between Baldiccione and the Founder, which show that the two professed a deep friendship (writings that almost all the Flambeau dismiss as fraudulent, given the Founder's well-known illiteracy).
>
> On the strength of this correspondence, some have ventured into the monastery that was once Campus to find some clue, but they have never learned anything more than that there is a cell which, despite the passage of time, is always coated in black soot, as if it had suffered a fire that the monks had been unable, or had not dared, to clean. Those who believe this theory are of the opinion that this must have been the cell of the Founder Flambeau. And what if it were true? Might some ancient possession of the Founder be hidden among the treasures of the monastery of Campus? Perhaps his talisman, Heart of Fire?

### Pico Sacro

>**Lifespan:** 913–1010<br>
>**Founder:** Ṭāmis ibn Baldiccione al-Išbīlī al-Gernikī<br>
>**Aura (type and strength):** Magic, strength 8<br>
>**Reputations:** Dragon-Haunted (Hermetic) 2

<!-- p. 126 -->

The covenant of Pico Sacro was founded by Baldiccione's first apprentice, a Mozarab from Seville named Ṭāmis. After his master's death, he left Campus Stellae (for he did not wish to turn his back on Hermetic life nor to shut himself away as a Benedictine monk in the monastery of Campus) and settled at a nearby place of power.

#### History

During its short life, Pico Sacro was a small covenant that never had more than two magi. Even so, it gained great renown in its early years thanks to the figure of its founder. Ṭāmis was not only one of Baldiccione's disciples; he also served many times as presiding Quaesitor, declined a seat in the upper chamber of Magvillus, brought about the peace with the *saḥirs* (continuing the work begun by his *parens*) and, despite his lineage, was one of those chiefly responsible for spreading the controversial Duresca manuscripts and one of the staunchest defenders of their authenticity. His principles and upright morals led him to defy Magvillus, which cost him his accreditation as a Quaesitor and possibly his life at the battle of Frías (see insert on page 78).

After his death, Pico Sacro disappeared from Hermetic life. Its only inhabitant, Mariña Sanchiz Ex Miscellanea, shut herself away in the little covenant so as not to be drawn into the intrigues that had done away with Ṭāmis, and discreetly ran it until the Schism War broke out in 1010. Mariña then collaborated with the Tremere during the conflict, giving them her vis and allowing them to use Pico Sacro as a base of operations in their fight against the Diedne. However, it was not the renegades who put an end to the covenant, but an enormous dragon that until then had lain asleep beneath Pico Sacro. The beast awoke for unknown reasons and laid waste to the buildings and their inhabitants. Since then no one has ventured near the mountain where the covenant of Baldiccione's heir once stood, despite its powerful aura.

#### Setting and Physical Description

The imposing Pico Sacro lies less than a day's journey from Compostela and from the old covenant of Campus Stellae. The peak, less than 500 meters high, stands out in the middle of flat land. On its summit nothing remains of the modest covenant but the base of a column; the rest was devoured by the flames of the dragon that dwells in the mountain (see insert).

> #### Story Seeds: The Dragon of Pico Sacro
>
> According to legend, the first place the disciples of the apostle Saint James chose for his tomb was the summit of this peak; however, when they climbed it, they found a dragon resting in one of its caves and decided to leave.
>
> The dragon of Pico Sacro is, therefore, an ancient magical being, a true dragon of immeasurable power that will test the most experienced magi. Use this resource however you see fit, for example as the starting point for further stories aimed at obtaining the information needed to defeat the dragon, or as the background for a Flambeau hunt.

## Asturias

During the ninth and tenth centuries the Asturian kings began to organize their territory into administrative units called *mandationes*, *commisos* and districts (*alfoces*). Alongside these units appeared the village community, made up of a grouping of small family cells, each of which held the right (granted by the king) to work a small part of the whole. The fact that the villages could govern themselves allowed the *concilium* to emerge (see page 17).

In almost every village in Asturias there is a church that acts as its social center; until the Gregorian reform, it operated as a proprietary church under the control of the community (indeed, it provided an important source of income).

The regional unit of Asturias stretches along the northern Cantabrian coast, from the Eo river to the Deva (a few kilometers east of the town council of Llanes), where it borders the kingdom of Castile. The terrain of Asturias is rugged: the imposing Cantabrian Mountains rise in its lands with peaks of over 2,500 meters, and it is crossed from north to south by watercourses such as the Narcea and the Nalón. Asturias holds important vis sources in its lands and, indeed, it was once home to what is believed to have been the richest of the entire Tribunal: the beach where the tempestarii worshiped their gods (see page 66). Needless to say, the most powerful covenant in the Tribunal, Duresca, has fed for centuries on the intrinsic power of this ancient region with its thousand-year-old magical tradition.

The territorial unit of Asturias is home to town councils such as those of Oviedo, Avilés, Pravia, Tineo and Llanes, among others. At present the only inhabited covenant in this whole territory is Duresca, the legislative center of Iberia.

<!-- p. 127 -->

### Duresca

*Human acts are sometimes performed solely so that the bodily form may exist. […] Within this kind fall drunkenness, the game of chess, and hunting done for pleasure. He who makes all these things his [ultimate] goal is [a man] purely corporeal […]. For such as these, spiritual forms have no value at all […].*[^p127-7]

[^p127-7]: Excerpt from *The Regimen of the Solitary* by Avempace (Spanish translation by Joaquín Lomba Fuentes).

>**Lifespan:** 780 (officially, 940)–Present<br>
>**Founder:** Tancoystl of Diedne (officially, Alvarra of Guernicus)<br>
>**Season:** Autumn<br>
>**Aura (type and strength):** Magic, strength 5 (inside the *regio* the aura reaches 9)<br>
>**Reputations:** Corrupt (al-Andalus) 4, Just (Iberian Tribunal) 3, Exemplary (Iberian Tribunal) 2<br>
>**Coat of Arms:** Its original emblem was destroyed in 1025 and is now unknown<br>
>**Votes:** 10

Duresca is so deeply rooted in the history of the Tribunal that neither can be understood without the other. The Guernicus who dwell there speak of it in the same terms as they speak of Iberia, and over the centuries that message has sunk in, turning the covenant into an institution in its own right — so much so that many magi believe that without it the Tribunal would cease to exist.

#### History

Duresca was the name that the Welsh maga Tancoystl of Diedne gave to her covenant, which she raised over a powerful sanctuary that had once belonged to the Asturian vates, although whether she won it by force or through some kind of agreement is not known for certain. Founded at the dawn of the Order, Duresca had its charter ratified at the first Rhine Tribunal in 780.

In its early years, Duresca worked to bring the Asturian and Galician wizards into the Order, succeeding with the vates but not with the tempestarii. During the war waged against the latter at the end of the eighth century, Tancoystl took their side so that they would not be exterminated, which led to the destruction of Brigantia, the deaths of several magi, and a reprimand and fine from the Grand Tribunal of 799.

Years later, during the Order's first crisis, the members of Duresca who had gone to Stonehenge to put an end to Damhan-Allaidh joined the Ordo Miscellanea of Pralix, which led to Duresca's expulsion. It would not return to the Order for almost two years, and when it did, it was under the aegis of House Ex Miscellanea, at the fourth meeting of the Grand Tribunal. On her return, Tancoystl began to notice how the Tremere of the covenants of Secunda and Tertia had started to amass great power through *certamen*. At the Grand Tribunal of 832 the maga confirmed that this was not a local matter, and she began to work with the Ronda covenant of Dār Malīḥaʾ to try to curb the House's megalomania. Moreover, in those same years many of Duresca's sources had begun to dwindle because of the discovery of the tomb of the apostle Saint James, and Tancoystl had to divide her efforts between the two causes.

Duresca was overwhelmed when, in 845, Ramiro I of Asturias condemned the wizards of his kingdom to the stake. That same year, Tancoystl asked the Iberian magi for help in trying to halt the advance of the Dominion and have the Christian monarch's edict revoked, at a meeting that was eventually dissolved by the Quaesitor of Secunda, Teodoric, when the maga's proposals finally overstepped the bounds of legality under the Code of Hermes. Tancoystl then tried to solve the problem within the law, but her progress was cut short when one of her *filiae* ended up burned at the stake, at which point the maga resolved to overthrow the Asturian king. The regicide never came to pass, however: Tancoystl was betrayed, and the aged maga was burned alive on the slopes of Mount Naranco.

The next maga to take charge of Duresca, the Diedne Briatiz de Moncharro, chose to distance herself from Hermetic and mundane intrigues in the Peninsula, and the covenant went unnoticed until 907, when Briatiz lost her apprentice in the brutal *saḥir* attack. In consequence, she killed in a Wizard's War the man she held responsible for that death, the Praeco Baldiccione. Having done away with him, she raided his *sanctum* and carried off all his possessions, among them the letters that would unleash the scandal of the Duresca manuscripts in 937, whose authenticity she defended to the end.

As is well known, Magvillus sent five Guernicus, led by Alvarra, to determine whether those manuscripts were genuine. After Briatiz's death at the battle of Frías, those same judges seized control of the covenant in 940. However, when a year later they declared the manuscripts fraudulent, their credibility suffered, and Duresca was pushed into the background while the Guernicus of Dār Malīḥaʾ dominated the legislative landscape of the Peninsula.

The Guernicus of Duresca had to wait more than fifty years for the magi to begin overlooking their stain: Alvarra took advantage of the corruption of the Tytalus to divert the attention of his *sodales*, whose suspicions were completely forgotten during the Schism War, in which Alvarra died at the hands of Duresca's last Diedne.

House Guernicus emerged from the Schism strengthened, and Duresca, now in the hands of Iustum (another of the Guernicus who had come from Magvillus), had to deal with the independence of al-Andalus. Iustum worked with Durato and Aedes Saturni to project the Order's errors onto the magi of al-Andalus, who came to be blamed for the losses of the Schism. Furthermore, they knew how to profit from the absence of the Andalusi covenants during their secession by laying down the new legislative foundations of the Tribunal with the rulings "On the Iberian Chamber" (1018) and "On the Diedne Legacy" (1025), after which they began to plan the absorption of the Tribunal of al-Andalus. Finally, in 1025 Iustum obtained the status of dedicated covenant for Duresca, so that it could act swiftly against any Hermetic crime and prevent another Order-wide war from ever breaking out. Thus the covenant of the Quaesitores came to receive an annual endowment of 60% of the treasury in the Tribunal's common coffers.

<!-- p. 128 -->

Duresca reached the height of its power in 1103, when it was handed the records of the Tribunal of al-Andalus and some Guernicus from the south (such as the distinguished judge Danāʾ al-Gernikiyya) joined its ranks, making it the sole sovereign of the Tribunal's legislative power. It went on to improve its position further: in 1123 it gained access to numerous African magical resources through the covenant of al-Minẓār; in 1151 it founded the pilgrims' hospital at Noreña (see insert on page 45) and took control of the Cordoban covenant of Jušjášun; in 1166 it wrested the custody of the hospital at Gares (and its pontage rights) from the Navarrese covenant of Andelos; and in 1179 it brought the hospital at Portomarín under its rule. Now Duresca hopes to close a deal in 1221 with the *triumvir* Nuño of Salionca and the Mercere of Aedes Saturni, by which it will obtain the right to work the salt pans of northern Castile (if the internal crisis it faces does not tear it apart first).

> #### The Way of Saint James
>
> *I, who have loved the apostle since my childhood, during my years as a student traveled through foreign lands and regions for the space of fourteen years, carefully noting down on a few poor, rough leaves whatever writings I found about him, in order to gather them into a single volume, so that those who love Saint James might find conveniently gathered together all that is needed for the readings on his feast days.*[^p128-II]
>
> At some point between 825 and 830, "burning lights" began to be seen at night at a hillfort (*castro*) near Iria Flavia, in a place where angels had often been sighted before. The news reached the ears of the bishop of Iria Flavia, Teodomiro, who went to the spot in person and discovered that the lights marked the resting place of the apostle Saint James (which came to be known as the *compositum tellus*). When Alfonso II the Chaste of Asturias learned of it, he supported the construction of the first buildings, which would be the seed of the city of Compostela.
>
> Soon the news of the discovery began to spread through Mythic Europe. Pilgrims came to the tomb from Iberia and from beyond the Pyrenees, for, apart from Saint Peter and Saint Paul (martyred in Rome), Saint James was the only apostle buried in the West. This made Compostela one of the three principal places of pilgrimage in Christian Europe, together with Jerusalem (whose pilgrims are called "palmers") and Rome ("romers"). Moreover, because of the millennium of Christ's death in 1033, pilgrimage gained fresh importance (besides which it allowed all sins to be washed away), and since Jerusalem was controlled by Islamic powers, the West turned its gaze to Compostela, a nearby destination free of the dangers of crossing the Middle East.
>
> It is estimated that in its peak years Compostela may have received between 200,000 and 500,000 pilgrims a year. Such a volume of people ended up concentrating wealth in the towns, and the monarchs of Iberia took advantage of it to organize and structure their lands, since the road encouraged immigration: many Navarrese towns were resettled by men and women from beyond the Pyrenees, such as Estella, founded in 1090 under the fueros of Jaca.
>
> In 1220 the road passes close to several covenants, such as Mare Iacum, in the Sierra del Bierzo (one of the hardest and most feared stages, as it passes by Mount Irago), and Salionca, which lies near Castañeda, where pilgrims stop to collect stones from the quarry and carry them to the city, thus helping to build the basilica of the apostle Saint James.
>
> To make the way easier for pilgrims, the *Codex Calixtinus* was written in the twelfth century: a manual describing the various routes, advice, the daily stages between stops, and the dangers, and indicating the most important places of pilgrimage in Iberia, namely:
>
> - Santo Domingo de la Calzada, where the eleventh-century canon who gave the town its name is buried; he built the stretch of the road between Nájera and Redecilla and the bridge over the river Oja. It is said that he brought a cock and a hen back to life.
> - Sahagún, which holds the mortal remains of Saints Facundus and Primitivus, Christian brothers who lived in the third century and refused to offer sacrifice to a Roman idol. As punishment they were tortured and killed, and their bodies thrown into the river (in fact, the town of Sahagún was built where their bodies washed ashore). Next to the town, moreover, is the poplar grove where the shafts of the lances of Charlemagne's warriors sprouted green again.
> - Leon, which guards the body of Saint Isidore, the seventh-century bishop and doctor of Seville. His remains were discovered in Seville thanks to a revelation received by the bishop of Leon, Alvito, and were taken to the royal city after al-Muʿtaḍid handed them over to Fernando I of Leon. Once they were in his possession, the Christian monarch built a church to house them.
> - Compostela, which keeps the mortal remains of the apostle Saint James the Greater.
>
> Besides these places described in the *Codex Calixtinus*, there are many other saints scattered throughout Iberia: Saints Emeterius and Celedonius in Calahorra, Saint Crispin in Écija, Saints Servandus and Germanus on the coast of Cadiz, Saint Eulalia in Mérida, Saint Leocadia in Toledo, and Saints Zoilus, Acisclus, Faustus, Januarius and Martial in Cordoba.
>
> [^p128-II]: Excerpt from the letter of Calixtus II that serves as the prologue to the *Codex Calixtinus* (Spanish translation by M. Bravo Lozano).

<!-- p. 129 -->

#### Setting and Physical Description

Duresca stands at the center of a potent magic aura that extends for about half a kilometer in every direction. The covenant lies in the eastern foothills of the imposing Ubiña massif (over 2,000 meters high), set on a rocky shoulder from which it commands all the surrounding land. A dense beech wood surrounds and hides it, and not far away is the source of the *rivum cavum*.

The complex of buildings that makes up present-day Duresca is enclosed by a wall with a wall-walk but no battlements (at most three meters high), and its architectural styles range from pre-Romanesque and Romanesque buildings to the great council chamber raised in the eleventh century, clearly of magical make. Duresca is a self-sufficient village in itself: within its walls live up to four hundred people devoted to the smooth running of the covenant.

Duresca has two clearly distinct areas within its walls: one for mundane use (stables, farms, smithies, ovens, tanneries, glassmaking and bookbinding workshops, and so on) and one devoted to the magi (library, council chamber, treasure room, *sancta*, the building housing the *Secundus* portal, and so on). The two areas are separated by a low wall, and the difference in the wealth and quality of the buildings is plain to the naked eye. The magi's buildings are opulent and receive the finest goods in the Peninsula: its magi wear robes of Malagan brocade (*wašy*), its halls are of polished marble (*mulūkī*) from Almería, its cellars are full of wine from Malaga, its soldiers ride Sevillian mares, and its chambers are scented with essences distilled in Murcia.

The oldest building in the covenant was commissioned by Tancoystl, after the destruction of the tempestarii's sanctuary at the end of the eighth century, to guard Duresca's center of power: an irregular monolith of dolerite some ten meters high and weighing about fifty tons, raised by the ancient vates (with no other sign of human working), which generates a *regio* that overlaps the mundane level within a radius of some thirty meters and acts as a gateway to the Magic Realm. The monolith was enclosed in a seamless hollow prism that Tancoystl sealed, buried and protected with spells to keep the Order from finding it. Adjoining the chamber, and wrapped around it, she built three Hermetic laboratories inside the *regio*, which could be reached through the single entrance she left open; she made it coincide with a mundane stone portico, which she also protected with numerous enchantments.

Over the years, the Diedne built their covenant around the entrance to the *regio*, and at some point at the end of the ninth century it was sealed off when the council chamber was enlarged, burying Tancoystl's secret. When the Guernicus arrived, almost a century after the Diedne maga's death, they did not even know the *regio* existed. In fact, the portico came to light barely ten years ago (during the latest refurbishment of the council chamber, still in progress), when one of the magi was led to it by the powerful magical residue it gives off. In 1220 they have still not managed to open it, nor do they know what it guards; although the magic protecting it is powerful, the magi of Duresca have not yet devoted their full efforts to it — after all, if they spent more than 200 years in the covenant without knowing it existed, a few more years will make no difference.

The next oldest building faces south, and if anyone took the trouble to draw a straight line to the summit of Peña Ubiña, they would find that it misses the highest point by a few scant centimeters. This building houses the *Secundus* portal that links to Aedes Saturni. Although the two covenants have historically been on good terms, the building is protected by enchantments, created in the eleventh century during the Schism War, that restrict not entry into it but exit from it. No Redcap is permitted to leave the building, and they must leave their correspondence in pigeonholes that the magi of Duresca have set up for that purpose: one for each magus and another for matters addressed to the covenant.

#### The Council Chamber

The great council chamber rises above the *regio* that holds the monolith of the vates. It is an immense space some ten meters high, with three cantilevered galleries at different heights running along the walls around its entire perimeter. In each corner a spiral staircase leads from one gallery to another. The ceiling is an impressive leaded stained-glass window depicting the Founders, except for Diedne, with Guernicus at its center, crowned by a triangle. The floor is decorated with the symbols of the Houses, made from more than twenty kinds of marble, and there is a marked-off area in the center for holding *certamina*. At night the glass gives off its own light, leaving the enormous hall in a multicolored half-light.

When Duresca hosts a Tribunal, each covenant has a space reserved in the galleries. The highest (some nine meters above the floor) is occupied by the Praeco and the Quaesitores. The one immediately below is taken by the Autumn covenants, while the one closest to the floor is reserved for the Summer covenants. The floor is usually occupied by the Winter and Spring covenants, whose members have to look skyward if they wish to follow the business conducted by the most powerful covenants of the Tribunal. The hall, like the walkways of the galleries, is completely bare: at Tribunals in Duresca everyone always stands, and it is bad manners to sit, whether on the floor or by means of any kind of magical or mundane contrivance.

#### The Pilgrims' Hospitals

Some three days' journey to the north lies the hospital in the town of Noreña, at the crossroads of two Roman roads (on the stretches linking Siero with Luarca and Gijón with Leon). This hospital takes in pilgrims passing through Oviedo on their way to Salas, where they take the road built during the eleventh and twelfth centuries that runs to Mellid, the last stop before Compostela.

Some nine days to the southwest of Duresca lies the small hospital of Portomarín, which is reached from Astorga, and, some two weeks' journey to the east, the hospital of Gares, where the French Way of Saint James meets the road from Jaca, in the kingdom of Navarre.

The magi keep Arcane Connections to a room in each of the three hospitals (always located on the first floor), which only members of the covenant may enter.

<!-- p. 130 -->

Duresca uses the hospitals as a means of gathering information of every kind, since travelers from every corner of Mythic Europe pass through them. The hospitals are run by companions of the covenant (unless some magus wishes to take on that commitment) and staffed by grogs.

#### Society and Customs

Duresca is a unicameral democracy that has the offices of the *disceptator* and the *rector* to help regulate its governing body. The inner chamber (as the charter calls it) meets annually and has the authority to decide on the covenant's affairs (resources, investments, improvements, addenda to the charter, renewal of the *Aegis*, and so on), for which each representative in the chamber (except the *disceptator* and the *rector*) has one vote. The autocrat may be invited to this meeting to make any request concerning mundane matters (although he has no vote), and it also hears the petitions of Iberian magi (from outside the House) who wish to become Quaesitores.

The *disceptator* acts as the covenant's representative at Tribunals and enjoys the following privileges: a casting vote and the power to censure any member of the covenant (except the *rector*). When the *disceptator* proposes to censure a representative of the chamber, the rest of the magi must vote for one of the following verdicts: loss of vote for one year, for seven years, or permanently; the last usually leads to expulsion from the covenant later on. The *disceptator* is elected democratically every seven years, at the meetings of the inner chamber that coincide with the ordinary Tribunals.

In addition, and independently of the workings of the chamber, Duresca has the office of the *rector*: an independent counselor who may advise and influence the *disceptator* in private audiences. When the *rector* takes office, he must designate a successor without delay. This choice may be secret, recorded in a document attesting to it, or public, announced to the *disceptator*. Although the *rector* may give his opinion at meetings of the inner chamber, he has no vote.

After the Schism War, the Iberian Tribunal passed the ruling "On the Iberian Chamber" (1018), under which Duresca is obliged to host in its halls a meeting of the powers of the Tribunal every ten years (see page 89). This meeting discusses the course the Tribunal as a whole is taking, examining the individual actions of each covenant and the points of friction between them, in an effort to achieve harmonious coexistence at the ordinary Tribunals. It also analyzes the situation of Iberia with respect to the Order and the mundane powers, in many cases setting out the measures needed for their approval at the ordinary Tribunals.

Any Guernicus who wishes to join Duresca would do well to bear in mind that the covenant follows the conservative school of interpretation of the Code, and that any deviation from its policy will lead to rejection. If these requirements are met, the applicant must pass a difficult three-day theoretical examination and then carry out some kind of work for the covenant. For the other Houses entry is even harder: only those with good connections, or whose fame and reputation precede them, may join.

As for its *custodes*, Duresca has an armed corps organized as follows:

- **New Guard.** The magi's shield grogs. These elite soldiers have access to horses, and within the covenant they cover their clothing with a white tabard. When they accompany their magi, they usually adopt clothing better suited to the purpose of their expeditions.
- **Covenant Guard.** Responsible for protecting the mundane area of Duresca. When on duty, they are required to wear dark blue tabards with the covenant's coat of arms embroidered in white thread on the chest.
- **Guard of the *Sancta*.** They are charged with protecting the magi's precinct of the covenant. Members of this corps must wear at all times a white tabard with a black circle embroidered on the chest. Many of these soldiers have Second Sight or some other kind of supernatural ability.

#### The Magi of Duresca

*These libertines are the ones who oppress the world with their injustices! May the curse of God, of the angels and of all men fall upon them!*[^p130-8]

[^p130-8]: Excerpt from *The Epistle of Holiness* by Ibn ʿArabī (Spanish translation by Miguel Asín Palacios).

There are two factions of magi in Duresca: those who support the *disceptator* and those who do not (although one magus seems to belong to neither). The first group makes up the majority, and the second has the talent the covenant needs to keep running normally. Fortún, Legiferi, Lía, Mal Anda, Fróila, Sepsis, Catena and Pedro Gutiérrez belong to the first group, and Jayrān, Bilanx and Rayya to the second. The odd one out is Indicium, a solitary, withdrawn man who seldom takes part in the social life of Duresca and supports one faction or the other as it suits him. To his misfortune, this has earned him the rejection of both groups.

For clarity, the magi are described below in that order.

##### Disceptator Fortún of Guernicus

Born to a Leonese noble family, Fortún was unanimously elected *disceptator* at the spring meeting of Duresca's inner chamber in 1187, inheriting the post from his colleague Jayrān. The then-young Fortún, a specialist in the Schism War rulings of the Peripheral Code, had already proven his talent at Magvillus, where he was apprenticed to the former Primus of the House, Arliandus. A passionate orator, Fortún could cite more than five hundred rulings from the Peripheral Codes of the various Tribunals of Mythic Europe and, as a conservative judge, he stood out among his peers and earned the respect of his *sodales* at Duresca.

Like many others at Duresca, Fortún took a liking to chess and to consuming poppy latex (see insert on page 134) within a few years of becoming *disceptator*. Unlike the rest, however, Fortún cannot go a single day without it: his addiction kept him from attending the meeting of the Iberian Chamber in 1210 and the ordinary Tribunals of 1207 and 1214, and he may well miss the 1220 and 1221 meetings of both bodies too.

>**Appearance:** Once brilliant, Fortún is now consumed by his addiction to the poppy, and although his position gives him access to the best longevity rituals, the drug has taken its toll in recent years, eroding his reason to the point of making him babble (Fortún makes one Aging roll per season because of his addiction).
