Always clean-shaven and perfumed with ambergris, the decay he suffers has forced its way through the false pretense of his finery. His sparse, snow-white hair reveals a sweaty scalp that gleams under the lights of Duresca's luxurious halls. His skeletal limbs usually hang lifeless at his sides while the drug feeds on his body. Fortún is the very image of decadence, a sight that moves to pity those who once held him in esteem.

<!-- p. 132 -->

Although some in the inner chamber have tried to remove him from office, until 1218 Fortún enjoyed the backing of his *parens* Arliandus, and those who challenged his authority ended up posted to some other covenant in Europe, generally against their will. In 1218, however, Arliandus met his Final Twilight, and since then the leadership of the House has been held by the archmage Bilera.

In 1220, Fortún neglects his duties and uses his office to squander part of the vis allotted to Duresca as a dedicated covenant on obtaining the drug to which he is addicted. In recent years his Longevity Ritual has failed several times and he has suffered marked physical decline. Even so, he defends his position and is intransigent toward anyone who disagrees with him. He is not yet aware that the support he relied on has vanished, and some of Duresca's magi have begun to challenge him and to mock his incoherence at meetings of the inner chamber.

Fortún is usually to be found in Duresca's high halls, lounging on cushions and silk carpets from Malaga, always beside his faithful servant, the Nubian slave Tienossi. He is also usually in the company of one or another member of his clique (Legiferi spends the most time with him), whether playing a game of chess, sharing some sumptuous meal, or consuming poppy latex.

##### Rector Legiferi of Guernicus

*A bad secretary is a foolish old man who turns up with his brains gone to liquid and breath so foul it seems a rat has died in his nostrils.*[^p132-9]

[^p132-9]: Poem from *The Treatise of Familiar Spirits and Demons* by Ibn Shuhayd (Spanish translation by Salvador Barberá).

Legiferi is Fortún's right-hand man and has never been a notable judge (something his *parens* always knew). Trained at Duresca by the aged Jayrān of Jaén, he saw his chance to get ahead in the covenant when Fortún arrived from Magvillus. And so he did. Through his intrigues and pressure, in 1215 he induced the former *rector* (a fierce opponent of Fortún named Chris of Guernicus) to resign her post in his favor, leave the covenant and depart the Tribunal. He was also responsible for Fortún's addiction to the white poppy, thanks to which he can spend a great deal of time with him. In their small, impassioned committees they "solve" the problems of Duresca, the Tribunal and the Order, and they always do so while drinking, playing chess and consuming poppy latex.

To those close to the *disceptator*, Legiferi is nothing but an unscrupulous opportunist. To Fortún, however, he is a trusted man and his chief adviser (not for nothing is he Duresca's *rector*). For their part, those who oppose the *disceptator* want to see Legiferi stripped of his post, and are waiting for the chance to depose him. To defend himself against them, Legiferi has all but persuaded Fortún to have the inner chamber censure them, which could cost them their votes indefinitely and end in their expulsion from the covenant, as the charter stipulates.

##### Lía al-Gernikiyya

The Jewish convert Lía al-Gernikiyya was trained at Dār Malīḥaʾ, where she already showed signs of her great ambition. Eight years after her Gauntlet she met Jayrān in secret to seek entry to Duresca. Lía passed the entrance examinations and Duresca granted her one of its coveted seats. Since then she has made her way among her *sodales*, though, unlike Legiferi, she has done so with subtlety.

An occasional consumer of poppy latex, Lía has used her excellent social skills to win the *disceptator*'s trust and so gain confidential information about Duresca and Magvillus. Her influence was such that in 1207 and 1214 she managed to be elected presiding Quaesitor and was able to take a seat in the lower chamber of Magvillus, a seat she still holds in 1220. Arliandus's Final Twilight, however, stopped her career dead: Lía's admission to Magvillus had been approved for 1219 (and with it a seat in the upper chamber), and with Bilera's arrival her application was canceled. In two years she has had no further word from the *domus magna*, and Lía is waiting expectantly. The silence from Magvillus seems to herald coming changes, so if Bilera were to withdraw her confidence from Fortún, Lía would prosecute him for his many crimes of corruption and hand him over to justice; if not, she would take advantage of the *disceptator*'s loss of power to leapfrog him in the chain of command and so negotiate her promotion with Bilera at the next meeting of the lower chamber.

Lía knows that the Trianomae of Durato, Nazhūn, does not approve of her methods, but she also knows that Nazhūn cannot afford to see Duresca discredited, so she will keep working with her to achieve her goals and thus draw closer to Magvillus.

##### Mal Anda of Guernicus

The Castilian Mal Anda was already a veteran when Lía arrived at the covenant. A dreadful politician and a mediocre magus, he has witnessed countless intrigues over his lifetime and has always managed to end up among the winners without taking sides. Now that Fortún seems on the verge of falling from grace, he will not hesitate to change sides if doing so brings him greater benefits.

Mal Anda was a regular at the *disceptator*'s revels and, like him, addicted to the poppy. Since 1218, however, he has been seen far less in his company, something the *rector*, Legiferi, has noticed. Mal Anda is a survivor and a good judge of men; he knows that Legiferi will soon ask him for some proof of loyalty to Fortún, but he senses that Fortún's road has come to an end. He will move ambiguously between the two factions until one proves victorious, just as he always has.

##### Fróila of Mercere (Redcap)

The Redcap Fróila arrived at Duresca barely four years ago to replace his uncle, who had grown too old to keep working at the covenant. Trained at Aedes Saturni, the young man has been dazzled by Duresca's wealth and Fortún's charisma. The *disceptator*'s closeness and the trust he has shown in him have led Fróila to devote himself entirely to the tasks Fortún gives him, and even to hold him in high regard. In 1220 he is a regular companion at play, and when he is at the covenant he is seldom seen doing anything but playing chess with the *disceptator*.

<!-- p. 133 -->

Those who do not know Fróila might think him another Legiferi, but that is not really so. The young man's only failings have been his naivety and his eagerness to work; Fróila is just a boy seduced by power.

##### Archmage Sepsis of Tytalus

Sepsis "the Dreaded," as she is known in the Tribunal, also holds the office of hoplite. The Tytalus maga lost her speech to leprosy (see insert on page 45), and she goes about wrapped in a shroud blackened by stains of sweat, dust and blood accumulated over the years.

Sepsis is Duresca's armed fist, and many consider her cruel and wicked. The magi of the Tribunal say that her mere presence has prevented many Hermetic crimes, and that more than one person has vomited as the maga passed by.

Sepsis is a calculating maga who enjoys the comforts Duresca provides her. Her support for Fortún is unconditional, at least as long as she can go on living such a life. She would certainly not give up her seat in the inner chamber for anything, although she would be willing to risk it to teach a lesson to the magi of al-Andalus, whom she hates above all things.

##### Catena of Verditius

Catena is a brilliant smith and a fine ivory carver. Her mistress, Faŷrun al-Verditiyya, initiated her into the Mysteries of House Verditius at what was then her covenant, Aẓm Alfíl, which Catena left before Faŷrun was murdered.

Catena has not stopped working since she arrived at Duresca. She has crafted all manner of devices for her *sodales*, and much of the covenant's magical defenses bear her mark. Thanks to her dedication, Catena enjoys a generous allowance of vis which, unlike her peers, she manages carefully so as to be able to carry out all her contrivances. Although she knows of Fortún's vices, she cannot forget the favors he has done her, and at Duresca she enjoys such abundant resources that her works can rival the crafts of Ajabeba. That is why Catena has always avoided the covenant's intrigues by taking refuge in her workshop, where she dreams of winning the competition held every eighteen years at Verdi (see *Houses of Hermes: Mystery Cults*, page 199).

Catena is an arrogant and proud maga, and it was precisely this that led her apprentice, Asur González, to leave Duresca and join Ajabeba.

Of all the magi of Duresca, Catena is the one who has shown the most interest in investigating the portal that has come to light beneath the council chamber.

##### Pedro Gutiérrez of Tremere

Pedro is an experienced Tremere magus who answers directly to Medea of Victrix, the House's Exarch for the Iberian and Provençal Tribunals. Pedro is charged with overseeing northern Iberia and reporting relevant events to his superior. He is also chiefly responsible for securing the pilgrims' hospitals that Duresca controls, and is on good terms with the primate of Toledo and the bishop of Compostela. Among his many other duties, he unravels the Tribunal conspiracies born at Duresca (thanks to his seat in the Iberian Chamber), and he has the authority to make decisions that have at times come to affect the whole Tribunal.

<!-- p. 135 -->

The elderly Tremere does not hold with the *disceptator*'s dissolute life, and has so far stayed at his side to keep his own privileges. Naturally, if Fortún lost his power, Pedro would not be the only one to abandon him. Needless to say, Pedro has never tried the poppy, although he is a great lover of chess.

Pedro is a good friend of Nazhūn, the Spring Tenens of the covenant of Durato, and trusts her as much as he trusts his superior, for he understands that their interests go hand in hand.

##### Jayrān al-Gernikī

Jayrān al-Gernikī is an aged magus who could have been elected Praeco were it not that he does not wish to give up his title of Quaesitor. Like all the Andalusi judges, he was trained at Dār Malīḥaʾ, but his vision of the Order led him to argue with his mistress on many occasions and, perhaps driven by the animal spirit of his youth, he left al-Andalus to seek his fortune in the north of the Peninsula. Although he tried to found a covenant, he lacked the initiative to do so (in truth he was afraid of failing) and ended up working at various covenants in northern Iberia until he was accepted at Duresca.

The old Diedne covenant has allowed him to pursue a brilliant career as a judge; not for nothing was he elected presiding Quaesitor at the Tribunals of 1137, 1158 and 1193, at which he led an active political life and showed great good sense in his judgments, even in the eyes of his colleagues in the south of Iberia. However, when Fortún was posted to Duresca, Jayrān had several arguments with him and, after a particularly violent encounter in which he insulted the *disceptator*, he was reprimanded by Magvillus, which made a deep impression on the veteran judge. Since then Jayrān has not been elected presiding Quaesitor again, and he has sunk into a despondency from which he has not yet recovered.

In 1220, Jayrān is now too old (which would not be a problem were it not that he truly feels old), and he has stepped aside so that his *filia* Bilanx can take the lead in the covenant's internal affairs. Lately, Jayrān spends much of his time reflecting on his life, and his thoughts are always filled with memories of his childhood at Dār Malīḥaʾ, where he spent the happiest days of his life.

Jayrān is a laconic, taciturn man, wholly different from the man he was in his youth and prime. At times he brightens at the memory of the smiles and embraces of his mistress, whom he misses deeply, and it is only now, in his last days, that he is beginning to come to terms with the grave mistakes he has made over the course of his life.

##### Bilanx al-Gernikiyya

Bilanx was trained at Duresca by the eminent conservative judge Jayrān. Her relative youth and having grown up surrounded by every comfort have made her a judge indifferent to anything that has nothing to do with Hermetic law. She is also an overbearing woman with complete confidence in her own abilities, who considers herself better prepared, more brilliant and more capable than the rest of the Tribunal's judges. Jayrān has at times rebuked her for her attitude, but Bilanx rarely listens: she does not understand the fears of her former master, whom she regards as a weak person.

Bilanx is the foremost critic of Fortún's corrupt regime, which she attacks harshly and always openly. Her defiant attitude has been a nuisance to almost everyone in the covenant (except perhaps her *amica*, Rayya), and, although she does not know it, in 1211 she came close to being expelled from it (which was prevented by her *parens*).

<!-- p. 136 -->

Since Bilera's arrival, Bilanx has begun to lash out more forcefully against Fortún and Legiferi, which is starting to discomfit the silent Sepsis, so that the archmage will probably end up declaring Wizard's War on her.

##### Rayya of Mercere (Redcap)

Rayya was born in Valencia shortly before the Almohads conquered the south of the Peninsula. Her father (a follower of Mercere) died in one of the raids (*algaras*) of Ibn Mardanīš, and her mother sold her to the Mercere of Aedes Saturni to keep her from being handed over to the Almohads as a slave. Since then, Rayya has traveled all over Iberia and sometimes even all over Europe. But she is now too old to keep traveling, and finds comfort only with her *amica* Bilanx, the only person who makes her forget her addiction to poppy latex, to which she became attached when young at one of the lavish banquets Duresca customarily holds during the meetings of the Iberian Chamber.

Rayya has been at Duresca for more than thirty years and considers that far too long. The elderly Redcap tries to spend as little time as possible at the covenant and, when she cannot avoid it, spends her days and nights with Bilanx. Although she has requested a transfer several times, Aedes Saturni has never granted it. The Mercer House needs someone it trusts at Duresca to keep it informed of what goes on there and, although they had thought Fróila might replace her, the young man has not proved trustworthy.

##### Indicium al-Gernikī

Indicium is a silent, solitary man whose past no one knows. Because of his dark complexion almost everyone assumes he comes from the lands of the *bilad al-Sūdān*; perhaps he was sold as a slave to some magus, or perhaps he came to the Peninsula with the Almoravids — who knows? To reinforce his enigmatic image, he always wears a veil (*liṯām* in Arabic) that covers his face in the Almoravid fashion and reveals only a pair of deep green eyes that contrast with his dark skin.

Indicium is a great expert in Hermetic law: no one has ever managed to refute him in a single case, and he is utterly incorruptible. Some suggest he might be a Perfect, which, together with his exquisite education, arouses all manner of hatred and envy.

> #### Story Seeds: The White Poppy
>
> *There are many kinds of poppy, and all of them are cold and moist. The white is so in the third degree and the black in the fourth. The white […] is useful against coughs caused by hot humors, strengthens the lung that has been eroded by this humoral mixture, and induces sleep. The black is harmful, [for it is] a narcotic that produces lethargy.*[^p135-V]
>
> Duresca's trading relationship with the Andalusi covenant of Jušjášun will soon be a hundred years old. Back then, the magi of Jušjášun paid the Iberian tax with the only source they had: some white poppies from which a few pawns of Mentem vis could be extracted.
>
> When, some time later, those poppies found their way to Duresca by chance, one of its magi used them to brew an infusion to soothe his lung ailment, since the same flowers in their mundane form had proved ineffective. To his surprise, their effects cured him and plunged him into an extremely pleasurable ecstasy. In this way the magus grew fond of them and began to consume them purely for pleasure. So, when his supplies ran out, he traced their origin to the covenant of Jušjášun, with which Duresca signed a seven-year trade agreement shortly afterward. When that time had passed, even though Jušjášun doubled the price of the poppies, the agreement was renewed for fourteen more years, and when the deal expired again, Jušjášun tripled its price and Duresca paid it — though not without consequences: the Asturian covenant did away with the magi of Jušjášun and sent a Bonisagus to take possession of the covenant and research the poppy plantation. Thus, when the magus finally managed to double its yield, Duresca granted Jušjášun the status of dedicated covenant for its work in Hermetic research (see page 238 for more information).
>
> Against this background, when the player characters' magi come across the *disceptator*, Fortún of Guernicus, wandering near their covenant, they know at once that his presence is going to bring them trouble. Fortún is staggering, his pupils are fully dilated, he keeps stopping to vomit, and the skirts of what was once a spotless brocade robe are soiled with his own excrement. To complicate the encounter further, the Quaesitor believes that Bilera is pursuing him.
>
> On recognizing the magi, he babbles a demand that they give him shelter in their covenant. Of course, the characters may refuse or take him in, although neither alternative seems very good. If they leave him outside, who knows where he might end up? In his state he is utterly incapable of casting magic. On the other hand, if they take him in, they will have to try to control his withdrawal and endure his pleas for a white poppy capsule. In any case, if he recovers, Fortún will remember the episode with humiliation, and if there is one thing Fortún will not tolerate, it is being laughed at.
>
> [^p135-V]: Excerpt from *The Book of the Generalities of Medicine* by Averroes (Spanish translation by V. de Benito and A. Morales).

### Mons Vindius

>**Lifespan:** 822–1016<br>
>**Founders:** Froiluba of Diedne, Theudechild of Diedne<br>
>**Aura (type and strength):** Divine, strength 1 (before the Schism War, Magic, strength 7)<br>
>**Reputations:** Diedne (Hermetic) 2

Under the Peripheral Code ruling "On the Diedne Legacy" (1025), all information relating to this House in the Peninsula was destroyed or archived at the covenant of Duresca. That is why the location of what was once the Diedne's defensive stronghold during the Schism War has fallen into oblivion: its ruins have stood silent and empty for almost two centuries, and any attempt to locate them is a violation of the Peripheral Code — so who would dare to look for them?

#### History

Mons Vindius was the heir of Diedne Duresca. When Tancoystl joined the Ordo Miscellanea, the Diedne of Iberian tradition (former tempestarii and vates) joined it with her. Two of the covenant's old druids, however, left to avoid being expelled. They spent some years wandering the north of the Peninsula in search of a site on which to raise their new home, and on their travels they met a Frankish druid named Theudechild, who had arrived fleeing the laws of the *Capitularia Regum Francorum*. The woman told them she had been captured in Lyon on the orders of Bishop Agobard, and had received 200 lashes and a brand on her forehead. According to her account, druids were being persecuted in France. Moved by her story, the two magi took her in and founded Mons Vindius with her.

The magi raised their covenant by magic beside a lake of glacial origin linked to many bodies of water scattered throughout Mythic Europe (see *Realms of Power: Magic*, page 137), with several nodes in the Peninsula (such as those near the covenants of Nebula and Ipagrum, also Diedne). Their covenant was constituted at the Rhine Tribunal of 822, at the same time as the Norman Bibracte and the Germanic Sirmium.

From the start, the Diedne of Mons Vindius lived discreetly, apart from the Order on their snowy peaks (though always in contact with the other members of their House), and when Ramiro I of Asturias ordered all wizards burned in 845, its magi gave shelter to some *sodales* of their House and pointed them to several places where there were other lakes with the same properties as theirs. Thanks to its isolation, the Asturian burnings never reached its halls.

Mons Vindius was not always inhabited solely by Diedne; its *sancta* housed everyone from Flambeau to Merinitae, and although as a covenant it always kept its distance, it never missed a Tribunal nor refused to cooperate with its *sodales*. But none of that could prevent what was to happen at the ordinary Tribunal of 996. With tensions between the Tremere and the Diedne at their height, the Praeco Ibn Sahl al-Tremerī of Tremébriga silenced the *ductor* of Mons Vindius, Tridio of Diedne, and expelled him from the meeting. The magus, however, refused to leave the hall, and the pent-up violence between the two covenants exploded. Tremébriga attacked the magi of Mons Vindius on neutral ground and the Diedne fled in terror. In his frenzy, Ibn Sahl pursued them as far as the Picos de Europa, where only the bad weather could save them. The Tremere then began systematically attacking the strongholds of Iberia, and Tridio contacted the other covenants of Europe and confirmed that it was happening everywhere: House Tremere wanted to wipe them out.

When the Order expelled House Diedne in 1011, Tridio summoned all the Diedne of the Tribunal to Mons Vindius and sought support among the covenants with which he had been on good terms. Brigantia offered to fight at their side, and Laminium offered them refuge in al-Andalus. The rest of the magi, however, who only a few years before had been drinking with them, turned their backs on them. And so the Diedne, together with the Flambeau of Brigantia, attacked the powerful covenants in the north of the Tribunal. As a result, Tertia, Salionca and Duresca saw their *Aegis* breached, their vis sources ravaged and their libraries burned. They saved their fury for Tremébriga, however: the headquarters of the Tremere in the Peninsula was razed and all its inhabitants killed. As they fled, the Diedne sowed salt on its foundations.

<!-- p. 137 -->

When it seemed the Diedne were going to win the war, the Order performed the ritual of *The Curse of Thoth*, and the tables turned. Tridio lost the Flambeau of Brigantia after the Concord of Fire, and the magi of the Order began to gain ground: the defenses of Mons Vindius fell in 1016, and only two Diedne managed to escape through Lake Enol to Nebula, and from there to the Glaslin at Stonehenge. There the only two surviving Diedne of Iberia continued the fight alongside their Primus, Llewelyn.

Mons Vindius fell in 1016. Tridio was tortured and killed, and his body thrown into the sea.

#### Setting and Physical Description

The ruins of Mons Vindius are nothing but rubble beside the lakes of Enol and Ercina. After the assault of 1016, the Order meticulously destroyed the buildings that made up the old Diedne covenant. Unlike Nebula, of which some remains were left, Mons Vindius was torn up by its foundations and wiped from the face of the earth; Lakes Enol and Ercina were evaporated and their magical connections destroyed. Moreover, to prevent those connections from forming again, the magi of the Order cast a consecrated image of the Virgin, together with a relic, to the bottom of the lake (the lakes filled with water again over the years), so that in 1220 the surroundings of the former Mons Vindius have a Divine aura of strength 1.

> #### Story Seeds: The Treasure of Mons Vindius
>
> Despite the Order's efforts, a small part of Mons Vindius was saved from the burning: when the Order expelled House Diedne, Tridio ordered two of his grogs to find a safe place in which to hide the covenant's secrets. The pair spent seven days searching for the right spot, until they settled on one of the limestone caves in the gorges that surround the peak of Torre Cerredo.
>
> To keep the treasure safe, Tridio removed all its Arcane Connections, handed the treasure to the grogs so that they could hide it without his knowing where, and on their return killed them, burned their bodies and destroyed their ghosts so that they could not be questioned. Thus, when the Order's attackers tortured Tridio, they obtained this information, but could not find the treasure's hiding place.
>
> Although during the first years after the Schism the Picos de Europa were combed in search of the hidden treasure, time and the destruction (perhaps by mistake) of the documents recording these events during the purge of 1025 consigned its existence to oblivion. Perhaps the time has come for it to see the light again. What would happen if the player characters found it? How could they justify possessing it while avoiding any association with the ruins of Mons Vindius?
>

## El Bierzo

The small regional unit of the Bierzo is bounded on the west by Galicia, on the north by Asturias, on the east by Leon and on the south by the kingdom of Portugal. Crossed from north to south by the Cantabrian Mountains, the Bierzo is a mountainous region with many watercourses, among them the Sil. In antiquity the Romans mined the gold of the Bierzo (poor deposits, in fact), which shaped the landscape in a distinctive way and put an end to the region's auriferous vis sources — to the magi's misfortune, since in their day they must have been important.

In the Bierzo are found the town councils (*concejos*) of Ponferrada, Villafranca, Bembibre, Molinaseca and Puebla, among others. The Bierzo has traditionally sheltered magi of Merinita, Bjornaer and Ex Miscellanea affiliation, all of them residents of Mare Iacum.

> #### Story Seeds: Lake Carucedo
>
> In the region of the Bierzo, where a village once stood, lies Lake Carucedo. The local people say that Charlemagne destroyed the village and drowned its ruins, cursing the inhabitants. Although the old folk say that Roland's sword, the one known as Durandarte, lies in its dark waters, the Verditius deny the story, for they say it is held by the magi of the Confraternity of Roland (see *Houses of Hermes: Mystery Cults*, page 206).
>
> The magi of Iberia have observed that roughly once a century an expedition is announced to explore (and plunder) the depths of Lake Carucedo, and everyone knows how it ends: no one returns from those waters. What secrets do the waters of the lake hold? Who or what rings the bells whose sound rises from those waters every year on Saint John's Eve?
>

### Mare Iacum

>**Lifespan:** 906–Present<br>
>**Founders:** Gizosto Bjornaer, Fronilde Bjornaer<br>
>**Season:** Spring<br>
>**Aura (type and strength):** Faerie, strength 3<br>
>**Reputations:** Poor (Iberian Tribunal) 3<br>
>**Votes:** 5

The ancient covenant of Mare Iacum has undergone profound transformations over time. Founded by two followers of Bjornaer during the second Iberian Tribunal, it came to be occupied by Ex Miscellanea when it had to change location and, later still, by the followers of Quendalon.

#### History

After its foundation, Mare Iacum lived in peace for almost a decade, until the Mozarabic monks of San Cebrián de Mazote (Valladolid) came to the lake to exploit its trout and its lands. What had been a tranquil region began to fill with clergy, and the vis sources dwindled one by one as the Dominion advanced. The members of Mare Iacum then debated the covenant's future: drive out the mundanes, or leave for other lands. However, since the threat of the *saḥirs* was still very much present, only Fronilde's supporters dared to set off southward, where they founded the covenant of Salama. Although not all of those who stayed at Mare Iacum agreed to attacking the mundanes, the covenant's eldest magi went out one autumn night in 917 and massacred the monks of the lake.

Far from driving the canons away, this deed brought down on Mare Iacum both an attack by the mundanes and the condemnation of the Order. Those who took part in the attack were expelled at the Tribunal of 920; those who did not went west, beyond the crest of the mountain that sheltered the valley of their former covenant, where the Dominion did not reach and the land was drier and more inhospitable, for they no longer had a forest to protect them. Although the Tribunal advised them to move farther away to escape the advance of the Dominion, the members of Mare Iacum disregarded its advice and raised their covenant beside a small lake a little over half a day's journey from the monastery of San Martín de Castañeda.

Time proved them right. The inaccessibility of the area has shielded Mare Iacum from the advance of the Dominion, and today it enjoys a weak faerie aura and a small community of faeries that the covenant's Merinitae take care of. Its old magical resources, however, have gradually been stifled by the advance of the mundane world, which, together with the indifference of its inhabitants, has meant that ever since Fronilde's heirs departed the covenant has lived in a perpetual Spring with which its inhabitants do not seem displeased.

#### Setting and Physical Description

Mare Iacum changed location in 922 and moved to a lake some five hundred meters across at its widest and two hundred at its narrowest. The covenant has only two buildings, which still have parts made of wood despite their almost three centuries of existence. Today Mare Iacum lies in the heart of the Sierra del Bierzo, one of the hardest stages of the Way of Saint James.

The ground floor of the magi's building is of stone and houses the covenant's only five *sancta*. On its upper floor (of wood, with unwhitewashed walls) are the meager library and the tiny council chamber. The building of the grogs and companions is somewhat smaller, though more luxurious: it is built of stone and has a roof of red tiles that is the pride of the covenant's inhabitants. The few Hermetic visitors who come to Mare Iacum are always surprised to discover that the grogs sleep in better beds than the magi.

#### Society and Customs

The magi of the Bierzo form a democracy that meets whenever some problem arises or when they feel the need to seek counsel, which tends to happen roughly every two years.

Mare Iacum is a poor covenant; its scant resources are obtained by its grogs, who work for the monastery that drove them from their lands and wager on games of chess. The magi know they would be lost without them, so eighty years ago they decided to improve the grogs' lives to keep them from leaving. To that end they granted full powers to their autocrat, Gudesteo, and they have not regretted it for a single day since. Gudesteo is a genius and a master of chess. Thanks to him, Mare Iacum is one of the favorite destinations of the Redcaps of Porta Pandere, where the Mercere have always sought to test themselves. Gudesteo has lost no more than a handful of games in his whole life, and every so often some unwary soul ends up wagering and losing against him, which has become the covenant's most important (though intermittent) source of income. Especially notable was the game he played fifty years ago against the head of the Mercer House of Porta Pandere, Parcus Minor. The Redcap arrived intending to humiliate him and wagered to defray all the covenant's Hermetic expenses in exchange for the autocrat's impressive chess set. Since then, Mare Iacum has not paid a single dīnār to the Tribunal.

Despite its age, Mare Iacum has always been a young covenant. With hardly any magical resources, the magi who grew up there spent only as much time as was strictly necessary before leaving for somewhere else, taking with them whatever little (or much) they had acquired. This has kept the covenant from prospering. Its lax charter permits this sort of behavior, and few magi who grew up at Mare Iacum have chosen to stay and watch the mundanes live better than they do (something too much to bear for the magi of the glorious Order of Hermes). Likewise, the few magi who have come to its gates have done so out of dire need and, once they have got back on their feet with the covenant's scant resources, have moved on.

<!-- p. 139 -->

In 1220, Gudesteo is an old man and, although the magi performed a Longevity Ritual for him, he is in the twilight of his life. The magi do not know how Porta Pandere will react when he is gone; they are trying by every means to have his son attain his father's mastery, though so far they have made little progress.

#### The Magi of Mare Iacum

##### Vieya of Merinita

When she was a girl, her mistress used to say she was like the *vieyas*, the ancient female numina who made the rainbow and set the air shimmering in summer. Vieya took her name from those days, for her sigil is tied to the primary colors.

Vieya is the eldest maga of Mare Iacum. At over ninety, she has lived through everything in the covenant she considers her home. Vieya still remembers the birth of Gudesteo, the autocrat; she helped at the delivery herself and still treats him as if he were her son.

Of all her mistress's apprentices, she was the only one who stayed at Mare Iacum and, as everyone else did, her *filii* also ended up leaving. Vieya does not mind; she is content to look after the small faerie community that lives in the streams and waterfalls that spill from the lake beside the covenant. Those who do not know the faeries think that Vieya must deal with gnomes or goblins or some other grotesque faerie of the night, for Vieya has *trasgu* blood and is small and wrinkled. Yet Vieya cares for beautiful, delicate faeries that the local people know as xanes (see the insert "*Agrestes foeminae*" on the next page).

Though at times she regrets having stayed at Mare Iacum, she shares those feelings with no one, for she knows that in the end everyone will leave and she will be left alone.

##### Ŷin-niy-yatun al-Merinitiyya

The young Ŷin-niy-yatun came from al-Andalus to study the xanes with Vieya; the covenant's council welcomed her and gave her the last free *sanctum* it had, asking nothing in return. During her stay, however, she has never quite grown used to the privations of Mare Iacum, and she means to learn all she can from the water faeries and get Vieya to teach her the Major Arcadian Mystery of Metamorphosis (see *Houses of Hermes: Mystery Cults*, page 161) before she leaves.

With every passing day Ŷin-niy-yatun finds Vieya's horrendous Latin accent and dreadful Arabic harder to bear. The smell of damp earth the old woman gives off disgusts her, and the little rituals she uses to protect herself and guard the covenant exasperate her. At the start of each day, the old woman checks that the boar's jawbone is on the covenant's small beehive and the laurel is still on the roof, makes sure the two milch cows still wear their seashells around their necks, asks about the chiastolite and the walnut with three seams she gave her two years ago (which, according to her, protect against witches, storms and the evil eye), and insists that she wear the *fascium* (a phallus-shaped amulet) for protection. To make matters worse, whenever she hears a dog howl or an owl hoot, or sees a crow fly on her right, Vieya foretells ill omens: "If only a moth would come into the house!" she then cries, as if that were a good thing. Ŷin-niy-yatun is tired of telling her to cast her Parma and renew the *Aegis*, because she cannot stand Vieya always giving the same answer: "Don't you want your friends to come into the house?"

<!-- p. 140 -->

Lately, Ŷin-niy-yatun has begun to think she made a mistake, for she has serious doubts about Vieya's magical abilities and no longer believes that the old woman knows (or ever knew) the Mystery of Metamorphosis.

##### Xanino Ex Miscellanea

Xanino was a changeling, born of a xane and one of the men of the monastery of San Martín de Castañeda. He was nursed by Vieya as a baby (since the xanes have no milk in their breasts), and from his faerie heritage he retains his hideous, hairy appearance and some exceptional abilities that his master was able to preserve when he initiated him into the Arts.

Although Vieya could have trained him, she handed him over to her *sodalis* Cresconio, who had helped her protect the child left by the faeries when his false mother discovered that her baby had been exchanged. Xanino was thus trained by a tempestarius and, like him, inherited his magical abilities (see page 299).

In 1220, he has just passed his Gauntlet and for the moment has no need (or prospect) of leaving the covenant. Of all the magi of Mare Iacum, Xanino is the youngest.

> #### Story Seeds: Agrestes Foeminae, Sylvaticae et Matres Campestres
>
> The xanes are faeries bound to rivers, and especially to waterfalls. They look like beautiful young women with long fair hair that they untangle with golden combs. Although they may dress in white, they usually go naked and, along with their comb, they often own golden hens and chicks and silver chalices, which they hide in riverbeds or in caves through which watercourses run.
>
> The xanes can leave the water for short periods, and they are customarily seen at night or on the morning of Saint John's Day in forest clearings, by waterfalls and in caves, where they like to pass the time dancing. Their treasures are always a lure for thieves and, when they are robbed, the xanes do what they can to recover their belongings. Usually, when the thief finds himself cornered, he hands the treasure over to the Church, for it is well known that the xanes abhor the name of God and the saints (which is why many small villages possess precious silver chalices they could never otherwise have obtained, as is the case with the parish of Santiago de Aguino, in southern Asturias).
>
> These faeries, associated with undines, have great knowledge of plants and use them to work enchantments, so it is not unusual to find them with aconite, opium poppy, wormwood, black poplar, angelica, celery, henbane, belladonna, sweet flag, hemp, hemlock, cinquefoil, ergot, foxglove, hellebore, thorn apple, nightshade, hound's-tongue, adder's-tongue, mandrake, fly agaric, bryony, parsley, white willow, yew or vervain, all of them herbs of virtue that can be enriched (see *Realms of Power: Magic* for some examples, page 154). In particular, they use *llanzuela* to heal the wounds of the men and women they love, and they fear rue, with which, so it is said, they can be disenchanted.
>
> The xanes of the streams and waterfalls of *mare iacum* (the lake beside which the first covenant of that name was founded) were decimated by the men who came with the monks who restored the monastery of San Martín de Castañeda. In 1220 they number fewer than a dozen, which worries the kindly old Vieya. The only way she can think of to stop men from wiping them out altogether is to finish the men off first, which she is not prepared to do under any circumstances. Vieya places little faith in Ŷin-niy-yatun's help, so if there were a Merinita among the player characters, she might ask them for help in saving the xanes' folk, though she will also warn them that neither the xanes nor Mare Iacum have much to offer in return.

> #### Story Seeds: Nabia and Ladico
>
> At some point in the history of Mare Iacum, one of its magae devoted herself to promoting among the people of the area the cult of Nabia (associated with fertility) and of the mighty Ladico (whom many liken to Jupiter), both of them magical beings who achieved their faerie apotheosis in ancient times. For her mission, this maga raised a small temple a little over a kilometer upstream along the Navea river, now in ruins. No one tends it any longer, and the few offerings the locals leave in the dead of night (lit candles, dead cockerels and mice) are not even addressed to Nabia and Ladico, for their names have been forgotten.
>
> Somehow (perhaps they discover these ruins on some expedition, or hear of them at some Tribunal or chess tournament), the player characters learn that there is an old temple near the ruins of Nemetobriga (the ancient capital of the Tibures tribe, *tiburi* in Latin). No one knows to whom it is dedicated, nor whether it was raised by a Hermetic magus. Perhaps they can discover to whom the altar was dedicated and learn the names of the ancient divinities, who, if the characters helped them return to the world, would shower them with gifts, though always in exchange for labors.

<!-- p. 141 -->

##### Cresconio Ex Miscellanea

Cresconio is the second-oldest magus of Mare Iacum and, although he is roughly half Vieya's age, he is considered an old magus by the covenant's standards. He is a tall, heavily built man, so tall that he looks like a *patarico*. His appearance is imposing, and he always wears his long beard knotted with a cord, which in the language of war signifies a bellicose and defiant attitude. At the few Tribunals he has attended, his beard has been mocked by some Flambeau, Jerbiton and Tremere. The jokes stopped, however, when Cresconio declared Wizard's War on an eminent and well-known Tremere of the Aragonese covenant of Victrix and ended up killing him within the first seven days. Since then no one has dared mock him again, and many have come to regard him as a threat.

##### Eva Ex Miscellanea

The maga known as Eva arrived a few years before Ŷin-niy-yatun: wounded, her eyes and tongue torn out, and with no memory of her past. Vieya took her in and named her Eva (for to the old maga there is nothing more dangerous than having no name), and from her robes and manners deduced that she was a *saḥira*.

Vieya and Cresconio took her to the Tribunal of 1214 to see whether anyone recognized her, but no one seemed ever to have seen her, so they began to think she might be a sorceress of the Order of Suleimān. To keep anyone from harming her, they begged Indicium al-Gernikī to register her at the Tribunal. In this way the young woman became part of the covenant. For her part, Eva spends the summer in the sun and the winter beside the fireplace of her *sanctum*. In the more than seven years she has been at the covenant, she has shown no interest in anything beyond what is needed to go on surviving.

## Leon

The extensive regional unit of Leon contains the populous city and royal seat that gives it its name, a city resettled in the mid-ninth century by the king of Asturias, Ordoño I, which grew in size and importance thanks to the Way of Saint James, along which came many merchants.

Leon is bounded on the north by Asturias, on the west by the Bierzo and the kingdom of Portugal, on the east by the kingdom of Castile, and on the south by the regional unit of the Extremadura. North of Leon, the land leaves the system of the Cantabrian Mountains and enters fully into the central plateau of the Peninsula, crossed from north to south by great rivers that flow into the Duero, the old frontier of the Andalusi realm.

In Leon are found the town councils (*concejos*) of Leon, Rueda, Mayorga, Mansilla, Benavente and Zamora, among many others. Because of its many mundane settlements and its scant magical resources, it has traditionally been a region unoccupied from the Hermetic point of view. Since 1215, however, it has been home to Septima Gemina, a covenant not yet legally constituted.

### Septima Gemina

>**Lifespan:** Not yet constituted<br>
>**Founders:** Miro Ponce de Cabrera Ierbitonis, Toda of Mercere (Redcap), Gonçalvo of Tytalus<br>
>**Season:** Spring<br>
>**Aura (type and strength):** Magic, strength 1<br>
>**Reputations:** None<br>
>**Votes:** 4

Septima Gemina is the youngest covenant in the Tribunal, and it has not even been legally constituted (its members hope to do so at the next ordinary Tribunal, in 1221).

#### History

Three of the members of Septima Gemina grew up in the Tribunal and, since their *parentes* were like-minded, they have been in fairly close contact with one another. So when they became magi in 1214, they decided to start a project together in the manor house of the wealthiest of them, Miro Ponce de Cabrera, near the city of Leon.

The *amici* went to Miro's house at the end of that same summer, and with them they took in two young magi exiled from al-Andalus who had nowhere else to go. Their host welcomed them, and together they chose the covenant's name: Septima Gemina, in honor of the Roman *legio VII gemina*, which had its base in the city of Leon during the fall of the empire. To celebrate, the five magi opened the bottles of Toledan wine in the manor's cellars, toasted, recited poetry, drank, played chess, sang, practiced archery, rode horses across the estate's grounds, went hunting, consumed white poppy, drew up the covenant's charter, danced, cast their spells on the dogs and servants of the manor, and swore one another eternal loyalty. Miro decreed that, after fifteen years devoted to magic and its study, it was time to take a sabbatical year. Everyone applauded, and the celebrations went on… for five more years.

In 1220, the two magi who came from al-Andalus are on the point of leaving, weary of the untimely noise, the disorder of the common rooms and the debauchery of their companions. They are so ashamed that they cannot bear to imagine their imminent reunion with their *parentes*. It is not that they lack for anything — Miro is a generous host (he regularly pays all the costs the covenant incurs and maintains all the laboratories) — but they cannot stop thinking about what will happen when the magi of the Order learn what goes on at Septima Gemina. The other three, however, do not seem worried, and have proposed not attending the Tribunal so as to avoid the problem; after all, no Redcap who is not trustworthy will come as long as their charter has not been ratified. And so, one after another, the days pass in this fashion at Septima Gemina.

One of the main problems Septima Gemina will face is its proximity to Duresca. The venerable covenant will not allow them to settle so close to it, and although this reason might be enough to bring them closer to Beit Midrash, the relationship between Raḥûm and Gonçalvo (see the magi below) will not allow it, at least not on friendly terms.

<!-- p. 142 -->

#### Setting and Physical Description

Miro's manor house lies north of the city of Leon, beside the groves on the alluvial terraces of the Torío river. The nearby woods belong to the estate, and deer and the occasional boar can be found there. Taking advantage of this hunting preserve, the magi organize hunts during the summer to test their magical abilities. Sheltered by the gentle slope, they do not suffer the rigors of winter so badly, although to the magi from the south it is still a cold, damp, mosquito-ridden place.

#### Society and Customs

According to the covenant's not-yet-ratified charter, Septima Gemina is a democracy that preserves the freedom of its members; that is, each has the right to express their opinion and to vote freely at any council without regard for anything or anyone. In practice, Septima Gemina has no governing body at all and is adrift: three-fifths of its members have no interest in any Hermetic protocol, and the rest try to get all the members to meet (sober) at least once a year… although sometimes they cannot even manage that.

As for non-Hermetic life, Septima Gemina makes use of the winters to gather in its halls to recite poetry and play chess, always accompanied by opium poppy and a good Toledan wine. Springs are usually given over to study and summers to hunting. In autumn the magi of Septima Gemina usually study, although if the summer has not been very abundant in antlers, they prefer to don their weapons and go out on the roads for sport, robbing merchants or protecting them from bandits. It would not be the first time they have clashed with the knights of the Order of Santiago! Their meager magical abilities are enough for them to keep their identities secret and enjoy their games. To wash away his sins, Miro always hands the loot he wins in autumn to the prelate of Leon, with whom he has had a close relationship since childhood.

#### The Magi of Septima Gemina

All the members of Septima Gemina are more or less the same age. Miro Ponce de Cabrera Ierbitonis is a young nobleman, son of the *ricohombre* Ponce Vélaz, and keeps up close ties with his family, which will become very powerful in the future. Miro shares his yearly allowance with his companions without asking for anything in return; animals, servants, books, laboratory improvements… he hands it all over freely and with a smile. If there is one thing to be praised in Miro it is his generosity, although if he goes on without managing it, he will ruin himself within a few years. Unfortunately for Miro, the wars being waged in the south will eventually force him to march under the banner of the king of Leon, so when he is summoned he will marry Toda to exempt himself (in accordance with the royal decree in force in both Castile and Leon since 1109).

His companion, Toda of Mercere, is a Redcap raised at Aedes Saturni who spent more than five years of her training traveling through al-Andalus, which is where her love of song, chess and poetry comes from. Toda admires Miro and would not mind spending the rest of her life by his side at Septima Gemina (although she still knows nothing of Miro's wedding plans). Toda is perhaps the only maga who has not neglected her responsibilities, for she has never failed to carry a message in all her years as a member of the Order.

The third of the trio is Gonçalvo of Tytalus, a native of the north of the kingdom of Portugal. Like his companions, Gonçalvo has no intention of giving up his way of life, for he knows that it will shame his hated and renowned *parens*, Raḥûm of Beit Midrash. In his lucid moments he composes poems satirizing his reunion with his former master, in which he usually ends up literally dying of shame at the sight of him.

The two magi who joined Septima Gemina later do not see life as their three *sodales* do. Sara al-Criamoniyya is a delicate Cordoban who, on meeting Miro, was dazzled by his magnetic charisma. As the months passed, however, her admiration turned to love, then to bewilderment, then to anger and frustration and, finally, to disgust. Sara has tried to leave the covenant, but she does not even know how to go about it; she is lost in Leon, where she knows no one, and she is afraid to take to the roads alone. For four years now she has left her *sanctum* only to meet with Vaasco each season and to renew the *Aegis*. For all these reasons, Sara feels lonely and sad. Her companion, Vaasco al-Bonisagī, went through a period of excess at the covenant (perhaps more than he would care to admit) and in the early years let himself be carried along by his companions. As a result, he still cannot look Sara in the eye and, although there has been no carousing for three years now, he has been unable to stop consuming poppy latex, to which he has become addicted. Vaasco is the only one who tries to bring some order to life in the covenant although, unfortunately, his former companions in revelry do not take him seriously and keep tempting him to go out raiding with them one last time.

> #### Story Seeds: The Highwaymen
>
> *Though I won fame as a libertine, I am wretched save in my verses. Was I, perchance, the first lover ever set aflame by eyes and cheeks?*[^p142-VI]
>
> While the companions and grogs of the player characters' covenant are traveling the roads of the kingdom of Leon in autumn, they are ambushed by a group of three people clad in magical shrouds that trail a wake of grey smoke, and whose hoods reveal nothing but a black hollow. The sight of the three magi of Septima Gemina is chilling, but perhaps not so much for someone used to fighting side by side with an experienced magus. After the attack, the encounter can have three possible outcomes, with or without casualties on either side:
>
> - the magi of Septima Gemina defeat the player characters' retinue and carry off their belongings;
> - the magi of Septima Gemina are defeated and captured;
> - the magi of Septima Gemina are defeated and flee without taking the grogs' loot.
>
> The storyguide should weigh each of the possible outcomes, bearing in mind that if anyone is wounded or killed, matters will not be so simple for either side.
>
> [^p142-VI]: Poem from *The Treatise of Familiar Spirits and Demons* by Ibn Shuhayd (Spanish translation by Salvador Barberá).

<!-- p. 143 -->

## The Leonese Extremadura

The regional unit of the Leonese Extremadura is a narrow strip of land comprising the territories south of the Duero as far as the point where the mountains of the Sierra de Gredos begin to rise. The region is bounded on the north by Leon, on the west by the kingdom of Portugal, on the east by Castile and on the south by the regional unit of the Transierra. This region is heavily fortified, and not so much for protection against the governors of al-Andalus as because of the constant border wars between Leon and Portugal.

In the Extremadura are found the populous town councils of Salamanca, Castelo Rodrigo, Ciudad Rodrigo, Salvatierra, Monleón and Miranda, among others. Given its long history as a frontier between kingdoms, it has never been chosen by the magi of the Order as a place to settle. The only Hermetic settlement it has had (intermittently) has been a Mercer House, which today the magi use as an inn or tavern. This is Occelum Durii.

### Inn of Occelum Durii (Mercer House)

>**Lifespan:** 899–986; 1032–1158<br>
>**Founder:** Violante of Mercere (Redcap)<br>
>**Aura (type and strength):** Divine, strength 1<br>
>**Reputations:** Inn (Hermetic) 6

#### History

The Mercere took advantage of Alfonso III of Asturias's resettlement of Zamora with Toledan Mozarabs to found their second Mercer House at the crossroads of two Roman roads, for Aedes Saturni was beginning to be unable to cope with the correspondence between the covenants of the Peninsula. Zamora, however, did not prove a suitable location: in 901 the city was attacked by al-Mahdī; in 907 the covenant was razed by the *saḥirs*; and in 986 it was besieged, sacked and burned by Almanzor's troops. These last two assaults carried off several Redcaps, and many letters and resources were lost, which is why Mercere portals were never built there (although they were planned).

After Almanzor's sack, the Mercere abandoned the city until Porta Pandere took the side of the covenants of al-Andalus. Aedes Saturni then sent a Redcap to restore the ruins where Occelum Durii had stood. The covenant served the Iberian Tribunal until the annexation of al-Andalus, when it came under Porta Pandere. For safety's sake, however, it was decided that the Mercer House should keep no important documents or riches, since there was no magus to protect it. It was thus used as a subsidiary house until 1158, when its administrator, the Redcap Vermuu Ordoniz, became caught up in the Trout Riot (see insert) and was burned to death with the rest of the nobles in the church of Santa María.

> #### The Trout Riot
>
> The story goes that one of the nobles of the city of Zamora claimed his right to buy the last trout in the market, which he was disputing with a shoemaker. Faced with the protests of commoners and burghers, the noble let the shoemaker have the fish to avoid a revolt. The nobles (Vermuu among them), however, would not let the matter rest: they gathered in the church to decide how to punish the shoemaker, and the mob seized the chance to bar the doors and set fire to the building.

After Vermuu's death, the Redcaps decided to abandon the site for good; they gathered their things and left. The place, however, was a habitual meeting point for a great many magi from all over the Tribunal, so at the ordinary Tribunal of 1165 resources were granted to Porta Pandere as a dedicated covenant to maintain Occelum Durii as a Hermetic inn. Since then, many members of the Order (and their companions and grogs) have used Occelum Durii as a meeting place to exchange news, or simply to play a game of chess while enjoying the sweets and wines of al-Andalus.

***1165 AD, On Occelum Durii, Hermetic Inn*** *(Jayrān al-Gernikī)*

The former covenant of Occelum Durii shall be made available as a Hermetic inn for all members of the Tribunal. Porta Pandere shall be responsible for renewing the *Aegis of the Hearth* each year and for providing as many invitations as necessary to any member registered in the Iberian Tribunal. Likewise, any recognized companion or grog shall have the privilege of requesting lodging at Occelum Durii, whose ground shall always be free of disputes.

<!-- p. 144 -->

#### Setting and Physical Description

Occelum Durii stands within the walled precinct of the city of Zamora, near the south gate that opens onto the old Roman bridge. The building currently belongs to the covenant and Mercer House of Porta Pandere and is run by one of its companions, the ever-stern Lianor of Coimbra, who knows the Romance tongue, Latin, Arabic and Hebrew.

The inn is a stone building with wooden floors and ceilings richly decorated with carvings and paintings depicting scenes of the Tribunal (especially of the Mercere). The building's façade is enchanted with several Imaginem spells that keep mundanes from noticing it. Should this protection be breached, the thresholds of the front and back doors are enchanted so that no human without an invitation can cross them, and above the door frame hangs a magical bell that rings when someone crosses it. In addition, the building is always protected by the *Aegis of the Hearth*. Because of the continual use of spells to disguise the inn's façade, the magi have begun to notice that the structure is being affected by Warping: parts of the outer walls are turning black, and they do not yet know what this means.

On the ground floor is a spacious hall with two great fireplaces and numerous round tables where the magi can sit and enjoy beer and wine. Although food and drink are free, other goods (such as white poppy) can also be obtained at a more affordable price than in other markets. On the same floor are the kitchens, the pantries (with a goods entrance from the street, which gives onto a small courtyard where they keep hens, a small vegetable garden, a cart and a horse), the stairs to the upper floor and the way down to the cellars, where the wine is stored and the rooms of Occelum Durii's residents are located.

The upper floor has six fully furnished rooms: individual bathing tubs, beds with feather mattresses and silk sheets, and curtains and rugs in the Andalusi style. On this floor there is also a fully equipped standard laboratory, although hardly anyone uses it because of the city's Divine aura. Finally, this floor also gives access to the attic, which, according to Lianor, is best not entered.

> #### Story Seeds: Board and Lodging
>
> The inn of Occelum Durii is an ideal setting for generating all kinds of stories. It could be the place where the player characters meet, where they go in search of news from the Redcaps, or where chess tournaments are held that serve as training for the Tribunal's tournaments. Occelum Durii might be crowded with strange magi when the player characters arrive weary after a long journey, or it might be mysteriously deserted. On the other hand, the inn might harbor infernal powers posing as old acquaintances, drawing the players' magi into a challenging story… Anything is possible at Occelum Durii, so storyguides should make use of this inn on almost any pretext.

## The Transierra

This regional unit is the smallest in the kingdom, for it comprises only the western foothills of the Sierra de Gredos and the basin north of the Tagus. The Leonese Transierra is constantly expanding, and in 1220 it reaches the course of the Tagus, where the frontier with the province of al-Andalus of the Almohad Empire lies. Its other borders are with the Extremadura to the north, the kingdom of Portugal to the west and the kingdom of Castile to the east. The most important town council in these lands is that of Coria, beside the Alagón river.

The rugged regional unit of the Transierra has spectacular natural landscapes that have traditionally been under the protection and stewardship of the venerable covenant of Salama.

### Salama

*Blue-grey as a cat's eye, pure as a stem of crystal. It comes from the Euphrates and is used after being left to rest for a night. It shows itself like the flame of a candle, with the purity of a tear.*[^p144-10]

[^p144-10]: Excerpt from *The Treatise of Familiar Spirits and Demons* by Ibn Shuhayd (Spanish translation by Salvador Barberá).

>**Lifespan:** 920–Present<br>
>**Founders:** Cisila Bjornaer, Bos Bjornaer<br>
>**Season:** Winter<br>
>**Aura (type and strength):** Magic, strength 6<br>
>**Reputations:** Debtor (Iberian Tribunal) 2<br>
>**Votes:** 2

Founded by former inhabitants of Mare Iacum, Salama has kept itself apart from the Order since its beginnings. Its isolation has allowed it to maintain a way of life entirely outside Hermetic law, but it has also contributed to its decline and the onset of its Winter.

#### History

In 917, the members of Mare Iacum who had not wanted to attack the monks of San Martín de Castañeda gathered their things and set off for the Lower March of the Caliphate of Cordoba, whose capital was Badajoz. For two years Cisila and Bos searched for the right place to raise their covenant, for, being so close to the frontier and in the heart of *saḥir* territory (although by then the peace negotiations were well advanced), they did not want to attract unwanted attention. They named their covenant Salama, in honor of the ancient water divinity of those lands: an ancestral spirit from which flowed the vast power of the untouched sierra.

<!-- p. 145 -->

After all they had been through, neither Cisila nor Bos had much desire to involve themselves in the affairs of the Order, so after attending the Tribunal of 920 to announce that they had founded the covenant, they never attended another. Indeed, according to the Redcaps of those days, their manners were so rough and their payments so meager that the Redcaps soon stopped calling at their door. Salama never allowed its vis sources to be registered, and it extended its domain over a perimeter of several kilometers all around. The covenant never paid the Iberian tax established by the ruling of 864 of the Peripheral Code, so that today its debt amounts to more than a queen of vis.

With the founding of Ciudad Rodrigo and the resettlement of Ledesma in 1161, the covenant's outlying vis sources began to dwindle, so Salama, inhabited entirely by *feritarii* (see *Houses of Hermes: Mystery Cults*, page 33), committed the same offense as its forebears at Mare Iacum and attacked the settlements being resettled by mundanes. Because of its isolation, however, the Tribunal was unaware of these attacks, and the magi of Salama preyed on those lands at will. Their isolation also made it hard for them to obtain new apprentices, however (the few they had ended up leaving or dying), and the covenant began to age. The youngest magus of Salama, an Ex Miscellanea tempestarius named Ríḥun, died in 1218, a few months before Pope Honorius III granted crusading privileges to those who took part in the assault on Cáceres: the columns of the mundane armies ravaged one of the covenant's vis sources on their way to the city, and Ríḥun set out after them to overtake them. When the crusader troops were encamped before Cáceres, Ríḥun summoned a mighty storm that killed several dozen men and forced them to abandon the siege. Days later, however, he was murdered by a band of those same men, Gascon soldiers who had strayed into the covenant's domain on their way home.

In 1220, officially there are only two magi resident at Salama, both *feritarii* and, like their forebears, devoted to preserving the ancestral spirit of the waters of the peak of Jálama. It is only a matter of time, however, before the Tribunal sends a delegation to settle the enormous debt they have accumulated, and the two worlds clash: that of the Order and that of Salama. The third, undeclared member is named Quercus Merinitae and is not even part of the Tribunal, although he may present himself publicly before it in the not-too-distant future.

#### Setting and Physical Description

Salama stands in the Sierra de Gata, a few kilometers from the peak of Jálama, in the midst of completely untouched country among chestnuts, oaks and walnut trees, home to the ancestral spirit that the covenant's magi defend. To protect the covenant's most powerful vis sources, Cisila and Bos raised a ring of enchanted menhirs enclosing vast tracts of slate mountains.

Salama has no buildings as such. Its inhabitants use the spell *Twist the Living Tree* (ReHe 25) when for some reason they need a covered space, although since Ríḥun died they have not needed it again, for its members spend most of their time transformed into their inner beasts. There is, however, a great oak that the magi keep permanently transformed to preserve Salama's only laboratory, currently occupied by Quercus. Beyond that, there are no other "buildings."

Because of its way of life, Salama has only two non-Hermetic inhabitants: a naturalist hedge wizard and a young orphan girl who is responsible for obtaining the few material things that the members of Salama cannot steal.

#### Society and Customs

Salama has no governing structure whatsoever. It keeps no minutes of any kind, nor anything of the sort. Its two members devote themselves to caring for the ancestral spirit of the place and sometimes go several seasons without seeing each other. When they deem it necessary, they launch targeted attacks on nearby mundane settlements to frighten them off, but even then they feel no need to meet; as a rule each acts on his own. For his part, Quercus Merinitae does not seem to mind, at least as long as they do not ask him to take part in their raids (*algaras*).

#### The Magi of Salama

##### Caronglo Bjornaer

Bos's former apprentice, Caronglo, is a powerful ox who spends his days and nights roaming Salama's domain, making sure no mundane dares set foot in it and keeping watch on the nearby settlements. Caronglo needs neither provocation nor deeds; when he believes something may threaten Salama's ancestral spirit, he tries to destroy it at all costs. That is why the mundanes of the surrounding area take care not to go near the forests of the sierra. Caronglo considers his task so important that he does not usually attend the twelve-year gathering (see *Houses of Hermes: Mystery Cults*, page 39), for he fears that in his absence the mundanes might invade Salama's untouched land.

If the magi of the Lucena covenant of ʿÔlām wā-ʿed could recognize him, they would remember that Caronglo was one of the eunuchs they raised, and that they sold him to Bos shortly before the Lucena covenant was razed. Caronglo does not want to remember those events and, should they ever become known, he would take revenge on those responsible (Caronglo's full character sheet can be found on page 76 of *Houses of Hermes: Mystery Cults*).

##### Sus Bjornaer

The wild sow Sus is just as zealous as Caronglo. Like him, she roams the ground her companion does not cover, to prevent the mundane advance into the area. Unlike Caronglo, however, Sus is somewhat more sociable. Thanks to this, she was able to meet Quercus of Merinita on the way back from the last twelve-year gathering, held in 1215 at the covenant of Crintera. Quercus, who claimed to be a follower of the True Merinita, asked to accompany them to Salama so as to pursue his research in peace. His leaning toward nature, wholly removed from the outlook of House Merinita, earned him entry to Salama, where he still lives.

<!-- p. 146 -->

##### Quercus Merinitae

Quercus is a native of Iberia. He was born in a village near the city of Salamanca, but was trained at Irencillia, where, after some years, he met Agnes, from whom he learned the House's lost nature mysteries. While he was at Irencillia, his *sodales* began to grow suspicious of his magic, so Quercus decided to leave for some remote place where he could go on learning those mysteries, preferably at the hands of some powerful spirit. To his good fortune, he came upon Sus on his way, and she, after long debates, allowed him to accompany her to Salama, which happened to be very close to where he had been born.

The naturalist magus has not stopped learning since then and, although he does not consider the covenant comfortable, it is the most pleasant place he has ever known. Although his two companions give it little importance, Quercus cannot stop thinking that he has not formally presented himself at the Tribunal, which makes him a wanderer who is not part of it, something that could lead to his banishment. Quercus may present himself at the Tribunal in 1221, though, unfortunately for him, he knows absolutely nothing about it (indeed, presenting himself while Salama owes so very much vis would be most inadvisable).

> #### Story Seeds: Salama's "Privilege"
>
> When, at one of the ordinary Tribunals, the player characters learn that the covenant of Salama owes a considerable debt to the Tribunal's coffers, they will surely want to know why they have to pay punctually while that covenant ignores its responsibility without the Quaesitores doing anything about it. What is more, they might raise the matter at the next Tribunal or try to persuade other covenants to protest jointly against Salama's "privilege," perhaps by not paying either. Alternatively, they might also offer to collect the debt on the Tribunal's behalf if they were allowed to keep a percentage as profit. Naturally, the last option will be the one the Quaesitores of Duresca favor most, for they will have no objection to letting others deal with something they find merely a nuisance.

<!-- p. 147 -->

# VI. The Kingdom of Castile

Since 1217 Castile has been ruled by the young Fernando III, son of Alfonso IX of Leon, who has brought his kingdom great stability thanks to the peace treaties he has signed with his father and with the monarchs of Aragon, Navarre and al-Andalus. Knighted barely a year ago, and recently married to Beatriz of Swabia, Fernando has not yet answered the call against the Muslims that Pope Honorius III issued in 1219 (see "The Crusades of Iberia," page 41). In fact, not until 1224 will Fernando III decide to fight to push the frontiers of his kingdom forward at the expense of the territories of the Almohad province of al-Andalus.

The vast kingdom of Castile is bounded to the north by the Cantabrian Sea (from Fuenterrabía in the east to just beyond San Vicente de la Barquera in the west), to the south by the Andalusi province of the Almohad Empire (the city of Baeza lies at the very edge of its frontiers), to the west by the kingdom of Leon (the cities of Sahagún, Tordesillas, Béjar and Plasencia lie on the border), and to the east by the kingdom of Navarre (with the city of Logroño at the edge of the realm) and the Crown of Aragon (the cities of Molina and Moya are close to the frontier).

## The Covenants of the Kingdom of Castile

The kingdom of Castile is divided into four great regions (from north to south): Castile, the Extremadura, the Transierra and Toledo, where the covenants of the Tribunal are located.

## Castile

*[…] past the Montes de Oca, toward Burgos, the Spanish land continues with Castile and Campos. It is a land full of treasures, of gold and silver, rich in cloth and vigorous horses, abounding in bread, wine, meat, fish, milk and honey. Yet it is bare of trees and full of wicked and vicious men.*[^p147-11]

[^p147-11]: Excerpt from the *Codex Calixtinus*, anonymous (Spanish translation by Millán Bravo Lozano).

The region of Castile is the northernmost part of the kingdom and is home to the important town councils of San Sebastián, Burgos, Santander, Lara, Palencia, Nájera and Logroño, among others. The north of Castile is dominated by the Cantabrian Mountains and their foothills, which make for very rugged terrain that grows gentler toward the south. Most of the kingdom's most powerful vis sources lie in this region and, as could hardly be otherwise, they are in the hands of the covenant of Salionca.

> #### Story Seeds: The Kingdom of the Pataricos
>
> According to the *Comentarii de Bello Iberico*, off the coast between the rivers Navia and Eo there is a *regio* that holds a lush island inhabited by giants. The pataricos (as they were known in ancient times) were forced to abandon their kingdom in northern Iberia after their king, the giant Equión, was slain by Grimoald Niger of Flambeau, and they have never returned since.
>
> When the characters meet a Redcap, he tells them that a group of whalers who put to sea from San Sebastián several months ago has been found in a makeshift boat near the coast of Asturias. Apparently, ever since they were found, they have talked of nothing but an island inhabited by giants.
>
> Such news is sure to spread quickly through the Tribunal, so if the characters do not hurry, they may not be the first to arrive. Will they set out at once to search the waters, or will they seek out the surviving whalers to look into what happened and so learn how to enter the *regio*?
