## Toledo

The territorial unit of Toledo covers the middle course of the Tagus basin and the upper course of the Guadiana basin. The southern frontier with the province of al-Andalus of the Almohad Empire is a troubled and ill-defined zone; the lands of Toledo border on Baeza and Úbeda to the south, take in the city of Plasencia to the west, and reach as far as the city of Moya to the east. Almost all the town councils (*concejos*) of this vast territory lie in its north — Toledo, Talavera, Escalona, Illescas, Uclés and Cuenca, among others — while in the south there is only that of Alcaraz.

The fact that Toledo was a frontier region until its conquest did not stop magi from seeking a place in its lands to grow their covenants, for it is well known that there are important vis sources in this area. At present there are two living covenants in the region of Toledo, with very little in common: the scholarly Iššáh and the venerable, isolated Laminium.

> #### Transhumance
>
> The regional unit of Toledo forms part of the great organization of lands that is beginning to be overseen by the newly created brotherhoods, or inter-council pasture communities (between the councils of Escalona and Plasencia, of Escalona and Segovia, and of Montalbán and Maqueda, for example).
>
> These brotherhoods are responsible for collecting the tolls for livestock crossing the pastures, setting the quotas of head of livestock per resident, and charging stockbreeders for their use of the land (taxes known as *montaticum* and *herbaticum*). To oversee all these payments, the councils rely on the well-known *caballeros de la sierra* (knights of the sierra) and *montaneros* (rangers), who are responsible for guarding the pastures to collect the transit fees and for regulating how long the livestock remain on them. Normally these two figures work only during the summer months, that is, from Saint John's Day (24 June) to Saint Vincent's Day (29 September).

> #### Story Seeds: The Stolen Flock
>
> The player characters' covenant controls the brotherhood of the neighboring inter-council pastures. At its last council, the *montanero* reports the disappearance of a flock of more than a hundred sheep. When he gave the shepherds free passage in the morning, he entrusted the land to them until dawn of the following day. When he returned in the afternoon, however, they were gone, and only the carcasses of the dogs remained. What could have made the sheep disappear? Could the owners of such a flock accuse the council (and therefore the covenant) of having stolen their livestock?

### The City of Toledo

Toledo was the Visigothic capital, capital of the Middle March under the Umayyad emirate and caliphate, a focus of numerous revolts against the central power of Cordoba, the center of a great taifa ruled by the ancient Berber clan of the Banū Ḏū-l-Nūn, and was finally conquered by Alfonso VI of Leon in 1085.

When the Christian monarch took the city, Rome succeeded in displacing the Mozarabic rite, and the archdiocese and the primacy of Iberia were restored: the church of Toledo became the most powerful Christian center in the Peninsula. The archbishops of Toledo, or "primates of the Spains," became the head of the ecclesiastical province, with several dioceses in their charge, numerous archdeaconries and more than twenty archpriestships.

In 1220, although the Roman rite is the official one, the Mozarabs (who still speak Arabic) outnumber the Latin Castilians, and these in turn outnumber the Mudéjars (who may be free or slaves) and the muwalladūn, who are few in number. Rarer still are Muslims converted to Christianity and Berbers, and Arabs are wholly absent. Because of the large number of Mozarabs, the city has two royal *alcaldes* (assisted by ten nobles): one to deal with the affairs of the Latin Christians and the other with those of the Mozarabs. The Jews, for their part, live in their aljama (*madinat al-yahud*), in numbers somewhat greater than the Muslims.

Moreover, in 1220 Toledo's commercial activity is such that it has no need of fairs (see page 58). In its markets one can find perfumers, bookbinders, spice merchants, potters, tailors, hosiers, cloth shearers, old-clothes dealers, shoemakers, saddlers, esparto workers, druggists, apothecaries (*alatares*), burnishers, moneychangers, smiths, dyers, velvet weavers, goldsmiths, butchers, fishmongers, scabbard makers, crossbow makers and armorers, which makes it a center of interest for all the magi of the Meseta, who can find their rare laboratory materials there without difficulty. Since its conquest, however, trade with al-Andalus has been increasingly restricted. Before 1085, the Toledans traded by mule train with Cordoba, Valencia and Murcia, exporting leather, livestock, weapons, horses, timber (which arrived down the Tagus), honey and rabbit skins, and importing textiles and jewels from the south. Over the years, however, the trade restrictions with the south of the Peninsula grew harsher. Thus in 1118 the export of hides and horses to al-Andalus was forbidden, and in 1138 Alfonso VII exempted Toledans who did not trade with al-Andalus from paying the tithe and the *portazgo* (or *portaticum*, the tax for bringing goods into the city).

#### The Pogroms of Toledo

Sadly, the city of Toledo has witnessed three terrible attacks on its Jewish population by its other citizens. The first pogrom took place in 1108, after the defeat at Uclés: the populace blamed the Jews for it, for having bought Christian prisoners to sell as slaves. The second took place in 1175 and ended with the murder of the city's rabbi. The last occurred in 1212, when the European crusader armies attacked the aljama, and the knights of the city came to the aid of their Sephardic neighbors.

<!-- p. 166 -->

> #### The Fall of Toledo (1085)
>
> *Andalusians, spur on your mounts, for to stay here is folly. Garments tend to unravel at the edges, but I see that the garment of the Peninsula has torn from the very start down the middle.*[^p166-IX]
>
> The city of Toledo, divided as it was between the Muslims (who favored rapprochement with other taifas) and the Christians and Jews (who favored alliance with the Christian monarch, Alfonso VI of Leon), ended up surrendering peacefully to Alfonso VI on the following terms:
>
> - the Muslims could remain in the city with their goods and families, provided they paid Alfonso VI the same tribute they had previously paid the Muslim governor;
> - any Toledan could leave with all his movable goods, with the option of returning to the city whenever he wished;
> - the great mosque of Toledo would remain in the hands of the Muslims;
> - Alfonso VI would keep the alcázar, the king's garden and the treasure of Ibn Ḏū-l-Nūn's grandson;
> - the Mozarabs could continue to practice the Visigothic Christian rite;
> - the Jews had to pay thirty *dineros* a year to the cathedral as a reminder of the sum for which Judas sold Jesus.
>
> As a result, almost all the Muslims left, except those who lacked the means to do so.
>
> When, barely a year later, the pact was broken (the mosque was turned into a cathedral and the seat of the archbishopric of the Peninsula), the Mozarabs' church lost its status as a cathedral. Since then the Christians of Toledo have used the eleven-aisled mosque as their cathedral, and in 1220 numerous houses near the mosque are already being expropriated, and there are plans to move the market so that the cathedral can be built, although its first stone will not be laid until 1226.
>
> [^p166-IX]: Written by ʿAbd Allāh al-ʿAssāl (1094) after the fall of Toledo (Spanish translation by E. García Gómez, 1987).

### Laminium

>**Lifespan:** 1012–Present<br>
>**Founders:** Modron Ex Miscellanea, Dwywai Ex Miscellanea<br>
>**Season:** Winter<br>
>**Aura (type and strength):** Magic, strength 6 (third level of the *regio*)<br>
>**Reputations:** None<br>
>**Votes:** 9

Laminium was founded as a result of the sentence passed by the king of Asturias, Ramiro I, on all the wizards of his kingdom. After Tancoystl's death, the Ex Miscellanea living at Duresca left and founded their own covenant amid the mists of the wetland of a *regio*. Although the magi settled there in the third quarter of the ninth century, they did not attend any Tribunal until 1012, when they were constituted as a covenant.

#### History

Laminium was the first covenant founded entirely by members of House Ex Miscellanea, apart from men and from the Order. Since its creation the covenant has had no political representation at Tribunals, and for years Redcaps have visited it only to announce the holding of the ordinary Tribunals. Its participation in the Hermetic life of Iberia has been so slight that today there are magi who do not even know it exists. Laminium has always been surrounded by a certain mystery, and in its entire history its members have attended only the Tribunal of 1012, where they voted in favor of the secession of al-Andalus.

A little more than ten years ago, the covenant's council decided to perform a ritual to increase the strength of the aura. After it was carried out, the fabric of the *regio* underwent no change, but a year later its inhabitants suffered a magical shock that sent them into Twilight (in some cases indefinitely) and hurled them, along with the covenant's buildings, into the highest level of the *regio* (see its description below). The magi who did not lose their sanity in the process discovered that this level had an aura of 9 and was apparently uninhabited, so they celebrated in grand style. In 1214, however, the level suffered what the covenant's elders call a pulse, and one of the magi and his *sanctum* vanished without a trace. Things grew worse four years later, when a second pulse brought forth an enormous mist serpent, and the magi had to flee the highest level of the *regio* to save their lives.

<!-- p. 167 -->

The elders have been trying to return to the highest level since 1218, since that is where the covenant lies, but as they have no guide they cannot reach it. Furthermore, although they meant to stay on the level immediately below, it proved extremely dangerous, so the magi have been forced to eke out a living in the ruins left after the catastrophe, on the third level of the *regio*. The elders hope that in 1222 (when the next pulse is due) the serpent will disappear and a door will open to the highest level of the *regio*, to which end they have not ceased praying and sacrificing animals to their ancient gods.

But these are not all of Laminium's misfortunes, for in the last few years the covenant of Iššáh has begun stealing the vis sources that the elders stopped harvesting after the catastrophe.

#### Setting and Physical Description

Laminium lies in the impressive wetland at the confluence of the Guadiana and its tributary, the Cigüela. Built on the highest level of a powerful magical *regio*, Laminium has buildings scattered among the water and the islands that dot the wetland.

Laminium has no buildings for common use; its members have always held their councils on the open ground of the *regio*'s central island, where they raised a menhir carved with the names of their Celtic gods. Likewise, they carved all their advances, their laboratory texts and their Hermetic books into stones brought there for that purpose, so that in its almost four centuries of existence the central island has become a stone forest filled with wisdom.

#### The Regio of Laminium

The *regio* in which Laminium lies has five levels, which can be reached only with a guide. The mundane level extends as far as the river's floodplain and is the gateway to the next level, which has an aura of strength 3. The third level has an aura of strength 6 and holds the ruins of old Laminium, now inhabited by the magi, which are no more than a reflection of the buildings that existed before the magical catastrophe. The fourth level was the highest before the catastrophe, and the founders avoided it, considering it very dangerous because of the beings that dwell there. In it are reflected the misty doubles (buildings, creatures and plants) of the highest level of the *regio*, which at times possess a certain corporeality. The fifth and highest level appeared after the catastrophe and has an aura of strength 9. It is here, shrouded in dense fog, that the buildings of Laminium are found. Every four years this level suffers a pulse that makes something vanish or appear within its bounds.

#### Society and Customs

Laminium has always been a gerontocracy, so its oldest members are the ones who govern the covenant. The council of elders meets at every equinox and solstice on the open ground of the central island, in the forest of menhirs, to discuss the covenant's affairs. The councils begin when one of the elders lights a fire on the island and last a full day and a full night, ending with the inhalation of the smoke given off by certain local roots when burned. After this the decisions taken are communicated to the young, who have no right of reply: the elders' ruling is final. After the catastrophe, however, the council of elders was left in the hands of insane magi, so the covenant is governed by their ravings.

Any magus may join Laminium. In exchange, the council of elders asks only that he obtain a new vis source and swear to set down all the knowledge he acquires (by inventing a new spell, enchanting an item or writing a book) on a menhir with enough space to hold it in full (when the menhirs run out, the elders have a new stone brought to the island to be carved, sometimes from distant quarries). These are the only two requirements for joining the covenant, and they have remained unchanged since the beginning of time.

When a member of Laminium reaches eighty years since his Gauntlet, he joins the council of elders. If he is already that age when he joins the covenant, he is admitted to it immediately.

#### The Magi of Laminium

##### The Council of Elders

The most senior member of Laminium is Anas Bjornaer, a magus over a hundred years old whose heartbeast is a red-crested pochard. Until the catastrophe, Anas migrated to North Africa every winter, but since he was hurled into Twilight he has left neither the covenant nor his duck form, and he is clearly deranged. Anas dwells in the ruins on the third level of the *regio* and bustles from place to place watching over the members of the covenant, telling them what to do and how. Anas no longer studies; he simply spends his days scolding his *sodales* in his shrill voice.

The next oldest magus is Pedro Ruiz of Tytalus, an ambitious man who came to Laminium fleeing the Almohads of al-Andalus with the idea of revitalizing the covenant and taking control of it. Unwisely, he persuaded the elders to improve the aura with one of his spells, which ended up destabilizing the *regio* and causing the catastrophe, from which he did not emerge unscathed either. When he returned from Twilight, Pedro could no longer cast spells and his personality had been deranged. Since then he has spent his days in the sun and sleeps in the shelter of the reeds by the river. He speaks only when spoken to, although on such occasions he seems lucid and even reasonable.

The next maga in age is Sol Ex Miscellanea. Sol is a *saḥira*, and she was the one charged with bringing new stones for the forest of menhirs. She carved them and also saw to the preservation of their writings. Since the catastrophe, her Twilight has left her out of her mind. Sol now has to be cared for by the covenant's inhabitants, since she cannot eat or walk on her own. Sol speaks only when the council is convened, which, like the other elders, she attends without delay.

Muŷāhid Ex Miscellanea is the last elder of Laminium and, like his companions, he too was gravely affected by the Twilight he underwent during the catastrophe. At first sight he does not seem to have lost his faculties: he still works in his ruined laboratory, he does not neglect his duties (such as lighting the bonfire on the central island that marks the start of the council of elders), and he goes on writing his research on the menhirs. Something in his perception has been unsettled, however: Muŷāhid reveres Anas

#### The Young Magi of Laminium

The young magi of Laminium live in the ruins of the covenant on the third level of the *regio*. With scarcely any resources, and led by elders who have been seduced by Twilight, they seek ways to survive, each in their own fashion.

Nuʿum Ex Miscellanea is the eldest of the young magi, a former apprentice of Sol. Nuʿum was not in the *regio* during the catastrophe; she was in Medina, where she had ridden on her steed Babieca to hear a minstrel sing the deeds of the Cid. Nuʿum loves tales of chivalry; indeed, she dresses as a knight herself, and on summer nights she often sings the exploits of the Cid to the rest of the covenant's inhabitants.

Since the catastrophe, Nuʿum has been in charge of her Hermetic sister, Buayna, whom she looks after and provides with every possible attention. This responsibility is partly why Nuʿum cannot devote as much time to the covenant as she would like. Moreover, the catastrophe cut short the negotiations she had been conducting with one of the *jinn* who dwell in the covenant's wetland. Since the incident, she has been unable to summon the magic spirit again, and she is beginning to suspect that it may have been affected in some way by the pulsations of the *regio*, or, worse still, that it has gone away. In any case, she knows of other, less powerful *jinn* on whom she can rely for lesser tasks.

At present Nuʿum has no thought of leaving the covenant, precisely because of her sister, despite the precarious conditions in which she lives. In fact, two years ago she performed her Longevity Ritual, which she knows will not stand up well to the passage of time, and she was forced to distill it in an improvised laboratory amid the ruins of the covenant's buildings. For the moment this does not trouble her, but sooner or later, if she cannot revitalize Laminium, she will have to leave and take Buayna with her. After all, she was the only one to come through the catastrophe unscathed, so the responsibility for keeping the covenant afloat rests on her shoulders.

Nuʿum's Hermetic sister, Buayna Ex Miscellanea, was not so fortunate. The catastrophe shattered her mind, as it did the elders', and ever since she has done nothing but repeat what she was doing that night: she spends her days distilling a brew in the ruins of what was once her laboratory.

The rest of the young magi, Ibn Muŷāhid Ex Miscellanea, Yulyān ibn Muŷāhid Ex Miscellanea and Clypeata Bjornaer, were affected by the catastrophe only superficially, and although they have their peculiarities, they go about their daily lives among the ruins their elders bequeathed them, restoring a covenant that, in time, they might bring back to Spring. However, since they know practically nothing of its resources (those being the elders' business), they gather only the vis they know about, which is the vis found inside the *regio*.

> #### Story Seeds: Laminium
>
> Laminium's abundant vis sources have been abandoned for more than ten years, so Iššáh began harvesting them when it learned that no one was exploiting them. The elders seem to have forgotten about them, and the young magi do not know they exist. Although in 1214 a Redcap brought them a notice announcing that if they did not exploit the vis sources of Ruidera, someone else might claim them, Anas drove him off with pecks and, in a fury, threw the letter into the water.
>
> The Redcaps know of Laminium's situation, so they might persuade the player characters to help the covenant or, on the contrary, to take the vis sources it still has and share them with the Mercer House. In the first case, the player characters will have to visit the covenant to unravel some of its mysteries and find out how to enter the last level of the *regio* to put an end to the mist serpent. In the second, they will have to obtain the location of its vis sources (for which they will very likely have to negotiate with the Mercere) and perhaps ally themselves with Iššáh to wrest the sources from it.
>
> Furthermore, Laminium is a good candidate for having served as a refuge for some Diedne during the Schism War. Being an isolated covenant, it might have taken in one of their apprentices, who would have finished his training as an Ex Miscellanea. It would not be a bad idea for a character with the Major Virtue Diedne Magic to come from here, although, as always, the storyguide has the last word.

### Iššáh

*Chess, backgammon, draughts and arrows must be forbidden, for they are games of chance, which are sinful and distract from the fulfillment of religious duties.*[^p169-17]

[^p169-17]: Excerpt from *The Treatise of Ibn ʿAbdūn* (Spanish translation by Emilio García Gómez and E. Levi-Provençal).
>**Lifespan:** 1025–Present<br>
>**Founders:** ʿĀtika al-Bonisagiyya, Salāmān al-Ŷerbitonī<br>
>**Season:** Summer<br>
>**Aura (type and strength):** Magic, strength 4<br>
>**Reputations:** Library (Iberian Tribunal) 6, Scribal Workshop (local) 3<br>
>**Votes:** 8

<!-- p. 170 -->

Iššáh (from the Andalusi Arabic for "chessboard square") was born after the fall of the caliphate and took root amid the disintegration of Iberia, together with the other covenants that made up the Tribunal of al-Andalus during the eleventh century.

#### History

When the fuqahāʾ of Cordoba condemned the leader of the covenant of al-Zahrāʾ and former Praeco, ʿAbbās ibn Munḏīr al-Bonisagī, ʿĀtika and Salāmān left the covenant and sought refuge at Fafḥṣ al-Luŷŷ, where, unlike its inhabitants, they voted in favor of the Tribunal's secession. Since the rest of their companions had decided to go off to war, the two magi left Fafḥṣ al-Luŷŷ to found a covenant in the city of Toledo, under the aegis of al-Andalus.

In those days they called their covenant al-Dhahabī (from the Arabic, "the golden one"), for they wished its name to evoke the profound meaning of an old Arabic proverb: "if speech is silver, silence is gold."[^p170-18]

[^p170-18]: Arabic proverb (Spanish translation by Ahmed-Salem Ould Mohamed Baba).

The Bonisagus and the Jerbiton lived through Toledo's splendor under the Banū Ḏū-l-Nūn: the city resounded with culture, its streets filled with music and its courtyards with fountains and gardens. ʿĀtika and Salāmān also explored the city's vast underground passages, where they found remains of their ancient occupants, by all appearances sorcerers of the cult of Mercury. From within they recovered great riches, which they stored in their covenant's coffers (see insert).

Al-Dhahabī enjoyed the protection and patronage of Ṣāʿid al-Andalusī and, if the records do not lie, counted among its ranks the astrologer Ibn al-Jayyāṭ (who remained there until his death) and the mathematicians Abū-l-Ḥasan ʿAlī al-Riŷal and Arzachel, the latter staying from 1068 until the conquest of Toledo in 1085, when he returned to Seville, his native city.

As the king of Leon advanced, ʿĀtika and Salāmān's covenant supported the Muslims in trying to prevent Alfonso VI from entering Toledo. However, since the Christians, Jews and Muslims could not agree on the matter, revolts broke out in the city and the looting began. Then the taifa of Toledo lost Cordoba and Valencia, and the emir of Badajoz, whom the Toledans had asked for help in resolving the situation, merely lined his pockets with the city's gold and departed. In the end, Ibn Ḏū-l-Nūn's grandson surrendered the city to Alfonso VI, and Toledo's cultural elite abandoned it. So did almost all the magi of al-Dhahabī, except for its *rector*, the Jewish doctor Ben Zômá al-Bonisagī, and a few other Jewish and Mozarabic magi.

When Ben Zômá joined the perfect Order in 1127, the leadership of al-Dhahabī fell to the rest of its members, who decided to rename the covenant Iššáh, for they were all great lovers of chess. The covenant's new era coincided almost exactly, in time and place, with the cultural movement that was to transform Mythic Europe: the Toledo school of translators. Sitt Nasim joined the enterprise and, from Iššáh, ensured that the covenant benefited from the arrival of scholars from all over the world, making Toledo the cultural capital of Europe. The newly renamed covenant began translating the Hermetic and mundane works that until then had been written in Arabic, and it set up a market that many magi of Iberia still enjoy today, for Iššáh's catalogue offers a great variety of books, both Hermetic and mundane.

> #### Story Seeds: The Riches of Toledo
>
> When ʿĀtika and Salāmān ventured into the Mercurian palaces of Toledo, they found all manner of riches inherited from the Visigothic kings. Although present-day Iššáh has never denied nor confirmed their existence, the Seeker of Aedes Saturni, Filemón of Bonisagus, has asked them to share their treasures with the Tribunal, or whatever research they may have carried out on them. Below we suggest some ideas of what Iššáh's coffers might hold.
>
> - **The table of Solomon:** carved from a single emerald, the table was a gift from the *jinn* to the Hebrew monarch, although one of its legs is now made of gold. It is believed that the table bears the inscription containing the secret name of God (the *Shem Hameforash* or *Shemaforash* of the Kabbalah).
>
> - **The mirror of the world:** this is a mirror in which whoever looks into it beholds the whole world before their eyes. It is made of dried clay, in a mixture of stones and drugs. Its rim and handle are engraved with Greek letters.
>
> - **The crowns of the kings:** it is said that among the treasures were twenty-five crowns of kings, whose powers are unknown.
>
> - **The books of the Law:** the treasure includes copies of the Torah, the gospel of the Psalms, and the books of Abraham and Moses.
>
> - **Books of alchemy:** describing the alchemical mysteries of the ancients, for which the riadiins would pay any price.

The covenant's prestige grew still further when, at the ordinary Tribunal of 1151, two magi from the destroyed covenant of ʿÔlām wā-ʿed joined Iššáh: the former *rosh yeshiva* of Lucena, Meʾir ibn Yosef, and the great critic of Maimonides' *Mishneh Torah*, Abraham ben David.

#### Setting and Physical Description

The covenant of Iššáh lies within the walls of the city of Toledo. Close to the Alcántara gate, it uses the front of a scribal workshop to deal with mundane society. Because Iššáh engages in very little political activity, the covenant has been able to live without attracting unwanted attention. However, the "privileged" location chosen by ʿĀtika and Salāmān is not entirely convenient for its current occupants, who miss having a more powerful aura to draw upon in their Hermetic research, for Iššáh is cloaked only by a weak Magic aura of strength 4, which emanates from the ancient Mercurian sanctuary over which the covenant stands. To make matters worse, at Christmas and on Palm Sunday Toledo's Divine aura swallows Iššáh's feeble aura and nullifies all its magical defenses.

<!-- p. 171 -->

The small workshop that serves as Iššáh's front stands on a narrow street. Once past the first mundane rooms, the covenant opens out and is arranged around a spectacular, light-filled inner courtyard planted with all kinds of ornamental plants (though without trees that might block the light the scribes need so badly). The great windows of Iššáh's large *scriptorium* face south onto this courtyard.

> #### The School of Translators[^p171-X]
>
> *Books of science must not be sold to Jews or Christians, except those that deal with their own law, for they then translate the scientific books and attribute them to their own people and to their bishops, when in fact they are the works of Muslims.*[^p171-XI]
>
> The fall of Toledo in 1085 gave Castile the treasure of the royal library of the Banū Ḏū-l-Nūn dynasty, the only one in the whole Peninsula devoted entirely to the sciences of the ancients. With such archives, the Cluniac monk Raymond de Sauvetat (named archbishop of Toledo in the twelfth century) began what would become the cultural reform that ushered in what might be considered the renaissance of the twelfth century.
>
> Raymond gathered and directed a group of translators, whom he lodged in rooms of the episcopal palace he had ordered built for that purpose. Following the translations made in Saragossa, Tarazona and Tudela during the first half of the twelfth century (and during the eleventh century at Ripoll; see page 205), Toledo took up the baton and produced the greatest number of translations of the books of philosophy, mathematics and classical knowledge that had reached the Peninsula after being copied in Baghdad. A great number of scholars came together in Toledo, working in two stages: first they translated from Arabic into the Romance tongue (generally a Jew or a Mozarab read the text and translated it aloud), and then another translator rendered the text into learned Latin or, from a certain point in the school's history onward, directly into Castilian. But it was not only translations: the sages who came to Toledo also sometimes left works of their own, almost always of great quality.
>
> From its beginning in the mid-twelfth century to its end in the early thirteenth, the life of the school of translators passed through two distinct stages.
>
> ##### The First Stage (Second Half of the Twelfth Century)
>
> Fostered and promoted by the cathedral chapter, with the following translators as its chief protagonists:
>
> - Gerard of Cremona. A native of Lombardy, he studied philosophy in Italy and during those years became interested in the works of Ptolemy. Seeking his writings in Arabic, he made his way to Toledo, where he learned the language and translated more than seventy works, such as Ptolemy's *Almagest*, Avicenna's *Canon of Medicine*, Al-Rāzī's *Medical Encyclopedia*, Abulcasis's *Surgery*, the works on spherical geometry of the Sevillian Abū Muḥammad Ŷābir ben Aflaḥ, Aristotle's *Cosmology* and *Analytics*, Euclid's *De elementa* and Galen's *Art of Medicine*. During his stay in Toledo he also taught astrology.
>
> - Dominicus Gundissalinus. Archdeacon of Cuéllar (Segovia) and protégé of the archbishop of Toledo, he collaborated on numerous translations of Al-Fārābī, Ibn Sīnā, Ibn Gabirol and Al-Gazālī. He also wrote the book of classifications entitled *On the Division of Philosophy*.
>
> - Johannes Hispalensis, who translated Abulmasar's books on astronomy *Introductorium maius* and *De magnis coniunctionibus et annorum revolutionibus*, as well as Avicenna's *Book of Healing*.
>
> - Hermann the Dalmatian. A Slavic cleric who translated Ptolemy's *Planisphere* with the commentaries of the mathematician Maslama (see page 287), and the *Introduction to Astronomy* of the Persian Albumasar, which had already been translated into Latin by Johannes Hispalensis.
>
> ##### The Second Stage (Late Twelfth and Early Thirteenth Centuries)
>
> This stage coincided with the archbishop of Toledo, Jiménez de Rada, and with the arrival in the city of the great Michael Scotus. Among the most notable figures were the following:
>
> - The Mozarab and canon Marcos de Toledo, who studied medicine in France and returned to Toledo to translate Galen. Among his works, he had to translate the Qurʾan and the *Treatise on the Unity of God* by Ibn Tūrmat, founder of the Almohad movement, so that the Muslim religion could be combated in Iberia.
>
> - Michael Scotus, who in 1217 translated into Latin (with the help of a Jewish translator) the work of the astronomer Abū Ishāq al-Bitrūŷī. He also translated Aristotle's great zoological compendium (*Historia animalium*) and, together with Hermannus Alemannus, Averroes' commentaries on the works of Aristotle, which brought about the entry and spread of Aristotle in the Christian world (indeed, it was in 1250 that Aristotle began to be studied in the classes of the university of Paris) and the triumph of rationalism.
>
> - Salio, a canon of Padua, who translated several Arabic works of astrology.
>
> [^p171-X]: The authors consulted agree that one cannot speak of a physical school as such, but rather of an infrastructure that allowed codices to be stored and circulated so that they were available, which suggests some kind of library, possibly that of the cathedral (although this theory seems unlikely for the twelfth century).
>
> [^p171-XI]: Excerpt from *The Treatise of Ibn ʿAbdūn* (Spanish translation by Emilio García Gómez and E. Levi-Provençal).

<!-- p. 172 -->

The magi's *sancta* are on the upper floor, as is the council chamber, and the great library lies in the cellars, where the books are more easily preserved. The chamber that holds Iššáh's countless tomes once housed the treasures of the Visigoths, and it is decorated with exquisite marble and jade. Moreover, this hall is protected by all manner of spells that keep its humidity and temperature constant and shield the precious codices from any outside agent (such as fire, water or vermin).

On the outskirts of Toledo, Iššáh keeps in working order the anaphoric clock (a forerunner of mechanical clocks) built by Al-Zarqālī, made up of great pools that fill and empty with the lunar cycles. As a result, Iššáh receives numerous requests from covenants all over Mythic Europe to review their astronomical calculations and check them against the fabulous record of time kept by the Toledan covenant.

> #### The Chess Tournament
>
> The members of Iššáh hold an ancient chess tournament every seven years (coinciding in place and time with the ordinary Tribunals of Iberia), for which any magus of the Tribunal may register up to one season in advance. For it to be held there must be at least 16 players, and there can be as many groups (in even numbers) as there are multiples of that number. That is, with 18 players registered a single group would be formed and the last two to sign up would be left without a game, and if 47 registered, two groups of 16 would be formed and the last 15 to sign up would not take part. The tournament is played by direct elimination; that is, a bracket is drawn up for each group of sixteen players. As a prize, Iššáh gives the winner a chess piece and a spectacular book (which may be Hermetic or mundane) with resonances (see *Covenants*, page 117).
>
> The tournaments begin three days before the ordinary Tribunals and last at most two days (although games may run on into the night). On the first day the first two rounds are played, and on the second the semifinals, the finals of each group and, if there are any, the play-offs between the champions of each group. The overall final is always played after sunset on the last day.
>
> ##### The Mechanics of Chess
>
> Each player draws lots for color, red or black (red moves first), and may bring their own pieces (there is a whole Hermetic market for them; see *Houses of Hermes: True Lineages*, page 95). To resolve the match, each round the players make opposed rolls based on the following total, using the new Chess Ability described on page 310.
>
> **Chess Total:**
>
> **Intelligence + Chess + concentration bonus + chess advantage + stress die**
>
> Here the concentration bonus equals the character's Concentration score divided by two (rounding up, and never greater than the Chess score), and the chess advantage equals the difference between the higher and the lower total generated in the previous round, so on the first roll the chess advantage is always zero. A botch reduces the player's Chess Total to zero and, at the storyguide's discretion, might carry other negative effects.
>
> Each game may last from ten minutes to four hours or more (depending on the opponents' Chess Totals and how the game unfolds), and in that time up to ten rolls may be made. If at any point one player doubles the opponent's total, checkmate occurs (from the Arabic *al-šah māt*, literally "the king is dead") and the game ends. If the game finishes without checkmate, it ends in a draw and both opponents are eliminated.
>
> The final is played as the best of three games; if all three games end in draws, there is no tournament winner that year.
>
> Although no rule forbids it, members of Iššáh who hold a position of responsibility (that is, the *maior*) do not usually take part in the chess tournaments.
>
> ##### The Prize
>
> The books awarded to the champions usually have Qualities of around 12 and, if they are *summae*, Levels of around 10. Along with the books, Iššáh awards the elephant chess piece (in Arabic *fīl*, which would be the modern bishop), made of gold, with the year of the tournament and the winner's name carved into its base. Moreover, the piece is a lesser enchanted device invested with 20 levels of effects (for example, resistance to outside agents such as damp and fire, the ability to move across the board following its owner's spoken commands, or the ability to change its appearance to match the style of pieces from other sets).
>
> The best players in the tournament also receive experience points in the Chess Player (Iberian Tribunal) Reputation: the champion gains 15 points, the finalists 5 and the semifinalists 3. For each tournament in which chess players with this Reputation fail to reach the semifinals (whether because they lose or because they do not take part), they lose one experience point, although their Reputation can never fall below zero.

#### Society and Customs

When al-Dhahabī's former rector left the covenant, its members changed not only its name but also its style of government, which went from an oligarchy to a bureaucracy in which the covenant's responsibilities were divided among three departments, each autonomous and without authority over the others: namely, the *scriptorium*, the *bibliotheca* and the *oeconomia*.

The *scriptorium* is in charge of copying the books, both Hermetic and mundane, that reach the covenant, and of their making (illumination, sewing, binding, creating resonances and so on), as well as the upkeep and manufacture of the materials needed to produce them. The *bibliotheca* is responsible for acquiring new manuscripts (by purchase or exchange), maintaining and preserving the books in the collection, keeping the covenant's catalogue up to date, and selling or recycling whichever volumes it sees fit. Lastly, the department of *oeconomia* handles the covenant's accounts (both Hermetic and mundane), and in its power lies the decision to approve or reject requests for money or vis from the other departments. This department is also charged with harvesting and maintaining Iššáh's vis sources.

<!-- p. 173 -->

Besides renting out and selling books, Iššáh owns several hectares of vineyards (next to the vines that the Castilian monarchs own in the fields of Toledo), keeps a small fishery of eels, barbel and lampreys (on the river meadows of the Tagus), and holds the rights to work several mills on the Tagus (where they grind wheat, barley and rye from the local fields).

Usually the Redcaps bring their orders to Iššáh, and the head of the *bibliotheca* delivers them at the ordinary Tribunals or at the covenants that placed the order, but never at Iššáh itself, for its charter forbids trading with other magi within the covenant, so as not to attract the attention of the mundane powers.

At Iššáh, all its inhabitants speak Arabic as their first language and Hebrew as their second, although almost all of them (the magi, of course) also speak Latin.

#### The Magi of Iššáh

##### Scriba maior Sitt Nasim al-Bagdadiyya al-Tremeriyya

Sitt Nasim is the oldest maga of the covenant and a possible candidate for Praeco (see page 333). She came to the Tribunal at the end of the eleventh century, after founding, together with Anteo, the covenant of Victrix, home to her superior, the Exarch of Iberia and Provence, Medea of Tremere. Sitt Nasim holds five voting *sigils*: her own, those of three of her apprentices, and one belonging to her apprentice's apprentice, and in the not-too-distant future she will try to get those of her lineage who remain at Iššáh to move to other covenants.

She is currently head of the *scriptorium* department. As such, she is responsible for copying every book that reaches the covenant and for assessing which ones may be in greatest demand so that they can be improved, and thus exchanged or sold for larger quantities of vis or better enchanted items. Sitt Nasim runs the covenant's binding workshops, which employ more than fifty workers (binders, copyists, ink-makers and so on).

Sitt Nasim organized the first chess tournament in 1151 and, although she has never taken part in any of them, no one has ever seen her lose a game. A devotee of the game, she owns an impressive collection of chess pieces, many of them enchanted.

##### Scriba minor Asāl al-Tremerī

Asāl does not hold his own voting *sigil* and works for his *parens*, Sitt Nasim, in the *scriptorium* department. To win his vote, young Asāl must beat his mistress at chess, so when he is not studying the Arts or enchanting some book for the covenant's library, he spends his few hours of free time reading treatises on the game and memorizing new moves with which to surprise his mistress.

##### Bibliothecarius maior Abū Dulaf al-Tremerī

Abū Dulaf was Sitt Nasim's first apprentice and still does not have his voting *sigil*. As *bibliothecarius* he is charged with preserving Iššáh's immense library and with enlarging it at any cost. Abū Dulaf behaves like a collector, so the covenant holds as many copies and translations of a single book as exist (especially if it is a valuable one). Although the Tremere relies on a dozen mundanes who travel across Mythic Europe to obtain new copies, he also travels a good deal himself; nevertheless, he tries to delegate to his subordinates so that he can look after the library.

Abū Dulaf is the one who chooses the volumes for the winners of the chess tournament, and he sometimes leaks his choice to other covenants to get something in return. As *bibliothecarius maior* he has a great number of Persian manuscripts on chess within reach, but not even with them has he managed to beat his former mistress, Sitt Nasim, a single time.

##### Bibliothecarius minor al-Aʿmaš al-Tremerī

Al-Aʿmaš was Abū Dulaf's apprentice and, as with his master, his voting *sigil* is held by Sitt Nasim. The young Tremere spends little time at the covenant, for he is almost always coming and going from one place to another to acquire the books his master demands. And he does it rather well, partly thanks to his good looks, his melodious voice, his skill with the *būq* and his overflowing charisma.

<!-- p. 174 -->

##### Bibliothecarius minor Abraham ben David al-Bonisagī

Abraham ben David is a great writer; his reflections and lucidity are valuable enough to Iššáh for the *bibliothecarius maior*, Abū Dulaf, to keep him on. Abraham is a philosopher who lives shut away in his treatises on Hebrew law; his only window on the world is his correspondence, vast and steady, with other covenants of philosophers and, of course, with his former Jewish companions from Lucena, now scattered between the kingdom of Leon and the Crown of Aragon. When he is neither studying nor writing, he spends as much time as he can with his friend, the *administrator maior*, Meʾir ibn Yosef.

##### Bibliothecaria minor Agar al-Merkeriyya

The Redcap Agar is a native of Egypt. She was trained at Porta Pandere, and her love of chess (as well as her Jewish faith) brought her to the covenant of Iššáh. Agar works for the Order and, as such, serves as messenger for several covenants near Toledo. However, she also travels the whole Tribunal to show Iššáh's catalogue of books to the covenants she visits, or to obtain the books the *bibliothecarius maior* commissions from her. Although she usually carries a volume or two with her, she generally gathers the requests and wishes of the magi she visits to discuss them with Abū Dulaf and Meʾir ibn Yosef, so that the purchase or sale can be closed at the next Tribunal. Naturally, as a keen chess player (see *Houses of Hermes: True Lineages*, page 95), Agar never misses the chance to play a game of chess and, as a keen collector, she works on new pieces which she then sells to the magi who are still interested in them.

##### Administrator maior Meʾir ibn Yosef al-Ŷerbitonī

The former *rosh yeshiva* of Lucena, Meʾir ibn Yosef, is responsible for the covenant's mundane and magical wealth. As such, he is charged with obtaining the greatest return from each of Iššáh's holdings. Meʾir has just acquired the important vis sources that belonged to the recently vanished Harra, and the secret of how to exploit some of the sources of forgotten Laminium. Thanks to his work, Iššáh is about to enter its Autumn and, after enjoying a Summer of almost 200 years, it promises to be a glorious period.

Meʾir is deeply involved in the Jewish affairs of the city of Toledo. In fact, he is one of the *dayaním* (see page 15) and still teaches at the city's *yeshiva* (Talmudic academy). During the pogrom of 1212, Meʾir was gravely wounded trying to defend his people. Since that year he has been weighing a move to another covenant, but for now he still prefers the refined life of Toledo to the ignorance of other, safer cities.

##### Administratrix minor Zaida al-Ŷerbitoniyya

The muwallad Zaida, a native of Granada, is the maga who has been at the covenant the shortest time: she was trained in the Roman Tribunal and, after passing her Gauntlet, decided to return home. However, when she found the Almohads there, she looked for covenants farther north where she could settle. When, in 1214, Meʾir ibn Yosef heard her recite poetry, he invited her to the covenant and, after she passed the *administrator maior*'s demanding test, she was admitted as a new member. As *administratrix minor*, her duty is to oversee the covenant's sources of wealth and to follow her superior's directions.

### Harra

*All fire gives off light as it burns, and without fail it burns combustible bodies. As a "true" prophetic saying puts it: "the splendors of His Face would burn up every creature His gaze reached."*[^p174-19]

[^p174-19]: Excerpt from *The Splendor of the Fruits of the Journey* by Ibn ʿArabī (Spanish translation by Carlos Varona Narvión).
>**Lifespan:** 934–1195<br>
>**Founders:** Eio of Flambeau, Raina Ex Miscellanea, Ibn Jalaf Ex Miscellanea<br>
>**Aura (type and strength):** Magic, strength 5<br>
>**Reputations:** None

The recently destroyed covenant of Harra (from the Arabic, "basalt desert" or "volcanic land of black stones") held great importance in the Hermetic politics of the Tribunal almost from its beginnings. Harra is the heir to Apromor's tradition in the Peninsula, for it is said that its founder was the very maga who carried out the negotiations with the *saḥirs*.

#### History

Harra was founded in 934, nine years after the *saḥirs* were admitted into the Order. The covenant's founding charter, preserved at Duresca, bears the names of its three founders: the *saḥiras* Raina and Ibn Jalaf and the Flambeau Eio. The fact that a Flambeau chose to found a covenant with two *saḥiras*, and that this same name, Eio, appears in the records of the centuries-old Brigantia, leads the Tribunal's Hermetic scholars to suppose that she must have been the one who carried out the negotiations with the *saḥirs* after the murder of Tareyja, and so the other two founders, Raina and Ibn Jalaf, may well have belonged to the destroyed covenant of Ribāṭ al-ʿAbraj.

Eio chose the name Harra for the ancient volcanic origin of the Campo de Calatrava, where her covenant stood and where an abundant source of Ignem vis could be harvested from the surrounding ignimbrites.

In the last quarter of the tenth century, Harra was chosen by the Tribunal to house the Mercere portal *Undecimus*, which linked it with Porta Pandere. As a result, the *praefectus praetorio* (or *ḥárisun*, as the office later came to be called) of the Portuguese Mercer House had to be chosen from among the Flambeau of the covenant of Harra, which thus became the first dedicated *saḥira* covenant (though always with a Flambeau presence).

<!-- p. 175 -->

As Andalusis, the magi of Harra did not take part in the Schism War and voted in favor of the secession of al-Andalus. During "the Disintegration" almost all its members were already Flambeau, and years later the covenant became involved in mundane intrigues, supporting the figure of the Wolf King. However, while Munio Alfonso Garcés al-Flambī was Praeco, Harra set aside its mundane interests so that the Tribunal could negotiate with the Almohads, which worked until, in 1190, the magi were condemned in Seville. Then, at the close of the Tribunal of 1193, the members of Harra convened an unofficial Tribunal whose attendees swore to stop the followers of Ibn Tūrmat, and in 1195 the opportunity arose to fulfill their promise. The magi of Harra who did not go to Alarcos were expelled from the covenant, while those who did go died. After the battle of Alarcos, the covenant of Harra was destroyed.

In 1220, there is a project to restore Harra, led by the triumvir Nuño of Salionca and the covenants of Duresca and Aedes Saturni (see above).

> #### Story Seeds: The Destruction of Harra
>
> After investigating the ruins of Harra, ʿUmar ibn Abī Ṭūṭ, of the Andalusi covenant of Chazāʾir, concluded that it had been destroyed by the *saḥirs* of the East. Although he shared none of his evidence, his suspicions spread through Iberia and other magi began to echo them, to the point that in 1214 the possible threat of the Order of Suleimān was discussed at the Tribunal.
>
> These magi maintain that Harra was destroyed not by the mundane forces of the armies of the Almohad caliph Abū Yūsuf Yaʿqūb al-Manṣūr, but by the Order of Suleimān, which was also involved in the strange withdrawal of the European crusader forces before the battle of Las Navas de Tolosa began. According to them, the threat is real, so the Tribunal ought to take measures to avert a catastrophe, preferably before 1225, for they believe that will be the year in which the *saḥirs* launch their decisive attack against Iberia.

#### Setting and Physical Description

The ruins of Harra lie beside the lagoons in the ancient volcanic craters of the Campo de Calatrava, specifically beside the lagoon of Lucianego. Although the surroundings are somewhat unhealthy, the Ignem vis sources that can be gathered each year are abundant enough to make it worth ignoring the stench given off by the nearby wetlands.

### Aẓm Alfíl

*Between the knowledge that the artist has of his work and any other knowledge of it there is a great difference. If the work has been executed in accordance with the artist's science, he performs it according to his knowledge; whereas for anyone who contemplates that work, and understands it in his own way, the knowledge follows upon the work.*[^p175-20]

[^p175-20]: Excerpt from *The Guide for the Perplexed* by Maimonides (Spanish translation by David Gonzalo Maeso).
>**Lifespan:** 1012–1177<br>
>**Founder:** Faŷrun al-Verditiyya<br>
>**Aura (type and strength):** Magic, strength 2<br>
>**Reputations:** None

The ruins of Aẓm Alfíl (from the Arabic, "ivory") have been occupied by mundanes. This Verditius covenant, which tried to rival the crafts of Ajabeba, fell when Alfonso VIII of Castile conquered Cuenca.

#### History

When Maslama foretold the ruin of the caliphate (before the Corruption of House Tytalus brought to light the negotiations of the Praeco ʿAbbās ibn Munḏīr with the caliph Al-Ḥakam II), the Verditius craftswoman Faŷrun al-Verditiyya left the covenant of al-Zahrāʾ and settled near Cuenca to found the covenant of Aẓm Alfíl.

Aẓm Alfíl was not officially constituted until the first Tribunal of al-Andalus, in 1012. Throughout its life it produced excellent work in ivory and continued the labor Faŷrun had carried out until then in the palatine city of Madīnat al-Zahrāʾ, from which she took her African contacts so that she could go on importing the precious ivory of the Maghreb.

Faŷrun made works for emirs and kings and trained two apprentices: Catena (who left for Duresca after completing her Gauntlet) and ʾAbyaḍun. All manner of exquisite crafts came out of her workshops and made Aẓm Alfíl prosper, but its fortunes changed when one of Faŷrun's agents secured the trading rights of an important client of Ajabeba. Relations between the two covenants grew strained and several vendettas were declared (see *Houses of Hermes: Mystery Cults*, page 199), until presumably one of them ended Faŷrun's life while she was traveling across the Mediterranean toward Barcelona. When the news reached the covenant, ʾAbyaḍun wrote to the Primus and swore revenge, but he could not keep his word, for a few months later (in 1177) Alfonso VIII of Castile conquered Cuenca. Soon all the Muslims had to leave the city: his workshop assistants departed, and ʾAbyaḍun had to emigrate and abandon the forge.

<!-- p. 176 -->

After the conquest, Cuenca was resettled as a royal town (*realengo*), a hospital for captives run by the Order of Santiago was established, it was made an episcopal see, and it was granted the famous fuero of Cuenca, with 950 laws, among them the one stating that anyone who went on a raid (*algara*) against the Moors would receive a fifth of whatever was won by it.

#### Setting and Physical Description

At the foot of the high walls of the gorges of the Huécar river there are hollows, long since plundered, that now shelter destitute folk. The old forge serves as a storehouse for the families who occupy the ruins of the covenant of Aẓm Alfíl; its rooms lie open to the sky and are wrapped in the vegetation of the river, which floods them seasonally.

> #### Story Seeds: Where Is ʾAbyaḍun?
>
> Faŷrun's former apprentice, ʾAbyaḍun, left Cuenca in the most utter destitution. Since he departed, more than fifty years ago, no one has seen him again. The Verditius of Ajabeba suspect that he may have drowned trying to cross the Mediterranean to carry out his revenge, but this is no more than speculation. ʾAbyaḍun is the only one who remembers the ivory-working techniques of the Umayyad Caliphate, a craft that has been forgotten over the years. The characters' covenant might find some evidence of this Verditius, perhaps one of his works, and follow his trail until they reach him. Perhaps they can persuade him to join the covenant or, if he is dead, they might gather up and study all his magical treasures.

# VII. The Kingdom of Navarre

*[…] the land of the Navarrese, rich in bread, wine, milk and livestock. […] The Navarrese dress in black clothes cut short to the knee, like the Scots […]. They wear, on the other hand, black woolen cloaks that reach down to the elbows […], which they call sayas. As can be seen, they dress badly, just as they also eat and drink badly, for in a Navarrese house it is the custom for the whole family to eat […], mixing all the dishes in a single pot, and with no spoons at all, but with their own hands; and they all drink from the same jug […]. They are a barbarous people […], steeped in wickedness […], of ignoble appearance […], equal in wickedness to the Getae and the Saracens, and sworn enemies of our Gallic nation. […] Nevertheless, they are held to be brave on the field of battle and vigorous in the assault […].*[^p177-21]

[^p177-21]: Excerpt from the *Codex Calixtinus*, anonymous (Spanish translation by Millán Bravo Lozano).

In 1220, the monarch of Navarre is Sancho VII, called the Strong, born of giants and noble of heart, sixty-six years of age. Sancho has filled his kingdom's coffers through the collection of tribute and through his part, ever since Las Navas de Tolosa, in numerous raids into Muslim lands. His triumphs against the Muslims earned him the recognition of Pope Honorius III in 1216, who confirmed his possession of numerous fortresses and granted him leave to build as many as he wished on the frontier of the Almohad Empire. On top of these holdings, Sancho has acquired numerous towns and castles on the borders of La Rioja and Aragon, and a great many urban and rural estates on Aragonese and Navarrese soil (especially in the district of Tudela).

Despite his age, Sancho has no legitimate offspring (his bastard son, Remiro, is bishop of Pamplona), so the sole heir to the crown is Theobald, son of his sister Blanca and the late count of Champagne, Theobald III. The boy will come of age in 1222, so his mother follows the news from Navarre with interest and, in 1225, will take advantage of Sancho's poor health (he will never again leave his fortress at Tudela) to win the favor of the lords of Moncada and Béarn, and so ensure that her son takes the throne of Navarre on her brother's death.

The kingdom of Navarre is the smallest in extent of the kingdoms of Iberia. To the north it borders the county of Gascony (the trans-Pyrenean towns of Mixa, Ostabaret, San Juan Pie de Puerto and Mauleón owe fealty to the king of Navarre), to the west the kingdom of Castile (the city of Laguardia lying at its westernmost point), and to the south and east the Crown of Aragon (with border towns, from north to south, such as Burgui, Javier, Peña, Buñuel and Monteagudo).

The end of this chapter includes a brief description of the independent lordship of Albarracín: although it is not part of the kingdom, its ruler, Pedro Fernández de Azagra, is lord of Estella and therefore a vassal of Sancho VII the Strong.

## The Covenants of the Kingdom of Navarre

After the Schism War, the boundary of the Provençal Tribunal was pushed southward: it now takes in the whole northeastern strip of the kingdom of Navarre, encompassing cities and places such as Pamplona, the Araquil valley and Ibañeta peak, from which pilgrims coming from France catch their first sight of the lands of Iberia and are accustomed to pray to Saint James. It is also traditional to plant a cross there, for when Charlemagne crossed the Pyrenees into Iberia he halted on the peak and left a cross behind (by 1220 they number in the thousands). As a result, a powerful Divine aura has arisen on the spot.

Leaving aside the territories of the Provençal Tribunal, the kingdom of Navarre can be divided into two large regions (from north to south), Tierra Estella and Tudela, described in detail below. The description of each region includes all the covenants found in this kingdom, namely:

| Inhabited Covenants | Lifespan | Votes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Barda | 1102–Present | 2 |
| Al-Quṣṣāṣ | 1158–Present | 2 (3) |

| Ruined Covenants | Lifespan |
| --- | --- |
| Secunda | 810–848 |
| Andelos | 1095–1165 |

<!-- p. 178 -->

## Tierra Estella

Tierra Estella is divided from west to east by the course of the Arga river and is the westernmost region of Navarre, with cities such as Estella itself (an important stop on the Way of Saint James, see page 127), Inzura, Marañón, Los Arcos, Viana, Laguardia, Mendavia, Cárcar and Olite, among others. The north of the region is dominated by the Sierra de Urbasa and the Sierra de Andía, home to the kingdom's highest point (Beriáin, more than 1,400 meters above sea level) and to abundant forests of beech, oak and Portuguese oak. The south of the region has a gentler relief, dominated by the depression of the Ebro valley (whose course marks the border with the Crown of Aragon), which is dotted with numerous stands of holm oak, evergreen oak woods and kermes-oak thickets.

Although Tierra Estella has abundant vis sources (once in the hands of Salionca), the greatest riches lie in the lands to the north, in the Provençal Tribunal, which has led to more than one dispute over resources between the two Tribunals.

At present, the region of Tierra Estella is home to the covenant of al-Quṣṣāṣ, which draws a wealth of magical resources from the beautiful landscapes of northern Navarre.

### Al-Quṣṣāṣ

>**Lifespan:** 1158–Present<br>
>**Founders:** Oriolfi al-Merinitī, Ibn ʿAbdūs al-Merinitī<br>
>**Season:** Spring<br>
>**Aura (type and strength):** Faerie, strength 6<br>
>**Reputations:** Foreigners (Iberian Tribunal) 1<br>
>**Votes:** 2 (3)

The covenant of al-Quṣṣāṣ (Arabic for "the storytellers") is a young Merinita covenant whose members belong to the group known as the Keepers of the Thousand Tales (see *Houses of Hermes: Mystery Cults*, page 145).

#### History

Both Oriolfi, a Valencian, and the Syrian Ibn ʿAbdūs al-Merinitī were trained at Fafḥṣ al-Luŷŷ and kept apart from the Tribunal's politics by the aged Damascene maga Šāhrazād al-Merinitiyya. When Šāhrazād met her Final Twilight, however, Oriolfi and Ibn ʿAbdūs began to take an interest in what was happening in Iberia, and when they discovered that Maksan (the leader of Fafḥṣ al-Luŷŷ) had allied himself with Zafadola, they denounced him to the Quaesitores and left the covenant on the judges' advice, since the latter meant to expel the magi of Fafḥṣ al-Luŷŷ at the Tribunal of 1151.

Although Oriolfi and Ibn ʿAbdūs had found a place in al-Andalus to raise their new covenant, on hearing the story of the covenant of ʿÔlām wā-ʿed they changed their minds and asked Duresca for help in finding a place to settle in the north of Iberia. The Asturian covenant provided them with a new site in the Sierra de Andía, in the kingdom of Navarre, where many faeries lived, in exchange for a share of the vis stocks they harvested in their domains. Oriolfi and Ibn ʿAbdūs accepted and, in 1154, raised their covenant in a powerful Faerie *regio*; its charter was ratified at the ordinary Tribunal of 1158.

The members of al-Quṣṣāṣ began to travel the towns and cities of northern Navarre to hear their legends and so compile them. Having been raised on Eastern and Andalusi tales, the two magi struggled to adapt to their new surroundings and to get the measure of the faeries of the place where they lived. In the early years, Ibn ʿAbdūs misread a fable and ended up offending an important local faerie. The faerie laid a trap for him, and he ended up accused of a mundane crime, which led to his capture while he was resting at an inn in Estella. To keep Oriolfi from searching for him, the faeries threatened him and offered him a bargain: if he completed the training of Roderick, a Gifted child the faeries held captive, they would tell him where Ibn ʿAbdūs was. So Oriolfi agreed and trained the boy, who had the blood of giants, until, in 1214, he was made a magus and given the Hermetic name Ojarra.

<!-- p. 179 -->

Although six years have passed since Ojarra swore the Code, the faeries have still not contacted Oriolfi. In fact, he will hear nothing from them until 1221, when he will receive a visit from a wolfish faerie who will tell him where Ibn ʿAbdūs is imprisoned. After more than thirty years, Oriolfi will go in search of him and, if possible, and if the Navarrese faeries and the judges of Duresca allow it, will flee with him back to al-Andalus, where perhaps his old allies, the faeries of the Valencian marshes, may be able to help them.

#### Setting and Physical Description

The covenant of al-Quṣṣāṣ is a beautiful structure of living wood that grows out of fertile soil, always carpeted with the golden leaves that fall from the magnificent beeches surrounding it. The wind makes a sweet melody as it tangles in the branches of the trees and, at night, it lulls the covenant's inhabitants, easing them into sleep. With the last light of day, the covenant is covered with fireflies that come from all around to sip the nectar of the night-blooming flowers that open on the gnarled walls of al-Quṣṣāṣ.

The covenant lies on the second level of a Faerie *regio*, where there are many dolmens and no trace of the damp or the mist of the mundane level. A few meters to the north lies the crest of a limestone shoulder that offers spectacular views over the whole valley. Were it not for its dark and twisted faerie inhabitants, one could say that al-Quṣṣāṣ occupies an idyllic spot.

Oriolfi is not permitted access to the third level of the *regio*, where, nonetheless, his *filius* Ojarra spends most of his time (although Oriolfi believes he knows how to reach it, he fears the faeries too much to try).

#### Society and Customs

The covenant of al-Quṣṣāṣ was founded as a democracy, although since the disappearance of Ibn ʿAbdūs in 1186 it has not held a single council. Ojarra's elevation to magus has not changed matters either; the young man spends most of his time on the upper level of the *regio*, and Oriolfi usually makes the covenant's decisions unilaterally.

As members of the Keepers of the Thousand Tales, Oriolfi and the wolfish, gigantic Ojarra travel the surrounding towns with their *nūras*, keeping the faeries' legends alive. While the former suffers through the harrowing stories he tells, the latter delights in them, despite the nightmares they conjure up.

> #### Tales of the Middle Ages
>
> Although Oriolfi and Ibn ʿAbdūs were raised on the tales of the *Thousand and One Nights* and, like the rest of the Andalusi *sodales*, know many Eastern tales brought from Baghdad by the Umayyads, in Latin-speaking Iberia the best-known Eastern tales are those collected in the *Disciplina clericalis* of Pedro Alfonso of Huesca (see the Mundane Library appendix).
>
> Like all tales, their aim is always didactic: by blending proverbs, fables, verses and comparisons (more or less abstract), they make teaching easier to grasp, which turns them into powerful tools for influencing cultures and societies. This might not go unnoticed by Durato, which could try to win the storytellers over in order to influence mundanes, although, of course, the aims of al-Quṣṣāṣ are quite different.
>
> #### Story Seeds: The Poisoned Water
>
> *Through Estella flows the Ega, its water sweet, wholesome and extraordinary. Through the town called Los Arcos runs a deadly stream; and beyond Los Arcos, beside the first hospital, […] flows a stream deadly to the horses and men who drink from it.*[^p179-XII]
>
> Every year, Oriolfi must harvest the abundant Perdo vis source concentrated in the waters of the Odrón river, which runs through the town of Los Arcos (near Estella), and hand two-thirds of it over to Duresca. Although mundanes have shunned the river ever since the *Codex Calixtinus* branded it deadly or harmful, in recent years the *merino* of Estella has decided to put an end to the matter by setting up crosses at its fords and paying a priest to bless its waters every year. As a result, Oriolfi has noticed that the river yields fewer pawns each year, so to avoid Duresca's fine he has to make up the shortfall from his own vis. But in 1220 he has not even managed to gather enough pawns to pay Duresca, so he will have to draw on the covenant's stores.
>
> Oriolfi believes the time has come to investigate what is making the stream's Perdo vis dwindle, which will mean confronting the local civil and ecclesiastical authorities. Will he seek the player characters' help?
>
> [^p179-XII]: Excerpt from the *Codex Calixtinus*, anonymous (Spanish translation by Millán Bravo Lozano).

#### The Magi of al-Quṣṣāṣ

##### Ibn ʿAbdūs al-Merinitī

*Seeing life slip away from me, and knowing for certain that the end draws near, I would dwell alone on a mountain, close to the summit where the wind blows, gathering dew in what remains of my life or drawing water from beneath the sand. My friends, who has tasted death but once? I have tasted it fifty times. Today, as I reach the end, it seems to me that my existence was like a flash of lightning.*[^p180-22]

[^p180-22]: Poem from *The Treatise of Familiar Spirits and Demons* by Ibn Shuhayd (Spanish translation by Salvador Barberá).

Ibn ʿAbdūs was clapped in irons by mundane soldiers in 1186, who threw him into a dark pit in one of the Almohad castles, where he was forgotten. When Sancho VII conquered Arcediello (on the border with Valencia) in 1216, the castle's garrison found Ibn ʿAbdūs during their occupation. No one knew who he was or what he had done, though he bore the mark of sorcerers on his cheek, so they left him where he was. The rigors of his captivity have cost Ibn ʿAbdūs his sight, his teeth and his hair, and left him unable to walk. Moreover, to keep from dying of thirst, he has been forced to suck at the mineral growths on the walls of his cell. As a result, his sanity falters with every passing year, and he no longer even remembers his own name.

##### Oriolfi al-Merinitī

Oriolfi is a mature magus who has spent the last years of his life at the mercy of the whims of the Navarrese faeries: they coerced him into training an apprentice, forced him to sing his story through the villages and towns of Navarre and, worst of all, made him fear them, so that he has lost his dignity. In 1220, he hopes to make amends for his mistakes by going to the rescue of his old brother, Ibn ʿAbdūs, with whom he will flee to al-Andalus, where the only thing they will have to worry about is not naming the Prophet in their tales.

##### Ojarra "Handia" of Merinita

The young magus Ojarra, whom the faeries call "Handia," is one of the bastard sons of Sancho VII the Strong. Like his father, he has the blood of giants in his veins (he stands nearly two and a half meters tall) and, through his contact with the Navarrese faeries, he has the head of a cynocephalus, with distinctly wolfish features. Thanks to the cloak his protectresses gave him, however, the young man can exchange his two and a half meters of height and his bestial face for a far more ordinary build. In this way he can pass unnoticed among mundanes, whom he often terrifies with his powerful, melodious bass voice when he sings the legends of the faeries he lives among.
