### Andelos

>**Lifespan:** 1095–1165<br>
>**Founders:** Morberga Ex Miscellanea, Agneta of Flambeau<br>
>**Aura (type and strength):** Magic, strength 6<br>
>**Reputations:** None

The ruins of the extinct Andelos are clear proof of the predation rife in northern Iberia, where the younger covenants must struggle against the hegemony of the Tribunal's oldest covenants.

#### History

The magae of the Normandy Tribunal, Morberga Ex Miscellanea and Agneta of Flambeau, arrived together with the settlers who resettled the banks of the Arga river at the end of the eleventh century. Responsible for their arrival was Sancho Ramírez, king of Aragon and Pamplona, who granted them a settlement charter (*carta puebla*), which the magae turned to their advantage by settling on the ruins of the ancient temple of Apollo in the Roman city of Andelos.

The covenant fared handsomely during its first twenty years, using its offensive might to launch raids against the settlements beyond the kingdom's border and so enrich itself. Its raids came to an end, however, when, at the Tribunal of 1123, the magae fell out with Munio Alfonso Garcés al-Flambī, of the covenant of Harra. Although neither party made the reasons for the quarrel public, the fact is that the Frankish magae of Andelos never again attacked the territories beyond the borders, and sought other sources of funding for their increasingly prosperous covenant. Thus Morberga and Agneta acquired the pontage rights of the bridge at Gares, an important crossroads where the French Way of Saint James meets the Jaca route, and then took control of the pilgrims' hospital at Gares, from which they began to control the town's trade. Freed from mundane needs, they at last concentrated on their Hermetic research, at least until 1146, when a Redcap delivered them a missive from Duresca accusing them of dealing with mundanes.

Duresca invited them to settle the matter in a closed trial a year before the next Tribunal, and the two magae presented themselves at the judges' covenant in the year 1150. The vis fine imposed on them was so great that they were forced to seek a loan from the Mercer House of Aedes Saturni, but not even that saved them: the interest was so high that, at the ordinary Tribunal of 1165, they declared themselves insolvent. As a gesture of goodwill, Aedes Saturni forgave the debt on condition that they hand over all the covenant's resources to Duresca, including the pontage rights and control of the hospital at Gares.

And so the two magae abandoned Iberia and their covenant. Over time its ashlars and marbles were stolen, and its old chambers came to be inhabited by folk best not crossed at night.

#### Setting and Physical Description

The ruins of Andelos rise over an ancient Roman temple dedicated to Apollo, from which the magical power of its aura springs. A few meters away runs the Arga river, whose water was used to irrigate the covenant's crops and meet its inhabitants' needs. Among the covenant's empty chambers one can still make out the wall-walk and the magnificent baths the two Frankish magae enjoyed.

Because Gares (Duresca's domain) lies so close, no magus has dared to settle there again, even though the site offers ideal conditions for housing a covenant.

> #### Story Seeds: A Piece of Jerusalem
>
> It is said that near Andelos, in the vicinity of the town of Olite, there stands a basilica dedicated to Our Lady of the Olive, somewhere within which lies a small wooden box holding a handful of earth from Jerusalem. This box was brought back by Saturnino Lasterra de Artajona, who served as captain of the troops of Don Ramiro, *infante* of Navarre, during the taking of Jerusalem in the year 1099. According to legend, Godfrey of Bouillon himself handed the box to Saturnino so that he could carry it back home, where the soldier hid it somewhere in the basilica. Perhaps, knowing this story, the magi will go there in search of this powerful relic when they find themselves in need of its divine power.

## Tudela

*First I set out from my city (Tudela) for the city of Saragossa; I went down the course of the river Ebro to Tortosa, and from there I journeyed two days to ancient Tarragona, (which) was of the construction of Greek Cyclopes, the like of which is not found in all the lands of Spain.*[^p182-23]

[^p182-23]: Excerpt from *The Book of Travels of Benjamin of Tudela* (Spanish translation by José Ramón Magdalena Nom de Déu).

The lands of Tudela[^p182-24] are the southernmost in the kingdom of Navarre, with towns such as Caparroso, Milagro, Valtierra, Corella, Tudela itself (from which the Jew Benjamin of Tudela set out in 1160; see Appendix I), Fontellas, Ablitas and Buñuel, among others. The east of the region is taken up by the Bárdenas, a semi-desert landscape full of gullies, mesas and solitary hills, while the south is dominated by the depression of the Ebro valley, with its rich farmland. The region is dotted with holm oaks, kermes-oak thickets and pine woods.

[^p182-24]: In the mid-thirteenth century the *merindades* of Tudela, Estella, Sangüesa and Pamplona will be created.

<!-- p. 183 -->

At present, the region of Tudela is home to the covenant of Barda, which is in dispute over vis sources with the Aragonese covenant of Caium.

### Barda

>**Lifespan:** 1102–Present<br>
>**Founder:** Yéñego of Flambeau<br>
>**Season:** Spring<br>
>**Aura (type and strength):** Magic, strength 3<br>
>**Reputations:** Thieves (Caium) 3<br>
>**Votes:** 2

The covenant of Barda survives through the systematic theft of the abundant vis sources of wintry Caium. Because of its criminal acts, its *ductor* stays politically active so as to keep abreast of everything that happens at the Tribunals and be ready to act in case of danger.

#### History

Barda was founded by Yéñego, the son of a nobleman from the town of Arguedas, during the Tribunal of 1102. The aged magus, who until then had lived in Provence, had inherited the right to graze the Bárdenas with his family's more than five hundred head of livestock, a right he owed to the privilege that the king of Aragon and Pamplona, Sancho Ramírez, had granted the town of Arguedas after conquering the territory from the Muslims.

Determined to strike out on his own, Yéñego returned to his family's land, where he settled in surroundings suited to his Study Requirement Flaw. Unfamiliar with the idiosyncrasies of the Iberian Tribunal, Yéñego supported the Andalusi magi at the Tribunal of 1109, which earned him the enmity of the northern covenants. In the aftermath, Barda's main vis source was destroyed and the covenant was left in deep isolation. Indeed, the only magus who joined the covenant was Ansour, a young Flambeau trained in Novgorod, who had been born in Estella and was returning to his homeland after passing his Gauntlet.

Yéñego shared his wealth with young Ansour until 1123. At that Tribunal, the news brought by Pasífae al-Merkeriyya of the destruction of the Mercer House of Tāfīlālt stirred Yéñego deeply. Despite Ansour's warnings, Yéñego set off for Africa in search of some clue that would unravel the mystery and expose what he believed to be lies spun by the corrupt covenants of the Tribunal's north. The old magus never returned, however, and when, five years later, someone spread word in Arguedas that Yéñego had died, the crown's *merino* seized the privilege to work the lands of Yéñego's family.

Overnight, Ansour found himself without magical or mundane income, in a covenant whose inhabitants, loyal to Yéñego, had begun to leave. Although Ansour was a young magus who knew nothing of the Tribunal and had scarcely any political experience, he decided to attend the ordinary Tribunal of 1130 on Barda's behalf. There he discovered the hostility his covenant aroused among the Flambeau of Salionca, and suffered firsthand the rejection of Duresca and Aedes Saturni. Not without considerable difficulty, he persuaded the Redcaps to show him the registered vis sources around his covenant and, on finding that there were unclaimed lands beyond the kingdom's southern border, began to explore that area in search of new vis sources. That was how Ansour came upon the sources of the century-old Caium, and that was how he decided to steal them in order to survive.

Although at first he stole in moderation, as year after year he saw that the magi of Caium did not even appear at the Tribunals, he began to take more and more pawns from them, until, at the end of the twelfth century, he decided to exploit to the full every source of the old covenant that he knew of. So, when Caium sent its grogs to investigate, Ansour had them murdered.

At times Ansour thinks this will not end well, but neither can he stop, for it is the only way he has of keeping going. Every seven years he promises himself he will do it no more, but he never keeps his word, and usually invents excuses to justify his thefts and murders. Indeed, in 1220 the covenant is beginning to flourish. Ansour has achieved a certain stability that the covenant's inhabitants are grateful for, and he even has two more magi: the young Šams al-Praliḥiyya, from Harra, and Tages of Tremere, one of the apprentices of Sitt Nasim, of the Toledan covenant of Iššáh.

#### Setting and Physical Description

Barda is perched atop a broad, arid mesa surrounded by deep gullies. From its vantage point, the covenant's inhabitants can see the surrounding land for kilometers around and enjoy spectacular sunsets. The violence of the *cierzo* in the area has shaped the covenant's layout, which is spread over three squat, single-story buildings joined by low walls that shelter the covenant's inhabitants from the wind. The three buildings have small, shuttered windows and flat roofs, all of them the same earthy color as their surroundings.

Barda's largest building has room for only three *sancta*, since Yéñego did not think it would ever be occupied by more magi. Barda also has a *castellum aquae*, an impressive cistern that stores the water drawn from a well that only flows in spring, guarded by magical protections so that no one wastes a single drop. The covenant's last building belongs to the grogs: a humble but functional construction. Because of the difference in temperature between night and day, Ansour is in the habit of heating the covenant's chambers by magic, and as a result Barda is beginning to be affected by Warping.

<!-- p. 184 -->

In 1220, Ansour keeps the few books Barda owns in his *sanctum*, since the covenant lacks a library and a council chamber (which Ansour plans to remedy by raising a magical building with the spell *Conjuring the Mystic Tower*, which he has managed to copy thanks to the covenant's surplus vis).

#### Society and Customs

Barda is an autocracy ruled by the *ductor*. Although it was a democracy in its early days, when Ansour began stealing Caium's vis sources the Flambeau amended the charter so that no one who came after could compromise him. However, since until recently the covenant had no members but him, this form of government has not yet been put into practice. For the moment, Ansour takes the newly arrived magi's opinions into account as though it were a democracy, but only because no important matter has yet come up. With a Tremere in the covenant, however, Ansour knows that the current situation will not last.

Since Yéñego's departure, the mundanes who stayed on at the covenant have developed a curious superstition concerning the *cierzo*: no inhabitant of the covenant leaves the buildings when the wind blows, for fear of going mad. Ansour is tired of hearing these stories and, although he does not give them much weight, he feels increasingly uneasy, since on windy days the covenant is left unprotected. Now that Šams is at Barda, he trusts that she will be able to master the jinn of the Bárdenas and defend the covenant against any threat.

For all their fear, Barda's grogs are thieves and murderers who carry out their raids beyond the Bárdenas. It is they who, on Ansour's orders, steal Caium's vis and murder the Bjornaer covenant's grogs as they arrive.

#### The Magi of Barda

##### Ductor Ansour of Flambeau

Ansour is a hypocritical and cynical magus who lives by lying. Nature has endowed him with kindly features and an innocent gaze which, together with his mild voice, incline hearts to trust him. Ansour is a self-indulgent monster who feeds on the feelings of those around him to build a better image of himself. His powers of persuasion are such that he often manages to deceive even himself, so that, despite his many crimes, he does not even feel guilty: Ansour has no remorse.

With Barda now prospering, he trusts that Šams and Tages will be the first of many magi to end up in the covenant, for which he has great plans. To that end, all he has to do is what he has always done: smile and lie.

##### Šams al-Praliḥiyya

Young Šams lived at Harra until 1195, when the rest of its members decided to go to the battle of Alarcos. Like other magi who disagreed, she was expelled from the covenant and had to seek a home in the north. That is how she met Ansour and came to join Barda at the beginning of the thirteenth century. Since her arrival, Šams has been following the trail of the *jinni* that dwells in the desert; she knows it is very powerful, so she keeps honing her abilities in order to be able to summon it without risk.

Šams is an intelligent and perceptive woman, so if she ever learns Ansour's secrets, she will end up denouncing him to the Tribunal.

##### Tages of Tremere

Tages's memory holds only happy moments from his childhood, and that memory is one of the most important parts of his person and his magic. Born into a humble Jewish family in Toledo, it was this very memory — as prodigious as it was selective about the recollections it managed to preserve in pristine form — that led his parents to go to the school of translators in search of a better future for the boy. As luck would have it, Sitt Nasim was present during the family's visit, and the Tremere maga did not hesitate for an instant to recruit the little boy who seemed blessed with such singular gifts.

Tages has been Sitt Nasim's last apprentice (to date, at least), but he has without doubt also been one of the most unusual. It took the maga only a few weeks to discover his Gift and the unique peculiarities surrounding it: the boy had a special facility with memories, both other people's and his own, which in turn gave him an astonishing ease in learning languages and, with the proper training, setting them down in books. As a scribe he was priceless, but as a Tremere apprentice… he was a diamond in the rough.

Sitt Nasim subjected the young boy to a brutal pace of learning: in the mornings he read the classics in every language possible, in the afternoons he devoted himself to learning magic and at night, without his *parens* knowing, the boy, who still wanted more, practiced one thing after another in his room, with his prodigious memory as his only tool. He would spend days without leaving the school's rooms or the halls of Iššáh, coming out only to eat, and always heartily, as if food nourished not only his body but his soul as well.

When Tages completed his apprenticeship, he knew he had traveled only half the road. His *parens* would keep his voting sigil until he had proven his worth. But he could never have imagined that Sitt Nasim would send him to a remote covenant in the heart of Navarre. What business did he have there? From the little he knew of Barda, it was nothing more than a minor covenant inhabited by irrelevant magi. His talents seemed utterly useless in such a setting, but most incredible of all was that his *parens* intended Tages to take control of the covenant, something that, *a priori*, struck him as a daunting task.

On his arrival at Barda in 1216, Tages's worst fears seemed confirmed. Ansour, for all his kindly manner and even kinder words, made his hair stand on end from the very first moment, although even now, several years later, he does not know whether he is judging the *ductor* unfairly. As for Šams, her dealings with the jinn rather unsettle someone as fond of peace and quiet as Tages. Yet the magus is also quite perceptive, and in the time he has spent at the covenant he has already seen enough suspicious things to understand Sitt Nasim's purpose in sending him there. Barda seems to have material resources far beyond what would be expected of such a covenant, and although Tages has not yet discovered where they come from, he knows that this is the key to taking control of the covenant and, with a little luck, getting rid of Ansour… if he can summon the courage to do it.

<!-- p. 185 -->

<!-- p. 186 -->

Recently, Tages has met Stellatus, one of the Bjornaer followers of Caium, who seems determined to rouse his covenant from its torpor and uncover those responsible for the thefts from its vis sources. Stellatus has spoken with Tages on a couple of occasions, trying to draw out of him what part Barda might have played in those thefts, but the Tremere, unaware of all Ansour's machinations, has not yet begun to put two and two together…

### Secunda

>**Lifespan:** 810–848<br>
>**Founders:** Somnus of Tremere, Átropo of Tremere, Scorilo of Tremere<br>
>**Aura (type and strength):** Magic, strength 3<br>
>**Reputations:** Schismatic (Iberian Tribunal) 1

The covenant of Secunda was established at the Rhine Tribunal of 810, at the same time as the Andalusi Alma Mater and the Norman Confluensis, and chose one of the meanders of the Ebro as its site. Today, almost everyone in Iberia remembers two of its founders' names with bitterness: the infamous Somnus and the twisted Átropo.

#### History

Scorilo of Tremere (the sole survivor of Prima) established the covenant of Secunda in the name of Somnus and Átropo. Having returned to Iberia after more than a decade at Lycaneon, he looked for a suitable place to raise the second Tremere covenant on the Peninsula. Scorilo chose to raise it in a weak magic aura beside the Ebro, not far from Tudela, in the domains of the governor Musā ibn Fortún, of the Banū Qasī. After years of study in the field, Scorilo wrote a report for Lycaneon singling out the Qasī as one of the clans that might wield the most power in Iberia, so the *domus magna* charged Átropo with establishing relations with them, and the aged Somnus with taking the reins of the Peninsula to consolidate the House's power at the far western edge of the Order.

In his first years, Somnus worked with Tello of Guernicus, *filius* of Ranemiro and then an eminent magus, to win the trust of one of the most representative figures on the Peninsula and learn from him everything the House needed, tentatively beginning his rise on the region's Hermetic stage. Secunda took part in the wars against Damhan-Allaidh and hosted in its halls the resolution of the second Grand Tribunal of 817, at which it was accepted that *certamen* should be decisive in settling any dispute.

By 822, Somnus had won the trust of many of his Peninsular *sodales*, and he finished writing his name into the history of Iberia when he acted as host for Priamitus's visit and, together with Tello, expanded the illegitimate Peripheral Code of the Peninsula, which granted the Mercere a series of privileges (still in force to this day). By that same year, Átropo had consolidated her relations with the Qasī of Arnedo and, thanks to them, was able a few years later to raise the covenant of Tertia, barely two days' journey to the west, to strengthen Tremere's plan to dominate the Order.

In his eagerness to strengthen the trust the magi had placed in him, Somnus expanded the Peninsular pseudo-code again in 836, and managed to have one of the Quaesitores of Magvillus join the covenant to cover up each of the violations of the Code he committed over all those years. Secunda was involved, together with Tertia, in the summons issued in 845 by the king of Asturias, Ramiro I (see page 69), and was finally abandoned in 848, after Somnus and the rest of the covenant's members were nullified following the Sundering.

#### Setting and Physical Description

Half a day's journey from Tudela, the ruins of Secunda lie beside a meander on the north bank of the Ebro, near a small river beach sheltered by abundant vegetation. In its day it was a majestic covenant with lush gardens where the magi could stroll beside the river. After the Sundering, its finest crafted works were plundered by other covenants, and the building was left abandoned and in ruins.

<!-- p. 187 -->

In 1220, the old walls rise no more than a meter from the ground and have been overrun by the abundant, lush vegetation of the Ebro's floodplain; no one could tell that these stones once belonged to a powerful Tremere covenant.

> #### Story Seeds: Dill
>
> *[Dill], when boiled with olive oil, makes the oil a solvent, soothes pains, ripens soft, unripe tumors and induces sleep.*[^p187-XIII]
>
> In life, Somnus planted a great deal of dill in his private garden from some magical seeds the Tremere had acquired in Barcelona. A keen lover of plants, Somnus managed to make these herbs grow up to two meters tall and produce pawns of Mentem vis (in their flowers) and Corpus vis (in their small fruits). However, like so many other secrets, knowledge of this vis source died with Somnus.
>
> This source might be in the player characters' possession, or they might discover it during a story. As mentioned above, the Mentem vis is obtained from the dill's flowers, which must be harvested in summer while they are still open. The Corpus vis, for its part, comes from the ripe fruits, in autumn, once the flowers have darkened. Obviously, if the flowers are harvested they cannot be pollinated, and so bear no fruit: in other words, if the Corpus vis is harvested, the Mentem vis cannot be, and vice versa.
>
> In 1220, the young people of nearby Tudela are in the habit of using the ruins of Secunda as a place for revelry, where they often drink until dawn. Yet none of them gets drunk. If the characters watch them, they will discover that all of them wear crowns made of green dill sprigs while they drink, since the plant's solvent and drying properties keep its wearers from becoming intoxicated. Their activities, however, are stripping the plantation bare, and the vis is disappearing. Matters could become complicated if some nobleman's son is among the revelers. How will the magi resolve this "minor" matter?
>
> [^p187-XIII]: Excerpt from *The Book of the Generalities of Medicine* by Averroes (Spanish translation by V. de Benito and A. Morales).

## The Lordship of Albarracín

The independent lordship of Albarracín is ruled by Don Pedro Fernández de Azagra (a vassal of the king of Aragon as lord of Estella), and, unlike the Crown of Aragon, some Muslims still live there. Albarracín has an active transhumant herding trade (see page 164) that stretches from the Sierra de Albarracín to the basins of the Júcar and the Segura, on a route twenty days long.

The lordship lies between the borders of the Crown of Aragon and Castile, and is crossed from east to west by the Guadalaviar river, the same river that encircles the hill on which the city and fortress of Albarracín are built. To the north and south, the region is guarded by mountain ranges under 2,000 meters high, where rivers such as the Tagus and the Júcar rise, and where towns such as Codoniat and Foya de la Grulla, among others, can be found.

Despite its natural wealth and its vis sources, the lordship of Albarracín has never been home to a covenant (the nearest is the extinct Aẓm Alfíl, in Castile), so it could make a good starting place for player characters.

<!-- p. 188 -->

# VIII. The Crown of Aragon

In the year 1220, the Crown of Aragon is divided into two main areas: the kingdom of Aragon and the Catalan counties, the latter being a series of lordships, once under French influence, that gradually won their independence from the ninth century onward. Several of them were annexed by or unified with the county of Barcelona, the most powerful of them all, and together with it became part of the Crown of Aragon, although others, such as the county of Urgell, still keep their independence. To the south, the marquisate of Lérida is also part of the Crown.

After the crushing defeat suffered at the battle of Muret in 1213, the Crown has lost a good part of its possessions north of the Pyrenees, such as Provence, and has a king who is barely more than a child, Jaime I. The defeat at Muret also put an end, for all practical purposes, to the possibility of forming a great Mediterranean state combining the Crown of Aragon with the Occitan possessions, so Jaime, who is destined to become a historic monarch, will expand the kingdom's borders in another direction, until they include Valencia and Majorca, among other cities. Young Jaime is now twelve years old; two years ago he took over from the former regent of the kingdom, Count Sancho I of Cerdanya, and he has held full rights over the kingdom since he was declared of age at the Cortes of Lérida in 1218.

The Crown of Aragon is bounded on the east by the Mediterranean Sea, from the northern tip of the county of Gerona down to Tortosa and Amposta, the kingdom's southernmost possessions in 1220. To the west it borders the kingdoms of Navarre and Castile, while to the south it borders the Almohad Empire, where the independent region of Albarracín serves as a neutral zone between the two realms. To the north it borders several Provençal regions, starting with the recently lost county of Roussillon in the east, and including Foix, Comminges and Bigorre, among others. Jaca is one of the towns closest to the border. The northern Hermetic boundary between the Iberian Tribunal and the Provençal Tribunal lies somewhat further south, running roughly as far as Gerona in the east and Pamplona in the west.

## The Covenants of the Crown of Aragon

The Crown of Aragon has had an almost constant Hermetic presence since the founding of the Tribunal, and although many of the oldest covenants no longer exist in 1220, others with several centuries of life behind them still stand, and some of them have carried great weight in the Tribunal at different times.

From a Hermetic point of view, the Crown can be divided into two great regions: the county of Barcelona and the kingdom of Aragon. The area also includes a small anomaly within the Order: a covenant located at Gerona, geographically within the Provençal Tribunal but politically belonging to Iberia. Indeed, that region has frequently been a source of conflict between the two Tribunals.

## The Kingdom of Aragon

The kingdom of Aragon occupies the northwestern half of the Crown and stretches from the county of Ribagorza in the north to the city of Teruel in the south, and from Alcañiz in the east to Calatayud and Tudela, its two westernmost towns. The kingdom is dominated by the city of Saragossa, conquered from the Muslims in 1118, which soon became its capital. It is a city in whose streets the presence of Islam can still be clearly seen, full of contrasts and exotic sights. It was the former capital of the Upper March and is now the base from which the Christian monarchs wage their struggle against the Almohads. Rivaling Saragossa in importance is the city of Huesca, conquered by Pedro I in 1096, which in 1220 is still a town of great political and social significance, not only within the kingdom and the Crown but throughout the Peninsula.

<!-- p. 189 -->

Aragon has always had an abundant Hermetic presence, and Saragossa in particular has hosted several covenants within its walls. Today, however, not a single inhabited covenant remains in the city. Even so, it is often visited by the many Redcaps who belong to the goliards, and who take advantage of the city's cosmopolitan character to conduct their business and trade information amid the bustle of its streets. It is one of the few places in all Iberia where goliards can still be found, for they have fallen into disgrace after enjoying great popularity in earlier decades. All manner of stories are told about these Redcaps, foremost among them one that astonished the city a couple of years ago, when the oliphant of Gaston of Béarn was stolen from the basilica of El Pilar for a few days, only to reappear later as if by magic. Although there is no conclusive proof, both the bishop of Saragossa and House Mercere itself suspect that the culprit may have been some unruly Redcap who wanted to play a cruel joke on the Church.

Outside Saragossa, almost all the Hermetic covenants that exist in 1220 occupy far less civilized places, such as Caium, on the Moncayo, and Mons Niger, in the arid Monegros.

### Caium

>**Lifespan:** 899–Present<br>
>**Founders:** Didericus Bjornaer (formerly Merinita), Luitgarde Bjornaer<br>
>**Season:** Winter<br>
>**Aura (type and strength):** Magic, strength 4 (main cave); Magic, strength 2 (gorge); Magic, strength 7 (Tomb of Cacus)<br>
>**Reputations:** Visionaries (Bjornaer magi) 3, Primitive (Iberian Tribunal) 2<br>
>**Votes:** 4

<!-- p. 190 -->

Caium is an exceedingly unusual covenant, for in more than four centuries of existence it has had almost no contact with the rest of the Tribunal. With a distant past closely tied to House Merinita, it is today an entirely Bjornaer covenant whose members form a fraternity devoted wholly and utterly to the study and investigation of a formidable magical resource.

#### History

After the founding of the Order of Hermes, many wizards came to Durenmar to join the newborn brotherhood and study under the auspices of one of its Founders. Such was the case of Didericus, a wizard of Germanic origin who traveled to the Black Forest to meet Merinita. The "lady in green" was a mysterious figure, possessed of great arcane knowledge, who always welcomed new followers, training them in her mysteries and asking them to travel the world. After spending a few years at Durenmar and learning the ways of House Merinita, Didericus left the Rhine to journey to the far south of Europe, to Iberia, a land of dense forests where he could settle and develop his newly learned Arts. He was accompanied on his journey by his own son, a boy in whom he had already detected the Gift, and by Luitgarde, a Bjornaer follower from Pomerania whom he had met at Durenmar and who was also looking to settle in a new covenant.

The group eventually reached the Ordesa valley, a mountainous, forested area south of the Pyrenees in the north of Huesca. However, after trying several possible sites without success, they moved further south until, drawn by the local legends, they came to the Moncayo, one of the highest peaks in the whole Iberian System. The mountain's origin varied from legend to legend: some said the Moncayo was born when a wizard of antiquity turned his three sons into three mountains, each taller than the last: the Moncayo, the Ocejón and the Alto Rey. Others said that in remote times the giant Cacus had taken refuge there, and was later slain by none other than Hercules. The Greek hero buried his enormous body beneath the mountain, which thus came to be known as Mons Cacus, the mountain of Cacus, or Moncayo. Whatever its origin, Didericus and Luitgarde soon found the ideal place to site their covenant. More than 1,000 meters up, in a narrow, hard-to-reach gorge surrounded by forest, they found an ancient cavern from which a strong magical aura emanated, and it was there that they finally decided to settle, at the end of the eighth century.

After Quendalon's victory during the sad events of the House Divided, Didericus was accepted into House Bjornaer by Luitgarde, and little by little the Bjornaer followers gained ascendancy in the covenant. Luitgarde, a member of the Arelie clan (see *Houses of Hermes: Mystery Cults*, page 34), became Caium's sole leader, and it was she who made the discovery that would completely change the covenant's identity. At the end of the ninth century, while enlarging the original cave, the magi found an even older cavern with a powerful magical aura, its walls covered in cave paintings depicting ancient men worshipping what looked like a gigantic humanoid creature with goatlike features, including a pair of great horns. Luitgarde spent months studying those paintings and reached a startling conclusion: this creature was what popular folklore had eventually turned into Cacus, but it was no ordinary giant. She was convinced it was a chimera, one of the mythological beasts around which one of the greatest Mysteries of House Bjornaer revolves (see *Houses of Hermes: Mystery Cults*, page 58). And most important of all, it was a chimera with a human component, something considered impossible in Bjornaer doctrine. Convinced that the chimera's body might lie there, and that its spirit indeed still pervaded that chamber, Luitgarde made the cavern a sacred precinct and abandoned the conventional doctrines of the Arelie clan to devote all her studies to discovering and better understanding the chimera. She thus formed a fraternity wholly independent of the clan, yet one that still followed its original precepts of honoring the memory of the ancestors, and she decided the time had come to approach the Order to constitute her covenant, which would come to be known as Caium, after the name of the mountain, which is covered in snow for much of the year and which the Romans also knew as Mons Caium, the "hoary mountain."

From then on, the covenant's direction changed radically. Luitgarde spent the last years of her life almost entirely in the Tomb of Cacus, as the painted cavern came to be called, and in her final months she did not leave her wolf heartbeast form until she vanished without warning in 905, when she was more than 150 years old. Her doctrines lived on through the other members of the fraternity. Although the Tomb of Cacus has always been its heart, from then on the covenant expanded both underground, into new caverns, and onto the nearby slopes, where the more solitary magi carved small dwellings in the rock to house their laboratories and *sancta*. And although Caium has had little contact with the Order, for centuries it has been a place of pilgrimage for many Bjornaer magi, especially the Arelie who wished to learn more about the chimerae. Access to the Tomb of Cacus is strictly controlled, but the members of the fraternity have always been willing to pass on much of the knowledge accumulated over the years.

Unfortunately, this scant contact with the Order has made Caium an oddity, living on the margins of many key events in Hermetic history and even of the protection the Order itself provides. The Schism War passed almost unnoticed on the Moncayo, save for the visit of a few fugitive Diedne from outside Iberia who sought refuge there before continuing their journey. Moreover, many of the vis sources the magi of Caium discovered in their first decades of exploring the Moncayo have been seized or stolen from them over the centuries. This has slowly sunk the covenant into a decadent Winter, with its members, all of them Bjornaer today, focused on the doctrines Luitgarde laid down more than three hundred years ago.

In 1220, the covenant is at a crucial moment that may end in its destruction or lead to a new Spring. On the one hand, they are suffering the harassment of Barda (see insert on page 192), which, combined with their ignorance of the Order, prevents them from defending themselves before a Tribunal. On the other hand, Stellatus, an elderly Arelie magus from the Normandy Tribunal, has recently arrived at the covenant, and although Stellatus and Lacerta share Hermetic ancestors, they hold completely opposed philosophical views. Most importantly, Stellatus knows the Order well, so he could mount a defense that would allow Caium to survive Barda's harassment. However, Stellatus opposes the covenant's central policy and its obsessive study of the Tomb of Cacus, which may provoke a confrontation with Lacerta with unpredictable consequences…

<!-- p. 191 -->

#### Setting and Physical Description

Caium lies halfway up the Moncayo, on one of its most rugged faces, half-hidden inside an almost inaccessible gorge that only the most experienced mountaineers can reach. Because of its remote location, the covenant receives very few visitors, Redcaps included, who do not include it on their usual routes. For the same reason, it is a self-sufficient, spartan covenant that lives off the resources around it, without needlessly exploiting Mother Nature.

The covenant consists mainly of two caves, one larger than the other, and several nearby structures built to take advantage of the natural surroundings: there are small artificial caves dug into the side of the ravine and, on a knoll above the gorge, several wooden huts raised on platforms in the trees, where much of the turb lives. A stairway carved into the side of the gorge gives easy access from that knoll down to the floor of the gorge, where the entrance to the cave lies, although a slip on any of its steps can be fatal.

The main cave is some forty meters across and is divided into several chambers separated by magically created stone walls that merge organically with the natural walls to form a curious labyrinth that disorients newcomers. The cave houses a couple of storerooms and meeting rooms, as well as a hall where the Arelie teach the covenant's visitors. All of it is rather spartan, and much of the furniture is made from the natural material shaped by magic into benches, shelves and the like. Several tunnels, some natural and others artificial, lead from the main cave to other rooms and private quarters. These include the *sancta* of the resident magi, as well as the treasury, which doubles as a library and holds Caium's few texts, most of them concerned with the wisdom of House Bjornaer and with disquisitions on the Mystery of the chimera.

One of the natural passages leads, through several twists and turns, to the Tomb of Cacus. The entrance to the passage is not only always guarded by a pair of grogs, but is also protected by several illusions and magical effects that will hamper any intruder. The Tomb is a much smaller cave than the main one, barely fifteen meters across, and a deathly silence always reigns within it. The paintings on the walls remain just as Luitgarde found them more than three centuries ago, and the only sign of human presence is a small circle marked out by stones on the floor, inside which lies the mystical paraphernalia of House Bjornaer; it is here that those who study the cave meditate on the Mystery. Only the leader of the fraternity and its most advanced members may enter the Tomb.

<!-- p. 192 -->

Visitors are forbidden to enter, and the youngest members of the fraternity must earn the right to enjoy it by demonstrating their wisdom. No one has ever found the body of Cacus, chiefly because no one has looked for it: the Bjornaer followers believe the chimera long ago transcended the physical state and exists solely on the metaphysical plane.

The *sancta* dug into the walls of Caium's gorge are occupied by the youngest members of the fraternity. Not only do they have a weaker magical aura, they are also exposed to the elements and very poorly equipped. Surviving in such an environment toughens the initiates, and it is sometimes one more of the ordeals they must overcome on their path through the Mysteries of the House.

#### Society and Customs

Caium is a covenant devoted almost exclusively to the study of the Tomb of Cacus. Everything revolves around it, and all the covenant's magi are Bjornaer followers who form a fraternity of the Arelie clan dedicated to the study of the chimera and to spreading that knowledge to those ready to understand it. The leader of the fraternity is usually a member of Luitgarde's lineage and guides the covenant's fortunes, although all decisions are made in a council in which each member's vote counts equally, so that Caium could be said to be governed by a primitive democracy. It is true, though, that the great majority of the fraternity's meetings and decisions revolve around its philosophy and studies, and mundane matters are delegated to the autocrat: Istebe, a sturdy mountaineer from nearby Tarazona who discovered Caium by chance on one of his climbs a couple of decades ago and ended up reaching an agreement with the Bjornaer magi to bring them supplies. Since then the arrangement has evolved until Istebe has become an essential part of the covenant's workings. The mountaineer has even taken an interest in Bjornaer wisdom, although he has no supernatural ability, and he supports Lacerta in almost everything.

Caium receives few Hermetic visitors, but nearly all of them are of House Bjornaer: magi who have heard of the covenant and wish to study there. Many spend only a while here, taking advantage of the Arelie's innate hospitality before continuing their journey; others, the youngest and most restless, apply for admission to the fraternity. Only those who show the curiosity, spiritual harmony and introspection needed to belong to the group are accepted. These are sent to the *sancta* on the slopes of the gorge, where for an indeterminate time they must prove their perseverance and fortitude before the leaders of the fraternity deem them worthy of reaching the higher levels of the group and of Bjornaer wisdom.

Although the Bjornaer followers have been studying it for centuries, they have not yet uncovered all the secrets of the Tomb of Cacus. Over the years Luitgarde and her disciples have discovered that the paintings on the walls have a mystical significance, and that by imitating the dances and rituals depicted on them while consuming certain plants with hallucinogenic properties, the initiate enters a trance in which the boundaries of reality dissolve and other places can be glimpsed, reachable through some of the small niches that dot the cave and that under normal conditions lead nowhere. The chimera, they say, roams the most remote of those places, spaces of enormous magical power, but it is elusive and appears only to the most exceptional initiates, sometimes enlightening them with its wisdom. According to the legends of Caium, the chimera imparts different knowledge to each magus. The experience profoundly transforms every Bjornaer follower who meets the chimera. They call it "the Encounter," and it is cause for rejoicing and celebration for the whole fraternity.

#### The Magi of Caium

At present Caium has four magi, all members of the Arelie clan of House Bjornaer, which is centered on reverence for the ancestors and on spreading their memory to the rest of the House. Three of them follow the alternative doctrine originated by Luitgarde, while the newly arrived Stellatus follows the clan's conventional philosophy.

##### Lacerta Bjornaer

Lacerta is the current leader of the fraternity. He is a magus in his nineties, of Luitgarde's lineage, who has been trained in the doctrines of the covenant's founder, with the same goal as every leader before him: to penetrate as deeply as possible into the Mystery of the Chimera and one day to become a chimera himself. The goal is a difficult one, but in his case it has become an obsession. Lacerta spends almost all his time in the Tomb of Cacus and shirks many of his responsibilities as the covenant's de facto leader. In another covenant this would be disastrous, but given Caium's lax organization, the management of Natrix and Istebe makes up for his negligence. Lacerta's heartbeast is a bright green lizard that has undergone certain transformations in recent years, probably as a result of his studies in the Tomb.

##### Natrix Bjornaer

Natrix is Lacerta's *filius*, although he is radically different from his *parens*. He too follows Luitgarde's precepts, but he does not share her convictions about the chimera so deeply, probably because he has not experienced any Encounter while in the Tomb. Natrix is an affable, outgoing magus, and it is often he who welcomes visitors to the covenant and imparts the fraternity's wisdom to those who decide to stay and study here or wish to learn more of the Mysteries before continuing their journey. Only his efforts to maintain the most basic logistics of the covenant have kept it from falling into utter chaos, given Lacerta's neglect. His heartbeast is a long grass snake almost two meters in length, which can sometimes unsettle the other initiates somewhat, at least until they discover that he is as harmless in serpent form as in human form. Although Natrix has access to the Tomb of Cacus, he does not often visit it. He is aware of the changes it is working on his *parens* and is not sure he wants to follow the same path. Nevertheless, he is fiercely loyal to Lacerta, and that is why he is one of the chief opponents of Stellatus's reforming theories.

<!-- p. 193 -->

##### Capra Bjornaer

Capra is the youngest maga at Caium and also a relative newcomer. Born in Cuenca and trained at Laminium, she came to the covenant a couple of years ago seeking to learn more about the House's doctrines concerning the ancestors and animal spirits, and out of curiosity about the figure of Cacus, since her own heartbeast is a goat. After some hesitation on Lacerta's part because of her prickly character, she was accepted into the fraternity and given one of the *sancta* dug into the mountainside. At first Capra reacted with hostility: she declared she refused to live there and left the covenant for a few days in a fit of rage. However, she soon thought better of it and returned, settled into the *sanctum* and showed her ability to adapt to and endure such a spartan life. At the same time, she tried to delve into the Mystery Cults of the House, although she has no liking at all for the rigid hierarchy that exists within the fraternity. She understands the value of Caium's resources, but would not mind seeing them managed differently, and for that reason she feels a certain sympathy toward the arrival of Stellatus.

##### Stellatus Bjornaer

The arrival of Stellatus has caused an upheaval at Caium. Stellatus is a venerable but taciturn magus from the Normandy Tribunal, where he should have been named Praeco after the recent death of Renita Bjornaer, being the oldest magus in the Tribunal. However, Stellatus did not wish to become entangled in the complex political plots that characterize Normandy and decided to emigrate, seeking his roots in the south. As a member of the Arelie clan, he had heard of the existence of Caium, where he learned that one of his Hermetic ancestors, Suspirium, had lived. That is why he decided to travel there: to ask to be accepted into the fraternity and follow the clan's philosophy. Unfortunately, Caium's organization proved to be the complete opposite of what he had expected, and its theory of the chimera baffles him. His medium-term intention is to transform the covenant, changing its philosophy and even its name from Caium to Suspirium, moving the covenant's focus away from the Tomb of Cacus. But Lacerta, who is also a Hermetic descendant of Suspirium, firmly opposes any change to a structure that has remained unaltered for several centuries.

Under normal circumstances Stellatus would not have many options: although he is an elderly magus, his standing within the clan is at most comparable to Lacerta's. But there is something that could work in his favor: Caium's dire situation and its Winter. The magi are defenseless against Barda's maneuvers out of sheer ignorance of Hermetic law, and there Stellatus could have a great deal to say. The old Bjornaer is willing to use this advantage to influence, or blackmail if necessary, the other magi of Caium into accepting his proposal for change. Lacerta and the others face a dilemma with no apparent solution: to accept their final Winter or to experience a new Spring transformed into something different from what they have always been.

> #### Story Seeds: Barda and Caium
>
> For more than half a century, the Navarrese magi of Barda have set their sights on Caium's ever scarcer magical resources, after discovering that the covenant had hardly any contact with the Order at large and was unable to defend itself at a Tribunal, having almost no presence there. In recent years their activities have intensified, and although the magi of Caium know that someone is actively working against them, none of them has the inclination or the time to look into the matter in depth. The situation is reaching the point where the Bjornaer followers find all their vis sources empty when they go to harvest them, and they have already lost several grogs who never returned from their journeys to collect the raw vis.
>
> Stellatus resolves to put an end to the thefts and uses his contacts to find a Quaesitor willing to investigate the matter "unofficially," in exchange for a substantial reward of vis from his private store brought from Normandy. The affair is delicate, and so it must be kept in the strictest confidence. Stellatus approaches the player characters' covenant to entrust them with this delicate mission, and if the Quaesitor also has the help of a Flambeau (preferably a hoplite), so much the better…

### Mons Niger

>**Lifespan:** 1032–Present<br>
>**Founders:** Gerardo of Tytalus, Guillermo of Tytalus<br>
>**Season:** Spring<br>
>**Aura (type and strength):** Magic, strength 4 (tower); Faerie, strength 1–3 (slopes of the Dark Mountain)<br>
>**Reputations:** None<br>
>**Votes:** 2

Mons Niger lies in the Sierra de Alcubierre, at the western end of the Monegros, atop the Dark Mountain (monte Oscuro), so called for the dense forests of black wood that cover its slopes. On the summit of the mountain rises a solitary, very tall tower, which commands unrivaled views over the uninhabited region. The tower is inhabited by only two magi, members of House Tytalus and descendants of those who occupied it in the eleventh century after it had been abandoned by its original occupants. The covenant has almost no dealings with the other covenants of the Tribunal, and many of Iberia's magi are not even aware that it exists.

<!-- p. 194 -->

#### History

The Sierra de Alcubierre has been as uninhabited as the rest of the Monegros since time immemorial. For that very reason, it has also occasionally been a refuge for highwaymen, criminals and others who did not wish to be troubled by mundane concerns. Perhaps that is why, during the Muslim invasion of the region in the first half of the eighth century, a pair of *saḥirs* settled on the mountaintop, drawn by its supernatural magical aura. It was they who, using powerful magic, raised the tower that still stands there today, of clearly eastern influence. Legend has it that to do so they enlisted the help of a formidable *jinni*, to whom, in exchange for its services, they granted freedom to roam the whole mountain, provided it did not interfere with the affairs of the tower's inhabitants and their servants (to learn more about the *jinn*, take a look at page 295).

The *saḥirs* and their descendants occupied the tower for more than two centuries, far from the madding crowd thanks to the terrible stories about the creature that dwelt on the slopes of the Dark Mountain. However, when news began to arrive of the Christian invasion of the kingdoms west of Aragon, the *saḥirs* suddenly and inexplicably abandoned their home. Some say it was for fear that the Sierra de Alcubierre would also be conquered by the Christians, something quite impossible given how inhospitable the region is. Other stories point to a very different reason: the *jinni* that had until then been their guardian had begun to behave erratically and aggressively, probably influenced by the progressive deforestation of the region and its effect on the area's supernatural aura. For several decades the tower stood abandoned until, at the beginning of the eleventh century, two Tytalus magi who were brothers by blood, Gerardo and Guillermo, came to the area, drawn by the legends that told of a strange creature prowling the slopes of the Dark Mountain. Setting themselves the challenge of confronting the creature and taming it for their own benefit, the Tytalus not only achieved their aims (not without problems, it must be said), but also discovered the abandoned tower, still in fairly good condition, on the mountaintop. Indeed, inside it they found something that would serve them to subdue the *jinni* once and for all: a dark gem made of an unknown material, which they would call the "Black Heart."

The Tytalus settled in the tower in the year 1027 and, although they announced their presence at the Tribunal of 1032, over these two centuries the covenant has had scarcely any contact with the outside world, nor has it been visited by the Redcaps, who seldom go to the Monegros except to deliver official notices of Tribunals or to catalog the area's few vis sources. Admittedly, the presence of the *jinni* on the slopes of the Dark Mountain does not exactly help in this regard: the magi of Mons Niger have never made public their relationship with the creature, with which the present Tytalus are in fact still playing a long game of power. For the same reason, the covenant has had almost no dealings with the Tribunal or the nearby covenants and, indeed, sends only a token representation to many Tribunals. Nor has Mons Niger had any need to intervene in any way in the conflict between Christians and Muslims.

#### Setting and Physical Description

Mons Niger lies atop the Dark Mountain, the second-highest summit in the Sierra de Alcubierre, after the Hermitage of San Caprasio (see insert). The mountain's slopes are covered with dense groves of juniper, savin and holm oak. The groves were denser still in times past, but even today they remain among the most luxuriant woods in the region. The groves are dotted with glens, ravines and streams, and a single path climbs roughly to the top of the ridge, where the covenant's tower rises: a slender structure forty meters high and eight wide, made of white stone that is barely weathered even today, cylindrical in plan and with beautiful, abundant carvings over its entire surface depicting legendary creatures intermingled with floral motifs and undulating forms. Slender windows mark each of the tower's eight main floors, the topmost of which lies beneath a majestic hollow dome of bluish marble. The tower is surrounded by a small wall four meters high, within which stand the covenant's few additional structures, essentially stables and stalls.

> #### The Hermitage of San Caprasio
>
> Less than two days' journey from Mons Niger stands the only summit in the whole Sierra de Alcubierre higher than the Dark Mountain. It is known as the Hermitage of San Caprasio, after the small hermitage that Saint Caprasius himself built centuries ago inside the caves on the summit. According to legend, Caprasius was a shepherd who one day saw the light of God; he threw his crook as far as he could and, when it landed on the summit of this mountain, it made a spring of water with healing properties gush forth. Caprasius soon settled there as a hermit, and ever since a small group of anchorites has lived in these caves, surrounded by medicinal waters and plants. Once a year the hermits receive the people of the nearby villages, who on Saint Mark's Day climb up here to bless their crops and livestock with the local waters. There is no record of any contact between the hermits and the inhabitants of Mons Niger, and no one knows what the former think of the creature that lives on the mountain's slopes (if they know of it at all). What the covenant's magi do not know either is that the hermitage's waters truly are healing, and can moreover remove fatigue prodigiously, though only at certain specific times of the year. Perhaps it is time to make contact with the hermits?

The covenant has few physical defenses because two factors protect it better than any wall: its remote location and the creature that dwells on the mountain's slopes. The *jinni* has reached a pact with the inhabitants of Mons Niger whereby it does not attack anyone who keeps to the path to the summit. However, the rest of the mountain is its domain, and it seldom shows mercy to any traveler who strays on the way up. Few survive an encounter with it.

>**Appearance:** In its physical form, the *jinni* is a vaguely humanoid creature with black skin, more than three and a half meters tall. It has various animal parts on its body, such as small dark horns growing from its head and features faintly reminiscent of a lion, always twisted in a ferocious expression. Its hands end in razor-sharp claws and it has a long, spiny tail. It walks slightly hunched, almost like an animal, but curiously it wears clothing and ornaments such as a human might: loose trousers and several gold or silver armlets and bracelets, which vanish like the rest of its body when it assumes its spirit form.
>
> The legends about the *jinni* of Mons Niger are, for the most part, false. The mountain had been a magical place since time immemorial, as it held the entrance to a *regio* that connected with the Magic Realm and in which a powerful *genius loci* dwelt. It is true that it was *saḥirs* who raised the tower on the Dark Mountain, but there were not two of them but three. And the formidable magic that allowed them to raise the tower (overnight, in fact) was obtained only through a terrible pact with the *genius*. In exchange for its help, the spirit demanded the sacrifice of one of them: a sacrifice to transcend the mortal veil and become an immortal magical being, who would serve it forever. In addition, the *genius* promised them a way to reach the *regio*, which was almost inaccessible from the mundane level.
>
> After a long debate, one of the *saḥirs*, Hashim, agreed to sacrifice himself. The *genius* kept its word: in a single night a majestic tower appeared, just as the *saḥirs* wished. But the price was terrible: Hashim was transformed forever into a *jinni*, a magic spirit, bound to the place where he had been created. His heart, torn from his chest at the moment of the sacrifice, became his only weakness, prodigiously transformed into a dark gem that not only allowed the *jinni* to be controlled but was also the way into the *regio*. The *saḥirs* carefully treasured the Black Heart, aware that it was the only thing protecting them from the one who had been their companion, and who, after his horrible transformation, prowled the mountain, maddened by his transformation and eternally serving his supernatural master.
>
> Soon the Dark Mountain acquired an even darker reputation as travelers began to disappear in its vicinity and stories began to circulate about the terrible beast that dwelt there, which many said was in the service of the sorcerers in the tower on the summit.
>
> For decades the *saḥirs* prospered in the tower, convinced of their control over the *jinni* that had been Hashim. The creature, in which a vestige of human mind still remained, inexplicably came to believe that if it managed to protect the mountain from all intruders, it would regain its human form, something that never happened.
>
> Then, with the Christian invasion of Alcubierre, disaster struck: a band of mercenaries eluded the *jinni* and reached the *saḥirs*' tower, intent on plundering it. The Muslim sorcerers tried to defend themselves but, outnumbered, decided to flee. In their headlong flight they left the Black Heart behind in the tower, which proved a fatal mistake for everyone involved: the *jinni*, weary of years of slavery and already half-mad, fell upon the fleeing *saḥirs* and killed them one by one. Then it made for the tower, where it surprised the mercenaries, who had taken the Black Heart for just another gem whose workings they did not understand. With the Christians exterminated as well, and unable to approach the gem that was its great weakness, the *jinni* left the tower and went back to roaming the mountain, guarding it and preventing anyone from reaching the summit.
>
> The tower remained abandoned for centuries… until the arrival of Guillermo and Gerardo of Tytalus. Thanks to their Parma Magica, the two Tytalus not only managed to repel the creature's attacks, but also discovered the tower and the Black Heart. The Tytalus restored the tower and investigated the heart, convinced that it had some connection with the creature, but they discovered only one of its powers, the one that allowed the *jinni* to be controlled. They then decided to take turns using the Heart, in the perverse game that Obstinatus and Oboediens still keep up today, centuries later. None of the magi has ever found the way into the *regio*. However, Scisco has recently discovered a hidden grotto in the tower's cellars, and is beginning to believe the Black Heart conceals more powers than it seems. Unfortunately, his magical ability is not yet enough to unravel those secrets, and so far he has also been unable to persuade his *parens* to spend time investigating the prodigious jewel anew.

<!-- p. 196 -->

<!-- p. 197 -->

As for the tower proper, because of its magical origin each of its floors has a similar layout, with a central chamber surrounded by a stone staircase that runs up the whole interior of the tower, broken by various landings. Four of the floors are reserved for the magi's *sancta*, although only two of them are usually occupied; the other four floors hold the treasury, the library, the meeting room and, on the topmost floor, an observatory that opens onto the hollow part of the dome, at whose base an outer walkway runs all the way around the dome and allows the landscape to be observed for several kilometers around.

#### Society and Customs

When Gerardo and Guillermo of Tytalus came to the Dark Mountain in 1027 and discovered both the tower and the area's supernatural inhabitant, it seemed to them the ideal setting not only for establishing a covenant, but also for embarking on a game that would go on for centuries. Each of the Tytalus would try to use the *jinni* of the Dark Mountain to prove the validity of his philosophy of conflict. Each brother followed one of the Tytalus schools of thought, the Calliclean and the Hippian, and they decided to prove the validity of their premises with their new neighbor: while one did everything possible to reinforce the *jinni*'s essential, natural behavior, the other did the opposite, trying to control the creature so that it would not wreak havoc in the region. All of this, of course, without the matter coming to the ears of the Tribunal's authorities.

The "game" between Gerardo and Guillermo lasted the rest of their lives, more or less eventfully depending on who had the upper hand. When Gerardo died, his *filius* Arnedo took his place in the game, as Arnal, Guillermo's *filius*, would do years later when Guillermo died. Arnedo and Arnal were not brothers by blood, but they did become Hermetic brothers, and they devoted their whole lives to continuing the game. Since then there have always been just two magi at Mons Niger, no more and no less. Always Tytalus, the only House whose members have been willing to keep playing this dangerous game, which on more than one occasion has ended in the death of a magus when the *jinni* ran out of control. At present the occupants of Mons Niger are Obstinatus and Oboediens, the sixth generation of magi. Both are getting on in years and, indeed, Oboediens is in the midst of training his apprentice, Scisco.

Given Mons Niger's structure, its system of government could be called a two-member democracy, the two usually agreeing on almost all decisions concerning the management and development of the covenant, matters to which, for that matter, they pay little attention. That is why, among other things, they remain in Spring almost two centuries after the covenant's founding.

#### The Magi of Mons Niger

##### Oboediens of Tytalus

Oboediens is a magus in his nineties, the current champion of Hippias's philosophy at Mons Niger. He has been here for more than four decades, having been recruited by his predecessor for his rigorous character and his conviction that the world makes no sense unless its inhabitants follow a set of rules, even artificial ones. He has applied this belief to the game that has been played at Mons Niger for centuries, trying to control the mountain's *jinni* so as to channel its lust for destruction toward more constructive ends, with the same meager success as many of his predecessors, for so far he has not managed to control the creature completely and turn it into a valuable resource for the covenant. In fact, it is rather the opposite: he is losing the game to Obstinatus. Oboediens is aware of this, and that is why in recent years he has concentrated more on the education of his *filius* than on the game, which has only strengthened Obstinatus's advantage. Oboediens has high hopes for Scisco, but the boy does not exactly see things the same way…

> #### The Black Heart
>
> The Black Heart is a gem the size of a human fist, made of a dark crystalline material of unknown origin. If someone gazes into it for more than a few seconds, they can make out black wisps that seem to float, although it is unclear whether this is a visual effect or the inside of the gem is really fluid.
>
> The Black Heart has three properties that can be investigated by Hermetic methods, described below with the levels needed to decipher them. Each power is protected by an effect similar to the level 40 spell *Shell of Opaque Mysteries*. Unlike the Hermetic spell, this protection conceals each power separately, which is why the magi of Mons Niger do not know there are two more effects in the gem.
>
> - *Lord of the Jinni* (Rego Mentem 40): By holding the gem in one hand and concentrating, the bearer can give mental commands to the *jinni*. The *jinni* must carry out the command to the best of its abilities, but if the sun sets or rises before it succeeds, the effect is canceled. The effect can be used only once a day.
>
> - *Vision of the Hidden* (Intellego Vim 45): In the least explored grottoes beneath the tower of Mons Niger there is a small hollow, a narrow passage that seems to end in a dead end. If the Black Heart is held aloft inside that tunnel in darkness, the gem gives off a gloomy glow that reveals a path where on the mundane level there is only a wall. This path leads to the Magic Realm and, it is said, to the City of Brass, inhabited by prodigious *jinn* and *ʿafārīt*. This effect is constant. Since no one has entered that *regio* for decades, it is unknown whether there are other ways into it, or even the details of its various levels.
>
> - *The Slave's Scourge* (Perdo Vim 55): The *jinni*'s magic is completely canceled if it is within ten meters of the Black Heart. Furthermore, it cannot attack either the bearer of the Heart or anyone within those same ten meters.
>
> The Black Heart is as fragile as any similar jewel, and its destruction would have no effect other than those arising from the loss of its powers: no one could enter the *regio* or control the *jinni* with it, and, naturally, the creature's powers would no longer be affected by the Heart.

<!-- p. 198 -->

##### Obstinatus of Tytalus

Obstinatus is thirty years younger than Oboediens. He was raised from childhood at Mons Niger, is the natural son of the covenant's previous Calliclean, and has an iron determination that very few before him have possessed. That is why in recent years he has gained the upper hand in the game, gradually making the *jinni* ever more faithful to its *physis*, its essence and its instincts. Obstinatus has also managed to transform the creature little by little, changing its nature through various encounters that were risky for his own person, in which he has achieved what seems impossible: the *jinni* carries out his designs convinced that it is in fact acting freely. To do this, Obstinatus has learned how to make offerings of vis to the *jinni*, which have accustomed it to savoring an energy and a power that it now seeks avidly. In his heart, Obstinatus dreams of turning the *jinni* into a kind of pet that will serve him both to find vis and as a scourge against possible enemies, even Hermetic ones, who may cross his path. To him, this would merely be a new phase of the eternal game being waged at Mons Niger. The challenge is to achieve his goal before he needs to train an apprentice.

##### Scisco

Scisco is Oboediens's apprentice and is barely three years away from facing his Gauntlet. He is a bright, perceptive boy and, although he should be the covenant's next Hippian representative, he knows the advantage Obstinatus has gained in the game and, indeed, is beginning to toy with the idea of following the theses of Callicles rather than those of Hippias. However, he also knows that Obstinatus is up to something that goes beyond the game, and he cannot allow him to get his way if he wants the game to go on being played at Mons Niger, as it should. He knows he will have to make a decision one way or the other when he faces his Gauntlet, but he cannot help seeing his master as a weak, failed magus, and deep down he admires Obstinatus, however little he shares his long-term goals. The decision will undoubtedly be a difficult one…

> #### Story Seeds: Dealings with the *Jinni*
>
> When the characters come to visit Mons Niger (perhaps because they are Redcaps, members of House Tytalus or for some similar reason), the *jinni* notices their presence and also that they are creatures similar to those who live in the tower. Instead of attacking them, it decides to show itself to them and offer them a pact: if they manage to recover the Black Heart for it, the *jinni* will show them the way into a *regio* such as they have never seen. Although the magi will very probably reject the proposal outright, they could certainly learn certain details about the magi of Mons Niger that might prove scandalous if made public…

### Prima

>**Lifespan:** Never constituted<br>
>**Founders:** Andrada of Tremere, Scorilo of Tremere, Decebalus of Tremere<br>
>**Aura (type and strength):** Magic, strength 2<br>
>**Reputations:** None

Raised at the behest of Tremere himself when the Order of Hermes was still young, Prima had a brief but intense life beneath the streets of Saragossa.

#### History

The eighth century was a period of conflict throughout a newly founded Order of Hermes. While Tremere himself was fighting in the distant south of Transylvania, he sent a small group of magi to Iberia to establish themselves in the region, perhaps as part of his grand plan to control the whole Order in the future, who knows. They were three Dacian necromancers named Decebalus, Scorilo and Andrada. The three crossed the Pyrenees at Roncesvalles and reached the city of Saragossa the White in early 778, which at the time was being besieged by none other than Charlemagne. The Frankish king was claiming the city from its governor Husayn, for that had been the price of his protection against the emir of Cordoba, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān I, in an agreement struck with Sulaymān, wali of Barcelona.

The Tremere immediately decided to profit from the situation and soon reached an agreement with Husayn: in exchange for their help against Charlemagne's assault, they wanted a place in the city's underground passages, resources to establish their dwelling there, and peace to study undisturbed. The wali agreed and, for a month, the Frankish troops fought without managing to break the siege, facing all manner of adversities, many of them inexplicable to mere mundanes. The necromancers proved their ability to contribute to the city's defense without drawing attention, and only on rare occasions did they have to resort to their ghostly allies, with the result that when Charlemagne ordered the retreat on learning that the Saxons were invading Francia, stories of a supernatural flavor were already circulating among his troops. Thus Saragossa remained unconquered and the Tremere were able to claim their reward. After putting the agreement with Husayn into effect, the Tremere planned the official constitution of Prima for the Rhine meeting of 791 (at which the covenant of Branugurix in Normandy would be founded). However, they were unable to carry it out, for they had to abandon the covenant in 789.

<!-- p. 199 -->

Although the city had a magical *regio* (which in the future would be used by the Unseen Tower), the Tremere preferred to settle underground after performing certain rituals that identified the spot where the ancient amphitheater of Caesaraugusta had once stood. The site was steeped in all the blood shed there in its day, much of it in honor of the Roman gods, and it still retained a faint magical aura. It was the perfect place for the necromancers, who partially restored the amphitheater and enlarged the underground spaces to house their laboratories and other chambers. They then threw themselves into a frenzy of warfare, taking part in many of the conflicts that shook the Tribunal during that decade and even aiding the wali of Saragossa again on a couple of occasions.

Prima came to an end in 789, when Saragossa was taken by the armies of the wali of Barcelona, Matruh ibn Sulaymān. Although the Tremere tried to win the trust of the new mundane powers, their attempts came to nothing and they were forced to leave Saragossa in haste (though why they did not take part in the city's defense remains unknown). With the meticulousness that characterizes their House, they brought down the walls of Prima so that no one could reach what had been their quarters, thus erasing every trace of their presence beneath the streets of Saragossa. But its members did not leave the Peninsula; they were taken in at Brigantia, where they began to plan where to raise a new covenant. They never saw that dream fulfilled, however: Andrada and Decebalus died in the fateful battles that preceded the fall of the tempestarii, and Scorilo returned to Coeris to recover from his wounds. He spent some years there before being sent back to Iberia with Átropo and Somnus to found the Navarrese covenant of Secunda at the beginning of the ninth century.

#### Setting and Physical Description

Prima once occupied a restored section of the ancient amphitheater that stood in Roman Caesaraugusta. The amphitheater's partially rebuilt tiers served as a forum and meeting hall, while new chambers excavated nearby housed the covenant's *sancta*, its library and its other quarters. Today all of it lies buried beneath tons of stone, after the Dacian necromancers brought down the walls of their own covenant in their hasty flight from the city in 789. No one has dug into those ruins since to try to recover whatever treasures may still lie hidden beneath them.

> #### Story Seeds: The Defixio Francorum
>
> Charlemagne's withdrawal from Saragossa ended in tragedy with the defeat the Basques inflicted on him at the battle of Roncesvalles. Learning of this, the necromancers of Prima traveled in secret to the battlefield and, using their magical arts, gathered a vast army of ghostly Frankish soldiers, whom they bound to a number of beads and ornaments that they carried back with them to Saragossa, so that they could summon them whenever needed.
>
> When they returned from their journey to Roncesvalles, the Dacians decided to hide those beads in plain sight: after unearthing part of the Roman amphitheater, they had a mosaic engraved around the perimeter of the tiers depicting the battle in which Roland died and the Frankish emperor suffered one of his worst defeats. To add insult to mockery, at various points in that engraving they set the beads to which the spirits of his soldiers were bound, sending a message as clear as it was macabre: even in death the Franks would remain unable to conquer Saragossa, and would in fact be subject to the necromantic powers of Prima's inhabitants. They called the engraving the *Defixio Francorum* and, it is said, on several occasions summoned its captive spirits to serve the Tremere.
>
> The hasty flight of the covenant's inhabitants forced the magi to abandon the beads and ornaments that adorned the amphitheater, and they remain there still, centuries later, buried under the rubble. Over the years the spirits held captive in the engraving were corrupted by other, even older spirits — those of gladiators who had fought in the amphitheater almost a thousand years earlier — and became something different and far more malign. No one has had contact with those spirits for several centuries, and indeed very few would know how to summon them from within the *defixio*. But all of that may change when one of the characters visits Saragossa following certain legends about the ancient Roman amphitheater and the magi of Prima…

### Tremébriga

>**Lifespan:** 871–1013<br>
>**Founders:** Acutus of Tremere, Tremula Flamma of Tremere<br>
>**Aura (type and strength):** Magic, strength 4<br>
>**Reputations:** Traditional (northern Iberian magi) 3, Intransigent (Andalusi magi) 2

In barely a century and a half of existence, the covenant of Tremébriga became one of the most powerful in Iberia. Founded by Tremere magi who came to the Upper March after the Sundering, Tremébriga was an example of the Tremere's ability to make the most of their resources while working at once for the Order and for their House (to which end they strove to restore their reputation, darkened as it was by the Sundering). Their involvement in the constant conflicts of the Upper March during their first decades, and their close ties first with the Banū Qasī and later with the Tujibids, strengthened their prosperity further still. However, the covenant was destroyed during the Schism War, at the very height of its power.

<!-- p. 200 -->

#### History

The Sundering of House Tremere had terrible consequences for the House. Its magi had begun to accumulate power in 822, and by 848 they controlled every figure of authority in the Order. However, the appalling events that wrecked the Founder's great dream changed everything. After some years in which the magi of the House were scarcely seen on the Peninsula, in 861 a pair of Tremere came to the Upper March intending to create a covenant in the region, to serve as a base from which to take part in the constant conflicts between Franks and Andalusis. Both had been trained at Lycaneon and sent from the House's *domus magna* to the Peninsula, but they could not have been more different in character: Acutus was an accomplished warrior, with both his sword and his magic, while Tremula Flamma, a woman of seemingly timid disposition, possessed on the contrary a superb mind for diplomacy, management and the administration of resources, as well as a keen artistic sensibility.

To avoid sharing the fate of their predecessors at Prima, who had carried on their activities beneath the soil of Saragossa, Acutus and Tremula Flamma followed the example of Secunda and acquired land where the Arba flows into the Ebro (halfway between the vanished Tremere covenants of Prima and Secunda), making use of the contacts that the late Átropo of Tremere of Tertia had established with the Banū Qasī before the Sundering. However, they also bought a property in Saragossa (near where Qasr al-Surūr, the Palace of Joy, would later stand, a place of light and learning that would host the Tribunals of al-Andalus; see below) in order to keep their influence over the city's governors.
