They then began building a fortified tower in which to establish their covenant. Although from outside it showed a uniform stone façade, the interior of the tower displayed an architectural style reminiscent of mosques and similar buildings, decorated with exquisite taste thanks to Tremula. Its construction completed in 865, the Tremere officially announced the creation of Tremébriga at the Rhine Tribunal of 871, along with a number of other Peninsular covenants.

Despite its efforts, Tremébriga could not bring about a recovery of the Banū Qasī, and when the feeble Lubb (Musā's firstborn) swore fealty to King Ordoño I of Asturias, Tremébriga pushed Tertia off the political stage and Tremula had a free hand in the city of Saragossa. Surprisingly, Tremébriga's situation improved still further in 884 when, in the midst of the Banū Qasī's crisis, the emir of Cordoba, Muḥammad I, acquired Saragossa for 15,000 dinars, taking advantage of the fact that another of Musā's sons had sworn fealty to him. The emir soon handed control of the city to the Banū Tuyib, or Tujibids, with whom the Tremere would forge a relationship even more beneficial to both sides.

Throughout the tenth century, Tremébriga enjoyed a true golden age, even though it never had more than three members. Fundamental to that development was Ibn Sahl al-Tremerī, the apprentice of Tremula Flamma, who combined the best qualities of the covenant's two founders. It was said of him that he held in the palm of his hand none other than Muḥammad al-Anqar, better known as "the One-Eyed," who governed the city for thirty-five years from the end of the ninth century. Ibn Sahl took care to avoid the sins of his Tremere forebears and always kept control of the covenant's development, which never ceased to operate in Saragossa and the Upper March from a distance. He was responsible, among other things, for a trade agreement with the Mercere of Aedes Saturni, whom he informed of the most significant cargoes coming down the Ebro, so that the Redcaps at Aedes Saturni's outpost at the river's mouth could profit from that privileged information. In return, it was always rumored that the vis exchange rates they granted Tremébriga were exceedingly generous, which swelled the covenant's coffers.

Ibn Sahl was as faithful in his service to the Order as to his own House, and served as a hoplite for many years. Despite his Mozarabic origins, he opposed the admission of the *saḥirs* into the Order, which earned him at once the enmity of the southern covenants and a certain popularity among the northern ones. His intransigence persisted when he was named Praeco in 996, a turbulent time, the prologue to the Schism War, in which Tremébriga would play a sorry part. Ibn Sahl, by then an aged magus, lashed out at the Diedne covenants of the Tribunal, beginning with the expulsion of all the magi of that House from the Tribunal meeting of 996 and the attack he launched against Mons Vindius on neutral ground. The latent violence between the two Houses only grew in the years that followed; from 1010, with open war between the two sides, Tremébriga became a frequent meeting place for the Tremere to prepare their attacks on the Diedne. In those years the covenant was fortified still further, becoming a stronghold and arsenal for the House.

During the chaotic years from 1010 to 1013, Tremébriga displayed a muscle and might unusual in so small a covenant. Its magical reserves were formidable, and it possessed not only abundant vis but also powerful magic items that made its few magi almost unstoppable in combat. The Tremere never forgave the Flambeau of Brigantia for siding with the Diedne, and in 1013 the final confrontation took place in Tremébriga's own halls, which were invaded by a Diedne contingent supported by the renegade Flambeau of Brigantia. The invaders arrived without warning, under cover of a potent illusion spell. Ibn Sahl and his companions, taken by surprise and sorely short of resources because of Porta Pandere's refusal to contribute to the war effort, fought with fire and sword through the corridors of their home and struck down many enemies, but their fate was sealed. The Diedne left no one standing (or so they believed), and after finishing off the Tremere they carried away all the considerable plunder they could gather, before setting fire to the interior of the tower. At dawn the next day, a plume of smoke was the only sign of Tremébriga's sorry end.

<!-- p. 201 -->

#### Setting and Physical Description

Tremébriga stood where the Arba flows into the Ebro, in a fortified tower raised by the Tremere. The tower was improved over the following century and a half, but after the Diedne attack little more than its outer walls remained. For years the tower was a place to be avoided, surrounded by dark legends that were probably born of the night on which Tremébriga was destroyed. Yet the memory of Tremébriga would outlast its halls by far, becoming an ominous warning of the terrible consequences that the unbridled use of magic can bring when human pettiness rules over reason.

> #### Story Seeds: The Ghost of Selim
>
> The night Tremébriga fell was a whirlwind of chaos and destruction. Although the Diedne emerged victorious, they had to gather up all the covenant's plunder and flee the place. In their haste they failed to notice that not all the covenant's Tremere had been slain. One of them, Selim al-Tremerī, took refuge in the underground passages when he found himself cornered by the attackers. A collapse caused by the magical forces unleashed that night buried the Tremere, who lost consciousness and awoke hours later with total amnesia. Wandering desperately in the darkness, his magic completely forgotten because of the blow, Selim slowly went mad over the following days until he died of starvation, forgotten by all. His frustration and despair kept his spirit in those sealed chambers long after his body had decayed. Become a tormented ghost, Selim has wandered the underground passages of Tremébriga for decades, unable to leave the place where he died.
>
> The Quaesitores send a group of magi to investigate rumors of ghostly apparitions, sounds from beyond the grave and spectral lights. What will the magi do when they discover that the cause is the ghost of Selim, and how can they give him eternal rest?

### The Unseen Tower

>**Lifespan:** 915–990<br>
>**Founders:** Conciatta of Bonisagus, Currito of Jerbiton<br>
>**Aura (type and strength):** Magic, strength 6 (in the *regio*), Divine, strength 2 (in the cellars)<br>
>**Reputations:** None

<!-- p. 202 -->

The Unseen Tower was a modest covenant that stayed on the margins of Tribunal politics, but it made a decisive contribution to the advance of Bonisagus's Hermetic theory.

#### History

This covenant was founded in 915 by the married couple formed by the Bonisagus Conciatta and the Jerbiton Currito. For it they chose the city of Saragossa, where they had found several supernatural auras and had perceived that only some of them seemed to benefit their magic. Since they wanted to understand those auras, and since the fall of Prima the city had not been claimed by any other magus of the Tribunal, they settled there after negotiating their presence with Tremébriga, which exercised powerful control in the city (although the terms of that agreement remain unknown to this day). Thus the covenant was able to settle within the shelter of a *regio* where Conciatta developed her Hermetic breakthroughs, many of them unprecedented in the Order, with which she carved out a place for herself in history.

The covenant was abandoned when, in 990, Conciatta left to end her days in the convent of San Ildefonso, in Toledo.

> #### Story Seeds: Conciatta's Research
>
> Conciatta published her first notable work in 930 and titled it *The Application of Vim to the Supernatural Humors* (a *tractatus* on Magic Theory, Quality 7). This great breakthrough showed that magic theory could be adapted to the four existing supernatural auras and could distinguish them from one another. It was a revolution for two reasons: it reduced the number of categories of auras to four, to match the known realms, and it showed that Vim could be used to affect them directly.
>
> In a short time the text spread through the Tribunals, and Conciatta signed her name into Hermetic history. However, although she continued to delve into that field of research, the maga never published her further advances. Rumors say that she found a way to ignore the Dominion's penalties on magic, so that if anyone were to bring her research to light, they could achieve the fame of the Founders themselves… but at what price? What did Conciatta have to sacrifice to attain such power?

#### Setting and Physical Description

The covenant lies in a *regio* to the northwest of the city of Saragossa, beside the sharp meander of the Ebro. The level of the *regio* where the tower stands has an aura of strength 6, while the strength 1 magic aura of the mundane level is subsumed by the Dominion (in a divine aura of strength 2).

The tower is several stories high, and each floor is spacious enough to hold several rooms and accommodate a Hermetic laboratory. Yet the building is not very large and never housed a great number of covenant inhabitants, a clear sign that its members led frugal lives or owned other estates nearby.

Today the site is occupied by the property of a wealthy merchant (named Reyes de Barbastro), which includes both his house and a large warehouse (in whose cellar lies the entrance to the *regio*).

### Qasr al-Surūr

>**Lifespan:** 1026–1103<br>
>**Founders:** n/a<br>
>**Aura (type and strength):** Divine, strength 1 (originally it had a magic aura of strength 4)<br>
>**Reputations:** None

Although it was never a covenant in the strict sense, Qasr al-Surūr (Arabic for "palace of joy") was an important Hermetic meeting place for the magi of the Tribunal of al-Andalus.

#### History

During the second ordinary Tribunal of al-Andalus, in 1019, the magi present agreed to create a neutral place where they could hold their meetings and share their knowledge and discoveries. At first they considered Cordoba, but the instability of the city, then mired in civil war and not yet fully recovered from the plague that had ravaged it in 1011, led them to reject that option. The Praeco of the Tribunal, Ḥafṣa ibn ʿAbbās al-Bonisagiyya, decided to turn to the riadiins, the mathematicians of Madrid (see page 287), whom she had already consulted to learn what role to adopt during the Schism War. Maslama himself answered Ḥafṣa's request once again with an augury: the Great Hall should be raised in the capital of the Upper March, Saragossa, "in a magical lagoon near where the Tower of the Wise Woman stood and where the Palace of Joy would soon rise." The allusions were far from clear: the Tower of the Wise Woman might refer to the vanished covenant of Conciatta of Bonisagus, while the reference to the "Palace of Joy" was entirely ambiguous. All this baffled the magi of the Order. What could the riadiin mean by those words?

Ḥafṣa was not willing to take any risks, nor to waste any time. Taking the reference to the "lagoon" as an obvious metaphor for some kind of magical aura, she sent several magi to the city of Saragossa to examine it. Soon the Hermetic embassy located a powerful magical *lacuna* to the north of the city, not far from where the Unseen Tower had stood, on a site that was soon to be built upon. The magi got ahead of events and managed to acquire the land, on which they would raise their Great Hall. For this they turned to Al-Halifa Zuhayr, an architect of Slavic origin living in the city, whom they commissioned to build a luxurious small palace to house their great project. The palace would consist of a great open chamber furnished only with shelves, tables and chairs, which would run without interruption around the perimeter of the enclosure designed and built by Zuhayr. In that inner courtyard a fountain was built and palms and other plants were planted, and the garden was scattered with couches, cushions and armchairs, creating an idyllic setting in which the magi of the whole Tribunal could not only share their knowledge but also enjoy one another's company and debate arcane questions at their ease. That courtyard would be known as the forum of Ḥafṣa and, together with the Great Hall itself, would be the stage for the Tribunals of al-Andalus. On the upper floor a gallery was built from which the garden could be seen in all its splendor, and which gave access to the laboratories fitted out on the premises for anyone who wished to use them.

<!-- p. 203 -->

In the Great Hall, Tribunals always began one day before the winter solstice; by then, those attending had to have taken part in the renewal of the *Aegis of the Hearth*. Then, between one Hermetic event and the next, banquets were held to the music of the artists present while knowledge, anecdotes and discoveries were shared.

Between Tribunals, the magi were free to meet informally during their visits to the Great Hall, but its only permanent occupants were the two *al-gayʿyūrun*, volunteers drawn from the Tribunal's covenants who had to live in the Great Hall permanently — at least one of them did. The *al-gayʿyūrun* were re-elected at the next Tribunal by popular vote, although they could not be compelled to remain in office. In 1061 these guardians received additional help in their task in the form of seven automata of bronze and silver donated by the Verditius of Ajabeba, as part of the agreement to introduce a clause into the Peripheral Code that would benefit them when selling enchantments to mundanes.

For almost the entire existence of the Tribunal of al-Andalus, the Great Hall became a repository for the finest books (both mundane and Hermetic) and laboratory texts that the magi of the Tribunal would create, as well as for all the spells and enchantments researched in the laboratories of the Great Hall itself. So great was its importance as a center of learning that the Bonisagi of al-Andalus made copies of their research for the Great Hall before sending it to Durenmar. Little by little, the Great Hall became the residence of a cultural elite of the Order, to which almost every covenant of al-Andalus contributed.

The situation of the Great Hall changed utterly with the arrival of Al-Muqtadir and the Banū Hūd in Saragossa. The city was transformed by the change of rule, reaching a splendor that rivaled, or even surpassed, that of cities such as Toledo and Seville. Al-Muqtadir, enamored of the idyllic spot where the Hermetic magi held their debates and conversed about art, culture and every other imaginable subject, described the place as a "Palace of Joy," thus fulfilling the second part of the prophecy Maslama had made long before. So infatuated was Al-Muqtadir with the place that he ordered the construction of a much larger and more luxurious palace beside the Great Hall. The site would be known as the Aljafería, and the petty king even tried to acquire the Hermetic quarters to incorporate them into the new palace. Only the diplomatic skills of Ḥafṣa, and later of her successor, Al-ʿĀsmarun al-Ŷerbitonī, made it possible to preserve the independence of the Great Hall without incurring the wrath of the Banū Hūd (or of the Andalusi Quaesitores). What is more, relations between the two sides were reasonably cordial, and it is said that the magi of the Order even cast enchantments over the whole of the Aljafería in exchange for the protection of the Banū Hūd in mundane affairs.

> #### Story Seeds: The Secret of Al-Halifa Zuhayr
>
> Not even the Hermetic magi ever learned the origin of the magic aura that reigned in the *lacuna* where the Great Hall rose, and they always sought some significant element or event that had taken place on the site to explain its existence, especially given that the aura grew stronger once the original construction was completed. The origin of that aura must in fact be sought in Al-Halifa Zuhayr, the creator of both the Great Hall and the Aljafería.
>
> Al-Halifa Zuhayr is a mysterious figure about whom very little was known when the Order of Hermes contacted him to commission the building of the Great Hall, drawn by his great reputation as an architect in Saragossa. Zuhayr simply accepted the commission and named a price. After completing the Great Hall, he disappeared from the city, only to return twenty years later, just as Al-Muqtadir was considering ordering the construction of the Aljafería. Despite the time that had passed, Zuhayr seemed to have aged barely a few years, and on the recommendation of the Andalusi magi's contacts, Al-Muqtadir decided to engage him to build his splendid palace. Once again, the architect accepted the commission.
>
> Zuhayr was in fact an undead creature of Transylvanian origin, a very rare variant of such creatures, distantly related to vampires but of magical nature. Not only did he lack the thirst for blood that besets those creatures, but he could move about naturally in broad daylight. Since time immemorial, Al-Halifa had wandered throughout Mythic Europe and North Africa, devoted to the study of the application of astrology to architecture, a wisdom that the Egyptians mastered in antiquity but that has since been lost. Traveling from school to school every few years to avoid arousing suspicion, Al-Halifa visited the south of Iberia and then traveled to Saragossa, where he got the Andalusi magi to commission the great work of his life: the plans of the Great Hall were in perfect alignment with several constellations, which reinforced its arcane significance. Strengthening that alignment with a blood ritual he performed without anyone's knowledge, Al-Halifa succeeded in increasing the magic aura of the area that would hold the Great Hall. Two decades later, he returned to the city, drawn by some strange intuition, and used Al-Muqtadir's commission to renew those rituals, maintaining the strength of the magic aura. Once his work was finished, he vanished from the city for good, though the aura endured, reinforced by the Hermetic presence, until the arrival of the Christian kings in the city and the alterations made to the palace irreparably destroyed the alignment, putting an end to the place's magic aura as well.
>
> While one of the magi is carrying out arcane studies, perhaps related to some breakthrough or mystery connected with architecture or astrology, he discovers a diagram that bears an uncanny resemblance to the plan of the Aljafería. The texts clearly indicate that the place could be used as a site of study in which to advance the research significantly. But… how can one gain access to what was once the Great Hall? And, most importantly, how could its astrological and architectural resonances be repaired?

<!-- p. 204 -->

But the history of the Great Hall was not free of controversy. In 1039 it was discovered that Yasmina al-Gernikiyya, an *al-gayʿyūrun* from Dār Malīḥaʾ, had used funds provided by Porta Pandere for personal projects and had never returned them to Qasr al-Surūr. She received a heavy fine and was barred from the office for life, and although she continued to carry out her duties as a Quaesitor, for some time there were suspicions that some more elaborate scheme hatched by her mother covenant lay behind her actions.

But the most important events that took place in the Great Hall came at the Tribunal of 1089, which, besides the usual attendees, was attended by representatives of Iberia at a time when the fate of al-Andalus hung by a thread. The clashes at the Tribunal, combined with the skillful intervention of those representatives, ended up bringing about the dissolution of the Tribunal of al-Andalus and the subsequent reunification of its covenants with Iberia. This decision caused great dismay among many of those present, including the Praeco himself, who thus saw their dreams of enlightenment and knowledge cut short. The Tribunals of Joy were held until 1103, when al-Andalus was officially absorbed by the Iberian Tribunal, while Al-Mustaʿīn II ruled in Saragossa, at a time of great conflict for all the taifas. Al-Mustaʿīn himself, who had to ask the Almoravids for help to keep his rule in Saragossa, played a sorry part in the twilight of the Palace of Joy and the Great Hall, threatening the magi with hostile reprisals if they did not immediately leave the Aljafería and the city. Unable to bring the petty king to reason, the magi sold him the Great Hall. Soon the Order of Hermes abandoned the capital of the Upper March, and although the city was reconquered by the Christians a few years later, the Order has not had a presence there to this day.

#### Setting and Physical Description

The Palace of Joy was located inside the Aljafería which, by 1220 and following the conquest of Saragossa by Alfonso I the Battler in 1118, has been converted into a Mudéjar palace where the Christian monarchs of Aragon reside. The structure, however, has not undergone substantial changes, although the wing once occupied by the Great Hall has been turned into royal apartments and meeting rooms; the courtyard where the forum of Ḥafṣa once lay will be known in the coming decades as the Courtyard of Santa Isabel.

### Praesidium Abditus

*Lubricus inc anguis fugiat in Tartara preceps,*<br>
*Pectora ne noceat rite dicata deo.*<br>
*ʽCrucis alme fero signum: fuge, demon.*[^p204-25]

[^p204-25]: Fragment of an anonymous exorcism, translated into Spanish by Miguel Rodríguez-Pantoja as: *Let the creeping serpent flee hence to Tartarus, swiftly, / let it not harm the souls that are consecrated to God. / "I bear the sign of the cross. Flee, demon!"*; taken from "Los mozárabes y sus poemas en el siglo ix" (in *Los mozárabes. Historia cultura y religión de los cristianos de al Ándalus*).

>**Lifespan:** 1123–1212<br>
>**Founders:** Iacobus Versutus of Jerbiton, Guzmán Garcés of Flambeau<br>
>**Aura (type and strength):** Magic, strength 3 (fortification), Infernal, strength 2 (underground cavern)<br>
>**Reputations:** None

#### History

In 1118, Alfonso I the Battler conquered the Aragonese town of Belchite, known until then as Belsid and part of the taifa of Saragossa. Shortly afterward he granted the town to Galindo Sanz, a magnate and soldier of the region, and in 1119 the town was given an unusual fuero that allowed it to take in criminals and offenders, who would have their sentences pardoned and gain the freedom to settle in the region. Among the offenders who came to have their guilt remitted was Iacobus Versutus, a young Jerbiton magus condemned for murder by mundane justice. Shortly after settling in Belchite and becoming a free man once more, Iacobus received a visit from Guzmán Garcés, an ardent Flambeau of noble birth from Salionca who had traveled to Aragon in search of a covenant that took an active part in the region's conflicts. After that meeting, the two were quick to ingratiate themselves with Galindo's circle and, taking advantage of the distribution of properties in the area, acquired a fortification not far from the town, built on a spot where, according to legend, an ancient Iberian hero had slain a demon and raised a small hillfort. There they established the covenant of Praesidium Abditus, founded in 1120, its charter ratified in 1123.

In its scant century of life, Praesidium Abditus underwent a profound transformation, brought about chiefly by the formation in 1122, under the auspices of Alfonso I himself, of the Confraternity of Belchite. Guzmán Garcés contrived to join the confraternity at once, which led Iacobus to abandon the covenant when he saw it receive two more Flambeau magi and another Tremere. Galindo Sanz himself led the confraternity during its first years, with Guzmán as his right hand, and Guzmán kept his preeminent position even when the confraternity was absorbed into the Confraternity of Monreal a few years later. By then the covenant was entirely Flambeau, and much of the turb was made up of some of the many former criminals who had flocked to Belchite, whose presence always made Praesidium Abditus a rather ungovernable and chaotic place.

<!-- p. 205 -->

During the second half of the twelfth century, the Flambeau of Praesidium Abditus took an active part in local conflicts. Skirting (and at times breaking) the limits of the Code of Hermes, Guzmán and his *sodales* took part in various clashes against Navarre and Castile, earning several fines from the Quaesitores and the enmity of the covenant of Victrix (see below). None of them imagined that the cause of their frenzied activity, and of the inexplicable unruliness of the turb, sprang from their own covenant: the body of the demon defeated there in antiquity had remained buried beneath the covenant's lands, generating an infernal aura that fostered anger and rage. This steadily eroded relations even among the covenant's own mundane inhabitants and drove the Flambeau to ever bolder acts; matters came to a head when, in 1193, they attended the Other Tribunal of Harra and swore common cause with other covenants to confront the Almohad threat. And so, when Guzmán's *filius* and the rest of the Flambeau set out in 1195 for the battle of Alarcos, where all of them would perish, the covenant disintegrated, sunk in the anarchy and disorder caused by clashing emotions.

Nevertheless, the fortification was never entirely abandoned. Some of the grogs descended from the members of the original turb — in many cases the grandchildren or great-grandchildren of confessed criminals — decided to adapt the covenant and turn it into the base of what would soon become a band of outlaws led by one Pello the Thief. The former grogs have now become bloodthirsty highwaymen who carry out brutal raids around Belchite, again as a consequence of the infernal aura. The rulers of Belchite have sent a couple of companies of soldiers to the old hillfort to deal with Pello's men, but none has returned. They are now considering asking the Templars of Monzón for help, which could once again attract the attention of the covenant of Victrix.

> #### Story Seeds: The Secret of Pello the Thief
>
> The authorities of Belchite are having serious trouble dealing with the highwaymen led by Pello. They know full well where the outlaw leader has his base, but the two groups of soldiers they have sent there have vanished inexplicably without a trace. When a third expedition results in the return of a single survivor who speaks of "possessed men with diabolical powers" living in the old castle, the authorities decide to turn to the Church to rid the region of this scourge.
>
> At the same time, a Redcap traveling through the region hears the same tales and, reading between the lines, concludes that Pello and his men have undoubtedly discovered and learned to use some of the artifacts created by the magi of the old covenant. After he sends word of this to Aedes Saturni, the Guernicus of the Tribunal soon decide that they cannot risk the mundane authorities establishing any link between these criminals and the Order of Hermes, and they offer a reward to whoever travels to Belchite, neutralizes Pello's band without drawing attention, and confiscates the enchanted items before the mundane authorities can do so. Might the characters be interested in such a mission?

#### Setting and Physical Description

Praesidium Abditus lay a little more than a day's journey south of Belchite, in a dense grove away from the main roads. It consisted of a small fortification built on the remains of an ancient Celtiberian hillfort, atop a low hill surrounded by a moat long since overgrown with vegetation. The fortification was a small square castle with a keep and a couple of outbuildings within a small courtyard. The covenant could never grow much because of the inexplicable anarchy that reigned among the turb and the mundane inhabitants, which provoked angry conflicts at the least opportune moments. In the keep, where the magi's *sancta*, the library and other chambers once lay, Pello and his most trusted men now live, while the rest sleep in the outbuildings.

Beneath the tower stretch cellars and small dungeons that saw almost no use while the covenant was active, but which Pello now uses from time to time to lock up a prisoner. What no one knows today, just as the covenant's original inhabitants never knew, is that beneath those chambers lies an ancient cavern where the remains of the demon that generate the infernal aura affecting the covenant still rest. There is no direct access to the cave, but on certain nights when the infernal powers are especially active, a supernatural mist seeps up into the castle's dungeons. Those who venture into it might end up discovering the cave and its disturbing contents…

## The County of Gerona

Established in the eighth century, after the city of Gerona was freed from Muslim rule and handed over to Frankish control, the county of Gerona has traditionally been part of the county of Barcelona since the end of the ninth century, when Wifredo the Hairy received it from Louis II of France, the Stammerer. Despite that dependence, the county minted its own coinage and had its own viscounts. Today it is bounded to the north by the county of Empúries and by Besalú, to the west by the county of Osona and to the south by the county of Barcelona; to the east it borders the Mediterranean Sea.

<!-- p. 206 -->

Gerona is the capital of the county and also its largest and most important town. Founded in the first century AD for its enviable strategic position, the city has passed through Roman, Visigothic, Muslim (for less than a century) and Carolingian rule, and perhaps for that reason it displays a cosmopolitan character in the thirteenth century, a time when the city reaches one of its greatest heights of splendor, thanks also to a population boom that forces it to expand in every direction and to build several bridges over the rivers that run through the city. Its Romanesque cathedral is dominated by the so-called Tapestry of Creation, a majestic linen tapestry of more than fifteen square meters depicting the creation of the world as described in the first chapters of Genesis.

> #### The Catalan Romanesque Monasteries
>
> Throughout Catalonia, and especially in the north, closer to the Pyrenees, there are many monasteries in the Romanesque style, famous as centers of spiritual retreat but also for their cultural and architectural importance. One of the most outstanding is Santa María de Ripoll, founded at the end of the ninth century as a Benedictine cenobium by none other than the count of Barcelona, Wifredo the Hairy, shortly after he had conquered that territory from Islam. The monastery prospered rapidly and became, during the tenth and eleventh centuries, an important cultural center, *scriptorium* and monastic school; it was enlarged several times in that period under the auspices of Abbot Arnulfo. Over the years some of the most distinguished figures of Europe have studied in its halls. Its period of greatest splendor came under the rule of Abbot Oliba, in the first half of the eleventh century. Oliba, of noble birth and a great-grandson of the monastery's founder, Wifredo himself, sent his monks traveling across half of Mythic Europe in search of documents of every kind, not only ecclesiastical, to copy and translate. At Ripoll books were translated from Arabic and Greek into Latin, which contributed to the formidable growth of the abbey's library. Also a fruit of those years is the dazzling Ripoll Bible (see Appendix I), an enormous volume of the sacred text copied by the monk Guifré and prodigiously illuminated by another, anonymous monk of great artistic gifts about whom very little is known. The work, which contains not only the sacred texts but is also a codex for liturgical use with additional exegetical texts, prayers and psalms, now rests in the abbey of Saint-Victor in Marseille.
>
> On Oliba's death the monastery entered a slow decline from which it has not yet emerged, although the place remains a majestic example of Romanesque art, as the monumental portal adorning the main entrance of the church amply attests.
>
> Not far from Santa María de Ripoll stands San Juan de las Abadesas, once the first convent for women in the Spanish March, also founded by Wifredo, who on his death left it in the charge of his daughter, Emma of Barcelona. Originally consecrated as San Juan de Ripoll and occupied by Benedictine nuns, in the decades under Emma's direction the monastery not only became a widely known cultural center but also amassed considerable wealth, which made it a coveted target for some of the nobles nearby. Perhaps for that reason the nuns were expelled from the convent at the beginning of the eleventh century for their supposedly lax morals, being branded "harlots of Venus." Since then the monastery has changed occupants and owners several times, even regaining a chapter of nuns at the end of the eleventh century, when it acquired its present name. Since 1114 the monastery has been occupied by Augustinian canons, who have given it a new cultural impetus.
>
> Throughout Catalonia there are many more convents, including several belonging to the Cistercian order, found especially in the south of Catalonia, among which those of Poblet, Les Santes Creus and Vallbona stand out, all of them of very recent construction.

> #### Story Seeds: The Third Bible
>
> The Ripoll Bible is not the only large copy of the sacred texts to come out of the Ripoll *scriptorium* in the time of Abbot Oliba. During those years the so-called Roda Bible was also copied, so named because Oliba himself sent it as a gift to the monastery of San Pedro de Roda on the occasion of its consecration in 1022. Written on vellum in Carolingian script, it too had Guifré as its copyist, and probably the same unknown illuminator as the Ripoll Bible.
>
> But there was a third Bible, far less known, even though the quality of its script and illumination was comparable to that of the other two. The monk charged with illuminating all three, a young novice named Gualterus with great artistic aspirations, had been tempted by the powers of Hell, with whom he had struck a bargain to obtain his enormous talent in exchange for selling his soul, something no one in the monastery knew. But Gualterus also became an unwitting tool of the infernal forces, which influenced him in ever subtler ways while he was illuminating the third Bible. The miniatures included in that copy were rendered ambiguously, and one well versed in the dark arts could use those illuminations to work terrible enchantments and witchcraft. Oliba himself discovered the connotations of those illuminations when the book was already finished, and he decided to keep the text under lock and key to prevent it from falling into the wrong hands, reluctant as he was to destroy a work of art of such caliber. Since his death, the existence of that Bible has been known only to the successive abbots of Ripoll. Now, decades after it was written, the third Bible has been stolen from the monastery in inexplicable circumstances. The abbot, or one of the monks of the monastery on good terms with the characters' covenant, comes to ask them for help in locating the lost sacred text, fearing that the culprit may be some worshipper of Satan.

<!-- p. 207 -->

Especially important is the city's Jewish community, which holds a special status in Gerona and will grow steadily throughout the thirteenth century. The Jews occupy an area near the cathedral, the so-called *Kahal Jueu*, in many cases in luxurious and monumental residences meant to convey the wealth of their occupants, a great many of whom are devoted to medicine and moneylending. Indeed, during the thirteenth century Gerona will at times be known as "the Mother of Israel."

At this time the city's Kabbalistic school is also becoming established, fully influenced by teachings arriving from Provence, and its principal figures are its first forerunner, Yiṣḥaq the Blind, his student ʿAzriʾel ben Menahem and, most especially, his disciple Naḥmanides, both born in Gerona itself. Naḥmanides, who in his early twenties is already a prominent figure in Kabbalistic circles, will stand out as a philosopher, Talmudist and poet, as well as a physician, during his long life. A champion of mystical spiritualism and an opponent of rationalism, the so-called Jew of the Four Names (for he was also known as Namban, Bonastruc Ça Porta and Mossé ben Naḥman) took part in many debates, both within his own doctrine and defending it against Christianity, and he is and will remain an essential figure for understanding the Kabbalah in Gerona.

### ʿĂrābôt

*ʿĂrābôt, where reign justice, equity and right, the treasures of life, of peace and of blessing, the souls of the righteous, the souls and spirits of those yet to be born, and the dew by which the Holy One (blessed be He!) will raise the dead.*[^p207-26]

[^p207-26]: Excerpt from *The Guide for the Perplexed* by Maimonides (Spanish translation by David Gonzalo Maeso).

>**Lifespan:** 1158–Present<br>
>**Founders:** ʿEzraʾ ben Šēlomoh al-Bonisagī, Abraham Sitjar of Jerbiton<br>
>**Season:** Spring<br>
>**Aura (type and strength):** Magic, strength 3 (palace), Magic, strength 4 (baths)<br>
>**Reputations:** Blasphemers (Kabbalists of Gerona) 2, Wise (followers of Maimonides) 2, Exiles (Iberian Tribunal) 2<br>
>**Votes:** 3

ʿĂrābôt (a Hebrew term referring to the last of the spheres that enfold the world, above which, according to the sacred texts, there is only God) is a Hebrew covenant full of contradictions: it is barely a century old, yet it is home to the Praeco of the Tribunal, and its members are fervent Rationalists who live in Gerona.

#### History

The destruction of the splendid covenant of Lucena caused a diaspora of many magi, who sought new surroundings and the most fitting place to mourn their loss in silence and rebuild their lives. One of them, ʿEzraʾ ben Šēlomoh al-Bonisagī, decided to cross half the Peninsula and return to his native city, Gerona, to establish a new covenant there in which to heal his emotional wounds and pursue his studies. After a long journey alone, he arrived in a city that had changed greatly since his last visit, when he was a newly made magus — a change in every sense, both physical, with a great expansion beyond the walls, and philosophical, with a strong presence of the Kabbalah, represented by the city's large Jewish population.

ʿEzraʾ sought to establish a place as paradisiacal as Lucena, but he had to settle for a small plot of land on the outskirts of Gerona, near the walls that bounded the city, with the episcopal palace and the aljama on one side and the church of Sant Pere de Galligans, which at that time held enormous influence outside the walls, on the other. Using the funds and resources the covenant of Harra had provided him, the Bonisagus commissioned the construction of a small palace on the land, where he had detected a *lacuna* of considerable size and strength. To undertake the construction he relied on the mediation of Abraham Sitjar, a Jerbiton magus accustomed to dealing with mundanes and, moreover, a scion of one of the town's most powerful families. Abraham was won over both by ʿEzraʾ's words and by his project, and he decided to join the magus, moved also by a deep compassion for someone in whom he saw a broken soul. Thus, in 1158, after almost two years of work, the small palace was finished and the covenant of ʿĂrābôt took its first steps. Its birth, however, was marked by controversy: although the city geographically belonged to the Provençal Tribunal, ʿEzraʾ was unwilling to renounce his roots and declared himself part of Iberia at the corresponding Tribunal. The matter inflamed the Provençal authorities and has remained a highly contentious question to this day. Fortunately, Abraham has contacts with a Provençal covenant, the recently reborn Bellaquin, whose Jerbiton are still master diplomats and try to defend ʿĂrābôt's independence before the rest of that Tribunal.

From its beginnings, ʿĂrābôt was more concerned with spiritual than Hermetic matters. ʿEzraʾ was almost more philosopher than magus, and an ardent champion of the rationalist teachings of Maimonides. During the early years he had constant meetings with other *sodales*, to whom he tried to impart his convictions, and at times he even taught the children of local noble families, almost always with Abraham as intermediary. However, his presence soon drew the attention of the city's Kabbalistic circle, which at that moment was beginning an age of ideological splendor as it received, through Yiṣḥaq the Blind, who lived in the city for a time, the influence of the intellectual movements arising in Provence. For a couple of decades the Kabbalists watched ʿEzraʾ and ʿĂrābôt with suspicion, and were defeated time and again in their debates whenever they tried to refute his theses. But it was precisely one of the local Jewish intellectuals who would become his fiercest ideological adversary: ʿAzriʾel "the Holy," a disciple of Yiṣḥaq himself, who engaged in several heated debates with ʿEzraʾ during the last years of the twelfth century.

<!-- p. 208 -->

<!-- p. 209 -->

In 1200, after the destruction of Harra and the death of the previous Praeco, ʿEzraʾ was named Praeco of Iberia at the Tribunal held at Aedes Saturni. A new era thus opened in the life of the venerable Bonisagus, who had believed he had reached a point at which he could devote himself to his philosophical disquisitions. But the new Praeco had to face the mass exodus of magi from al-Andalus that took place in those years. Accompanied by his inseparable Abraham, ʿEzraʾ has tried to concentrate on stemming the migration from Iberia, setting aside his debates and theses for a time. Unfortunately, he has not been able to do so as fully as he would like, for in the Kabbalistic circle of Gerona a new and formidable dialectical adversary has arisen: Naḥmanides, a former follower of Maimonides' theses who now embraces the Kabbalah with a fervor worthy of Yiṣḥaq himself.

#### Setting and Physical Description

ʿEzraʾ always wished to emulate the luxury and splendor of Lucena in Gerona. When he had the small palace built in which ʿĂrābôt would rise, he invested every last coin he had, yet obtained only a pale reflection of his former home: even so, it is an elegant two-story building with porticoes around a central courtyard, adorned with trees and plants, where ʿEzraʾ usually teaches his students when the weather and his time allow. The ground floor is taken up by common rooms, the mundane library, a small storeroom and a couple of small classrooms used when the weather is bad or the group of students is very large. The upper floor holds four *sancta* (one of them usually empty), the treasury and the arcane library. The whole structure stands within a powerful *lacuna* of strength 4 and is protected by an *Aegis of the Hearth* of the sixth magnitude.

ʿĂrābôt also owns a second structure barely two streets from the main palace: baths that ʿEzraʾ had built, in the style and in imitation of those the Muslims used in al-Andalus, shortly after the palace was completed. The *lacuna* reappeared there even more intensely and, most interestingly, as the Bonisagus discovered, it was aligned with healing magic (see *Realms of Power: Magic*, page 16). ʿEzraʾ and Abraham have visited the baths often since they were built, retiring there to debate among the magically heated waters. Moreover, in 1193 the two magi opened the doors of the place to any citizens who wished to enter to shelter from the famine caused by the flooding of the Ter. That act not only saved many lives but also improved the covenant's reputation throughout the city, including among the mundane and ecclesiastical authorities, some of whom were themselves saved by taking refuge in the baths of ʿĂrābôt.

#### Society and Customs

There are two clearly distinct phases in the brief history of ʿĂrābôt: before and after ʿEzraʾ's appointment as Praeco. During its first fifty years, ʿĂrābôt was a twilight retreat for the Bonisagus, who devoted himself more to his philosophical meditations than to his Hermetic affairs, whether magical or political. Abraham, for his part, devoted himself body and soul to making the covenant a place not only known but even esteemed by mundane society; he tried to hide its more arcane side and turn it into a kind of forum for academic and philosophical debate. For that reason, ʿĂrābôt has neither great magical resources nor a very complete arcane library, but it does have an extensive network of contacts throughout Gerona. Its contacts reach even the city of Barcelona, where some of the most prominent members of the Jewish community have dealt with the covenant at one time or another. Maintaining that network demands constant effort from Abraham, since the Kabbalists of the aljama still do not look kindly on the presence and theses of the magi of ʿĂrābôt, and so they often try to defame them or even to reveal their magical activities in a sinister light. So far Abraham has managed to thwart almost all of these attempts, but he must remain constantly on his guard.

With ʿEzraʾ's appointment as Praeco, everything changed. Mindful of his responsibilities, the covenant became almost an extension of the Bonisagus's Hermetic persona; its social activity was reduced (partly also because of a long and deep Twilight suffered by Abraham), and ʿEzraʾ abandoned much of his philosophical activity to concentrate on the Order. Over the last twenty years the Bonisagus has traveled constantly through the Tribunal, visiting many covenants and trying to impose some order on the chaos that has reigned in recent times. Once again this has held back the covenant's Hermetic development, though for different reasons, and it remains mired in a Spring that could stretch on for a long time.

#### The Magi of ʿĂrābôt

##### ʿEzraʾ ben Šēlomoh al-Bonisagī

The life of ʿEzraʾ ben Šēlomoh al-Bonisagī was shattered in 1148 with the fall of Lucena, the covenant where he had lived almost all his life. He was then barely fifty years old, and the blow broke his heart. Unlike his *sodales*, who emigrated to Toledo and to Monforte and with whom he has kept in constant touch all these years, ʿEzraʾ decided to return to his native Gerona to sink into a self-imposed exile. He knew that to do so he would have to form a covenant, which caused him many headaches that added to the deep nostalgia he has always felt for Lucena. Had it not been for Abraham, who has become a constant support to him, he would probably have ended up renouncing the Order or even taking his own life. For many years the only light in his life in Gerona was that of philosophy, and only when he became embroiled in heated debates with the local anti-rationalists did he seem to recover the energy that had once characterized him in al-Andalus. The rest of the time he was a taciturn, sullen magus with very few social relationships.

All that changed in 1200 with his appointment as Praeco. Suddenly ʿEzraʾ not only had a purpose once more, but held an office that allowed him to pursue his dream, which was none other than to try, even from afar, to restore Lucena. Unfortunately, the bureaucratic and logistical realities of the office soon consumed all his time and have kept him from developing that plan beyond a few simple ideas floating in his head, already somewhat senile with age. What cannot be denied is that since his appointment he has been a new man, full of vitality and ready to fulfill his responsibilities for as long as the Order asks it of him. He even took an apprentice shortly after his appointment, Benjamín ben Judá, determined to perpetuate his lineage in a covenant in which he once did not even much believe.

<!-- p. 210 -->

### Abraham Sitjar of Jerbiton

Abraham was born into one of the most powerful and wealthy families of Gerona, the Sitjar. His Gentle Gift remained hidden for several years, but when it became clear that the boy had unusual qualities, his family sent him to study in Provence, where he was trained at the covenant of Bellaquin, which made the necessary arrangements to adopt him as a Hermetic pupil. After his Gauntlet, aware that the covenant where he had studied was entangled in a web of risky social relationships, Abraham decided to return for a time to his native city to ponder his future. It was then that he met the taciturn ʿEzraʾ. His request for help in formalizing the construction of the palace that would become ʿĂrābôt drew in the young Jerbiton, who threw himself body and soul into the project and ended up joining the covenant. Since then, he has worked tirelessly to maintain good relations with every estate of society, avoiding the mistakes that led to the destruction of Bellaquin, with whose heirs he remains in constant contact. Abraham is a jovial, talkative character, although he is now nearly a hundred years old and the subtleties of social diplomacy are beginning to weary him.

### Benjamín ben Judá al-Bonisagī

Young Benjamín was the son of a Jewish cobbler who lived not far from ʿĂrābôt, near the Ter river. When he was barely ten years old, he fell ill with a severe fever that brought him to the brink of death. In desperation, his father went to the owners of the Arab baths, about whom strange stories were told, ready to pay any price to save his son's life. When ʿEzraʾ and Abraham brought young Benjamín to the baths to try to cure him, they were greatly surprised to detect the Gift in the boy. Once he had recovered from the fever, ʿEzraʾ asked the cobbler, as payment, to let him adopt his son, compensated by a more than generous reward in coin. The grateful man accepted, on condition that he could see his son regularly. With the agreement concluded, Benjamín became ʿEzraʾ's apprentice. Although his Gift was strong, his ability to control it has never been great, and he had serious trouble passing his Gauntlet in 1217. By then ʿEzraʾ was already immersed in his duties as Praeco, and where another master would have been ashamed of his pupil's limitations, the Bonisagus saw only a soul that had to find its place, as had happened to him. Since then, Benjamín has tried different aspects of Hermetic magic to determine which of them he has the greatest affinity for, but so far he has not found the answer. His frustration has made him a somewhat embittered young man, and although Abraham tries to make light of the matter, telling him that time will help him find his way, both the Jerbiton and ʿEzraʾ are beginning to worry about the young man's limitations.

> #### Story Seeds: Sacrilege in Gerona
>
> The *Sefer Ha-Bahir* is a fundamental Kabbalistic text, the first volume to set down in writing some of the basic precepts of the Kabbalah, codifying them in a practical sense. First appearing in 1176, the text is attributed by many to Yiṣḥaq the Blind, and the members of the Gerona Circle regard it as almost a sacred text. That is why there is widespread consternation when it is discovered that the book has been destroyed, reduced to ashes for some inexplicable reason.
>
> Inflamed, the Kabbalists of Gerona cry to heaven at the affront, and evidence soon begins to appear pointing to ʿEzraʾ ben Šēlomoh, who over the years has engaged in several heated debates with members of the Kabbalah. The magus denies any involvement in the attack, but the repercussions that the Praeco's participation in such an attack could have, both for the covenant and for the Order of Hermes in general, are unpredictable. Since the magi of ʿĂrābôt are known in the city, the Quaesitores decide to send a small group of magi who can go unnoticed while they investigate what has happened and try to clear the Praeco's name in both mundane and Hermetic eyes.

## The County of Barcelona

The county of Barcelona was created in the year 801, when Louis the Pious of France conquered the city of Barcelona and incorporated it into the Frankish kingdom, establishing it as a county dependent on the king. Over the following centuries, the counts of Barcelona steadily strengthened their autonomy, drawing away from Frankish influence until, with the fall of the Carolingian dynasty and the rise of the Capetians at the end of the tenth century, the counts seized the opportunity to break free of the Franks entirely and become an independent county.

The county continued to strengthen its power in later centuries and to grow in size, coming to include Majorca and the county of Gerona itself. When Ramón Berenguer IV of Barcelona and Petronila of Aragon married in 1150, creating the Crown of Aragon, the county had reached Lérida and Tortosa to the south and west, bordered the counties of Gerona and Osona (both under the authority of Barcelona) to the north, and the county of Urgell to the west. In the latter, the towns of Vich and Ripoll stand out, cities with a strong ecclesiastical character.

In addition to the counties of Gerona and Osona already mentioned, the county of Barcelona also governs those of Berga, Besalú and Manresa. Barcelona is the capital of the county and also its most important town, although there are other notable cities, such as Lérida or Besalú.

<!-- p. 211 -->

### The City of Barcelona

*[…] there is a holy community there (of Jews) and wise and learned men, and great princes […]. It is a small and beautiful city on the seashore, to which merchants come with their wares from every land: from Greece, Pisa, Alexandria in Egypt, the land of Israel, Africa and all its borders.*[^p211-27]

[^p211-27]: Excerpt from the *Book of Travels of Benjamin of Tudela* (Spanish translation by José Ramón Magdalena Nom de Déu).

Barcelona is one of the main centers of trade and activity in the kingdom, a city that has grown enormously rich thanks in part to the weakening of the taifa kingdoms in previous decades, and which boasts a large commercial fleet (see insert). After the Battle of Muret in 1213, which wrecked Aragon's dreams of creating a trans-Pyrenean kingdom reaching into Occitania, the city has turned its sights east and south thanks to the peace treaties signed with Sancho VII the Strong, monarch of Navarre, something that will also benefit it with the future conquests of Jaime I.

In 1220 the city has a wall of Roman origin that encircles its oldest quarter, but outside the walls urban life is also very lively, which will lead Jaime I to extend the wall during his reign, dotting it with gates and entrances to control the access of travelers and goods into the city. Barcelona is currently governed by the Council of One Hundred, a newly created municipal body made up of 128 jurors. The city's commercial prosperity has led many merchants to settle permanently in the city, and will bring about the creation, in 1258, of the Consulate of the Sea, an institution that will regulate maritime trade. That same prosperity will lead to the building of a new wall at the end of the thirteenth century, which will enclose a much larger area and offer the city greater protection against outside threats.

> #### Barcelona, Maritime Power
>
> For decades Barcelona has been one of the leading commercial powers of the Mediterranean, especially since, after the conquest of Almería in 1147 and the disappearance of Muslim piracy, the route along the Mediterranean coast was opened up as far as the Pillars of Hercules. In fact, some of the Anglo-Normans who took part in the crusade against Almería stayed on to live in the county of Barcelona after it ended. Its shipyards, at the Regomir gate, produce mighty ships, and during the reign of Jaime I other, even larger arsenals will be built at the foot of the hill of Montjuic, which will bolster the vigor of the Catalan seafarers.
>
> The maritime might of the county's capital is on a par with cities such as Genoa, Venice or Pisa, although, unlike the Italian powers, which reach both East and West, Barcelona's ships have concentrated more on the eastern coast of the Peninsula and on trade with the Mediterranean islands. Yet although this is their main sphere of activity, some Barcelona seafarers will reach as far as Holland during the thirteenth century and will travel to the Levant from 1230 onward.
>
> Barcelona's relationship with the Italian powers of the Mediterranean has fluctuated over the years. Thus, although in 1167 it agreed to allow safe passage to the ships of Genoa and Pisa along the whole northwestern coast of the Peninsula, a few years later it renewed the pact only with the Pisans. Paradoxically, in 1204 a Genoese vessel pursued by a Pisan one arrived in Barcelona, and the Catalans came to the aid of the Genoese and protected them from the Pisans, who had to promise to harm neither Genoese nor Aragonese before they were allowed to dock and take on supplies.

### Aedes Saturni (Mercer House of Yubal)

>**Lifespan:** 832–Present<br>
>**Founders:** Priamitus of Mercere, Don Šaybān of Mercere (Redcap)<br>
>**Season:** Autumn<br>
>**Aura (type and strength):** Magic, variable strength (between 1 and 4)<br>
>**Reputations:** Efficient (Iberian Tribunal) 3, Profiteers (Andalusi magi) 2<br>
>**Motto:** *Ad triumphum per discretionem* "Toward triumph through discretion"<br>
>**Votes:** 4

Barcelona is home to the most important Mercer House in Iberia, an extensive covenant that spans several structures throughout the city and the county. The Mercer House of Yubal, as it is known, has over the centuries maintained a well-deserved reputation as reliable messengers and trustworthy bankers. Today its members are an important element in the politics of the Tribunal, dealing frequently with the main Hermetic powers of Iberia, while taking care to keep a low profile in the mundane sphere to avoid possible conflicts. They are without doubt one of the powers behind the scenes in the Tribunal.

#### History

The origin of Aedes Saturni is to be found in the Peninsular meeting of 822, where Priamitus of Mercere offered to establish the first Mercer House in Iberia, moved by his interest in discovering more about the region's Mercurian past. He was accompanied in his project by one of his sons, a Mozarabic Redcap without the Gift called Don Šaybān. After discussing it with the magi of the region and agreeing to take the project to the next Grand Tribunal, both parties undertook to buy a large building in Barcelona, inside the Roman wall that then bounded the city, at that time under the control of the Carolingian dynasty. Priamitus named the project Aedes Saturni and began to work with his son to build several Mercere portals in the Peninsula; he also entrusted his son with the first census of vis sources after the Grand Tribunal of 832 approved its construction.

<!-- p. 212 -->

Priamitus was also a far-sighted magus, and, foreseeing that the city would prosper and become an important commercial hub in the Mediterranean, he considered it an ideal place from which the followers of Mercere could carry out their work, and not only in the service of the Order. Thus, in 878, Aedes Saturni lent a substantial sum to Wifred the Hairy to pay his troops in the struggle against Bernard of Gothia, then count of Barcelona, who had rebelled against Charles the Bald. Wifred would go on to become the first count of Barcelona truly independent of the Frankish kingdom. The nobility of Barcelona would not forget Aedes Saturni's help for decades, but this was not the only source of the covenant's economic prosperity: the Mercere of Barcelona managed to profit from numerous entries in the Iberian Peripheral Code, beginning with "On the Iberian Treasury" (899), which from its very inception made the covenant one of the nerve centers of Iberia.

> #### The Almogavars
>
> *[…] and therefore the adalids and the almocadens must take great care to bring with them, on raids and in the other deeds of war, foot soldiers who are accustomed to doing these things we spoke of before, and moreover who are light and always go well provided with good lances and darts, knives and daggers; and likewise they must bring with them foot soldiers who know how to shoot the crossbow well […].*[^p212-XII]
>
> The almogavars are among the first "professional" troops in Iberia, if by "professional" we mean those who know that profession alone as a means of living. The term "almogavar" comes from the Arabic *al-mugāwir* ("he who stirs up raids"), and although the word was already known in al-Andalus during the tenth century, it referred to a certain kind of guerrilla fighter specializing in lightning attacks; it soon came to be used also for the mountain folk and shepherds of the north of the Peninsula who, faced with the hardships caused by the constant conflicts in the area, were forced to come down from the mountains and become bandits and highwaymen in order to survive. They launched swift raids of plunder and pillage, accustomed by their upbringing to surviving in harsh circumstances. Little by little this became their main means of living and, in time, they became fierce guerrilla fighters whom the Christian kingdoms began to employ in their clashes with the Muslims, above all in frontier areas, despite their reputation as cruel plunderers.
>
> The almogavars usually act as infantry, since their relatively light armor gives them great mobility on the battlefield. Their main weapons are the *azcona* or short spear, the falchion, and the *coltell*, or long knife (in game terms, the falchion uses the same statistics as the short sword, and the *coltell* is equivalent to the knife). They are fierce troops, capable of striking fear into their enemies with their terrible war cries and by striking sparks from their weapons with the flints they always carry.
>
> The almogavars have played an important role, especially in the Crown of Aragon, contributing in several battles to the Crown's advance southward, for example in the reconquest of Saragossa or at the Battle of Las Navas de Tolosa. King Alfonso X himself will describe in the *Siete Partidas*, a few years from now, the requirements to be met by the different ranks into which the corps is divided, from the *adalid*, or chief leader, down to the *almocadén* (or captain) and the almogavar who makes up the main body of troops.
>
> The almogavars will grow ever more important over the course of the thirteenth century (not only in Aragon, but in other kingdoms of the Peninsula) and much of the fourteenth; they will come to travel across half of Mythic Europe and will be among the main exponents of the so-called Great Company led by Roger de Flor. Nor are they strangers to contact with the Order of Hermes, and they have offered their services to various Iberian covenants.
>
> [^p212-XII]: Alfonso X, *Siete Partidas*, Second Partida, Title XXII, Law 7.

> #### Story Seeds: *Desperta, ferro!*
>
> *Desperta, ferro!* ("Awake, iron!") is one of the most famous war cries of the almogavars, which they chant before going into battle to intimidate their enemies. In an encounter with a band of almogavars, the magi of the covenant watch in astonishment as many of their grogs, men hardened in a thousand battles, flee in terror on hearing the cry of the enemy warriors. After the inevitable reprimand to their soldiers, the magi may want to investigate, or perhaps hire, that company of almogavars. They are astounded when they discover that the troop's *almocadén*, an Aragonese named Balero, is chiefly responsible for that terror, thanks to a *coltell* that seems to be invested with a potent magical effect that sows fear in those who hear the two dreaded words as the knife is struck against a metal surface. How did Balero come by that knife? Is a covenant involved and, if so, has it broken the law?

<!-- p. 213 -->

Throughout its history, the members of Aedes Saturni have taken an active part in many Hermetic tasks: they have served as a link of communication between magi, they have influenced the distribution of vis sources, and they have manipulated the Tribunal's *status quo* more or less subtly. Moreover, in recent years the covenant has more than once made use of the *víbria* company of almogavars (see insert on the previous page) to carry out all manner of raids, and in 1221 it will close an important deal with the triumvir of Salionca (see page 152).

At the beginning of the thirteenth century, Dulcia, the eldest Gifted Mercere maga of Aedes Saturni, entered Final Twilight and was replaced by the next most senior magus of the covenant, Arnau de Sant Vicenç, a native of Mataró, a Gifted Mercere who still holds the office of covenant leader today.

#### Setting and Physical Description

The Mercer House stands inside the Roman wall, near the Riera d'en Malla, a small watercourse that comes down from the mountains and crosses the city to empty out near the harbor. The covenant occupies a large building, not far from the church of Saints Justus and Pastor, a small Romanesque structure outside the walls that is several centuries old. Aedes Saturni consists of a large guild building acquired by the Redcaps on the pretext of using it as a center for commercial operations, and which hides its true purpose underground: beneath the bustling building on the surface, full of halls, storerooms and chambers, stretches a network of ancient tunnels that begins beneath a small cellar and runs for several hundred meters under the soil of Barcelona. There lie the magi's laboratories, as well as the library, the storerooms, the treasury and the meeting rooms used by the messengers of the Order of Hermes.

Aedes Saturni owns two other buildings in the city that also form part of the covenant: on the one hand a small house in the carrer de l'Estruc (see insert), and on the other a building in the *Kahal Jueu*, the city's Jewish quarter. The Mercere keep a close watch on everything that happens in l'Estruc: they are aware that the great majority of those who work there are hucksters and swindlers, but now and then valuable goods turn up, even raw vis, which always attracts their attention. As for the building in the *kahal*, it was an abandoned house at the time they acquired it, owing to a tragic story involving a Jewish alchemist who had once lived there. Despite its bad reputation, the Mercere discovered that its interior contained a couple of small *lacunae* and decided to acquire it to set up a branch there.

#### The Main Building

To all appearances, the covenant's main building is the headquarters of a commercial organization that serves as a front so that the magi of Aedes Saturni can go about their activities undisturbed. Many of the covenant's mundane members form a mercantile body that trades with other merchants, providing the covenant with funds; at the same time, this front avoids arousing suspicion about what goes on beneath the building's floor. There, reached from a cellar, lies an ancient network of tunnels and caverns that has been enlarged and adapted over the years to house the covenant's main chambers and laboratories. This whole network has auras of different strengths. In the parts nearest the building, many of these auras are small, low-intensity *lacunae*. The *lacunae* closest to the main building have a Magic aura of 1 or 2 at most, and are reserved for the covenant's youngest magi or for the Redcaps' meeting rooms.

However, the Magic aura grows stronger and more uniform as one advances along the tunnels that lead, after a few hundred meters, to the ruins beneath the church of Saints Justus and Pastor. The present Romanesque structure of that church was raised in the ninth century on the remains of an old Visigothic church, but even earlier, in Roman times, a temple dedicated to Mithras stood here. Although these Roman remains are no longer in use today, their Magic aura still persists and extends consistently through the tunnels, with an average strength of 3–4. For years the Mercere of the covenant extended the tunnels until they reached the ancient temple of Mithras, but although they partly cleared the Roman area, hardly any of the covenant's magi make regular use of it.

There are several notable underground chambers in Aedes Saturni. One is the hall of portals, a spacious chamber almost twenty meters across whose perimeter is lined with portals, nearly a dozen of them, many now deactivated. Only four work at present. Three of them are among the oldest portals in Iberia: *Primus* (which connects with Harco), *Secundus* (which connects with Duresca) and *Quintus* (which connects with Salionca). The fourth working portal, *Decimus*, leads to Porta Pandere. In the center of the hall rises a four-meter-tall marble statue of the Founder himself, one arm outstretched and pointing a finger forward. The statue is enchanted so that it turns to point at the portal through which someone will arrive most imminently, a few seconds before the event takes place. In this way the two Redcaps usually posted in this hall (accompanied by guards) can tell where the next visitors will arrive from. The statue, made in the covenant's early years, is said to have other hidden properties, but no one has been able to unravel them, as it is protected by powerful concealment enchantments.

> #### The Carrer de l'Estruc
>
> The carrer de l'Estruc (a word meaning "fortune" or "witchcraft" in Old Catalan), outside Barcelona's Roman wall, is known throughout the city for the soothsayers, sorcerers and witches of every stripe found along the barely 200 meters of its length. The street has something of a bad reputation, for some rather unpleasant legends are told about it, but it is also a common place of visit for the more superstitious, who go there when they suffer some ill that cannot be remedied by mundane means… or when they want to cause some harm to another person. Many of those who live or work in the street are in fact swindlers, or simply people able to perform tricks with which to deceive the populace. Some of them, however, do possess some minor magical ability, although these are precisely the ones who tend to be least active. One of them is the *astruc* ("witch") Sacanera, an old man gifted with minor healing abilities who, they say, uses a black magic stone to work miracles.

<!-- p. 214 -->

The treasury holds the common coffers of all the covenants of Iberia. It is a spacious chamber protected by a sturdy door of solid iron with several locks, enchanted with abundant defensive spells that can strike down any intruder who does not utter the words that allow safe entry. The covenant's treasurer is currently Martí, a Redcap only slightly younger than Yubal, endowed with a prodigious memory and an exceptional head for figures. Faustus of Flambeau also tends to spend a great deal of time in the treasury, and has his laboratory very close by.

The last notable chamber is the covenant's library, located near the ruins of the temple of Mithras. The arcane section of the library specializes in Rego and Corpus magic, but that is not what is remarkable about this chamber: to one side, on several racks divided into shelves that stretch almost to the cavernous ceiling, barely lit by torches, are piled ancient volumes, folios, parchments and engraved tablets, the accumulated travel notes of the various generations of Redcaps who have lived at Aedes Saturni. Anyone wishing to learn some detail of the history or geography of Iberia over the last few centuries can request special permission from Yubal to research these documents, always under the strict supervision of one of the Redcaps.

It is also worth mentioning that in Aedes Saturni's establishment in the carrer de l'Estruc there is a small cabinet containing what at first glance seem to be small objects of every kind and condition, with no apparent relation to one another: pebbles, bits of bone, fragments of clay, pieces of tree bark... In fact this is the covenant's collection of Arcane Connections, to which the magi and Redcaps turn when they need to travel urgently to some place. The cabinet, of sturdy wood, is not only locked with a key but also magically protected with a version of *Watching Ward* that triggers the spell *The Call to Slumber* on anyone who opens or forces the cabinet without first uttering certain words known only to the Redcaps of Aedes Saturni. Naturally, the Arcane Connections are carefully stored to prevent them from losing their mystical links or replacing them with others.

#### The Ebro Premises

Aedes Saturni also has a building outside Barcelona, in the city of Tortosa, at the mouth of the Ebro. This town, which is enjoying a time of unusual prosperity since it was reconquered by Count Ramón Berenguer IV, now sees all manner of goods and products pass along the waters of the river: metals, cotton, alum, silk, timber, kermes, indigo, spices, sugar... The town had no Hermetic presence while it was Turtusha and ruled by the Muslims, but with the reconquest, Aedes Saturni opened a small establishment there, a moneylending house overseen by a Jewish Redcap, Simón the Fair, which serves as a cover for keeping a close eye on the river trade of the region. In addition, the covenant also holds certain rights of commercial exploitation in the area, granted by Templars sympathetic to the covenant of Victrix (see below).

<!-- p. 215 -->

#### Society and Customs

Almost since the beginning of its existence, Aedes Saturni has been governed by a rigid autocracy combined with a democracy. The upper council is usually made up of the Gifted Mercere magi and the current *quaestor aerarii*. Each of these magi has one vote, although the *quaestor aerarii* usually acts as an impartial witness and votes only on matters concerning the common coffers. Below that council there is a second tier made up of the covenant's non-Mercere magi, each of whom has half a vote, or, what amounts to the same thing, half the decision-making power of the Gifted Mercere. In this way plurality within the covenant is guaranteed, without ever forgetting that it is a Mercer House and that, therefore, the magi of that House must have a certain preeminence.

The offices of *praefectus praetorio* and *quaestor aerarii* are traditional posts created more than four centuries ago, when in the year 822 it was agreed that the common resources of the Tribunal would be moved permanently to Aedes Saturni. The first is usually held by a Flambeau magus charged with personally protecting those resources (see the corresponding Flaw in the "New Virtues and Flaws" section, page 305). The duties of the *praefectus* are to protect at all times the common coffers kept at Aedes Saturni, even at the cost of his own life. The *praefectus* usually has his laboratory near the treasury and often takes charge of supervising its guards and even designing its protections. Just as holding the office is an honor for the magus in question, any damage to or theft from the coffers is an affront very difficult to wash away in the Tribunal. This is a title that stirs mixed feelings among the magi of Iberia: some value it for being temporary and for granting the holder a good reputation, while others consider it a waste of time (the title does, however, bring significant economic benefits to the home covenant of the magus who holds the office, as described in the new Flaw).

As for the *quaestor aerarii*, the office is usually held by a member of House Guernicus, and its role is much more administrative and, at the same time, more important than that of the *praefectus*, for it consists of making sure that no one improperly appropriates any of those funds, and that they are used just as each Tribunal determines. The *quaestor* is therefore both manager and watchman of the funds. Unlike the *praefectus*, the *quaestor*'s presence in the treasury is not so necessary, and he usually visits it only occasionally. Even so, he watches over the safety of the coffers at all times, for their integrity is key to the Tribunal. The conditions for the election and re-election of the *quaestor aerarii* are the same as those for the *praefectus praetorio*, as are the benefits in terms of reputation. While both magi hold their offices at Aedes Saturni, they are considered full members of the covenant, and as such they may draw on its resources.

#### The Magi of Aedes Saturni

Aedes Saturni has four Gifted magi and eight Redcaps. One of the magi is a Mercere who serves as the covenant's leader, while another is a Bonisagus Seeker. The other two magi are a Flambeau and a Guernicus who fill the traditional offices of *praefectus praetorio* and *quaestor aerarii*. Among the Redcaps is the eminent Yubal (after whom many know the covenant), and at present they offer their services as messengers to almost the entire western half of the Tribunal. Another of them, Bernat de Sabastida, is a passionate chess player who often takes certain liberties on his travels to visit Toledo and the covenant of Iššáh, home of Agar al-Merkeriyya, with whom he has a healthy rivalry at the game, and with whom he is also hopelessly in love. Although his love is not returned, the two sometimes make stretches of their journeys together, sharing experiences as well as games of chess.

##### Arnau de Sant Vicenç of Mercere

Arnau is an anomaly within House Mercere. Orphaned of both father and mother, he was adopted as a boy by Dulcia of Mercere, a veteran maga of Aedes Saturni. Her intention was to train him as a Redcap, making use of the qualities she saw in the lad, who was as bright and quick-witted as he was eloquent and restless. Imagine her surprise when, some time after Arnau's training had begun, it was discovered that he had the Gentle Gift. Dulcia then faced a curious dilemma, for it is the custom among the Mercere to initiate Gifted children only if they are direct descendants of the Founder. In a bold move, and convinced that she was doing the right thing for the Order and the House, Dulcia decided to take Arnau as her apprentice, causing something of a stir not only at Aedes Saturni and in Iberia, but throughout the House.

It soon became clear that Dulcia had made the right decision. As a pupil, Arnau displayed uncommon perseverance and dedication and, what is more important, an absolute commitment to the House, which he supported entirely selflessly. It soon became clear that he had a certain affinity for healing magic, which clearly decided his specialization, but both before and after his Gauntlet, Arnau closed no doors and trained in the most diverse ways, always with the benefit of the House as his ultimate goal: he dabbled in Mutantum magic, learned unusual but useful spells, and even grew accustomed to traveling with some of the Redcaps of Aedes Saturni when they visited places he had not seen. He used those journeys to get to know new lands and also to get to know the messengers better, whom he considered his equals in their role within the House. He also showed a keen nose for business, and has often used his Gentle Gift to take a direct part in the activities of the mercantile enterprise behind which his covenant hides. Some say that all this is nothing more than an attempt on Arnau's part to clear his name of any stain stemming from his "illegitimate" lineage, something many have not yet forgotten.
