He absorbed the Mercere doctrines concerning Gifted magi so thoroughly that, even today, he tries to avoid casting magic in public and pretends to need special tools to do so, some small colored stone beads forming an exotic rosary that in fact serve no real purpose at all.

For all these reasons, when Dulcia died a few years ago and Arnau put himself forward as her successor, several members of the House were outraged by the proposal. However, there could only be one decision: the only blemish on Arnau's record was precisely the one in which he had had no part: his origin outside the lineage of Mercere. The rest of his life had been marked by absolute commitment and devotion. So there was no doubt about his election within the covenant, and since his appointment as leader, Arnau has only redoubled his devotion. The covenant is more prosperous than ever, and although there are some who still regard him with suspicion within the covenant itself and occasionally try to undermine him covertly, very few in his inner circle doubt that he is the best person to guide the destiny of Aedes Saturni.

##### Filemón of Bonisagus

Filemón is a Bonisagus Seeker of Greek origin who came to Iberia from the Theban Tribunal after hearing rumors about the ruins of the temple of Mithras beneath Aedes Saturni. Since his arrival, a couple of decades ago, the Bonisagus has tried to unravel the mysteries of the ruins with rather little success, owing both to the deplorable state of the site and to his limitations with Intellego magic. Even so, he has not given up. Moreover, ever since he heard that the Toledan covenant of Iššáh possesses the ancient treasures of the Visigoths, he has also shown an interest in having its members share their secrets with him.

<!-- p. 218 -->

Filemón is a man loyal to the covenant and will do whatever it takes to keep his privileged position so that he can go on researching the ruins.

##### Faustus of Flambeau, *praefectus praetorio*

Faustus was trained at Salionca, in the years after his *parens*, Florentius, had left the office of *praefectus praetorio* that he had held for several decades at Aedes Saturni. Florentius believed that Faustus had everything it took to become one of the most promising Flambeau magi in the House and the Tribunal: intelligent, sharp and skilled with magic, he had captivated Florentius from the start, and Florentius had given him a varied and refined education. Faustus's imposing physique was the perfect complement to these gifts, and Florentius was convinced that his *filius* was destined for things far greater than he himself had achieved. Unfortunately, the peculiarities of Faustus's character ended up slowing, if not cutting short, what might have been a meteoric rise through the ranks of the House.

The trouble was that Faustus combined two personality traits that never work well together: he was an inveterate snoop, and utterly incapable of keeping a secret or a relevant piece of information to himself. A couple of rather serious slips at Salionca sent Faustus's reputation plummeting shortly after he passed his Gauntlet, when he learned certain sensitive information relating to Marco Gayo, by then already *dictator* of the covenant. Faustus's slip almost caused a schism in the covenant, and the magus was not only severely reprimanded, but his reputation was badly damaged by the incident, even though the Flambeau never quite understood what had happened.

He soon discovered that his indiscretions had spread through half the Tribunal and that few in Iberia were willing to accept someone like him into their covenants. With a heavy heart, Florentius decided to pull some strings and contact what had been his home for many years, Aedes Saturni, to find a place for his *filius* as *praefectus praetorio*. The negotiation was far from easy: both Yubal and Collegiata refused to accept someone like Faustus. In the end, however, the will of Arnau prevailed; although he shared their doubts, he saw in the young man a reflection of what he himself had lived through in his past. The negotiation with the magi of the Tribunal was not simple either, but in the end the Flambeau voted in favor so as to have a representative of their House in Barcelona (after all, Florentius had carried out his task in exemplary fashion, so perhaps Faustus deserved a vote of confidence), and almost all the Andalusi magi backed them. Thus Faustus was appointed guardian of the magical treasury of the Mercer House and the Tribunal.

Once in Barcelona, Faustus did everything he could to continue the legacy of integrity and honor set by his *parens*. So far he has only partly succeeded. Faustus fulfills all his duties rigorously, guarding the treasury and accompanying Collegiata in all her dealings. It would never even cross his mind to take advantage of the office to steal a single pawn of vis. However, the temptation to snoop in a place like Aedes Saturni is very strong for him. The frantic comings and goings of the Redcaps, the constant exchanges of information in every room of the covenant and the complex financial transactions carried out by Yubal and his family are torture for Faustus, who cannot help listening to every conversation that takes place near him and keeping the juiciest details, which has occasionally led him to neglect his duties as guardian of the treasury. More than once Yubal has caught him "spying" and has lodged complaints with Arnau, whose only argument in reply is Faustus's efficiency in his official duties. The leader of Aedes Saturni trusts that Faustus will learn to control this flaw in his character and so become a guardian as long-serving and reliable as his own *parens*.

##### Collegiata of Guernicus, *quaestor aerarii*

Aedes Saturni and Duresca have always had a very close relationship, especially since they had to join forces to prevent a definitive separation of the Tribunal of al-Andalus. The figure of the *quaestor aerarii* is fully accepted in the Mercer House, and Collegiata is merely the latest in a long line of Guernicus who have served the Tribunal and Aedes Saturni (in that order, according to them), and she matches the same profile as her predecessors. She is a middle-aged maga, shrewd and steadfast, who keeps a close eye on the state of the coffers, but an even closer eye on the political state of the Tribunal. She will do anything to preserve the cohesion and integrity of Iberia... even if it means committing some irregularity in the administration of the coffers that other magi would consider intolerable.

##### Yubal of Mercere (Redcap)

Yubal (also known as Yuval) is the leader of the Redcaps of Aedes Saturni, a veteran messenger with almost a century of experience behind him. Besides that, he is a seasoned businessman — not for nothing has he spent almost half that time as the public face of the mercantile house that serves as Aedes Saturni's mundane front, which is why many call it the House of Yubal. The Redcap had to step down from that position a little over five years ago, to avoid drawing too much attention because of his unusual longevity, and he now divides his time between overseeing the running of the business and hovering about the library, as well as making sure that messages between covenants are delivered punctually — not for nothing is he a member of the Followers of Belin (see *Houses of Hermes: True Lineages*, page 91).

Yubal is quiet and taciturn, and prone to fits of self-absorption from which it is increasingly hard to rouse him. They say that at such moments his memory drifts back to his younger years, when Queralt, the love of his life, was still alive. Unfortunately, those happy times now exist only in Yubal's memory, and he has never fully overcome that loss despite the years that have passed. Even so, when he has a job to do he does it impeccably, and he tolerates no irregularity in the workings of the Redcaps. From time to time, he still takes up his old magic staff and accompanies one of the younger messengers on their journeys, to experience once again the pleasure of traveling.

> #### Story Seeds: The Awakening of Mithras
>
> While some mundane members of the player characters' covenant are visiting Barcelona on a trading mission, some of them go to the church of Saints Justus and Pastor. There they witness an incident in which one of the altar boys falls into a strange trance that many attribute to heavenly intervention. But doubts soon arise when the boy begins to show even stranger behavior: whenever he is inside the church he suffers violent physical reactions (vomiting, epileptic fits, and so on), speaks in ancient pagan tongues, and even produces supernatural manifestations around him.
>
> While the ecclesiastical authorities lean toward possible possession, the magus leading the expedition receives a clandestine visit from Filemón: the magus, deeply worried, asks the visitors for help in getting him out of an awkward predicament. On one of his recent visits to the temple of Mithras he made an unexpected mistake: he fell into a brief but intense Twilight while examining what looked like an ancient sepulcher. When he emerged from Twilight he found the sepulcher open, with clear signs of a strong magical presence, and he fears he has released some supernatural spirit. Afraid to reveal this slip to his superiors at Aedes Saturni, and aware of the presence of the expedition from the player characters' covenant, Filemón asks them for help, in exchange for which he offers his services as a teacher for a few seasons.
>
> Whatever Filemón awakened has taken possession of the church's poor altar boy, whose days are numbered if the characters do nothing to remedy the situation. The creature in question is a faerie spirit that had been imprisoned beneath the ruins for centuries, and which might assume the identity of the Roman Mithras. Before doing so, however, it wants to get to know the new world around it better through the eyes of a human. And everyone knows that faerie curiosity knows no bounds…

### Zaloquia

>**Lifespan:** 927–1162<br>
>**Founders:** Assilem ḅint Cadira Ex Miscellanea, Fateh Ex Miscellanea, Jaled Ex Miscellanea<br>
>**Aura (type and strength):** Magic, strength 2 (inside the mountain); Divine, strength 1–4 (monastery and mountain surface)<br>
>**Reputations:** Illegitimate Origin (Iberian Flambeau) 3

For several centuries the covenant of Zaloquia stood on the summit of Mount Escornalbou, although both the mountain and its fortification have a far older history. After more than two hundred years of a more or less peaceful existence, during which it was inhabited almost entirely by *saḥirs*, Zaloquia was abandoned and later destroyed by the Christian troops of Alfonso II, who retook the region in the mid-twelfth century.

#### History

In Roman times a fortification stood on Mount Escornalbou (so called by the locals because the mountain resembles a bull's horn). Its remains were conquered and restored by the Muslims during the eighth century, when the Saracens overran the whole region of Tarragona and created the so-called emirate of Xibrana. It was then that a group of *saḥirs* in the service of the Muslims discovered a magical aura of some strength on the mountain and asked the local wali for permission to restore and enlarge the fortification, where they settled in the year 852. From then on the place would be known as Zaloquia, or *zahaloquia* in Arabic, meaning "watchtower."

For almost a century Zaloquia was a stronghold of the *saḥirs* who opposed the Order of Hermes. Some of the most powerful non-Hermetic sorcerers who fought on the Mediterranean coast in that era came from there, and when peace between Hermetic magi and *saḥirs* was made official in 925, not everyone at Zaloquia took it the same way. Several of its most important members emigrated south, and only three *saḥirs* remained in the fortress and joined the Order. Hermetic chronicles record them as Assilem ḅint Cadira, Fateh and Jaled, and they are considered the covenant's official founders.

For more than two centuries the members of Zaloquia tried to keep apart from the constant clashes between Islam and the Christians in the region, which had become a frontier zone that saw a great deal of fighting. The Flambeau of the Tribunal still regarded the *saḥirs* with suspicion, however much they had joined House Ex Miscellanea, and any false step could have meant a Wizard's War. Even so, there were isolated cases, not always known, in which some of Zaloquia's *saḥirs* are said to have taken part directly in those conflicts to help the wali of Xibrana. Many of the magi who took part covertly in those battles are said to have belonged to the lineage of one of the founders, Fateh. He had wavered until the last moment over whether to go with the *saḥirs* who fled south, but in the end he decided to give the Order a chance. He soon regretted it, so the story goes, and only his good relationship with the maga Assilem kept him from leaving the Order at once. His Hermetic descendants, however, kept up a belligerent attitude for as long as the covenant existed; they were repeatedly fined by House Guernicus and, on at least one occasion, threatened with expulsion. Only the Schism War forced the *saḥirs* of Zaloquia to keep a lower profile, for fear of suffering the same fate as the Diedne. Assilem's Hermetic descendants, for their part, made Zaloquia a refuge for many Saracens fleeing the Christian advance, who used the stronghold as a place to rest and take on supplies before continuing on their way.

When the troops of Alfonso II of Aragon finally conquered the region in 1162, they launched an attack on Zaloquia, drawn by its enviable strategic position. Most of the covenant's members fled south, warned of the attack beforehand by friendly inhabitants of Xibrana. The members of Fateh's lineage, however, stayed behind to defend the covenant. For all their magical power, the Christian troops, led by Arbert de Castellvell, lord of Ciurana, had no trouble taking the stronghold, and Arbert himself soon held the crag. He ceded it to Joan de Sant Boi on condition that he resettle the place by building a castle and a monastery in honor of Saint Michael, since the little fort had finally fallen on that saint's day. The building of the castle and monastery went on through the second half of the twelfth century and the first half of the thirteenth, and in 1220 the monastery is still unfinished (it will be consecrated in 1240). Today almost nothing remains on the summit of Escornalbou to recall that a Hermetic covenant once stood there.

#### Setting and Physical Description

Zaloquia rose on the top of Mount Escornalbou, almost 650 meters high, whose slopes are covered in thick forest and whose summit commanded a superb view of the whole surrounding area. The covenant was built on the remains of an ancient Roman fortification, and at the height of its splendor it had a main fortress with four towers on the mountaintop. Zaloquia also extended underground, with a number of subterranean chambers that housed the treasury and the *sancta* of some of the magi. Almost the whole place was razed when the troops of Alfonso II retook the region in 1162, although some say that a few underground areas might still hold treasure or documents belonging to the old covenant. This is very hard to confirm, however, since where the covenant once stood there now rises a half-built Augustinian abbey, protected by an imposing adjoining castle. Not far from the site lies the small village of Segura, which grew up while the monastery and castle were being built.

<!-- p. 222 -->

> #### Story Seeds: The Moorish Queen's Leap
>
> Legend has it that in the days when the troops of Alfonso II conquered Xibrana, a young princess named ʿAbd-l-Azia, famed for her incomparable beauty, lived in the town. The daughter of the local wali, she lived surrounded by every kind of luxury and wealth, convinced that nothing could ever take the town, defended as it was by an impregnable castle. When the Christians at last broke into the fortress (with the help, some say, of a Jew who let them in through a window), the princess, on hearing the news, resolved to kill herself rather than be captured by the enemy. She mounted a horse and galloped off toward a nearby precipice. The horse, far less desperate than its mistress, tried to stop before the inevitable fall, but nothing could keep horse and rider from plunging down the mountainside. Ever since that day, the hoofprints the horse left as it tried to stop and escape its terrible fate can still be seen at the place now called the Moorish Queen's Leap.
>
> The characters hear rumors of a possible vis source at the foot of the Moorish Queen's Leap. Looking into the rumors, they confirm that there is indeed a powerful source in the area, but it is guarded by the ghost of ʿAbd-l-Azia herself, who wanders there in eternal torment. The characters could try to destroy the ghost, but before they can do so they hear a story that tells of the princess's passionate romance with one of the last inhabitants of Zaloquia. Might seeing an object that belonged to her beloved bring the Moorish queen's ghost to rest? And how can they get into the tunnels beneath the monastery of Escornalbou, where they might find such an object?

## The Marquisate of Lérida

The area of the marquisate of Lérida was one of the last in the northeast of the Peninsula to be conquered by the Christian kingdoms. The city of Lérida itself was not taken until 1149, by the count of Barcelona, Ramón Berenguer IV, as part of his military campaigns beyond the eastern limits of his domains. Because of its frontier position, the whole region came to be known as a "marquisate," which included other towns also taken in those years, such as Fraga, Monzón, Alguaire and Bell Lloc. It never had a noble house as such, however, and some of its towns soon had their own settlement charter, as Lérida did in 1150, and their own municipal charter, which Pedro II granted Lérida in 1197. Lérida is in fact the most important city in the whole region, with a cathedral in full construction in 1220, commissioned from the recently deceased master Pere de Coma, which rises on the same hill where the city's old Muslim alcazaba once stood, now a royal castle.

### Victrix

>**Lifespan:** 1095–Present<br>
>**Founders:** Anteo of Tremere, Sitt Nasim al-Tremeriyya<br>
>**Season:** Summer<br>
>**Aura (type and strength):** Magic, strength 4<br>
>**Reputations:** Templars (Iberian Tribunal) 3<br>
>**Votes:** 5

The covenant of Victrix continues the long Tremere tradition in Iberia. Besides the explicit meaning of its name (Latin for "victorious"), the Tremere chose it because its initial is the Roman numeral five (it being the fifth Tremere covenant in the Tribunal).

#### History

After the Schism War, the only Tremere to survive in Iberia was in fact an apprentice: the very young Fata. Although the girl tried to keep the covenant of Tertia going, in 1046 she had to leave Iberia and join a covenant of the Normandy Tribunal, because Duresca had sentenced her to pay a heavy fine on pain of exile. The Tremere did not return to the Peninsula until 1089, when Coeris sent Sitt Nasim al-Tremeriyya, a maga born in Baghdad, and the future Exarch of Iberia, Anteo of Tremere *filius* Gaia, with the aim of regaining political representation there and supporting the Order in the territory of the Peninsula.

Although they were newcomers, Coeris provided them with all the information it had on Iberia and the contacts left by the Tremere who had come before them. Sitt Nasim and Anteo settled not far from where the covenants of Prima, Secunda, Tertia and Tremébriga had once stood. To choose the right site they spent a few years studying the area, and settled on the newly formed kingdom of Monzón. In 1083 the town of Monzón had been conquered by the Cid for the Hūdid king of Saragossa, and in 1089 it had passed to the king of Aragon, Sancho Ramírez, who had given it to his son Pedro, who in turn had made it the capital of the small kingdom of Monzón, a fief of Aragon. So the Tremere settled near the town, on the banks of the Cinca, and soon approached the ecclesiastical powers of the area. The founders of Victrix had also taken note of the newly created church of San Juan (which had been named a royal chapel), hoping it might become an important center (indeed, in 1220 thirty churches depend on it).

In those years Monzón was a defensive bastion that protected the kingdom's southern frontier and held back raids from the taifa of Lérida. By the time the fortress passed, in 1104, to the husband of doña Cristina Rodríguez (one of the Cid's daughters), Anteo and Sitt Nasim had already won the favor of the clergy and lesser nobility of the kingdom, so the Tremere maga was able to leave and join the Toledan covenant of al-Dhahabī (the future Iššáh), where Coeris had posted her. Anteo then became Exarch of Iberia and was left at the head of the Tremere of the Peninsula and Provence, just as the mundane situation was beginning to turn against them. In 1126 the covenant was attacked by the Muslim forces that took Monzón, and the Tremere of Victrix had to take refuge at Iššáh, which they did not leave until 1130, when the area was recovered by Alfonso I the Battler. But the peace did not last. In 1136 the covenant again witnessed the conquest of the town, although this time Anteo was able to save the situation with magic and there was no need to abandon it. Monzón thus remained in Muslim hands until 1141, when it was conquered by Ramón Berenguer IV, *princeps* of Aragon. With the Concord of Gerona of 1143 (see insert), Anteo turned his relationship with the Templars to Victrix's advantage. The Knights of the Temple renounced the will of Alfonso I in exchange for grants from the kingdom of Aragon in the form of commanderies and castles: the town of Monzón passed into their hands, they were granted customs rights, and they made the church of San Juan the commandery of Monzón. In return, Anteo helped them build their irrigation channels and a pilgrims' hospital, and work their lands. In time the Templars built a mint, and the commandery became the most powerful in the kingdom, to the profit and glory of Victrix.

<!-- p. 223 -->

> #### The Templars in Iberia
>
> The first Templar in the Peninsula was Ramón Berenguer III, count of Barcelona. In 1126 he managed to have the Templars establish themselves in his county, and in 1130 he joined the order; the first Templar grant in the Peninsula, the castle of Grañena, followed in 1134 at the Count's request. But the order's power did not arrive until the settlement of the Concord of Gerona in 1143. In that settlement, the Templars rejected the will of Alfonso I the Battler in exchange for a series of concessions to the order, which in the end made possible its rise in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries. For example, Ramón Berenguer IV granted them a fifth of everything they helped to conquer, exempted them from paying tribute to the Church and the crown, and gave them autonomy of decision in military matters, the right to collect tithes, and the right to build castles, provided these were for fighting the Muslims. In addition, the Count ceded them several strongholds, including Monzón and Chalamera, over which they gained permanent rights of usufruct and exploitation (all these places were confirmed by Pope Eugenius III at the Lateran in 1150, and six years later Ramón Berenguer IV held a Concord at which he obtained from Pope Adrian IV a bull confirming all his concessions). Finally, the Concord laid down fines and punishments for anyone who wronged the Templars.
>
> The Templars and the count of Barcelona, Ramón Berenguer IV, were the protagonists of the conquest of Tortosa (see page 42). After the spoils were divided, the Genoese sold their share to the Temple, and in 1182 Alfonso II (son of Ramón Berenguer IV) also handed over his share, which was confirmed in 1202 by Pedro II the Catholic. By 1210 the power of the Templars was such that they had become moneylenders to the crown, issuing it written promissory notes.
>
> The counts of Portugal, for their part, made donations to the order in its early years (such as the town and fortress of Soure, which the order would keep until its dissolution), with the aim of defending the southern frontier against the Almoravids. And they gave the order not only strongholds and towns but also vassals and properties, both in Portugal and in Galicia.
>
> In 1220 the Templars hold numerous fortresses in Iberia, some of which are listed here: the castle of La Zuda (headquarters of the commandery of Tortosa, conquered by Ramón Berenguer IV); the fortress of Miravet, from which they control traffic on the Ebro toward Tortosa and oversee the collection of taxes (conquered from the Muslims by Ramón Berenguer IV and ceded to Pere Rovira, master of the Temple in Provence); the castle of Gardeny (in Lérida, also conquered by Ramón Berenguer IV); Ucero (in Soria, which served as a base for Alfonso I of Aragon during the civil war with his wife Urraca); Ponferrada, from which they control the Way of Saint James on the stretches between Astorga and Villafranca del Bierzo; the castle of Alba Aliste (Zamora, granted to the Temple in September 1220); and that of Alcañices since 1211 (also in Zamora, on the border of al-Andalus and Portugal), which in 1220 is disputed with the Order of Santiago (although in 1230 Pope Honorius III will intercede on the Templars' behalf).

Anteo met Final Twilight in the mid-twelfth century, and the maga Medea of Tremere took the title of Exarch and the leadership of the covenant. Medea ruled Victrix forcefully, and although she suffered a hard blow with the death of Prosérpina of Tremere at Alarcos, she more than made up for it in 1214, when she took advantage of the arrival of the *infante* Jaime and his cousin Ramón Berenguer (future count of Provence) at the castle of Monzón. Both were placed in the care of the renowned Catalan Templar and master of the Temple, Guillem de Montrodón, who brought them up as Templar knights until the age of nine, which is why Jaime remained close to the order for the rest of his life. Thanks to her close relationship with the Templars, then, the Tremere maga was able to oversee very closely the education and upbringing of the future Jaime I the Conqueror.

In 1220 Medea wields great power and enjoys a great reputation, for she has managed to draw close to the Order of the Temple in the Peninsula, and as Exarch she governs the Tremere of the Provençal and Iberian Tribunals (Pedro Gutiérrez of Duresca and Sitt Nasim of Iššáh report directly to her). She also controls the castle of Chalamera (under the commandery of Monzón), at the confluence of the Alcanadre and the Cinca, through which passes the secondary Catalan route of the Way of Saint James, and where its garrison (of between ten and fifteen Templars) is charged with protecting the roads. Her influence reaches a small church of the Order of the Temple dedicated to Saint James, beside the pilgrim road (near Chalamera), whose revenues are a constant source of dispute with the bishop of Lérida. Thanks to Medea, the Templars have ceded part of their rights to exploit the trade at the mouth of the Ebro and its important seaport to the covenant and Mercer House of Aedes Saturni, which has added to the general wealth of the Tribunal, and of Victrix in particular.

<!-- p. 224 -->

#### Setting and Physical Description

The covenant of Victrix stands on a small hill beside the Cinca, some eight kilometers south of Monzón. Partly fortified (it has an outlying tower built with the Temple's permission), from the outside it looks like a castle, although it has no keep. All its buildings lie behind a curtain wall some five meters high, with a crenellated wall-walk on the west and north to watch the flanks not exposed to the river. The "fortress" has no parade ground, however. The mundane buildings are in the northern and western parts, while the magi's quarters (council chamber, library and *sancta*) are to the south and east, overlooking the Cinca and arranged around a courtyard that resembles a cloister in every respect, except that at Victrix it has two stories.

The mundane quarters are separated from the magi's by three guarded passages, which only the covenant's highest-ranking grogs may pass. In the mundane quarters there is a well and a garrison of knights commanded by a companion who belongs to the Order of the Temple and holds certain privileges in the commandery of Monzón.

The covenant's presence has begun to draw a small suburb around the fortress, and a small chapel has been founded there, which Medea watches closely to keep the divine aura from growing. Victrix has a network of underground passages that the Tremere architects built after the first Muslim attack on the covenant. The tunnels reach as far as the town of Monzón and have an entrance on the southern slope of the hill on which the covenant stands. In 1215 Medea arranged a meeting with the *infante* Jaime in that very cave: disguised as an old man, she told him to bathe his sword in the spring of El Saso, for if he did so he would never be defeated while defending Christendom.

#### The Castle of Chalamera

Victrix controls the castle of Chalamera, at the confluence of the Alcanadre and the Cinca, a day's journey south of Monzón. The town of Chalamera is a place where pilgrims coming from Catalonia stop to rest, which brings great wealth to the Temple in the first instance and to Victrix in the last. The fortress of Chalamera is a small castle with a parade ground where the ten or fifteen Templar knights who guard it can train and stable their horses. Among their duties is protecting the roads so that they can be traveled safely, both by merchants and by the pilgrims who follow the secondary route of the Catalan Way of Saint James. These Templars obey Guillem de Montrodón, so Victrix can only count on them in the absence of any order from their master. That is why Medea always keeps a small garrison of two or three soldiers loyal to Victrix, who as a rule place themselves at the service of any order issued by the Templar garrison.

#### Society and Customs

The inhabitants of Victrix live under the autocrat's strict rules. Within its walls no one may raise their voice, work must be done in silence, and sensual pleasures such as music, poetry or drink are strictly forbidden (although chess, of course, may be played). In many respects life at Victrix is like life in a monastery. Because of its relationship with the Templars, the autocrat may require Victrix's inhabitants to perform tasks for the Temple, and the magi themselves sometimes have to carry out some errand or support the activities (in peace or war) that the master Guillem de Montrodón requires of them.

The magi's council is an autocracy ruled by the *ductrix* Medea. The post is held for life and is tied to the office of Exarch of Iberia and Provence, so it can only be obtained through *certamen* or by direct appointment from Coeris. Below that figure come the rest of Victrix's magi, then the autocrat, and finally the captain of the turb (one or both of these must come from a noble family of Aragon and belong to the Order of the Temple). Medea strictly regulates the attendance of Victrix's members at council; it is a rare meeting that all the covenant's members attend, except for the customary meeting at the winter solstice, when they gather to renew the *Aegis of the Hearth*, always cast by the *ductrix*.

Victrix is on good terms with the powers of the Tribunal and has always cooperated with them. Its presence in Iberia has nothing to do with the earlier Tremere settlements in the Peninsula, so in 1220 it is a covenant that inspires trust among the magi of the Tribunal. So much so that, of the three vacant seats in the Iberian Chamber, one is usually reserved for the Exarch Medea of Tremere, invited by both Duresca and Durato, for those who know her speak wonders of her, as much for the good sense of her counsel as for her pragmatism.

#### The Magi of Victrix

##### *Ductrix* Medea of Tremere, House Exarch and Archmage

Medea is an elderly maga holding the title of archmage, who appears to be in her thirties thanks to a powerful Longevity Ritual. She is said to have been born in Pembroke, in the south of Wales, and to descend from a line of magae that the Tremere know as the lineage of Diana. Medea holds the office of Exarch of the Iberian and Provençal Tribunals and answers only to the Prima Poena; the Tremere of experienced rank report directly to her. When she speaks, she usually does so in a calm but firm tone that forces those present to lower their voices in order to hear her. For all her beauty, her features are unsettling, since she rarely moves anything but her mouth when she speaks and seldom blinks. Few magi have seen her so much as raise an eyebrow.

<!-- p. 225 -->

<!-- p. 226 -->

Medea rules Victrix with an iron hand, and although her House comes first, her covenant does not lag far behind. Her relationship with the Temple has cost her more than one investigation by House Guernicus, from all of which she has emerged unscathed. For Medea, honor and one's given word are everything, as the powers of the Tribunal well know, and they always reserve one of the free seats in the Iberian Chamber for this implacable maga.

Medea holds three voting *sigils*: her own and those of her former apprentices, Alexírroe (at Victrix) and Dánae (at the Andalusi covenant of Qasr Dār al-Muchaddad).

##### Alexírroe of Tremere

The maga Alexírroe is Medea's *filia*, and so does not yet hold her own voting *sigil*. As such, she is at the service of her mistress, the covenant and the Tribunal (in that order), and, thanks to Alexírroe's Gentle Gift, Medea often negotiates through her. Alexírroe is loyal, with an unbreakable will. She lacks initiative, however, which makes her an exceptional subordinate and a dreadful leader. This weakness worries Medea, and although she has tried to remedy it, she has not yet managed to get Alexírroe to step forward on her own initiative.

##### Lop Garcés Cajal of Tremere

Lop comes from an important noble family of Aragon to whom Alfonso I granted lands and honors back in the eleventh century. His family's relationship with the Temple fostered its good relations with Victrix, to the point that, when the Gift was discovered in the boy, the family handed him over to the covenant to take charge of his education, so he is both Templar and magus. Lop holds two voting *sigils*: his own and that of his *filius* Deucalión (at Victrix).

Lop is a mature, ambitious magus with a brilliant career in the House. But his ambition frightens Medea. Lop is no more capable than Alexírroe, but he does have enough drive to leave her behind. Medea believes that maintaining Victrix's position is a delicate matter and, somewhat arrogantly, thinks that no one could do it better than she. She fears that in her absence Lop would lean too far toward the Temple and Victrix would fall into a Hermetic crime, something Medea has no intention of allowing.

As a Templar, Lop must do his duty by the order and answer to Guillem de Montrodón. Thanks to the negotiations Medea has conducted with the Templars, however, Lop usually stays out of the Temple's affairs unless Victrix decides otherwise.

##### Deucalión of Tremere

The young Deucalión is the *filius* of Lop Garcés and, unlike his *parens*, has not been made a Templar knight, for besides being of humble origins, his character has never been to his *parens*'s liking. Deucalión has developed an impractical poetic streak that Lop loathes and that clashes head-on with the atmosphere at Victrix. He is a talented young man, however, so Medea has always protected him and promoted his advancement, even against Lop's wishes. Medea does not intend Deucalión to spend much longer at the covenant and is negotiating his admission to one of the covenants of al-Andalus, where he can better serve the House and the Tribunal and can begin to live after the years of psychological torment he has suffered under his master.

##### Creúsa of Mercere (Redcap)

The Redcap Creúsa has served Victrix ever since she finished her apprenticeship at Aedes Saturni. Over time her diligence and attitude earned Medea's respect, so at the beginning of the thirteenth century the Exarch asked the Mercer House to allow her to join Victrix. The main seat of the Mercere in the Tribunal was not about to pass up such a deal, so Creúsa became a member of the covenant at once.

> #### Story Seeds: The Child of Time
>
> *[…] God's bringing the world into existence does not imply a beginning in time, since time is itself among the created things. Indeed, if you assert that time existed before the creation of this world, you are bound to admit its eternity […], which must be avoided.*[^p226-XV]
>
> Recently many magi in the Tribunal have sensed a strange pulse in the flowing vis of Iberia. Although no one has been able to put it into words, those who have tried agree in describing it as a sensation like a void with consciousness. The Criamon of the Tribunal say the cause is a boy with a strange Gift, whose sigil may be related to time. According to them, his magical crises are linked to painful events in his life, and when they happen, it is as if time stopped for an instant.
>
> Although it seems no more than gossip, the boy, named Carles, has caught Medea's attention. If it is true, the boy's sigil would breach a Limit of magic, and his Gift might hide the secrets of that Limit. It seems that the Criamon of Barzaj have been watching him for a year, and other magi have already gone to the farmstead in the county of Barcelona where he lives with his family. The magi who have seen him already call him "Tempus."
>
> If what is said of the boy is true, Medea would be willing to take him as her apprentice, even though he is male. Will the player characters' magi be interested in this child? Could he spark a confrontation among the magi of the Tribunal? As always, how this singular child develops and what becomes of him will ultimately depend on each gaming group's storyguide.
>
> [^p226-XV]: Excerpt from *The Guide for the Perplexed* by Maimonides (Spanish translation by David Gonzalo Maeso).

# IX. The Almohad Empire

*I praise God for having caused me to be born in al-Andalus and for granting me the grace of being one of its sons. My arm may be raised with pride, and the nobility of my condition spurs me to perform meritorious deeds.*[^p227-28]

[^p227-28]: Excerpt from *In Praise of Spanish Islam* by Al-Šaqundī (Spanish translation by Emilio García Gómez).

Al-Andalus is the northernmost region of the Almohad Empire. In 1220 the twenty-three-year-old caliph, Abū Yaʿqūb Yūsuf II al-Muntanṣir, "rules" from his palace in Marrākeš, the capital of the empire, though only in name, for he has delegated his powers to various members of his family: his third cousin governs in Tunis and his uncles govern in Seville, where, beyond the borders of the *kūra*, the unity of the empire is crumbling.

The Almohad army has not recovered from the defeat it suffered in 1212 at Las Navas de Tolosa. The Christian monarchs have kept pushing the frontiers of their kingdoms southward, and while the younger kings of the north have not yet begun to expand (Fernando III of Castile will sign a truce with the Almohads in 1221, and Jaume I will not begin his advance into Valencia until 1229), the older ones have never stopped doing so (in 1217 Afonso II of Portugal inflicted a terrible defeat on the Almohad armies at Alcázar do Sal, and Alfonso IX of Leon will attack the *kūra* of Seville in 1220). On top of all this, the governors of the other *kuwar* of al-Andalus will themselves take advantage of the weakness of the Almohad central power to defy it and proclaim themselves independent emirs, in what will become the third period of the taifa kingdoms (beginning with Baeza in 1224 and continuing with Malaga and Ceuta in 1229).

Meanwhile, on the other side of the strait, the Almohads have managed to put down a rebellion that shook their empire for four years. The Banū Marin (who fought alongside the Almohads at Alarcos) began to levy their own taxes on small villages far from the central power in 1213, and in 1217 they tried to occupy the east of the Maghreb. Although the Almohad armies managed to defeat them and drive them back into the Rif mountains, they did not destroy them. Indeed, the Banū Marin will remain in the mountains for nearly thirty years, after which they will attack the empire again until they conquer its capital, Marrākeš, in 1269, at which point the Almohad dynasty will come to an end.

Although in 1220 the government in Tunis is relatively stable, the loss of the peninsular territories is undermining its authority, and in the near future the Almohads will have to face further rebellions: in 1229 the governors of Ifrīqiya, the Banū Hafs, will break away from the empire, which will only hasten its disintegration.

In spite of everything, the caliph lives oblivious to all the problems of his empire; in his short life he has left the palace of Marrākeš only twice, and he will die in 1224 without having fathered a male heir.

## The Covenants of the Almohad Empire

The covenants of the Almohad Empire are scattered between al-Andalus and North Africa. In Iberia they are spread among the various *kuwar* of al-Andalus: al-Gharb, Seville, Cordoba, Granada, Jaén, Valencia, Murcia and the Balearic archipelago; in Africa only the covenant of al-Minẓār, in Madīnat Fās (Fez), still stands, since the Order's advance into the lands of the *bilad al-Sūdān* was halted after the passing of the Peripheral Code ruling "On al-ʿIdwa" (1123).

## Al-Gharb

The administrative region of al-Gharb (from the Arabic, "the west") is the westernmost *kūra* of Iberia. Although its frontier has shrunk considerably since 1217, it is home to important cities such as Silves (its capital), Beja, Ṭabīra and Šanta Marīyat al-Gharb (Faro). The terrain of al-Gharb is gentle across most of its extent but somewhat more rugged toward the south, where the mountains do not exceed 1,000 meters in height. Its coasts are lined with beaches and low cliffs riddled with caves. Because of the nature of its landscape, al-Gharb has traditionally held numerous vis sources of moderate power, which has led many covenants to use the area as a place for gathering vis rather than for settling.

Al-Gharb is bounded to the west and south by the Atlantic Ocean. To the north it borders the kingdom of Portugal, and to the east the Almohad *kūra* of Seville. At present the region is home to the covenants of Ŷezirat Tennyn and Chazāʾir.

### Ŷezirat Tennyn

*For knowledge, water represents the domain of life, in the sensible as much as in the spiritual sense.*[^p228-29]

[^p228-29]: Excerpt from *The Splendor of the Fruits of the Journey* by Ibn ʿArabī (Spanish translation by Carlos Varona Narvión).

>**Lifespan:** 1130–Present<br>
>**Founders:** Fāṭīma al-Praliḥiyya, Sankhambi al-Merkerī (Redcap)<br>
>**Season:** Summer<br>
>**Aura (type and strength):** Magic, strength 5<br>
>**Reputations:** Ocean Explorers (Hermetic) 3<br>
>**Votes:** 2

Ŷezirat Tennyn (from the Arabic, "dragon island") is a seafaring covenant devoted to the exploration of the Green Sea (as the Arabs call the Atlantic) and to the search for the magical resources it holds. Although it is relatively young, in its almost one hundred years of existence it has reached strange lands, from which it has brought back curious specimens of animals, plants and minerals and, on occasion, extraordinary vis never seen before.

<!-- p. 229 -->

Their exceptional knowledge of the ocean has earned its members a certain renown in the Tribunal and the Order. It would not be the first time that other magi have hired their services for ocean voyages or to reach some distant archipelago. While other vessels sail without losing sight of the coast (even the sailors of Barcelona, held to be the finest navigators in the Mediterranean), Ŷezirat Tennyn has spent months on the high seas and lived to tell the tale.

#### History

Fāṭīma and Sankhambi were members of the Mercer House of Aedes Iris in the lands of the *bilad al-Sūdān*. When the two of them proposed exploring the Green Sea to obtain more magical resources, Porta Pandere, Aedes Iris and Aedes Saturni all agreed, and so they were given a fast ship and several men and women to help them handle the vessel and defend themselves against the pirates of the Atlantic.

On their first voyages they sailed within sight of the coast and put in at every archipelago they came across. During those journeys they suffered numerous pirate attacks and discovered new vis sources and the portal at the Pillars of Hercules (see the covenant of Qasr Dār al-Muchaddad, page 250). Over the years, Fāṭīma proposed to Aedes Iris that they venture out into the open sea, and although the proposal was rejected at first, they were eventually granted a magical ship and a crew capable of enduring such a voyage. Fāṭīma and Sankhambi then put to sea, far from piracy and the known world, and discovered extraordinary things, all of them recorded in their precious logbooks (among the many wonders described is their encounter with the old woman of Jurāsān, who stood upright on the waters praising God while the waves caressed her legs).

At the end of their long voyage they reached a group of seven islands peopled by strange and learned folk, whose description matched the eternal Fortunate Isles (in Arabic, *al-jalidāt*), to which wise men and women go after they have passed on all their knowledge to the community. Each of the two largest islands had a column forty meters high, adorned with beautiful bronze statues and crowned by two human figures with their hands stretched out toward the sea; the sages of those lands told them that the figures pointed toward *Ŷezirat Tennyn*, the "dragon island," a magical place guarded by a terrible creature fallen from the lunar sphere that watched over immeasurable treasures of antiquity. On their return, laden with vis and riches, they found that Aedes Iris had been destroyed, so they set course for Porta Pandere, where Fāṭīma and Sankhambi were told of everything that had happened during their long absence (such as the resolution the Tribunal had passed in 1123). Despite the riches they brought, the Tribunal forbade them to return to *al-jalidāt*, and, after demanding that they hand over their sea charts, Porta Pandere took from them the magical ship that Aedes Iris had given them. It was then that Fāṭīma and Sankhambi decided to found their own covenant, which they named Ŷezirat Tennyn.

The two magi persuaded the Quaesitores of Duresca to sign the covenant's founding charter in 1130, three years after their return from *al-jalidāt*. Fāṭīma and Sankhambi worked to acquire a ship and to raise their covenant on an island off the coast, a few kilometers south of the town of Sines. Over the years (some say through piracy, though in truth it was through their ambergris) they amassed enough wealth to sail the Green Sea once more with the sole purpose of finding *Ŷezirat Tennyn*. However, time passed and they never managed to reach that island.

When the crusaders took Alcázar do Sal, Sankhambi and Fāṭīma, by then elderly, boarded their enchanted ship and put to sea for the last time. The newly made maga, Manjuza *filia* Fāṭīma, was not even able to bid them farewell, for they left before dawn without saying goodbye. Since that year, Ŷezirat Tennyn has tried to carry on the founders' task. In 1220, however, there has been hardly any progress, for although Darfílun's heart-beast is a dolphin, Manjuza has asked him not to leave her alone, since every year there are more sightings of Christian ships near the coasts of al-Gharb. The absence of the two founders has weakened the covenant, and Darfílun doubts that anyone will want to join them, for the war between Portugal and the Almohads is about to reach their doors.

If no one helps them in the coming years, Ŷezirat Tennyn could fall back into its Spring. What is more, when the Tribunal learns of Fāṭīma and Sankhambi's departure in 1221, Aedes Saturni and Porta Pandere may try to seize the covenant's priceless sea charts. Then both Manjuza and Darfílun will have to seek the support of other covenants (such as Ajabeba).

#### Setting and Physical Description

Ŷezirat Tennyn stands on the small island of Pessegueiro, some 300 meters off the coast. From north to south the island is about 350 meters long, and from east to west a little over 150 at its widest point. The island's surface is fairly even, which makes life in the covenant easier. Taking advantage of some rocky stacks on its western side, the founders built a landing stage there where the boats that carried Redcaps (or any other guests) to the covenant could tie up, and which, until 1217, were used to row out to Ŷezirat Tennyn's great enchanted ship (which was kept anchored offshore). After the founders took the ship away, the carpenters built a longboat that Manjuza uses to reach the covenant's vis sources.

Ŷezirat Tennyn consists of two small buildings separated by a courtyard. As is common in Andalusi architecture, the covenant's exterior is rather austere: its monotonous gray walls have only a few small windows set more than two meters above the ground. The covenant's roof is flat, and on clear days the columns of smoke rising from its chimneys can be seen from the mainland. Around the perimeter of the island the founders raised a stone wall that bars any mundane approach except at the point farthest from the coast, where the harbor is located.

The interior of Ŷezirat Tennyn is luxurious and opulent: ceilings and walls are hung with carpets, and the common rooms are full of cushions, chairs and divans. The covenant is perfumed with the costly essence of ambergris, which the former founders traded in the port cities of Cadiz and Almería. Unfortunately for Manjuza and Darfílun, the founders did not record the sources of this perfume in any of the many navigation charts the covenant keeps, so although they have enough reserves to live comfortably for centuries, if they were to lose them they would be unable to restock.

<!-- p. 230 -->

For all the covenant's luxury, if there is one thing its magi are proud of, it is their courtyard. Adorned with every kind of plant brought from impossible places, it has a pool at its center in which live two small blue fish from beyond *al-jalidāt*. The fish have proved to be extraordinarily long-lived and, although there is one of each sex, they seem to feel no need to breed, eat or sleep. The founders observed a close connection between the fish and the local weather. By paying attention to the hue of their skin, one can work out how far away the next storm is: when one is very close, their scales take on a deep, dull tone, whereas when there are none about they are turquoise. Although the founders never put to sea without them, they did not take them when they left in 1217, which only added to young Manjuza's bewilderment.

The island provides several pawns of Vim and Aquam vis a year, and it is the covenant's only vis source that does not lie out on the high seas.

#### Society and Customs

The covenant has never had a governing body, since it has always been ruled by two magi. After Darfílun joined the covenant in 1205, Fāṭīma and Sankhambi went on making their decisions unilaterally. The covenant always functioned as an oligarchy, though there were never any records of meetings or of ordinary councils. The only thing that involved all the members of the covenant was the yearly renewal of the *Aegis of the Hearth*.

Ŷezirat Tennyn holds the largest library of sea charts in the whole Tribunal, and no one from outside its walls has ever had access to it. In all its existence the covenant has neither sold nor allowed the copying of any of its charts, and its inviolability is written into the covenant's charter. Its two present residents are expert navigators and, although they do not know all the founders' secrets, they could steer any ship to the places mapped on their charts.

Until 1217, the covenant's magi went every four years to some small islands west of the coast of al-Gharb, where they spent a season meditating in the midst of nature. Although they could have used magic to reach them, they always made the crossing by ship. Manjuza has been to that place several times since her *parens* abandoned her, but she has never found any trace of her or of her companion, the Redcap Sankhambi.

#### The Magi of Ŷezirat Tennyn

##### Darfílun al-Biŷornī

Darfílun is a middle-aged Bjornaer from the east of al-Andalus whose heart-beast is a dolphin (see *Houses of Hermes: Mystery Cults*, page 82). He came to the covenant looking for a place near the sea that was far from the wars between Christians and Almohads, and Ŷezirat Tennyn met both requirements, at least until 1217. When its two founders left, leaving him alone with a newly made maga, Darfílun began to reconsider his choice. Nevertheless, he feels responsible for young Manjuza and he is a man of honor, so he has no intention of abandoning the covenant.

Although Manjuza believes that the founders put to sea in search of *Ŷezirat Tennyn*, Darfílun suspects that they actually sailed for *al-jalidāt*, to walk one last time through the lands they had fallen in love with in their youth, like two sages who have already given back to the world all that they have learned. Darfílun understands that *Ŷezirat Tennyn* was never the destination, only the way.

<!-- p. 231 -->

##### Manjuza al-Praliḥiyya

Fāṭīma bought Manjuza in the slave market of Madīnat Fās when she was no more than a three-year-old girl. Like Fāṭīma, she came from the lands of the *bilad al-Sūdān* and, like her, she too bore the strength of Africa. Fāṭīma gave her the name of her own mother as a gift, Manjuza of Guleni, for the girl had the same lips and the same dimples in her hands.

Manjuza grew up in Ŷezirat Tennyn, where she learned all the secrets of the Green Sea. In more than fifteen years of apprenticeship she has sailed the northern seas, the Mediterranean and the waters of the deep Atlantic Ocean. She believes that her *parens* has gone in pursuit of *Ŷezirat Tennyn*, and her wish is to go in search of her, although she does not yet have a ship sturdy enough for the task.

> #### Story Seeds: Ŷezirat Tennyn
>
> The "dragon island" is a great opportunity for storyguides to develop all kinds of stories around the search for it and the mysteries it holds. It might be part of the Magic Realm, or it might be nothing more than a mundane island. It could be the mythical Isles of the Seven Cities, founded by the Christians who left the Peninsula before the Muslims invaded it; it could hold wonders of immeasurable power, or be nothing more than a fantasy of Fāṭīma and Sankhambi. What *Ŷezirat Tennyn* is will depend on each troupe in general and on each storyguide in particular. In any case, the covenant could be a good starting point for developing the ideas set out in the insert on page 23 of *Realms of Power: Magic*.

### Chazāʾir

>**Lifespan:** 1137–Present<br>
>**Founder:** Ibn Qasī al-Criamonī<br>
>**Season:** Spring<br>
>**Aura (type and strength):** Magic, strength 4<br>
>**Reputations:** Close Ties to Mundanes (Iberian Tribunal) 6, Troublesome (Quaesitores) 4<br>
>**Votes:** 3

The covenant of Chazāʾir (from the Arabic, "islands," referring to the marshes) is a stain on the Criamon, a nuisance to the Quaesitores and a scourge to Durato. Chazāʾir is an irreverent covenant born of the Kharijite movement, a hotbed of resistance to all authority that is always looking for ways to serve its own interests.

#### History

When the magi of Bayt al-Ḥikma were arrested in 963, one of its members (a young Criamon named Ibn Abdullah) refused to be captured and, betraying the principles and ethics of the covenant, fled Bayt al-Ḥikma and took refuge in the desert of Almería until 970. For the next fifty years Ibn Abdullah lived by turns between Barzaj and Pechina, where he learned from other Ṣūfī masters and where he trained his apprentice, Ibn Qasī al-Criamonī.

When Ibn Abdullah surrendered himself to Twilight to attain personal salvation, Ibn Qasī went on living in Pechina, where he studied under Ibn al-ʿArif and from where he was finally forced into exile by the persecution the Ṣūfīs suffered at the hands of the Almoravids. Ibn Qasī fled to the *kūra* of al-Gharb, where he began to spread his master's Ṣūfī ideas and, to the shame of his House and the alarm of the Quaesitores, started to organize a religious militia against the Almoravids and to call for rebellion in Ṭabīra. To hide from the mundane authorities, he founded the covenant of Chazāʾir in the marshes near that city.

Ibn Qasī was expelled at the ordinary Iberian Tribunal of 1144 and executed by the hoplites the following year: they caught up with him on the border of the *kūra* of Seville as he tried to flee Hermetic justice. His former apprentice, ʿUmar ibn Abī Ṭūṭ, took charge of Chazāʾir, left House Criamon to join House Ex Miscellanea, and pursued his master's course of action.

The revolts begun by Ibn Qasī spread through the rest of al-Andalus after the death of the caliph Tāšufīn. Two years later, however, cities such as Cadiz, Cordoba, Jerez and Seville submitted to the sovereignty of the Almohad caliph. ʿUmar ibn Abī Ṭūṭ then led a pocket of resistance from Ṭabīra which, with the help of Munio Alfonso Garcés al-Flambī, managed to hold back the Almohad forces until 1150, when political pressure finally broke the mundane population. Ṭabīra signed its surrender at Salé and recognized Almohad sovereignty over its territory. A year later, however, ʿUmar ibn Abī Ṭūṭ and his covenant-mate, ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUbayd Allāh al-Praliḥī, rebelled against the Almohads once again. As a result, Ṭabīra remained independent until 1167, and during that period it surrounded itself with a mighty wall to defend itself against the armies of Seville. Although the city was taken again that same year, its inhabitants and the members of Chazāʾir managed to drive the Almohads out once more, and in 1220 the Almohads still control neither the city nor its port.

Since ʿAbd Allāh's death at Alarcos (see page 94), ʿUmar has had to defend himself against numerous charges of mundane interference and to pay costly fines in vis and in time devoted to the Tribunal, which has hindered Chazāʾir's development to the point of sending it back into a bitter Spring.

<!-- p. 232 -->

#### Setting and Physical Description

Chazāʾir lies almost eight kilometers southwest of the city of Ṭabīra, deep in the marshes. Ṭabīra is a prosperous city (although it has lost some of the importance it enjoyed during the Almoravid period) where ships from the Gulf of Cadiz and North Africa put in, and where many of the pirates who sail the strait take refuge.

Chazāʾir is a covenant built by magic. Except for the harbor, which sits in the middle of the covenant's main block, the rest of the structure rises on mighty pillars of black stone that hold its rooms some two meters above the surface of the water. Chazāʾir is not a large covenant; it has two main blocks joined by a bridge that hangs over the reeds and marshes. In the westernmost block (where the mundanes' quarters are) is the small boat harbor, which has a stairway leading to the cellars (below the water) and to the guardroom on the ground floor of the mundanes' building. A walkway runs around both buildings, which the soldiers use to keep watch over the surroundings. When they light the lanterns at night, those who see them from the mainland take them for will-o'-the-wisps, which has helped to keep most mundanes away. The covenant's second block houses four *sancta*, the (meager) library and the council chamber, where Chazāʾir keeps numerous maps of the area with which it has planned all its attacks on the Almohad forces.

All of Chazāʾir is tastefully decorated; the rooms have Arabic poems written on the walls and the materials are of very high quality (it even has glass in its windows). However, the marshes are not a very healthy place, and Chazāʾir's refuse does nothing to improve them. In 1220, ʿUmar ibn Abī Ṭūṭ has given the autocrat an ultimatum to clean up the covenant's surroundings, since over the past year the miasmas have made many of the inhabitants ill, and ʿUmar himself has suffered a Crisis, which he survived only thanks to his Longevity Ritual.

#### Society and Customs

Chazāʾir is an autocracy ruled by an emir or an *umm walad* (the titles given to men and women, respectively). This figure is the only one in the covenant to hold a title, and it passes in direct line from *parentes* to *filii*. The magus who holds this office is the only one who may make decisions concerning the covenant, and the other members must delegate their votes to him at ordinary Tribunals. Although Chazāʾir has never had more than four magi, this system of government (or rather the ideas of the current emir, ʿUmar) has meant that many magi have been unwilling to join its ranks, and a few others have left after some years.

The emir of Chazāʾir rules over the autocrat, who is responsible for managing the three ships the covenant keeps moored in the port of Ṭabīra, which it uses to trade or to raid other vessels of smaller draft. At Chazāʾir the autocrat is considered a member of the covenant and, though not a magus, bears greater responsibilities than the magi. As with the emir, the post of autocrat passes by descent, unless the emir or the *umm walad* decides otherwise.

All the inhabitants of Chazāʾir speak Arabic among themselves, and although they also know Latin, they use it only with members of the Order who are not of the Iberian Tribunal.

#### The Magae of Chazāʾir

##### Emir ʿUmar ibn Abī Ṭūṭ al-Praliḥī

ʿUmar abandoned the Ṣūfī precepts and House Criamon when his *parens* was executed by the Order's hoplites, and so he lost the stigmata on his skin. He considers Bayt al-Ḥikma a mistake, though a lesser one than the Order itself. ʿUmar is rebellious toward everything to do with the Code and, whenever he believes it stands in the way of his own survival, he ends up breaking it, which has earned him severe fines, ultimatums and reprimands from the judges and the Trianomae.

<!-- p. 233 -->

After the disaster of Las Navas de Tolosa, Duresca issued a communiqué forbidding any magus or affiliate to go to the battlefield, not even the *quiñoneros*.[^p233-30] As was only to be expected, ʿUmar ignored the request and went to Jaén to investigate what had happened. From his inquiries he deduced that those responsible had been the *saḥirs* of the East, and although he never made his conclusions public, he did mention them to other magi, and the news spread throughout the Tribunal (see "The Destruction of Harra," page 174).

[^p233-30]: The *quiñoneros* were royal officials charged with gathering, valuing and sharing out the spoils after a battle, and with counting the enemy's dead. To do so, they had to walk the battlefield and inspect it once the fighting was over.

In 1220, ʿUmar faces numerous fines and has run up debts with Porta Pandere in order to pay them, which has not stopped him from breaking the Code again on repeated occasions.

> #### Story Seeds: The Ravens of Saint Vincent
>
> In the fourth century, Vincent of Huesca was condemned and executed in Valencia under the edicts of the emperor Diocletian. It is said that his body was left out to be devoured by wild beasts, but a raven protected his mortal remains from the other scavengers. Ever since, the bird's descendants have always accompanied the martyr.
>
> The Christians recovered his body and buried it in Valencia, where it was exhumed in the eighth century for fear that ʿAbd al-Raḥmān I might desecrate it. A group of the city's clergy thus set off with the saint's remains in search of a place where they could keep them safe. On their pilgrimage the clerics passed through Saragossa, where they left some of his relics, and, after crossing the Peninsula, they decided to settle on the southernmost cape of al-Gharb, where they raised a shrine and a hermitage in which ten ravens nested. At the beginning of the twelfth century, however, the church was razed and the ravens shot down by the Almoravids. The saint's remains thus lay hidden until 1173, when they were moved to Lisbon, where they still rest.
>
> When the player characters discover that a raven is hanging about the covenant, they may not think much of it. However, once they notice that their Gift does not frighten it off, they may begin to look into it. If they do, they will find that the bird is always near children or near people or magae of upright morals (whatever their religion), and that it tends to cause small annoyances to the vicious and wicked (it fouls their clothes, pecks at their grain, caws at their windows, and so on). Where does this raven come from, and what is its nature? Is it here to help the magi, to punish them or to ask them for help? Depending on the saga and on the player characters, the storyguide must decide what the raven's motives are and the reason for its visit. Perhaps their paths will cross with Chazāʾir when it leads them to Cape Saint Vincent, where some of the saint's relics are waiting to be returned to Lisbon.

##### Al-Gassāniyya al-Praliḥiyya

Al-Gassāniyya is ʿUmar's *filia*, and so she will be the next *umm walad*. Despite her master's Kharijite past, Al-Gassāniyya has not been raised in its precepts (she does not even know that ʿUmar was once a Criamon) and, although she is relatively young, she has already taken part in several raids against Almohad detachments (some of them while she was still an apprentice). In fact, a few years into her training, ʿUmar ordered her to accompany ʿAbd Allāh to Alarcos, a tragedy that Guiomar averted by interceding to keep her from going, on the pretext that she needed her help in the laboratory. Ever since that day, Al-Gassāniyya has never stopped thanking Guiomar for her gesture, for she knows that her foresight saved her life.

##### Guiomar al-Praliḥiyya

The Portuguese maga Guiomar was trained as a tempestarius in the north of Iberia. After passing her Gauntlet she went to the south of al-Gharb, where her *parens* had told her there was an ancient center of power of the tempestarii (at least until the arrival of the remains of Saint Vincent; see the insert on the previous page), known today as the *Promontorium Sacrum*. Guiomar spent two seasons roaming among the menhirs and megaliths around the cape until she decided to settle there for the time being. However, when she met ʿUmar at the Tribunal of 1179, she decided to join Chazāʾir, partly because of its closeness to the *Promontorium*.

Guiomar fought the Almohads alongside ʿUmar and ʿAbd Allāh, and proved especially deadly against the ships that crossed the strait: nothing escaped her storms, friend or foe. Precisely because Guiomar was the most powerful maga in Chazāʾir, ʿUmar sent ʿAbd Allāh to the Other Tribunal of Harra in her place; he did not want to risk his most valuable asset in what seemed an easy battle. But fate decided otherwise, and the Hermetic magi fell at Alarcos. From that day on, the emir decreed that the priority must be Chazāʾir and Ṭabīra, and Guiomar concentrated on defending the city and the covenant.

In 1220 two things worry Guiomar. The first is the advance of the kingdom of Portugal into the lands of al-Gharb; the second, and more important, is the feelings she harbors for Al-Gassāniyya: if she does not see her every day she feels a tightness in her chest, and she suffers when they argue over trifles or when the young woman shows her affection for other magi of the Tribunal. Although Guiomar has repressed her feelings, she fears that Al-Gassāniyya may perceive them and use them to hurt her, or, worse still, that they may be returned.

## Seville

*Among its excellences Seville counts the mildness of its climate, the magnificence of its buildings, the adornment both of its precinct and of its surroundings […]. Its villages surpass all other villages in the fineness of their construction and in the care with which their inhabitants tend them inside and out, so much so that, whitewashed as they keep them, they look like white stars in a sky of olive trees.*[^p233-31]

[^p233-31]: Excerpt from *In Praise of Spanish Islam* by Al-Šaqundī (Spanish translation by Emilio García Gómez).

> #### Some Notes on Seville
>
> Seville is a splendid city built around the Guadalquivir river (which is navigable down to its mouth), whose bustling river port supplies it with goods of every kind. The banks of the Guadalquivir are full of music, with no lack of poetry or good wine (even though it goes against the Qurʾan), which makes its people quick-witted and gives them a great sense of humor — so much so that they may take offense if one does not play along with the joke. The Guadalquivir largely governs the life of Seville's inhabitants, and its use is regulated by the civil authorities. Throwing rubbish into the river is forbidden and punished with flogging and a considerable fine. Moreover, not everyone may draw water from the river for drinking, nor may it be done just anywhere (one must always avoid the water among the legs of beasts and places that are muddy or where the river runs cloudy). This task falls to the water carriers, or *azacanes*, who are assigned stretches of the river that the tide does not reach. From there they may draw buckets of water from plank pontoons built for the purpose, and they may share that space with no one. Needless to say, washing clothes nearby is forbidden.
>
> Seville is a *kūra* of great private estates, since its governors have always seen to it that the viziers hold large personal farmlands. To estimate their harvests, Seville has the *jurrās* (singular *jāris*), officials who work during the month of June in the mills where the cereal grain is stored. The *jurrās* are paid by the owners of the estates and not by the state treasury (in Arabic, *bayt al-māl*), which breeds corruption in the office: landowners often pay more money to obtain better estimates, and the *jurrās* take the opportunity to enrich themselves. But it is not the only office prone to corruption: the magistrates charged with safeguarding the interests of the treasury, called *ʿummāl* (*ʿāmil* in the singular), work with the tax collectors, or *qubbād* (singular *qābid*), who, because of how easily they can grow rich at the people's expense, must be supervised by the city's *qādī* and by the *almojarife*. Indeed, the popularity of the government depends to a great extent on these measures of oversight.

<!-- p. 234 -->

In 1220 Seville is the capital of the Almohad province of al-Andalus and the largest *kūra*, although, like the rest, its northern frontier has been falling back before the advances of the king of Leon, Alfonso IX.

Seville is divided by the gentle range of *Ŷabal al-ʿArus* (Sierra Morena), which separates the plateau from the basin of the Guadalquivir. Its geology has encouraged the working of deposits of gold, silver, copper and lead, and its soil yields the olives from which the finest oil in al-Andalus is pressed, exported to important cities in Iberia and North Africa.

Although in the past it sheltered many non-Hermetic wizards (such as the Mercurians of Mérida), during the Order's dominion it has not been a region much frequented by magi, perhaps because of the poverty of its vis sources or because of its many mundane settlements, a tendency that has only grown stronger with the arrival of the Almohads and the passing of the ruling "On Mundane Relations in al-Andalus" (1193).

Besides Seville, the province is home to important cities such as Mérida, Cáceres, Badajoz, Niebla, Cadiz, Carmona and Huelva. To the north the *kūra* of Seville borders the kingdom of Leon; to the west, the kingdom of Portugal and the *kūra* of al-Gharb; to the south, the Atlantic Ocean and the *kūra* of Granada; and to the east, the *kūra* of Cordoba. At present the *kūra* of Seville is home to a single inhabited covenant, the "perfect" ʾAlif.

### ʾAlif

*Man, like the rest of the animals, is composed of that first mover which grammar designates with the "alif" and by which I can say "I."*[^p234-32]

[^p234-32]: Excerpt from the *Letter of Farewell* by Avempace (Spanish translation by Joaquín Lomba).

>**Lifespan:** 1130–Present<br>
>**Founders:** Ḥayy ibn Yaqẓān al-Bonisagī, Absāl al-Criamonī, Salāmān al-Gernikī<br>
>**Season:** n/a (Winter)<br>
>**Aura (type and strength):** Magic, strength 2<br>
>**Reputations:** Troublesome (Hermetic) 3, Progressive (Andalusi magi) 2, Subjugated (Iberian Tribunal) 1<br>
>**Votes:** 0 (2)

The covenant of ʾAlif takes its name from the first letter of the Arabic alphabet, which is also the first letter of the word *ʾana,* meaning "I." ʾAlif is the unity to which the men who make it up aspire: the reviled *mutawaḥḥid* or Solitaries (or *nawābit*, as they prefer to call themselves), who in the middle of the twelfth century began to build *al-madīna al-fāḍila*, the perfect society, whose aspirations were cut short by the Order. They are the perfect magi.

#### History

When, at the beginning of the twelfth century, the *falāsifa* Ḥayy ibn Yaqẓān al-Bonisagī, Absāl al-Criamonī and Salāmān al-Gernikī met in Saragossa, their souls connected. Each found himself facing one of the fragments of a single spirit, severed at the dawn of creation. They soon shared their ideas on the decadence of the Order and the reasons for the tragic events that had marked its history over more than four centuries of existence. Their poems from those days reflected their dejection and the helplessness they felt: to them, apprenticeship was nothing but an indoctrination meant to break men's freedom. Ḥayy, Absāl and Salāmān were not only great poets but exceptional musicians and scientists, polymaths who also had a deep interest in the Hermetic history of the Tribunal. Their research in that field led them to the corruption of al-Zahrāʾ, the Kharijites of Bayt al-Ḥikma and the struggle against the tempestarii: the history of the Tribunal was full of examples of corruption, a reflection of the imperfection of mundane societies. The three set out to create a philosophy of their own that would solve the Order's endemic problems, drawing on the ideas of Avempace of Saragossa, Ibn Ṭufayl of Granada and the Persian Al-Fārābī. Their efforts took shape in an ambitious project that they began to preach at the ordinary Tribunals. When Ḥayy set out the foundations of his philosophy in 1116, the Andalusi magi showed interest, and the *falāsifa* built up a network of correspondence that came to overwhelm the Tribunal's Redcaps. Their philosophy took hold, and the community that grew up around those first ideas put down strong roots; thus arose the figure of the *mutawaḥḥid* or *nawābit* (singular *nābit*, "sprout"). So when, in 1123, Ḥayy demolished the theses of the Ṣūfīs of Barzaj and publicly insulted them, the powers of the Tribunal began to worry. Their antimaterialist theories spread like wildfire through the Tribunal and attracted influential scholars such as Ben Zômá al-Bonisagī, *rector* of al-Dhahabī (the future Iššáh). The covenant of Durato then began to watch them and intercept their correspondence. That was how it discovered that the perfect ones had begun drafting a new Code of Hermes.

In 1130 the *nawābit* decided to build a covenant, ʾAlif, which grew steadily during its first two decades: from three magi they went to twenty, making it the greatest power in the Tribunal. However, the *nawābit* never voted at Tribunals: they merely gave their opinions without exercising their right to vote, which only deepened the concern of the other covenants. In 1150 the Iberian Chamber met to deal with the problem of the *mutawaḥḥid* and the perfect society, or *al-madīna al-fāḍila,* they wanted to build. To that end, it bribed one of ʾAlif's founding members: Salāmān al-Gernikī. In exchange for admission to Duresca, Salāmān helped them dismantle the philosophy of the perfect ones, attacked their doctrines from within, and the Chamber was able to study their weak points in order to dissect them at the Grand Tribunal of 1162.

When Ḥayy and Absāl discovered Salāmān's corruption, they learned a bitter lesson: their perfect order was not safe from the corruption inherent in men; the *nābit* had shown that he was not always upright, and it had become plain that a single individual could ruin the society they wished to build. And so the traitor Salāmān won his seat in Duresca while Jayrān was *disceptator*, which allowed him to amass great riches (both mundane and magical) and gain a position of responsibility at the Tribunal's center of jurisprudence. He was an old man, however, and his fondness for the white poppy finally put him in the grave: he died before Fortún became *disceptator* (see "Duresca," page 126).

<!-- p. 235 -->

The Grand Tribunal cut short ʾAlif's aspirations. The covenant was accused of having committed a high crime and could save itself only by handing over the copies of the code it was drafting and recanting it. As a result, most of the covenant's members left, and those who stayed set aside their Hermetic reformism and went back to working on the foundations of their philosophy, incorporating the ideas of Maimonides and Averroes.

ʾAlif suffered another severe setback with the edict of 1190 issued by the Almohad caliph Abū Yūsuf Yaʿqūb al-Manṣūr (see page 92). To avoid persecution, almost all its members emigrated to the East in the hope of being able to build the perfect society in safety. ʾAlif was then left occupied only by its founders, and it was at that time that one of the Tribunal's magi denounced it in Seville. So it was that in 1193 the covenant was stormed by Almohad troops: they arrested all the mundanes, burned its library, poems and musical instruments, and ordered the building demolished. Dismayed, the two remaining magi had to flee and abandon their people to their fate. So as not to be found, they sought out a cave in which to spend their days and achieve union with the agent intellect (or the Enigma, as Absāl used to say).

#### Setting and Physical Description

*[…] he confined himself to resting [motionless] at the bottom of his cave, head bowed, eyes closed, withdrawn from sensible things and from the bodily faculties, all his cares and thoughts concentrated solely on the necessary Being, associating nothing with Him.*[^p235-33]

The three founders of ʾAlif chose a place far from human society, in the hills north of the city of Niebla, far from the Almoravid capital in Granada. Although nothing remains of this first building today, it was large enough to house up to twenty magi with their respective laboratories. At that time the covenant had a single *sanctum* symbol carved at its entrance, representing the communal rather than personal protection of the magi. It was in that period that the covenant gathered an impressive library on the Hermetic history of the Tribunal and acquired the important vis sources of the rivers Luxia and Urius.
