After that magnificent building was destroyed by the Almohad forces, the only two magi who remained decided to isolate themselves from humankind and shut themselves away in the caves of the Covachos mountains, in the Sierra Norte of Seville, some two kilometers north of the town of al-Madīnat Bālat, in an area of many quarries that the Almohads worked for marble, certain metals and dyes. Despite the size of the cave mouth (fifteen meters wide and six meters high), the founders chose it for the protection offered by its inner galleries: at the entrance there were traces of human activity and refuse, but in its depths there was nothing but darkness and silence. Isolated at last, the two *nawābit* devoted themselves to the search for salvation in the depths of the limestone caverns.

ʾAlif is no longer a place but a concept, where all the spirits that have walked the Path of Negative Attributes gather (see insert on the next page). Transcending matter, they ascend to the perfect society, or *al-madīna al-fāḍila*, where there is neither vice nor corruption.

#### Society and Customs

*As for happy men, if it is possible for them to exist, they have happiness only by isolating themselves, and consequently the right regimen will be solely that of the isolated [man], whether there be only one or more, so long as the community or the city does not unite in their doctrines.*[^p235-34]

The covenant of ʾAlif revolves around the perfect society. Within it dwell the spirits of the *nawābit*, mystically united through the attainment of the final milestone of the Path of Negative Attributes, which Ḥayy ibn Yaqẓān al-Bonisagī developed while he still had access to the laboratories of the material ʾAlif. In that state, the members dissolve their identities until they reach the oneness of their collective self-soul. Thus, although the magi of ʾAlif are scattered between the East and Iberia, they consider themselves members of the same covenant and part of *al-madīna al-fāḍila*. Of course, from a legal point of view, the only magi registered at ʾAlif in 1220 are its former founders, Ḥayy ibn Yaqẓān al-Bonisagī and Absāl al-Criamonī, who gave up their voting sigils in 1130.

#### The Magi of ʾAlif

The magi of ʾAlif were the scholars who named the events of the Hermetic history of the Peninsula and who delved into the memory of Iberia to keep it alive.

##### Nābit Ḥayy ibn Yaqẓān al-Bonisagī

*I see a human figure; but, if I use my reason,* *I find that your body is a celestial body.*[^p235-35]

Ḥayy ibn Yaqẓān means "the living one, son of the watchful one." In his youth Ḥayy was a great musician who plucked the strings of an extremely costly *kanīra* made by the Verditius of Ajabeba, and a misfit who shunned all his fellows, whom he regarded as fools and illiterates. When he met his *amici*, Absāl al-Criamonī and Salāmān al-Gernikī, something changed inside him. His spirit was freed from the heavy burden of the emptiness from which all his pain sprang, all that hatred that turned the rhyme of his poetry into a sharp blade with which he made the world bleed. His anxiety vanished on contact with those kindred souls, from their meeting the philosophy of ʾAlif was born, and he himself began to be transformed. This transformation culminated in the burning of the *kanīra* he called *rúḥun*, the last of his material ties. After the destruction of his covenant, Ḥayy resolved to take refuge from the corporeal world together with Absāl.

[^p235-33]: Excerpt from *The Self-Taught Philosopher* by Ibn Ṭufayl (Spanish translation by Ángel González Palencia).

[^p235-34]: Excerpt from *The Self-Taught Philosopher* by Ibn Ṭufayl (Spanish translation by Ángel González Palencia).

[^p235-35]: Excerpt from *The Ring of the Dove* by Ibn Ḥazm (Spanish translation by Emilio García Gómez).

<!-- p. 236 -->

##### Nābit Absāl al-Criamonī

Absāl was already a friend of Salāmān before he met Ḥayy in Saragossa. Like him, he was a great historian and poet, a lover of music and a renowned physician, and, like Ḥayy, Absāl found a part of his soul when he met him. From their union was born a universal revolution which, because of the tyranny of the Order, ended up confined to the *nawābit* of ʾAlif.

After enlightening their Hermetic brothers, the *mutawaḥḥid* withdrew from Hermetic society and shut themselves away in Covachos, where Absāl trusts he will find the answer to the Enigma before the end of his days. He knows that the perfect order is the solution, but he has not yet found a way to relate the answer to the problem.

> #### Story Seeds: The End of the Perfect Order?
>
> *We cannot see the intellect in itself; rather, we contemplate it in the traces [it leaves] in other beings.*[^p236-XVI]
>
> When the Almohads destroyed ʾAlif, they burned all the Initiation Scripts for the Mystery of the Path of Negative Attributes and those containing the ritual of *al-madīna al-fāḍila*, written by Ḥayy ibn Yaqẓān in the covenant's early years. Their knowledge is now spread among the *nawābit* of the East and the West (that is, those who stayed at ʾAlif after the Grand Tribunal condemned their philosophy), all of them elderly. Despite having rejected it, the Order is in fact very interested in the Mystery that allows the minds of magi to be united and, it is said, raises them above the third circle (according to emanationist theory; see page 304). To all appearances, the ritual of the final milestone was achieved through a Hermetic breakthrough, since it breaches the lesser limit of the lunar sphere, and, although many consider the idea absurd, a few suspect that it might breach the Divine Limit, since it is based on non-Hermetic knowledge of interplanetary magic (see "The Astra Planeta" in *Realms of Power: Magic*, pages 112 and 113).
>
> The Criamon of Barzaj do not believe in the theses of the *Perfect* and consider their quest selfish and therefore barren; although they would never admit it, they would rather this knowledge were lost to oblivion. The Order, however, does not see it that way, and so the Tribunal is interested in recovering it. Perhaps the characters will have to seek out the Perfect of the Tribunal and somehow persuade them to initiate them into that Path. Could the ideas of the Perfect be reborn within the Order?
>
> [^p236-XVI]: Excerpt from the *Letter of Farewell* by Avempace (Spanish translation by Joaquín Lomba).

### Ribāṭ al-ʿAbraj

>**Lifespan:** 927–930<br>
>**Founder:** Aḥmad al-Praliḥī<br>
>**Aura (type and strength):** Magic, strength 1<br>
>**Reputations:** None

The magi of Iberia who know the history of al-ʿAbraj can be counted on the fingers of one hand. Its brief existence is of interest only to scholars and lovers of history; not even the Flambeau remember it. All that remains of it are a few scattered records in the covenants of Salionca, Duresca, Porta Pandere, Aedes Saturni and al-Minẓār.

#### History

The *saḥirs* of al-ʿAbraj (Arabic for "the towers"), led by Aḥmad, joined the Order in 925, after the peace treaty signed by Al-Muzaffar. Aḥmad attended the ordinary Tribunal of 927 on behalf of al-ʿAbraj to have its covenant constituted. Just three years later it was destroyed by a group of Flambeau led by the infamous Ruiz Sánchez de Esco. The fire fused flesh with rock, and the smoke from its embers could be seen from Cordoba. No one survived that night; the attackers left behind only a hole of ash and oblivion.

#### Setting and Physical Description

The only records of the location of al-ʿAbraj are kept at Salionca, but not even its current inhabitants would be able to find them, since they are more than three centuries old and may well have been damaged by the salt that is swallowing the covenant. Scholars of the Tribunal's Hermetic history place it between Mérida and Cáceres, on high ground close to al-Balat (the Vía de la Plata), because in the twelfth century a single reference bearing the name al-ʿAbraj was found in the basilica of Santa Lucía del Trampal. It must surely have served as a defensive bastion between the northern kingdoms and al-Andalus, and as a bulwark against an Order that could not bring the *saḥirs* to heel until 925.

<!-- p. 237 -->

### Ribāṭ Ŷibāl al-Raḥma

*What I shall do is go to the frontiers of Islam, facing the enemy, and in any one of its rápitas I shall devote myself to holy war until I die.*[^p237-36]

[^p237-36]: Excerpt from *The Epistle of Holiness* by Ibn ʿArabī (Spanish translation by Miguel Asín Palacios). A rápita is a *ribāṭ*.

>**Lifespan:** 927–1091<br>
>**Founder:** Al-Muzaffar al-Mursī al-Praliḥī<br>
>**Aura (type and strength):** Magic, strength 6<br>
>**Reputations:** *Saḥirs* (Iberian Flambeau) 1

The ancient military and religious fortress (*ribāṭ*) of the mountains of mercy (in Arabic, *Ŷibāl al-Raḥma*, in the part of the Sierra Morena closest to Seville) was a stronghold used by the *saḥirs* to defend al-Andalus against the Flambeau during the first two centuries of the Order. Today it is nothing but ruins, badly decayed by the constant desecration they have suffered over the years at the hands of the most diehard Christian Flambeau.

#### History

The *ribāṭ* north of Seville was the place from which the *saḥirs* set out who attacked the north of the Peninsula in 907. In their advance they destroyed the covenants of Inverneira and Ipagrum and damaged Occelum Durii, Fafḥṣ al-Luŷŷ and Duresca. The attack was a response to the breaking of the truce they had signed with the Hermetic magi after the destruction of the *ribāṭ* in northern Jaén, where the Hermetic envoy Tareyja al-Apromoriyya and the judge Qatr al-Nadà were negotiating with the *saḥirs*; all of them died that day. Although Al-Muzaffar al-Mursī had planned another attack, this time on Salionca, Ṭāmis ibn Baldiccione al-Išbīlī al-Gernikī and Zaynab ḅint Qatr al-Nadà secured a new truce that finally brought the longed-for peace between the *saḥirs* and the Order in 925. The only condition Al-Muzaffar imposed was a ban on founding Hermetic covenants in Africa for 300 years (see insert on page 77).

Al-Muzaffar then joined the Order and turned his old fortress into a Hermetic covenant. During the first years he had to face some sporadic attacks by the Flambeau of Ruiz Sánchez de Esco, and he realized that joining the Order had made them weaker: from being ahead, they had ended up at the back of the line, ignored by an organization almost two centuries old.

In 930 the Flambeau of Salionca destroyed the covenant and *ribāṭ* of al-ʿAbraj and wiped out its inhabitants, all of them good friends of Al-Muzaffar. The Flambeau took advantage of the fact that the *saḥirs* did not know the secrets of the Parma Magica and had no copy of the *Aegis of the Hearth* to slaughter them at will. Al-Muzaffar denounced these deeds to the Quaesitores of al-Andalus, and at the end of that same year the Andalusi covenants of Bayt al-Ḥikma, Dār Malīḥaʾ and Qasr Dār al-Muchaddad undertook to teach the *saḥirs* Parma Magica and Hermetic theory and to give them copies of the *Aegis of the Hearth*, finally achieving their true integration into the Order.

In 940, Ŷibāl al-Raḥma took part in the battle of Frías, and its members witnessed the murders of Briatiz de Moncharro of Diedne and Ṭāmis al-Išbīlī by the men of Alvarra of Guernicus, which only deepened their disenchantment with the Order. But the last straw came in 963, when the magi of Iberia sat on their hands after Bayt al-Ḥikma was condemned by the mundane powers: refusing to obey the Tribunal, Al-Muzaffar went to Cordoba to help his friends. Not only did he fail in his undertaking, but he was gravely wounded. On his deathbed he said to his daughter Muhŷa: "Sealing our union with the Order of Hermes has been the greatest mistake of my life; I hope you can forgive me."

When in 976 the Order approved the Hermetic colonization of Africa, Muhŷa al-Praliḥiyya could not believe what was happening: although she opposed it in the vote, not even a small share of the covenants of al-Andalus supported her veto. Ŷibāl al-Raḥma then disappeared from Hermetic life and concentrated on strengthening its ties with the city of Seville. Thus, when the *fitna* ended, the members of the covenant were able to enjoy the splendid taifa kingdom of the sultan Ibn ʿAbbād; when the Almoravids attacked the city, Ŷibāl al-Raḥma came to its aid, but both its members and the city's inhabitants were defeated by the Veiled Ones. Yet within its walls the kin and servants of Al-Muzaffar's family, none of them Gifted, still remained safe.

When the Tribunal of al-Andalus was annexed to Iberia in 1103, the *ribāṭ* of Ŷibāl al-Raḥma was attacked and laid waste by a band of Flambeau. Since it lay outside the Order's protection (there being no Hermetic member), the crime went unpunished. The few survivors had to abandon the ancestral seat of Al-Muzaffar's family.

> #### Story Seeds: Justice!
>
> When some magi of the Tribunal end up at the ruins of the *ribāṭ* of Ŷibāl al-Raḥma, they look on in dismay at the many desecrations it has suffered over the years. Weary of the Tribunal's passivity in the face of Flambeau violence against the *saḥirs*, they decide to take matters into their own hands and bring the case before the Tribunal, so as to have the harassment the *saḥirs* have endured over the centuries defined as an offense once and for all. In their plea they will have the support of the maga Šarīfah Muhŷa al-Praliḥiyya of the African covenant of al-Minẓār, who will become their chief representative. Will the player characters' magi support the initiative?

<!-- p. 238 -->

#### Setting and Physical Description

The blackened ruins of Ŷibāl al-Raḥma lie on the southern slopes of the Sierra Morena, almost a day's walk from the city of Seville. Its remains are strewn with refuse, the product of the pilgrimage that some Iberian Flambeau have been making (ever since the Tribunal of al-Andalus was reunited) to reaffirm their sovereignty over the *saḥirs* and to commemorate those who died fighting them. Despite the many petitions brought before the ordinary Tribunals to forbid this practice, no such ruling has ever quite been passed, and it may no longer be necessary to pass one. By 1220 hardly anyone remembers these old ruins, or the names, carved into their ashlars, of the countless Flambeau who came here to celebrate the supremacy of their House and of the Order over the non-Hermetic magical traditions.

> #### Story Seeds: The Sorrel Horse
>
> *It was a sorrel horse with which battle was kindled as if by a brand of courage. Its coat was the color of the pomegranate flower; its ear, the shape of the myrtle leaf. And in the midst of its ruddy color a white star rose upon its brow, like the snowy bubbles that laugh in a glass of red wine.*[^p238-XVII]
>
> Some Criamon of the Tribunal believe that the wars between the Flambeau and the *saḥirs* during the first two centuries of the Order's existence brought about the creation of a terrible adulteration (see *Houses of Hermes: Mystery Cults*, page 99), which takes the form of a magnificent, tall, red-coated steed with a majestic gaze. The Iberian Criamon are convinced that this adulteration has been responsible for every war in which the Order has been embroiled, the Schism War included. According to them, the adulteration can only be resolved if the Order confronts its past and, as a whole, tries to change its bloody nature; the time has come for it to atone for its sins if it does not wish to meet a tragic end. Of course, any attempt to defeat it through violence would only feed it.
>
> Of the few who have ever glimpsed the supposed sorrel horse, none has been able to prove that it is an adulteration. Nevertheless, more than twenty sightings have been recorded in recent years, which to the Criamon heralds the imminent arrival of the next global conflict, quite possibly the last, as they somberly add. Few magi outside House Criamon believe these stories, and the Christians accuse them of plagiarizing the rider of the red horse of the Apocalypse. Despite their discredit, the Criamon do not lose heart, and they seize on every Tribunal to make their *sodales* reflect on the violent history of the Order.
>
> [^p238-XVII]: Verses by Ibn Jafāŷa (twelfth century) taken from *In Praise of Spanish Islam* (Spanish translation by Emilio García Gómez).

## Cordoba

*Cordoba was of old the seat of empire, the center of learning, the beacon of piety, the abode of nobility and primacy. […] You will already have heard that its inhabitants held canon law in great veneration and competed eagerly to attain primacy in this science, and that kings knelt before the ulama, extolling their rank and acting in accordance with their opinions, and that they chose no minister or counselor who was not learned.*[^p238-37]

[^p238-37]: Excerpt from *In Praise of Spanish Islam* by Al-Šaqundī (Spanish translation by Emilio García Gómez).

As in the province of Seville, both the Sierra Morena and the Guadalquivir river cross the *kūra* of Cordoba from west to east. North of the mountains the *kūra* is more rugged, while to the south the land is flatter, suitable for establishing large tracts of farmland that take advantage of the rich Guadalquivir plain. In the tenth century, at the height of the Umayyad dynasty under the caliph Al-Ḥakam II, the city of Cordoba was the most important center of learning in Mythic Europe. The magi of the Tribunal then settled in the palatine city of Madīnat al-Zahrāʾ and attained a prosperity that no magus of the thirteenth-century generations could even imagine.

The province borders the kingdom of Castile to the north, the *kūra* of Seville to the west, that of Granada to the south, and the *kūra* of Jaén to the east. Cordoba is the capital of the *kūra*, which is also home to the important towns of Lucena, Baena, Poley and Cabra, among many others. Cordoba currently hosts a single inhabited covenant, the nursery of white poppies, Jušjášun.

### Jušjášun

>**Lifespan:** 1075–Present<br>
>**Founders:** Rebeca al-Praliḥiyya, Al-Layt al-Mursī al-Criamonī<br>
>**Season:** Summer<br>
>**Aura (type and strength):** Magic, strength 6<br>
>**Reputations:** White Poppy Supplier (Iberian Tribunal) 3, Duresca's Puppet (Iberian Tribunal) 1<br>
>**Votes:** 2

The covenant of Jušjášun (Arabic for "poppy") is small but tremendously rich. Today it is known for supplying white poppy to the entire Tribunal, a trade through which it began to grow wealthy in the early twelfth century and by which it earned the title of dedicated covenant at the ordinary Tribunal of 1158. Jušjášun, however, was not always rich, nor always interested in trading the small capsules of the poppy family.

<!-- p. 239 -->

#### History

The maga Rebeca, of the Lucena covenant of ʿÔlām wā-ʿed, met the Criamon Al-Layt of Barzaj at the Tribunal of al-Andalus in 1068. The two were young and beautiful then and, without meaning to, let themselves be carried away by passion. Within a few months they had left their home covenants and settled in a small covenant in the village of Zuheros, in the gorges of the Bailón river, under the protection of the Zirid kingdom of Granada. In their search for vis sources they found, up on the mountainside, a deep cave hidden in a wood of holm oaks, Portuguese oaks, wild olives and scrub. There they discovered some delicate white poppies, watered by the slow dripping of the speleothems and fertilized by the droppings of enormous albino bats. When, in 1075, the two magi announced the founding of their covenant at the meeting of the Tribunal of al-Andalus in Saragossa, they named their venture Jušjášun and gave it the image of the lovely white poppies they had found in the bat cave.

In 1090 the Almoravids conquered Granada, and Rebeca renounced her religion, converting to Islam under the name Danāʾ so that she could go on living with Al-Layt. When, thirteen years later, al-Andalus was absorbed by Iberia, Jušjášun, which until then had been more a home than a covenant, was absorbed into Hermetic society and began to pay the Iberian tax. Since the couple had no vis other than the poppies and the bats, they handed the delicate white flowers over to the Tribunal and, to their surprise, in 1123 Duresca offered them a seven-year exchange of vis for the poppies. At first Danāʾ naively believed that the powerful Asturian covenant needed Mentem vis. A year later, a Redcap confessed to them that Duresca wanted the flowers for their properties and not for their inherent magical power. The magi of Jušjášun then tried to grow them outside the cave or to increase their yield, without success. When, in 1130, Duresca proposed extending the exchange for fourteen more years, Jušjášun doubled the price of the poppies and Duresca accepted; for the first time in their lives, the magi of Jušjášun began to have a surplus of vis. In 1144 Jušjášun tripled the price of the poppy and Duresca accepted again; neither of the two saw the danger. After the covenant had weathered the arrival of the Almohads in 1151, Al-Layt was summoned to appear at Duresca over an alleged mundane violation of the Code of Hermes. The magus did not even notice the trap, and went, alarmed, to prove his innocence. He never stood a chance: he was cast out of the Order in a private hearing and murdered as he fled back toward Jušjášun. His wife never even learned of his fate: she was killed by drunken mundanes who had broken into Jušjášun in search of a few dīnārs. A few days later Al-Ŷannan al-Bonisagī of Duresca arrived at the covenant. The magus buried Danāʾ and settled there, carrying out some remarkable research that soon doubled the yield of the poppy crop. Al-Ŷannan thus claimed the covenant of Jušjášun at the Tribunal of 1158, shortly before it was named a covenant dedicated to Hermetic research.

In 1220 Jušjášun supplies white poppies to several covenants at a price of ten to one (that is, a rook of vis in exchange for one pawn of poppy Mentem), and sends a third of its harvest, along with half the profits from its exchanges, to Duresca free of charge.

#### Setting and Physical Description

The small covenant of Jušjášun stands in the gorge of the Bailón river canyon, surrounded by holm oaks, Portuguese oaks, kermes oaks, wild olives, mastic trees and scrub, which are home to wild boar, wildcats and peregrine falcons. Beside it is a beautiful waterfall that once delighted its inhabitants. Despite Jušjášun's wealth, the covenant is no larger than it was in its founders' day: a two-story building with room for two *sancta*, a central courtyard and space for at most ten servants. Everything in it, however, is of the very finest quality. Jušjášun also has a small building beside the bat cave, which is always guarded by a grog. The mouth of the cave is protected by a ring, inscribed with the *sanctum* symbol and enchanted to repel animals and humans. The entrance can also be watched from the pool in the covenant's courtyard, where its inhabitants can ask to be shown the cave by speaking the command word *kahfun*.

#### Society and Customs

The covenant of Jušjášun depends on Duresca in every respect: it is managed from the Asturian covenant. In minor matters, however, the little covenant has enough freedom to make its own decisions.

Its magi are no more than guardians of the poppy crop: Al-Ŷannan is in charge of improving the sowing and harvesting, and Al-Barrāḍ makes sure that no magus is tempted to raid the covenant. Beyond that, Jušjášun has no other identity. At Tribunals, the two magi of Jušjášun may vote as they please unless Duresca says otherwise. The truth is that, even without instructions, they end up voting the same way as Duresca, which has earned them a reputation as its puppet (something that does not seem to bother them much).

#### The Magi of Jušjášun

##### Al-Ŷannan al-Bonisagī

Al-Ŷannan (Arabic for "the gardener") is the *laqab* of this Valencian Bonisagus, a byname he earned for his exceptional skill with plants. Al-Ŷannan cares very little for politics and does not meddle in any affairs of Duresca or of the other covenants. He lives for Hermetic research into plants, a goal he achieved in 1158, when he took charge of the small covenant of Jušjášun. Al-Ŷannan is a magus without the slightest empathy for people; the pain and injustice of the world leave him entirely unmoved.

##### Al-Barrāḍ al-Praliḥī

Al-Barrāḍ is likewise a *laqab*, the byname of a pre-Islamic Arab warrior whose violence gave rise to the saying: "you are more vehement than the attacks of Al-Barrāḍ."

<!-- p. 240 -->

Al-Barrāḍ is a *saḥir* and a powerful soldier in Duresca's pay. His job is to defend Al-Ŷannan and the white poppy plantation. The magi of the Tribunal prefer to avoid this magus, for he has no honor and no scruples in carrying out his work. To many he is nothing but a hired killer, which only reinforces the image Duresca wishes to project of its faithful soldier.

> #### Story Seeds: The Faithful Hound's Prey
>
> In one of his ravings as Duresca's *disceptator*, Fortún has issued an order to Al-Barrāḍ to "frighten" Collegiata of Guernicus, the *quaestor aerarii* of Aedes Saturni, since he believes the maga is diverting part of Jušjášun's money into the coffers of the Tribunal.
>
> One rainy night the player characters are woken by their servants and find a gravely wounded maga at their gates, begging for refuge. The maga, who is none other than Collegiata, explains that she has been attacked by a stranger who is hard on her heels. From then on, the players must get through what remains of the night while Al-Barrāḍ tries to reach his victim. Will they hand the maga over in exchange for some favor from Duresca? Will they protect the *quaestor aerarii* regardless of the consequences? If this is their first contact with the powers of the Tribunal, this encounter could be an important moment in the saga.

### Alma Mater

>**Lifespan:** 810–863<br>
>**Founder:** Tello of Guernicus *filius* Ranemiro<br>
>**Aura (type and strength):** Unknown<br>
>**Reputations:** Martyr (Iberian Tribunal) 1

#### History

During the early years of Lucis, Tello acted as intermediary between Ranemiro and the Mozarabs of Cordoba and Toledo, and over time he came to spend more time in those cities than in his *parens*'s covenant. When Ranemiro was condemned at the Grand Tribunal of 799, Tello was in Cordoba, completing the purchase of a modest property in the city's suburbs. Unaware of what had happened, he returned to Lucis to find nothing but ruins. After praying for months on the spot, he came to know that his *parens* had ascended to the Divine realm. Tello returned to the Rhine, where he registered his Cordoban covenant at the Tribunal of 810, together with the covenants of Secunda and the Norman Confluensis. He then went straight back to Cordoba where, years later, he was joined by another of Ranemiro's apprentices, Qatr al-Nadà, who had been wandering al-Andalus without founding or settling in any covenant.

Throughout the covenant's life, the rooms of Alma Mater served as classrooms for teaching theology, medicine and philosophy, and amid the comings and goings of people its inhabitants discovered several students with the Gift, whom they also trained in the Arts and Hermetic theory. During the revolt of the suburb in 818, Alma Mater had to take refuge in Secunda, where it remained a whole year before returning to Cordoba. Years later, when the tomb of the apostle Saint James was discovered, Alma Mater put on its festive best and made a pilgrimage there with its students, which eventually became a tradition and kept Alma Mater and Campus Stellae on good terms throughout its existence.

Tello won great fame as a judge within the Order, and Alma Mater became a byword, which, it must be said, Somnus of Tremere did not hesitate to exploit for his own benefit. Tello's life changed at the Council of Cordoba of 839. The magus was deeply impressed by the speech of Esperaindeo (see "The Voluntary Martyrs," page 24), and his tolerance turned into intransigence. Tello took to crossing himself whenever he heard the call to prayer from the minarets and to arguing frequently with Qatr al-Nadà. The tensions between them erupted at the New Year council, when Tello's *filia*, María, sided with Qatr al-Nadà. Tello insulted her and told her she was defending a heretic who had converted to Islam. To settle the argument, Tello expelled both women from the covenant, and from that moment on he devoted his life to atoning for his sins and helping the Christians who lived subjugated by Islam.

In 851 Tello ended up in prison for having accepted a girl of Muslim parents into his classes, and he had to recant before the *qādī* to win his freedom a year later. His submission, however, did not please Álbaro of Cordoba, who shamed him before the city's Christian community. So when, seven years later, Saint Eulogius was executed, Tello sank into a deep depression. That autumn, at the end of the afternoon prayer, the magus publicly accused Muḥammad of being a false prophet and was imprisoned. When asked to recant, he reaffirmed his opinion before the *qādī*, who had no choice but to sentence him to death.

The only magus left in Alma Mater departed after Tello's beheading in the autumn of 863. With his departure the covenant ceased to exist, but the cathedral chapter of Cordoba continued to use it as a center of learning.

#### Setting and Physical Description

Alma Mater was sacked and burned during the *fitna*. Nothing of it remains. Other houses were raised on its foundations, so it is not even possible to tell where it was built, or whether it was bathed by the Divine aura that now lies over the area.

<!-- p. 241 -->

### Ipagrum

>**Lifespan:** 871–907<br>
>**Founders:** Boudica of Diedne, Huctia Ex Miscellanea<br>
>**Aura (type and strength):** Magic, strength 5<br>
>**Reputations:** None

The covenant of Ipagrum was founded by magi of Duresca who sought their fortune in the south after the death of Tancoystl. As was the custom among the Diedne, they raised their covenant beside a lake, a day's journey from the town of Lucena and five kilometers from the Muslim town of Poley.

#### History

When Tancoystl plotted the murder of the king of Asturias, Ramiro I, Boudica and Huctia fled south from the Christian king's justice and the machinations of the magi of the north of the Peninsula. After speaking with the magi of Mons Vindius, they decided to go to al-Andalus and settle beside the huge lagoon of Zóñar, a little over two days' journey south of the city of Cordoba, since it held a communication node with Lake Enol at Mons Vindius. In the same year that the magae of Ipagrum founded their covenant, their former *sodales* at Duresca founded the covenant of Nebula. This was the Rhine Tribunal of 871.

For its first ten years Ipagrum was able to grow and live in peace, always in contact with its twin covenant in the central massif. At the end of the ninth century, however, the rebel ʿUmar ibn Ḥafṣūn used the town of Poley as a stronghold from which to take Cordoba, whereupon the armies of the emir and future caliph, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān III, besieged the town's fortress and assaulted the stronghold, which surrendered in 891. Unfortunately for Ipagrum, the fighting spilled over onto the covenant: it was attacked, and the magae had to defend themselves against the Cordoban troops in a battle that ended in the defeat of the mundanes and cost Huctia her life. But the armies of the capital did not give up, and returned on several occasions, until in 907 Ipagrum was razed by the *saḥirs*.

Ipagrum was the first covenant the *saḥirs* attacked before crossing the frontier and destroying Inverneira. The Muslim sorcerers left no one alive: the magae and an apprentice died that night, and not even Nebula could help them through the lake portals that linked the two covenants. After the ruling "On the Diedne Legacy" (1025) was passed, the Tribunal erased the last traces of the covenant: its location, its coat of arms and its history were destroyed, so that in 1220 very few know its name.

> #### Story Seeds: The Incorrupt Finger of Saint Tello of Guernica
>
> On one of their journeys through northern Iberia, the player characters are approached by the parish priest of a village. With impeccable manners, the monk informs them that they have the opportunity to pray before the relic of Saint Tello of Guernica, for a few coins, of course. A Perception + Awareness roll against an Ease Factor of 6 lets them notice that the priest wears an old silver ring bearing an almost indistinguishable symbol of House Guernicus. If they ask about the saint, the priest tells them that he was martyred in Cordoba by the Moors, having been the sole survivor, in the early eleventh century, of the cholera outbreak that devastated the town of Guernica, abandoned ever since. An Intelligence + Iberian Tribunal Lore roll of 9+ lets them connect that Tello of Guernicus martyred by Muḥammad I with this saint, Tello of Guernica, whose past is anachronistic. If they visit the church and examine the relic (after making a small donation), they discover that it has True Faith. Where did the parish priest get that finger? Does it have anything to do with the ring? Could these be the remains of Tello of Guernicus? Might these priests possess anything else from Alma Mater?

> #### Story Seeds: An Offering to the Diedne?
>
> *Is it not worship of the devil to light candles beside stones, trees, springs and crossroads? To divine what is to come and to celebrate the day of idols, is that not paying worship to the devil?*[^p241-XVIII]
>
> When the player characters find a vis source at the lagoon of Zóñar, they also come upon the ancient ruins of Ipagrum. These are not, however, entirely abandoned. In one of the corners where the pagan magae's old altar used to stand there is a stone that is not from the area, bearing traces of fresh blood. The surface of this makeshift altar carries some rather crude inscriptions that depict something the player characters cannot recognize at all (unless, improbably, they know something of the symbolism of House Diedne). Any InVi spell designed to detect magical traces can identify them, and if there is a Quaesitor in the group, he or she could try to decipher the caster's sigil. Which magus or maga of the Tribunal is making sacrifices to the Diedne? Whose sigil marks those spells?
>
> [^p241-XVIII]: Excerpt from *De correctione rusticorum* by the sixth-century Hispanic bishop Martin of Braga (taken from A. Peña, 2004).

<!-- p. 242 -->

#### Setting and Physical Description

The few ruins left of Ipagrum lie on the shore of a seventy-hectare lake that reaches a maximum depth of sixteen meters. The lagoon, named Zóñar, with slightly brackish waters, is ringed by a belt of marsh vegetation of reeds, rushes and bulrushes. Waterfowl (purple swamphens, shelducks, pochards, greylag geese, white-headed ducks, great crested grebes and mallards) use the vegetation to nest under its shelter. In the past, the inhabitants of Ipagrum harvested vis from some of these birds' nests.

### ʿÔlām wā-ʿed

*[…] since man is distinguished by something very singular in him, which exists in none of the beings that people the lunar sphere, namely his intellectual capacity, for which neither sense nor any bodily part nor limb is used, it has been likened to divine apprehension, which is independent of any medium […]. For this reason, I mean on account of the intellect "that is joined to man," it has been said that he is in the image of God and His likeness, not that God […] is a body endowed with shape.*[^p242-38]

[^p242-38]: Excerpt from *The Guide for the Perplexed* by Maimonides (Spanish translation by David Gonzalo Maeso).

>**Lifespan:** 920–1148<br>
>**Founders:** Malʾāk al-Gernikī, Petuel al-Ŷerbitonī<br>
>**Aura (type and strength):** Magic, strength 2 (main building), Divine, strength 1 to 6 (in the rest of the city's buildings)<br>
>**Reputations:** Slavers (Iberian Tribunal) 3, Greedy (Iberian Tribunal) 1

The covenant of ʿÔlām wā-ʿed (Hebrew for "for ever and ever," in its sense of perpetuity and as a synonym for God) was a powerful urban covenant forged during the Umayyad Caliphate, when Lucena belonged to the *kūra* of Cabra. ʿÔlām wā-ʿed reached the height of its splendor during the eleventh and twelfth centuries, coinciding with the independence of the Tribunal of al-Andalus and the arrival of the taifa kingdoms (in the Zirid kingdom of Granada) and of the Almoravids (by then in the *kūra* of Cordoba).

#### History

The town of Lucena (in Arabic, al-Yusana), halfway between Cordoba, Granada and Malaga, based its economy on trade and viticulture, and was the most important Jewish enclave in al-Andalus until the arrival of the Almohads in 1148. During the caliphate the town stood on a cultural par with resplendent Cordoba, for its rabbinical academy came to enjoy more prestige than that of the former caliphal capital, and it was where the Iberian genius Moses ben Maimon studied (see page 321).

The Jews Malʾāk and Petuel took the risk of founding their covenant in their native Lucena when Ṭāmis ibn Baldiccione al-Išbīlī al-Gernikī announced in 920 that peace negotiations with the *saḥirs* were still under way. To buy the building they wanted (a modest property in the medina, bathed by a weak *lacuna*), the two magi had to take a loan from Aedes Saturni, which they extended a year later to purchase several lots of young slaves in Almería. Having brought them to Lucena, they operated on the males and separated the slaves by sex to educate them for ten years. On reaching maturity, the eunuchs were sold in the souks of Cordoba to work as servants in the harems, as administrators in the civil service or as soldiers in the army, and the women were delivered to serve in the palaces as scribes (for their delicate calligraphy), singers, dancers or musicians. At that time the trade in people from the land of the *ṣaqāliba*[^p242-39] was booming: slaves were carried down the Rhône to its mouth at Arles, and from there shipped by sea to al-Andalus. Their first investment yielded such profits that ʿÔlām wā-ʿed extended its influence to the cities of Barcelona and Almería, where the slave ships arrived from northern Europe. In time they began to trade in slaves from southern Provence and northern Iberia, since Basque women were especially coveted by the Cordoban upper classes. Their slaves became so famous that ʿÔlām wā-ʿed reached the cities of North Africa and the Mediterranean, and many Christian covenants in northern Iberia paid them in vis. In the markets and souks of al-Andalus, the slaves of ʿÔlām wā-ʿed fetched prices of more than 1,000 dīnārs.

[^p242-39]: A territory that the Arab authors of Iberia identified with regions of central and northern Europe, where there were important cities such as Prague and Verdun devoted to the export of slaves.

In 974 the caliph Al-Ḥakam II engaged the services of ʿÔlām wā-ʿed and received Malʾāk with gifts and honors at Madīnat al-Zahrāʾ, where he signed a commercial contract with him to supply the eunuchs for his harem and his court. ʿÔlām wā-ʿed thus came to be protected and supported by the Umayyad public treasury, but it did not entrust its livelihood to it, continuing instead to trade with cities across the known world. In those days the magi used the titles *ʾāḥôt* and *ʾāḥ* (Hebrew for "sister" and "brother," respectively), under the leadership of the *rosh yeshiva* (head of the Talmudic academy of Lucena), and its solvency was such that it lent money to numerous covenants, and once even to the Mercer House of Aedes Saturni.

After the Schism War, ʿÔlām wā-ʿed supported the independence of al-Andalus and, as the mundane powers rose and fell, showed a great capacity to adapt. Thus, when the *fitna* broke out, its finances did not suffer, thanks to its foreign trade; during the taifa kingdoms it was one of the main suppliers of eunuchs to the Zirid court of Granada; and with the arrival of the Almoravids it was able to buy its freedom, and its business was barely affected. In 1148, however, everything changed. The town of Lucena and the covenant were razed by the Almohads, and the magi had to flee in haste. Although they tried to return, they managed to recover only an insignificant part of all they had amassed in their two centuries of existence: the governor of Granada, Abū Saʿīd ʿUṯmān, took everything from them. The mundane Jews of Lucena did not escape unscathed either, and had to go into exile in Provence,[^p243-40] in the Christian kingdoms of Castile and Aragon and, above all, in the Islamic lands of the East and North Africa.

<!-- p. 243 -->

When, at the Tribunal of 1151, Meʾir ibn Yosef al-Ŷerbitonī announced the destruction of ʿÔlām wā-ʿed, the Tribunal was left breathless, for it confirmed that no one was safe from the power of the Almohads. The magi of ʿÔlām wā-ʿed then dispersed among cities with a notable Jewish presence, such as Toledo (in the covenant of Iššáh), Gerona (where they founded the covenant of ʿĂrābôt) and Monforte (where they raised the unruly Beit Midrash).

[^p243-40]: The physicians who took refuge in Montpellier, France, gave rise to an important school of medicine that eventually became a faculty in 1220.

#### Setting and Physical Description

The covenant of ʿÔlām wā-ʿed was spread among numerous buildings within the walled town of Lucena. The magi lived in an impressive building, inside a *lacuna*, divided into four wings named according to the Jewish tradition that associates the four letters of the divine name (YHVH) with living beings: in the complex of humans (the "Y"), to the south, were the magi's private synagogue and *micvé*, where incense always burned so that the stench of the sacrifices of oxen and lambs would not seep into ceilings and walls; in the complex of the lion (the "H"), to the east, were the *sancta*; in the wing of the ox (the "V"), to the west, was the treasury; and in the quarters of the eagle (the other "H"), to the north, was the fabulous library.

ʿÔlām wā-ʿed maintained trade relations with the main coastal cities of the Mediterranean and also with Constantinople, from which it imported purple-dyed silks reserved exclusively for the emperors. On one occasion, one of the magi of ʿÔlām wā-ʿed managed to send one of his apprentices to study schedography, Greek and Armenian at the court of Alexios I, where he shared lessons and games with the eldest of the emperor's daughters, the then little Anna Komnene, who had a lion cub that the Fatimid caliph of Egypt had given to her father, the *basileus*. Every year the magi of ʿÔlām wā-ʿed went to Constantinople on the day of the Nativity of Jesus, when the emperor displayed in the city's great hippodrome all manner of human beings discovered by the armies of the *basileus* on their campaigns. There they acquired rare specimens to educate and trade (bear in mind, however, that at this time the Jews lived under repression in Constantinople: they could not ride horses, live in the city, or trade with its inhabitants).

> #### Story Seeds: Ṭalāl the Eunuch
>
> *O you who ride on horseback, though in truth there is no rider when the testicles are not set upon the steed's back! You have surpassed Moses and his miracles, for you make the water flow while hiding the rod.*[^p243-XIX]
>
> During the Almohad assault on Lucena, one of the covenant's eunuchs managed to escape with the shepherd's staff *nōʿam* (Hebrew for "grace" or "favor"), which the prophet Zechariah used to tend his flock. The staff is a powerful relic with four Faith Points that in time can raise a Divine aura of strength 6 (see *Ars Magica Fifth Edition*, pages 274 and 275). This relic was one of the most treasured possessions of ʿÔlām wā-ʿed, although, truth be told, it was just one among the many other marvels the covenant owned.
>
> During the winter, the player characters' covenant receives a visit from an old man with Armenian features who speaks Arabic, Latin and Greek. He introduces himself as Ṭalāl and asks for lodging until the bad weather passes. He explains that he has spent many years searching for his former masters and lords of ʿÔlām wā-ʿed, and he is grateful for any help they can offer him. In return, he offers to spend the following season educating one of their apprentices or writing a book of mundane knowledge that interests them.
>
> During that season, the covenant's aura is eclipsed by a powerful Divine aura of strength 6 that ruins the player characters' Hermetic research and hampers spellcasting. Will they discover the source of the aura? Will they help Ṭalāl find his masters?
>
> [^p243-XIX]: Verses by Al-Majzūmī that appear in *In Praise of Spanish Islam* (Spanish translation by Emilio García Gómez).

### Al-Zahrāʾ

>**Lifespan:** 941–1000<br>
>**Founder:** ʿAbbās ibn Munḏīr al-Bonisagī<br>
>**Aura (type and strength):** Divine, strength 1 (in the medina), Magic, strength 1 (in the *almunia*)<br>
>**Reputations:** Glorious (Iberian Tribunal) 1

When the caliph ʿAbd al-Raḥmān III built the palatine city of Madīnat al-Zahrāʾ in the middle of the tenth century, ʿAbbās al-Bonisagī was dazzled by its majesty and power. Its spell over him was such that the elderly magus bought a small *almunia* on the nearby slopes of *Ŷabal al-ʿArus*, where he founded the covenant of al-Zahrāʾ.

#### History

ʿAbbās ibn Munḏīr was elected Praeco at the close of the tumultuous Tribunal of 941, a couple of days after formally founding his covenant, so he had to take on the difficult task of turning the small *almunia* he had acquired into a structure capable of hosting an entire Tribunal in only seven years. ʿAbbās almost regretted, then, having left the covenant of Qasr Dār al-Muchaddad.

<!-- p. 244 -->

Making use of the relationships that he and the Praeco Ǧamīla al-Ŷerbitoniyya had established with certain dignitaries of the Umayyad court, he began to weave numerous intrigues and hand out numerous gifts to secure a small monthly stipend from the public treasury; and although he tried to approach ʿAbd al-Raḥmān III, to whom he gave a beautiful enchanted carving of Venus in 947, all he achieved, to his despair, was to have it placed over the southern gate of the city. Despite his income, ʿAbbās had to take a loan of almost 500,000 dīnārs from Aedes Saturni and from the Lucena covenant of ʿÔlām wā-ʿed in order to hold the sumptuous Tribunal of 948 at al-Zahrāʾ.

ʿAbbās continued to rise at court, and he invented a genealogy making him a descendant of Abū Bakr (the first caliph chosen to govern the Islamic community after the death of the Prophet) to obtain his first audience in the halls of the palace of Madīnat al-Zahrāʾ. At that meeting Al-Ḥakam II took a liking to him, as much for his lineage as for his wisdom, and showered him with gifts. The caliph raised his stipend to 1,000 dīnārs a month (more than ten times that of the *ḥaŷib*!), granted him seventy *almudes* of wheat a month, and gave him a palace in the medina, lands for his *almunia* and slaves to work them, mounts, jewels, garments, tapestries and numerous books. ʿAbbās then used his influence to have the caliph sign an agreement with the covenant of ʿÔlām wā-ʿed to supply him with slaves and eunuchs. In return, the Lucena covenant forgave his debt and paid Aedes Saturni what ʿAbbās owed it.

ʿAbbās arranged for one of his fellow covenant members, the eunuch Ṭalīd, to take charge of the caliph's library of learning (*jizanatu-hu l-ʿilmiya*); he founded an important workshop for copying Qurʾans, directed by the freedwoman and woman of letters ʿAʾisha ḅint Ahmad ibn Muḥammad ibn Qadim; and he set up an ivory workshop so that the exceptional Faŷrun al-Verditiyya (see "Aẓm Alfíl," page 174) could work the tusks the caliph brought from the Maghreb. In less than twenty years al-Zahrāʾ had acquired several stalls in the souk, public baths, mills and a small fleet of ships that it leased out to enrich itself. But the price was very high: at the end of 962, ʿAbbās denounced the Kharijites of the Almería covenant of Bayt al-Ḥikma in order to advance at court and achieve something unprecedented in the Order, the integration of the Tribunal into mundane society through the Peripheral Code ruling "On the Great Mosque of Cordoba" (969).

After the death of Al-Ḥakam, however, ʿAbbās won the trust of the *ḥaŷib* Almanzor, though not for long. Despite his efforts to prevail, the approach of the end of the millennium (when many Christians predicted the end of the world) marked his fall. Before the turn of the century, the Redcaps of Aedes Saturni published the minutes of the meetings ʿAbbās had held with Al-Ḥakam in 962, and an anonymous figure denounced al-Zahrāʾ to the *fuqahāʾ* of Cordoba. The Praeco was condemned by the *qādī* in the Great Mosque and fled; the rest of the members scattered throughout the Tribunal. The covenant's riches were seized by the civil authorities of Cordoba and, with the fall of the palatine city, its halls were sacked and plundered.

The enchanted statue of Venus remained atop the city gate until, in 1190, the caliph Abū Yūsuf Yaʿqūb al-Manṣūr ordered it destroyed. According to the chronicles, when it was taken down a hurricane-force wind arose that did great damage to roofs and ropes and even uprooted some trees; the people of Cordoba believed that the statue protected the city.

#### Setting and Physical Description

The covenant of al-Zahrāʾ lies in ruins, both its old palace and its *almunia*. Decay and oblivion shelter those walls; its chambers and alcoves are mute. In 1220 its ruins are indistinguishable from the other palaces and buildings around it; nothing remains that could identify it as a former Hermetic palace.

> #### Story Seeds: The Giant of Maryah
>
> In the summer of 971, Al-Ḥakam II heard of a boy in the farmstead of Maryah, in the *kūra* of Rayya (Malaga), who at the age of four already looked like a youth. Intrigued, he asked for him to be brought to court, for he wished to meet him. The boy arrived accompanied by his grandfather, Jalaf, and at the end of the visit both returned home laden with gifts. ʿAbbās told the magi of Lucena about the boy, and they went to his village and kidnapped him. Two years later the boy with giant's blood slipped away from his captors and returned home, where he found that he had grown considerably. The villagers greeted him as a monster, so he took the caliph's gifts and fled north, where he found refuge in the hills of roses (*Ŷibāl al-ward*) of the Cordoban highlands. The boy grew up, grew old and, after a long life, died.
>
> In 1220 some of his children might still be living in those hills, perhaps with the gifts the caliph gave their father, perhaps with the Gift. Storyguides could use this story to supply the history of a Hermetic apprentice with the Giant Blood Virtue, or to introduce the riches that were lost in the hills of roses.

## Granada

*Granada is the Damascus of al-Andalus, pasture for the eyes, elevation for the soul. […] God has adorned it by placing it high above its broad plain, where the silver ingots of the streams branch out among the emerald of the trees.*[^p244-41]

[^p244-41]: Excerpt from *In Praise of Spanish Islam* by Al-Šaqundī (Spanish translation by Emilio García Gómez).

<!-- p. 245 -->

After Seville, the *kūra* of Granada is the largest. To the north it borders the provinces of Seville, Cordoba and Jaén, to the west the Atlantic Ocean, to the south the Mediterranean Sea, and to the east the *kūra* of Murcia. Granada is crossed by the Sierra Nevada (*Ŷabal Šulayr*), which twelfth-century chroniclers said always had snow, winter or summer, and where the highest peak in Iberia rises, more than 3,700 meters high. In 1220 its slopes are dotted with farmsteads whose lands, watered by the Genil river, produce walnuts, apples and mulberries.

The *kūra* of Granada is home to towns such as Almuñécar and Salobreña (whose sugar cane rivals that imported from Tyre), Malaga, Almería, Gibraltar, Ceuta, Ronda, Guadix, Pechina, Algeciras and, of course, Granada. Because of its exceptional landscape, many magi chose it for their covenants, and in 1220 it shelters two of the oldest covenants in al-Andalus: Dār Malīḥaʾ of Ronda (which many regard as the flagship of the Tribunal, above moribund Salionca or decadent Duresca) and the faded Qasr Dār al-Muchaddad of Granada.

### Dār Malīḥaʾ

*Now, it is for you to decide. If you strive for your perfection to be achieved through means, [for example,] through wealth, then your perfection will be like that of one who dreams. [If you want it to be] through health, you will be a servant by nature, whether or not a man possesses you as your master. If your perfection [is attained] through the moral virtues, then you will be directed by someone other than yourself and will need a director […]. And if you are perfect in the practical arts, then, by my life, you will be a man, for you will command that [which you do] and will not be governed [by another].*[^p245-42]

[^p245-42]: Excerpt from the *Letter of Farewell* by Avempace (Spanish translation by Joaquín Lomba).

>**Lifespan:** 843–Present<br>
>**Founders:** Qatr al-Nadà al-Gernikiyya, María of Guernicus<br>
>**Season:** Autumn<br>
>**Aura (type and strength):** Magic, strength 7<br>
>**Reputations:** Just (Iberian Tribunal) 4, Even-Handed (Iberian Tribunal) 3<br>
>**Votes:** 8

Dār Malīḥaʾ (Arabic for "gracious house" or "good house") was founded by two magae of the line of Ranemiro of Sahagún, one of the *filii* of Guernicus. For this reason, the Quaesitores trained within its walls tend to pride themselves on their ancestry, since they consider themselves the true judges of Iberia, unlike those who came to Duresca from the Roman Tribunal in the first half of the tenth century.

#### History

Qatr al-Nadà of Ronda (Arabic for "dewdrop") was a disciple of Ranemiro and stayed with him until the magus shared everything he knew about the tempestarii with the Rhine Tribunal. Her *parens*'s lack of integrity led her to renounce her religion and return to al-Andalus, where she wandered for almost twenty years far from Hermetic life. On her travels through the cities of al-Andalus she had a few encounters with the *saḥirs*, from whom she learned something of their customs and concerns. Weary of her wandering, when she learned in 810 that her Hermetic brother Tello had founded the covenant of Alma Mater, she joined him and caught up on what had happened in the Order: the defeat of the tempestarii, Ranemiro's expulsion at the Grand Tribunal of 799, the disappearance of Lucis and the supposed ascension of her *parens* to the Divine realm.

During her early years at Alma Mater, relations with Tello were not easy: the magus kept his distance and would not let her take part in the life of the covenant because she was a Muslim. Although Qatr al-Nadà took it philosophically, the situation became untenable after the Council of Cordoba of 839; that winter, Tello expelled his *filia* María and Qatr al-Nadà from Alma Mater, and the two went to Ronda, where they founded their own covenant.

Since Tello had begun to neglect the affairs of the Order in favor of the Christian community of Cordoba, the judges of Dār Malīḥaʾ took over from him. Particularly noteworthy was their collaboration with Tancoystl Ex Miscellanea of Duresca, with whom they worked until his death in 845 to unmask the Tremere conspiracy, a task that culminated in 848 with the Sundering.

From then on, Qatr al-Nadà concentrated on achieving peace with the *saḥirs* alongside Baldiccione, with whom she persuaded the *saḥirs* to sign their first truce with the Order in 870, and she worked for more than thirty years toward a peaceful union with the Muslim sorcerers. She did not, however, see her dream come true: Qatr al-Nadà was murdered in 907 by the Flambeau while meeting with the *saḥirs* in a *ribāṭ* in Jaén. On her death the covenant passed into the hands of her *filia* Zaynab (of the Banū Qurra, a notable family of Ronda) and María, who had converted to Islam under the name Maryam. Zaynab was responsible for continuing the negotiations with the *saḥirs* (which finally bore fruit in 925), and years later, during the scandal of the Duresca manuscripts, Maryam provided the evidence needed to declare them fraudulent at the Tribunal of 941. Maryam then left for Duresca, and Zaynab withdrew from political life for fear of ending up like her colleague Ṭāmis (see page 77).

The covenant was revitalized by the arrival, at the end of the tenth century, of the Trianomae Ḥafṣa ibn ʿAbbās. The maga launched an ambitious project to improve the infrastructure of Dār Malīḥaʾ and extend its influence in Iberia. Within a few years the covenant had built an astronomical observatory near al-Ŷazīra al-Jaḍrāʾ, raised a spectacular building in the gorges of the Guadalhorce river (to which the magi moved), fitted out the old quarters of Dār Malīḥaʾ to serve as the seat of the Banū Qurra, opened a school of Mālikī law, acquired a building in Malaga, and widened its contacts among the Cordoban elite and the astrologers of Almanzor's court, taking advantage of its good relations with the covenant of al-Zahrāʾ, which was ruled by her *parens*, ʿAbbās.

<!-- p. 246 -->

When the Schism War broke out shortly afterward, Ḥafṣa attended the extraordinary Grand Tribunal of 1011 and voted against the expulsion of House Diedne. When the meeting decided otherwise, she was consumed by frustration and issued a communiqué inviting all the covenants of Iberia not to respect the Order's verdict. Almost all the Andalusi magi backed her and, as a result, the Tribunal broke apart into two smaller units: Iberia and al-Andalus. Curiously, Ḥafṣa met the greatest resistance in her own covenant: her *filius*, Domingo Garcés, and two of its most eminent members, the musicians and poets Maʿbad and Al-Garīd al-Ŷerbitonī, left Dār Malīḥaʾ and went off to fight the Diedne.

As the foremost representative of the Andalusi movement, Ḥafṣa was elected Praeco of the illegitimate Tribunal of al-Andalus, and Dār Malīḥaʾ hosted the first two Tribunals before they moved to the Great Hall of Saragossa. To reward the invaluable part the mathematicians of Madrid had played in its construction, in 1035 Ḥafṣa funded the school of mathematics and astronomy of Granada, founded by Asbay ibn Muḥammad, one of the disciples of Maslama (see page 287).

Dār Malīḥaʾ also produced the second and last Praeco of al-Andalus, the charismatic poet Al-ʿĀsmarun al-Ŷerbitonī. During his tenure he persuaded Porta Pandere to approve the creation of the Mercere portal *Vicesimus*, and he contributed to the enrichment of the Tribunal through the Mercer House of Aedes Iris. He did not, however, manage to have the Order recognize the independence of al-Andalus, and he ended up supporting its reunification in 1089. With the return to Iberia, Dār Malīḥaʾ was pushed into the background under the strict watch of Duresca and Durato, though this did not stop it from continuing to set an example with its high moral standards and sound judicial practice.

#### Setting and Physical Description

Dār Malīḥaʾ is spread across the cities of Ronda, Malaga and Almería and the gorges of the Guadalhorce river, where the magi's *sancta*, the covenant's stores of vis and its library are located.

#### The Treasury, the Tailor's Workshop and the House of the Ulama of Ronda

In Ronda, pristine Dār Malīḥaʾ has two stone buildings joined by an underground passage; the first is in the lower part of the city and the second in the upper part. The buildings, of flawless workmanship, are built of first-rate materials from Persia, al-Andalus and Constantinople. Both have two stories and a cellar, and both stand within the medina. The first, which bears the name of its founder, Qatr al-Nadà, lies very close to one of the city gates, where there are baths and a bridge spanning the Guadalevín river. The building, which once housed two *sancta*, now serves as a school of Islamic law, from which Dār Malīḥaʾ extends part of its influence over al-Andalus. In the cellar is a passage connecting it to the building in the upper town, called Ḥafṣa, raised in the middle of the tenth century to house another pair of *sancta*. The Ḥafṣa building stands some hundred meters above the Guadalevín river, beside an impressive cliff. Its cellars reach down to the riverbed, where a small landing stage gives access to the *Vicesimus* portal, the covenant's treasury, the wine cellars and the stores of grain and victuals that arrive from Malaga. Unlike the Qatr al-Nadà building, the Ḥafṣa building is protected by the *Aegis of the Hearth* and guarded around the clock by companions loyal to the magi. Attached to it, the covenant owns a workshop that makes the gold-tissue tunics (*al-ḥulal al-mawšiyya*),[^p246-43] the brocades and the magnificently colored silks worn and displayed by the refined magi of Dār Malīḥaʾ.

[^p246-43]: *Wašy* is a multicolored silk cloth embroidered with gold, known in Europe as algüexi, albexi, albeci, alveici, oxi, oxsi, etc. The Arabs used these tunics as a symbol of sovereignty.

#### The Harbor House of Malaga

*Malaga unites the two prospects of sea and land, with vineyards that follow one another without interruption, so that you cannot see among them a patch of uncultivated ground; with country houses that resemble the stars of heaven in their great number and the splendor of their brilliance; and with the river, which crosses it, visiting it in the two seasons of winter and spring, the depths of its plain, and encircles it to learn its contours.*[^p246-44]

[^p246-44]: Excerpt from *In Praise of Spanish Islam* by Al-Šaqundī (Spanish translation by Emilio García Gómez).

The city of Malaga is the gateway through which the goods of Genoese merchants enter on their way to the city of Granada (where the Italians have a quarter). Dār Malīḥaʾ took advantage of this to acquire a small building in the city from which to charter its ships, which it uses to buy the sumptuous materials its magi are accustomed to in Mediterranean cities such as Valencia, Almería, Barcelona, Pisa, Genoa, Tunis or Constantinople. The building, with two stories and a cellar, is protected with enchantments so that mundanes cannot break into it, since until the goods are carried to Ronda they are stored in the strongrooms beneath the harbor house.

To avoid the piracy of Majorca, the covenant has struck a deal with Ajabeba, although even so its ships are sometimes boarded.

#### The Observatory, Farm and Exchange of Almería

*Almería is a city of renowned fame and great importance, whose inhabitants are distinguished by their even temper, their brilliant pomp, the softness of their skin, the beauty of their faces and their manners, and their nobility in dealings and friendship.*[^p246-45]

[^p246-45]: *Ibidem*.

Almería (al-Mariyyāt Baŷŷāna) received the title of city in 955, when ʿAbd al-Raḥmān III made it the capital of a *kūra*. Its souks offer a great variety of goods: Iraqi glass has been imported there since the ninth century (after Ziryāb made it fashionable), to be worked in its own workshops or in those of Murcia, Malaga or Seville. The city has more than 800 silk looms and the finest marble workshops, where the marble, once carved or polished, is called *mulūkī*. Dār Malīḥaʾ bought a building in the city's Christian exchange (within the walled enclosure), where Christian goods are distributed throughout the domains of al-Andalus.

<!-- p. 247 -->

The covenant's other building in Almería, an astronomical observatory, was built by Ḥafṣa at the end of the tenth century on the highest peak of the Sierra de Alhamilla. The slender tower, twenty meters high, is crowned by a chamber with no entrances or exits: it can only be reached by means of magic. There lies the observatory, whose floors and walls are made of Iraqi glass worked in the workshops of Almería. The floor, inspired by the chamber King Solomon built for Bilkīs, imitates a lovely pool that shimmers in the starlight. On clear nights the magi can see the sky distinctly and take their measurements in the observatory's small study. In time the magi of Dār Malīḥaʾ built a laboratory there.

Dār Malīḥaʾ also exploits the kermes oak (a relative of the holm oak) in the area of Senés, home to an insect from which a valuable pigment known as "grain" (*kermes vermilio*) is obtained, which dyes fabrics red and provides an abundant source of income (see the agriculture source of income in *Covenants*, page 80).

#### The Sancta in the Gorges of the Guadalhorce River

More than a hundred meters above the ground, between the sheer walls of the river's gorge, Ḥafṣa raised by magic a building that seems to float in the air. The structure rests on the rock walls by means of two superimposed arches, and inside, its rooms are carved into the stone. As in Ronda, passages pierce it vertically, from the very top (where there is a lookout post) down to the turbulent river. Spread over five levels are nine *sancta*, an impressive library, the council chamber and the chamber where the vis stores are kept. On the highest level are the three *sancta* of the advisory council or *maŷlis al-rāʿy* (occupied by the covenant's Quaesitores), and immediately below are six *sancta* spread over two floors (which may not be occupied by Quaesitores). On the fourth floor (counting from the top) are the mirror room and the huge council chamber, which can host an ordinary Tribunal, and on the lowest floor (still more than fifty meters above the riverbed) are the immense library, the chamber of the magical treasury and the room holding the various Arcane Connections to the covenant's outposts throughout al-Andalus. Separate from the main body are the guest quarters, which are carved into the rock and have only two entrances: one opening to the outside and one leading to the council chamber. Although they do not connect directly with the covenant, they lie under the protection of the *Aegis of the Hearth.*

#### The Mirror Room

Only the members of Dār Malīḥaʾ (present and past) know the command word needed to work the door leading to the mirror room. Once the way is unlocked, a Magic Resistance of 20 or more is required to cross the threshold (because of a magical effect). Beyond the portal a staircase leads to a small square room, fifteen meters on a side, without windows or furniture, with a great mirror covering the whole of the wall on the left as one enters. The mirror is enchanted with a level 50 effect of *The Invisible Eye Revealed*

<!-- p. 248 -->

(InVi) and works on anyone who looks into its surface with a Magic Resistance of 40 or less. It is also invested with a permanent *Lamp without Flame* effect (CrIg; Target Room), and with an effect similar to *Frosty Breath of the Spoken Lie* (InMe 20; with an effect Penetration of 50), which shows a murky reflection of those who lie when they speak. Finally, the mirror is linked to a tiara, usually worn by the covenant's Redcap, which lets the wearer record in writing whatever thoughts she wishes to share. On the first day the recorded messages are black; from then on they take on an ever redder hue until they vanish on the seventh day (the members of Dār Malīḥaʾ visit the room at least once a day to check that there are no new messages).

The covenant's councils are held in this room, so all its members must remain standing and exposed to the mirror's scrutiny. Under the charter, participants are obliged to lower their Parma when they speak, so that the mirror can probe them. Only in the face of a grave threat is this rule set aside.

#### Society and Customs

The charter of Dār Malīḥaʾ is most peculiar. Its code defines the covenant's government as democratic, although a few points qualify this.

- The covenant may have no more than nine magi, of whom at most three may be Quaesitores (*Ḥafṣa introduced these changes into the code to prevent legislative power from becoming concentrated in the covenant*).

- The covenant may house up to three Redcaps, who have one vote between them.

- The covenant may have only one Tremere among its ranks (*Ḥafṣa introduced this rule during the independence of al-Andalus, although at that time the Tremere were barred from entry altogether, lest the hierarchy of* *the House override the covenant's independence. However, when the Tribunal was annexed to Iberia, the judges of Duresca amended it. To date, no Tremere has ever lived in the covenant*).

- The Quaesitores make up the advisory council or *maŷlis al-rāʿy* and vote as a bloc in the covenant's councils, so they have only one vote.

- The remaining members each have one vote with which to cast their judgment, with the following exceptions: to keep the covenant from being swayed by Tribunal politics, the Praecones of Dār Malīḥaʾ (should there be any) may not vote on council decisions, while the Trianomae, by contrast, hold a casting vote.

Apart from the advisory council or *maŷlis al-rāʿy*, the magi hold no other title within the covenant. Anyone who wants something from Dār Malīḥaʾ must speak before all its members at the ordinary meetings held at each solstice and equinox, attendance at which is not compulsory.

At Tribunals, the magi of Dār Malīḥaʾ are usually the first to volunteer to work for the common good (provided no other interests are at stake), and they offer their legal services free of charge when they consider a case legitimate and just. For these reasons they often work shoulder to shoulder with the members of Durato. The judges of Dār Malīḥaʾ are thus famous for their steadfast loyalty to the magical community and for their progressive interpretation of the Code. In this way, the covenant generally remains true to the ideal that sustains it.

Traditionally, all the covenant's magi have been pacifists, and neither ambition nor competitiveness has ever been encouraged within its walls. When one of its members displays either of these two faults, the council meets and gives him a warning. After this first warning, the magus has the chance to mend his ways. If his conduct does not change, the council meets again and votes either for his expulsion or for a second chance. As a rule nobody is given a second chance, but if it happens, the magus has a year to reform. If at the end of that time there is no sign of improvement, he is expelled at once and all his possessions and inventions are confiscated. This point of the covenant's code usually keeps anyone with personal ambitions from joining Dār Malīḥaʾ. Perhaps that is why the covenant has never had an archmage among its ranks.

> #### The Spells of Dār Malīḥaʾ
>
> The judges of Dār Malīḥaʾ invented variations of some spells popular among the Guernicus, and by 1220 they are known to almost all the Quaesitores of the Tribunal.
>
> ##### Finding the Egg of the ʿAnūq
>
> InAn 20<br>
> R: Arc, D: Conc, T: Ind<br>
> As *Tracing the Trail of Death's Stench* (InCo20), but with dead animals.
>
> The name refers to the ʿanūq, a bird the size of a raven that feeds on carrion and lays no eggs; hence the saying "harder to come by than the eggs of the ʿanūq."
>
> (Base 3, +4 Arcane Connection, +1 Concentration)
>
> ##### Nimrod's Fire
>
> ReMe 30<br>
> R: Eye, D: Moon, T: Ind<br>
> This spell is used to torture people. For its duration, the target convinces himself that he is being burned alive. The sensation is so vivid that, after suffering it day and night for a lunar month, the target must make an Aging roll at +3 the following winter (even if he is under thirty-five). Two castings in a year modify the roll by +6, and if it is used more than twice in the same year, the subject modifies the roll by +9.
>
> The spell's name refers to the Jewish tale in which Nimrod cast Abraham into the furnace for seeking to put an end to idolatry, and God commanded the fire to grow cool so as not to harm the prophet.
>
> (Base 10, +1 Eye, +3 Moon)
>
> ##### The Sincerity of the Qaṭā
>
> ReMe 35<br>
> R: Eye, D: Sun, T: Ind<br>
> This spell is a variation of *The Penitent's Confession* (ReMe 30; see *Houses of Hermes: True Lineages*, page 79), but with Sun duration.
>
> The name refers to the qaṭā, a bird the Arabs consider truthful because its call sounds like its name.
>
> (Base 20, +1 Eye, +2 Sun)

<!-- p. 249 -->

Dār Malīḥaʾ has an extensive network of mundane contacts spread throughout Iberia and North Africa. To coordinate them it uses the services of Chamua, a Redcap who rides a beautiful Sevillian mare with a pearl-colored coat.

#### The Magi of Dār Malīḥaʾ

The magi of Dār Malīḥaʾ are divided between those who are Quaesitores and sit on the advisory council or *maŷlis al-rāʿy* (all of whom hold a seat in the Iberian Chamber), and the rest.

##### Jayāl al-Gernikiyya (maŷlis al-rāʿy)

*I would like to know who it was and how it came by night. Was it the face of the Sun, or was it the Moon? Was it an idea that reason brought to light in its reflections? Was it a spiritual image that thought raised up before me? Was it a phantom forged from the soul's hopes, which the eye had the illusion of reaching? Perhaps it was none of these, but a misfortune that fate brought me as the cause of my death.*[^p249-46]

[^p249-46]: Excerpt from *The Ring of the Dove* by Ibn Ḥazm (Spanish translation by Emilio García Gómez).

Jayāl (or tayf) is the name the Arabs give to the phantoms that appear in dreams. Jayāl took this *laqab* on passing her Gauntlet, for she is a Mentem specialist with a weakness for the study of dreams and oneiromancy.[^p249-47] She is said to be a descendant of the Banū ʾUmayya, who ruled the city of Cordoba until the eleventh century.

[^p249-47]: Oneiromancers have always been present at the courts of al-Andalus. When, in the tenth century, the Zirid Bādīs ibn Ḥabūs dreamed that all the poplars of Granada fell to the ground, he summoned one of them to tell him whether this meant he would lose the battle.

Jayāl is a mature maga with great analytical powers. Although she has been elected presiding Quaesitor on more than one occasion, she has never accepted the post. Her word carries considerable weight with all the judges of the Tribunal, who listen closely to learn how she interprets the Code in each case, and despite her open opposition to Duresca, Jayāl is always willing to work with them.

In 1220, Jayāl is possibly the most influential maga of the Tribunal in legislative matters, something that Nazhūn, the Trianomae of Durato, often turns to her own advantage.

##### Dāmis al-Gernikiyya (maŷlis al-rāʿy)

The maga Dāmis (from the Arabic for "pitch-dark night") is the *parens* of Jayrān of Duresca (who was expelled for his ambition) and of the outstanding Jayāl. Dāmis was once a woman of great strength and influence, but she is now an extremely aged maga consumed by Twilight: she does not speak, she does not rise from her bed, and her bedridden image flickers, showing how she looked in times past. Her only contact with the world is through her *filia* Jayāl, who often visits her to search her mind for possible solutions to complex Hermetic cases. Dāmis, however, seems unaware of this and does not even react when it happens. Although what remains of Dāmis is not even a dream, all the magae of the covenant still regard her as a full member of Dār Malīḥaʾ.

##### Fāṭīma al-Saraqusṭiyya al-Gernikiyya (maŷlis al-rāʿy)

Better known by her *nisba*, Al-Saraqusṭiyya ("the woman of Saragossa"), she was Jayāl's apprentice and passed her Gauntlet only seven years ago, which makes her the youngest member of the covenant.

Fāṭīma met Lía al-Gernikiyya of Duresca at the Tribunal of 1214 and, contrary to what the covenant thinks of her, did not find her a monster at all. In fact, she felt as though they had known each other for years. During the days the Tribunal lasted they talked of poetry and music, and Lía told her she was a maga of great potential. Since then Al-Saraqusṭiyya has written to Lía some ten times, always in secret. Fāṭīma sees nothing wrong in talking to her — after all, they never touch on any important Hermetic matter — but she would rather nobody in the covenant found out, for she knows the covenant's prejudices against Duresca. The maga longs for the Tribunal of 1221 so that she can see her friend and, though she would not admit it, she dreams that one day Lía will invite her to Duresca.

##### Labwatun al-Biŷorniyya

The Bjornaer Labwatun (from the Arabic for "lioness") was born in a coastal village in Gāna and came to Seville with her family, where her parents lost her in the crowd. Labwatun lived on the streets until a magus found her and took her to Crintera. There she was educated, and her inner beast proved to be a lioness. When she passed her Gauntlet she returned to Iberia and joined the pacifist covenant of Dār Malīḥaʾ, ignoring invitations from the Bjornaer covenants of Caium and Laminium. Although Labwatun cuts a fearsome figure, she has in fact never been involved in a fight. She prefers the tranquility of the halls of Dār Malīḥaʾ to the tumult of Hermetic society. She is seldom seen at Tribunals, for she barely understands men, whom she considers shallow and banal. For Labwatun, happiness is a walk through the woods around Dār Malīḥaʾ, whether in silence or in the company of her covenant siblings.

##### Ḥannûn al-Criamonī

Ḥannûn (from the Hebrew for "merciful") is the *filius* of Offilo, and despite his age he is still very childish (his favorite book is still *The Travels of Fedoso*; see *Houses of Hermes: Mystery Cults*, page 101).

He spent the best years of his life with his inseparable friend, Al-Saraqusṭiyya, and now that she has drifted away from him, he resigns himself to walking his path alone. The void his friend has left is hard to fill, and he still cannot understand how, barely a few years ago, they could have sworn eternal friendship. In his despair, Ḥannûn committed a terrible crime of which he is still ashamed: he spied on his former friend's correspondence and discovered that she was writing to a member of Duresca. He now knows that her distance is due to a change of priorities, which has only tarnished the image he has of her.

<!-- p. 250 -->

> #### Story Seeds: Dār Malīḥaʾ
>
> Although Dār Malīḥaʾ can give rise to many stories, here are two examples that troupes can easily introduce into their games.
>
> ##### The Ulama
>
> The chroniclers say that in the Cordoba of the second half of the tenth century there were some 500 ulama, scholars specializing in disciplines such as Islamic law, the interpretation of the Qurʾan and theology. The life of the ulama is devoted to these disciplines, so they often travel to places such as Ifrīqiya, Egypt and Iraq to study under renowned masters of law and other juridical sciences. The ulama may work as qadis, prayer leaders, preachers, notaries or supervisors of market activities. They are charged with preserving the religious heritage against the threat of the world's corruption, which they face armed only with their dignity. Because of their integrity they usually enjoy the trust of the people, and the caliphs try to win them over to their cause by offering them posts and lavish gifts. For example, the Toledan faqih Abū Ibrāhīm Isḥāq al-Tuŷībī served as jurisconsult to Al-Ḥakam II, yet he would not greet the caliph when he came to his house and never tired of reminding him that the wealth of Cordoba was not his, but belonged to the Muslims. His attitude won him the people, and the caliph ended up fearing him.
>
