> The school of Dār Malīḥaʾ educated the son of a celebrated qadi of Seville, who in 1220 works as a preacher in the Great Mosque of the capital. When Nazhūn of Durato learns of this, she goes to Dār Malīḥaʾ to ask that this companion be used for the benefit of the Order: with such lineage and position, he could help stifle Almohad rule in al-Andalus. Dār Malīḥaʾ will refuse, however, and Nazhūn will begin to work her way into the scholar's circle and to seek allies among the magi of the Tribunal. So, when a letter from Durato reaches the player characters' covenant offering them a vis source if they can get the scholar to preach against the Almohads, they will have to weigh whether it is worth meddling in such affairs.
>
> ##### The Caged Lioness
>
> On one of their journeys, the characters meet a merchant carrying a caged lioness. The animal seems the very epitome of its kind, and the magi suspect it may be a magical creature. If they ask the merchant, he tells them that he found her in the forests of Malaga and that she has been bought by the king of Leon, Alfonso IX, to keep company with the old male he has at court. Attempts to detect magic reveal PeAn and ReAn enchantments on the ring around the animal's neck, but nothing more. A closer mundane examination (Perception + Awareness 9+), however, reveals that the metal is covered in runes betraying its magical manufacture (a Verditius can recognize them as the work of his House). The lioness, who is none other than Labwatun, roars loudly at the characters and is unaffected by the Gift. How was she captured? Where did the magic ring come from, and how did the king of Leon come by the lioness? Do the magi of Dār Malīḥaʾ know anything? The characters will have the chance to win the trust of one of the most powerful covenants of the Tribunal while investigating a possible mundane violation… by Ajabeba? Perhaps the Verditius will want to buy their silence!

<!-- p. 251 -->

##### Offilo al-Criamonī

The Mozarab Offilo was readmitted to the covenant after the verdict of the Grand Tribunal of 1162 condemned the perfect ones of the covenant of ʾAlif. Fearing a tragic fate, and quite unwilling to leave the Tribunal, Offilo abandoned the search for the perfect society and asked to return to Dār Malīḥaʾ. Although he was once more sociable, since Ḥannûn's apprenticeship ended he seldom spends much time with his covenant-mates (with the exception of Labwatun), and on the rare occasions he is seen, his silence speaks louder than his words. Apart from these brief encounters, Offilo spends his seasons immersed in his meditations, which is why the *maŷlis al-rāʿy* believes he is still one of the perfect ones.

##### Al-Tawwād al-Praliḥī

*Though valiant, I am the plaything of fate; my cup overflows with misfortunes. I fell like a steed from on high, and asses of men laughed. Their braying has not ceased to this day.*[^p251-48]

[^p251-48]: Verses from *The Treatise of Familiar Spirits and Demons* by Ibn Shuhayd (Spanish translation by Salvador Barberá).

Al-Tawwād (from the Arabic for "he who accepts repentance") is descended from the important Cordoban family of the Banū Fuṭays and was a powerful *saḥir* who left the Peninsula after passing his Gauntlet. It is said that Al-Tawwād attained the title of archmage in the middle of the twelfth century and was in contact with the great powers of the Order in Europe, at least for a time. When he reappeared at the Iberian Tribunal of 1179, the *saḥir* had renounced his title and had every appearance of a man who had given up. It was at that very Tribunal that he met the members of Dār Malīḥaʾ, who invited him to join the covenant.

Although the Tribunal's Redcaps say he renounced his title because of an incident in Novgorod, his past remains a secret, and Al-Tawwād clings to a vow of silence and nonviolence that has caused him more than one problem. At the meeting of 1214, the archmage Sepsis humiliated him in front of everyone, and Al-Tawwād did not even react.

Al-Tawwād always wears an *almaizar* (a veil worn as a turban) of many-colored silk with abundant gold tinsel, and he usually keeps his hands clasped behind his back.

##### Chamua of Mercere (Redcap)

The Galician Chamua asked to join Dār Malīḥaʾ almost sixty years ago. Trained at Porta Pandere, she works almost exclusively for the covenant, since Dār Malīḥaʾ generates a great deal of correspondence throughout Iberia.

Chamua is the bearer of the tiara linked to the covenant's mirror room, so she can relay her messages to the covenant's magi, although as a rule no matter is urgent enough to disturb them.

Chamua knows that Al-Saraqusṭiyya is in contact with Lía of Duresca and, although her oath forbids her to speak of the correspondence she carries, she hopes to attend one of the covenant's councils in the coming seasons and somehow contrive for the maga to have to refer to the matter, so that she is forced to tell the truth or be exposed by the mirror.

##### Marŷān al-Bonisagiyya

Marŷān is a learned maga who has contributed many advances to the covenant. For some years she has been working with Osoro of Pallantia (see page 157), although lately her colleague has neglected his studies to concentrate on teaching. Marŷān thinks this a waste, so she has invited him to found a covenant with her. Indeed, if he accepted, she would leave Dār Malīḥaʾ, much to the sorrow of her brothers and sisters.

### Qasr Dār al-Muchaddad

>**Lifespan:** 878–Present<br>
>**Founder:** Ǧamīla al-Qurṭubiyya al-Ŷerbitoniyya<br>
>**Season:** Winter<br>
>**Aura (type and strength):** Magic, strength 3<br>
>**Reputations:** None<br>
>**Votes:** 2

A little more than a century after the founding of the Order, Ǧamīla created the covenant of Qasr Dār al-Muchaddad (from the Arabic for "palace of the new house"), which was destined to become the Tribunal's first Islamic point of reference and the prime mover in the Arabization of the Order in Iberia.

#### History

The Cordoban Ǧamīla was taken to the Baghdad of the sorcerers when she was barely five years old. Her master trained her in the East, surrounded by every kind of luxury and with access to all the writings of the great Greek thinkers. After passing her Gauntlet, Ǧamīla set out on a long journey through the Middle East and North Africa which, almost three decades later, brought her to the city of Algiers, where she met one of the Redcaps of Aedes Saturni. When the Mercere told her that the Order had signed a truce with the *saḥirs*, she took ship for the Peninsula to continue her travels, unaware that she was heading for her final destination. On her arrival, Ǧamīla fell in love with the al-Andalus of the Umayyads and founded the covenant of Qasr Dār al-Muchaddad north of the medina of Elvira, which at that time had a large Jewish population. In those days she met the Trianomae ʿAbbās ibn Munḏīr, newly arrived from Durenmar, with whom she forged many alliances with the most powerful families of Cordoba and the governors of the *kuwar*. So busy were they that they spent hardly any time at the covenant, which, incidentally, saved them from being attacked when the *saḥir* truce was broken in 907. But the brutality of the attack changed her: Ǧamīla threw herself into Hermetic politics and was elected Praeco, demonstrating her commitment to the Tribunal in seeking peace with the *saḥirs*. She was the champion of the cultural revolution that bore her name in the tenth century and that gave the Tribunal its distinctive identity. Ǧamīla's popularity, however, ended in 941 with the affair of the Duresca manuscripts: at the height of the Tribunal, and under pressure from Magvillus's envoys, the maga chose to silence those who defended the authenticity of the manuscripts, which led ʿAbbās and other companions at Qasr Dār al-Muchaddad to abandon her. Ǧamīla died eight years later, practically alone. The covenant vanished from the Hermetic scene and, during the Schism War, supported the independence of al-Andalus. In time it sank into the Winter in which it remains trapped.

<!-- p. 252 -->

The fate of Qasr Dār al-Muchaddad seemed to be inevitable oblivion until Fāṭīma and Sankhambi (the founders of Ŷezirat Tennyn) discovered the uncontrolled portal at the Pillars of Hercules. Aṣbag Ḏū l-Sayfayn al-Merinitī, one of the magi of Aedes Iris, then undertook to watch over it, but since the African covenant was too far away, he asked the covenants of Dār Malīḥaʾ and Qasr Dār al-Muchaddad for lodging during the ordinary Tribunal of 1123. Although the former turned down his request, the aged Jewish magus Hālôm, the sole resident of Qasr Dār al-Muchaddad, gave him leave to live in his covenant with complete freedom. And so, after the destruction of Aedes Iris, Aṣbag became a nominal member of Qasr Dār al-Muchaddad, which gladdened the aged Hālôm, who feared the covenant would disappear after his death.

In 1220, Aṣbag and Hālôm devote themselves to watching the gate, so as to keep in check any creatures that might threaten Europe. To this end they are trying to have some Tribunal (even outside Iberia) recognize them as a dedicated covenant but, for some reason, everyone believes the Granadan covenant has its own motives for guarding the portal of the Pillars of Hercules.

#### Setting and Physical Description

Qasr Dār al-Muchaddad lies north of Granada, in Alfacar. Its lands are watered by the irrigation channel of the great spring (or Aynadamar), which has been used to irrigate Granada since the time of the Zirids. Aynadamar is a karst spring that rises at the foot of the Sierra de Alfaguara (from the Arabic *al-fawwāra*, "fountain" or "spring"), and it has allowed the area north of Granada to fill with orchards and myrtles, with land given over to fruit trees and vines.

The covenant's buildings make up a rich *almunia* (country estate) in the hands of the Banū Gómez, who are responsible for running the covenant's finances and managing its mundane resources with the Almohads. The *almunia* of Qasr Dār al-Muchaddad has pastures, gardens, woods and even a quarry, which the Gómez family works. To maintain all its lands the family makes use of slaves, oxen and donkeys, as well as the old magic items left by the covenant's former inhabitants to ease the work of the fields and improve the fertility of the farmland.

The *almunia* has three large buildings on its grounds (and many others scattered about that house the covenant's workers). The largest is called *al-maŷlis al-šarqī* (from the Arabic for "eastern hall") and is built on two terraces stepping down to the south. At its northern entrance there is a pool of more than 1,500 square meters and five meters deep, built of ashlar and finished with red-ochre plaster. In Ǧamīla's day this building hosted the Tribunals, which, weather permitting, were held in the open air, around the pool by day and on the southern terraces by night. The second building is called *al-magānī* ("the dwellings"), and it houses the *sancta* (up to six), the covenant's library and a watchtower for the grogs. All its rooms are very luxurious and spacious, although in 1220 only two laboratories are equipped, since the Banū Gómez are unwilling to maintain facilities that are not used. The third and last building is the autocrat's palace, or *qasr al-luʾluʾa* ("palace of the pearl"). This impressive building has nothing to envy in the palaces of Seville, although it is in the Umayyad style rather than the Almohad. In it live the Banū Gómez, who hold the title of autocrat. As such, they run the finances and manage all the covenant's resources, which makes them powerful mundane lords, in the *kūra* of Granada as well.

#### Society and Customs

Qasr Dār al-Muchaddad is inhabited by two mundane families at odds over power in the covenant: the Banū Gómez (descended from Gómez, a magus of the covenant in the late eleventh century) and the Banū Ǧamīla (descended from the son of Ǧamīla and ʿAbbās). The rivalry for the post of autocrat arose in the middle of the twelfth century, when Gómez's son rebelled against the power of Ǧamīla's descendant. The magi of Qasr Dār al-Muchaddad were unaware of the dispute until the autocrat was found hanging from one of the orange trees of the *almunia*. Although at first they managed to keep the quarrels in check, as the covenant sank into Winter the magi turned to their own concerns and stopped dealing with the problem. In 1220 Anrric Gómez rules, occupying the sumptuous palace of the autocrats of Qasr Dār al-Muchaddad.

In Hermetic matters, the covenant is an autocracy governed by the *pontifex*. To keep watch on the portal (which lies in the middle of the water), the covenant raised an artificial islet by magic, on which it built a small lookout post. The magi use faeries to watch it, although they sometimes stand guard themselves, mainly when they have detected too much activity or have some sign that a serious threat is about to appear (which, so far, has not happened).

#### The Magi of Qasr Dār al-Muchaddad

##### Pontifex Aṣbag Ḏū l-Sayfayn al-Merinitī

*Slung across my shoulder I bore a damascened sword, and in my hand a lance from the hive of Jatt. Both pull my fortune out of its stumbles. They have not left me since my youth: one is a stream from which glory springs, the other grows like a branch and bears fruit.*[^p252-49]

[^p252-49]: Poem from *The Treatise of Familiar Spirits and Demons* by Ibn Shuhayd (Spanish translation by Salvador Barberá). Jatt is a port in Bahrain famous for exporting lances.

Aṣbag bears the noble *laqab* Ḏū l-Sayfayn, which means "he of the two swords." Descended from an Arab family of warriors, he came to Aedes Iris to help the Redcaps explore the African territories. When the portal of the Pillars of Hercules was discovered, however, Aṣbag volunteered to guard it. With the destruction of Aedes Iris he took up residence at Qasr Dār al-Muchaddad, where he was granted the title of *pontifex*.

<!-- p. 253 -->

Aṣbag uses his influence with the faeries to enlist their help in watching the portal, and although he has not yet persuaded any Tribunal to grant them the status of dedicated covenant, he expects that things will change when some catastrophe occurs (one he trusts he will survive).

##### Hālôm al-Praliḥī

The Jew Hālôm (from the Hebrew for "dream") is an Ex Miscellanea who has spent his whole life shut away in Qasr Dār al-Muchaddad. As an apprentice he grew up surrounded by aged magi and, as a magus, watched them vanish one by one, whether through death, Twilight, or of their own accord by leaving for other covenants. Over the years he realized that the Banū Gómez did not want him and began to fear for his life, since he was the only thing preventing them from fully joining the mundane politics of Granada. Yet nothing ever happened to him: the men went on fighting for power without paying him any attention.

With Aṣbag's arrival, Hālôm shed the responsibility of leading the covenant and negotiating with the autocrat, Anrric Gómez. Since then he has lived for the portal of the Pillars of Hercules alone and, selfishly, dreams that some terrible creature will appear and sweep the world away, for he is terrified by the idea of dying and history going on being written without him.

##### Dánae of Tremere

The very young Dánae of Tremere is the *filia* of Medea of Tremere of Victrix. Aṣbag admitted her in 1219, so she is a newcomer. Even so, her attitude and willingness have quickly won Aṣbag's favor, and her presence at Qasr Dār al-Muchaddad has become essential.

> #### Story Seeds: the ʿanzʾ ayyal
>
> Aṣbag comes to the Tribunal of 1221 to announce that an animal half goat, half deer has been sighted, which by all accounts matches the description of the ʿanzʾ ayyal. To many, this animal is nothing more than an ancient legend, said to possess the powers of the phoenix. It apparently swam across the strait and headed north, where it was last sighted near Occelum Durii. Aṣbag seizes the occasion to ask once more for resources to have Qasr Dār al-Muchaddad named a dedicated covenant, and calls for volunteers to hunt the creature down. Will the player characters support the nomination? Will they volunteer to go after this quarry?

### Bayt al-Ḥikma

>**Lifespan:** 913–963<br>
>**Founders:** Muḥammad al-Criamonī, Wāṣil al-Criamonī<br>
>**Aura (type and strength):** Magic, strength 7<br>
>**Reputations:** Kharijite (Iberian Tribunal) 3, Gorgiastic (Iberian Criamon) 2

The Criamon who founded this covenant left Barzaj when they were young and traveled to Baghdad, where they learned from the great masters at the House of Wisdom (in Arabic, Bayt al-Ḥikma), and from there they returned to Iberia to continue their studies, this time with the masters Aḥmed and Omar al-Harranī and the great Ibn Masarra (see page 79). This covenant was the seed of the Kharijite movement.

#### History

The *amici* Muḥammad and Wāṣil were raised at Barzaj and, after passing their Gauntlets, continued on their path without the supervision of their *parentes*. In 857 they traveled to Baghdad to go on learning from the great sages of the Islamic world, and in their late-night conversations they decided to call their future covenant Bayt al-Ḥikma, inspired as they were by the tales of the East.

When the *amici* returned to Iberia, they did not even bother to announce their arrival or to raise their covenant; they lived in Cordoba while they studied at the Great Mosque. It was not until the Tribunal of 913 that the presiding Quaesitor, Ṭāmis al-Gernikī, obliged them to build their covenant within seven years on pain of expulsion. By then the *amici* had already left Cordoba, and they chose as their home the lands bordering the desert, some thirty kilometers north of the coastal city of al-Mariyyāt Baŷŷāna (Almería), where, unbeknownst to them, a powerful *genius loci* dwelt (see *Realms of Power: Magic*, pages 117 and 118).

The covenant went unnoticed until the ordinary Tribunal of 948. After the scandal of the Duresca manuscripts, Muḥammad and Wāṣil called the magi of the Tribunal to disobedience and, in response to Magvillus's repression, Bayt al-Ḥikma declared that it would open its doors to every member of the Order who wished to study from its fabulous library, offering to teach any magus without asking anything in return. The Redcaps spread the news and, in barely seven years, Bayt al-Ḥikma became a center of learning for many magi of the Tribunal and the rest of Europe. The adherents of this social movement came to be called Kharijites.

When mundanes reached its gates, the Quaesitores grew alarmed. But that was not what brought about its downfall; rather, it was a disagreement with the philosophy of the Founder Criamon: one of the magi of Barzaj denounced them to the Praeco, who used the news to denounce them to the caliph and so draw closer to him. Almost all the members of Bayt al-Ḥikma were crucified at the end of the summer of 963 on the roof terrace of the Azuda Gate, or bāb al-Sudda, facing the Guadalquivir; their bodies were used as targets by the archers of the alcázar. The few survivors (mostly mundanes) stayed in Almería and joined the Masarrī schools they had founded there, or went off to the nearby *rābiṭas*.[^p254-50] Of the two magi who escaped, one founded the covenant of Chazāʾir and the other left the Order. The impressive library of Bayt al-Ḥikma was plundered by the covenants of the Tribunal in the summer of 963 and, a month later, the mundane forces finished razing what was left of the covenant.

[^p254-50]: *Rābiṭas* are a kind of hermitage where Muslims withdraw to lead an ascetic life (not to be confused with the *ribāṭ*). Some five kilometers from Almería stood the *rābiṭa* of ʿAmrūs, and near Granada were the *rābiṭas* of al-ʿUqāb, al-Maḥrūq and al-Liŷām. Farther afield, in Seville, stood the *rābiṭa* of Bāb ʿAmbar.

<!-- p. 254 -->

#### Setting and Physical Description

*Halt, both of you, and ask the ruins where their former dwellers are. Have the day and the night, passing over them, consumed them? All is erased, abandoned, bare. One would say the dwellings have vanished and become mere ideas.*[^p254-51]

[^p254-51]: Excerpt from *The Ring of the Dove* by Ibn Ḥazm (Spanish translation by Emilio García Gómez).

The ruins of Bayt al-Ḥikma lie on the northern edges of the desert of al-Mariyyāt Baŷŷāna. From them one can tell that it was once a large covenant; it was said that its library occupied the westernmost wing and its enormous *scriptorium* the southern wing. The library catalog was stolen, and the registers in which the members of Bayt al-Ḥikma noted who copied what and when were seized by Duresca.

> #### Story Seeds: qaḥṭ ("drought")
>
> The records of Duresca state that Bayt al-Ḥikma was raised around the year 913 on the edges of the desert. Yet in 1220 the ruins sit amid a landscape of hard sand and low scrub; the desert has advanced at least four kilometers since then. It seems that the *genius loci* is making its way across those lands, relentlessly drying up everything it touches.
>
> The storyguide may introduce the spirit of the place into the saga however she pleases. Perhaps the characters wish to settle nearby, or try to win the favor of some mundane lord whose lands are threatened by the advancing desert, or are simply looking for vis sources. In any case, the statistics on page 118 of the supplement *Realms of Power: Magic* can be used, or the storyguide can create her own. Of course, the desert can be the setting for many other stories.

## Jaén

*Jaén is the castle of the lands of al-Andalus, for it is the city most abundant in grain, the most valiant in heroes, the most impregnable.*[^p254-52]

[^p254-52]: Excerpt from *In Praise of Spanish Islam* by Al-Šaqundī (Spanish translation by Emilio García Gómez).

The Andalusis call it Jaén of the silk, land of the silkworm, because of the great number of people who raise silkworms. During the caliphate, the district of Iqlīm de Naška, in the Sierra de Segura, became the chief supplier of timber for building in Cordoba. The timber was floated down the Guadalimar river to Cordoba. From there, some lots were sent along with tar and pitch to Seville, whence they traveled to Algeciras to build the fleet of the Umayyad state. Besides its silk and timber, the saffron of Baeza (under Castilian rule until 1224) is a commodity the *kūra* exports by sea and land to many places, and the vineyards of Úbeda (also under Christian rule in 1220) produce so many grapes that they can neither eat nor sell them all.

The northern frontier of the *kūra* of Jaén fell back to the south (practically to the course of the Guadalquivir) after the defeat of the Almohad forces at the battle of Las Navas de Tolosa, and it is now the smallest of all the provinces the Almohads rule on the Peninsula. It was once home to the Castilian covenants of Laminium and Harra, but with the advance of the Christian kings of the north, by 1220 none remains. The *kūra* of Jaén includes cities such as Linares and Jaén itself. It borders the kingdom of Castile to the north, the *kūra* of Cordoba to the west, Granada to the south, and Valencia and Murcia to the east.

If your troupe is thinking of starting a saga in this area, the Sierra de Cazorla would be suitable, for besides lying on the northern edge of the *kūra* (which can give rise to stories tied to the advance of the mundane forces), it offers a perfect setting for those who wish to live far from society and surrounded by nature (the source of the Guadalquivir would be ideal for this purpose).

## Valencia

*Valencia is called the nosegay of al-Andalus for its many gardens. […] In this region lies the famous Albufera, full of light and brilliance, and it is said that, because of the reflection of the sun on this Albufera, light is so abundant in Valencia that the city is known for it.*[^p254-53]

[^p254-53]: *Ibidem*.

The *kūra* of Valencia borders the Crown of Aragon and the Catalan counties to the north, Jaén and the kingdom of Castile to the west, the *kūra* of Murcia to the south, and the Mediterranean Sea to the east. Almost all of it is mountainous, the mountains giving way only to the narrow coastal strip in the east. This province contains cities such as Vinaroz, Peñíscola, Chelva, Valencia, Denia, Sagunto and Ayora.

<!-- p. 255 -->

Despite its exceptional land, the vis sources of this *kūra* have been in the hands of the Verditius of Ajabeba since the beginning of the tenth century, which, together with their well-known acts of piracy and the strong *saḥir* presence in the Order's early days, has kept most of the Peninsula's magi away. In 1220 it is home to no living covenant, perhaps awaiting resettlement with the coming conquests of Jaume I the Conqueror.

### Fafḥṣ al-Luŷŷ

>**Lifespan:** 871–1151<br>
>**Founder:** Ziyād al-Ŷerbitonī<br>
>**Aura (type and strength):** Magic, strength 2<br>
>**Reputations:** Cursed (Iberian Tribunal) 2, Traitor (Andalusi magi) 1, Mundane Ties (Iberian Tribunal) 1

The covenant of Fafḥṣ al-Luŷŷ (from the Arabic for "field of the wood") was founded by a Jerbiton from Valencia educated in Thebes, and despite its long life it suffered many mishaps and never fulfilled its potential. Indeed, its last attempts to prosper brought about its final downfall. Thus Fafḥṣ al-Luŷŷ was expelled from the Order at the Tribunal of 1151.

#### History

Ziyād al-Ŷerbitonī was a member of the Theban League, and when Jerbiton returned home he went with him and stayed there until, toward the end of the third quarter of the ninth century, he decided to return to his family, taking advantage of the peace with the *saḥirs*. On the Peninsula he clashed many times with the Tremere of Tremébriga, until he finally died in a Wizard's War against Acutus of Tremere. After his death his *filia* Selene carried on his work for a few more years, but she shared his fate when in 907 the *saḥirs* razed Fafḥṣ al-Luŷŷ and massacred all its inhabitants. The covenant then stood empty until it was resettled by Jerbiton magi from beyond the Pyrenees.

During the Schism War, Fafḥṣ al-Luŷŷ voted against the secession of al-Andalus and, as if under a curse, all its members perished fighting the Diedne. Its chambers stood empty once more until Yulyān ibn Muhŷa al-Bonisagī claimed them under the jurisdiction of the Tribunal of al-Andalus.

The Bonisagus enjoyed the peace of the Tribunal until 1067 when, in exchange for numerous benefits and the office of Praeco, he handed the powers of Iberia first-hand information on everything that was happening in al-Andalus. Although his betrayal led to the peaceful reunification of the Tribunal in 1103, the magus earned the hatred of all his Andalusi *sodales*. Such was the pressure brought to bear on him that he ended up taking his own life. With his death the covenant plunged into Winter and, with little left to lose, his *filius* Maksan decided to ally himself with Zafadola (see page 47) in an attempt to take control of all the Almoravid domains of al-Andalus. But Fafḥṣ al-Luŷŷ had no luck on that occasion either: Maksan was denounced to Duresca by the Merinitae who lived with him, who abandoned him to his fate and went off to Navarre, where they founded the covenant of al-Quṣṣāṣ.

After Zafadola's death in 1146, the Tribunal expelled Maksan in 1151, and his covenant was plundered in accordance with Hermetic law and destroyed so that no other magus could ever live there again, for the Tribunal believed it was cursed.

#### Setting and Physical Description

The former site of Fafḥṣ al-Luŷŷ lies two days' journey east of the city of Albacete, on some hill surrounded by farmland. The covenant was destroyed in 1151, burned to its foundations by its attackers. Although the Redcaps know where it stood, they prefer not to reopen old wounds and, unless strictly necessary, never reveal its location in public. Over time the covenant ceased to arouse any interest, and by 1220 almost nobody remembers it.

> #### Story Seeds: the Horses of Fafḥṣ al-Luŷŷ
>
> In the middle of the tenth century, the members of Fafḥṣ al-Luŷŷ took a liking to the horse races and jousts held in summer on the esplanade before the Azuda Gate of the alcázar of Cordoba. To achieve better times and hardier horses, the Jerbiton bought the finest stallions from the Cordoban stables and crossed them with mares of virtue from the marshes of the Guadalquivir. The magi obtained an exceptional breed of magic horses able to tolerate the Gift and the wounds suffered in combat. It is said that when the Tremere saw them they wished to emulate them, which is why the *vexillation* of the Burning Acorn strove to obtain similar mounts (see *Houses of Hermes: True Lineages*, page 129), though with poorer results. Certainly, if the texts these Jerbiton wrote on breeding those animals were found in 1220, they would be greatly coveted by the Tremere as well as by the Merinita and the Mercere. Could they somehow come into the hands of the player characters?

## Murcia

*Murcia is the capital of the East of al-Andalus. […] Its river is an arm of the river of Seville […], and beside it there are as many gardens of swaying branches, as many waterwheels singing musical notes, as many warbling birds and rows of flowers, as you will have heard. It is one of the lands richest in fruits and perfumes.*[^p255-54]

[^p255-54]: Excerpt from *In Praise of Spanish Islam* by Al-Šaqundī (Spanish translation by Emilio García Gómez).

<!-- p. 256 -->

The *kūra* of Murcia is crossed by a range of gentle mountains whose highest peak reaches little more than 1,000 meters. To the north, in the valley of the Segura river, stretch extensive irrigated lands dotted with waterwheels and irrigation channels. To the south the terrain softens down to the coast, where there are broad beaches and an enormous coastal lagoon of salt water, separated from the Mediterranean by a tongue of sand more than twenty kilometers long.

Once home to the Mercurian wizards and a stronghold of the *saḥirs* of the eastern Peninsula, the south of Murcia saw many pitched battles in the ninth century between the Flambeau and the *saḥirs*, whose places of power were scattered among the region's beaches, capes and hills. This area has always been rich in vis, although nowadays almost all its sources are exploited by Ajabeba.

Murcia borders the Crown of Aragon and the Catalan counties to the north and the *kūra* of Jaén and Granada to the west, and is washed by the Mediterranean Sea to the south and east. Within its borders lie cities such as Cartagena, Orihuela, Alicante, Elche and Murcia, among others.

In 1220, Murcia is home to the oldest covenant in al-Andalus, possibly the first in the Tribunal (older even than Salionca, although it was not legally constituted until several decades later). This is the cryptic Barzaj, inhabited entirely by magi of House Criamon.

### Barzaj

*Journeys […] are of only three kinds […]: the journey from Him, toward Him, and in Him. This last is the journey of bewilderment (altīh) and perplexity (ḥayra). As for the voyage that comes from Him, its benefit lies in being, while by the journey in Him one gains nothing less than Him Himself. The two journeys ("from" and "toward") have an end that is reached and where one stops, whereas the journey of bewilderment has no limit.*[^p256-55]

[^p256-55]: Excerpt from *The Splendor of the Fruits of the Journey* by Ibn ʿArabī (Spanish translation by Carlos Varona Narvión).

>**Lifespan:** 836–Present<br>
>**Founders:** Lubnà al-Criamoniyya, Jalaf al-Criamonī<br>
>**Season:** Autumn<br>
>**Aura (type and strength):** Magic, strength 3 to 9 (the *sancta* have an aura of strength 5)<br>
>**Reputations:** Inaccessible (Iberian Tribunal) 3<br>
>**Votes:** 5

*Barzaj* is an Arabic word that refers to the intermediate world. It means "isthmus," something that both separates and joins two substances. For the Ṣūfīs it has a double meaning: it is the period beyond time and space through which the souls of mortals wander from death to resurrection, and it is the intermediate world between the invisible (accessible through the active or creative imagination) and the visible. The *barzaj* is inhabited by the creative imagination, caught between those two shores represented by the spiritual and material worlds. Indeed, the Criamon who live there truly believe that the *regio* they guard is the *barzaj* itself.

Barzaj is the heart of the Iberian brood, and all its members belong to a single mystical brotherhood (*ṭarīqa*) and follow the Path of Walking Backwards, which was introduced into the House after the long time that Abdkypris (a former member of Barzaj and Primus of the House) spent among the Ṣūfīs.

Throughout their history, the Criamon of Barzaj have not reacted well to change: when the Kharijites came they did not support them (although they later absorbed some of their Ṣūfī doctrines), and when the Rationalists came they despised them too (and to this day they maintain that they are nothing but Gorgiastics).

#### History

*Know that whoever continues along the path of distrust is led from the sensible to the spiritual, from bliss to torment, from the veil* (sitr) *to theophany* (taŷallī)*, and from death to the life of beings […] After this journey, the easts of the lights become known, as does the rising of the new moons of all secrets. […] Those who distrust will in the end be saved […], enjoying prodigious gifts, such as walking on water or vanishing before their enemies […].*[^p256-56]

[^p256-56]: *Ibidem*.

When Criamon died, a few years after the Order's First Tribunal, two of his apprentices left the Cave of Twisting Shadows for the distant lands of Iberia to found a brood where they could continue seeking answers to the Enigma. The two magi were Lubnà of Damascus and Jalaf of Cordoba. Although their journey was arduous, they managed to cross the Pyrenees and reach southern Iberia, where they looked for a place like the one they had left in the Greater Alpine Tribunal. After a few more months of travel, in 772 they at last found a cave that served them as a refuge. If this were true, it would make it the first covenant on the Peninsula; the Criamon, however, do not consider this relevant, and there is no written record of its history that could prove it.

It was the apprentices of Lubnà and Jalaf who went to the Rhine Tribunal of 836 to declare the existence of their covenant, which they called Indal Eccius. After training a second generation of apprentices (who would become the Kharijites of Bayt al-Ḥikma), the founders returned to the Cave of Twisting Shadows and left their first apprentices in charge of the cave they called a covenant. The cycle repeated itself for a generation or so more, and Indal Eccius went on existing outside the political life of the Tribunal until the Kharijites Muḥammad and Wāṣil of Criamon turned against the Order after the scandal of the Duresca manuscripts. Then Taʿlab, a young magus of Indal Eccius, denounced them to the Praeco of Iberia, thus bringing about the end of the Kharijite movement. His betrayal, however, also caused a terrible adulteration to be created at the moment of his Final Twilight.

<!-- p. 257 -->

When the Schism War broke out, the magi of Indal Eccius voted in favor of the secession of al-Andalus, for violence repelled them. By then most of the covenant's Criamon had embraced Ṣūfism, and they decided to rename their covenant Barzaj. In this time of prosperity, one of its members, Sibila al-Criamoniyya, returned from the *ʿālam al-mithāl* (see below) with a clue she believed was the key to solving the Enigma. The maga spent a year setting down her thoughts in a gallery on the third level of the *regio* and, in the autumn of 1073 (when Pope Gregory VII had launched his great reform movement), she summoned her *sodales* to tell them of her discovery. However, her finding was never passed on. Sibila died at the hands of Taʿlab's adulteration and vanished without a trace; she was its first victim. All that remained of her research was the enormous chamber the maga had used for her meditations, which came to be called Sibila's gallery and which became a place of perfect transmission (see below). Despite the years, Sibila's discovery remains hidden, and the Criamon have come to think that perhaps the answer does not lie in the meaning of the thousands of words that cover the gallery.

During the eleventh century, Barzaj accepted as a member the illustrious Criamon and future Primus Abdkypris, who spent several years with the Ṣūfīs of Almería before traveling to North Africa and the Levant to converse with the greatest thinkers of the Islamic world. Abdkypris introduced the Path of Walking Backwards into the House and, when he left Barzaj, the covenant became the brood of the Path.

> #### The Ṣūfī School of Almería
>
> The Ṣūfī school of Almería flourished during the eleventh century, and its most distinguished master was Abū-l-ʿAbbās ibn al-ʿArif. With the arrival of the Almoravids in 1086, one of his disciples, Al-Qasī, had to flee with his own disciples to al-Gharb (in the south of Portugal), where he held out for twenty years until his death in 1151. Many Ṣūfīs then emigrated to the East, and others stayed on to live as solitaries in the Moroccan mountains. The Criamon of Barzaj, for their part, were able to go on living in their covenant thanks to its isolation, so none of them had to leave the Tribunal.

Barzaj did not return to the Hermetic life of the Tribunal until the maga Fawd ḅint Abī Yaʿqūb al-Criamoniyya was elected Praeco in 1109. Barzaj thus hosted the magi of the Tribunal in 1116; however, since the cave was too gloomy and uncomfortable (because of the damp and the echo), the assembly decided to hold the following Tribunals at Duresca, and Fawd offered no resistance. What is more, as she had little interest in moderating Tribunals, the Praeco delegated part of her responsibilities in the Iberian Chamber to the members of Duresca.

The second Tribunal with Fawd as Praeco (that is, in 1123) was marked by the conflict between Barzaj and the perfect ʾAlif. Ḥayy ibn Yaqẓān al-Bonisagī attacked the principles of the Ṣūfīs and insulted their philosophy before the assembly, which led the members of Barzaj to take a stand against him and criticize his rationalist ideas in turn, for as mystics they did not believe salvation could be reached through the pure intellectual act. The conflict between the two covenants lasted until 1162, when the Grand Tribunal condemned the doctrines of the magi of ʾAlif. Fawd, however, did not live to see it. The maga vanished at some point in 1147, consumed by Taʿlab's adulteration.

<!-- p. 258 -->

After Fawd's disappearance, Barzaj once again withdrew from the political scene and kept its attention fixed on the search for the Enigma. The exodus from the Tribunal did not go unnoticed by the covenant, however. After the account given by Meʾir ibn Yosef al-Ŷerbitonī at the Tribunal of 1151, two members of Barzaj left for North Africa to live as hermits.

In 1220, Barzaj is a peaceful covenant that keeps clear of the Tribunal's intrigues and still does not understand the origin of the adulteration of Taʿlab (see insert on page 261).

#### Setting and Physical Description

*The origin of existence is movement. There can be no stillness in it, for it would then return to its origin, which is nonexistence (*ʿdam*). Never does the journey cease, neither in the higher world nor in the lower, and even the divine Realities (*ḥaqāʾiq al-ilāhiyya*) never end their course, coming and going.*[^p258-57]

[^p258-57]: Excerpt from *The Splendor of the Fruits of the Journey* by Ibn ʿArabī (Spanish translation by Carlos Varona Narvión).

Barzaj is a hypogenic cave bored into the mountains in the northwest of the *kūra* of Murcia, whose slopes are dotted with esparto grass, junipers, mastic shrubs and hawthorns. Unlike other caves in the area, Barzaj was uninhabited until the arrival of Lubnà and Jalaf. The cave of Barzaj is a labyrinth of more than four kilometers of galleries, great chambers filled with spectacular speleothems, and numerous vertical shafts that plunge as deep as a hundred meters. As such, the cavern itself serves as a labyrinth for the purposes of meditation. All its galleries lie within a *regio* with four known levels (of strengths ranging from 3 to 9), between which one must travel both vertically and horizontally, coming and going. The cave is a metaphor for the inner journey the magi of Barzaj undertake in search of the Enigma, an endless journey, since it takes place within oneself.

The mundane level of the *regio* has an almost constant temperature of about twenty degrees centigrade and a humidity close to saturation point (any book kept in these conditions is ruined in a matter of minutes).

The first level of the *regio* is reached by a vertical climb (the magi of Barzaj usually employ *Rise of the Feathery Body* [ReCo 10]) from the first great cavern, some 200 meters from the entrance on the mundane level. Once on this level (where there is an aura of strength 3), the walls take on a faint bluish luminescence and the condensed droplets give off greenish sparks as they fall through the air. At this point there are barely any visions to disturb daily life, and the few there are fade quickly. Here live Barzaj's few grogs, and here the magi keep their stores of vis and their meager library (fewer than a dozen books, kept in several cabinets enchanted to repel the damp). It is meager because in Sufism teaching passes orally from master to apprentice, since that is the only way to express the inner energy, which, being sustained by the breath of life, reaches further than the written letter.

The second level of the *regio* (strength 5) is reached by continuing through the cavern to the next great chamber, at whose center stands a rock column several meters across, supporting a ceiling crowded with mineral formations that glow with the green of the water that caresses them. This column is the gateway to the next level. Once past the boundary of the *regio*, the darkness of the cave grows deeper, the light in the grotto more intense and the humidity more stifling, to the point that some stretches seem drowned in a green-tinged mist, home to tiny lentil-sized arachnids with bluish legs called *opiliones*. Here lie the magi's *sancta*, and the visions of the *regio* are somewhat sharper, though they still pose no real threat and cause no distraction.

To reach the third level of the *regio* (strength 7), visitors must go back to the mouth of the cavern and pass through the portal into the dim light of the "outside." Once on this level, the magi of Barzaj have found no way to return to the second level except by ReVi magic. Here the floor is waterlogged and the humidity makes breathing extremely difficult (any normal physical activity requires a Stamina roll of 6+ to avoid losing a Fatigue level). The walls seem farther away and more uniform, and the speleothems vast and terrible; images abound, though they lack solidity, and they begin to trace the patterns of motion of the luminaries of the eighth sphere. Walking through this level of the *regio* creates a feeling of emptiness that soon brings on an attack of anxiety (in game terms, each Diameter the character must pass an Intelligence + Enigmatic Wisdom roll of 6+ to keep walking). On this level there is a laboratory of General Quality +3, with a Major Feature (see *Covenants*, page 153) that grants +3 to Mentem Lab Totals. This laboratory may be used by any member of the covenant with a score of at least 1 in Enigmatic Wisdom (otherwise it counts as a standard laboratory). It was here that Sibila made her notes, which, after her death, turned the gallery into a place of perfect transmission.

The last known level of the *regio* (strength 9) is reached by descending the great shaft that pierces the grotto, some 400 meters from the "entrance." The magi of Barzaj call it *ʿālam al-mithāl* (or "world of likenesses"), where pure images reign, the raw material of the creative imagination. The shaft, flooded with water, acts as a portal which, once crossed, reveals the mirror image of Barzaj, where the traveler passes from one world to another (*ʿabara iʿtibār*); that is, from the spoken material word to its unveiling. Here the apparent motion of the stars is represented with absolute precision, showing the whole of the luminaries regardless of the season in which the traveler enters. Without a spell to prevent condensation, however, life is impossible: the traveler has 5 + Stamina minutes to live before dying with waterlogged lungs. Those who manage to defeat the damp must still interpret the images that dwell in the cave. The magi of Barzaj who have been to this level describe it as "meeting oneself," for the grotto shows images related to the essence of its visitors and alters them with new ones; at this point the images can be lethal. Symbolism is fundamental on this level of the *regio*, for meanings are hidden from the human senses, and those who cannot interpret them cannot continue the journey. Visitors must make an Intelligence + Enigmatic Wisdom stress roll every hour and compare the result with the following table (note that the modifiers to the rolls apply only within a single journey; that is, the first roll of each journey is never modified):

<!-- p. 259 -->

| Roll | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Botch | The traveler gains a non-botching stress die of Warping Points, loses his Intelligence, and is lost on the road forever. If he suffers a Twilight and returns, he appears on the level immediately below, and if he must roll on the table again, he does so at a –9 penalty. |
| 0 or less | The traveler gains a simple die of Warping Points, his Intelligence drops to 0 or falls by one point (whichever is worse), and he gains the Simple-Minded Flaw. If he suffers a Twilight and returns, he appears on the level immediately below, and if he must roll on the table again, he does so at a –6 penalty. |
| 1–6 | The traveler gains two Warping Points and tries to leave the grotto as soon as he can. If he must roll on the table again, he does so at a –3 penalty. |
| 7–13 | The traveler gains one Warping Point and suffers a –1 to his next roll on this table. |
| 14–21 | The traveler continues on his way and gains a +1 bonus to his next roll on this table. From this point on, the traveler may return and claim the title of *ḏū al-ʿaynayn*. |
| 22–27 | The traveler gains a simple die of experience points in an Art and a +3 bonus to his next roll on this table. |
| 28+ | The traveler reaches the Lote Tree of the Boundary (*sidrat al-muntahā*); what he finds there is up to the storyguide. |

According to the Ṣūfīs of Barzaj, the goal of the journey is to reach the Lote Tree of the Boundary (*sidrat al-muntahā*), which marks the end of the ascent, being the place where being becomes light. Beyond the Lote Tree of the Boundary, mortals encounter the totality, where the human senses are of no use (the Criamon speculate that it may be an entrance to the Divine or Magic Realm). However, no one who has managed to return from this level has been able to confirm the existence of the Lote Tree of the Boundary.

The covenant's grogs keep a record of the time spent by the magi who have entered this level. Generally, one magus in three does not return, and the record belongs to a maga of the early twelfth century who spent an entire season inside. On her return her body was flooded with light, though it was nothing but an empty shell. The magi of Barzaj believe she may have reached the Lote Tree of the Boundary, though they suppose she was not prepared for what she found there.

#### The Council Chamber (Mundane Level)

Here was held the only Iberian Tribunal that Barzaj ever hosted. Since then, the great grotto has stood empty.

#### Sibila's Gallery (Level Three)

*When a house appears before you, you declare that in it lies the end of your journey, whereas in truth another road opens to you there, and to set out upon it, you take provisions there.*[^p259-58]

[^p259-58]: Excerpt from *The Splendor of the Fruits of the Journey* by Ibn ʿArabī (Spanish translation by Carlos Varona Narvión).

When Sibila vanished, the words in the gallery where she had written down her discoveries took on a blue-green hue and an intermittent luminescence. Since her disappearance, the Criamon of Barzaj have studied both their content and the relationships between the pulses of light, the words of greater and lesser intensity, and the concepts traced in the air.

To study Sibila's words, a character must have Enigmatic Wisdom and spend a season noting the luminous relationships created between the words, so as to decipher the riddles they pose. Sibila's gallery has a Source Quality equal to a stress die plus the aura of the place (7 on this level), and magi may study any Art they choose there, but only once, unless their Advancement Total exceeds 21. If they exceed that figure, the magi may spend another season unraveling Sibila's riddles.

The magus Félez of Criamon achieved the greatest number of consecutive seasons in 1178. After the third season, however, he vanished, consumed by the adulteration of Taʿlab. Since then, the magi of Barzaj have been studying the possible relationships between the adulteration and Sibila's gallery.

#### The Shaft (Portal to the Fourth Level)

*If this course is called a "journey," it is because it unveils (*yusfiru*) the characters of men, laying bare both those that are blameworthy and those most praiseworthy.*[^p259-59]

[^p259-59]: *Ibidem*.

On the third level of the *regio*, the shaft is entirely flooded, which is not the case on the lower levels. The magi of Barzaj believe that the adulteration takes refuge in the last level of the *regio* (since all the other levels have been mapped), but given the inherent difficulties of that level and its mystical significance, no one has dared go looking for it.

#### Society and Customs

*[…] when man journeys to the world of his imagination, he must go beyond it in order to reach that of the (higher) Realities. There he will see things as they are, and he will receive the absolute gift (*wahb muṭlaq*), provided he has not mortgaged himself (*yataqayyad*) to gain […].*[^p259-60]

[^p259-60]: *Ibidem*.

<!-- p. 260 -->

Barzaj is a quasi-autocracy guided by the *ḏū al-ʿaynayn*, that is, by the one who has two eyes (see "The Ṣūfī Mystics" on page 303). This leader is no more than a figure who serves as a guide to the other magi who make up the mystical brotherhood (*ṭarīqa*) of Iberia. Normally the title is earned only by those who have reached the fourth Station of any Path, and only after returning from the *ʿālam al-mithāl* following forty days (*arbaʿniyya*) of spiritual retreat (*jalwa*), during which the aspirant usually brings back some clue about the Enigma (forty is an important number for Muslims since, among other things, it is the number of days souls remain in purgatory before being reunited with their creator). In theory, two magi of Barzaj could hold the same rank, but that has never happened in the covenant's history.

Those who review Barzaj's charter are often surprised to find the following clause: "magi bearing the title of *ḏū al-ʿaynayn* are the only ones empowered to decide on the affairs of the covenant, both internal and external." Barzaj adopted this form of government in 1103, after the Tribunal of al-Andalus was annexed to the Iberian Tribunal, because its members feared the covenant would fall into the hands of other Houses and be perverted. Although the model was criticized by some members, it was finally approved by the presiding Quaesitor at the ordinary Tribunal of 1109, the same year Fawd was elected Praeco. In practice, no magus of Barzaj has ever made use of the privileges that come with the title of *ḏū al-ʿaynayn*.

At the end of each season, nearly all the magi of Barzaj (the magus Yehudá is usually the exception) gather in one of the cave chambers on the first level of the *regio*, on a carpeted dais strewn with brocade cushions, where they discuss their findings, communicating with one another through poetry, music or dance. Every member of Barzaj ends up growing fond of these gatherings, and almost all of them own magical musical instruments, usually made at Ajabeba. These objects are the only exceptions to the ethic of the journey followed by Barzaj's members, which entails a strong detachment from all things material. Through this detachment they avoid putting down roots that might keep them from letting themselves be carried by the perpetual flow, so as to remain subject to constant change.

#### The Magi of Barzaj

*Each faculty perceives only that for which it was specifically created; thus the gaze grasps nothing but sensible and visible things, and the senses turn back "driven away" (*jāsāʾn*) when they see no crack through which to enter.*[^p260-61]

[^p260-61]: Excerpt from *The Splendor of the Fruits of the Journey* by Ibn ʿArabī (Spanish translation by Carlos Varona Narvión).

Above and beyond what the covenant's charter says (and titles such as *ḏū al-ʿaynayn*), each maga and magus of Barzaj calls himself or herself a *sālik*, "one who follows a spiritual path" through a series of states (*aḥwāl*), halts and stations (*maqāmāt*), which the magi liken to the *regio* where they live and to their own imaginative intellect.

##### Ḏū al-ʿaynayn, sālik, Wallāda al-Criamoniyya

*Man was created with the knowledge needed to (govern) his appetites with reason, and it is by wielding reason that he can resist them.*[^p260-62]

[^p260-62]: *Ibidem*.

Wallāda is the oldest maga at Barzaj. Her features still keep something of their beauty, and not a single gray hair has appeared in her red hair. Wallāda was born blind, which has not prevented her from unraveling the mysteries of her Path, for the organ of mystical vision is the heart. During her stay in Baghdad she learned the Qurʾan by heart, thanks to which she can heal the sick with the touch of her hands.

Given how close she is to Final Twilight, she should already have left the covenant to die in the Cave of Twisting Shadows, but the adulteration holds her back. She has a feeling that she is close to resolving it, though in fact she has not approached the problem correctly. She is aware that the adulteration was created in the past by the faults of Barzaj's former inhabitants, but she has not acknowledged her own. Like the rest, she regards the perfect ones as Gorgiasts, and does not believe the resolution of the Grand Tribunal of 1162 brought about any harm, quite the contrary. As long as Wallāda persists in refusing to accept her share of the blame, the adulteration will keep growing in power and claiming the lives of Barzaj's inhabitants (Wallāda's full statistics appear on page 130 of *Houses of Hermes: Mystery Cults*).

##### Sālik, Yehudá al-Criamonī

*The most poetry can attain is this: to be something mixed of the perfect and the imperfect, without ever achieving pure perfection; and from this* summum *it can, naturally, descend to the very lowest point on the scale of the imperfect and the base.*[^p260-63]

[^p260-63]: Excerpt from *The Epistle of Holiness* by Ibn ʿArabī (Spanish translation by Miguel Asín Palacios).

Yehudá, a Jew, is an elderly magus and a former apprentice of Fawd, who spends most of his time wandering the labyrinthine grottoes of the third level of the *regio*.

Yehudá has never approved of his *sodales*' seasonal gatherings, which he considers in poor taste and, of course, hardly ascetic. In fact, he hates music and poetry, and if he hears either, he presses his hands hard over his ears until the noise stops. Unlike Wallāda, Yehudá is not much interested in resolving the supposed adulteration that dwells in Barzaj, and concentrates on following his Path in order to find some clue to the answer of the Enigma. For all the disdain he shows toward the adulteration, Yehudá always avoids Sibila's gallery, for which he harbors an irrational fear; something, of course, he has never admitted in public.

Unfortunately for Barzaj, Yehudá's contemptuous attitude toward the adulteration is of little help in resolving it. Indeed, even if Wallāda accepted her own faults, the malignancy would most likely stay hidden behind Yehudá's disdain.

#### Sālik, Crespo of Criamon

<!-- p. 261 -->

Crespo is a magus of Castilian origin who came to Barzaj barely ten years ago and who, perhaps because of his youth, is fascinated by the adulteration. His dearest wish is to resolve it and, although he has no idea how to go about it, he usually volunteers for anything connected with the matter. For all his enthusiasm, Crespo is afraid to enter the higher levels of the *regio* for fear of meeting the angel of death, Asrāʾil, who according to Sunni angelology is responsible for carrying the souls of the dead to judgment, the threshold of their final destiny. These are mere superstitions, of course — or are they?

#### Sālikiyya, Wardatun al-Criamoniyya

The maga Wardatun (a native of Algeciras) came from Normandy after traveling across Europe in search of places of perfect transmission. Wardatun studies such places in search of some pattern that might bring her closer to the answer of the Enigma. Since arriving at the covenant more than twenty years ago, however, she has changed Paths and devoted herself to the study of Sibila's gallery. Wardatun has not yet used the gallery as such; rather, she has compared it with the other similar places she has visited in order to continue her overall study. The covenant's damp makes things very difficult, however, and she has had to resort to wax tablets to record her discoveries. As a result, she is beginning to have trouble storing them and has chosen to keep them in one of the galleries on the mundane level.

Wardatun knows little of Barzaj's history, but she believes its magi are wrong to reject the Rationalists of ʾAlif. If anyone can defeat the adulteration that plagues the covenant, it is she.
