### Sālik, ʿĀqīl al-Criamonī

ʿĀqīl abandoned the Path of Walking Backwards to follow the Twisting Path. Along the way he was seduced by the Rationalist doctrines of the perfect ones, and since 1162 he has dreamed of joining the magi of ʾAlif so that they might teach him what they have learned. Yet in the nearly sixty years that have passed since, he has not found the courage to leave Barzaj and set out on a new road.

<!-- p. 262 -->

ʿĀqīl lives prey to his fears and dreads leaving his roots behind. If ʿĀqīl managed to uproot himself and join the perfect ones, the resolution of the adulteration would draw nearer, for he is a respected member of the covenant, and perhaps his departure and his acceptance of the perfect ones' philosophy might spur the other members to reflection. On the other hand, if Barzaj were to condemn his departure, the adulteration would grow more powerful and might end up swallowing another magus.

> #### Story Seeds: The Malignancy of Taʿlab
>
> *Whoever [...] journeys toward the world of his heart sees the angelic world as the vastest (of the universes), and before him is manifested (*taŷallī*) the supreme world (*al-ŷabbarūt*) in its greater sublimity. He also sees the secret of life, the spirit that spreads through all that lives. And he distinguishes between the spirit of the many and of the few [...].*[^p262-XX]
>
> When Taʿlab suffered his Final Twilight, the detritus of his psyche created a terrible adulteration, born of his betrayal of the Kharijites of Almería. The adulteration took refuge in Barzaj and remained hidden until it claimed the maga Sibila in 1073. The magi of Barzaj then concluded that a powerful adulteration dwelt in their covenant, but they did not know which of them had produced it.
>
> The adulteration grew more powerful with each of Barzaj's mistakes until, in 1162, with the threat against the perfect ones, it reached the rank of a malignancy. Yet the three lives it has claimed (Sibila in 1073, Fawd in 1147 and Félez in 1178) show no pattern the magi of Barzaj can use to discover the origin of the problem.
>
> In 1220, the poet Wardatun is the one closest to finding the solution, but the fact that the other members have still not accepted their own guilt has allowed the malignancy to keep eluding her. Perhaps the player characters can be the mirror the magi of Barzaj need in order to see their own faults and so finally overcome them (though that might entail defending the perfect ones before the Order and an apology from Barzaj).
>
> The storyguide should design the malignancy with a Magic Might of at least 45 or, if he prefers it to be a place within the *regio*, it should be dangerous enough to put the players to the test. Likewise, he must decide whether or not the *regio* vanishes when the malignancy disappears (for more ideas about adulterations, we recommend taking a look at the insert on page 98 of *Houses of Hermes: Mystery Cults*).
>
> [^p262-XX]: Excerpt from *The Splendor of the Fruits of the Journey* by Ibn ʿArabī (Spanish translation by Carlos Varona Narvión).

## The Balearic Archipelago

*The island of Majorca is one of God's most populous lands and one of the richest in grain, provisions and livestock. Despite its isolation from other lands, it can do without them, and even sends them the surplus of its produce.*[^p262-64]

[^p262-64]: Excerpt from *In Praise of Spanish Islam* by Al-Šaqundī (Spanish translation by Emilio García Gómez).

The Balearic Islands were under Umayyad control from the early tenth century and, in 1030, after the *fitna*, they were conquered by the governor of Valencia. After little more than two centuries in Muslim hands, Majorca was conquered in 1115 by the armies of Pisa and Catalonia together with soldiers from Rome, Lucca and the south of France, who freed the Christian captives and slaughtered the island's Muslim inhabitants. When, a year later, the Catalans learned that the Almoravids were about to attack the islands, they abandoned their houses, burned them and left, leaving the islands deserted.

The Balearic archipelago was the last Almoravid stronghold in Iberia (in the hands of the Banū Gāniya) to be conquered by the Almohads. In 1204 the Almohads put the islands to fire and sword, killed their governor and hung his body from the walls of his own fortress.

In 1220 the islands remain under the rule of the Almohad Empire, though both Ibiza and Formentera have few mundane inhabitants.

Majorca grows cereals, olives and vines, and has abundant pasture for livestock. The islands also have an important coral fishery, controlled mainly by the Catalans. Horses and donkeys are bred there too, but its mules are the best in all Iberia, for the absence of predators, the excellent pastures and the lack of epidemics favor the breeding of these animals, which can fetch as much as 500 dīnārs in the markets of the Peninsula (it is also said that the herdsmen who tend these animals are skilled with the sling).

The Balearic archipelago (in the waters of the Mediterranean) is made up of the Gymnesian Islands (Majorca, Minorca and Cabrera) and the Pityusic Islands (Ibiza and Formentera), with numerous islets around them. Majorca, the largest of the islands, has a mountain range in the north that rises above 1,000 meters at several points and, in the east, holds the largest city in the whole archipelago, called Palma by the Romans and Mallorca by the Muslims. Throughout the history of the Order (and almost from its earliest days), the archipelago has been home only to the controversial Ajabeba.

<!-- p. 263 -->

### Ajabeba

*You must consider our conditions with regard to attainment, for the more indispensable a thing is to the living creature, the more readily it is found and at the lower cost; and the less necessary it is, the harder it is to find, and at the higher price.*[^p263-65]

[^p263-65]: Excerpt from *The Guide for the Perplexed* by Maimonides (Spanish translation by David Gonzalo Maeso).

>**Lifespan:** 871–Present<br>
>**Founder:** Megaris Angelina Palaiologina of Verditius; Hermongenes of Verditius (officially)<br>
>**Season:** Autumn<br>
>**Aura (type and strength):** Magic, strength 7<br>
>**Reputations:** Artisans (Iberian Tribunal) 3, Reclusive (Hermetic) 2, Opulent (Iberian Tribunal) 1<br>
>**Votes:** 6

The covenant of Ajabeba (the Arabic name for a kind of flute made from bone) was founded by one of the apprentices Verditius trained at Verdi (Sardinia) in the early years of the Order. It has been dominated by Verditius magi ever since.

#### History

Some years after Verditius was murdered in Corsica, the maga Megaris, a native of one of the Greek islands, left Verdi with her apprentice, Hermongenes, for the island west of Sardinia that Milo (Verditius's second apprentice) had described as almost deserted and rich in natural resources. Megaris and Hermongenes roamed the Gymnesian Islands for years in search of a suitable site for their forge, until in 842 they found a hidden beach in the north of Majorca, in the heart of the Sierra de Tramontana. The spot was perfect, for the maga wanted a private harbor from which to sail to the other cities and islands of the Mediterranean. It had one small drawback, however: for two years the cove had been occupied by Andalusi pirates who had fled Crete to escape the Greek forces commanded by Theophilus, emperor of Byzantium. Megaris managed to reach an agreement with them at the end of 842, under which, in exchange for a handful of magic items, the pirates offered her their fleet and protection and a share of whatever plunder they took, as well as permission to raise the covenant's first building, which the maga named the Forge of Megaris.

At the start of the new year of 843, Hermongenes passed his Gauntlet in his master's new forge and, two months later, the pirates sailed into port with two impressive ships whose crews (save for a ruddy-cheeked girl named ʿAyša) had been put to the knife. Megaris and Hermongenes inspected the ships and discovered that they were enchanted with Hermetic magic and that the holds had been sealed with warding spells. The first thing they did was eliminate any Arcane Connection the ships might have and, after investigating them for two seasons, they uncovered their secrets and gained access to the holds, where they found a treasure that included three queens of vis, numerous magic items and great quantities of gold, rock salt and precious stones, worth more than seven million Mythic dīnārs. On the night Megaris entered the hold, a faction of the pirates mutinied and tried to seize the treasure, and although the revolt was put down and the surviving rebels were hanged, Megaris lost her life and Hermongenes took over the leadership of his master's forge.

Hermongenes supposed that both the ships and the treasure belonged to some Hermetic covenant; nevertheless, he did not hand them over, for two reasons. On the one hand, he had no wish to become embroiled in legal affairs and, on the other, he did not want his *parens*'s death to have been in vain. So, overnight (in the most literal sense), the Forge of Megaris became an extremely wealthy covenant. The treasures from the ships filled the coffers and workshops of the Verditius, who did not hesitate to share them with the pirates who had remained loyal to him. But what Hermongenes did not suspect was that the greatest treasure was not among all those riches, but was living alongside the rest of the covenant's inhabitants. A few days after the revolt, one of his laboratory assistants brought the sole survivor of the Hermetic ships' crews to his *sanctum*. To Hermongenes's surprise, the girl had the Gift.

Hermongenes took ʿAyša as his apprentice and initiated her into the mysteries of the House. During her training, the girl showed great aptitude for music and spent much time in the covenant's workshop making beautiful instruments, with which she later enlivened her master's hours of research. In the fifteen years her apprenticeship lasted, ʿAyša came to love Hermongenes as a father, and the magus learned to love her as a daughter. So, when Hermongenes attended the Rhine Tribunal of 871 for the first time, he announced the founding of his covenant in the Gymnesian Islands and chose the name Ajabeba, rather than the one his master had given it, because that was ʿAyša's favorite instrument. Shortly afterward, ʿAyša passed her Gauntlet and took the Hermetic name Xanthippe.

Ajabeba remained secluded on its island and had little contact with the outside world. The two magi took on more apprentices and kept increasing their wealth through piracy in the Mediterranean and the many items wrought in their furnaces and workshops. Although the covenant faced some difficulties when the Umayyads conquered the island at the beginning of the tenth century, Ajabeba was able to recover, for it already had contacts in cities such as Barcelona, Arles, Valencia, Pisa, Pechina, Algiers, Almería, Melilla, Genoa and Cartagena, and it exploited the vis sources of the Valencian coast and of the volcanic islands of the Mediterranean (Columbretes, Blanāsīa, Grosa, and so on), which its pirates used as hiding places. Moreover, it was on good terms with the Fatimid caliphs (who had ruled Ifrīqiya since 916) and the Umayyad caliphs, to whom it sold its devices.

<!-- p. 264 -->

During the reign of Al-Ḥakam II, Ajabeba negotiated free passage with the caliphate for ships bound for its harbors, and began acquiring rare copies of mundane and Hermetic books that swelled the library of this singular covenant. By then Ajabeba was known throughout the Tribunal for its extraordinary craftsmanship, from which many magi benefited. From Ajabeba came the artificers who built the marvelous automata of the palatine city of Madīnat al-Zahrāʾ and the other enchantments that filled those halls at the height of Umayyad splendor (see "The Verditius Devices of Cordoba," page 85).

True to its policy of isolation, Ajabeba stayed on the sidelines during the Schism War and the secession of the Tribunal of al-Andalus, at least until 1061, when the Order ruled that Hermetic magi could no longer sell the items they created directly to mundane society, but had to use intermediaries without the Gift to do so. House Verditius then reduced to one per year the number of items a magus could sell to mundanes, which did not go down well at Ajabeba. Although the covenant had many contacts scattered through the most important port cities of the Mediterranean, it began negotiating with the Iberian Tribunal for an entry in the Peripheral Code that would soften the impact of the edict, but since no agreement was reached, Ajabeba turned to the illegitimate Tribunal of al-Andalus, where, in exchange for seven impressive automata destined for the Great Hall, the unofficial Tribunal introduced the entry "On the Exchange of Enchantments with Mundanes" (1068).

During the period of the taifa kingdoms, Ajabeba took advantage of the diversity of princes in al-Andalus to put numerous magic items into circulation. With the annexation of the Tribunal of al-Andalus to Iberia, Ajabeba secured the validation of the 1068 ruling in 1119, so its annual sales only began to decline with the Almoravid conquest of the taifa kingdoms. In those years Ajabeba also had problems with the port cities of other Tribunals which, obviously, were not governed by the Peripheral Code of Iberia. The covenant was brought before the Provençal Tribunal and the Roman Tribunal for its expansionism, and had to pay a heavy fine and stop selling its magic items in those Tribunals. In response, Ajabeba concentrated on the cities of North Africa and monopolized the sale of enchantments there. These events gave rise to numerous *vendettas* between the Verditius of other Tribunals and those of Ajabeba.

In 1115, when the crusading armies of the Catalans and Pisans reached the island, the inhabitants of Ajabeba had to take refuge on the island of Grosa, off the coast of Murcia, which the Verditius used as a quarry to extract pawns of Ignem and Terram vis. Ajabeba's main building was razed by the Christian forces and, although they never reached the forge, the covenant suffered heavy losses. The arrival of the Almohads on the island in 1204 was also dramatic for Ajabeba, which once again had to abandon the covenant and take refuge on the island of Sardinia, where the magi of Verdi gave them shelter. This time, however, the covenant suffered no damage thanks to its magical defenses, and the magi of Ajabeba were able to return home having suffered no more than a few casualties among their mundane contacts.

In 1220, Ajabeba is a powerful, independent covenant that houses the finest crafters of enchantments in the whole Tribunal, and although its networks of intermediaries are occasionally hampered by Durato's agents, its members are usually careful in this regard so as not to draw unwanted attention to themselves. Although in 1221 they hope to meet the founders of Ŷezirat Tennyn to reach an agreement with them, they will have to negotiate with Darfílun and Manjuza instead, for they are the only members left in that covenant (see page 229).

#### Setting and Physical Description

The buildings of the covenant of Ajabeba are spread across several Mediterranean islands, while its trading networks reach much farther, through numerous port cities where the Verditius of Ajabeba have freed slaves over the course of their history. This has allowed them to earn the trust of these people for generations, so that they act as the covenant's agents either occasionally (for specific payments) or permanently (on the covenant's payroll).

Ajabeba's main forge, the one Megaris Angelina Palaiologina raised, lies in the north of the island of Majorca, at one of the few points where the Sierra de Tramontana reaches the sea. Set in the light of spectacular, narrow cliffs 200 meters high, the covenant sits in a cove of rounded pebbles that floods at high tide. Part of the covenant building is carved into the rock, where the Verditius have their workshops, which boast natural springs of saline water and great hollows that serve as windows. They are also fitted with enchanted chimneys that eliminate the smoke they give off, so that the settlement cannot be spotted from afar. The building also houses six spacious *sancta*, the council chamber, the library and the covenant's common treasury (which usually holds less than the magi's personal treasuries).

Next to the main building, also in the cove, is Ajabeba's small private harbor, where only the magi's ship may moor. Less than 500 meters' sail to the west lies another cove where the covenant has shipyards and a larger harbor where the rest of its ships ride at anchor. In the eleventh century, the Verditius dug a tunnel through the mountain connecting the shipyards with Ajabeba's workshops, for transporting materials or as a refuge in case of attack.

The way out to the open sea from these two coves is guarded by the sphinxes, two monstrous automata more than twelve meters tall that can raise waves of up to five meters at sea, hurl missiles of Greek fire, create a curtain of thick fog, and freeze the surface of the water to trap any vessel in the ice. The sphinxes were built over two centuries by several generations of Verditius from the three workshops that govern the covenant (see below). It was thanks to them that the Almohad assault of 1204 ended without any material loss to the covenant.

Most of the covenant's vis sources lie on Mediterranean islands belonging to the *kūras* of Valencia and Murcia. To harvest them each year, Ajabeba keeps a series of refuges it can reach by means of the Arcane Connections stored in the covenant's treasure room. All these refuges have a small harbor where rowing boats can be tied up, and are guarded by mundane soldiers equipped with various magic items. The most notable refuges are the following:

<!-- p. 265 -->

- A tower some twelve meters tall on the largest of the Columbretes islands (which is shaped like an open arch, a legacy of its former volcanic activity).
- A large fortified building and a shipyard on the island of Blanāsīa (where there is an abandoned forge and a small mundane population affiliated with the covenant).
- A simple structure beside the lagoon on the island of Plumbaria.
- A supply fort for the grogs at the top of the volcanic cone of the island of Grosa (some two and a half kilometers off the coast of Murcia), where the *orovales* (small shrubs that cover the island) produce a modest amount of vis each year. On this island there is a small magical *regio* that sinks into the treacherous seabed surrounding the island (where many ships have been wrecked).

#### Society and Customs

Ajabeba is a bureaucracy run by the heads of the covenant's three workshops, namely: carpentry (and cabinetmaking), goldsmithing (metals, minerals and ceramics) and tanning (all work involving animal products, such as sinew, bone or ivory). The master of each workshop is responsible for drawing up the designs of every project produced, or for correcting and approving the designs of his subordinates or journeymen. He also receives the title of *amīn*,[^p265-66] which makes him responsible for seeing that the work meets the required standards of quality. In workshop meetings the masters have the last word on any matter under discussion, while in the council they hold a casting vote on covenant decisions related to their field of work. If two or more workshops are involved in a vote and it ends in a tie, the members of Ajabeba settle it by lot with an ancient ivory die (six-sided) that they found in a wreck beneath the waters off Grosa and carved with the symbols of each workshop (using two opposite faces of the die for each one). In this way no workshop gains greater weight than the others and no one's pride is wounded.

[^p265-66]: The *amīn* is the syndic of a guild.

> #### Musical Instruments
>
> Since Xanthippe's time there has always been some Verditius at Ajabeba with a love of music and poetry, so its workshops have produced the most refined musical instruments in all Mythic Europe. The Verditius magi of Ajabeba have always held that responsibility for a fine sound rests equally on the instrument and the player, so they have almost never enchanted their instruments for that purpose. Normally the enchantments are meant to make the object last, making it resistant to damp (indispensable for the magi of Barzaj, for example), to fire or to blows.
>
> Among the instruments they make are the following: the karrīŷ (reed pipe), the ʿūd (lute), the rūṭa (rote), the rabāb (rebec), the qānūn (psaltery or harp), the kanīra (a kind of zither), the qitār (guitar), the šuqra (a baritone flute), the nūra (a triple flute), the būq (hornpipe), the duff (square frame drum), the aqwāl (a kind of drum), the yarā (pipe or shawm) and, of course, the ajabeba (a Moorish recorder).

<!-- p. 266 -->

The title of master is conferred by the masters of each workshop and the investiture takes effect immediately. If no appointment has been made when a master dies, the title passes to the next most senior craftsman in the workshop. If there are no candidates, the workshop stands empty until someone takes it up. In this rare case, the first to join it is automatically named master.

The workshops work in concert to produce the finest enchantments, but when it comes to the House competition (see *Houses of Hermes: Mystery Cults*, page 199), the magi shut themselves away in their workshops to work alone.

To orchestrate the networks of mundane *venditores*, the council relies on the powerful figure of the autocrat of Ajabeba, who is usually a forge-companion of the magi. Curiously, the office of autocrat is inherited through the maternal line. In 1220 the autocrat is named Fajr.

Every year, beginning at the summer solstice and lasting a whole week, Ajabeba holds a festival in the cove where the magi's building stands, to which all the covenant's inhabitants are invited. A few days beforehand, the harbor begins to fill with ships from every corner of the Mediterranean carrying Ajabeba's most distinguished mundane members (*venditores*, fences, former workers, and so on). During the celebration, the finest players among magi and mundanes play the most exquisite instruments the covenant has produced, recite beautiful poetry, and present valuable gifts to renew their loyalty. For the Verditius magi of Ajabeba, this event is almost more important than the House competition.

#### The Magi of Ajabeba

##### Master Carpenter Muṣawwir al-Verditī

Muṣawwir (Arabic for "maker") is the master of the carpentry workshop and a mediocre musician. His creations, however, are unequaled. No member of Ajabeba can recall ever having had a craftsman like him. Such is his skill that the previous master of the workshop appointed him while he was still very young. Now that he is old and his hands and fingers have lost their steadiness, he directs the designs and passes on his knowledge to his journeyman, whom he hopes will become a great master when he is gone.

##### Journeyman Carpenter Layla al-Verditiyya

Layla is the daughter of one of the nieces of the covenant's previous autocrat, so it can be said that she has always been part of Ajabeba. As an inhabitant of the covenant, Layla spent some time traveling among the various Mediterranean cities assigned to her father as a *venditor*. Perhaps that is why it took so long to realize she had the Gift. At the age of seven, Layla was brought to Ajabeba and handed over to the magi to be raised as one of them. For showing such loyalty and trust, her parents were showered with gifts and treated with greater consideration from then on, which no doubt contributed to their prosperity in the city of Arles, where they lived. And so Layla was handed over to the master carpenter Muṣawwir.

When Layla became a maga, she specialized in making musical instruments and items that could help Ajabeba's *venditores* and pirates sail the Mediterranean. In time, magical aids became her work, and making musical instruments her passion. And it is a lucrative passion: Ajabeba sells her masterpieces (both enchanted and unenchanted) to numerous mundanes and covenants, in Iberia and in other Tribunals alike, so much so that they account for a good share of the covenant's mundane income. As one might expect, Layla is well aware of this and enjoys her triumphs within the covenant.

In 1220, Layla is focused on acquiring the knowledge needed to be initiated into House Verditius's Inner Mystery of Harmonic Items. She is also worried, however, about reaching the level of experience needed to be named master carpenter, for her skill, though outstanding, cannot yet compete with that of her *parens*. These tribulations are not entirely unknown to her workshop *sodales*, who have devotedly kept helping her to improve. Layla's problem, though, is her lack of constancy in the laboratory: her creativity drives her to let herself be carried away by her fancies for a season every few years, and her introverted spirit compels her to withdraw now and then to some cove on the island, where there is room only for her daydreams, her prayers and her music. Even so, Muṣawwir is proud of her, for he enjoys her music as much as, or more than, the rest of her creations.

>**Appearance:** Despite her true age, Layla retains an exceptional Basque beauty, thanks to the powerful Longevity Ritual she was able to afford with Ajabeba's riches. The maga has a thick mane of curly blond hair in which not a single gray strand can be seen. Her eyes, blue (inherited from her father), are bright and luminous, and her smile reveals a row of perfect, mother-of-pearl teeth, which tends to draw the gaze (and stir the envy) of those who hear her sing. By contrast, her skin is dark and weathered by water and sun, which only accentuates the radiance of her face. Accompanying her extraordinary beauty, Layla's gestures are graceful and elegant, and her limbs slender and delicate. The whole is so harmonious that those who behold her rarely notice the hardness of her hands, the product of her ceaseless work in the covenant's carpentry workshop.
>
> Layla is a taciturn, aloof woman who enjoys solitude, which has no doubt earned her a certain reputation among the covenant's inhabitants. Those who manage to get close to her, however, discover a vibrant, optimistic person, loyal and devoted enough to be trusted.
>
> Layla was Muṣawwir's apprentice and, unlike him, is an exceptional musician and poet. The power of the melodies that flow from her instrument is such that it can move the most taciturn or the most jovial of mortals to laughter or tears. Her favorite instrument is the *rabāb*, and she has an impressive collection of them, both magical and mundane. During the summer solstice festivities she usually chooses one she calls *al-ʾafuww* (Arabic for "the forgiving"; in fact, one of the ninety-nine names of God), whose neck is made from a single piece of mother-of-pearl taken from an enormous shell found by the magi of Ŷezirat Tennyn in the depths of the Green Sea.

##### Journeyman Carpenter Alfonso Téllez of Verditius

Alfonso Téllez was trained at Verdi and is the youngest of Ajabeba's Verditius. Despite the time he has spent at the covenant, he has yet to acquire a taste for music. He does, however, show a passion for the *regio* on the island of Grosa and the old forge on Blanāsīa, which do not seem to interest his other *sodales* much. Alfonso dreams that the forge on the little island is one of the ancient forges of Hephaestus, and spends his free moments imagining himself working in such a mythic place.

##### Master Goldsmith Țarūb al-Verditiyya

Țarūb is a maga in her seventies who rose to the post of master without having been chosen. Her companions at Ajabeba are worried about her, for ever since her *filia* Ferraria left for the covenant of Beit Midrash, she has been trapped in an undying melancholy that shows in all her compositions. Since she has still not overcome her loss, the goldsmith's workshop still has no journeyman.

<!-- p. 268 -->

Despite her tribulations, Țarūb is an exceptional cabinetmaker and, contrary to what one might expect, her work has not suffered from her melancholy; it has been heightened by that powerful sense of loss… which in the end might also bring her gloomy genius to a premature end.

##### Master Tanner Rāʾiq al-Verditiyya

The maga Rāʾiq is Țarūb's *filia*. To her misfortune, she is neither an outstanding craftswoman nor a great musician. Since Asur arrived she has been pushed aside in the workshop, and she is certain that as soon as Ajabeba receives an application from another tanner, they will do without her. That thought has embittered her toward the covenant, and her attitude toward it is defiant. Her *parens*, of course, is perfectly aware of this and, much against her wishes, may well end up requesting her expulsion.

Her sense of inferiority runs so deep that in 1214 she pretended she could not attend the ordinary Tribunal, on the excuse that she had to finish a piece of work still pending. Taking advantage of being alone in the covenant, she broke into Asur's *sanctum* and enchanted a piece of unworked ivory with a PeCo Watching Ward with enough Penetration to wound the magus mortally. Six years later, Asur still seems not to have worked that piece, though Rāʾiq trusts she will see him die in agony before she is expelled from the covenant.

##### Journeyman Tanner Asur González of Verditius

Asur was the apprentice of Catena of Verditius, the craftswoman of Duresca. As such, he is the heir to an ancient tradition of craftsmen known as the finest ivory workers in all al-Andalus (see the covenant of Aẓm Alfíl).

Asur left Duresca because of his stormy relationship with his *parens*, the oppressive atmosphere of the covenant, and the glorious fame of Ajabeba, where there was moreover no ivory craftsman. In fact, Asur is Țarūb's favorite, not only for his magnificent works of craftsmanship but also for his great gifts as a musician, which has poisoned his relationship with Rāʾiq, his workshop companion.

<!-- p. 269 -->

> #### Story Seeds: Ajabeba
>
> Here are three story seeds connected with Ajabeba. Naturally, the storyguide and the troupe can draw on its history to create many more.
>
> ##### The Andalusi Pirates
>
> When one of the ships of the characters' covenant is attacked, they witness the pirates making use of powerful magic items, which makes them formidable opponents. If the characters manage to defeat them, they can study the items and conclude that they were made by Verditius magi. The items will set them on the trail of the legendary Ajabeba, for they are not only magically powerful but also superb works of art. How will they handle this situation? Will they denounce Ajabeba or come to terms with it? What would happen if the Verditius wanted their magic items back?
>
> ##### The Blood of Mercurius
>
> The ship that the pirates of Megaris captured in the ninth century belonged to the Mercere of Aedes Saturni. Mercurius's heirs brought the case before the Rhine Tribunal of 843, where, besides the lost treasures, they reported that a girl named ʿAyša, who carried the blood of Mercere, had vanished along with the ships. Although the assembly was moved by the story, the Redcaps were not popular in those years, and their plea for aid was dismissed. The family history born of her loss was a terrible one for the Redcaps, but time passed and Aedes Saturni gave up searching for ʿAyša and the ships it had lost in the Mediterranean.
>
> When in 1215 Ajabeba's autocrat gives birth to a healthy baby named ʿAŷab, everyone in the covenant rejoices at the continuation of her line, and when four years later the little girl turns out to have the Gift, the melancholy Țarūb adopts her as her apprentice. However, while introducing her to the Arts, the maga comes up against certain supernatural abilities she cannot master, capacities that have traditionally been linked to the Mercere of the Order. The old woman, who wishes to fill the void left by Ferraria, knows Ajabeba's history and wonders whether ʿAŷab might be ʿAyša's descendant. If so, the line of Ajabeba's autocrats would carry the blood of Mercere. What might such news provoke at the Tribunal if it proved true and came to light?
>
> ##### The Swords of the Cid: Colada and Tizón
>
> *He who was born in a good hour has won this battle; he has taken Count Don Remont prisoner; there he won Colada, which is worth more than a thousand marks. [...] He slew Búcar, the king from beyond the sea, and won Tizón, which is worth a thousand marks of gold.*[^p268-XXI]
>
> Colada was the Cid's first famous sword: the Campeador took it in battle from the count of Barcelona, Berenguer Ramón the Fratricide. Tizón was a battle trophy won from the emir of Marrākeš, Búcar, when the Cid was defending Valencia against the Almoravid armies. According to tradition, both swords have the power to strike fear into enemies if wielded by someone worthy.
>
> If what is said is true, both swords are in Ajabeba and have been studied by its members over the years. While Colada was made by the Confraternity of Roland (see *Houses of Hermes: Mystery Cults*, page 206) and is comparable in power to Durandarte, the mysteries of Tizón have yet to be unveiled.
>
> [^p268-XXI]: Excerpt from the *Cantar de mio Cid*, anonymous (Old Spanish text edited by Ramón Menéndez Pidal).

## Africa

Thanks to the influence of the Cordoban covenant of al-Zahrāʾ, the Iberian Tribunal took advantage of the protectorate over the western and central Maghreb that the caliph ʿAbd al-Raḥmān III had created to launch itself into the conquest of Africa. However, the Peninsula's magi were cautious because of the clause they had signed with the *saḥirs* in 925, and in 976 they sent a small group of Redcaps and magi, led by the maga Umm al-Kirām al-Merkeriyya. When the Redcaps pushed into southern Africa, they discovered that mundane power was split among a complex web of Berber dynasties which, unlike the Umayyad and Fatimid caliphs, never went so far as to create a state as such, and so leaned toward one power or another according to their own interests or the political maneuvers of one caliphate or the other.

Today, the only covenant still standing in Africa is the *saḥira* covenant of al-Minẓār, some eighty kilometers as the crow flies south of Madīnat Fās, a city conquered by the armies of Al-Ḥakam II in 974.

> #### Al-Qāhira
>
> By 969 the Fatimids had already occupied Egypt and conquered Fusțāț, so the caliph Al-Muʿizz ordered the founding of the city of Cairo (al-Qāhira), to which he moved in 972. Al-Qāhira thus became the new capital of Egypt and, over the years, grew into an impressive medieval metropolis which, like other Mediterranean cities, eventually became a port of call for the magi of Iberia. Storyguides should not miss the chance to create exotic stories connected with this magnificent city.

### Al-Minẓār

>**Lifespan:** 1012–Present<br>
>**Founders:** Iliyās al-Praliḥī, Zarwāl al-Praliḥī<br>
>**Season:** Spring<br>
>**Aura (type and strength):** Magic, strength 7<br>
>**Reputations:** Underhanded (Iberian Tribunal) 2<br>
>**Votes:** 4

<!-- p. 270 -->

Al-Minẓār (Arabic for "the mirror") was the project of two *saḥirs* who longed to escape the persecution of the Tribunal's Flambeau and the partiality of the magi of Iberia. They founded the covenant outside the law, and for more than a century they went unnoticed in almost complete Hermetic solitude. With the attacks that razed Aedes Iris, however, the Tribunal discovered the covenant and took control of it.

#### History

When the ordinary Tribunal of 976 permitted the exploration of the African continent, Iliyās and Zarwāl al-Praliḥī, two magi of the Andalusi covenant of Ŷibāl al-Raḥma, eagerly awaited news of the progress of the explorer Umm al-Kirām al-Merkeriyya. So when the maga returned and the Tribunal approved the creation of the Mercer House of Aedes Iris, they decided to try their luck: they left their covenant and set off for the African continent. The two magi found a good place to settle in the Middle Atlas, mapped the area, and returned to Iberia to have the charter they had drawn up ratified. The Tribunal, however, rejected their petition on the grounds of the treaty signed with the *saḥirs* in 925 — which did not stop them either. Determined to fulfill their dream, the two magi defied the will of the Tribunal and returned to Africa at the beginning of the eleventh century to build their "covenant," which they named al-Minẓār.

Al-Minẓār lived in peace, apart from what was happening in the Order, until in 1124 the group of magi the Tribunal had sent to investigate the destruction of Aedes Iris arrived at its gates. By then Iliyās had already died, and Zarwāl had to appear alone before the judges of Duresca, who gave him the choice between letting a Quaesitor into the covenant or being expelled from the Order for having contravened the Tribunal's mandate. With few alternatives, Zarwāl accepted the admission of Gonçalvo of Guernicus. A year later, however, Zarwāl gathered his belongings and, without saying farewell to the other members, set off southward. When Gonçalvo noticed his absence he went after him, but never found him.

Zarwāl was expelled at the Tribunal of 1130 (though no one ever saw him again), and Gonçalvo took advantage of the situation to proclaim himself leader of the covenant and change its charter and its form of government to an autocracy. In this way, to the misfortune of the *filii* of al-Minẓār's founders, the covenant came under the control of Duresca and ended up returning to a bitter Spring because of the constant restrictions imposed by the "infamous" Guernicus.

In 1220, the *filii* of the founders are mature magi and are beginning to consider the possibility of shaking off the yoke unjustly imposed on them years ago.

#### Setting and Physical Description

The covenant of al-Minẓār stands in the depths of an ancient volcanic caldera, fifty meters below ground level, in the heart of the Middle Atlas. The covenant was built of red sandstone by a fire jinni that Zarwāl had commanded and, like many *saḥir* buildings, it has the shape of a tower. The slender structure has five floors, among which are distributed the *sancta*, the covenant's various chambers, and a basement housing the unknown door, so called by the covenant's members because not crossing it was one of the conditions Zarwāl negotiated with the jinni of the place (what lies beyond this threshold is left in the hands of storyguides and their troupes).

The building is surrounded by a dense forest of impressive cedars that are home to many birds. At the bottom of the crater, beside the covenant, there is a small hydrothermal pool from which thick wisps of steam rise during the winter. On the surface, the crater is sunk into a rocky plateau where there are many other craters and inactive volcanic cones.

#### Society and Customs

Since 1130, al-Minẓār has been an autocracy ruled by the *pontifex*, who, according to its charter, can only be appointed by Duresca. Among the *pontifex*'s powers is the ability to require the members to delegate their voting sigils to him so that they vote as a bloc at the ordinary Tribunals of Iberia.

When Gonçalvo took up the post of *pontifex*, he destroyed the covenant's charter and past records, so that in 1220 not even those who were apprentices of the founders remember them.

#### The Magi of al-Minẓār

##### Pontifex Gonçalvo of Guernicus

Gonçalvo is an old magus who feels he has wasted his life. Although in 1123 Duresca flattered him with his new post as *pontifex*, since accepting it he has done nothing but carry out the orders of his superiors in Duresca. When he came to terms with this fact, Gonçalvo took to consuming poppy capsules, which he now cannot do without. For some reason, Gonçalvo has not suffered the degradation their use entails, and he shows no outward signs of addiction (although they would surface if he went without it for more than a day).

By 1220, Gonçalvo has lost hope that Duresca will send him a replacement or an assistant (which he has been requesting since the start of the century), for he believes his superiors intend to finish off al-Minẓār for good, which has only fed the resentment the magus feels toward the Asturian covenant.

##### Šarīfah Muhŷa al-Praliḥiyya

*I learned that some harbor hatred against me in their breasts, but my heart stands free and empty before them.*[^p270-67]

[^p270-67]: Poem from *The Treatise of Familiar Spirits and Demons* by Ibn Shuhayd (Spanish translation by Salvador Barberá).

Šarīfah Muhŷa al-Praliḥiyya, a Fatimid and a descendant of Al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib (one of the Prophet's grandsons and the son of Fāṭīma), was brought up in the bosom of a powerful Cairo family, where she spent her childhood until one of the magi of al-Minẓār took her away.

Šarīfah Muhŷa is the *filia* of the late Iliyās and, after Gonçalvo, is the oldest maga in the covenant. She is tired of living far from Iberia, and for years she has been involved in a movement for the full acceptance of *saḥirs* in the Peninsula (see insert on page 236). As for ʿAmrīl, although she suspects he is plotting something, she has not yet managed to find out what.

<!-- p. 271 -->

In 1200, Šarīfah Muhŷa went to Egypt to help her people, for a great famine, brought on because the Nile had not risen that year, was ravaging the country. In those times food was so hard to come by that people ate rotting flesh and even went so far as to eat one another. By the time Šarīfah Muhŷa arrived, plague had struck the cities and villages so hard that Egypt was almost deserted.

> #### Story Seeds: The Nasnās
>
> *[…] is it not said that Iblīs*[^p271-XXII] *was, in the Creation, among its […] greatest worshippers? And yet what he reaped was to be cast out, and set apart from bliss […]. When the word of punishment came upon him, he returned to his origin: the fire, which was created for him, and in which he alone is tormented.*[^p271-XXIII]
>
> Gonçalvo and his immoral acts toward al-Minẓār drew the attention of a tempter demon (*shayatin*) known as a nasnās in the middle of the twelfth century. Since then, the demon has managed to feed Gonçalvo's resentment toward Duresca (which drove him to consume the latex of the poppy) and has also worked its wicked arts on ʿAmrīl, whose hatred of the Quaesitor's mismanagement has only grown over the years, to the point that he wants to murder him. Its insidious workings have also affected ʿAmrīl's *filius*, who shares his *parens*'s aims and hatreds. The only one who has escaped the nasnās's schemes (for the moment) is Šarīfah Muhŷa, whose Magic Resistance it has been unable to penetrate. However, the demon may yet manage to set her against ʿAmrīl if she gets in his way.
>
> The nasnās's time is running out, however, for Šarīfah Muhŷa has been alerted by the powerful jinni who serves her and is beginning to investigate, which could cause the nasnās to act rashly and expose itself in order to finish its work. In any case, the demon will not dare fight the jinni, which it will try to avoid at all costs.
>
> [^p271-XXII]: Iblīs, the devil, is named in the Qurʾan some fifteen times, although he appears more often as Šayțān, a word of Aramaic origin meaning "enemy." Because of his rebellion, and because he was the only angel who refused to prostrate himself before man, he was cast out of Paradise and condemned to the flames of eternal fire.
>
> [^p271-XXIII]: Excerpt from *The Splendor of the Fruits of the Journey* by Ibn ʿArabī (Spanish translation by Carlos Varona Narvión).

<!-- p. 272 -->

> #### The Nasnās
>**Order:** Tempters (*shayatin*)<br>
>**Infernal Might:** 20 (Corpus)<br>
>**Characteristics:** Int +3, Per +3, Pre –4, Com +0, Str +2, Sta +1, Dex +3, Qik +4<br>
>**Size:** 0<br>
>**Virtues and Flaws:** Tough, Puissant Athletics; Weak-Willed<br>
>**Personality Traits:** Selfish +5, Cruel +2<br>
>**Reputations:** Servant of Iblīs (Hell) 1<br>
>**Hierarchy:** 1<br>
>**Combat:**<br>
>*Claws:* Init +3, Atk +11, Dfn +13, Dam +4<br>
>**Soak:** +4<br>
>**Fatigue Levels:** OK, 0, –1, –3, –5, Unconscious<br>
>**Wound Penalties:** –1 (1–5), –3 (6–10), –5 (11–15), Incapacitated (16–20), Dead (21+)<br>
>**Abilities:** Awareness 3 (listening), Athletics 6+2 (running), Intrigue 3 (infernal politics), Brawl 5 (claws), Stealth 5 (desert)<br>
>**Powers:**<br>
>*Coagulation*, 2 points, Init –1, Corpus<br>
>The nasnās can shape its physical appearance from the formless matter of the universe. The nasnās must spend twenty rounds to assume this appearance. The nasnās can end this effect at any time to return to its natural ethereal state, and does so almost instantly (it must concentrate for one round to do so, so it can be interrupted, as dictated by the rules on page 132 of *Ars Magica Fifth Edition*). The nasnās's statistics do not change with its form (whether physical or spiritual), although in spiritual form it cannot use its physical Characteristics. Ramadan forces the nasnās to abandon its coagulated form (in Christian lands, this happens only on Easter Sunday).
>
>*Obsession*, 1 to 3 points, Init –5, Vim<br>
>The nasnās's Obsession Trait is spite, and it can impose it on a mortal when the latter commits a venial sin (that is, the nasnās can only use this power when the victim's virtue falters and he gives himself over to sinful thoughts or deeds). At such moments, the nasnās can impose its spite on the victim if it penetrates his Magic Resistance. If it succeeds, the victim is assailed with sinful thoughts and acquires the Personality Trait Spiteful with a score equal to the number of Might points the demon spent (one to three points). When the victim is next presented with the opportunity to act spitefully, he must roll a simple die and add his Spiteful score: to resist these impulses, the result must be lower than the total of another simple die plus any other Personality Trait opposed to that spite, such as Loving, Affectionate, etc. (if the victim has any other Personality Trait similar to Spiteful, its score is subtracted). If the spite total is lower, the nasnās's power fails and the victim loses the Spiteful Trait. If, on the other hand, it is higher, the victim gives in to sin and permanently acquires the Personality Trait Spiteful at +1 (or increases it by one if he already has it). From then on, whenever the victim succumbs to spite again, it counts as a sinful act and not as one induced by the nasnās. Given this power's low Initiative, the nasnās rarely uses it in combat.
>
>*Envisioning*, 1 or 5 points, Init +0, Mentem<br>
>With this power, the nasnās can slip into the dreams of a sleeping target (at a cost of one point) or make the target experience a waking dream or vision (at a cost of five points). When it assails a sleeper, the nasnās cannot make substantial changes to the dreams immediately, but must twist them little by little so that they grow ever darker and more frightening, and it can speak through any figure from the victim's subconscious. When the nasnās induces a vision, on the other hand, the victim suffers a sudden and powerful hallucination, to the point of being stunned for a round and having to make a Brave Personality Trait roll against an Ease Factor of 9. If the roll fails, the victim has an extreme reaction, such as retching, convulsions or abject terror. This is the only way the nasnās can communicate with mortals while in its spiritual form.
>
>*Flay*, 5 points, Init +3, Corpus<br>
>The nasnās can flay the skin from mortals it touches (in combat, its claw attack must inflict damage) if it overcomes their Magic Resistance. If the victim has been affected by its *Obsession* power, he suffers a Heavy Wound; otherwise he takes +1 damage. Armor offers no protection against this power.
>
>**Weakness:** Running water (the nasnās cannot cross natural watercourses).<br>
>**Vis:** 4 pawns of Corpus vis in its arm and its leg.<br>
>**Appearance:** In Arab folklore, the nasnās is an apelike monster with a single foot and a single arm, which moves about in great leaps at high speed. The Arabs believe it was begotten by a demon called Shiqq and a human being, and it is said that its touch can kill mortals, who are flayed within seconds. The nasnās's body is covered with thick dark hair, with patches of even blacker hair spattering its back and limbs. Its hand and foot end in powerful claws, and its face, twisted into a terrible grimace, frames a great mouth of pointed teeth that opens within a bristling beard.

<!-- p. 273 -->

##### ʿAmrīl al-Muntaqim al-Praliḥī

As Zarwāl's former apprentice, ʿAmrīl cannot stand Gonçalvo, but he has had to tolerate him because of the power of Duresca, the senior covenant — a power he has watched dwindle since Fortún of Guernicus became *disceptator*.

Since 1137 ʿAmrīl has not missed a single Tribunal, and he follows every move of Duresca and House Guernicus closely; he even breaks the Code by reading Gonçalvo's correspondence. In 1220 he is determined to change al-Minẓār's course, for he knows of the appointment of the new Prima of House Guernicus and that Fortún's days are probably numbered. Now that he is a mature magus and has the help of his *filius* (the young magus Maḍà, who calls his master by the *laqab* Al-Muntaqim, meaning "the avenger"), ʿAmrīl will seek the best moment to murder Gonçalvo and be rid of the Order of Hermes once and for all, for he has no intention of returning to it once he achieves his aim. Distasteful as he would find it, if his companion Šarīfah Muhŷa stood in his way he would confront her, and might even end up killing her.

##### Maḍà al-Praliḥī

Maḍà was named a magus at the Tribunal of 1214 and, for as long as he can remember, he recalls every injustice the *pontifex* Gonçalvo has committed against the covenant. As such, he is a great ally of ʿAmrīl and, although he does not possess a jinni as powerful as his *parens*'s, he knows that any help is worth having.

### Aedes Iris (Mercer House)

>**Lifespan:** 983–1123<br>
>**Founders:** Umm al-Kirām al-Sayyida al-Kubrà al-Merkeriyya, Ibn Ḥawqal al-Merkerī (Redcap)<br>
>**Aura (type and strength):** None<br>
>**Reputations:** None

Named in honor of the goddess Iris (sister of Arke, both messengers during the Titanomachy), this Mercer House was founded by the explorer Umm al-Kirām after she returned to Iberia from her journey through African lands. Of all the places she might have chosen to raise the Tribunal's Mercer House in Africa, she picked the beautiful oasis of Tāfīlālt, a few kilometers north of the city of Siŷilmāsa, an important crossroads between Marrākeš and the gold lands of *bilad al-Sūdān*.

#### History

Umm al-Kirām traveled across North Africa with a group of Redcaps that included the excellent cartographer Ibn Ḥawqal. Her expedition sailed from the port of Malaga and took on supplies at Ceuta, from where it traced a route through the coastal settlements of Melilla, Hippo, Skikda, Jijel, Algiers, Cherchell, Tenés, Aršqūl and Tunis, a city where the group rested before heading down to the populous city of Qayrawān in order to travel overland along the main North African communication route. The expedition then crossed the Hodna corridor (leaving the Aurès massif to the south) until it reached the city of Ṭubna, from which it followed a route stopping at the towns of al-Māsila, Tāhart, Tlemcen, Madīnat Fās and, finally, Siŷilmāsa, where almost all the members of the expedition remained. From that point Umm traveled the gold route until she reached what would be her destination, the city of Kumbi Sāliḥ (capital of Gāna), where the king lived in a glass palace surrounded by forests inhabited by pagan sorcerers and hierophants unknown until then.

To earn the king's respect, Umm and Ibn Ḥawqal had to defeat the evil spirit Ashmeday[^p273-68] (once captured and banished to the Egyptian desert by the archangel Raphael), who proved a terrible adversary. When the maga showed that the demon had been annihilated, the monarch of Kumbi Sāliḥ heaped treasures upon them and granted them great tracts of land containing rich and plentiful vis sources. Thanks to their deeds, the hierophants of Kumbi Sāliḥ taught them some of their rites and even, as her journals hint, initiated her into their mysteries. With the riches she had been granted, Umm al-Kirām crossed the desert back to Siŷilmāsa, from where, together with the Redcaps she had left there, she returned to Iberia.

[^p273-68]: This demon of ancient Persia, responsible for the deaths of Sarah's first seven husbands, is credited with many ancient constructions, such as the Roman bridges or the aqueduct of Segovia.

> #### The Mystery of *bilad al-Sūdān*
>
> The Hermetic scholars of the Peninsula do not believe in the truthfulness of the *risāla* that recounts Umm's travels, since the theories that exist about the peoples living beyond the Sahara rule out any possible contact. The most extreme of them suggests that the Sudanese may be faeries and that their lands exist only in the Faerie Realm. To accept the truth of Umm's *risāla* would therefore mean admitting that the Order had reached the end of the world and crossed it… and that is something almost no one is willing to accept.

The charter of Aedes Iris was ratified at the Tribunal of 983, which led to the creation of Porta Pandere seven years later. When the Iberian assembly allowed communication between Aedes Iris and the Portuguese Mercer House by means of the *Tertius Decimus* portal, the Andalusi magi began to call Umm al-Kirām Al-Sayyida al-Kubrà ("the great lady").

During its lifetime, Aedes Iris mapped many vis sources, which Umm al-Kirām kept secret, and indirectly controlled many places of importance for kilometers around (among its most notable holdings was the prosperous Maghrebi port city of Masrsā Farrūj). When the Schism War broke out, the African Mercer House stayed on the sidelines and supported the breakup of the Tribunal by joining the magi of al-Andalus, which led Porta Pandere to follow suit (wagging tongues claimed that the Redcaps of Iberia wanted to get their hands on the vis sources that Umm al-Kirām jealously guarded in the lands of *bilad al-Sūdān*, and so, even at the risk of upsetting the outcome of the Schism War, they joined the Tribunal of al-Andalus).

<!-- p. 274 -->

Umm al-Kirām and Ibn Ḥawqal lived their best years in Africa and brought prosperity to the Tribunal of al-Andalus, sharing with it the riches they carried from *bilad al-Sūdān* so that the hated Iberian tax could be abolished. Their management of Aedes Iris was always exemplary, so much so that when the Almoravids reached Siŷilmāsa in 1055 they were able to adapt to the new circumstances without losing a single one of their privileges. Not without reason, the maga was one of the most beloved figures among the magi of al-Andalus.

In old age they withdrew from political life and, in their last days, were able to enjoy the Tribunals of Joy, when the Tribunal was governed with justice and fairness. Fortunately, they did not live to see the Tribunal of 1082, nor did they witness the handing over of al-Andalus's records to Iberia, which would surely have broken their hearts.

After the deaths of Umm al-Kirām and Ibn Ḥawqal, Porta Pandere wrote to the new head asking him to send to Lisbon the documents and maps showing the locations of Aedes Iris's vis sources. However, only a few vague notes and the locations of minor sources reached the Portuguese Mercer House. The head of Aedes Iris kept stalling until, in 1103, Porta Pandere sent a delegation to take over the covenant. To their surprise, the records of Umm al-Kirām and Ibn Ḥawqal were incomplete: rather vague at best and wholly nonexistent at worst. When they asked the head for an explanation, the Redcap replied that Umm al-Kirām and Ibn Ḥawqal had never shared that information with anyone. Porta Pandere put all the inhabitants of Aedes Iris on trial and placed a new head in charge. The Redcaps who had covered for Umm al-Kirām were abandoned in the desert without food or water, and the African covenant came under the direct tutelage of Porta Pandere.

From then on the Redcaps tried, without success, to find the rich vis sources of *bilad al-Sūdān*, and after twenty years of fruitless searching the covenant was mysteriously destroyed (see page 90). All the Tribunal learned of that night was that the *Tertius Decimus* portal was hastily sealed. When the magi made use of their Arcane Connections to Aedes Iris, they discovered that these had been severed, and so they had to prepare and fund a costly expedition to reach Africa once more. When they reached their destination a year later, they saw that not only the Mercer House but also the city of Siŷilmāsa had been destroyed. With its disappearance, Porta Pandere stopped receiving the gold of *bilad al-Sūdān* and had to close its mint.

#### Setting and Physical Description

The local mundanes made use of the ruins of Aedes Iris to build their own houses. In 1220, those ashlars carved with Hermetic symbols can be found scattered among many of the buildings of the magnificent oasis of Tāfīlālt. The few magi who have returned to the site have not even managed to locate the old underground chamber that housed the *Tertius Decimus* portal, although it seems inconceivable to them that it should simply have vanished. In any case, with the law against them ("On al-ʿIdwa" [1123]) and for fear of being attacked, few have dared to venture into African lands again.

> #### Story Seeds: "By the Lord of the Kaaba!"[^p274-XXIV]
>
> *When you desire my presence, recite these verses:*
>
> *Come to my aid, loving Zuhair, 'Azza. If memories call upon him, he will come to them. If one day a mouth speaks my name, I think that I kiss it; I go to the houses of those who call upon me, though sands lie between us, for my love answers theirs.*[^p274-XXV]
>
> When one of the player characters' poet *saḥirs* summons a jinni, it demands that the character beat it in a contest of wits before it will begin negotiating with him. During the contest, if the character succeeds on an Intelligence + Iberian Tribunal Lore (history) roll of 6+, he will notice that its rhymes contain references to Aedes Iris and Umm al-Kirām.
>
> The jinni is none other than Láfiz ibn al-Láfiz, an ancient and powerful spirit that served Imru-l-Qays in antiquity, and Umm al-Kirām after she visited the priests of Kumbi Sāliḥ and became imbued with the spirit of the great priestess Al-Kāhina. The jinni may well know the secrets of the legendary sources that Umm al-Kirām took to her grave. How can the player character obtain that information?
>
> [^p274-XXIV]: This is an expression commonly used by the Muslims of Iberia.
>
> [^p274-XXV]: Poem from *The Treatise of Familiar Spirits and Demons* by Ibn Shuhayd (Spanish translation by Salvador Barberá). In the story, Xuhaid's familiar spirit is Zuhair ibn Numair, of the jinn tribe of Axya'.
