<!-- p. 276 -->

# X. Magical Traditions

*[…] the magician is without any doubt devoted to idolatry, even though he follows special and strange ways, different from those usual among the multitude, in the worship of the false gods.*[^p276-1]

Although the Order of Hermes is the most powerful magical organization in the Peninsula in the thirteenth century, it is by no means the only one. Other, lesser traditions coexist with the Hermetic magi, not always harmoniously, and some of them trace their origins back even further than the founding of the Order itself. This chapter describes some of the most important, along with the information needed by anyone who wishes to create a character from one of them. It also describes two Ex Miscellanea traditions and presents some ideas on the Rationalist, Kabbalistic and Ṣūfī philosophical currents. Finally, at the end of the chapter you will find the new Abilities, Virtues and Flaws named throughout the book.

## Non-Hermetic Traditions

This section provides information on the riadiins of Madrid, the astral sorcerers of Cordoba, the tiryāqi and the distaurnanja, along with some ideas for introducing the vitkir, or rune wizards, into your saga.

### The Distaurnanja

This minor hedge tradition counts some three dozen practitioners across all of Iberia, and its lineage is said to reach back to the original clans of the Visigoths who first invaded the Roman Empire. The distaurnanja (from the Gothic, "those who shatter") imbue with magic short phrases written on scraps of parchment, engraved on strips of metal or painted on small ribbons, in order to protect themselves from the enchantments of other wizards and to create tools or weapons capable of shattering the spells and effects of other hedge wizards, faeries and lesser demons. As a rule, its members pass on their knowledge orally, and they do so in Gothic: since very few speak the language fluently, and written texts are fewer still, the tradition is a rather fragile one.

Despite their ancestry, the distaurnanja are Christians (the Visigoths of the Peninsula embraced Christianity in the sixth century). Nevertheless, many have taken them for pagans throughout history, so in 1220 their few members are wary of displaying their magic or their leanings in public. This would be of interest to most covenants, which would be more than happy to welcome them as companions. However, almost no distaurnanja can overcome the mistrust the Gift provokes.

#### History

When the Visigoths crossed Gaul and established their kingdom in the Peninsula, the distaurnanja were a minor tradition devoted to hunting the many wyverns that infested the Pyrenees. Before the arrival of the Muslims, the distaurnanja had already had a couple of encounters with the tempestarii and the sorginas, but being so few in number, they had given way before the power of the local wizards. After all, the seat of the distaurnanja had always been Toledo, and the north of the Peninsula was a distant place to them.

With the coming of the Muslims, the Visigothic capital passed into the hands of the emirate, and the distaurnanja took part in the city's many revolts to win independence from Cordoba. It is said that the leader of the distaurnanja and several of his apprentices died on the Day of the Ditch (see page 21), which thinned their ranks and made their members far more secretive; they restricted knowledge of their arts to the sons, daughters, nieces and nephews of the distaurnanja, and only on rare occasions taught them to their closest friends.

#### The Coming of the Order and After
It seems unlikely that the distaurnanja were aware of the Order's arrival in the Peninsula. They must, however, have come into contact with it when Grimoald Niger reached Toledo (at least according to a small fragment of the *Comentarii de Bello Iberico* in which they are named; see page 63). According to the records, the distaurnanja rejected the offers of Val-Negra's emissaries, and the Flambeau responded by burning their three representatives. When the rest of the distaurnanja learned of the massacre, despite their warlike spirit, they fled the city and headed north. In Saragossa they discovered that the newborn Order was there to stay, and for years their contact was reduced to small, violent encounters with the Hermetic magi. The distaurnanja were no match for the Order, however, and they ended up scattering even further and cutting their gatherings and the transmission of their knowledge to the bare minimum.

[^p276-1]: Excerpt from *The Guide for the Perplexed* by Maimonides (Spanish translation by David Gonzalo Maeso).

<!-- p. 277 -->

Some distaurnanja had the chance to settle the score at Alarcos, where the Flambeau of Harra had gone to fight (see page 94). Led by Arturo de Compostela, a small group of distaurnanja took advantage of the Muslim armies to attack their Hermetic enemies. They never had the chance to take their revenge, however: the magi had already been crushed by other, superior and unknown forces. Although the Christians lost the day at Alarcos, Arturo faced the future with hope for the first time: the Order was not omnipotent in Iberia, and the distaurnanja had to take advantage of its weakness to end the centuries of ostracism to which they had been subjected. And so Arturo traveled the Peninsula, telling the distaurnanja he knew what he had seen and inspiring them to begin training new members (indeed, one of them fought at Las Navas de Tolosa). In 1220, the distaurnanja seem ready to take on a more active role.

#### Current Situation

The distaurnanja have no real organization. They have no declared leader and no seat of government. Normally each knows only two or three practitioners of this magic, so no distaurnanja knows all the others. The victories of the last two generations have inspired the younger distaurnanja, allowing them to relive the victories of their forebears in Toledo and the Pyrenees. Some of their members take an active part in the struggle against the Muslims, although most are content to protect their immediate communities and survive.

Some of the distaurnanja who ended up in the kingdom of Navarre after their diaspora have come into conflict with the sorginas by using their magic to break the witches' curses. The distaurnanja do not mean to make enemies of them, however, but only to help the communities in which the Visigothic wizards live. Of course, the sorginas' coven does not see it that way, and has decided to drive the distaurnanja out of its territories or, in extreme cases, to do away with them.

Elsewhere, the distaurnanja devote themselves to protecting the roads, or the shepherds' flocks, from the hungry wyverns of the Pyrenees.

Most of the distaurnanja live in northern Iberia, among the kingdoms of Leon, Castile, Navarre and Aragon. The distaurnanja have roughly eighteen known active factions, the most important in Compostela, Toledo, Pamplona and Jaca. Arturo leads Compostela, where he has trained his two sons, the illegitimate son of a priest, and two nuns who do not practice. They often argue in Toledo with Pedro del Mar, a former pirate, and with the children of Pedro's late brother (who died during a raid on Majorca), whom the pirate is raising as his own. Another group operates in Pamplona, and a fourth group is said to be established in Jaca, where two brothers devote themselves to hunting *saḥirs*.

> #### Story Seeds: The Sorgina's Curse
>
> A group of grogs slips off without permission to get drunk in a nearby village, and later discovers that a witch has put the evil eye on them. They cannot ask the magi for help, because they would get into trouble for having broken the covenant's rules, but neither can they go home while the spell still affects them. So they will have to seek out the distaurnanja who lives on the outskirts of the village and carry out one of his commissions in exchange for the ritual needed to undo the sorgina's hex. Although that might solve their most immediate problems, the sorginas do not take insults lightly: the grogs may have earned themselves an enemy who will be waiting for them when they go back without the magi.

#### Customs

Despite their lack of organization, there is one place that all the distaurnanja know: a cave hidden in the Montes de Toledo. On the walls of the cavern's deepest grottoes, the creed of the distaurnanja is carved in Gothic. If read by a distaurnanja with a score of 4 in Gothic and 5 or more in one of the tradition's Abilities, it can be used to initiate others, or himself, into the Virtues of Abjuration or Protective Bindings, provided he has a score of 3 in Distaurnanja Lore. Written as a symbolic parable detailing scenes from the Gothic Bible, the carving has made the cave a place of pilgrimage for the tradition's members. Nevertheless, a few distaurnanja (above all in the south) have never even visited it, despite knowing it exists.

Likewise, since they lack structure, they also have few defined rituals. Even so, slaying a wyvern in the Pyrenees is usually considered the final test before one may train apprentices of one's own or be considered a master. Being a tradition of oral transmission, there are almost no written books on their magical arts (in fact, only some three *tractatus* and one low-Quality *summa* exist). Magi who wish to incorporate these powers into Hermetic theory (chiefly, they emulate Hermetic Perdo magic and Penetration) will have to achieve a minor breakthrough (see *Houses of Hermes: True Lineages*, page 29).

The distaurnanja are not pagans, and they believe their abilities are a divine gift (although they belong to the Magic Realm). To them it would be unthinkable to create protections against angels or other divine creatures, although they are aware that many priests do not understand the origin of their magic. This situation forces them to keep their powers hidden (revealing them only to those they trust most) or to disguise them as blessings or prayers. When discovered by more zealous priests, most distaurnanja flee, preferring not to risk explaining their practices to the less tolerant; the Order is aware of the existence of some of these fugitive distaurnanja.

<!-- p. 278 -->

#### Distaurnanja Magic

The magical Abilities of the distaurnanja, Abjuration and Protective Bindings, are Accelerated Abilities (see page 309). A character with the Gift can learn these Abilities, which can also be acquired during character creation as Major Supernatural Virtues. The distaurnanja do not consider hedge wizards from other parts of the world with similar abilities (such as the columbae or the African settuten) to be part of their tradition. The distaurnanja are mostly of the lineage of the ancient Visigoths. This relative isolation means that no Gifted distaurnanja has yet been found who was trained as a Hermetic magus after learning Abjuration or Protective Bindings.

The powers of the distaurnanja are aligned with the Magic Realm.

#### Abjuration

The distaurnanja know Abjuration, a kind of magic that can directly harm supernatural creatures or cancel their powers or active spells. Depending on its strength, an abjuration can prevent a single type of spell from affecting the bearer or the target to be protected, or even weaken or kill a supernatural creature affected by the bearer of the abjuration.

Once the distaurnanja has completed the spell he imbues into the ribbon, it must be wrapped around the object to be protected and its two ends joined together with pitch, glue or sap. They can also be tied or nailed. The symbols are inscribed in the Gothic alphabet, and they define the type of spells or creatures that will be affected or harmed by the magic. These types of spells must be roughly equivalent to those a Minor Magical Focus would cover, that is, a specific area within a Hermetic Form, such as "controlled bodies" (Corpus), "created fire" (Ignem), "altered minds" (Mentem) or "exploding stones" (Terram). Types of creature are defined by the supernatural realm to which they belong. The definition can be more specific (for example, to affect a particular spell), and Arcane Connections can be incorporated into the ribbon to include or exclude a subject from the abjuration and give it additional power.

Once the ribbon has been tied or fastened, the distaurnanja imbues his magic into it, which always costs him a Fatigue level. To do so, he makes a stress roll, adding his Stamina, his Abjuration score, any aura modifier and any other appropriate modifier, including the distaurnanja's Penetration score.

**Abjuration Casting Total: Stamina + Abjuration + Penetration + aura + stress die**

The total represents the highest effect level the abjuration can cancel, or the highest creature Might it can affect; the abjuration total is also its Penetration Total, and indicates the number of Abjuration points it holds. When the abjuration cancels a spell or harms a creature, it loses a number of Abjuration points equal to the magnitude of the spell or the creature's Might. When it is used to attack a creature of the specified realm with a Might equal to or less than the total, a successful attack permanently reduces the creature's Might points by one fifth of the abjuration total (rounding up). Creatures reduced to Might 0 are destroyed. When the abjuration loses a number of Abjuration points equal to its total, it unravels and is destroyed. If the abjuration is used to attack a creature whose Might exceeds its total, the abjuration is also destroyed. The same happens if the abjuration tries to cancel a spell of a level higher than the abjuration total.

<!-- p. 279 -->

Incorporating an Arcane Connection to a specific creature doubles the abjuration total, but further limits the abjuration's potential targets.

A distaurnanja can have only one abjuration active at a time.

#### Protective Bindings

The distaurnanja practice the art of Protective Bindings, a kind of magic that can protect its target against supernatural creatures and their powers and spells. A protective binding acts directly on supernatural creatures and magical effects, preventing them in turn from affecting the protected target. Depending on its strength, a protective binding can prevent a specific type of spell from affecting the protected target, or prevent a supernatural creature from touching or harming the target.

Once a distaurnanja has completed the spell he imbues into the ribbon, it must be wrapped around the object and its two ends joined together with pitch, glue or sap. They can also be tied or nailed. The symbols are inscribed in the Gothic alphabet and define the things against which the ribbon will protect. These types must be roughly equivalent to those a Minor Magical Focus would cover, that is, a specific area within a Hermetic Form, such as "mundane fire" (Ignem), "serpents" (Animal), "metal weapons" (Terram), "demons" (Vim) or "a sorgina's evil eye" (Vim). The definition can be more specific, and Arcane Connections can be incorporated into the ribbon to include or exclude a subject from the protective binding and give it additional power.

Once the ribbon has been tied or fastened, the distaurnanja imbues his magic into it, which always costs him a Fatigue level. To do so, he makes a stress roll, adding his Stamina, his Protective Bindings score, any aura modifier and any other appropriate modifier. Vis can be used on this roll: each pawn adds +2, and he may spend as many pawns as half his Protective Bindings score (rounding up).

**Protective Binding Casting Total: Stamina + Protective Bindings + aura + stress die**

If the protective binding is designed to affect a natural object or type of material, treat the result as the Casting Total of an equivalent Hermetic Rego warding spell of the corresponding Form and level to determine whether the protection affects the target. However, distaurnanja magic is inferior to Hermetic magic in Penetration. Incorporating a suitable Arcane Connection allows the distaurnanja to double his protective binding total. When affecting supernatural creatures or protecting against a magical effect, calculate the Penetration Total as if the spell level were 0, and treat the final Penetration Total as the final effect level. If the distaurnanja has the Penetration Ability, it is added after doubling the total for an Arcane Connection. For example, if the skin of a lord's watchdog is added to a protective binding with a total of 6 to protect the bearer against that lord's pack of dogs, the final total would be 12 (6 × 2 for the penetration multiplier), and that protective binding would prevent the lord's mundane hounds, as well as his magical hound of Might 10, from attacking whoever wears the binding. If the binding protects its bearer from the effect of a spell, the spell's Penetration Total must exceed the protective binding total. If the spell's Penetration exceeds that total, the bearer is affected by the spell and the binding is destroyed.

A distaurnanja can have a number of protective bindings active equal to his Protective Bindings score divided by five, rounding up.

**Active protective bindings: Protective Bindings score/5 (rounding up)**

Thus, a distaurnanja with Protective Bindings 7 could have two protective bindings active. A protective binding ceases to take effect when the ends of the ribbon are no longer joined, when someone cuts it, or when the distaurnanja creates a new protective binding that exceeds his permitted limit, which makes the oldest protective bindings stop working.

> #### Story Seeds: Non Statu Quo
>
> A local merchant has been subtly influenced by magic so that he ignores the Gift and the peculiar behavior of the grogs who frequent his establishment. However, his family, worried by his behavior and by the possible "curse" afflicting the shopkeeper, has hired a distaurnanja. The latter has removed the enchantment that affected the merchant, and is now working for him temporarily as an assistant, intending to discover who was responsible for that enchantment. When he discovers that the covenant has come to restore the cancelled spell, the distaurnanja destroys it again and launches a campaign to bring the wrath of the Church down upon the covenant. Will the magi find out who is destroying their spells, and will they be able to reach some agreement with the Visigothic wizard?

### The Astral Sorcerers of Cordoba

*Were this knowledge revealed to mankind, it would destroy the universe.*[^p279-2]

[^p279-2]: Excerpt from *Ghāyat al-Ḥakīm* (*Picatrix*) by al-Qurṭubī (English translation by Dan Attrell and David Porreca; Spanish translation by Mario Donaire).

<!-- p. 280 -->

#### History

At the beginning of the tenth century, Abū-l-Qāsim Maslama ibn al-Qāsim Ibrāhīm al-Qurṭubī al-Zayyāt was born in Cordoba, and his genius soon made itself known among his peers. It was a happy chance that Petuel al-Ŷerbitonī happened to be in Cordoba at the same time: the man who would found the covenant of ʿÔlām wā-ʿed in Lucena recognized the boy's Gentle Gift and extraordinary intellectual capacities and, without much ceremony, took him with him.

To avoid any conflict with the *saḥirs*, Petuel went to Egypt with the young Maslama al-Qurṭubī, where he began to train him as his apprentice. Egypt was not the only place where the boy had the chance to live, however. For ten years he traveled with his master through North Africa, Greece, Nabataea, Babylonia, Persia and India, and afterwards they finally settled in Lucena, where Petuel founded the covenant of ʿÔlām wā-ʿed. But those journeys sowed a seed in Maslama al-Qurṭubī's soul that stayed with him all his life. He thus completed his apprenticeship with what would become the first *Itinerarium* of House Jerbiton (organized by the archmage Anna of Naples), and, once named a magus, he traveled the whole of the Islamic world on a pilgrimage that took up almost his entire life.

On his travels, al-Qurṭubī (his name as a magus) came to understand that Bonisagus's magic theory showed no regard for God, since it enjoyed its power irreverently and selfishly, and he concluded that the Gift had been perverted by the Order. In his view, the rejection that magi suffered because of the Gift was nothing but a warning from the Most High to mend their ways. On his return to Iberia, al-Qurṭubī joined the Kharijite covenant of Bayt al-Ḥikma, where he developed an alternative magic theory called *ṭillasm* (from the Arabic, "talisman"), which used the magical energy of the stars to work its magic, God willing. Al-Qurṭubī compiled his new magic theory in four voluminous books, which he titled *Ghāyat al-Ḥakīm* (see Appendix I).

Quite apart from the social movement of Bayt al-Ḥikma (see page 78), when al-Qurṭubī finished his magic theory in 956, he underwent an ordeal to align his Gift with that of the stars, and left the Order together with his two *filii*. Al-Qurṭubī failed to gauge the consequences of his actions at the time: although the ritual had left him unable to cast Hermetic magic, he still knew the mysteries of the Parma Magica, and that is what ultimately cost him his life.

Al-Qurṭubī initiated his two students into his magic theory, but he did not teach them Bonisagus's Parma Magica, since he considered it part of the "impious" Hermetic theory, and it was precisely this that saved their lives and allowed his knowledge to survive. In 964, a year after the Kharijites were condemned, the hoplites hunted down al-Qurṭubī and killed him as he was traveling by ship to Egypt. His tradition lived on in those two initiates, who, however, had not been able to learn from their master all the Rationalist secrets of a theory that had only just been born. Consequently, in 1220 the practitioners of this magic are few in number, since they need Gifted boys and girls in order to initiate them into their mysteries. Indeed, this factor (together with their characteristic humility) is essential to their survival, since if they recruited many aspirants, the Order would find itself competing with them for those born with the Gift and would surely end up annihilating them.

Although many members of al-Qurṭubī's lineage have continued to travel throughout their lives, in 1220 there is a "school" in the city of Cordoba where these conjurers can be found in small numbers (no more than three). If a Hermetic maga ever took an interest in their rigid and restricted magical scheme, and came to discover that this theory breaks many of the Hermetic limits, her interest could resonate throughout the whole Order.

#### Philosophy

These sorcerers belong to the magical tradition of Platonic Orientalism (see the insert "Emanationist Theory" on page 304), which holds that all magic derives from a single, imperishable tradition that unites all the sages of the known world and whose origins can be traced back to Plato, Pythagoras, Orpheus, Moses, Hermes Trismegistus, Enoch, Zoroaster and Adam. In reality, this "tradition of knowledge" is a manifestation of the mystical Platonic idealism of Antiquity, syncretized with the religions of the peoples conquered by Hellenism.

The magic of this tradition is based on natural magic rather than theurgic mysticism, and its foundations rest on Aristotle's *Theology* (translated in Baghdad in the ninth century, although it also has roots in Greek, Egyptian, Babylonian, Arabian and Indian natural philosophies), which was the principal Neoplatonic source in the medieval Arab world. This tradition manipulates the invisible flow of cosmic energy that radiates from the firmament of the stars and that, on its way to the Earth, passes through the planetary spheres, pervading everything in its path. According to the astral sorcerers, behind this "magical" energy there are spirits with whom the wise (that is, those of upright and pious life and great learning in natural philosophy and the liberal arts) can communicate by following complex rituals. Indeed, the fundamental basis of this theory regards the planetary powers as volitional forces that constitute the hidden mechanisms of a cosmos governed by the will of God.

For the astral sorcerers, magic is a noble and hieratic art; it is the mark of the true mystic, not of the madman who has given himself over to infernal pacts (as the Hermetic magi have). The pursuit of magic must be a pure act aimed at knowing God and His creation, since He alone is above all things. For this reason, the impure and the foolish must not have access to this magic. Magic is thus the inevitable consequence of a fervent contemplative life, and its practitioners are required to show wisdom, ritual purity and discretion. Only upright people who are astrologically predisposed (see the insert "The Astronomers" on page 74) will be able to use this power.

This type of magic works through talismans (*telsam* in Latin, *ṭillasm* in Arabic), or "images," which channel stellar energy from the macrocosm to the microcosm. This magic is thus the art of binding spirits to matter, and so there is nothing "demonic" about it.

<!-- p. 281 -->

> #### Cosmology
>
> The universe is made up of a series of concentric spheres composed of ethereal substances. At the center of the cosmos lies the material world, made up of the four elements, which arrange themselves naturally according to their density. The densest elements (water and earth) sink to the center of the cosmos, and the lightest (fire and air) rise toward the heavens. Ascending beyond the realm of the four elements, one leaves behind the microcosmic (lesser) world and enters the macrocosmic (greater) world.
>
> The first of the planetary spheres, the Moon, is a silver gate leading from the sublunar world (the world of matter and corruption) to the supralunar world (the world of spirits and creative source). From the lunar sphere onward, the cosmos is not made of elemental matter: the planets (in the following order: the Moon, Mercury, Venus, the Sun, Mars, Jupiter and Saturn) are formed of immaterial spiritual substances that radiate their power downward. Beyond the planetary spheres lies the eighth sphere, the ring of the zodiac, through which the planets move. Beyond the eighth sphere lies the *Primum Mobile*, or the veil covering the empyrean, which produces the daily turning of the firmament and acts as a perforated shield before the light and glory of God. Beyond these cosmological spheres is God, whose dwelling is infinite space.

#### Magic

*We call "magic" those acts whose performance absorbs the spirit and the senses, and which result in a miracle worthy of contemplation that produces wonder.*[^p281-3]

Everything that exists between the Earth and the divine principle can be affected by magic. It is not known, however, at which level of the cosmology magic acts, since it can affect everything equally. The sorcerer must bear the responsibility of understanding all the hidden correspondences (called "affinities") between the plants, animals and minerals of the sublunar world and the spiritual forces of the heavenly bodies of the supralunar world. With this knowledge he can gather all the necessary sympathetic materials and use them to invoke the planetary spirits that belong to the nature of his goal. For example, invoking Venus in rituals of love or seduction might require copper plates, fumigations of saffron and "things of moderate heat and excessive moisture."

Through the sympathetic resonances between the gathered objects and their respective heavenly bodies, the sorcerer can use his power to bring about a change in the world. It is thus the sorcerer's task to gather materials tirelessly, to make talismans, to spend countless nights watching the sky, to read astrological charts and celestial maps carefully, to pay close attention to the slightest detail of astronomical positions, and then, by the grace of God, to make nature act.

Each planet governs its own set of plants, animals or minerals, but also its own psychology, professions, places, languages and peoples. Astrological considerations are fundamental to magic, to the point that the sorcerer might have to wait for years (in game terms, this only happens if the roll to determine the lunar mansion is botched; see below) for the right celestial circumstance to occur that will let him carry out what he wishes. In the meantime, the sorcerer must prepare himself by choosing the best locations, clothing, fumigations, sacrifices, tinctures and, most importantly, magical images. In astrological magic, all particulars contain universals, and all things in the sublunar world have their reflection in the supralunar world.

#### The Mystery of the Gift of the Zodiac

The upright individual becomes wise by adhering to divine law; through his wisdom, the sage is naturally inclined to acquire knowledge and is drawn toward God's creation (through the study of the liberal arts, medicine and so on). The natural conclusion of leading an upright life while appreciating the natural order of creation (that is, loving God's creation) is thus a kind of gnosis (a holistic knowledge of Neoplatonic cosmology that places mortals as mediators between God and the material world). Once the knowledge of how the world is truly ordered (that is, its threefold division into matter, spirit and intellect) is revealed, one obtains the metaphysical framework within which to perform magical operations. For this reason, the astral sorcerers use the Artes Liberales Ability to initiate others into the Mystery of the Gift of the Zodiac.

These magical operations are carried out through complex rituals in which a *ṭillasm* is made from sympathetic and Arcane Connections to summon the supralunar energy of the celestial spheres. To be able to work magic, the sorcerer must be initiated through the only Script al-Qurṭubī left behind, for which he must have one of the following Virtues: the Gift, Failed Apprentice, a suitable variant of Mythic Blood, or Latent Magical Ability. In addition, he may not have any of the following Flaws: Tainted with Evil, Infamous, Ambitious, Avaricious, Envious, Gluttonous, Wrathful, Lecherous, Hatred, Proud, Compulsion, Obsessed or Dark Secret. Once initiated, the sorcerer gains the Major Supernatural Virtue The Gift of the Zodiac, which grants him the Accelerated Ability Ṭillasm at 1 (see "New Abilities" on page 309).

### Initiation into the Mystery of the Gift of the Zodiac

**Ease Factor:** 21 (Major Virtue known by the mystagogue)

**Script Bonus:** +16

**Script Details:** The initiate must make a pilgrimage to Mecca (Quest, +1) and then sacrifice his Gift to align it with the stars, gaining in turn the Major Flaw Pious (Major Ordeal, +9). Once this is done, he must spend a season with the mystagogue (Time Commitment by the mystagogue, +3) studying the mansions of the Moon and the conjunctions with the planets (Sympathetic Bonus, +3). Note that the mystagogue's Initiation Total will be equal to his Presence + Artes Liberales + the Initiation Script Bonus.

[^p281-3]: Excerpt from *Ghāyat al-Ḥakīm* (*Picatrix*) by al-Qurṭubī (English translation by Dan Attrell and David Porreca; Spanish translation by Mario Donaire).

<!-- p. 282 -->

#### The Rituals of the Zodiac

All astral conjurations require rituals in order to be performed, and these take a season to cast. No one without the Virtue The Gift of the Zodiac can use this magic.

The rituals of astrological magic are based on observing the heavenly bodies and making a talisman (*ṭillasm*), a word meaning "that to which power over something is granted." The sorcerer cannot make a useful talisman if he lacks the necessary ingredients (each five points of the conjuration's Ease Factor represent one pound in ingredient costs, rounding up) or if he fails to determine the necessary conjunction with the lunar mansion during that season, for which he must succeed in an Intelligence + Artes Liberales roll against an Ease Factor of 9.

**Determining the lunar mansion: Intelligence + Artes Liberales + stress die**

If the roll succeeds, the sorcerer determines the horoscope precisely and can undertake the task of creating the talisman in order to carry out the ritual (so the ritual materials are spent at this point). If the roll fails, the sorcerer loses the season trying to draw up the astrological chart. If the roll is botched, the sorcerer believes the desired conjunction will occur later on, and wastes four seasons searching for ingredients, drawing up astrological charts and creating a talisman that will be of no use, so he also loses whatever material components he has used in the process. He still gains Exposure experience, however.

> #### The Mansions of the Moon
>
> The sorcerer uses the power of the mansions of the Moon (the thirteen days the Moon spends in the signs of the zodiac) to channel the power of the stars. According to the *Ghāyat al-Ḥakīm* there are twenty-eight mansions, each suited to a different purpose (see "Conjurations" below).
>
> | Mansion | Zodiac |
> | --- | --- |
> | *Alnath* | Aries |
> | *Albotain* | Aries |
> | *Azoraya* | Aries and Taurus |
> | *Aldebaran* | Taurus |
> | *Almices* | Taurus and Gemini |
> | *Athaya* | Gemini |
> | *Aldirah* | Gemini |

Once the astrological chart has been successfully drawn up, the sorcerer can use the talisman to draw down the influence of the spirits of the supralunar world through the energy they emanate, and undertake the performance of the ritual over the rest of the season. It is at this point that the sorcerer generates a Casting Total, which he compares against the Ease Factor of the conjuration he is casting (see "Conjurations" below) to learn whether he has succeeded. This Casting Total is also used to calculate the Penetration Total (just as it is calculated for Hermetic magic, although no Penetration bonus can be applied, since these rituals always consume the magical energy of the sympathetic connections in their casting), treating the conjuration's Ease Factor as its level for these purposes.

**Casting Total: Intelligence + Ṭillasm + bonuses + aura + stress die**

The bonuses may be the following.

- **Vis**. Vis related to the conjuration being cast grants a bonus of +2 per pawn to the Casting Total. A sorcerer can use as many pawns of vis as his Ṭillasm score, and rolls one additional botch die per pawn used (all the vis is consumed by the casting).

- **Sacrifices**. The most powerful act in the rituals is the sacrifice of animals (the animal to be sacrificed is determined by astrological influences, at the storyguide's discretion). This act creates a resonance upon the tangible world thanks to the solemnity of the sacrifice and to the force imparted by imposing human will upon the life of another being. The explanation for this lies in the powerful impact on the material world created by the sudden release of the animals' energy (called *rūḥāniyyāt*, or spiritual powers) when they are killed violently. The shock wave of the *rūḥāniyyāt* disturbs the universal harmony and affects the natural world, which allows it to be altered by magic. Animal sacrifices grant a bonus to the Casting Total equal to the creature's Size +1. A sorcerer can perform as many sacrifices during a ritual as his Ṭillasm score, and rolls one additional botch die per animal sacrificed. Animals smaller than Size 0 grant no bonus.

<!-- p. 283 -->

- **Exceptional ingredients**. The sorcerer may have used quality ingredients (that is, three times as costly as normal ingredients) while making the talisman, which grants +5 to the Casting Total.

- **Mastered conjuration score**. The sorcerer can add one point for each level he has in the Ability for the mastered conjuration (see below).

Supernatural auras influence astrological magic as set out in the "Supernatural Realms Interaction Table," and also add as many botch dice as the absolute value of the modifier they apply to the Casting Total.

> #### Supernatural Realms Interaction Table
>**Divine aura:** +3 × level<br>
>**Magic aura:** +level<br>
>**Faerie aura:** –level<br>
>**Infernal aura:** –3 × level

If the roll meets or exceeds the conjuration's Ease Factor, the desired effect occurs and the sorcerer loses one Fatigue level from exhaustion. If the roll fails by ten points or less, the conjuration works, but the sorcerer loses three Fatigue levels from exhaustion. If the roll fails by more than ten points, the sorcerer loses three Fatigue levels from exhaustion and fails to channel the magic, so the conjuration has no effect. If the roll is botched, the sorcerer stirs up the forces he is trying to control and receives a punishment of greater or lesser severity depending on the number of zeroes rolled (the storyguide decides what kind of punishment he receives, but it could mean losing The Gift of the Zodiac for some years, acquiring a Supernatural Flaw, or even a misfortune associated with the place where he lives).

#### Twilight and Warping

As true users of magic, the astral sorcerers are subject to Twilight, as set out in the magic rules on page 141 of *Ars Magica Fifth Edition*. Likewise, the targets of their conjurations also gain Warping (just as with Hermetic magic; see *Ars Magica Fifth Edition*, page 248), treating the conjuration's Ease Factor as the effect level.

#### Learning Conjurations

The astral sorcerers take a season to learn any of the thirty conjurations that al-Qurṭubī codified (all of them collected in the *Ghāyat al-Ḥakīm*). To learn them, they need fulfill no requirement other than possessing The Gift of the Zodiac and having a laboratory (see "A Riadiin's Laboratory," page 288).

#### Laboratory Texts

Any astral sorcerer can spend a season producing a legible laboratory text of all the conjurations he knows.

#### Mastered Conjuration Abilities

Every astral sorcerer can master the conjurations he knows, thereby gaining an Ability named after each. This Ability has no specialty, and its score is added to the Casting Total of the zodiac ritual, with no other benefit.

#### Conjurations

Below are the descriptions of the thirty conjurations that al-Qurṭubī taught his two apprentices; there are, however, other conjurations that were lost in the tenth century after his death, and whose rituals remained obscure in the *Ghāyat al-Ḥakīm*. Among them are *Grant Someone Good Fortune*, *Bring Things into Balance*, *Poison the Besiegers*, *Enhance the Works of Alchemy*, *Destroy Ships*, *Curse Those Who Travel by Ship*… Today's astral sorcerers wonder whether an additional mystery rite will be needed to uncover all these secrets, because when they have tried to use those rituals they have generally ended in catastrophe.

None of the following thirty conjurations can be varied in the slightest, and all must penetrate any Magic Resistance to take effect; the approximate Form of each is given for this purpose (the Technique is added for information only). In addition, all conjurations with a duration longer than Momentary can be dispelled with Hermetic spells: for these purposes, their level is considered equal to their Ease Factor. Finally, the sorcerer can manipulate as many sympathetic Arcane Connections as his Ṭillasm score.

All these conjurations (that is, determining the mansion of the Moon, the necessary preparation and the casting itself) take a season to perform (so the sorcerer gains two experience points from Exposure). For the sake of simplicity, the Moon is assumed to be in the right mansion for the sorcerer once per season.

For benevolent rituals, the Moon must be safe from Saturn and Mars alike and from the rays of the Sun, and the reverse must hold to conjure malevolent rituals.

<!-- p. 284 -->

### Protect Travelers by Land (PeMe 35)

The sorcerer can beseech the favor of the stars so that a group of travelers may go their way safe and sound from mortal snares. The number of travelers under this protection is decided when the conjuration is cast, and the sorcerer must have some Arcane or sympathetic connection to each of them in order to perform it. Otherwise the ritual fails, regardless of the success of the Casting Total.

This protection is similar to the effect of *Closed Mouth of the Nightwalker* (PeMe 40; see *Houses of Hermes: Mystery Cults*), with a duration equal to that of the journey. Along the way, the travelers will be ignored by highwaymen, ruffians, tax collectors and the like, as long as the sorcerer's Penetration Total exceeds any Magic Resistance. This conjuration does not, however, protect against natural adversities (storms, landslides and so on). As a drawback, if the travelers need lodging, the innkeeper might give their room to others, having forgotten that he gave it to them (in any case, they will not have to pay for any services).

### Create Enmity between Two People (CrMe 30)

As long as any Magic Resistance is overcome, this conjuration spoils the good relationship between two people (partners, friends, spouses and so on). To do so, the sorcerer must have an Arcane or sympathetic connection to the targets. If he succeeds in invoking the astrological forces, the targets feel a revulsion toward each other to the point of making the relationship impossible. This does not mean that, for example, partners are able to dissolve their business dealings or spouses to divorce, but they will speak to each other only to convey what is strictly necessary, and will often quarrel over the smallest things. This enmity lasts for as long as the targets live.

### Free Captives (ReCo 40)

With an Arcane or sympathetic connection to the captive, the sorcerer can transport him to the point farthest from the prison's entrance, beside its walls or boundaries. This conjuration does not guarantee the target's safety once he is set free.

### Dig Channels or Wells (PeTe 20)

With this conjuration, the sorcerer can create a channel, irrigation ditch or well up to twenty meters in length or depth. To do so, he must have one or more Arcane Connections to the exact place where he wishes to create it; the works will materialize at the beginning of the next lunar mansion. These works appear finished, with any supports or linings needed, and can bore through rock as well as soil. The duration of the structure created by this conjuration depends on its upkeep; that is, it suffers normal wear.

### Discover Hidden/Buried Treasure (InTe 15)

The sorcerer obtains a mental vision of the place where a treasure is hidden in a building or plot of land to which he has an Arcane Connection. This effect only detects treasures of metal or minerals, and must penetrate any Magic Resistance to be effective (such as an *Aegis of the Hearth*). The vision lasts only a few seconds.

### Destroy Buildings or Houses (PeTe 25)

By raising his prayers to Jupiter in the mansion of *Albotain*, the sorcerer can bring down a single structure to which he has an Arcane Connection at the beginning of the next lunar station. This effect is similar to *End of the Mighty Castle* (PeTe 25).

### Make a Prison More Secure (MuTe 20)

With this conjuration, the sorcerer improves the locks and bars of a cell to which he has an Arcane Connection, making them more complex and more resistant (respectively). In game terms, the Soak of the bars and the Ease Factor to pick the locks increase by +3. The effect of this conjuration remains active until its prisoner escapes, dies or is released.

### Protect Travelers by Ship (ReAq[Au] 35)

The sorcerer can beseech the favor of the stars so that a group of travelers may have a sea crossing free of swells and storms. The number of travelers under this protection is decided when the conjuration is cast, and the sorcerer must have some Arcane or sympathetic connection to each of them in order to perform it (as well as having to penetrate any Magic Resistance). This conjuration does not protect against animals or mortals (such as pirates), and its protection lasts until the end of the voyage.

### Protect One Who Works with Fire (ReIg 25)

With a sympathetic or Arcane Connection to the target, the sorcerer protects him against fire so that he can work with it without fear of being burned (+15 to Soak against fire). This effect lasts seven lunar stations (some three astronomical seasons) and works similarly to *Ward against Heat and Flames* (ReIg 20).

### Bring About a Good Hunt (InTe 25)

This effect grants the hunter a sense similar to that of *Sense the Feet That Tread the Earth* (InTe 30). To do so, the sorcerer must have an Arcane or sympathetic connection to the target and, at the end of the mansion of *Azoraya* or *Athaya,* bless the talisman he has made for that purpose. The conjuration's effects dissipate when the day's hunting ends.

### Create Affection/Friendship/Love between Two People, or Win Someone's Favor (CrMe 20)

As long as any Magic Resistance is overcome, this conjuration makes affection blossom between two people, or wins someone's favor. The people need not know each other or get along, although if they already do, the effect will be stronger. To do so, the sorcerer must have an Arcane or sympathetic connection to the targets. If he succeeds in invoking the astrological forces, the targets feel an attraction that impels them to seek each other's company. If the relationship was already good, they might feel a romantic attraction. The duration of this feeling is momentary, so the course of the relationship will depend on the deeds and words of those involved.

### Destroy Cities and Villages (ReTe 75)

This terrible conjuration shakes the earth beneath a city, causing collapses and great material damage, so it can injure many and kill as many more. For this reason, the sorcerer must be sure that the city and its inhabitants deserve such a punishment, or else he might bring misfortune down upon himself.

<!-- p. 285 -->

With an Arcane Connection to something highly representative of the city, the sorcerer summons Mars to shake the foundations of the earth. At the end of the mansion of the Moon, the city suffers a terrible earthquake that damages the stone buildings and destroys everything else. The catastrophe takes no more than a few seconds to complete.

### Taint Springs and Wells (MuAq 15)

With an Arcane Connection, the sorcerer corrupts a spring or a well so that its waters are no longer fit to drink. Drinking them occasionally causes indigestion; prolonged consumption could cause terrible diseases and leave serious aftereffects. This corruption is permanent, at least until the conjuration's effects are removed.

### Kill Any Reptile or Venomous Animal (PeAn 15)

On completion of the conjuration, the creature of this kind to which the sorcerer has an Arcane or sympathetic connection dies.

### Improve the Education of Students (CrVi 30)

By summoning the powers of Mercury in the appropriate mansion of the Moon, the sorcerer grants the target the Virtue Apt Student, whose benefits he enjoys for as long as his training lasts.

### Shore Up/Finish/Build Structures (CrTe[He] 25)

On completion of this ritual, the talisman the sorcerer has created allows him to finish, raise or repair any structure to which he has an Arcane Connection. Bear in mind that buildings created with this spell are not furnished with any furniture or plumbing, so the owner might consider them crude. The building takes one night to be completed or raised.

### Besiege a City with an Army (ReMe 50)

The sorcerer, who must have an Arcane or sympathetic connection to everyone with authority over the army, completes this ritual by fumigating the powerful talisman he has made for that purpose. At the end of the mansion of the Moon, if the sorcerer manages to penetrate his targets' Magic Resistance, the leaders summon their armies (which might take up to a year to muster, depending on their numbers) and lead them toward the chosen city. This army's march through cities and kingdoms will cause a great stir and alert the affected monarchs before it reaches their gates. Needless to say, using this conjuration could have grave consequences for the peoples involved, who could be plunged into war for years.

The effects of this conjuration last until the moment the army lays siege to the target city. After that, the generals are once again entirely free to decide what to do with their troops.

### Embolden the Target / Foment Conspiracies against Kings / Enable Slaves to Flee (CrMe 15)

To cast this conjuration, the sorcerer must make a talisman with the Arcane Connections of his targets. When the ritual is consummated, the targets gain the Personality Trait Brave at +3, or increase it by one point, spurring them to do things they would not otherwise dare. Of course, if the target has no need to do anything risky, he will not do it.

The effect of this conjuration dissipates the instant the target carries out his task (or at the moment it is cast, if he has nothing risky to do).

### Ruin Crops, Harvests and Plants (PeHe 25)

On completion of the conjuration, the plants in a cultivated field of up to ten hectares wither and die after seven days. The sorcerer needs a representative Arcane Connection to the target to cast the conjuration successfully.

This is a very dangerous conjuration, since the economy of nations rests on agriculture. Ruining a nation's crops would endanger hundreds of thousands of people and bring disease and death.

### Improve Trade and Profits (CrAn[HeTe] 100)

This powerful ritual raises the category of a source of income by one, although never above "Abundant" (see *Covenants*, page 79). The talisman takes one lunar year to take effect, but thereafter the source of income yields its benefits naturally.

<!-- p. 286 -->

Al-Qurṭubī once said that this conjuration should be performed only on those who deserved it, and never twice on the same business.

### Improve Crops, Harvests and Plants (CrHe 25)

This conjuration has the same effect as *The Bountiful Feast* (CrHe 35), and its use brings bounty and well-being to the people. Good rulers will be those who store the grain to use it in hard times.

The crops take one lunar mansion to flourish, and they must be suited to the sowing season; that is, the conjuration will not make grain planted out of season bear fruit. Naturally, the sorcerer needs a significant Arcane Connection to the harvest he wishes to improve.
