### Keep Vermin Out of a Place or Drive Them Out (ReAn 15)

With an Arcane Connection to the place he wishes to cleanse, the sorcerer completes this simple ritual and makes all the vermin (bedbugs, rats, flies and so on) leave it, preventing them from returning for a lunar year. After that time, it is up to the inhabitants to keep the vermin from infesting it again.

### Curse, Ruin or Harm Someone (CrVi 35)

At the conjunction of the Moon with Saturn, Mars or the Sun, the sorcerer calls upon the powers of the celestial spirits to curse someone to whom he has an Arcane or sympathetic connection, permanently giving the target the Minor Flaw Lesser Malediction (pious or virtuous people are not affected by this conjuration).

### Cure Diseases (CrCo 35)

With an Arcane or sympathetic connection, the sorcerer conjures the energy that flows from beyond the Moon to cure a person of any disease. The sorcerer must have correctly diagnosed the affliction in order to remove it, must penetrate any Magic Resistance, and can eliminate only one disease per casting. The target gains no immunity whatsoever and may develop the same affliction again should the occasion arise.

### Drive People from a Place (ReMe 30)

The sorcerer can drive out of any place as many people as he has Arcane or sympathetic connections to (a number limited by his Ṭillasm score). If he overcomes their Magic Resistance, the people leave the place as soon as possible, and it will take someone summoning them again, or chance bringing them together once more, for them to gather in the same place.

### Stand Out from the Rest (MuIm 15)

With his power, the sorcerer can bless a target's talisman to make him more respectable and charismatic. This effect is exactly the same as that produced by *Aura of Ennobled Presence* (MuIm 10), but with Moon duration.

### Kill Captives (PeCo 25)

With an Arcane or sympathetic connection to a captive (that is, a prisoner, regardless of who has taken him prisoner or the reasons for his captivity), the sorcerer can call upon the power of Mars (which must be in conjunction with the Moon) to end the wretch's life instantly (provided he overcomes his Magic Resistance).

### Tame Wild Animals (ReAn 20)

By fixing the Arcane or sympathetic connection to the animal in question in the talisman, the sorcerer can make any wild beast docile, as if it had been tamed. If he overcomes its Magic Resistance, the animal will neither shun people nor behave aggressively toward them. This effect lasts until the animal's death or until it is dispelled.

### Make the Target Come to You as Soon as Possible (ReMe 25)

To cast this conjuration, the sorcerer must know the name of the person he wishes to draw to him, as well as have an Arcane or sympathetic connection in his possession. If he overcomes the target's Magic Resistance, the target drops whatever he is doing and sets out as soon as possible. It does not matter whether he knows how to reach the sorcerer; the magic will guide him. Even so, there are some obstacles the magic cannot overcome: the target will not risk his life to reach the sorcerer. If, for example, he had to cross a sea to get there and did not have enough money to pay for passage, he would not throw himself into the water, but would save up or look for some way to overcome the obstacle without endangering his life. As a result, depending on the target's whereabouts, he might take years to arrive.

The effect of the conjuration ends when the target reaches his destination or dies before reaching it.

### Cripple a Limb (PeCo 20)

By representing the limb to be crippled on the talisman, the sorcerer uses an Arcane or sympathetic connection to the target to maim him. If he overcomes the target's Magic Resistance, the limb goes limp and strengthless. This effect has the symptoms of a curse, since no natural remedy can cure it and time does not improve the condition.

### Al-Maŷūs

During the history of the Order in the Iberian Peninsula, the Northmen (whom the inhabitants of al-Andalus called *al-Maŷūs*, in reference to their pagan nature and their fondness for fire, since they reminded them of the pre-Christian followers of the Zoroastrian religion of the East) ravaged the coasts and interior of the Peninsula many times. Also known as *vikingr* (Old Norse for "pirates"), the Northmen reached the shores of Iberia on several occasions.

- In 844, a Viking squadron attacked Gijón, Corunna (where they were defeated by Ramiro I of Asturias), Lisbon and Cadiz, and sailed up the Guadalquivir to Seville, which they sacked for forty days. The men were killed and the women and children carried off as slaves.

- In 859, the brothers Björn Ironside and Hastein attacked Iria Flavia and sacked it. They then besieged Compostela, where they were driven back. Part of their fleet split off to attack Lisbon and al-Gharb, although many of the ships were intercepted and defeated by the troops of the emir Muḥammad I. The rest of the fleet did greater damage beyond the strait: at Algeciras, Murcia, Melilla and the Balearics. Afterward they managed to sail up the Ebro and captured the king of Pamplona, García I Íñiguez, who had to pay 70,000 gold dīnārs for his ransom.

- In the summer of 966, after ravaging the lands of Galicia, twenty-eight Norse ships attacked Lisbon. The fleet of the caliph Al-Ḥakam II set out from Seville and defeated them near Silves.

- In 971 there was a sighting of Viking ships that turned out to be a false alarm.

- In the summer of 972 Viking ships were sighted for the last time, when Al-Ḥakam II was about to begin his North African campaign against the Berber leaders allied with the Fatimids. As had happened in 971, the caliphal forces found no trace of the Norse enemy. After two months patrolling the area, the Andalusi spies in the north of the Peninsula confirmed that the threat had left Galicia, and the troops returned to Cordoba without having seen battle.

<!-- p. 288 -->

On many of these raids, the ships carried a vitkir, or Norse rune wizard, on board. The magi of Iberia had never had contact with this kind of magic, and for a time they were taken aback by these wizards and by the fact that their magic seemed to affect them differently from anything they had known until then. Reactions differed considerably between the north and south of the Peninsula: while in the north the Flambeau fought these strange wizards with fire and sword without asking many questions, in al-Andalus there were some who tried to come to terms and negotiate with the strangers in order to learn something more of their unusual magic. Unfortunately, many of the vitkir cared only for plunder and the gathering of booty, and turned a deaf ear to such requests. That evident hostility, and the mutual ignorance, soon gave rise to the belief in a so-called Order of Odin, an organization of Norse wizards comparable to the Order of Hermes, of which the vitkir would be the representatives. The existence of such a group has never been definitively confirmed.

The vitkir use a magic that works in a radically different way from Hermetic magic, based on inscribing or carving runes on various objects or surfaces. The runes bring about a change in the object they affect that is considered natural, so that in many cases it is not considered an active magical effect and therefore does not need to overcome Magic Resistance. Each rune has a different effect, and the various combinations of runes must be studied, much as a Hermetic magus would in his laboratory, before they can be used.

> #### Story Seeds: al-Maŷūs
>
> ##### The Ship of Fire
>
> Although no Viking ships have been sighted since 972, these antagonists can easily be brought into the story when the characters' covenant is asked for help against a sighting of Norse ships. It is said that their decks spew fire that can burn on water. What if some wizard of the dreaded Order of Odin were among them?
>
> ##### Two Orders, One Magic
>
> The characters' covenant receives a request for help from one of their acquaintances, a rather faint-hearted Bonisagus in whose covenant a Jerbiton died not long ago in mysterious circumstances. The Bonisagus would have gone to the Quaesitores, but he has discovered some strange old notes in the Jerbiton's laboratory that speak of a possible integration of Hermetic magic with that of the vitkir.

### The Riadiins, the Mathematicians of Majrīṭ

*[…] mathematical intelligibles do not exist in a state separate from matter, as the intellect represents them to itself. If that were so, the very act of thinking them would be their existence; they would be intellect in themselves […].*[^p288-4]

[^p288-4]: Excerpt from *On the Intellect* by Averroes (Spanish translation by Abdelali Elamrani-Yamȃl).

When the mathematician and astrologer Maslama al-Majrīṭī founded a school in 1004, he was already an aged scholar, but one renowned throughout the Peninsula. Among other things, he had helped the Order of Hermes make several delicate decisions in earlier years (see Chapter III). The school soon became famous throughout Iberia. Mathematics (*taʿlīm* in Arabic), astrology and alchemy were taught there and, according to some, thaumaturgy and other more esoteric disciplines as well. Before long, Maslama (who died in 1007) and his acolytes became famous for the precision of their calculations — not only mathematical ones, but also those that could only be regarded as divination. They could discern where a person was, when an event would come to pass, or even what the outcome of a battle would be.

Soon prominent members of the courts of all Iberia and al-Andalus were vying for their services as palace soothsayers. For years the mathematicians served these nobles accurately, but not without self-interest. They grew rich not only materially; some also rose socially and attained high office in certain places. If Maslama became Almanzor's astrologer and foretold the civil war that would scourge Cordoba and bring about the fall of Madīnat al-Zahrāʾ and Madīnat al-Zaḥirāʾ, no less famous were the predictions of his daughter Fāṭīma, who served many nobles and kings and is said to have lived to almost two hundred years of age.

After her father's death, Fāṭīma carried on his teachings and trained new riadiins (a Romance adaptation of the Arabic term for "mathematicians"). She also enlarged the school's so-called "inner circle," a select group chosen from among the most brilliant students, which included, among others, Al-Kirmānī of Cordoba and Asbay ibn Muḥammad, who would found another school of mathematics in Granada that went on to forge a fruitful relationship with the jurists' covenant of Dār Malīḥaʾ (see Chapter IX). To these riadiins was revealed the true knowledge the brotherhood possessed: that of the most hidden properties of the world around them, the threads that bound its various elements together, and their relationship with the celestial spheres and even with what lay beyond them. Knowledge, in short, of the world in its broadest and most philosophical sense. This group has survived into the thirteenth century, and although its members are not magi properly speaking, few can match the learning they have amassed.

The founding in 1217 of a Dominican friary in Madrid has posed an unexpected threat to the school. Founded by the preachers Suero Gómez and Pedro de Madrid, the friary is intensely active in philosophy, and voices have already begun to be heard branding some of the riadiins as pagans and frauds.

<!-- p. 289 -->

#### Customs

The riadiins are in fact experimental philosophers, or empiricus: scholars who seek to uncover the secrets of the world around them, from what lies beneath their feet to what the highest celestial spheres conceal. They are not magi and have no magical power, but they do know (something very few people know) the properties of many of the elements around them, which they know how to exploit until those properties seem almost magical. Although they deal with all kinds of subjects, from alchemy to mathematics by way of logic and rhetoric, their specialty today remains the same as Maslama's in his time: astrology. This takes shape in two specific philosophic activities: the making of ligatures and astrological charts.

#### Ligatures

A ligature is an enchantment consisting of a small pouch containing parchment, stones or herbs, which is usually worn hung around the neck. It also usually includes an Arcane or sympathetic connection to whatever it is meant to affect. Ligatures use the natural principles of experimental philosophy to enhance a specific action, and generally affect a single die roll. In the case of the riadiins, the preparation of these ligatures derives from their knowledge of the liberal arts, and more specifically of astrology; therefore, they can only affect actions that fall within the scope of that Ability (see accompanying insert), and they never affect a seasonal activity or a Lab Total.

> #### Possible Ligature Bonuses for Artes Liberales
>
> Grammar (interpreting or translating a text), logic (solving a logical problem), rhetoric (persuading others to follow a course of action, casting a Mentem spell), arithmetic (a complex calculation), geometry (designing a building), astronomy (calculating a horoscope, casting an Intellego spell), music (performing music, composing).

Making a ligature takes a few hours, during which the character performs astrological calculations, gathers items with the appropriate properties (or visits an apothecary to obtain them), and writes the necessary texts. The ligature is made with a specific purpose in mind, including a specific period during which it will be valid and the target who will benefit from its effects. It lasts for one year, although it only works during a particular six-hour period of the day, which must be specified when it is made. Once the process is complete, the maker rolls a stress die and adds his Intelligence and Artes Liberales score.

#### Ligature Creation:

Intelligence + Artes Liberales + stress die

Compare the result to the following table to find the bonus the roll will receive:

| Result | Bonus |
| --- | --- |
| 9 | +1 |
| 15 | +2 |
| 24 | +3 (maximum) |

On a botch, the components have the opposite effect: the action suffers a –2 and also has two extra botch dice. The character should not know that he has botched a ligature.

A ligature can be used only once; once it has modified a roll, its conjunction of elements loses its value, although its ingredients can be reused in another ligature. A character can benefit from only one ligature at a time, as otherwise their properties would interfere with each other.

Ligatures are not exclusive to the riadiins, and anyone with a score in Artes Liberales can use them, although the riadiins gain a benefit in this respect from one of their Mysteries. Nor is the Gift needed to make them or to benefit from them.

#### Astrological Charts

Where the riadiins' talent shines brightest is in applying their astrological and mathematical knowledge to what are called astrological charts. Each astrological chart has a specific purpose, and making one has two stages: first its formula must be researched, by learning it from some source or by investigating it personally; then the necessary seasons must be invested in preparing a specific astrological chart from that formula. A formula is described much like a Hermetic spell (even though it is not a magical effect but an entirely mundane procedure), since both rest on the same foundations of natural philosophy and are developed over seasons of study or work.

> #### The Laboratory of a Riadiin
>
> *[…] I followed him into a room in which there were pots covered in smoke like storm clouds, giving off so fetid a stench of sulfur, arsenic, cinnabar and sarcocolla that I recalled: "… the day when the sky brings forth a visible smoke that covers the people; that will be their painful punishment." I felt the presence of evil and resolved to flee. On turning around I found myself among heaps of embers, apparatus with gold dust, and black and yellow figures.*[^p289-I]
>
> All experimental philosophers have a laboratory, and the riadiins are no exception. Although in concept and overall size they are comparable to those of a Hermetic magus, in practice they are not such complex and sophisticated places. They do not need to be in any supernatural aura, however, and their specific equipment depends on the specialty of their occupant. Astrolabes and armillary spheres are common in riadiin laboratories, as is every sort of implement for drawing up astrological charts. Player and storyguide are free to adapt the contents of the "Laboratory" section of *Covenants* (page 142) to the laboratory of an empiricus.
>
> [^p289-I]: From Ibn Shuhayd, taken from *The Treatise of Familiar Spirits and Demons* (Spanish translation by Salvador Barberá).

<!-- p. 290 -->

Researching (or creating) the formula of any astrological chart requires the acquisition of experience points. When a character gains experience points in Artes Liberales, he may assign them, instead of to the score itself, to learning a formula based on that Ability. Once he has accumulated 5 experience points in that formula, he is considered to have learned it and may use it to create a physical version (an "empiric"). This is why some riadiins who concentrate their efforts on creating formulas build up a certain "disadvantage" compared with more abstract philosophers, which is reflected in their scores. The storyguide may limit which astrological chart formulas can be learned from a book according to its specific subject matter. Besides reading books, these experience points can also be obtained by practicing different combinations of the natural principles (that is, by investing in it the 5 experience points gained from a season of practice; see *Ars Magica Fifth Edition*, page 245). An empiricus can therefore learn a formula in a single season by this method. It does not matter if the level of the formula is beyond the empiricus's reach; he can still learn it, which is not the same as preparing it.

#### Preparing an Astrological Chart

A riadiin's Lab Total is as follows.

#### Lab Total:

Intelligence + Artes Liberales + philosophic bonuses\*

\*Shape and material bonuses (see *Ars Magica Fifth Edition*, page 173); risk bonuses — as with experimentation in the laboratory, but without adding the simple die — and laboratory bonuses. In total, these bonuses can never exceed the empiricus's Artes Liberales score.

The Lab Total is compared with the level of the formula, adapted as if it were a Hermetic spell, although it has only one parameter, Detail (see insert on the next page). Preparing a formula takes at least one season, and only if the empiricus's Lab Total equals or exceeds the level of the formula; for every point by which it exceeds it, he accumulates one point, until he has accumulated the level of the formula. Thus, if the Lab Total is double the effect level, it can be completed in a single season. Work on an astrological formula need not be continuous.

An astrological chart is an astrological formula designed to answer a specific question about a character, object or future event. It requires close contemplation of the stars and complex mathematical calculations and research, but once created it is relatively easy to use. The riadiin completes the chart with the horoscope related to the target (be it a person, object or event) by making the final calculations, at which point the answer is revealed. Each astrological chart is therefore generic when created, but specific when used.

Using the astrological chart requires the target's natal horoscope, which means that the riadiin must know the place and date of birth (or of creation, in the case of an object, or of beginning, in the case of an event) of the target. Calculating the target's horoscope takes a day, but it need only be done once per target. If the chart has two targets ("Does Yasmin love Abdul?"), the horoscopes of each of them are needed. No astrological chart can affect more than two targets.

<!-- p. 291 -->

#### Calculating the Natal Horoscope:

Intelligence + Artes Liberales + stress die versus an Ease Factor of 9

It is impossible to calculate a horoscope if the target's date and place of birth are not known. Once the horoscope is known, one minute per level of the astrological chart suffices to complete the calculations and learn the answers. Although they are written products, astrological charts cannot simply be copied with parchment and ink; the corresponding laboratory texts are required, since they include their own horoscopes, marked by the day on which they were completed.

> #### Guidelines and Levels of Detail
>
> These are the four basic guidelines available for astrological charts:
>
> **Level 2:** learn a visible property (such as the whereabouts) of a person or object.
>
> **Level 3:** learn a mundane property that could be discerned through close examination (such as the state of consciousness or the age) of a person or object.
>
> **Level 4:** learn a specific fact that could not be discovered without a particular Ability (such as an emotion, or who made an object) about a person or object.
>
> **Level 5:** learn complex information that would require the sustained use of an Ability (such as the truth of a statement, or all the properties of an object) about a person or object.
>
> Detail defines the extent and quality of the information obtained through an astrological chart, and is the only parameter that governs it. These are the different levels of Detail a chart may have, and their modification to the chart's base level:
>
> **Binary:** a one-word answer between two options (+0 magnitudes).
>
> **Basic:** provides the equivalent of a three-word answer (+1 magnitude).
>
> **Brief:** provides one sentence of information (+2 magnitudes).
>
> **Detailed:** reveals all the relevant information associated with the chart's target (+3 magnitudes).
>
> In addition, a chart that seeks to decipher events in the distant future (more than one astrological month away) increases by one magnitude, as do questions concerning the past. Questions about the near future (within the same astrological month) add two magnitudes. Questions about the present add no magnitudes. Predicted future events are subject to the acts of creatures with free will and might not come to pass.

#### Sample Astrological Charts

In the following sample charts, "N" stands for "name" and "ON" for "other name," referring to the targets represented by the chart.

### Is N in Good Health?

Chart Level 3

**Detail:** Binary

By consulting the relative position of Saturn (the planet of death) and the Sun (the planet of life) in the horoscope, the astrological chart reveals which planet has the greater influence on the chart of the person in question.

### Is N Inclined to Love ON?

Chart Level 4

**Detail:** Binary

Requires two horoscopes, one for each target. It does not reveal the targets' feelings, only whether they have compatible astrological charts, according to the position of Venus.

### Is N Telling the Truth?

Chart Level 5

**Detail:** Binary

Mercury and Scorpio determine whether the target is the kind of person given to lying, and whether today his aspect leads him not to tell the truth.

### What Will the Weather Be Tomorrow in N?

Chart Level 5

**Detail:** Basic

The angle between the Moon and Mercury, and the stars that bisect it in the horoscope of an event taking place the following day (such as a fair), will reveal the weather likely to prevail in that place tomorrow.

### Will N Declare War?

Chart Level 10

**Detail:** Binary

Requires the horoscope of a person who is likely to go to war. The ingress of Mars into the horoscope indicates whether war is to be expected or not.

### Where Is N?

Chart Level 4

**Detail:** Brief

Reveals the current location of the named person within an area of roughly fifty kilometers around, in relation to a particular feature; for example, "in the *kūra* of Seville, beside still waters."

### How Goes the Battle of N?

Chart Level 10

**Detail:** Detailed

By tracing the movement of Mars, the astrologer can discern the course of the fighting in terms of relative numbers of casualties. To do so he must have the horoscope of the day the battle began.

### Who Made the Object N?

Chart Level 15

**Detail:** Detailed

The Moon's north node exemplifies beginnings, and Mercury represents craftsmanship. The position of both in an object's horoscope will reveal information about its maker: his complexion (and therefore his approximate appearance), occupation, interests and current location.

<!-- p. 292 -->

### Who Caused the Death of N?

Chart Level 20

**Detail:** Brief

From the horoscope of a deceased person, the astrologer can determine a single characteristic of the likely murderer, such as his complexion or his approximate location in relation to where the victim was at the time of the murder. If no murder took place, the answer may be misleading.

#### The Mysteries of the Riadiins

Although ligatures and astrological charts are processes within reach of anyone versed in the liberal arts, the most brilliant riadiins are chosen by the group's leaders to have revealed to them the existence of a series of mysteries, ceremonies and private knowledge that make them especially skilled at carrying out their activities. Although they are not an esoteric order properly speaking, nor do they possess any "magical" power *per se*, these small mysteries enhance their astrological and divinatory skills. There is talk of additional mysteries known only to Maslama himself (and his daughter, Fāṭīma), which allowed him to make truly complex prophecies, but that knowledge was irretrievably lost long ago.

As with all Mysteries (see *Houses of Hermes: Mystery Cults*, page 6), an initiate's advancement depends, among many other things, on his knowledge of the organization and its wisdom (represented in this case by the new Ability Riadiin Lore) and on the sacrifices (material, of time, or even spiritual) he is willing to make. Some options for this group's Mysteries are suggested below.

**First Outer Mystery:** Mystery of the Primary Qualities.

**Minor Virtue gained:** Mystery of the Primary Qualities (see "New Virtues and Flaws" below).

**Initiation modifiers:** +1 (material sacrifice to acquire unusual components), +3 (quest: obtain a mineral or plant regarded as legendary, chosen by the mystagogue), +1 (sacrifice of time: the initiate spends a season in the mystagogue's service), +3 (symbolic sacrifice: the initiate renounces all family ties to concentrate solely on his studies).

This level is the only one that is public and known to all riadiins, and anyone may try to attain this knowledge, which reveals the primary qualities of many mundane objects and the benefits that can be drawn from them. Moisture, heat, cold or any other primary quality of an object can be manipulated if the philosopher is skilled enough.

**Second Outer Mystery:** Mystery of the Sublunary Spheres.

**Minor Virtue gained:** Puissant Artes Liberales (or Affinity with Artes Liberales if Puissant is already possessed).

**Initiation modifiers:** +1 (material sacrifice to acquire special laboratory equipment), +1 (sacrifice of time: the initiate spends a season in the mystagogue's service), +3 (quest: obtain valuable studies by other empiricus, to be determined by the mystagogue).

At the second level of the brotherhood, the initiate is taken under the personal tutelage of one of the most experienced riadiins, who employs him as a laboratory assistant and trains him intensively in the liberal arts, and in astrology in particular. His training culminates in a special commission by which the initiate demonstrates his absolute commitment to his studies: he must obtain the writings of some other empiricus, chosen by the mystagogue. How he gets them is left to the initiate, but he is strictly forbidden to do anything that might cause harm to the riadiins. The time spent in study and the new ideas about the discipline allow the initiate to gain Puissant or Affinity with Artes Liberales.

**Inner Mystery:** Aligned with the Stars.

**Major Virtue gained:** Aligned with the Stars (see "New Virtues and Flaws" below).

**Initiation modifiers:** +1 (material sacrifice to acquire special laboratory equipment), +1 (sacrifice of time: the initiate spends a season in the mystagogue's service), +3 (quest: the initiate must travel in winter to the ruins of Madīnat al-Zahrāʾ and meditate there while contemplating the firmament for several moons), +3 (minor ordeal: the rigors of the experience at Madīnat al-Zahrāʾ give the initiate the Minor Flaw Fragile Constitution).

For the deepest mystery of the riadiins, the mystagogue once again takes the initiate under his tutelage, employing him as an assistant in his most delicate and complex studies. After devoting time and material resources to these studies, initiate and mystagogue set out on a journey to the ruins of Madīnat al-Zahrāʾ, where both spend several weeks meditating and contemplating the firmament. While the mystagogue does so in a measured and prudent way, the initiate must remain in a state of deep meditation every night out in the open, watching the sky and straining his mind regardless of any hardship he may suffer.

At the end of this process, the initiate gains the Major Virtue Aligned with the Stars. Only a few of the group's most distinguished members have ever reached this level.

### The Tiryāqi

After Averroes's banishment to Marrākeš in the mid-twelfth century, the Cordoban philosopher set down part of the medical knowledge he had acquired in a book he titled *Kitāb al-Kulliyyāt fīl-ṭibb*, or "Book of the Generalities of Medicine." In it he sought to set out the most elementary and essential knowledge for any physician, combining, in a revolutionary way never seen before, subjects such as anatomy, therapeutics and even the hygiene of patients. Within the book Averroes also devoted a large section to the medicines and foods best suited to treating the various ills that might afflict a person. The former qadi of Seville went back even to the philosophers of antiquity, making a thorough study of the Hippocratics and of Galen, to whose theories he added the advances made by Averroes's own Arab predecessors, such as the Persian Al-Rāzī and the Sevillian Ibn Zuhr.

Although the *Kulliyyāt* has not yet been translated into Latin (it will be in the coming years, under the name *Colliget*), many students of the Cordoban master's work threw themselves headlong into studying this formidable text, some of them traveling to Seville, Cordoba or Marrākeš, where he was in exile, to consult him. The most brilliant of these students (or the luckiest, who enjoyed Averroes's own advice) were able to see beyond the separate texts and sections of the *Kulliyyāt*. Following one of the sage's maxims ("The visible can afford a glimpse of the invisible"), they managed to fit together the various pieces contained in the book to uncover a hidden philosophic science that allowed medicine to be taken further than anyone of that age thought possible. By combining certain ingredients named by Averroes in the right way, and applying his philosophical theories, his followers discovered that they could make medical preparations of prodigious power: they called them theriacs, also known as treacles, from the Arabic *tiryāq*, "remedy," and Averroes himself would go on to explore them further in the *Maqāla fīl-tiryāq*, or "Treatise on Theriac."

<!-- p. 293 -->

Soon these privileged few had not only formed their own group (they called themselves the tiryāqi) but had begun to take Averroes's teachings further, researching new formulas for new theriacs, which they jealously guarded among themselves. Despite their valuable discoveries and creations, they very rarely shared either with anyone outside the group: they supplied theriacs only to those few men or women whose worth as philosophers, physicians or scholars they judged to make them deserving of their preparations. More than one qadi and more than one wealthy merchant have tried in vain over the last few decades to obtain one of these fabulous theriacs, although word of the small group's existence has not spread far, and its slight renown extends only through the southern half of the Peninsula.

The sage Averroes's most accomplished disciple, Abū‑l‑Haŷŷaŷ ibn Tumlūs, has for years been the leader of this select group, although by 1220 he is beginning to tire of the responsibility of seeking out and training new pupils, and he may soon hand the position over to one of his most accomplished disciples.

#### The Secrets of Theriacs

The members of the tiryāqi can prepare theriacs, pharmaceutical remedies that many charlatans claim to know but that very few actually know how to make. The theriacs of the tiryāqi are philosophic preparations beneficial to the human body, described in books such as the *Kitāb al-Kulliyyāt fīl-ṭibb*, the *Maqāla fīl-tiryāq*, and other works both earlier and later. The tiryāqi take the human body, its humors and its elements as their focus and principal element, and only after many years of study are they able to prepare the most potent remedies this discipline allows. The basic Ability they use for all their philosophic activities is therefore Medicine.

Note that any student of philosophy with medical knowledge and a suitable laboratory (whose conditions would be similar to those of the riadiins; see page 288) can create theriacs. The tiryāqi are simply able to prepare far more potent theriacs, although it is true that their field of work is not as broad: where other philosophers can create theriacs that are poisonous or harmful to men, the tiryāqi are devoted solely to preserving the health of the body. On the other hand, only the tiryāqi can create theriacs that grant bonuses to Aging rolls or that restore Fatigue, something that, were it discovered by the Order of Hermes, could lead to inevitable contact between the two groups, who until now have been unaware of each other's existence.

<!-- p. 294 -->

> #### Base Guidelines for Theriacs
>
> **Level 2:** Gives +1 to the character's next wound recovery roll. Gives +1 to the character's next disease recovery roll, but only for a specific humor (see *Ars Magica Fifth Edition*, page 265).
>
> **Level 3:** Relieves pain. The patient loses a number of Fatigue levels equal to the theriac's potency, and penalties from wounds and diseases are reduced by the same number. Gives +3 to the character's next wound recovery roll. Gives +3 to the character's next disease recovery roll, but only for a specific humor. Reduces the potency of a poison by one level.
>
> **Level 4:** Gives +6 to the character's next wound recovery roll. Gives +6 to the character's next disease recovery roll, but only for a specific humor.
>
> **Level 5:** Cures a specific disease, in a time equal to that disease's usual interval. Restores Fatigue.
>
> **Level 10:** Cures a wound of a particular kind (a poison, crushing damage, a cut). The wound heals completely in a time equal to the normal healing interval for a wound of its type.
>
> **Level 15:** Adds +1 to Aging rolls until one is failed.
>
> **Level 18:** Adds +2 to Aging rolls until one is failed.
>
> **Level 21:** Adds +3 to Aging rolls until one is failed. This is the maximum bonus a theriac can provide to an Aging roll.

### Initiation into the Mystery of the Tiryāqi

**Ease Factor:** 15 (Minor Virtue known to the mystagogue; see page 308)

**Script Bonus:** +10

**Script details:** The initiate must spend a season in the service of a tiryāqi, learning his methods and procedures with patients (+3), and must also invest time and money in acquiring and properly preparing the materials needed to set up his laboratory (+1); finally, he must complete the quest for a specific and unusual ingredient, named by his master within the order (+3), and, having concluded that quest, solemnly pronounce the vow of the tiryāqi, which gives him the Flaw Vow: pacifist (+3). Note that in this case the mystagogue's Initiation Total is equal to his Presence + Medicine + Initiation Script bonus.

#### How Theriacs Work

To create a theriac, the first step is to research its formula, which can be done in various ways, such as reading it in a book or practicing Medicine to discover it on one's own. In either case, the student may "sacrifice" 5 experience points to research the formula of a theriac instead of investing them in the Ability; although the storyguide could, and should, limit the number and variety of theriac formulas available in books. (For example, you can find information on the *Kitāb al-Kulliyyāt fīl-ṭibb*, and its statistics, on page 323, in the "Mundane Library" appendix, and decide that it contains one or more theriac formulas, which any reader willing to sacrifice the corresponding experience points would learn.)

Once the formula of a theriac is known, preparing it requires a laboratory, at least one season, and a number of unusual ingredients and items that vary from formula to formula; for this reason, it is recommended that the tiryāqi have the Ability Profession: Apothecary, or know someone who does and can supply those ingredients. Research of the formula is based on the following total.

#### Lab Total:

Intelligence + Medicine\* + philosophic bonuses\*\*

\* Those who possess the Tiryāqi Virtue add their Medicine score twice to this Lab Total, but can only create theriacs based on the guidelines in the insert on this page.

\*\* Includes shape and material bonuses (see *Ars Magica Fifth Edition*, page 173); risk bonuses — as with experimentation in the laboratory, but without adding the simple die — and laboratory bonuses. In total, these bonuses can never exceed the tiryāqi's Medicine score.

If the Lab Total exceeds the level of the theriac's formula, the tiryāqi can prepare the formula as if it were a Hermetic spell: accumulating one point per season for every point by which the Lab Total exceeds the level of the theriac. Thus, if the Lab Total is double the level of the theriac, he can prepare the formula in a single season. The seasons of work on a theriac need not be consecutive, but for the most complicated theriacs even the wisest tiryāqi take years or decades to create them.

This preparation creates a laboratory text with all the details of the process, which the tiryāqi can use in the future to reproduce the theriac more quickly: with such a text, the tiryāqi produces one dose of that theriac for every five points of his Lab Total in a season (rounding up). It is said that the tiryāqi have a library, built up over the last few decades, in which they have set down the most complex theriacs, although no one outside the group has ever seen such texts.

**Example.** *The tiryāqi Raquel of Cordoba has managed to research the formula for the agrimony poultice (described on the next page), and now sets about preparing it in her laboratory. Her Lab Total is 22, while the poultice's level is 15. Therefore, unless she experiments, it would take her three seasons to create one dose of the poultice. However, once that first dose is complete, if she wished to prepare more she would automatically prepare five doses in a single season.*

<!-- p. 295 -->

#### Potency of Theriacs

A theriac is based on two main parameters: the base guideline, which defines its effect, and the potency, which represents the severity of the wound or ailment it is meant to relieve. Potency adds a number of magnitudes to the base guideline, from which the final level of the theriac is calculated.

In the insert on the previous page you will find the base guidelines for the theriacs of the tiryāqi. For purposes of potency, a minor disease or poison is one with an Ease Factor of 6 to overcome its effects; serious ones have an Ease Factor of 9; major ones an Ease Factor of 12; and critical ones an Ease Factor of 15. The possible potencies of theriacs are described below.

- **Faint:** affects minor pains or symptoms of wounds or diseases. It can also affect the Winded Fatigue level (+0 magnitudes).

- **Light:** affects a Light Wound, a minor disease, or the Weary Fatigue level (+1 magnitude).

- **Medium:** affects a Medium Wound, a serious disease, or the Tired Fatigue level (+2 magnitudes).

- **Strong:** affects a Heavy Wound, a major disease, or the Dazed Fatigue level (+3 magnitudes).

- **Formidable:** affects an Incapacitating Wound, a critical disease, or the Unconscious Fatigue level. Aging rolls also fall into this category (+4 magnitudes).

A theriac can only affect wounds or ills of the potency for which it was designed, or lower. Thus, a character with one Heavy Wound and two Medium Wounds would need a theriac of Strong potency for all three wounds to benefit from the bonus. In addition, theriacs of Faint potency have a therapeutic effect: by imitating the symptom of a disease, they can purge a humor, allowing the patient to reroll a failed disease recovery roll, although he can never improve as a result of this second roll.

Theriacs that grant a bonus to Aging rolls are compatible with Hermetic Longevity Rituals and other magical or mundane factors that may affect those rolls. However, a person can benefit from only one theriac of this kind at a time.

#### Sample Theriacs

### Reinvigorating Sponge

Level 10

**Potency:** Light

Mixing crushed willow bark with bergamot and other plant ingredients, and diluting it in sweet wine, yields a thick, brownish liquid with which a sponge is soaked. When the sponge is applied to a person's body, that person automatically recovers the Weary Fatigue level.

(Base 5, +1 Light)

### Agrimony Poultice

Level 15

**Potency:** Strong

This agrimony-based poultice, supplemented with crushed thistle, pyrite powder and jasper, gives +6 to a character's next wound recovery roll. It affects any Heavy, Medium or Light Wound, but not Incapacitating Wounds.

(Base 4, +3 Strong)

### Mithridate

Level 30

**Potency:** Formidable

Mithridate takes its name from the fact that its invention is attributed to King Mithridates VI of antiquity, who was obsessed with the fear that someone would try to kill him by poison. It is one of the most potent theriacs in existence, and immediately cures any wound (save mortal ones) caused by a poison ingested by the bearer. Mithridate is made up of a great many ingredients, among them sweet flag, poppy, frankincense, myrrh, turpentine and storax, to name only a few.

(Base 10, +4 Formidable).

### Universal Theriac

Level 35

**Potency:** Formidable

This is the most potent formula in the whole repertoire of the tiryāqi. With as many as seventy different ingredients in its composition (from hellebore to aloe, by way of viper's flesh and *terra sigillata*), the liquid derived from this preparation adds +1 to the Aging rolls of whoever drinks it until one of them is failed, at which point it ceases to have effect. The only known written description of this formula is found in the *Kitāb al-Diryāq,* by the Persian Abū al-Fatḥ al-Bustī. According to some of Averroes's followers, there may be more potent versions of this formula, but so far no one has been able to reproduce them.

(Base 15, +4 Formidable)

> #### Optional Rule: Wound and Disease Recovery Rolls
>
> Unlike what is described in the *Ars Magica* core rulebook, the base guidelines for theriacs divide recovery rolls into two types: those made for wounds and those made for diseases, since each has a different diagnosis, symptoms and treatment. That is why they are given as separate guidelines. If you decide to use this rule, you should also do the same with the Creo Corpus guidelines in the core rulebook that have similar effects, and decide, when inventing a spell, whether the bonus it grants applies to recovery from diseases or from wounds. If you decide not to use this rule, you can merge the theriac guidelines that affect diseases and wounds separately into a single guideline for each level.

<!-- p. 296 -->

## Ex Miscellanea Traditions

This section describes the Hermetic *saḥirs* and the tempestarii, whose magic is the heir of the first storm wizards of the Peninsula.

### The Hermetic Saḥirs

*You practice magic, and your payment shall be the sword and the fire.*[^p296-5]

[^p296-5]: Excerpt from *The Treatise of Familiar Spirits and Demons* by Ibn Shuhayd (Spanish translation by Salvador Barberá).

According to the Qurʾan, mankind learned *siḥr* (magic) from the fallen angels Harut and Marut, whose intent was to tempt men away from the straight path of Islam. The knowledge was handed down from generation to generation and, over time, it became corrupted in some cases and forgotten in others, leaving behind a fragmented trail of its original lore.

Today there is a tradition that claims to practice this magic in its purest form. These wizards are the *saḥirs* (feminine *saḥiras*), whose existence is confined almost exclusively to the Iberian Tribunal. Among Hermetic magi there are legends of an Order of Suleimān (Solomon), an organization of Islamic wizards that might rival the Order in power and that is supposedly based in the Levant Tribunal. Its aims, and indeed its existence, are often debated, above all in the southern Tribunals of the Order, and especially in Iberia.

#### Key Points

Major Non-Hermetic Virtue: Siḥr (see "New Virtues and Flaws" below).

Minor Hermetic Virtue: Minor Magical Focus (*jinn*). This focus applies only to the *jinn* (singular *jinni*, from the Arabic for "genie"), and not to any other spirit creatures.

Major Hermetic Flaw: Twilight Prone. Wielding a powerful magic that compels spirits to appear means that *saḥirs* may succumb to Twilight more easily.

#### History

In the Umayyad emirate of the Iberian Peninsula, the *saḥirs* who murdered Flambeau's *parens* were hunted down by Flambeau, who believed (wrongly) that they were diabolists. His followers continued the witch hunt to avenge Flambeau's death, although in truth the *saḥirs* had not been to blame. The *saḥirs* of Iberia took advantage of the negotiations conducted by the magi of the Tribunal and officially joined the Order in 925 through House Ex Miscellanea. As is well known, the most important Flambeau of the Tribunal rejected the agreement and swore to wipe out the lineage of the Saracen wizards (see Chapter III).

> #### The Jinn
>
> *[…] we crossed the skies and the deserts until we came to a land unlike our own, full of trees and fragrant flowers. I noticed that the air was different.*[^p296-II]
>
> When God made the world, He granted the gift of intelligence to three kinds of creatures: the angels, created from light; the *jinn*, from pure elemental matter (also called "smokeless fire" or ether); and mankind, molded from clay.
>
> A *jinni* (or *jinnī*; feminine *yinniyya*, for one verse of the Qurʾan states that they have sex) is a spiritual reflection of human beings. Like humans, they can be saved or damned and, according to the Qurʾan, they are bound to worship God. The Prophet was commanded to preach the Qurʾan to them and, in return, won almost all of them over to the new religion (among the seven *jinn* who listened to the Prophet was the mighty Zawbaʿ, an evil spirit whose plural, *zawábiʿ*, means "calamities" or "misfortunes"). Although legends say that at the Last Judgment God will reproach the *jinn* for having abused men, some *jinn* seem to be (or at least feign to be) uninterested in mankind, so they disdain to imitate it and are usually pagans (these *jinn* draw their power from the Magic Realm). Others, by contrast, seem unable to keep from meddling in mortal lives; they live very close to humans and often seek salvation by professing the faith of Islam (this group is similar to the Arabian faeries). There is also a third kind of *jinn* that seems bent on destroying mankind, abounding above all in literature, where the line separating them from demons tends to blur — such as the *jinni* Nadr ibn al-Hárith, an evil genie of the Quraysh, who bore animosity toward Muḥammad and claimed that his Persian tales were better than the Prophet's.
>
> The *jinn* dwell in a valley of Yemen called ʿAbqar, whose fragrance is evoked by many poets in their verses. According to tradition, the *jinn* write through men, and their vanity sometimes leads them to take human form to present themselves as the authors of certain compositions. According to pre-Islamic legends, there is no poet who is not accompanied by his genie. Thus Láfiz ibn al-Láfiz is the *jinni* of Imru-l-Qays, and Mashal ibn Uthama that of Al-Aʿxa, for example.
>
> The *jinn* are a variety of *genii loci* (spirits of a place), and as such they possess a spiritual form and a physical one built from elemental matter. The spiritual form inhabits a feature of the landscape, such as a sand dune, a rock or a pool. The *jinni* of a mountain is likely to have a higher Might than that of a stone (Might generally ranges between 5 and 40). Its material form is essentially human, although its size matches that of the physical feature its spiritual form inhabits and it is generally made of the same substance. If this form is destroyed, the spirit can shape it again once it has regained the Might points it spent to create it; the *jinni* will most likely cry out for vengeance for its murder. The *jinn* need neither eat nor drink, and they do not age. In addition, all of them have the Virtues Ways of the (Land) and Second Sight.
>
> [^p296-II]: Excerpt from *The Treatise of Familiar Spirits and Demons* by Ibn Shuhayd (Spanish translation by Salvador Barberá).

<!-- p. 297 -->

#### Culture

This tradition is deeply rooted in the southern part of the Iberian Peninsula and is rarely found beyond these lands. The ancient pacts made by the pre-Hermetic forebears of the *saḥirs* allow them to summon the spirits of natural features (called *jinn*) that inhabit the lands occupied by the Muslims, from Cordoba to the Holy Land, by way of North Africa and Egypt. *Saḥirs* who travel away from these lands can still use this unique magic to summon such spirits, but the *genii loci* of Christian lands that answer the call are usually unknown to them, and it is harder for them to make pacts with them. Because of the hostility they have historically aroused among the most diehard followers of Flambeau, the *saḥirs* tend to be very close-knit and often help each other in times of need. Nevertheless, owing to the scarcity of the resources they require (the *jinn* themselves, and the vis needed to bargain with them), they do not usually live near one another.

*Saḥirs* are usually on good terms with the *jinn* that dwell near their homes, and they often regard the most powerful as companions, friends or even family. The weaker *jinn* are given the respect due to a valued servant or grog. Foolish is the *saḥir* who mistreats a *jinni* whose services he will need again, for a disgruntled *jinni* might twist its master's orders and, once released, plot revenge against him.

*Jinn* bound to a *saḥir* by their agreements usually follow him in spirit form, although they can also take animal or human form. Summoning a *jinni* is a slow and complicated process, and it can be costly in vis, but the spirits summoned by *saḥirs* can remain at their side for seasons and can be summoned again throughout the *saḥir*'s whole life. With good forward planning a *saḥir* can become a powerful enemy, although he should not neglect his Hermetic abilities for those times when he must face adversity with no *jinni* at hand.

*Saḥirs* often have to accept some obligation on the *jinn*'s behalf in order for them to enter their service, and they are bound to fulfill this duty for the length of the contract. The storyguide should make sure that at least one event related to this obligation occurs. If the *saḥir* fails to fulfill this duty, the contract is broken and the *jinni* becomes his enemy, which means temporarily gaining the Flaw Plagued by Supernatural Entity (*jinni*) or Supernatural Nuisance.

Most of the *jinn* with which Hermetic *saḥirs* deal are aligned with the Magic Realm. Some practitioners of this magic specialize in faerie *jinn*. However, most of these *jinn* profess Islam, and that religion forbids one Muslim to enslave another. More worrying is that some spirits that appear to be *jinn* are really demons, although, fortunately for the *saḥirs*, infernal *jinn* are usually easy to identify by their bloodlust and brutality (there is more information on the *jinn* on page 110 of the *Realms of Power: Magic* supplement).

#### Relations with Non-Hermetic Saḥirs

Hermetic *saḥirs* have very little contact with the non-Hermetic branch of their tradition. Since almost 300 years have passed since the Iberian *saḥirs* placed themselves under the protection of the Order, a non-Hermetic *saḥir* will rarely be found in Iberia today. However, rumor has it that, after the Other Tribunal of Harra, some may have made their way into the Peninsula (see page 174).

Non-Hermetic *saḥirs* are believed to be members of an association of Muslim wizards similar to the Order of Hermes, though with much closer mundane ties. Non-Hermetic *saḥirs* have much greater control over the *jinn*. Instead of relying on contracts to win their favors, they can compel them if necessary. The powers that non-Hermetic *saḥirs* demand of their *jinn* include immortality, the healing of any ailment, instant transport, spying on others, transforming into something else, and even magic resistance. Hermetic *saḥirs* crave the knowledge of this magic, but all their attempts to contact their Levantine brethren have ended in hostility.

#### Characters

All Hermetic *saḥirs* are Muslims. If the saga is set anywhere other than Islamic Iberia, characters should have the Flaw Judged Unfairly to represent the prejudice that magi may hold against Muslims (it would be the same for mundanes, although compared with the negative effects of the Gift it would be a minor matter). *Saḥirs* are also likely to have the Flaw Feud, owing to the enmity between their lineage and some members of House Flambeau.

Certain Virtues are very useful to Hermetic *saḥirs*, above all Second Sight; in addition, a few are Elementalists, and the Virtues Student of (Realm) are also common, as are Puissant or Affinity with Bargain. Botches in negotiations with the *jinn* during apprenticeship may bring with them the Flaw Plagued by Supernatural Entity, Supernatural Nuisance, or Greater or Lesser Malediction. Occasionally a *jinni* may choose to accompany a *saḥir* of its own free will, granting him a variant of the Flaw Faerie Friend (although in this case the *jinni* will have Magic Might rather than Faerie Might).

#### Assessing a Jinni's Might

Before summoning a *jinni*, the prudent *saḥir* studies it to estimate its relative power. If the *saḥir* has the Virtue Second Sight, or a spell that lets him see spirits, this estimate takes only a round, since he can observe the *jinni* directly in its habitat. Without magical aid, the *saḥir* must use his knowledge of the local area to gather enough information about the spirit that dwells there. To do so, he must make an Intelligence + (Area) Lore roll against an Ease Factor of 6 to discover the center of its power, the form the *jinni* takes and its possible powers. This examination takes the *saḥir* about an hour. Once this preliminary investigation has been carried out, the *saḥir* may try to discern the *jinni*'s approximate Might from its appearance (if visible), its dwelling and his own knowledge of these matters. First he must decide whether the *jinni* is faerie, magical or infernal from its behavior and attitude (at this point the *saḥir* can rely only on his experience), and then make an Intelligence + appropriate Realm Lore roll (that is, Magic Lore, Dominion Lore, Infernal Lore or Faerie Lore) against an Ease Factor of 9. If he succeeds, the *saḥir* infers the magnitude of the *jinni*'s Might. If he fails, he cannot guess it, so summoning the *jinni* would be dangerous. If he botches, the inferred magnitude is determined by rolling a simple die. Note that choosing the correct Realm Lore is vital; if the player chooses wrongly, he adds nothing but his Intelligence to the roll. However, since the player need not have any experience with *jinn*, the storyguide should make the differences between their various kinds clear.

<!-- p. 298 -->

**Assessing the Might of Jinn:** Intelligence + appropriate Realm Lore + stress die vs. Ease Factor 9

#### Summoning a Jinni

Once he has assessed the *jinni*'s Might, the *saḥir* can summon it and bind it to his service. This summoning must be performed in the presence of the *jinni* (in its physical state) or at the place it inhabits (the more common of the two options, as it provides an Arcane Connection to the spirit). Once the summoning has begun, the *jinni* can interfere with the process (although most do not), so it is advisable to raise a Hermetic ward that can hold it at bay. The summoning takes about fifteen minutes and causes the spirit to assume its material form. During it, the *saḥir* chants the words of command codified by Solomon while performing the prescribed ritual movements and writing Arabic numerals on the ground. The summoning also requires vis appropriate to the Form of the *jinni* summoned. The standard cost of the summoning is one pawn per magnitude of the *jinni*'s Might, although the *saḥir* may choose to spend less (one pawn at minimum) or more (up to a maximum equal to his Siḥr score). Note that the *saḥir* has only his estimate of the *jinni*'s Might (assuming he tried to assess its Might before the summoning), so he may unknowingly spend more or less than the standard cost. The amount of vis spent does not affect the summoning, but it plays an important part in the negotiation that follows.

The *saḥir* generates a Summoning Total based on his Siḥr Ability. A successful summoning that penetrates the *jinni*'s Magic Resistance forces it to take its physical form before the *saḥir*. The amount by which the *saḥir*'s Summoning Total exceeds the Ease Factor is the Summoning Strength. A botch on the Siḥr roll may cause an enraged *jinni*, or a spirit entirely different from the one expected, to appear.

**Summoning Total:** Presence + Siḥr + aura + stress die

**Ease Factor:** jinni's Might

**Summoning Penetration Total:** Summoning Total + Penetration bonus – jinni's Might

**Summoning Strength:** Summoning Total – Ease Factor

<!-- p. 299 -->

A *saḥir* may spend more time on his summonings; for every additional fifteen minutes, the *saḥir* loses a Fatigue level after the summoning, adds one botch die to the summoning roll and gains a +2 bonus to the Penetration Total. *Saḥirs* take more time when summoning *jinn* whose Might is close to the limit of their Ability.

#### Negotiating with a Jinni

Once the *jinni* has manifested, the *saḥir* must negotiate with it to obtain its services. The power of the Siḥr Virtue prevents the *jinni* from leaving or attacking until it has reached an agreement with the magus, or until both decide that no agreement is possible. However, if the *saḥir* refuses to negotiate, the *jinni* need not make a pact with him. In this context the word "negotiation" can be somewhat misleading, since an experienced *saḥir* can secure the services of a weak *jinni* without offering anything in return.

If an agreement is reached, the magic enforces its terms: the *jinni* cannot break its word unless the *saḥir* breaches the terms of the agreement, and as long as the *saḥir* does not abuse it, most *jinn* also tend to keep faith with what was agreed.

A *saḥir* can try to reach an agreement with any *jinni*, not only the one he has summoned (for example, when renegotiating after an earlier agreement has expired), although he will not have the advantage of the Summoning Strength, which is often necessary.

**Negotiation Total:** Communication + Bargain + Summoning Strength + stress die

**Ease Factor:** 18 + negotiation modifiers

The Ease Factor carries a negotiation modifier that depends on what the *saḥir* is asking of the *jinni* and what he offers in return.

If the negotiation roll fails, no agreement is reached and the *jinni* is not obliged to remain. If the roll botches, the *saḥir* gains the Flaw Supernatural Nuisance (for a weak *jinni*) or Plagued by Supernatural Entity (*jinni*) (for one of moderate or great power) for at least a month. If the negotiation succeeds, the *jinni* is entirely at the *saḥir*'s disposal for as long as the agreement lasts. The *saḥir* can ask it to do anything within its capabilities, although when a *jinni* spends its last Might point in the *saḥir*'s service, the bond ends, regardless of what remains to be done. The *jinni* cannot break any solemn oath it made before being summoned, such as, for *jinn* who profess a religion, disobeying the tenets of their faith. The *jinni* cannot swear any new oath during its service without the *saḥir*'s permission. Furthermore, a *jinni* that has remained in a magus's service for a season or more can be used to teach Siḥr, an appropriate Hermetic Form or one of the Realm Lores (that is, Magic Lore, Dominion Lore, Infernal Lore or Faerie Lore, as appropriate). A *jinni* can instruct the *saḥir* only once in each Ability and Art. A *saḥir* can have as many *jinn* in his service at one time as his Leadership score, although every *saḥir* can command at least one *jinni*.

> #### Typical Tasks for Saḥirs
>
> **Simple tasks:** cleaning or guarding the *jinni*'s home, protecting a human family to which the *jinni* is attached, recovering riches stolen from it, writing a poem praising the *jinni*, obtaining rare goods (such as incense or rubies).
>
> **Complex tasks:** fighting wizards who seek to enslave *jinn*, freeing *jinn* from captivity, playing a prank on a local figure of some importance, delivering the heart of an enemy, obtaining a rare item (such as a book written by Solomon himself).
>
> #### Negotiation Modifiers
>
> | Condition | Modifier |
> | --- | --- |
> | The terms of the agreement are general in scope ("Follow me and do as I say") | +3 |
> | The terms of the agreement are specific in scope ("Help me find the table of Solomon") | +0 |
> | The terms of the agreement involve a single task ("Take me safely across the Strait of Gibraltar") | –3 |
> | The service lasts for a day | –3 |
> | The service lasts for a week | +0 |
> | The service lasts for a month | +3 |
> | The service lasts for a season | +6 |
> | The service lasts for a year | +9 |
> | The *saḥir* accepts a simple task | –3 |
> | The *saḥir* accepts a complex task | –6 |
> | The *saḥir* has spent less vis than the standard cost | +2\* |
> | The *saḥir* has spent more vis than the standard cost | –2\* |
>
> \* The modifier applies per pawn spent above or below the standard cost.

<!-- p. 300 -->

**Quality of a Jinni as a Source:** 3 × Might magnitude

**Maximum Number of Jinn a Saḥir Can Control at Once:** Leadership (minimum 1)

#### Hermetic Magic

*Saḥirs* are usually good at the elemental Forms, because they can learn from the *jinn* they summon. They should also always know spells that protect them against *jinn*, in case they fail to negotiate an agreement. The most cautious *saḥirs* usually raise wards around themselves before beginning a summoning.

Since Hermetic magic lacks a specific protection against *jinn*, and *saḥirs* favor the elemental Forms, they usually create powerful wards against a specific type of *jinn* (of water, of earth, and so on), although to do so they must learn different variants according to the nature of the *jinn*: faerie, magical or infernal. The *saḥirs*' magical arsenal includes apotropaic spells (those that strip spirits of their Might).

*Suleimān's Wrath upon the Treacherous Jinni*, PeVi Gen

R: Voice, D: Mom, T: Ind

This spell weakens, and can destroy, creatures with Magic Might. If the spell penetrates the creature's Magic Resistance, it loses as many Might points as the spell has levels. If the creature's Might falls to zero, it is permanently destroyed. For the spirit to be a valid target, the caster must be able to detect it in some way, so another spell may be needed to perceive it.

(General base, +2 Voice)

> #### Saḥirs in the Saga
>
> Playing a *saḥir* character in a saga poses some challenges that differ from those of other magi. The *saḥir*'s work is done in advance: before a story begins, he must summon the *jinni* and bind it to his service. However, his non-Hermetic magic depends heavily on the amount of vis available in the saga, which determines his capacity to summon *jinn*. Moreover, *saḥirs* do best on familiar ground, where they have investigated the local *jinn* and know their capabilities well. The storyguide should create several *jinn* in the covenant's surroundings and let other players use them as supporting characters during stories. Although *jinn* must obey the agreements made with *saḥirs*, they need not do so servilely. *Jinn* can have different personalities: some will be friendly and willing to negotiate, while others will be hostile and try to turn the pact they have made on its head. Remember too that as a *saḥir* grows in power, he will want to summon a more powerful *jinni*, so the storyguide should make sure there are spirits of varying power in the area, or that the *saḥir* can find them on his travels.

### The Tempestarii

#### Key Points

Major Non-Hermetic Virtue: Tempestarius (see "New Virtues and Flaws" below).

Minor Hermetic Virtue: Affinity with Auram.

Major Hermetic Flaw: Chaotic Magic.

Typical Virtues and Flaws: Special Circumstances (storms), Puissant Auram, Mythic Blood; Magic Addiction, Hedge Wizard, Warped Magic, Infamous Master.

#### History

Before the Order of Hermes came to Iberia, before its very founding, and even before the Romanization of the Iberian Peninsula, there lived in the northern reaches of Iberia a group of wizards feared and hated in equal measure by the locals. They were descendants of the ancient worshipers of the god of thunder and storm, known in the regions of Galicia and Asturias as Nuberu (paired with the Celtic Taranis, the Roman Jupiter or the Germanic Wotan), and so these sorcerers were originally called *núberos*, although they should not be confused with the supernatural creatures of similar nature (see insert on page 301). They were unsettling and mysterious figures who from time to time appeared unexpectedly in the lives of the inhabitants of those regions, bearing cryptic messages and strange requests, only to vanish again just as swiftly. Their arrival was usually marked by violent storms and rain, and so, when the Romans reached the north of the Peninsula, they began to call them by the name by which the Order of Hermes would come to know them: *tempestarii*.

The tempestarii lived all along the Cantabrian coast, and the common folk attributed strange powers to them, all of them related to storms: it was said that they could summon torrential rain, hail and snowfall, but some told of even more incredible feats, such as divining the future merely by watching the lightning fall from the sky, or even riding the storms to travel at great speed from one place to another. The Romans, who respected any wizard able to read omens or auguries in the elements of nature, had an ambivalent relationship with the tempestarii, fighting them (and executing them) when they resisted, yet going so far as to employ their services to learn the fate of their battles. The wizards survived the fall of the Roman Empire and are still present today, especially in the most rural parts of the region.

#### The Coming of the Order of Hermes

The arrival of the Order of Hermes brought a radical change for the tempestarii. The first Flambeau, and Grimoald Niger in particular, made the ancient priests one of their main targets during their expansion through the north of the Peninsula. However, the tempestarii put up formidable opposition to the Order, mounting an organized resistance with strong support from the very rural folk in whom they inspired such fear. Not a few Flambeau were struck down by their lightning in the duels between the two traditions.

<!-- p. 301 -->

For a long time the tempestarii were a thorn in the Order's side, and it even tried diplomacy to subdue an enemy that proved unyielding. Some records speak of tempestarii attending the meetings held at the vanished covenant of Lucis, and of how they might perhaps have joined the Order. However, the negotiations grew complicated (as explained in Chapter III, see page 64), and in 792 the tempestarii presented a series of demands that the Order found unacceptable, dashing any possibility of alliance.

The Flambeau of Brigantia took matters into their own hands and resolved to finish off the storm wizards once and for all. They prepared a great joint attack on their main centers of power but, surprisingly, the tempestarii were ready for them. Although some accused the maga Tancoystl of Diedne of having warned them (something that could never be proven), the *núberos* stood up to the Flambeau for months in a conflict that laid waste to entire regions. When the conflict threatened to spill over into the mundane sphere, in 794, it was decided to attack the main sanctuary of the tempestarii, which was also the most important vis source in northern Iberia: a beach on the western coast of Asturias. Almost all the magi of the Peninsula took part in a brutal attack that razed the beach. Stripped of one of their great sources of power, the vast majority of the tempestarii chose to fight on to the death rather than join the Order, and only a few agreed to convert and join the ranks of Duresca.

#### The Surviving Lineage and the Ordo Miscellanea

Nevertheless, those few tempestarii were always viewed with suspicion by many magi of the Order, and more than one died in some incident during those turbulent years. By the time the war against the Spider had ended and Pralix had returned from Britain at the head of the Ordo Miscellanea, only two tempestarii remained at Duresca: Nicero and his young apprentice Aria, who did not hesitate to join the new order, which in 817 would become the thirteenth Hermetic House. Unfortunately, by then many of their inner mysteries had been lost, and those two magi could pass on to the later members of the lineage only the knowledge they possessed: the summoning, and limited control, of storms and other weather phenomena. Although no documents on the rest of the mysteries have ever been found, since the tradition of the *núberos* was handed down chiefly by word of mouth, there are still some today who try to recover that lost knowledge to expand the capabilities of the lineage of the *tempestarii*.

#### The Tempestarii Today

From then until now, the tempestarii have remained a very minor lineage within House Ex Miscellanea, and they exist only in the Peninsula. They usually go unnoticed, with rare exceptions (such as Aria Ex Miscellanea, who summoned a hailstorm in high summer over Oviedo at the end of the eleventh century), and they number barely ten members. Despite the centuries that have passed since their tumultuous inclusion in the Order, there are those who have not forgotten that their ancestors spilled a great deal of Hermetic blood. Nor does the tempestarii's strange tendency to lose control of their magic unpredictably help their reputation (some even summon hail mixed with goat hair, represented by a possible Warped Magic Flaw). That is why there are some, especially among the Flambeau, who feel an undying hostility toward them. Many tempestarii live in covenants in the kingdom of Leon, where they feel protected by like-minded magi who have lived alongside them for many years. They seldom travel beyond those regions, and meeting a tempestarius in the south of the Peninsula, or elsewhere in Europe, is quite unusual, and generally means that he is immersed in some important research that has led him to leave his usual surroundings.

Perhaps because of the hostility they arouse, the tempestarii usually keep a rather low profile at every level: they almost never take an active part in Tribunal politics and, although they will defend the Order if necessary, they will do so only as a last resort. More than once they have been accused of refusing to help other magi in some conflict, which has only reinforced the stigma they still bear; not a few believe that one day they will betray the Order. On their own, their small numbers would make them no threat, but if their contacts with other minor traditions of a similar nature elsewhere in Europe were discovered, the Order would doubtless take that danger far more seriously.

#### Customs

The few tempestarii who exist today try to keep alive the traditions they inherited from the *núberos* of old. Although their knowledge and powers are quite limited compared with those of their forebears, they feel themselves the legitimate heirs of a tradition that it is their responsibility to keep alive. For that reason they guard this knowledge jealously, passing it from master to apprentice in private ceremonies about which nobody knows anything — another reason that feeds the suspicions of the more mistrustful. Besides a magus's official naming within the Order, it is customary for the tempestarii to perform an initiation ritual for an apprentice in which they reveal to him the outer secrets of the tradition. This ritual is usually held on a beach on the western coast of Asturias, a place still shunned by mundanes today and about which all manner of strange stories are told, doubtless a consequence of the attack carried out centuries ago by the Hermetic magi. The tempestarii, however, know the place well and, if the gossips are to be believed, they know of one or more *regiones* where their ancestral magic is still active, and it is precisely there that these initiations take place.

Although almost no one in the Order knows it, the tempestarii maintain constant and stable communication with other traditions of a similar character scattered across Europe, such as the weather witches of Germany and the Saxon lands, or the lineage of Muj (from which Myanar descended), both within the Order of Hermes, or certain Transylvanian wizards in the distant Carpathians. It is even said that there have occasionally been conclaves attended by the leaders of these different traditions, although only they know what matters were discussed there.

<!-- p. 302 -->

> #### The Ñuberu
>
> The ñuberu is one of the most ancient creatures of the northwest of the Peninsula, and the oldest legends of the kingdoms of Leon, Castile and Navarre already speak of similar beings. Although their exact appearance may vary from case to case and from region to region, for they are creatures with distinct personalities and purposes, all these legends credit them with the same powers: a command of storms, blizzards and hail that sows terror among the inhabitants of the most remote towns and villages. The same legends ascribed a certain mischievous character to these creatures, which delighted in tormenting the inhabitants of the villages they visited, threatening to destroy crops and houses if their whims were not satisfied — whims that could be of very diverse kinds: sometimes they were content to carry off food from the local granaries, but at other times they demanded animals or even newborn babies. The consequences of ignoring the ñuberus' demands could be disastrous: if the creature was in a good mood, it merely lifted whoever crossed it into the air, using its control over the clouds to give them a hard time. If they truly flew into a rage, the outcome was worse: more than one poor father was struck dead by lightning summoned by one of these creatures when it wanted to carry off his child. Many fishermen have lost their lives in the waters of the Cantabrian Sea, victims of an unexpected tempest. That is why many coastal villages still perform various rituals to drive the ñuberus away. Here are some examples.
>
> - Burning a branch of blessed *lloreu* (laurel) (the *lloreu* and the *noceu*, or walnut, are sacred trees that lightning can never strike).
>
> - Lighting a candle called a *tinieblina* (brought from the Maundy Thursday Mass).
>
> - Placing an axe pointing at the cloud.
>
> - Turning a cart upside down (forming a cross with the crossbar and the body).
>
> - Ringing the church bells (ñuberus hate the sound of bronze and are frightened off by the pealing of bells).
>
> - Praying to Saint Barbara or Saint Bartholomew.
>
> The ancient tempestarii had regular dealings with the ñuberus, although no one, not even the few members of the tradition who still exist today, remembers what those dealings consisted of. The destruction of the tradition forced the ñuberus to hide high in the mountains, and they disappeared for a time, perhaps for fear of crossing paths with the Hermetic magi who had wiped out their protégés. Over time, however, they gradually began to lose their fear and came down once again to the villages and towns to commit their mischief anew. Today, the inhabitants of those regions still flee at once when they see a traveler whose appearance recalls, however remotely, a ñuberu.
>
> Although the ñuberu described here is magical in origin, faerie ñuberus also exist in the Peninsula, with powers and weaknesses very similar to these, which makes it very hard to tell one from the other. In fact, in the tenth century there was a tempestarius named Abel who postulated that his lineage might have a faerie origin, citing as proof the characteristics they shared with the ñuberus. Abel disappeared in the midst of a terrible storm off the coast of Galicia, supposedly while trying to contact one of the most powerful ñuberus of the area.

<!-- p. 303 -->
