#### The Power of Storms

To summon a storm, the tempestarius must make a stress roll of Communication + Tempestarius + Auram/5. The basic Ease Factor is 0, modified as follows according to the size and duration of the storm.

**Total to Summon a Storm:** Communication + Tempestarius + Auram/5 + stress die

***Size of the storm:***

**+3 Local range.** The storm affects an area five kilometers in diameter. It costs one pawn of Auram vis.

**+6 Provincial range.** The storm affects an area seven leagues (thirty kilometers) in diameter. It costs two pawns of Auram vis.

**+12 National range.** The storm affects an area 250 kilometers in diameter. It costs four pawns of Auram vis.

***Duration of the storm:***

**+3.** The storm lasts a Diameter.

**+6.** The storm lasts an hour.

**+9.** The storm has Sun duration.

**+12.** The storm has Moon duration.

Summoning a storm also requires the expenditure of Auram vis, without which the natural forces cannot be controlled as the tempestarius wishes. The storm is centered on the place where the tempestarius stands when he summons it, and if he moves, it does not move with him. The storm takes a number of rounds equal to the Ease Factor to appear, and if summoned indoors, it breaks outside. Although the storm is summoned magically (and counts as a magical effect for the purposes of auras), once summoned it is entirely natural and need not penetrate any Magic Resistance to affect a target.

<!-- p. 304 -->

The tempestarius can also move a storm (whether he summoned it or not) at a rate of one kilometer per Diameter. To do so, he must make a roll similar to the one above, but whose Ease Factor depends only on the size (and not the duration) of the storm. While it is being moved in this way, the storm does count as a supernatural effect for the purposes of Penetration.

To travel in a storm, the tempestarius must make a stress roll of Perception + Tempestarius + Auram/5 of 12+, modified by +3 if he is inside the storm. If he can see his destination, the magus will arrive there without difficulty. Otherwise, he must specify a distance and direction when making the roll. With a roll of 15+ he can do the same with another person he is touching.

**Total to Travel in a Storm:** Perception + Tempestarius + Auram/5 + stress die

Finally, the tempestarius can use the devastating power of a storm to attack people or structures, provided he can see them and they are within the storm. The form of the attack depends on the Ease Factor; some examples are given below. The roll in this case is always a stress roll of Strength + Tempestarius + Finesse + Auram/5.

**Total to Attack with a Storm:** Strength + Tempestarius + Finesse + Auram/5 + stress die

**3: Deluge.** Affects all targets within a thirty-meter diameter. Anyone who wants to move within that area must make a Dexterity roll of 6+ or stumble and fall. This counts as an aimed attack and ignores Magic Resistance.

**6: Hailstorm.** Affects all targets within a thirty-meter diameter, who suffer +3 damage. This counts as an aimed attack and ignores Magic Resistance.

**9: Erosion.** Affects a single structure (such as a tree, a house, a small tower, and so on), eroding the earth at the structure's foundations so that it collapses. The attack may have no effect against especially solid foundations or those cut into rock.

**12: Lightning.** A bolt of lightning strikes a single target, causing +20 damage. If the roll succeeds, it automatically hits its target, although it must penetrate the target's Magic Resistance (in this case, Finesse is not added to the total).

> #### Story Seeds: The Resurgence of the Tempestarii
>
> The inhabitants of a village near the characters' covenant come to ask for their help after suffering the depredations of a ñuberu that recently visited the village. However, when the magi go to investigate and speak with the locals, they discover certain clues that are somewhat baffling. It seems that the ñuberu was accompanied by a young man, something extremely unusual. According to the witnesses, the youth also seemed to share some of the ñuberu's powers. More worrying still: if the magi investigate the scene with Intellego magic, they will find what are undoubtedly traces of Hermetic spells. The possible consequences, should a link be discovered between the Order and a creature such as the ñuberu, could be unpredictable, but the case will become more complicated still as the characters continue their inquiries: they soon discover that the description of the youth who accompanied the ñuberu matches that of a young apprentice who went missing from an Ex Miscellanea covenant a couple of years ago, and who belonged to the minor tradition of the tempestarii. Could the ñuberu be instructing the young man in the oldest and most forgotten arts of the tempestarii? What is its purpose? Perhaps to restore the tradition to its former glory? Might the Order have to face once again what was one of its worst enemies in its early years of settlement in Iberia?

## Falāsifa

*And no one shall be permitted to say: this kind of reflection through rational analogy is a heresy, for it did not exist at the beginning of Islam. For reflection through juridical analogy and its kinds was deduced after the first moment of Islam, and yet it is not considered heresy.*[^p304-6]

[^p304-6]: Excerpt from *The Decisive Treatise* by Averroes (Spanish translation by A. Yacine and P. Chabrera Calpe).

In recent years the Tribunal has undergone a veritable philosophical revolution thanks to the wisdom distilled in the writings of the great Maimonides and Averroes. Indeed, the Praeco ʿEzraʾ is a great champion and disseminator of Maimonides' ideas among the members of the Order, although this has earned him the enmity of the Kabbalists of his native city, who, like the ṣūfīs, are anti-rationalists. In 1220 many magi call themselves *falāsifa* (from the Arabic for "philosophers"; singular *faylasūf*).

### The Ṣūfī Mystics

*Those who travel in Him are divided into two groups: (first) there are those who travel in Him by means of thought and the mind, and have strayed from the path, having found no guide in their quest but their reason. These are the philosophers, and those who follow that course. The (second) group is that of those who travel with Him, that of the messengers and the prophets, of the elect among such saints, such as the men of Sufism […].*[^p304-7]

[^p304-7]: Excerpt from *The Splendor of the Fruits of the Journey* by Ibn ʿArabī (Spanish translation by Carlos Varona Narvión).

<!-- p. 305 -->

All the ṣūfīs of Iberia belong to a mystical community or brotherhood (*ṭarīqa*) where they can share teachings and knowledge in order to reach the state of purification needed to attain the original unity, or *tawḥīd*. To reach this state, the ṣūfīs follow a very strict ascetic life and hold to a very rigid morality, so they commit no crimes or sins and cannot accept gifts or alms from those who they do not know to have acquired them lawfully (for example, gifts from the civil authorities are always refused, for there is no ruler who is not a tyrant).

Different schools are followed among the ṣūfīs, such as the malāmī, which originated in the East and whose chief rule consists of avoiding vanity by hiding spiritual perfection beneath a false appearance of moral imperfection that draws the scorn of the faithful; or that of Al-Ḥāriṯ ibn Asad al-Musḥāsibī (born in the ninth century in Basra), whose essential rule consists of the scrupulous examination of conscience to attain moral perfection (the followers of this school often write down in a notebook each night everything they have done, so as to see their faults more easily and be able to amend them the following day).

According to Ibn ʿArabī there is a complex hierarchy among the ṣūfī mystics, with different degrees of dignity and esoteric perfection. There is a single *quṭh* ("pole") around which the spiritual life of the whole world turns; two *imām* ("chiefs") who serve as the *quṭh*'s vicars and succeed him when he dies; four *awtād* ("pillars"), charged with carrying his mission to the four cardinal points; seven *abdāl* ("substitutes") who carry out their mission in the seven geographical climes; twelve *naqīb* ("prefects") for the twelve signs of the zodiac; and eight *naŷīb* ("nobles") for the eight celestial spheres.

As for their philosophy, the ṣūfīs, who oppose the rationalist ideas of Averroes (the Rationalists proclaimed reason superior to the sensible delight proclaimed by the ṣūfīs), draw on the Andalusi works of Ibn ʿArabī and Al-Gazālī, and start from the premise that human reason is nothing more than an obstacle to finding the true light of knowledge, which can be reached only with the heart (hence the path toward the light must be traveled through love and not through reason). This light of knowledge (called the wisdom of illumination, or *ḥikmat-al-išrāq*) gathers in the *tawḥīd* (meaning unity), from which everything emanates and to which, after completing a cycle, it is reunited (according to the theory of "the unity of existence," or *waḥdat al-wuŷūd*, in which knowledge and reality are joined together; see insert).

The ultimate goal of the one who walks the path of light is to reach the summit of purification (that is, the revelation of God), which the ṣūfī mystics call *kašf* or *mukašafa* (meaning discovery). After that stage comes the passing away, or *fanāʾ*, in which the self is annihilated to become part of the whole, like a drop in the ocean. Then comes *baqā*, the resurrection, in which one exists outside of nothingness. One who reaches this state is called *ḏū al-ʿaynayn*, he who has two eyes, the right of which sees unity and the left multiplicity, while knowing that both visions are one and the same.

> #### Emanationist Theory
>
> *[…] since wisdom is in a certain way something proper to men […], it is considered impossible that the whole inhabited earth should abandon philosophy, just as one must think it impossible that it should abandon the natural arts.*[^p305-III]
>
> Neoplatonic emanationist theory and the Plotinian doctrine of the "One" and the many became known in Iberia through the *Epistles* of the Brethren of Purity. Rationalists and ṣūfīs alike used them to argue part of their cosmological ontology. A general summary of their postulates follows.
>
> ##### Neoplatonic Emanationism
>
> According to Neoplatonic emanationism, everything derives from the One, or first cause, from which flow the rest of the intelligibles, distributed in three circles:
>
> - the first circle, closest to the One, corresponds to the decad of the intelligences or pure immaterial forms, among which is the agent intellect;
>
> - the second circle is made up of the decad of the souls, ten celestial spheres among which is the universal soul (which emanates from the agent intellect);
>
> - the third and last circle is made up of the decad of material beings, where are found the forms, matter, the four elements, the three natural kingdoms (vegetable, animal and mineral) and mortals.
>
> The first two circles are immutable, but the third (the sublunar world where mortals live) is not. This makes it the most imperfect circle of all. However, since mortals are the most perfect form of the sublunar world (above the three natural kingdoms), they can attain the perfection of the tenth sphere of the third circle through the intellectual act. The circles contain the motors of human existence, namely: the perfect ideas; the agent intellect that contains them (which actualizes the human intellect); the human intellect; the soul in which the intellect and the other cognitive faculties reside; and, finally, the whole of the self-soul.
>
> ##### The Unity of Existence
>
> According to the ṣūfīs' theory of the unity of existence, the intelligibles are distributed in three orbs of existence (*wuŷūd*), which can in turn be subdivided:
>
> - the first is the Essence of God (the divine immensity, or *al-ŷabārūt*), which is the Absolute Unity (*aḥadiyya*), having no manifestation or direct bond with anything; to mortals it is unknowable. From it flows creation;
>
> - in the second, separated from the first tier by a barrier impassable to human perception, the divinity makes itself known through its Names (*al-malakūt*), through which everything exists in the mystery of the absolute secret;
>
> - in the third tier are the concrete or particular Essences (*aʿayān*), arising from the Names after the Holy Effusion (*al-fayḍ al-muqaddas*). This is the intermediate world, where forms have not yet taken shape, and where the Criamon of Barzaj believe the *regio* of their covenant lies (see page 255).
>
> [^p305-III]: Excerpt from *On the Intellect* by Averroes (Spanish translation by Andrés Martínez Lorca).

<!-- p. 306 -->

Given how closely their philosophies resemble each other, the Criamon are staunch followers of this mystical current, and many have found in Iberia the setting they need to devote themselves to the pursuit of the Enigma. At present the Iberian brood (whose heart is the covenant of Barzaj) follows the Path of Walking Backwards (see *Houses of Hermes: Mystery Cults*, page 120), although your troupe could develop another Path based on the philosophical concepts of the ṣūfīs. Bear in mind that, in 1220, the ideas of the ṣūfīs are persecuted by the Almohad fuqahāʾ.

#### The Kabbalistic Circle of Gerona

The Kabbalists of Gerona champion esoteric knowledge and mysticism as the road to God. Like the Muslim ṣūfīs, the Jewish Kabbalists oppose the rationalism voiced by Averroes and Maimonides.

The Kabbalistic circle of Gerona formed in the twelfth century, inspired by the teachings of Yiṣḥaq the Blind of Provence, a preacher of a contemplative mysticism based on meditation upon the Sefirot and the symbolic interpretation of the Bible. The first two members of the circle were the blind man's pupils, ʿEzraʾ and ʿAzriʾel. They were later joined by the celebrated Yaʿāqoḇ ben Šešet Girondí, a defender of the creation of the world in Kabbalistic terms and a bitter enemy of Maimonides' theses. The most influential member of the circle, however, is probably the physician Mošeh ben Naḥman, known as Naḥmanides.

#### The Rationalists

*It is a fact that true entitative reality is known through demonstration, in which there is no room for divergence, nor for rejecting or denying what has been proven, unless one is dealing with an ignoramus who clings to so-called "apodictic contradiction." In this respect you will find people who dispute the sphericity of the earth, the circular motion of the celestial sphere, and things of that kind. Such sorts of people are not our concern.*[^p306-8]

[^p306-8]: Excerpt from *The Guide for the Perplexed* by Maimonides (Spanish translation by David Gonzalo Maeso).

The Rationalists are followers of the writings of Averroes and Maimonides, so nearly all the magi of the Tribunal could be considered Rationalists, since the foundations of Hermetic theory rest on these theses and their predecessors. For them, truth can be reached through reason, independently of faith (in a clear separation of philosophy and theology). Reason is a divine Gift that must be used to explain the mysteries to which man has had no access since his creation; once the power of reason is accepted, every concept can be interpreted through philosophy.

Many magi in Iberia revere these ideas and devote much of their study to philosophy. It is thus rare for a covenant not to own Maimonides' *Guide for the Perplexed*, or not to use it to teach apprentices the philosophical foundations of Hermetic theory.

> #### On the Fourth Lateran Council
>
> In 1215 the Fourth Lateran Council was held in the city of Rome. Among other things, it issued canons to condemn heretical ideas, regulate the conduct of the clergy and the formation of religious orders, make confession (at least once a year) and communion compulsory for the laity, and impose new measures on the Jews, such as the compulsory wearing of garments that identified them, a ban on their holding public office, and a ban on converts returning to their former faith.
>
> Although the council ended in 1216, its conclusions did not reach the Peninsula until 1228–1229, so their strict application does not clash with the canonical starting year of *Ars Magica* in the Iberian Tribunal.

The magi of ʾAlif built on these theses to create a Mystery of their own (based on the Enigmatic Wisdom of House Criamon and on a Hermetic breakthrough), which they called the Path of Negative Attributes (see *Houses of Hermes: Mystery Cults*, page 123). This Path arose with the Rationalist movement led by the members of ʾAlif and the Perfect Order, and it has no representation in any other Tribunal. Although the Path of Negative Attributes might seem to have no brood (like the Path of Beacons), this is not so; its followers call it the agent intellect: the state of the solitary can raise a solid barrier against the discord of the world, based on the physical isolation of its members and on the search for the answer to the Enigma through the negation of its attributes, for the members of this Path hold that the nature of the Enigma can be revealed by no other method.

## New Abilities, Virtues and Flaws

### New Virtues and Flaws

Muslim and Jewish characters, whether of urban or rural origin, are generated in the same way as any other character. However, some Virtues and Flaws are forbidden to them or, at least, very rarely seen among them (at the storyguide's discretion, you may rename them or modify them slightly). They also have access to some additional Virtues and Flaws available only to them.

Muslim characters living in non-Muslim lands are generated in the same way as other Muslim characters, but they must take the Major Social Status Flaw Outsider to reflect their relationship with the local people around them.

As a general rule, characters of another faith living under Islam cannot belong to the religious class (ʿĀlim, Qādī, Sufi), although many Christians living under Islam serve in the civil administration, and Jews may be merchants. Almost all non-Muslim characters living in a Muslim state should have the Minor General Flaw Dhimmi, described below, which reflects their status as non-Muslims in the lands of Islam. The exceptions tend to be people who stand outside the social order and therefore escape the notice of the Muslim authorities. Hermetic magi are the most obvious example of these exceptions.

## Virtues

### Abjuration

*Major, Supernatural*

This Virtue grants the Accelerated Ability Abjuration at level 1.

#### Faqih

*Minor, Social Status*

Plural *al-fuqahā*. You are a member of the religious elite and possess knowledge of *fiqh* (jurisprudence); you are also a specialist in the juridical religious sciences (*fiqh* and *šarīʿa*) and, above all, in what may be derived from them. As such, you have good prospects for advancement in public life and, if you excel in your duties, you may join the qadi's court, where you must advise him so that his judgments are as just as possible according to the law. You may take Academic Abilities during character generation. This Virtue is only available to male Muslim characters.

#### ʿĀlim

*Minor, Social Status*

You are a member of the religious elite and possess the quality of science, knowledge and learning. As such, you are both jurist and theologian. Your influence in society is great, and thanks to your acknowledged holiness and a great deal of preaching you could even sway the policies of the ruler of your city or region. However, you are a conservative element in any Muslim government and always put the brakes on any innovation. Governors will try to buy you with offices and salaries, which you must refuse if you wish to keep your status. Most likely you are regarded as a holy man and subject yourself to all kinds of ascetic mortifications. Your status as an ʿālim (one of the ulema) does not prevent you from taking up arms, provided it is to wage holy war.

You begin play with a positive Reputation of 4 as incorruptible and independent of power. You may take Academic Abilities during character generation. This Virtue is only available to male Muslim characters.

#### Aligned with the Stars

*Major, Supernatural*

This Virtue is gained after the riadiin is initiated into the cult's Inner Mystery. The initiate doubles his Artes Liberales score (including Puissant, if he has it) when casting an astrological chart. He also gains a Reputation as Wise at level 2 in any academic circle near his area of study.

#### Soul of Salt

*Major, Supernatural*

The character is immune to cold, both magical and mundane; he is also immune to insects of every kind, begins making Aging rolls at fifty years of age, and has a +3 bonus to Aging rolls.

This Virtue grants the character the Minor Virtues Unaging and Tough. However, the character also loses his appetite for temporal things; as a result, he feels no need to change his routine or leave his place of residence: what he likes best is to remain in one place. Finally, when the character reaches five Decrepitude points (or suffers a terminal crisis; see *Ars Magica Fifth Edition*, page 252), he turns into a (rather crude) statue of salt.

#### Protective Bindings

*Major, Supernatural*

This Virtue grants the Accelerated Ability Protective Bindings at level 1.

<!-- p. 308 -->

#### Bureaucrat

*Minor, Social Status*

You are a member of the civil administration, probably a *kātib* ("secretary"), a muhtasib, a market-tax collector, a *ṣāḥib al-šurūṭ* ("notary"), a *ṣāḥib al-madīna* ("city prefect") or a *warrāq* ("copyist"). You may take Academic Abilities during character generation. This Virtue is only available to male Muslim characters.

#### Doctor

*Major, Social Status*

You are a doctor, practicing one of the few learned professions that non-Jewish authorities allow to Jews. You are at least twenty-five years old, minus your Intelligence score, and have been educated at an academy. You may purchase Academic Abilities during character generation, and you must have a score of 5 or more in Artes Liberales and in Hebrew. Because of your highly specialized education, you begin with 240 additional experience points, which must be spent on Arabic, Greek, Latin or Academic Abilities. You must also have a score of at least 3 in Medicine and in Philosophiae.

You must work two seasons a year to keep your position. If you have the Poor Flaw, you must work three seasons to survive. If you are Wealthy, you need only work one season a year. This Virtue is only available to male Jewish characters.

#### The Gift of the Zodiac

*Major, Supernatural*

This Virtue is gained after the astral sorcerer is initiated into the cult's Mystery, and it grants the Accelerated Ability Ṭillasm at 1. With it, the sorcerer can manipulate astral magic.

This Virtue is incompatible with the Gift and with the Flaws Tainted with Evil, Infamous, Ambitious, Avaricious, Envious, Gluttonous, Wrathful, Lecherous, Hatred, Proud, Compulsion, Obsessed or Dark Secret.

#### Emir

*Minor, Social Status*

This Virtue is the same as Knight, although, owing to the rather different upbringing of Muslim emirs, you are likely to be as skilled at hunting, as cultured and as versed in religious teachings as you are in martial skills. You are most likely a *ḥāŷib*, a *wazīr* or a *wālī*.

#### Educated (Hebrew)

*Minor, General*

You have been educated in Hebrew at a yeshiva, synagogue, school or academy, or by a member of your family. You may purchase Academic Abilities during character generation, and you gain 50 additional experience points (you must spend at least 10 of these points to reach a score of one in Hebrew and in Artes Liberales). All Jews have a religious duty to see their children properly educated, so all Jewish characters are advised to take this Virtue.

#### Educated (Islamic)

*Minor, General*

You have been educated in a mosque or Qurʾan school. You gain 50 additional experience points, which must be spent on some or all of the following Abilities: Arabic, Persian, Greek, Latin, Theology: Islam, Islamic Law and Artes Liberales.

#### Member of the Mucaddemim

*Minor, Social Status*

You belong to the council of elders of the aljama (which handles its internal affairs and represents the royal authority), so you must be at least thirty-five years old. You might be a judge (or *dayaním*), a treasurer, an officer, and so on. This office is hereditary, so your family enjoys some standing in the city (you cannot have the Poor Flaw). To take this Virtue you must have the Minor General Virtue Educated (Hebrew) and some version of the Outsider Flaw. This Virtue is only available to male Jewish characters.

#### Milites

*Minor, Social Status*

You belong to a military order, and it is your duty to be ready to fight the infidel at any time. You have sworn a lifelong vow of obedience, poverty and chastity, and are answerable only to your superiors and the pope. As a knight you must wear the symbol of your order on your surcoat (Calatrava, Santiago, etc.; see page 56) and, unless you are Poor, you may have high-quality weapons and armor and two horses. You may take Academic and Martial Abilities during character generation.

<!-- p. 309 -->

#### Mystery of the Primary Qualities

*Minor, Supernatural*

This is the Virtue the riadiins gain after being initiated into the First Outer Mystery. In game terms it is equivalent to the Special Circumstances Virtue, but it only affects rolls to make ligatures.

#### Qādī

*Major, Social Status*

The caliph or a state authority of similar rank has invested you with the power to judge, and your judgments are final (although you must consult the fuqahāʾ). Your competence covers civil and criminal cases, although you might also have other administrative duties. You have a positive Reputation at level 3 in the region where you serve as judge. You may take Academic Abilities during character generation.

This Virtue is only available to male Muslim characters.

#### Rabbi

*Minor, Social Status*

You are an ordained rabbi. This makes you a leader among the surrounding Jewish communities and a respected figure. The title carries certain responsibilities tied to the well-being of the community. Your position earns you considerable respect among Jews, while non-Jews regard you with resentment.

The Wealthy Virtue and Poor Flaw affect you normally. You must take the Minor General Virtue Educated (Hebrew) and some version of the Outsider Flaw. This Virtue is only available to male Jewish characters.

#### Ṣaqāliba

*Minor, Social Status*

You were bought as a child, trained at a military school and educated in Islam, and then freed upon reaching adulthood. You are probably a Slav, though you may also be Basque or African. You are likely to have been trained in the use of lances, bows, shields, chainmail and lamellar armor (both have the same statistics) and one or two swords, both on foot and on horseback, though this does not necessarily mean that you will own all this equipment at the start of the game (storyguide's option).

You may take Martial Abilities during character generation and, as a special case, you may also take the Ability Theology: Islam, even if you do not have the Minor General Virtue Educated. This Virtue is only available to male characters and (for companion characters only) is compatible with the Emir Virtue, as many *ṣaqāliba* have climbed high in the Muslim hierarchy.

#### Siḥr

*Major, Supernatural*

The Siḥr Virtue is used to summon a *jinni* and to lend mystical power to the agreement that places it in the service of the *saḥir*. This Virtue grants a score of 1 in the Accelerated Supernatural Ability Siḥr (see "New Abilities" below). You will find more information on Accelerated Abilities in the insert on the following page.

#### Sufi

*Minor, Social Status*

You are a Muslim mystic, seeking union with the divine through asceticism and rituals. You are a member of a *tariqa* of Sufis led by a *shaykh*. While the group supports you in times of need, your *shaykh* expects equal commitment from you; you automatically gain the Minor Story Flaw Mentor, which does not yield any points for buying Virtues.

Most Muslims treat you with respect for your pious lifestyle. You may purchase the Abilities Theology: Islam, Islamic Law and Dominion Lore during character generation. This Virtue may be taken by both male and female characters.

#### Tempestarius

*Major, Supernatural*

This Virtue confers a score of 1 in the new Accelerated Supernatural Ability Tempestarius, which covers all the non-Hermetic abilities of this tradition (see "New Abilities" below).

#### Tiryāqi

*Minor, General*

The character has been schooled in the wisdom of Averroes and the secrets of his books, such as the *Kitāb al-Kulliyyāt fīl-ṭibb* and the *Maqāla fīl-tiryāq*, as well as other related texts and authors. When preparing theriacs, the character may add twice his Medicine score (including Puissant, if he has it) to his Lab Total (instead of applying the score only once, as in conventional theriac making). Tiryāqi can only create theriacs based on the guidelines in the insert on page 293 and cannot create any harmful theriac; in exchange, they are the only known philosophers able to understand Averroes' texts well enough to create theriacs that grant bonuses to Aging rolls.

## Flaws

### Dhimmi

*Minor, General*

You are a non-Muslim living under Muslim rule. If you are adult and male, you must pay the *ǧizya* head tax. The amount dhimmis have to pay in *ǧizya* varies, but it rarely exceeds a dīnār (a gold coin) per year. All dhimmis must abide by certain social restrictions in return for being tolerated and protected by the Muslim authorities.

#### Eunuch

*Minor, General*

You are a eunuch, and so cannot father children. Whenever the operation was performed, you show outward characteristics that mark you as such, which may lead other characters to see you as an anomaly. In return, you enjoy a certain freedom of movement between the sexes, and you may have been made a eunuch to work in a harem or a military school. This Flaw is only available to male characters.

#### Excommunicate

*Minor, Social Status*

You have been excommunicated by the pope, so Christians are forbidden to eat or drink with you; they may not kiss you, greet you or speak with you (except about repentance), and when you die you cannot be buried in consecrated ground and no one may pray for your soul. This Flaw is only available to Christian characters, both male and female.

> #### Accelerated Abilities
>
> Accelerated Abilities are Supernatural Abilities that use the advancement table for Arts rather than the one for Abilities, because they are designed to be compared against Ease Factors well beyond the usual values (where 21 is extremely difficult, even for specialists). Instead, the normal Ease Factors for Accelerated Abilities are spell levels or the Might scores of supernatural creatures. The other difference between Accelerated Supernatural Abilities and normal Supernatural Abilities is that the equivalent spell level for Accelerated Abilities is equal to the Casting Total, rather than to five times the Ability score.
>
> Accelerated Abilities are not Arts, however. The main difference between an Art and an Accelerated Ability is that the former is useless on its own: it must be used with at least one other Art to produce any effect (even if that Art's score is zero). An Accelerated Ability, by contrast, appears in a total without being paired with other Abilities. For all purposes other than advancement and equivalent spell level, Accelerated Supernatural Abilities are treated as standard Abilities; for example, Accelerated Abilities cannot be improved by studying vis, receive only a +1 bonus for each pawn of vis spent, and receive a +2 bonus, rather than +3, from the Puissant (Ability) Virtue.

#### Outsider

*Minor, Social Status*

You belong to a group that is readily identifiable and is despised or distrusted by the social majority (you might be a Jew in Toledo, a Christian in Seville or a Muslim in Barcelona). You have a bad Reputation of level 1 to 3 (depending on how easy it is to identify you) among the dominant culture of your region, and people outside your closed community shun you, persecute you or threaten your life and freedom when you have to deal with them. There is no way to remove this Flaw.

Normally, this Flaw is only appropriate for grogs; companions and magi should take the Major version instead.

#### Praefectus Praetorio (Ḥárisun)

*Minor, Story*

You are charged with guarding the coffers of the Iberian Tribunal kept at the Mercer Houses of Aedes Saturni (*praefectus praetorio*) and Porta Pandere (*ḥárisun*, Arabic for "guardian"). You are most likely of House Flambeau (although since 1116 this has not been a requirement), and you live in one of the Mercer Houses or nearby. You were elected at a Tribunal and may hold the office for life, although your resignation may be demanded (if you neglect your responsibilities) and you may step down of your own accord at any time. As such, you are entitled to a seat in the Iberian Chamber (see page 89), and your covenant receives the status of dedicated covenant, so it receives an annual stipend of vis or is exempt from the Iberian Tribute (storyguide's choice).

#### Quaestor Aerarii (Jāzin)

*Minor, Story*

You are charged with keeping the accounts of the coffers of the Iberian Tribunal kept at the Mercer Houses of Aedes Saturni (*quaestor aerarii*) and Porta Pandere (*jāzin*, Arabic for "treasurer"). You are most likely of House Guernicus (although since 1116 this has not been a requirement), and you live in one of the Mercer Houses or nearby. You were elected to the office at an ordinary Tribunal and may hold it for life, although your resignation may be demanded (if you neglect your responsibilities) and you may step down of your own accord at any time. As such, you are entitled to a seat in the Iberian Chamber (see page 89), and your covenant receives the status of dedicated covenant, so it receives an annual stipend of vis or is exempt from the Iberian Tribute (storyguide's choice).

## New Abilities

### Abjuration

*Supernatural (Accelerated)*

Abjuration is a kind of magic that can directly harm supernatural creatures or cancel their powers or active spells. To create an abjuration, a distaurnanja paints, sews, embroiders or otherwise inscribes his spell onto a strip of ribbon or other material, which he then wraps around a character, an object, a room or the hilt of a weapon.

<!-- p. 311 -->

#### Chess\*

*General*

This game, which the Arabs received from the Persians and spread through Christian Mythic Europe, is played on a board that represents the world, on which the cosmic cycles (which frame the foundations of Hermetic theory) appear in symbolic form: the four central squares stand for the four basic phases of every cycle (the seasons), the squares surrounding them correspond to the orbits of the sun and the twelve signs of the zodiac, while the outer squares of the board are mirrored in the twenty-eight mansions of the moon. On the board, moreover, the alternation of white and black is what distinguishes dawn from dusk.

The tournament of Iššáh on page 171 gives an applied example of the rules for chess. For the different styles of chess, take a look at the insert on page 143 of *Houses of Hermes: True Lineages*.

**Specialties:** first round, second round, ancient chess, prima or adventurer.

#### Protective Bindings

*Supernatural (Accelerated)*

Protective bindings are a kind of magic that can protect their target against supernatural creatures and their powers and spells. To create a protective binding, a distaurnanja paints, sews, embroiders or otherwise inscribes his spell onto a strip of ribbon or other material, which he then wraps around a character, an object, a room or the hilt of a weapon.

#### Distaurnanja Lore

*Academic*

This Ability covers knowledge of the organization of the distaurnanja, their hierarchy, their history and their background. As such, it is essential for advancing in the cult's Mysteries.

**Specialties:** history, initiating others, personalities.

#### Riadiin Lore

*Academic*

This Ability covers knowledge of the organization of the riadiins, their hierarchy, their history and their background. As such, it is essential for advancing in the cult's Mysteries.

**Specialties:** history, initiating others, personalities.

#### Islamic Law\*

*Academic*

Islamic law, or *šarīʿa*, encompasses all legislation rooted in the Qurʾan, the sunna, the *iŷmāʿ* and the *qiyās*. In game terms, this Ability is the Muslim version of Civil and Canon Law.

In Iberia the Mālikī version of Islamic law is taught, and it is independent of the rest of the eastern Islamic world. Mālikī law is based on ordering and regulating communal life so as to respect the social order, although, given its ambiguity, one must not only regulate but also improvise, for at times the strict application of justice is unjust (this subjectivity was partly curbed by the Almohads; see the insert "Islamic Law: The Mālikī School" on page 21). For this reason, every qadi must have a certain intuition about the facts and heed any presumption of innocence. In addition, the social repercussions of the trial must always be weighed, taking into account the harm or benefit the qadi's ruling may bring to the community. In practice this usually means that the more witnesses one has, the more likely one is to win a case.

Islamic law is an orientation, a guide to action with ethical and religious connotations, so if a judge knows little of the law, he must adhere to *taqlīd* (Arabic for "imitation": literal adherence to the law, applying it by analogy with the precedent case).

**Specialties:** any one of the sources of Islamic Law, a particular topic, customs of a particular area, *taqlīd*, Qurʾanic verses.

#### Rabbinic Law\*

*Academic*

This is the civil and canon law of the Hebrew people. This Ability covers all the civil and religious laws, as well as the customs, of rabbinic Judaism.

**Specialties:** laws of a specific place, laws on a particular topic.

#### Siḥr

*Supernatural (Accelerated)*

This Accelerated Ability allows you to summon and negotiate with a *jinni* according to the rules set out in the section on *saḥirs* (see above).

#### Tempestarius

*Supernatural (Accelerated)*

This Accelerated Ability reflects the tradition's control over storms, and it essentially breaks down into three fields: summoning storms, traveling in storms and attacking with storms. All Tempestarius rolls receive a bonus equal to the tempestarius's Auram score divided by five (rounded up).

**Specialties:** summon storms, travel in storms, attack with storms.

#### Theology: Islam\*

*Academic*

This is the Islamic equivalent of Christian theology. The main sources of Islamic theology are the Qurʾan and the sunna.

**Specialties:** the Qurʾan, debates, history, prophets.

#### Theology: Judaism\*

*Academic*

This is the Jewish equivalent of Christian theology. The main source of Jewish theology is the Talmud.

**Specialties:** the Talmud, the Torah, mysticisms, heresies, history.

#### Ṭillasm

*Supernatural (Accelerated)*

This Accelerated Ability allows you to manufacture the talismans needed to cast astral magic (see above). Talismans must be crafted from the appropriate materials at the appropriate time and must be consecrated and strengthened with the proper rituals and sacrifices; only then can the sorcerer draw the celestial spirits down onto the image to work this kind of magic.

<!-- p. 312 -->

# XI. Places of Power

Iberia is a Tribunal with many places where the power of one of the four supernatural realms is concentrated. By way of example, we have developed two of them to encourage you to design others with your gaming group. To do so you can use some of the many places named in this book, or draw on your own knowledge and experience of the Peninsula.

## The Punic Temple on the Islet of Sancti Petri

On the outer edge of the Bay of Cadiz, on a rocky promontory at the southern tip of the islet of Sancti Petri, stands a partly ruined watchtower that juts above the waters. The Frisian crusaders almost destroyed it entirely when they sacked the island in 1217 during the Fifth Crusade. Today all that remains standing of the ancient Punic temple that once stood here is the shell of a square tower and the steps of a stairway leading up to the ruins of the chamber of the temple of Melqart. On either side of the temple threshold, set against the building, two columns of worn stone still stand, and in front of them is a great stone pedestal on which a rough circle of faded verdigris can be made out. Here once stood an eighteen-meter-high bronze statue of Hercules, which was taken down and melted by Abū-l-Ḥasan ʿAlī ibn Maymūn (admiral of the Almoravid fleet) in 1145. Anyone who crosses the threshold at sunset while touching either of the two columns can enter a Magic *regio* with an aura of 3 that overlies the whole temple complex.

The *regio* has one main level, although it has other, deeper levels that can be reached from the temple. Those who enter through the threshold guarded by the temple's two old mundane stone columns, whether by following the necessary ritual or by using magic, find that the sacred precinct is much larger than on the mundane level (almost fifteen meters wide by fifty-five meters long). Although nominally dedicated to the Punic god Melqart, the temple is clearly consecrated to Hercules, or Hercules Gaditanus, as he is named on many sculptures. Within the *regio*, the temple precinct is enclosed by high walls that shelter a group of ancient buildings gathered around a courtyard. The bronze leaves of the huge gates that close the complex are carved with the labors of Hercules. On either side of them, above braziers of undying flame, rise two imposing bronze columns bearing inscriptions in Punic, Greek and Latin that tell sailors and explorers they may make their sacrifices in the flames. The path from the great gates to the temple steps is lined with twelve bronze altars, each with a sacred fire and bas-reliefs showing scenes from the life of Hercules. At the very center of the complex grows the tree of Pygmalion, whose fruits are emeralds.

The columns that support the temple pediment correspond to the columns on the mundane level through which the *regio* is entered. One is carved from a single emerald crystal, within which beats a fire that makes it gleam, and the other is made of solid gold. The phrase *Non Plus Ultra*, also written in Greek and Punic, is carved on both the base and the capital of both columns. The columns switch sides at random, although the emerald one is more often on the right as you look from the temple toward the tree of Pygmalion. The golden column bears a faint engraving of a man holding the world on his shoulders, while the fire inside the emerald column varies in intensity between the light of a star, the first light of dawn and the last rays of sunset.

Entering the temple is like entering a cave. The chamber lies in half-darkness, and the fires visibly dim inside it. In fact, this chamber is a gateway to other *regiones*, whose destination varies according to the visitor's wishes. Those who seek absolution or purification find at the far end a staircase descending into darkness until it reaches the Divine *regio* of purgatory. The way back is not always clear, and only those who have recently confessed or have lived without falling into sin return quickly. Travelers who follow in the footsteps of Hercules end up in the network of *regiones* that stretches across the distant Pyrenees, and may even come out on the Via Domitia, outside the shattered remains of Béziers. Wyverns lurk along these roads, however: greedy lizards that hunt travelers for food and to swell their motley hoards with their belongings.

<!-- p. 313 -->

### Vis Sources

The emeralds of the tree of Pygmalion provide two vis sources when they are harvested on the last day of summer. Those gathered from the side of the tree facing the emerald column contain five pawns of Intellego vis. The fruits harvested from the side facing the golden column contain a total of five pawns of Rego vis. One pawn in five (of either kind of vis) is extraordinary vis that emulates lesser enchanted devices (see *Realms of Power: Magic*, page 147) with one of the following effects.

#### Splinter of Atlas's Strength

ReTe 10<br>
Penetration 0<br>
R: Touch, D: Conc, T: Ind

By pressing the emerald against a larger object, such as a chest or a stone, you can lift it and carry it slowly, as if you had a Strength of +5. You can do no more than walk slowly, and the emerald must stay in contact with the object being carried. Moreover, you can carry only inanimate objects in this way, and you cannot lift them more than two meters off the ground.

(Base 3, +1 Touch, +1 Concentration; the emerald maintains concentration)

#### Lens of Clear Sight

InAu 10<br>
Penetration 0<br>
R: Per, D: Conc, T: Vision

Looking through this crystal, you can see clearly through the particles that cloud the air, such as smoke, fog and dust, even if they are of magical origin. You can walk slowly while looking through the emerald, but if you want to move faster you must make a Concentration roll against an Ease Factor of 12 to avoid stumbling and falling.

(Base 1, +1 Concentration, +4 Vision)

> #### Story Seeds: A Door to Anywhere
>
> A Jerbiton arrives at the covenant gate, terribly ill and certain of one thing: the temple of Sancti Petri is not only a gateway to the mythical Hesperides, but to anywhere at all, if the traveler performs the proper ritual. According to him, there is a site on the outskirts of Tangier that is paired with the Gaditan temple, and if one performs the proper ritual at both, one can go anywhere one wishes by setting out from the Peninsular temple. It worked for Hercules, Hanno and Hannibal, and it has worked for him. The magus's bulging eyes and dry cough unsettle the members of the covenant, but the promise of so longed-for a harbor could tempt anyone.

<!-- p. 314 -->

## The Tumulus of Zalamea

At the beginning of the sixth century BC, the Tartessians built a temple of Phoenician inspiration in the interior of the Guadiana valley, several days' journey from the Tartessian heartland of the Peninsula (see insert) and far from the main routes of the age. This complex was dedicated to the Phoenician-Carthaginian deities Astarte (or her native equivalent) and Tanit, and served as a frontier sanctuary for trade between the communities of the area, allowing transactions to be carried out safely. Like so many other sanctuaries built on the banks of the Guadiana, it would surely have become a magnet for the Phoenicians, who would have come there to buy or sell goods or services.

Lying on the edge of the Tartessian cultural horizon, the sanctuary survived the crisis of the mid-sixth century BC and endured until the dawn of the fourth century BC, when it was destroyed and buried as the culmination of a great ritual that went on for several days. Among the ritual proceedings, sixty animals were sacrificed to Astarte, and their remains were thrown into the ditch surrounding the complex together with the pottery used for the banquet. Sheep and cattle were the most numerous of the animals, but pigs, a deer, a wild boar and a fox were also sacrificed, along with sixteen sacred horses (bred for the purpose), which were first beheaded and their heads laid out in order at one end of the ditch. While most of those present enjoyed the feast outside, the priests poured libations and enjoyed their own banquet inside the temple. To end the ritual, those present emptied the sanctuary of all its riches and set it on fire. Once it had been consumed by the flames, the remains were covered with the mud bricks of the partly demolished walls, and the whole site was carefully sealed with a thick layer of clay to preserve it from any possible desecration.

What remained was an enormous artificial mound (which eventually disappeared beneath the sediment) and a powerful magical aura of level 6 that still endures in 1220.

> #### Tartessos[^p314-IV]
>
> *[…] When they reached Tartessos, they made friends with the king of the Tartessians, whose name was Arganthonius, and who reigned over Tartessos for eighty years, while he lived a hundred and twenty in all.*[^p314-V]
>
> Tartessos (*Tartessos* in Greek) was the culture of the southwest of the Peninsula (from the mouth of the Tagus to Valencia) that arose from the contact of the native population with several waves of Phoenician settlers and other Mediterranean groups. The heart of Tartessos lay between Huelva and the lower Guadalquivir, an area that has always been well suited to mining, farming, herding and the exploitation of marine resources. The arrival of the Phoenicians in the Peninsula, and their settlement west of the Pillars of Hercules, allowed their culture to permeate the native communities, which adopted their technical and social innovations without losing their own identity. In this way the Tartessians improved their farming and mining, as well as their crafts, through the introduction of new advances of Phoenician heritage, such as ironworking, cupellation, lost-wax casting, the potter's wheel, the cultivation of vines and olives, the development of the salting industry, and the use of poultry, the donkey and the mule in their farms. And, also thanks to the Phoenicians, the Tartessians were able to make the most of their strategic position by using the Phoenicians' international trade networks, which allowed them to act as intermediaries between Mediterranean and Atlantic trade.
>
> In return, the Phoenicians gained privileged access to local resources and trade, possibly to the exclusion of other competitors.
>
> In the mid-sixth century BC, however, Tartessos suffered a crisis that stopped its development dead, possibly because of the transformation that trade in the western Mediterranean was undergoing at that time (the isolation Tyre suffered in the seventh and sixth centuries BC strengthened Carthaginian dominance, which ended up harming the Greeks' activity in the south of the Iberian peninsula) and the devaluation of silver. In addition, a deep-focus earthquake may have struck in the Atlantic, which could have caused a tidal wave that would have destroyed the most flourishing ports and industries of the Phoenicians on the coasts of Huelva and at the mouth of the Guadalquivir, the heart of Tartessian culture. And so flourishing Tartessos reached its winter and, although it lingered on for a few more years on the fringes of the area this cultural horizon had occupied, it finally disappeared.
>
> Shortly before it breathed its last, the ruins of Tartessian civilization and their inhabitants were trapped in an enormous Faerie *regio*. The only known entrance lies in the marshes at the mouth of the Guadalquivir, where it is said to be impossible to enter without a guide. Indeed, the fact that the temple of Zalamea has a Magic aura rather than a Faerie one could be a matter of debate for groups interested in such things. In any case, a faerie replica of the temple can be found in this *regio* and, at the storyguide's discretion, the answer to the tablets in the insert "Story Seeds: The Ritual Tablets" on the following page.
>
> [^p314-IV]: The name Tartessos is not attested within the culture it refers to; that is, none of the Tartessians ever called themselves by that name. In fact, the first mention of the name appears in the *Geryoneis* of Stesichorus of Himera, a poem about the encounter between Geryon (see page 118) and Hercules, which says that the giant was born beside the river called Tartessos, opposite the island of Erytheia. This river was later called the Baetis by the Romans and the Guadalquivir ("great river") by the Arabs.
>
> [^p314-V]: From Book I of Herodotus's *Histories* (Spanish translation by Carlos Schrader García).

### Setting and Physical Description

The tumulus of Zalamea lies less than ten kilometers north of the Muslim castle of the same name, which in 1220 stands on the edge of the Almohad province of the Peninsula. The tumulus (entirely imperceptible to mundane eyes) rests in a hollow beside a small, ever-flowing stream, covered by a dense holm oak forest.

Besides the powerful aura of the area, anyone searching for underground water (whether with the Dowsing Virtue or some other Hermetic effect designed for that purpose) will detect a vein of water running through the whole area. These two factors make the site an excellent spot for a covenant (at least from a geographical point of view, since, with the help of the Order of Alcántara, the area will be conquered in the 1230s by the forces of King Fernando III, who by then will rule not only over Castile but over Leon as well).

<!-- p. 315 -->

Beneath the tumulus, the ruins of the complex are laid out around a courtyard paved with pressed red clay, in the center of which a deep well was dug to reach the vein of water mentioned above. The buildings and chambers around the courtyard face east (associated with the dawn and the creative forces of Astarte), and the whole complex is surrounded by a ditch four meters deep cut into the rock.

### Vis Sources

Crimson flowers that are a source of Animal vis also grow on the tumulus of Zalamea. The flowers, nourished by the remains of the ritual banquet held at the beginning of the fourth century BC and by the underground vein of the aquifer that runs through the area, grow in clumps along the strip of the buried ditch. They are bright red, and the filaments of their stamens stand out for being a brilliant white. Although they have short stems and are not very large, when they appear (at dawn on the spring equinox) they are plainly visible. In addition, their heady, musk-tinged perfume usually acts as a repellent to animals, which rarely come near them except by accident.

The flowers open during the day and close at nightfall, and they last for seven days, withering at the seventh nightfall of spring. Any attempt to transplant them is useless, since as soon as they are taken from their soil they lose their perfume and their leaves wither within a few hours. Nor, of course, is it enough to transplant them with the soil they grow in: their health depends on the magical aura and the lingering traces of the ritual that was performed there centuries ago.

Although harvesting the vis is easy, since it is enough to distill the musky perfume the flowers give off (for example, with a ReVi 15 effect similar to *Distill the Crystal Stream*; see *Covenants*, page 103), the hard part is working out that the vis lies in the olfactory (and therefore intangible) *species* the flowers give off.

This source can provide up to five pawns of Animal vis, although the storyguide may increase or reduce that number.

> #### Story Seeds: The Ritual Tablets
>
> Hidden among the ruins, beneath the remains of the mud-brick walls, the layer of clay and the sediment of more than sixteen centuries, lie the slate tablets inscribed with the Tartessian ritual used by the priestesses of Astarte. The inscription is utterly illegible, however, since it is written in Tartessian, a *sui generis* adaptation of the Phoenician alphabet used in the south of the Peninsula from the seventh century BC as part of the sweeping revolution that reached the Peninsula with the Levantine peoples (indeed, Tartessos was the only region west of the present-day Roman Tribunal where a local alphabet was developed to write the native languages).
>
> The script combines a semi-alphabetic and semi-syllabic system, and uses signs that represent the guttural consonants and other semivowels of Semitic speech to represent vowels. It also invents new signs to complete the syllabic system beyond Phoenician, so even if the characters know Phoenician they will not be able to decipher the content, which will require much deeper research. If they manage to decipher it, it might represent an advance similar to the one Fenicil brought at the end of the ninth century.
>
> We leave it to each group to design this effect to suit their saga, although it should be of a power similar to that of Fenicil's rituals (see *Houses of Hermes: True Lineages*, page 81).

# Appendix I: Mundane Library

*It is not generous wine that pleases me, nor the melody of song, nor the chords of instruments. My delights are the books I study, and the servant I employ is my pen.*[^p316-9]

[^p316-9]: Verses by a poet from Malaga who lived in the time of the caliph Al-Ḥakam II (Spanish translation by A. Martínez Lorca).

This appendix gathers information on the authors of the Iberia of Mythic Europe, among them the authorities responsible for the "first European renaissance." The authors are listed alphabetically and grouped according to the periods into which the second section of this book is divided. Each entry includes a few notes on the author's life and the most important works that the magi of the Tribunal may own or seek out for their libraries. Unless otherwise stated, all the books are written in Arabic.

## Before the Order of Hermes

#### Isidore of Seville

A native of Cartagena, the man who would become archbishop of Seville was a great author and compiler of the seventh century. An excellent theorist and philosopher, he established a teaching tradition in his city that made it one of the leading intellectual centers of Christian Europe. Although his theses survived the arrival of the Muslims, his reforming current was eclipsed by the Islamic reform.

##### Originum Sive Etymologiarum Libri Viginti

*Summa* on Artes Liberales, Level 4, Quality 7

*Summa* on Philosophiae (natural philosophy), Level 2, Quality 7

*Summa* on Theology, Level 4, Quality 7

*Summa* on Civil and Canon Law, Level 2, Quality 7

**Description:** Written in Latin and organized into twenty books, this work is a compendium of all the knowledge gathered up to its time (that is, up to the seventh century).

##### Historia Gothorum, Vandalorum et Suevorum

*Tractatus* on Iberia Lore, Quality 7

**Description:** A history in Latin of the kings of the Goths, Vandals and Suevi up to the seventh century.

### The Emirate of Cordoba

During the emirate of Cordoba, the Andalusis traveled to Baghdad and Damascus to learn from the scholars of the East. This period is not remarkable for its literary output, for these were years of learning and of receiving knowledge, but Arab chroniclers abounded; they placed greater importance on the reliability of historical transmission, and on exalting the glorious names of their protagonists through historical deeds, than on setting down history truthfully.

#### ʿAbbās ibn Firnās

A mathematician, poet and astronomer from Ronda. In his laboratory he had a dome that emulated the firmament and imitated the noise of thunder, and in Cordoba he installed a water clock fed by the Guadalquivir to predict the hours of prayer in case the weather was bad. It is said that, in an attempt to emulate the flight of birds, he launched himself from the Ruzafa of Cordoba in a harness to which he had attached two wings, and glided for twelve seconds before crashing to the ground. After breaking both his legs, he realized that he had forgotten to build a tail to stabilize his flight.

##### Kitāb nasafa (apocryphal work)

*Tractatus* on Artes Liberales (geometry), Quality 5

*Tractatus* on Philosophiae (natural philosophy), Quality 5

**Description:** The "Book of Flight" contains the laboratory texts for the device Ibn Firnās devised.

#### ʿAbd al-Wāḥid ibn Isāḥq al-Ḍabbī

An Andalusi astronomer (possibly from Algeciras) of the caliph Al-Ḥakam I (here recast as a magus of the Order of Hermes; see page 74).

##### Al-urŷuza

*Summa* on Artes Liberales (astronomy), Level 5, Quality 8

**Description:** A book on methods of prediction according to the weather and the stars. This *summa* was used by an entire generation of Umayyad astronomers.

#### Ibn ʿAbd Rabbihi

A writer and poet from Cordoba, born to a freed slave of Hišām I.

##### Al-ʿiqd al-farīd

*Summa* on Artes Liberales, Level 3, Quality 7

*Summa* on Philosophiae, Level 3, Quality 7

*Summa* on Theology: Islam, Level 3, Quality 7

**Description:** "The Unique Necklace" is a monumental encyclopedia of literature, which demonstrates that Andalusi poetry is comparable to that of the East. Its twenty-five chapters are named after precious stones and metals, such as *pearl* (on poetics), *topaz* (proverbs on human generosity), *coral* (protocol), *silver* (stories of embassies and delegations), *sapphire* (the sciences), *gold* (language)… and many other subjects besides, such as religion, the stars or elegies.

#### Aḥmad al-Rāzī

This Cordoban is considered the founder of Andalusi historiography.

### The Caliphate of Cordoba and the *fitna*

At the end of this period, the magi of Iberia were able to acquire books from the library of knowledge (*jizanatu-hu l-ʿilmiya*) of Al-Ḥakam II during its public auction. It is therefore possible that copies of these volumes exist in covenants founded before that date.

#### Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr

A native of Cordoba, he was qadi of Lisbon and Santarém and lived to the age of ninety-eight. He was a great scholar respected throughout al-Andalus.

##### Bahŷat al-maŷālis

*Summa* on Philosophiae (moral philosophy), Level 3, Quality 7

**Description:** A work on morals and human customs that discusses the activities of man as a social being in relation to his fellows, the world around them, and death.

#### Abū-l-Qāsim Maslama ibn al-Qāsim Ibrāhīm al-Qurṭubī al-Zayyāt

Known as Al-Qurṭubī, he was an Andalusi scholar described by his contemporaries as "a man of spells and talismans." Here he has been recast as a magus and the creator of the non-Hermetic tradition of the astral sorcerers.

##### Ghāyat al-Ḥakīm

*Therefore I tell you, if you wish to apply your intellect to the lofty, noble and important realms of knowledge, do not stint in it, and do not neglect the study of the books and the words of the sages, for it is by that path that you will make your dreams come true.*[^p317-10]

[^p317-10]: Excerpt from Al-Qurṭubī's *Ghāyat al-Ḥakīm* (*Picatrix*) (English translation by Dan Attrell and David Porreca; Spanish translation by Mario Donaire).

*Summa* on Artes Liberales (astronomy), Level 5, Quality 9

*For those initiated into astral magic (see page 278), this compendium gathers all the known conjurations of that tradition.*

**Description:** "The Goal of the Wise" is written according to ideas drawn from many places, such as Iberia, North Africa, Greece, Egypt, Nabataea, Arabia, Babylon, Persia, India and beyond, and its learning is encyclopedic. This compendium in four books reflects the personal needs, ambitions, fears and longings of magicians and their clients, and it binds together into a coherent framework the magic, philosophy and astrology of Antiquity with those of the Islamic culture of the Middle Ages.

In these books you can find practical sections with the recipes and ingredients needed to perform more than two thousand rituals, prayers to invoke the planets and their spirits, instructions for the making of talismans, formulas for fumigations, remedies to cure specific afflictions, and so on, as well as theoretical sections that explain the underlying mechanisms of magic, include admonitions to initiates, aphorisms of the sages, and astrological instructions concerning the celestial figures (decans, constellations, planets, and so on), and set out the foundations of magic and of the making of images or talismans.

"The Goal of the Wise" will be translated into Castilian in 1256–58 under the name *Picatrix* by the Jew Yehudā ben Moshē, one of the translators of Alfonso X the Wise. Later (no one knows when, perhaps in 1300), it will be translated into Latin in Montpellier, and it will not be widely disseminated until 1450.

#### Abū-l-Qāsim al-Zahārawī

Known to the Latins as Abulcasis, he was the most famous physician of the caliphs of Cordoba. He lived in Madīnat al-Zahrāʾ until the fall of the caliphate.

##### Kitāb al-tasrif

*Summa* on Medicine, Level 6, Quality 9

**Description:** A monumental encyclopedia in thirty volumes covering every branch of medicine and its surgical methods.

##### Mujtasar kitāb al-filāḥa

*Summa* on Philosophiae (natural philosophy), Level 3, Quality 9

**Description:** A compendium of agriculture.

A poetess of Umayyad blood who always refused to wear the veil (for which she was much criticized). She inherited a fortune with which she opened a literary salon in Cordoba, frequented by the most distinguished poets and nobles of the city.

### The Taifa Kingdoms

During this period, poetry and literature flourished in al-Andalus. The authors of this time are true points of reference for the magi of the Tribunal, for they served as the standards by which they wrote their own works.

#### Abū ʿAmir ibn Šuhayd

*If you must compose and your soul invites you to it, do not weary your talent, and when you finish, rest for three days, no fewer. Then begin to correct and prune what you had composed […].*[^p318-11]

[^p318-11]: By Ibn Shuhayd, taken from *The Treatise of Familiar Spirits and Demons* (Spanish translation by Salvador Barberá).

Of Arab descent, his family was one of the most distinguished in al-Andalus. The poet lost his father at the age of eleven and rose to the office of minister before he was seventeen. However, he could not rise to the post of secretary for two reasons: he was hard of hearing, and he had a scandalous reputation (immodesty, overindulgence in wine, and generosity to the point of excess, which led him into poverty).

Šuhayd remained in Cordoba during the *fitna* with one of Almanzor's wealthy grandsons, with whom he shared his fondness for poetry and wine. Twenty years later he was accused of murder and condemned to exile, where he died of a paralysis that afflicted his entire body.

##### Risālat al-tāwābiʿwa-l-zawābī

*You must not weep for those nights whose memory keeps you from drinking, and in which you see the sword of death unsheathe gray hairs from your head. You lose your life, which slips away in moments; its perfume flees at its finest hour. If you weep, weep for the brief life that passes as swiftly as the course of the stars.*[^p318-12]

[^p318-12]: Poem from Ibn Shuhayd's *The Treatise of Familiar Spirits and Demons* (Spanish translation by Salvador Barberá).

*Summa* on Magic Lore, Level 5, Quality 9

**Description:** The "Treatise of Familiar Spirits" is a journey to the supernatural realms inhabited by the genii who inspire poets (for every good poet is possessed by a genius who speaks through his mouth). The mission of these genii is to enlighten the noblest of men with a vision of the beauty and perfection of the spiritual world, to which they could not otherwise aspire because of their inherent natural imperfection.

#### Abū Muḥammad ʿAlī ibn Ḥazm

The poet Ibn Ḥazm belonged to an important muwallad family of high officials of the Umayyad state (indeed, his father was a minister of Almanzor). He was persecuted by the Mālikī fuqahāʾ for not following their school, and so he left the Peninsula and died in Baghdad. It is said that he wrote 80,000 folios in more than 400 volumes.

##### Tawq al-hamāma

*[…] love is a rebellious ailment whose medicine lies within itself, if we know how to treat it; but it is a delicious ailment and a desirable malady, to the extent that whoever finds himself free of it renounces his health, and whoever suffers from it does not wish to be cured. It makes beautiful in a man's eyes what he once abhorred, and smooths for him what once seemed difficult, to the point of overturning his innate character and his inborn nature […].*[^p318-13]

[^p318-13]: Excerpt from Ibn Ḥazm's *The Ring of the Dove* (Spanish translation by Emilio García Gómez).

*Summa* on Philosophiae (moral philosophy), Level 5, Quality 12

*Tractatus* on Arabic (poetry), Quality 12

**Description:** "The Ring of the Dove" is a treatise with Neoplatonic roots, in which love is the reunion of the two halves of a spirit that was created as a single sphere. Ibn Ḥazm places love in the sphere of the spiritual, for he always rejects sexual union. He admits, however, that the two halves recognize each other only through physical attraction.

##### Taqrib li-hadd al-mantiq

*Tractatus* on Artes Liberales (logic), Quality 12

**Description:** A book of logic.

#### The Ripoll Bible

The Ripoll Bible is the latest of the three Bibles produced at the monastery of that name. It is a book more than half a meter tall and almost forty centimeters wide, written in Latin in Carolingian script, with abundant illustrations that illuminate the sacred texts so delicately set down by the monk Guifré. Another of its peculiarities, which make it even more valuable, are the dozens of prologues and additional texts that complement the Holy Scriptures, from apocryphal texts to commentaries by Saint Jerome or Saint Isidore, among others.

Note that, from around the year 1170, the Ripoll Bible no longer remains in the monastery where it was created, being moved to Marseille.

*Summa* on Theology, Level 10, Quality 6

*Summa* on Church Lore, Level 3, Quality 6

The additional texts count as a commentary (see *Covenants*, page 121) on Theology of Quality 7.

#### Ibn Baṣṣāl

This eminent Toledan botanist was born in 1050 and served at the court of the taifa petty king Al-Maʿmūn. His name means "the tender of buds." During his life he visited Sicily, Egypt, Syria, Iraq, Persia and northern India, where he was able to observe the different agricultural techniques of those lands. From his travels he brought back several species to Toledo, where he planted them in the city's botanical garden to carry out his experiments. Shortly before the fall of Toledo, Ibn Baṣṣāl left for Seville, where he joined a group of agronomists and scholars.

##### Dīwān al-filāḥa

*Summa* on Profession (Agronomist), Level 5, Quality 7

*Tractatus* on Philosophiae (natural philosophy), Quality 7

**Description:** The "Agricultural Anthology" is an impressive compendium of agronomy that Ibn Baṣṣāl wrote in Toledo.

<!-- p. 319 -->

Its pages focus above all on the author's own observations, and so their approach is eminently practical. Later, in Seville, Ibn Baṣṣāl adapted his anthology to reduce its length (the abridged book, called *Kitāb al-qaṣd wa-l-bayān* or "The Concise and Clear Book," is a *tractatus* on Profession (Agronomist) of Quality 6, and will be translated into Castilian in the thirteenth century).

The Avicebron of the Christians. A native of Malaga, he left very early for Saragossa, where he joined a literary circle made up of great Muslim and Hebrew figures. He later enjoyed the patronage of Ismāʿīl ibn al-Nagrela of Granada, and died in Valencia before it had been conquered by the Cid.

#### Al-Zarqālī

Named for his blue eyes (the Arzachel of the Latins), he invented the *azafea*, an instrument that reproduces the movements of the heavenly bodies on a single surface, and he built an anaphoric clock on the outskirts of Toledo (for which he constructed two great pools that filled and emptied with the lunar cycles). After the fall of Toledo, he returned to Seville, his native city.

This Barcelonan Kabbalist (the Savasorda of the Latins) spread Arabic algebra to the West through his translations.

Considered the most influential of the Jewish scholars of the High Middle Ages, the Abenezra of the Latins was born in Tudela and spent his most productive years outside Iberia. The Tremere of the Peninsula usually know by heart his poem on chess, known as the *Delights of the King*.

#### Anonymous (attributed to Calixtus II)

##### Liber Sancti Iacobi (Codex Calixtinus)

*Tractatus* on Way of Saint James Lore, Quality 6

**Description:** A book made up of material written at different times and independently of one another, revised and compiled by a goliard in 1160, possibly Aymeric Picaud. This treatise consists of five sections: the first is a collection of sermons, liturgical texts and formularies for the liturgy of Saint James; the second is a collection of twenty-two miracles wrought through the intercession of Saint James; the third recounts the translation of Saint James's body to Compostela; the fourth is the *Pseudo-Turpin* (attributed to the archbishop of Reims), which tells of the crusade of Charlemagne and Roland; and the last corresponds to the *Liber peregrinationis*, a treatise and travel guide for the pilgrim to Santiago.

#### Abū Bakr ibn Bāŷŷa

The Avempace of the Latins was born in Saragossa and lived in Játiva, Almería, Granada, Oran and Fez (in exile), where he died, poisoned with an eggplant by a famous physician. This philosopher, scientist, physician, poet and musician (he fused Christian-style music with Arabic music in the form of the *muwaššaḥa*, and called it zajal) reached the Christians through Averroes' commentaries on Aristotle, despite having been the first to translate and comment on the Stagirite philosopher.
