##### Tadbīr al-mutawaḥḥid

*The perfect city is characterized by the absence within it of the art of medicine and that of jurisprudence, and this is because love unites [its inhabitants] to one another [who, in consequence] do not quarrel among themselves at all. Therefore, if love is lacking in one of the members [of that city] and discord arises, it is then necessary for justice to be restored, and so someone to carry it out will inexorably be needed, namely: the judge. Moreover, all the acts of the perfect city are upright, for this quality is a necessary concomitant of it. That is why its inhabitants do not nourish themselves with harmful foods, […] nor do they need to know [how to] cure the [abuse of] wine, since nothing there is disordered. Thus, if they abandon exercise, a multitude of illnesses follow as a consequence, which evidently are not proper [to the perfect city, in which] perhaps, in most cases, there will be no need to cure [anything more than] […] illnesses whose particular causes come from outside and which a good and healthy body is by itself unable to avoid. […] the further a city is from the perfect one, the greater its need of [physicians and judges], and the higher the [social] status of both kinds of people.*[^p320-14]

[^p320-14]: Excerpt from Avempace's *The Regimen of the Solitary* (Spanish translation by Joaquín Lomba).

*Summa* on Philosophiae (moral philosophy), Level 5, Quality 9

**Description:** "The Regimen of the Solitary" is a moral protest against the materialism and worldly life of the ruling classes. It speaks of the attainment of wisdom through the theoretical life in the Aristotelian manner, and of detachment from all that is material in order to unite mystically with the agent intellect.

##### Letters Completing *The Regimen of the Solitary*

*Tractatus* on Philosophiae, Quality 9

**Description:** A set of letters that complete the *Tadbīr al-mutawaḥḥid* and are studied in a single season. Their titles and descriptions follow:

##### Risālat al-waddāʿ

*And since perfection either exists or does not exist, and since, when the habit of science is present [without the virtues], the subject of that habit will not have attained the supreme end of science, for that reason Abū Naṣr [al-Fārābī] says: "I say that if one man knows all that Aristotle wrote without practicing anything of what is [in his books], and another practices it though he knows nothing, the ignorant man who acts will be more excellent and virtuous than the wise man who abandons [the practice of virtue]."*[^p320-15]

[^p320-15]: Excerpt from Avempace's *Letter of Farewell* (Spanish translation by Joaquín Lomba).

**Description:** The "Letter of Farewell" completes "The Regimen of the Solitary," and is dedicated to his friend, Ibn al-Imām of Saragossa.

##### Min kalāmi-hi fīʿumūr allātī yumkin bi-hā al-wuqūf ʿalà al-ʿaql al-faʿʿāl

**Description:** The "Treatise on the Agent Intellect" is a complex philosophical treatise.

##### Risāla ittiṣāl al-ʿaql bi-l-insān

*The situation of the common people with respect to the intelligibles is similar to that of those who see but are inside a cave in which the sun does not rise for them, and so they do not see it, yet they can see all the colors in the midst of the darkness. He who is in the [inner] space of the cave [only] sees in a manner resembling one who [is wrapped] in shadows. And he who is at the mouth of the cave sees the colors, [but] in shadow. All the common people see beings only in a situation resembling darkness, without ever seeing that brightness. Therefore, just as light separate from colors does not exist for the people of the cave, so that intellect does not exist for the common people, nor can they become aware of it. But those who devote themselves to speculation occupy the place of one who leaves the cave for the open air, where the light separate from colors shines, and who sees the colors in their totality and in their very essence. As for the blessed, there is nothing in physical sight that resembles them, since they themselves are transformed into the thing [known]. If they were transmuted into seers and became light, this would be the situation of the blessed.*[^p320-16]

[^p320-16]: Excerpt from Avempace's *Treatise on the Union of the Intellect with Man* (Spanish translation by Joaquín Lomba).

**Description:** Translated as "Treatise on the Union of the Intellect with Man."

##### Fī l-gāyat al-insāniyya

*For the perpetual, from the point of view of time, is not perpetual, since the perpetual is that which is not contained in time, for it is perpetual in itself, not because its time is perpetual.*[^p320-17]

[^p320-17]: Excerpt from Avempace's *On the End of Man* (Spanish translation by Joaquín Lomba).

**Description:** Translated as "On the End of Man."

##### Fī saʿādat al-madaniyya wa-l-saʿādat al-ajariyya aw difāʿan Abī Naṣr

**Description:** Translated as "On Political Happiness, or the Happiness of the Other [Life], or a Defense of Abū Naṣr [al-Fārābī]," he wrote it in response to the accusation made against him of not believing in the afterlife.

#### Abū Bakr al-Ṭurṭūšī

This Muslim jurist from Tortosa opposed Fatimid ideology and was a teacher in Alexandria.

##### Sirāŷ al-mulūk

*Summa* on Intrigue (politics), Level 3, Quality 6

**Description:** The "Lamp of Princes" covers numerous anecdotes on royal conduct.

<!-- p. 321 -->

#### Al-Fatḥ ibn Jāqān

A master of rhymed prose, he showed the way for the men of letters who were to come. He was a state administrator who used to arrive drunk at the qadi's sessions and who, through his attitude, earned the enmity of Avempace. All his biographers agreed that his prose was beautiful, but also that his behavior was reprehensible. He died, tortured and with his throat cut, in a brothel in Marrākeš in 1134, where he was impaled through the anus with a stake, possibly because of his avowed homosexuality.

*O God! A gazelle has visited me on your behalf, strutting proudly among the veils of evening. I had to restrain myself in my love for her, as if I were Marwān, terrified by the squadrons of al-Saffāḥ. But I lost my restraint and left it in the desert, and gave free rein to my delight. She offered me the rose of her two cheeks, and I gathered it with my gaze, without sin. I wished to abstain from her love, but could not, showing her gravity in the midst of jest. And I let my heart become, through ardent affection, like a bird with which desires fly without wings.*[^p321-18]

[^p321-18]: Poem by Al-Fatḥ ibn Jāqān (Spanish translation by Celia del Moral Molina).

##### Qalāʾid al-ʿiqyān

*Summa* on Iberia Lore (personalities), Level 3, Quality 10

**Description:** Biographies of selected authors arranged in four categories (princes; viziers and secretaries; judges and fuqahāʾ; men of letters and poets). Within these four groups, the author ranks them according to criteria of quality (entirely subjective ones).

##### Maṭmaḥ al-anfus

*Tractatus* on Iberia Lore (personalities), Quality 10

**Description:** An anthology that complements the previous one (*Qalāʾid al-ʿiqyān*), but covers a longer period of time.

#### Al-Idrīsī

A cartographer and geographer from Ceuta of the Banū Ḥammūd dynasty. He produced almost all of his work at the court of Roger II of Sicily.

##### Nuzhat al-mushtāq fī ikhtirāq al-āfāq

*Summa* on Mythic Europe Lore, Quality 8

**Description:** Known as the *Tabula Rogeriana*, the book is divided into the seven climatic zones of the Ptolemaic system, which are in turn subdivided into ten sections, all described in detail (relief, culture, politics and socioeconomic characteristics) and accompanied by a map. The book also contains a map of the Eurasian continent and North Africa.

#### Mosé ibn Ezrá

A Jewish philosopher, linguist and poet, a native of Lucena, the city of poetry.

##### Maḳāla bi ʿl-ḥadīḳa fī maʿnāal-madj̲āz wa ʿl-ḥaḳīḳa

*Summa* on Hebrew (poetry), Level 3, Quality 9

*Summa* on Philosophiae, Level 2, Quality 9

**Description:** A theory (with philosophical references) of how to construct Hebrew poems following the structure of Arabic poems.

#### Pedro Alfonso

Astronomer, mathematician, physician, cosmographer… and one of the most important figures of the so-called renaissance of the twelfth century. A native of Huesca, Pedro (called Alfonso after his protector, Alfonso I of Aragon, the Battler, whose physician he was) was a Jew converted to Christianity who fiercely refuted the Christian theses in his famous Latin work *Dialogus contra iudaeos*.

##### Disciplina clericalis

*[…] I composed my little book partly from the proverbs of the philosophers and their teachings, partly from Arabic proverbs and counsels, and from fables and verses, and partly by making use of comparisons with birds and beasts.*[^p321-19]

[^p321-19]: Excerpt from Pedro Alfonso's *Disciplina clericalis* (Spanish translation by Esperanza Ducay).

*Tractatus* on Teaching, Quality 10

**Description:** Written in Latin, this little work draws on Aesop and on famous Eastern works such as the *Barlaam*, the *Calila* and the *Sendebar* (which would not be translated into Castilian until the middle of the thirteenth century), as well as on Hebrew folk tradition and biblical proverbs. It is an educational book from which a religious lesson can be drawn (although that is not its aim). The book is built from dialogues and comprises thirty-four tales that became widely known in the Middle Ages (more than sixty manuscripts scattered through every library in Europe).

### The Almohad Dynasty

#### Abū Bakr ibn Ṭufayl

Known to the Latins as Abubacer, the renowned polymath from Guadix practiced as a physician in Granada before serving the son of the Almohad caliph, Abū Yaʿqūb Yūsuf, and being appointed vizier and physician to the caliph. Three years before his death, he ceded his post to his friend Averroes, whom he had introduced to the Almohad court.

##### Risāla Ḥayy ibn Yaqẓān fī asrār al-ḥikma al-mašriqiyya

*[…] the thesis of the creation of the world, after it had not existed, cannot be conceived except together with the idea that time preceded it; but time is a part of the totality of the world, inseparable from it; therefore one cannot imagine the world as posterior to time. Furthermore, [...]: "If the world was produced, it must necessarily have a producer; why did he make it arise at such a moment and not before? Did some novelty befall him, when nothing exists outside him, or was it through a change wrought in his essence? But then, who produced that change?"*[^p321-20]

[^p321-20]: Excerpt from Ibn Ṭufayl's *The Self-Taught Philosopher* (Spanish translation by Ángel González Palencia).

<!-- p. 322 -->

*Summa* on Philosophiae, Level 3, Quality 9

**Description:** "The Self-Taught Philosopher" is a philosophical work that deals with the attainment of supreme truth through the exercise of the human faculties in solitude. The tale this book tells is that of Ḥayy ibn Yaqẓān, a man who grows up on an island in the care of a gazelle (which exemplifies beauty for the Arabs). When the gazelle dies, the child must learn what life is through the contrast of its loss (starting from the premise that knowledge springs from within, clearly reminiscent of Avempace): he must reach supreme truth through solitary reflection and the observation of the natural world.

#### Benjamin of Tudela

Little is known of him, save that he was a learned rabbi, perhaps a merchant.

##### Séfer-masaʿot

*Tractatus* on Mythic Europe Lore (Jewish communities), Quality 7

**Description:** This is an edited compilation of Benjamin's travel notes, written in Hebrew. The book aimed to examine three matters: the socioeconomic and politico-religious situation of the Jews in western and eastern Europe; the politics between the nations of the western Christian world and those of the eastern Islamic sphere; and the commercial and craft centers of both worlds, together with the routes that link them or could link them.

#### Abū Ishāq Nūr al-Dīn al-Biṭrūyī

Known to the Latins as Alpetragius, Al-Biṭrūyī (a native of Pedroche) was an apprentice of Ibn Ṭufayl.

##### Kitāb al-haiʾa

*Summa* on Artes Liberales (astronomy), Level 4, Quality 8

**Description:** "The Astronomical Theory" delves into the Ptolemaic thesis of the universe, criticizing and expanding upon it.

#### Abū Marwān ibn Zuhr

The Avenzoar of the Christians was born in Seville at the end of the eleventh century. He was a great chess player and a friend of Averroes, whom he considered the greatest physician of his age.

##### Kitāb al-ağḏiya wal-adwiya

*Tractatus* on Medicine, Quality 7

**Description:** "The Book of Foods" discusses their properties and their applications in medicine.

The book might contain one or more theriac formulas, described on page 293.

##### Kitāb al-iqtiṣād fi islāh al-anfus wal-asḫsad

*Summa* on Medicine, Level 6, Quality 7

*Summa* on Philosophiae, Level 3, Quality 7

**Description:** The "Book of the Middle Course on the Reform of Souls and Bodies" is an encyclopedia in seven volumes on organs, epidemics, hygiene, treatments and diseases.

##### Kitāb al-taysīr fi-l-mudāwāt wa-al-tadbīr

*Summa* on Medicine, Level 5, Quality 7

**Description:** The two books that make up this work facilitate the study of therapeutics and diet, and were written at Averroes' request as a complement to his Kitāb al-kulliyyat al-tibb. These books discuss and describe the practice of tracheotomy for the first time.

#### Rabbi Mosé Ben Maimón

Known as Maimonides to the Christians of the Renaissance, in Hebrew literature he was called Rambam (an acronym of his name). Of an illustrious family (of the line of the redactor of the Mishnah, Rabbi Yehudá ha-Nasí, and even of King David himself), both his father and his grandfather were *dayaním* of the community. Maimonides received his first lessons from his father before studying at the rabbinical school of Lucena and, with the arrival of the Almohads, he had to emigrate with his family to Fez, whence they fled to Palestine (Acre, Jerusalem), then to Cairo and, finally, to Fustat, where he was appointed *raís al-Yahud* ("head of the Jews") of the city and physician to Saladin, and thus achieved worldwide fame (in those days many came to consult him on Jewish law or on medicine).

For him, the study of philosophy and science (especially medicine) was a biblical precept, a religious commandment (the body must be healthy so that the soul may be in harmony with God), for both give man a better knowledge of God. Maimonides raised his scientific studies within religious life and granted a great role to reason, not only empirical reason; in them he sought to bring man closer to God through intellectual knowledge rather than directly through faith.

His writings clashed with (anti-rationalist) Jewish orthodoxy, and he was criticized by Abraham of Posquiēres (father of Yiṣḥaq the Blind, the inspiration of the Kabbalah of the Gerona circle) and by the Toledan Meʾir ben Ṭodros ha-Leví Abulafiah, who in 1202 wrote to the scholars of Lunel in France (admirers of Maimonides) urging them to make him recant his ideas. But not all his detractors were Jews. In Castile, *The Guide for the Perplexed* was denounced as heretical before the Christian authorities. In the Crown of Aragon, on the other hand, his theses were supported by the Barcelonans Abraham Šēmuʾ ha-Leví ibn Ḥasday, Yosef ben Yēhudá ben Yaʿāqoḇ ibn Aknin, and the physician and poet of Alfonso II and Pedro II, Šēšet ben Yiṣḥaq ben Yosef Benveniste.

##### Dalāt al-ḥaiʾrīn

*[…] the account of the creation, which is […] physical science. But, because of the gravity and importance of this matter, and because of the limitation of our capacity to apprehend the most transcendent of matters in its full reality, recourse has been had […] to parables, enigmas and extremely nebulous expressions. That is why the sages […] declared: "To explain to mortals the whole substance of the account of the creation is impossible. For that reason Scripture tells you covertly: 'In the beginning God created'..." They warn you, then, that the matters in question are recondite. […] To express these concepts, recourse has been had to terms of many meanings, so that the common people might understand them according to their intellectual capacity and their feeble conception, while the perfect man, already instructed, may interpret them otherwise.*[^p322-21]

[^p322-21]: Excerpt from Maimonides' *The Guide for the Perplexed* (Spanish translation by David Gonzalo Maeso).

<!-- p. 323 -->

*Summa* on Philosophiae, Level 4, Quality 9

*Summa* on Theology: Judaism, Level 6, Quality 9

**Description:** "The Guide for the Perplexed" (written in 1190) was translated into Hebrew in Maimonides' lifetime by Samuel ibn Tibbon, under the title *Moreh ha-Nevuchim*, and in 1220 it was translated into Latin at the court of Frederick II of Sicily under the name *Dux neutrorum vel dubiorum*. The book has an Aristotelian and Neoplatonic lineage (with its harmonization of faith and reason, and of religion and philosophy), and argues that one can be faithful to the Bible and the Talmud while remaining interested in intellectual inquiry, for to know God one must study creation and, therefore, the natural sciences, in a pure demonstration of rationalism.

##### Mishneh Torá

*Summa* on Rabbinic Law, Level 4, Quality 9

**Description:** This fourteen-volume commentary on Jewish law (translated as "Repetition of the Law") was written in Hebrew to make clear to his colleagues what they should do at every moment, and to serve as a replacement for the Mishnah (as an updating on rites, liturgy, jurisdiction, ethics, and so on). The first volume, Séfer ha-madda ("The Book of Knowledge"), sets out the theological and philosophical foundations of Judaism.

##### Sefer ha-maʾor

*Tractatus* on Rabbinic Law, Quality 9

**Description:** "The Luminary" deals with Talmudic law, that is, Jewish law. Together with the *Mishneh Torá*, it gathers the whole of rabbinic jurisprudence (written in Hebrew).

##### Fī tadbīr al-ṣiḥḥah

*Tractatus* on Medicine, Quality 9

**Description:** Every physician must have ties to philosophy (prevention is more important than cure, and the physician must be the one with a great moral code, for he must cure not a disease but a person). "The Regimen of Health" speaks of holistic remedies and psychosomatic responses, establishing a relationship between mental and physical health. The book might contain one or more theriac formulas, described on page 293.

#### Muḥammad ibn al-ʿArabī

Ibn ʿArabī of Murcia wrote hundreds of works and coincided with Averroes and Maimonides during what may have been the greatest moment of cultural fulfillment of al-Andalus. Over the course of his life he earned the honorific epithets of *Muḥiyy al-Dīn* ("reviver of religion"), *Šayj al-akbar* ("greatest doctor") and *Ibn Aflaṭūn* ("son of Plato").

His metaphysical ideas are structured on the eastern Ṣūfī syntheses that reached al-Andalus at the hand of the Cordoban Ibn Masarra (see above), built upon the theses of Plotinus and the Gnostics. His doctrines are anti-Mālikī, for they argue for the direct search for God without any intermediary: individuals can attain the original unity through purification. He also holds that illumination is a play of light and shadow, and that all beings are a mixture of light and darkness. Because of this he was persecuted and had to emigrate at the beginning of the thirteenth century. In his travels he visited many cities of the East (such as Fez, Tunis, Mecca, Jerusalem, Baghdad, Konya, Aleppo and Damascus, where he died), in which he both gave and received lessons from great masters.

##### Kitāb al-isfār

*[...] in Paradise one enjoys bliss and delights, whereas in this world one aspires to the increase of knowledge, for through seeking, man comes to know here what he does not know of there.*[^p323-22]

[^p323-22]: Excerpt from Ibn ʿArabī's *The Splendor of the Fruits of the Journey* (Spanish translation by Carlos Varona Narvión).

*Tractatus* on Philosophiae (metaphysics), Quality 6

**Description:** "The Splendor of the Fruits of the Journey" was written in Fez during his youth (1198). It describes the kinds of spiritual journey that exist: from God, toward God and in God, exemplified by those who undertook them (such as Moses or Enoch).

##### Risālat al-quds

*From the first moment I arrived in these lands, I asked after the people of this exemplary way of life […]. They led me to a certain community of Ṣūfīs who lived together in a monastery with high walls and a broad courtyard; at once I noticed that the goal of their aspirations and the target of their longings lay in keeping their habits very clean, and even more so the showy colored trimmings on the hems of their tunics, and in keeping their beards well combed. […] If you look at their faces, you will see eyes with a hard, restless and wrathful gaze; if you look at their souls, you will see souls swollen with pride; if you look at their hearts, you will see dissipated hearts, empty of inner life, holy and sublime, already reduced to utter ruin down to their very foundations, veritable dens of fierce lions and lairs of howling wolves.*[^p323-23]

[^p323-23]: Excerpt from Ibn ʿArabī's *The Epistle of Holiness* (Spanish translation by Miguel Asín Palacios).

*Summa* on Sufism Lore, Level 3, Quality 6

*Tractatus* on Philosophiae, Quality 3

**Description:** "The Epistle of Holiness" is divided into three parts. The first is a critique of the eastern Ṣūfīs, the second is an exercise in self-criticism by Ibn ʿArabī himself, and the third is a biographical compilation of the masters he had access to on his travels.

##### Fuṣūṣ al-ḥikam

*Summa* on Philosophiae, Level 6, Quality 3

**Description:** "The Bezels of Wisdom" is Ibn ʿArabī's most celebrated book. The Ṣūfī wrote it in an abstruse manner to keep profane eyes from understanding the esoteric doctrine it holds, which is always controversial with respect to Islamic orthodoxy.

#### Ibn Rušd

The Averroes of the Latins was a philosopher (Aristotelian and Platonic) and a Mālikī jurist who served as qadi in Cordoba and Seville. Averroes was also physician to the Almohad caliph Abū Yaʿqūb Yūsuf and, after Alarcos, he was banished by the caliph Abū Yūsuf Yaʿqūb al-Manṣūr to win the favor of the fuqahāʾ in the campaign against the Castilians; the caliph burned his books at the stake, although he made amends by granting him a post at the court of Marrākeš.

Averroes wrote commentaries on Aristotle, but also on Ptolemy, Alexander of Aphrodisias, Nicolaus of Damascus, Galen, Al-Fārābī, Avicenna and Avempace. Thanks to his commentaries on the works of Aristotle, the ideas of the Stagirite philosopher were able to enter Europe.

<!-- p. 324 -->

##### Fasl al-maqa´l

*[…] rational reflection does not contradict what the Law commands, because truth does not contradict Truth, but rather confirms it and bears witness to it.*[^p324-24]

[^p324-24]: Excerpt from Averroes' *The Harmony of Philosophy and Religion* (Spanish translation by A. Yacine and P. Chabrera Calpe).

*Tractatus* on Philosophiae, Quality 12

*Tractatus* on Theology: Islam, Quality 12

**Description:** In the treatise on "The Harmony of Philosophy and Religion," he postulates that philosophy needs no theological concessions and defines the Averroist method of free thought, in which theology and philosophy must not be mixed. In this treatise, Averroes defends reason as a method for knowing God and existing things, and the use of philosophy to resolve the contradictions between reason and the law.

##### Bidāŷat al-muŷtahid wa nihāyat al-muqtaṣid fi-l-fiqh

*[…] before making war, an invitation [to embrace Islam or pay parias] must be addressed [to the enemy], which is as much as to say that he must not be fought until the said invitation has been made to reach him […].*[^p324-25]

[^p324-25]: Excerpt from Averroes' *The Book of the Ŷihād* (Spanish translation by Carlos Quirós).

*Tractatus* on Islamic Law, Quality 12

**Description:** "The Starting Point of the Authoritative Doctor and the Supreme End of the Moderate Doctor on Islamic Law" is a legal manual in fifty-seven books that regulates the life of the believer according to the life of the Prophet Muḥammad (always from an Aristotelian point of view and in accordance with the Mālikī school).

##### Kitāb al-kulliyyāt fī-l-ṭibb

*Our purpose in composing these books has been to offer a code and a canon to serve as a guide for those who wish to complete their knowledge of every aspect of the art of medicine, following an order and a plan in doing so.*[^p324-26]

[^p324-26]: Excerpt from Averroes' *The Book of the Generalities of Medicine* (Spanish translation by V. de Benito and A. Morales).

*Summa* on Medicine, Level 5, Quality 12

**Description:** "The Book of the Generalities of Medicine" was conceived as a manual of basic ideas, to serve as an introduction to medicine or to remind those already versed in it of its concepts. The work is divided into seven books: anatomy, physiology, pathology, semiotics, therapeutics, hygiene and medication.

The book might contain one or more theriac formulas, described on page 293.

# Appendix III: The Peripheral Code of Iberia in 1220

#### 899 AD, On the Iberian Tax

*(Ṭāmis al-Išbīlī al-Gernikī)*

Any covenant of the Iberian Tribunal that can demonstrate its work on behalf of the Order may request a payment to defray the costs of its labors. To meet such demands, every covenant of the Tribunal must deliver to the Iberian treasury an amount of vis determined by the wealth of its declared sources[^p332-27]. The vis may be of any Art and must be delivered every seven years, coinciding with the ordinary meetings of the Iberian Tribunal.

[^p332-27]: In game terms, Spring covenants pay one pawn of vis, Summer covenants five, Autumn covenants seven and Winter covenants two.

No covenant may request this service twice within a period of less than ten years. Requests shall be assessed by the Quaesitores of the Iberian Tribunal, and the vis shall be kept in the Tribunal's treasury.

No war, whatever its nature, may be financed with the funds of the treasury.

#### 899 AD, On the Privileges of the Mercere

*(Ṭāmis al-Išbīlī al-Gernikī)*

The treasury shall set aside 5% of the Iberian tax for the use of the Mercere, to be used to create and maintain the network of portals of Iberia.

#### 899 AD, On Vis Sources

*(Ṭāmis al-Išbīlī al-Gernikī)*

Every declared vis source shall be reviewed, assessed and registered by a Quaesitor and a Mercere, so that its possession does not come into conflict with other covenants.

#### 906 AD, On the Praeco

*(Ṭāmis al-Išbīlī al-Gernikī)*

The Praeco shall be chosen at the close of each Tribunal from among the five eldest magi (unless there is no Praeco at the start of the Tribunal). Furthermore, the candidates must be members of a covenant of Iberia, and must therefore belong to the Tribunal and be registered in it.

Once the business of the Tribunal has been concluded, the presiding Quaesitor must ask the assembly whether it wishes to choose a new Praeco. In the vote, each member of the Tribunal has a single vote (Tremere without their voting sigils may vote, and those who hold their *filii*'s sigils may cast only their own),[^p332-28] and neither the Quaesitores, the Redcaps nor the Praeco may vote. The five candidates must be in full possession of their mental faculties, and may not all come from a single covenant or belong to the same House. Should that be the case, the youngest of them must be replaced by the next-eldest magus of the Tribunal. Furthermore, the five candidates may not excuse themselves from their obligations, and therefore may not decline the office; to do so is classed as a high crime and may therefore lead to the magus's expulsion.

[^p332-28]: Note that this overrides the delegation of votes; see *Houses of Hermes: True Lineages*, page 55.

Finally, Quaesitores, archmagi and Primi may never be Praecones.

#### 906 AD, On the Gentle Gift

*(Ṭāmis al-Išbīlī al-Gernikī)*

A magus's first apprentice with the Gentle Gift may be claimed from his masters by the Quaesitores of Iberia. This claim does not outrank that of the Bonisagus; that is, if a Bonisagus wants the same apprentice as a Guernicus, the Bonisagus's preference shall always prevail.

#### 920 AD, On Court Astronomers

*(Ṭāmis al-Išbīlī al-Gernikī)*

No Hermetic magus may serve as a court astronomer.

#### 941 AD, On the Records of Iberia

*(Maryam al-Gernikiyya)*

The records of Iberia shall be kept at the covenant of Duresca.

#### 948 AD, On the Duresca Manuscripts

*(Alvarra of Guernicus)*

Any reference to or dissemination of the proven-fraudulent "Duresca manuscripts" contributes to undermining the integrity of the Order and shall therefore be considered a low crime. Repeated offenses may come to be considered a high crime.

#### 969 AD, On the Great Mosque of Cordoba

*(Qāsim ibn Muṭarrif al-Gernikī)*

Any magus with the Gentle Gift, or any of his agents, may claim a free column of the Great Mosque of Cordoba at which to teach Hermetic or mundane knowledge. The lessons must keep within the bounds of Mālikī doctrine so as not to violate the Code of Hermes. In any event, responsibility rests with the teacher, who must under no circumstances make his connection to the Order of Hermes known, on pain of expulsion. Naturally, lessons must be suspended for the day's prayers, and the teacher must always visit the ablution hall beforehand, in accordance with the precepts of Islamic law. If there are children present, the teacher shall be responsible for looking after them and for making sure they do not soil the mats on which the faithful prostrate themselves. Under no circumstances shall teachers be entitled to receive any payment for their lessons.

<!-- p. 333 -->

#### 1018 AD, On the Iberian Chamber

*(Iustum of Guernicus)*

Duresca shall host every decade (from 1020 onward, at the autumn equinox) a meeting of the Tribunal's magi in what is called the Iberian Chamber, which may be attended by the members of Duresca, the Trianomae, the heads of the Tribunal's Mercer Houses, the Praeco, the Quaesitores, and the *praefectus praetorio* and *quaestor aerarii*. In addition, the chamber shall have three additional seats, which may be used by any other member invited by the *disceptator* of Duresca, the Praeco or the Trianomae (one seat for each of these powers).

The purpose of the chamber shall be to discuss the state of the Tribunal as a whole: under no circumstances shall it serve as a legislative instrument, and so the Iberian Chamber shall have no power over the meetings of the Tribunals and shall to all intents and purposes be considered of lower rank. However, the Iberian Chamber shall have the authority to audit the accounts of the Tribunal's treasury, and may take control of them if the ordinary Tribunal approves.

#### 1025 AD, On the Diedne Legacy

*(Iustum of Guernicus)*

House Diedne shall be erased from the records of Iberian history. All knowledge of or reference to it shall be purged, and its possession shall be grounds for punishment (deemed a high crime) by the forces of the Tribunal.

Deliberately seeking any knowledge related to this House shall be considered a low crime, for which the person responsible must answer before the Tribunal. Likewise, protecting or sheltering a magus of this House shall be grounds for expulsion.

#### 1116 AD, On the Iberian Treasury

*(Danāʾ al-Gernikiyya)*

The Tribunal's treasury shall be divided between the Mercer Houses of Porta Pandere and Aedes Saturni. The former shall keep the Tribunal's treasury for the covenants of the territory of al-Andalus and the kingdom of Portugal, and the latter that of the territories of the kingdoms of Leon, Castile and Navarre, the Crown of Aragon and the Catalan counties. To this end they shall be regulated and protected by two magi (traditionally a Flambeau and a Guernicus), who shall hold the titles of *praefectus praetorio* (*ḥárisun*) and *quaestor aerarii* (*jāzin*), respectively.

#### 1116 AD, On Arabic

*(Danāʾ al-Gernikiyya)*

The Iberian Tribunal recognizes Arabic as a second language. Under these terms, the magi of the Iberian Tribunal may address their *sodales* in Arabic, both orally and in writing.

#### 1116 AD, On the Exchange of Enchantments with Mundanes

*(Danāʾ al-Gernikiyya)*

A single magus may sell as many magical enchantments per year as he has clients under the rule of different mundane princes, and always through mundane intermediaries.

#### 1123 AD, On al-ʿIdwa

*(Danāʾ al-Gernikiyya)*

The founding of any covenant beyond the Pillars of Hercules shall be considered a high crime. This prohibition shall remain in force until the year 1225.

#### 1165 AD, On Occelum Durii, Hermetic Inn

*(Jayrān al-Gernikī)*

The former covenant of Occelum Durii shall be made available as a Hermetic inn for all members of the Tribunal. Porta Pandere shall be responsible for renewing the *Aegis of the Hearth* each year and for providing as many invitations as necessary to any member registered in the Iberian Tribunal. Likewise, any recognized companion or grog shall have the privilege of requesting lodging at Occelum Durii, whose ground shall always be free of disputes.

#### 1193 AD, On Mundane Relations in al-Andalus

*(Jayrān al-Gernikī)*

No covenant or magus may enter into an agreement with a mundane party, whatever its terms. Furthermore, any agreement already under way must be handled by a Quaesitor, so that he may take the appropriate actions and advise on the course to follow at every stage.

Finally, no magus may use magic or employ any magic item in a settlement of al-Andalus or its surroundings, or in any other place where his life would be endangered by a possible denunciation to the authorities.

#### 1207 AD, On Tenure in the Tribunal

*(Lía al-Gernikiyya, pending approval by the Grand Tribunal of 1228)*

Every magus Gauntleted in Iberia must remain in the Tribunal for at least seven years. If after this period he has found no covenant to take him in, his *parens* shall be obliged to give him shelter.

#### 1214 AD, On the Southern Frontier

*(Lía al-Gernikiyya, pending approval by the Grand Tribunal of 1228)*

The southern boundary of Iberia shall extend southward as far as the limits set by the Atlas Mountains, namely the Anti-Atlas, the High Atlas, the Middle Atlas and the Saharan Atlas. All covenants in these new territories shall fall under the jurisdiction of the Iberian Tribunal.[^p333-29]

[^p333-29]: Note that this conflicts with the Tytalus cabal of the Shining Eye, which aims to have the Rhine Tribunal colonize North Africa.

# About The Iberian Tribunal

*The Iberian Tribunal* covers the mundane and Hermetic history of the Iberian Peninsula across the more than four centuries of the Order of Hermes' existence. The Peninsula is divided among the kingdoms of Portugal, Leon, Castile and Navarre, the Crown of Aragon, and the Almohad Empire's province of al-Andalus. The political intrigues of all of them form a complex tapestry that also reflects the influence of the papacy after the Gregorian reform of the late eleventh century. This is the land that fostered an early renaissance of arts and letters at the hands of Muslim and Jewish authors such as Rabbi Mosé ben Maimón and Ibn Rušd, and that resounds with the echoes of the Way of Saint James, the Toledo school of translators, the Iberian crusades, the Peninsula's military orders, and the evocative history of al-Andalus.

Iberia is also a land of great Hermetic importance. It was in Iberia that Flambeau fought both before and after joining the Order, in Iberia that the scandal of the Duresca manuscripts broke, and Iberia is the Tribunal that looks out over Africa, a source of endless mundane and magical riches. This book describes in detail thirty-one inhabited covenants and twenty-seven ruined ones, for a total of 155 magi.

*The Iberian Tribunal* is designed so that you can play at any point in the history of the Order on the Peninsula. You can set your saga among the first Hermetic settlers, at the time when peace was made with the *saḥirs*, during the celebrations of the Tribunals of Joy in Saragossa, or during the persecution carried out by the fuqahāʾ when the Almohads arrived. Discover all the secrets of the Iberian Tribunal!

**Finis Terrae, the Iberian Tribunal** was crowdfunded on 22 December 2021 thanks to the participation of 322 backers. What is more, thanks to its warm reception, the book was enriched with the following additional content:

- a map of the Iberian Tribunal;
- a mundane library, added in Appendix I of the book;
- coats of arms for every covenant in the book;
- the stat blocks of six notable figures of the Tribunal, with their illustrations (the *filia* Ágata, Fortún of Guernicus, Nuʿum Ex Miscellanea, Tages of Tremere, Faustus of Flambeau and Layla of Verditius);
- the non-Hermetic traditions of the tiryāqi, the astral sorcerers of Cordoba and the distaurnanja, all with their illustrations;
- the stat blocks of the ñuberu, the nasnās and the jinni of Mons Niger, with their illustrations;
- the places of power of the Punic temple of Sancti Petri and the Tartessian barrow of Zalamea, with their illustrations;
- an insert with possible locations for Calebais in the Iberian Tribunal.

From the bottom of our hearts, thank you all.

This book is yours.
